$ JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 ./app

options.name: Keep today's behavior
options.detail: jet keeps refusing to start under the variable, so the checked allocator stays unusable until another design lands.
options.technical: No code change. environment.md is corrected to say checked builds are unavailable.
options.code:
$ JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 jet build app.jet
jet checked allocator: this program was built without the checked allocator (exit 70)

comparisons.note: The race detector is a build choice; the built program checks itself. Source: https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector
AddressSanitizer is a compile flag; ASAN_OPTIONS only tunes a checked program. Source: https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html

recommendation.why: A asks for checking where Go and Clang do, at build time, and the built program always checks itself. That needs no reserved names, no toolchain special case and no run-time variable, so unchecked programs carry no start-up check at all.
gains: Checked builds work again with one signal.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two variables and makes every program scan its environment at start-up.
C leaves the memory debugging aid unusable.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: one signal, and no start-up cost in any other program.

decisions.title: Service calls name the file and wait effects they reach
decisions.situation: The service runtime is moving from Rust into Jet. Its file and wait steps are effect-free today, so a tree writes its state store, rollout journal and delivery log with an empty effect row. A package that allows only reading files can therefore write them, and a function with an empty ceiling can start a tree. The vote decides whether service calls must name what they reach. We recommend they do.
decisions.gist: Should a service call that writes files say FS in its signature?
decisions.lesson: An effect row lists what a call may do, such as read files, write files or wait. The package grant and each function's ceiling are checked against those rows. A call with an empty row is trusted to do none of them. A row that hides a file write makes both checks pass when they should not.
decisions.story: Ana's billing package allows FS.Read so it can load a price file. She adds a service tree with an event log. Today the tree writes the log and its rollout journal anyway, and no check notices. Under A, `jet run` stops with E1803 and asks her to allow FS.Write.
decisions.detail:
Today. The port keeps the user surface unchanged, so its file and wait steps are effect-free core.service rows. Only `service.state_store()` asks for anything, and it asks for FS.Read. Start, stop, durable sends, snapshots, events, rollouts and delivery calls read and write files with an empty row.

What a tree touches. With a store at `orders.state`, a tree writes that file plus `orders.state.rollout`, `orders.state.workflows` and the delivery authority log. Every access also creates and removes a `.lock` file beside its target. While another process holds a lock, the call sleeps 1 ms at a time, for up to 30 s.

Probes. A package that allows [IO, Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait] and calls `service.state_store()` stops with E1803 for FS.Read. A package that allows [FS.Read, IO, Mem.Alloc] and appends to a file stops with E1803 for FS.Write. A function `boot() -[IO]>` that reaches that append stops with E0740 naming FS.Write. A package that allows only [IO, Mem.Alloc] ran `time.sleep(1ms)` with no grant.

What A does. The port's file steps flip from no effect to FS.Read or FS.Write, and the lock sleep to Time.Wait. Inference then carries those effects to every service call that reaches them. Calls that only touch memory keep an empty row: tree, worker, send, receive, show and observe. Each flip is one line in the effect table.

Who changes under A. All four durable service examples already allow FS, so none changes. Up to four test programs start a tree with no store and no FS grant, and each adds one allow line. Time.Wait needs no grant, so it only matters to function ceilings.

Beginner and expert paths under A. A beginner's lone file runs with `jet run --allow=FS run.jet`, and the E1803 fix line says how to keep that grant. An expert library writes `-[FS, Time.Wait]>` on its own service helpers. Helpers that only show or route, like `label`, keep `-[]>`.

Precedent. Core's file calls name their leaf even through a held handle. `Directory.remove` and `FileWriter.set_mode` both declare FS.Write. Under B the service store would be the one handle that does not.

Review. Author: Claude (LiveUI lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Each service call names the file and wait effects it reaches
options.detail:
A service call that can reach the state store says so: reads give FS.Read, writes and lock files give FS.Write, and lock waits give Time.Wait. Calls that only touch memory keep an empty row. The package grant and every function ceiling then see the real file writes.

A tree with no store still asks for FS to start, because start writes the rollout journal when a store is set.
options.technical: The port's core.service file rows (read, append, reserve, finish, rename, fsync, lstat, mkdirs) take FS.Read or FS.Write; the lock sleep row takes Time.Wait. Inference gives start, stop, send_durable, commit_snapshot, append_event, restore_snapshot, rollout and delivery calls FS plus Time.Wait. Status reads take the store lock, so they need FS.Write too. tree, worker, send, receive, show and observe stay `-[]>`.

options.name: The store asks for all of FS once; tree calls stay effect-free
options.detail:
`service.state_store()` asks for FS, reading and writing, when the program opens the store. Every tree call keeps an empty row, because holding the store value already proves the grant.

This is how Deno KV works: permission is checked when the store opens, not on each write.
options.technical: state_store's row widens from FS.Read to FS. The port's file rows stay effect-free. Package grants become honest, because no store can open without FS.Write. Function ceilings do not: a `-[]>` function handed a tree can still write its files.

options.name: Keep the port's effect-free rows
options.detail:
Only `service.state_store()` asks for FS.Read, as today. Every tree call keeps an empty row, including the ones that write files.

This is what the port ships now, so it costs no change.
options.technical: state_store stays `-[FS.Read]>`. Every core.service file and sleep row stays effect-free, as the Rust runtime rows were. A package that allows only FS.Read can write the state store, the rollout journal, the workflow store and the delivery log.

comparisons.note: Effects are inferred into every function type; a function that touches the file system carries `fsys` all the way up. Source: koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html, effect types.
comparisons.code:
fun save(p : path, s : string) : <fsys,exn> ()
  write-text-file(p, s)

comparisons.note: Permission is checked when a KV store opens; later writes ask nothing. Source: docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security and docs.deno.com/deploy/kv/manual.
comparisons.code:
const kv = await Deno.openKv("./orders.db") // --allow-read --allow-write
await kv.set(["order", 1], "paid")

comparisons.note: No effect system: a gen_server or dets table writes files with nothing in its type. Source: erlang.org/doc/apps/stdlib/dets.html.

recommendation.why: A makes the rows tell the truth. Today a package that may only read files can write the state store, and an empty ceiling can start a tree. A closes both, as Core's file calls already do.
gains: Package grants match what the program writes.
Function ceilings hold for service calls.
Memory-only service calls stay effect-free.

whyNot.reason: B fixes the package grant but not ceilings: an empty-ceiling function can still write the store through a tree it was handed. Core's own file handles name FS.Write on each call.
C lets a package that allows only FS.Read write four files, and no function ceiling sees those writes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A store-less tree asks for FS to start. The port ships C now, and each A row is a later one-line flip.

decisions.title: The state a durable delivery reads right after send_durable
decisions.situation: A durable send records the message, puts it in the worker's mailbox and returns a Delivery. The example golden says that Delivery reads Accepted. The runtime says Delivering, as the Rust runtime did. No spec line says which is right. The vote decides when a delivery becomes Delivering. We recommend the mailbox moment, as today.
decisions.gist: After send_durable returns, is the delivery Accepted or Delivering?
decisions.lesson: A durable delivery moves through states that are written to a log on disk. Accepted means the log has the message. Delivering means the worker has been handed it. Delivered means the worker committed it. A restarted program reads the log to know what to send again.
decisions.story: Ben sends an order with send_durable and prints its status to check it worked. Under B he sees Accepted until his worker calls receive. Under A he sees Delivering at once, because the order is already in the worker's mailbox.
decisions.detail:
Today. send_durable writes an acceptance record, puts the message in the worker's mailbox, then writes a Delivering record before it returns. The Rust runtime did the same: Services.rs 3215 calls mark_delivered, which appends Delivering (ServiceAuthority.rs 1862-1873). The base's Jet source keeps that order.

The golden. Examples/features/tooling/service_authority expects `first:accepted` and then `duplicate:delivering`. The duplicate send returns the same delivery, and nothing happens to it between the two prints. So the two lines cannot both hold under one rule. Line 1 was written by hand in 198561770c and never ran against this runtime.

What Accepted means under each. Under A, Accepted marks a message that is recorded but not yet in any mailbox: a retried delivery, or one recovered after a restart, waiting for the next receive to admit it. Under B, Accepted also covers a message already sitting in the mailbox.

What B costs. receive would write the Delivering record, so every durable receive adds one locked log append. send_durable would stop writing it. The receive path must also tell a first take from a re-take after a restart.

Who changes. Under B, lines 1 and 2 of the golden read accepted, and the runtime moves its marker. Under A, only line 1 of the golden changes, to delivering. No other golden or test prints this state right after a send.

Review. Author: Claude (LiveUI lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Delivering starts when the message enters the worker's mailbox
options.detail: send_durable writes Delivering as soon as the message is in the worker's mailbox, before it returns. A status read right after the send says Delivering, and so does the duplicate's. This is what the runtime does today.
options.technical: No runtime change: send_durable and pending admission keep calling mark_delivered after the mailbox send. Golden line 1 becomes `first:delivering`; line 2 already says delivering.
options.code:
use core.service as service
use core.testing as testing

fn orders_worker() {}

fn label(delivery: ^Delivery) -> String {
    state :: delivery.status() ?? panic("status")
    if state == {
        .Accepted -> "accepted"
        .Delivering -> "delivering"
        else -> "other"
    }
}

fn run() {
    store :: Path.from(testing.temp_dir("orders")).join("orders.log").to_string()
    tree := service.tree("orders")
    &tree.set_delivery(service.delivery_durable()) ?? panic("delivery")
    &tree.set_state_event_log(service.state_store(store) ?? panic("store"), "orders", 1, "reversible") ?? panic("log")
    endpoint :: &tree.worker("orders", orders_worker, capacity: 2) ?? panic("worker")
    &tree.start() ?? panic("start")
    first :: &tree.send_durable(endpoint, "order", key: "order-1") ?? panic("first")
    print("first:{label(^first)}")
    duplicate :: &tree.send_durable(endpoint, "order", key: "order-1") ?? panic("duplicate")
    print("duplicate:{label(^duplicate)}")
    print("delivered:{&tree.receive(endpoint) ?? panic("receive")}")
}

// A: Delivering starts when the message enters the worker's mailbox
$ jet run run.jet
first:delivering
duplicate:delivering
delivered:order

decisions.title: How `jet fix` moves callers off an old function when the new one takes different arguments
decisions.situation: Libraries retire functions with a deprecation marker that names the replacement. Callers get a warning, and `jet fix` edits their code, but only by renaming the call. When the replacement takes different arguments, the rename breaks the caller, and the only safe path is a hand edit in every program. The owner decides how `jet fix` should handle that case. We recommend three steps in order: inline a wrapper, else use the author's pattern, else print the exact edit.
decisions.gist: When a library retires a function whose replacement takes different arguments, how should `jet fix` update the callers?
decisions.lesson: A library marks an old function as deprecated and names its replacement. Callers get a warning, and `jet fix` edits their code. Today that edit can only rename the call, so any change in arguments needs a hand edit in every program that uses the library.
decisions.story: Sam's charting package replaces `double(x)` with `scaled(x, 2)`. Two hundred programs call `double`. Each owner sees the warning and runs `jet fix`, which should leave every program building without a hand edit.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #6376, report Docs/research/language-release-notes-2026-10-30.md. Probe $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-4/probes/rel/r11_deprecated.jet on jet 03c64ad0c4: `jet fix` applied 2 fixes, and the fixed copy fails with E0766 because `double(4)` became `scaled(4)`. That misapplied rename is card #6405, a defect under any option.

Related law: D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A (#2052, `#Deprecated(since:, use:)`, rename-only fix), #6068 (every break ships a `jet fix` rewrite). Go 1.26 release notes, Tools section: go fix is the home of modernizers and a source-level inliner driven by `//go:fix inline`.

options.name: Inline, else a pattern, else an exact step
options.detail:
First, if the old function's body is one returned expression, `jet fix` puts that expression at each call with the caller's arguments. A plain rename is the simplest such body, so today's markers keep working.

Second, for any other body, the author may add a call pattern to the marker, and `jet fix` fills it in.

Otherwise `jet fix` leaves the call alone. The warning then prints the exact edit, such as which new argument `scaled` needs.
options.technical:
Step 1 needs no new marker word: `use:` plus a body of `return <expr>` whose names are all visible to callers. The rewrite works on the checked call and binds an argument to a local first when it is used other than exactly once, in order.

Step 2 is `rewrite: "scaled({a}, 2)"`, checked against the old signature when the library builds. A pattern on a wrapper body is refused with a registered error, so there is never a second copy.

Step 3: L2001 names the replacement's signature and each parameter without a default. `jet fix` re-checks every edited file and rolls back a failing edit.

options.name: Rename only
options.detail: The marker keeps `use:` for renames. `jet fix` applies it only when the replacement accepts the old call's arguments unchanged. Otherwise the warning says to edit the call by hand.
options.technical: No new marker form. The fix engine checks that the renamed call type-checks before applying it, and the L2001 text stops promising automatic migration when it would not.

options.name: Pattern only
options.detail: Every automatic migration is written as a text pattern in the marker, with holes named after the old parameters. `jet fix` fills the holes with each caller's arguments. Without a pattern, only plain renames are applied.
options.technical: Marker `#Deprecated(since: "1.2", rewrite: "scaled({a}, 2)")`. The pattern is parsed and checked against the old signature when the library builds. Argument binding follows A's evaluate-once rule. The checker does not compare the pattern with the body.

comparisons.note: `go fix` gained a source-level inliner; authors mark wrappers with `//go:fix inline` to migrate their own users.
comparisons.code:
//go:fix inline
func Double(a int) int { return Scaled(a, 2) }

comparisons.note: Breaking changes shipped with deprecated aliases and compiler fix-its, so code moved forward without hand edits.
comparisons.code: # old name kept as a deprecated alias; the compiler suggests the new spelling

comparisons.note: `#[deprecated(since, note)]` prints free text; stable Rust has no automatic rewrite for library deprecations.
comparisons.code:
#[deprecated(since = "1.2.0", note = "use scaled(x, 2)")]
pub fn double(x: i32) -> i32 { scaled(x, 2) }

recommendation.why: Most retirements are thin wrappers, so inlining the checked body handles them with nothing new to write. A pattern covers the rest, and an exact step covers what no tool can.
gains: Package upgrades need no hand edits whenever a wrapper or pattern exists.
`jet fix` never leaves a broken call behind.

whyNot.reason: It leaves every argument change as a hand edit in every program that uses the library.
It makes authors restate each wrapper as text, which can then disagree with the real body.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives each case its best tool: the body when it is a wrapper, the author's pattern when given, and an exact instruction otherwise.

decisions.title: A module's effect cap is `#FX(...)` on its `module` line
decisions.situation: Jet limits what code may do at four levels: a block, a function, a package and a single run. A module has no limit of its own, so a team that wants its pricing code never to touch the network or files must repeat the promise on every function. Writing the same `#FX` marker on a module line is accepted today but silently does nothing. The vote decides where a module's cap is written. We recommend the `#FX` marker on the module line, the way a block already takes it.
decisions.gist: Where should a cap on what one module of code may do be written?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network or file access. Jet caps effects on a block with `#FX(...)` and on a function with its row. A package caps them with `authority:`, and a run with `--deny`. Modules are the missing step. A module cap covers every function inside, so the promise is written once and checked everywhere.
decisions.story: Ana's shop app keeps its price rules in `module pricing`. The team promises that pricing never reaches the network or the disk, so prices are reproducible in tests. Today that promise lives in a code-review checklist, and a helper that reads a file slipped in last month.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rzkb53. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot, which the owner rejected; this is its module question alone. Ratified and not on this ballot: function rows in the arrow (D-SHAPE8=A), `#FX` on blocks (D-ABILITY-NAME2=A) and denials through calls (D-PROP1). Also settled: inferred rows (D-EFFECT-OMIT1=A) and package `authority:` (D-AUTH-AMBIENT3=A, D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A).

What the probes found, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. modcap.jet: `#FX(!Net, !FS)` above `module pricing { }` parses. modcap_breach.jet: the same cap over a function that reads a file checks clean, so the marker is accepted and ignored today.

fn_marker.jet: `#FX(!FS)` above a `fn` is an internal compiler error ("the function marker `#FX` is not supported by the self-hosted checker yet"). rungs_a/run.jet is option A's program; it checks clean today because the cap is ignored. These findings are notes for existing cards, not new cards.

Central review. A lead who wants one place still has it: package `authority.deny` applies to every module, and `jet explain effects --caps` lists each module cap with its file and line.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 asks whether types and traits get their own cap; under A here, a type's promise comes from its module's cap. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 puts the same `#FX` above an `effect` declaration with the same "at most" meaning. D-MARK-SCOPE1 already lets `#Policy` sit on module lines; A here gives `#FX` the same place. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 adds the artifact limit below the package.

options.name: `#FX` on the module line
options.detail:
A module takes the `#FX(...)` marker on the line above its `module` declaration, exactly as a block takes it. The cap covers every function inside, including nested modules. An inner cap or function row may only tighten it.

The cap sits in the parent file, so code inside the module cannot loosen its own cap. `#Policy` already sits on module lines the same way. `jet explain effects` lists every cap in force, nearest first.
options.technical:
Ladder after A: `#FX` block, `-[ ]>` function, `#FX` module, package `authority:`, run `--allow/--deny`. The marker already parses on module declarations (probe/fx/modcap.jet) but sema ignores it: probe/fx/modcap_breach.jet reads a file under `#FX(!Net, !FS)` and checks clean.

A makes the module cap a ceiling plus denials, the function-row rule (Effects/Checks.jet:2207-2219). E0712 and E0749 gain the cap line as a secondary label. D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix mode for `#FX` on modules: tighten (intersect). Grants stay site-bound: `#FX(grant: …)` is still block-only. Note: `#FX` above a `fn` today is an internal compiler error (probe/fx/fn_marker.jet), not a refusal; a function's limit is its row.

options.name: Caps in package `authority:`
options.detail:
The package file's `authority:` gains a `modules:` table naming each module and its cap. The project's rights and its module caps then sit in one file that one person can review, as Deno and LavaMoat keep policy in one place.

The cost is that each module name appears twice. A module renamed in code keeps no cap until package.jet is updated, so the checker must refuse unknown names.
options.technical: New `authority.modules: { path: { allow?, deny? } }` in package.jet, parsed beside allow, deny and grants (packages/typed_settings/package.jet shape). Unknown module paths are an error. D-TEAMPOLICY1's parsed-but-unenforced `policy.effects` is retired into it.

options.name: Rows on each function
options.detail:
Modules stay without a cap. A team that wants pricing free of network and files writes `-[!Net, !FS]>` on each function, as Koka and Flix put every effect on functions. Callers see the promise exactly where they look.

The promise is repeated on every function, and a helper added without a row is inferred instead of capped. The silent marker on module lines becomes an error.
options.technical: Today's rule kept. `#FX` on a module declaration becomes a refusal naming the per-function row as the fix, closing the silent no-op found in probe/fx/modcap_breach.jet.

comparisons.note: Lint levels on a `mod` line cover the whole module; forbid cannot be loosened inside. Source: Rust reference, lint attributes.
Permissions are listed in one config for the whole program, as option B lists caps. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
Effects live only on function types; there is no module-level limit, as in option C. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html

recommendation.why: A adds the missing step with the marker blocks already use, written once where the module is declared. Code inside cannot loosen it, and beginners never see it.
gains: One promise covers every function in the module.
The marker that silently did nothing now works.

whyNot.reason: B writes each module name twice, and a rename silently drops the cap until package.jet is fixed.
C repeats the promise on every function, and a new helper slips past it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Caps live beside the modules they cover rather than in one file; `jet explain effects` gathers them.

decisions.title: `process.args()` is the one raw argument list; the program path comes from `sys.executable()`
decisions.situation: A Jet program reads its raw command-line words through two functions. One puts the program name first, and one does not. Agreed texts name a third, which is really the argument parser library. Most examples use the form with the program name and skip it by hand. A few use the other. A job and a command with one name both pass the check. An agreed rule forbids that, so it is fixed as a defect. The vote picks one raw function.
decisions.gist: Should `process.args()`, the user's words only, be the one raw argument list?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `process.args()` gives the user's words; `sys.executable()` gives the program path.
decisions.story: Sam's first script loops over `process.args()` and greets each name. No index arithmetic, and no program name in the output.
decisions.inWild:
Option          First word         Like
A args only     the user's first   Deno, Java, C#, Dart
B argv only     program path       Python, Go, Rust, C
C both          either             no peer
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Core/Process/Process.jet:76-78: `args()` stays (`args_from_argv`, :441-444); public `argv()` is removed with no alias; the intrinsic stays private to Core.
- `ArgsSpec.parse` takes `process.args()`; its E1304 hint names it. L0515 retires. The program path is `core.sys.executable() -[Env]> String` (Core/Sys/Sys.jet:302); there is no `core.os`.
- Migration: 67 files move from `process.argv()`: 14 examples, 44 tests, 5 Tools, 3 Compiler and 1 Core (BallotReview-2 count).

FIXED UNDER EVERY OPTION (no vote)
- Job and command clash: D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C reserves job names in the shared command table. Yet `#Job(.Ship) fn deploy()` beside a `#CLI` command `deploy` passes (probes q01, r18). The fix is a check error naming both lines; different visibility still clashes; `.Internal` jobs never clash.
- Seen in passing (need defect cards): `jet run job_runner.jet -- greet` runs `fn run`, not the job (q02). A typed `fn run(args: T)` gives E2105 "has no fn run to build" (q02).

EVIDENCE (r14 jet)
- r12: `process.args()`, `process.argv()` and `sys.executable()` all work with `--allow=Env`.

IDS
Under A amends S12 (SD:342-343): the raw entry becomes `core.process.args`. D-SHAPE-CLI1=A's `core.args` is the ArgsSpec parser of D-ARGS1, not a raw list. Fixed: D-CLI-GLOBAL1=E, D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C (SD:7172-7181). Hosts #6057 (L-19).

decisions.title: Whether Int.parse accepts a leading plus sign and surrounding spaces
decisions.gist: Should Int.parse accept only an optional minus sign and digits, refusing "+5" and " 5"?
decisions.lesson: Int.parse turns text into a whole number. It also reads command-line numbers. Today it accepts "+5" and lets some stray spaces through, and no spec line says whether it should.
decisions.story: Sam runs `tool --count ' 5'` after a copy-paste. Today the space slips through and the tool runs with 5. Under A and B the tool says ' 5' is not a whole number, so the stray space is caught. Under C it keeps working.
decisions.inWild:
Rust: "+5".parse::<i64>() is Ok(5), " 5".parse() is an error. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i64.html#method.from_str_radix

Go: strconv.Atoi("+5") is 5, strconv.Atoi(" 5") is an error. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/strconv#Atoi
decisions.detail:
Core/Text/Parse.jet parse_int_base accepts an optional '-' or '+' then digits in the base. Int is exact (arbitrary precision), so very large values are correct and are not errors. core.args reads every Int option and argument through Int.parse (Args.jet), so the rule also decides what a command line accepts. No spec line covers sign or space handling.

Under B, the grammar is: optional '-', then one or more digits; nothing else. "+5", " 5", "5 " and "" all return None, and core.args reports the usual 'not a whole number' error.

Under A, '+' stays accepted, and spaces are refused. Two pieces remove the cost of refusing spaces. Core's typed row decoders (CSV and TSV) accept spaces around a number in an Int column, as pandas does, because such a column cannot hold a meaningful space. core.args names the stray space in its error, so a command-line typo explains itself.

Under C, today's text stays: '+' accepted, and surrounding spaces trimmed.

options.name: Plus allowed, spaces refused
options.detail: `[+-]?digits` parses; spaces return None. Typed CSV and TSV Int columns still accept padding, and core.args names a stray space in its error.
options.technical: Keep the '+' branch; refuse whitespace. Typed row decoders trim an Int column before Int.parse. core.args reports "has a space" for a padded number. Corelib cases cover each rule.
options.code:
Int.parse("+5")   // Val(5)
Int.parse(" 5")   // None

options.name: Strict: optional minus, then digits
options.detail: Only `-?digits` parses. A plus sign or any space returns None.
options.technical: parse_int_base drops the '+' branch; a doc comment states the grammar; a corelib case covers "+5", " 5", "5 ", "-0" and a 30-digit value.
options.code:
Int.parse("5")    // Val(5)
Int.parse("+5")   // None
Int.parse(" 5")   // None

options.name: Lenient: plus and surrounding spaces
options.detail: Spaces around the number are trimmed, and a plus sign is accepted.
options.technical: Trim ASCII whitespace before parsing; document it.
options.code: Int.parse(" +5 ")  // Val(5)

comparisons.note: Accepts a leading '+', refuses spaces. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i64.html#method.from_str_radix
Accepts a leading '+', refuses spaces. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/strconv#Atoi

recommendation.why: It matches Rust and Go, so numbers written with a plus sign keep working, while stray spaces from copy-paste are caught.
gains: Stray spaces in a command-line number become a clear error that names the space.
Text that other tools write with '+5' still parses.
Padded number columns in CSV and TSV files still decode with no extra code.

whyNot.reason: Refusing '+5' breaks text from tools that print an explicit sign, with little safety gain.
Silently trimming hides copy-paste mistakes on the command line.

recommendation.tradeoff: None left: padded files decode as before, and only hand-sliced text sees the stricter rule.

decisions.title: Whether machine-readable error reports name files by absolute or project-relative path
decisions.gist: Should machine-readable error reports name files relative to the project root, with the root written once, so reports are identical on every machine?
decisions.lesson: Tools read Jet's JSON error reports to jump to the failing line. An absolute path always opens from any folder. A project-relative path hides the machine's folder layout but needs the project root to open.
decisions.story: Kim's editor runs `jet check --json` from a subfolder and opens each reported file. With absolute paths every report opens. With project-relative paths the editor must first find the project root. Her CI logs, though, show her home folder in every report.
decisions.inWild:
Rust (cargo): JSON messages give file names relative to the workspace root. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html#json-messages

TypeScript (tsc): diagnostics print paths relative to the working directory. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/compiler-options.html
decisions.detail:
Docs/spec/diagnostics.md says every jet.report/v3 `file` field is absolute. The one exception is E2702 crypto misuse, which is project-relative so it never carries the machine's folder layout. Card #6531 asks to make every report project-relative.

Under A, paths are relative to the folder jet ran in. The tool that ran jet opens them with no join, and CI runs from the same folder on every machine, so saved reports match byte for byte.

Under B, the spec stays: absolute everywhere except E2702.

options.name: Paths relative to the folder jet ran in
options.detail: Every file under the folder jet ran in is reported relative to it, with `../` for other files in the project. The tool that ran jet opens each path directly, as with gcc and tsc. Runs from the same project folder give the same bytes on every machine.
options.technical: Report projection makes file fields relative to the invocation folder inside the project. No `root` field and no special rule for E2702 are needed. Files outside the project keep absolute paths, as today. The spec rule and the resolvable-paths case change in one cutover. Editors use the language server, which sends absolute `file://` URIs as the LSP protocol requires (Compiler/JetLSP/Source/LSP/Diagnostics.jet:150).
options.code: {"code":"E0102","file":"src/main.jet","line":3}

options.name: Keep absolute paths; E2702 stays the exception
options.detail: Reports keep absolute paths. Only crypto-misuse reports are project-relative.
options.technical: No change. #6531 c1 and c3 are dropped; c2 is met.
options.code: {"code":"E0102","file":"/home/kim/app/src/main.jet","line":3}

comparisons.note: JSON messages use paths relative to the workspace root. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html#json-messages
Diagnostics print paths relative to the working directory. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/compiler-options.html

recommendation.why: The tool that ran jet opens every path directly, and reports from the same folder match on every machine.
gains: Reports show no machine folder layout, so E2702 needs no special rule.
Saved CI reports match byte for byte across machines.
Scripts and editors open every reported file with no extra step.

whyNot.reason: B keeps machine-specific folders in every report and a second path rule for E2702.

recommendation.tradeoff: Paths follow the folder jet ran in, as gcc and tsc do.

decisions.title: How does an author ask jet fix to move a declaration's markers inside or back above?
decisions.situation: D-MARKER-INBODY1 A lets a declaration write its markers above it as #X(args), or inside its body as #X :: value lines. Card #6562 says jet fix moves a declaration's whole marker set inside and back above. jet fix today only applies the edits that diagnostics carry, and it has two flags, --dry-run and --all. When a declaration is not mixed there is no diagnostic, so nothing tells jet fix which way to move.
decisions.gist: Which command moves markers between above and inside?
decisions.lesson: jet fix applies the fix that comes with each error. A declaration that writes all its markers in one place is correct and has no error, so moving its markers needs an explicit request.
decisions.story: Ana's struct has five markers above it and twenty fields. She wants the markers inside, after the fields, as the owner allowed. She also wants a way to put them back above before a release.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:1848 JetCLIPlan.Fix{file: file, dry_run: jet_argv.contains("--dry-run"), all: jet_argv.contains("--all"), …}
Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Diagnostics/Diagnostic.jet:259 fn diagnostic_with_alternative_edit(…)
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS RATIFIED

D-MARKER-INBODY1 A: both placements fill one marker list. Mixing on one declaration is refused, with a jet fix that moves the whole set either way. jet fmt keeps the author's placement.

WHAT IS OPEN

How to ask for the move when nothing is mixed. The mixing error can carry one fix plus one alternative edit (diagnostic_with_alternative_edit), but jet fix applies only the primary one.

options.name: A placement flag on jet fix
options.detail: jet fix --markers inside FILE moves every declaration's marker set in FILE into its body; jet fix --markers above FILE moves them all above. Each line is added at the end of the body, in the original marker order. Without the flag, jet fix fixes a mixed declaration by moving its whole set above. An editor offers both directions as code actions on any declaration.
options.technical: One new flag on the existing Fix plan, parsed in Front.jet beside --dry-run and --all. The rewrite is one TextEdit per declaration over its marker and body span, so jet fix's apply path stays unchanged.

options.name: Editor code actions only
options.detail: The move is a code action in the editor (LSP) on a declaration's markers. On the command line, jet fix only fixes mixed declarations, using the primary fix (above). The card's round-trip proof uses the LSP fix path.
options.technical: No CLI change. The round trip cannot be run from a script without an LSP client.
options.code: // editor: "Move markers inside" / "Move markers above" on `struct Point`

options.name: jet fmt chooses placement
options.detail: jet fmt --markers inside|above rewrites placement as a formatting option.
options.technical: Against the ratified rule that jet fmt keeps the author's placement.
options.code: jet fmt --markers inside src/shapes.jet

recommendation.why: The card asks jet fix to move markers both ways. A flag is the smallest addition that does this from the command line, and it keeps jet fmt placement-neutral as ratified.
gains: The round trip runs in a case test.
No change to how jet fix applies edits.

losses.mitigation: It sits beside --dry-run and --all in jet fix --help and the CLI docs.

whyNot.reason: B cannot be scripted, so the card's round-trip case cannot run in the suite.

decisions.title: How a program starts another copy of itself
decisions.situation: Some programs start a fresh copy of themselves, for example to test crash cleanup in a separate process. Jet's example does this by running os.executable() with one extra argument. After jet build, os.executable() names the program file, so that works. Under jet run, the program runs inside the jet tool, so os.executable() names jet itself. Each child then runs a command like `jet return`, which fails, and the example quietly prints the wrong output. You are deciding how a program reliably relaunches itself in both modes. We recommend a new process.self_cmd(args) call that always reruns this same program, while os.executable() keeps naming the real file of the running process.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet program start another copy of itself so it works the same under jet run and jet build?
decisions.lesson: A process is one running program. os.executable() returns the file the operating system started. After jet build that is your program. Under jet run it is the jet tool, which runs your program inside itself. A adds process.self_cmd(args), which always reruns this program. B makes jet run hand out a small launcher file instead. C only documents the difference and leaves relaunching to each author.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A process is one running program, with its own memory and its own exit code. A child process is a process another program starts.

Jet has two ways to run code. jet build makes a native program file you can start directly. jet run compiles your program and runs it inside the jet tool's own process. Jet's law says both must behave the same.

os.executable() asks the operating system which file started the current process. After jet build that file is your program. Under jet run it is the jet tool.

process.cmd(argv) builds a description of a child process from a list: the program file first, then its arguments. process.run_spec runs that description and returns a receipt with the exit code and output.

The example cleanup_matrix starts itself six times, each with a case name, to watch cleanup happen in a separate process. Under jet run each child becomes `jet return` or `jet error`. jet does not know those commands, so every child exits with an error.

Relaunch means starting a new copy of the same program. The question is which call names that copy correctly in both modes.
decisions.story: Omar writes a test harness that starts his program again in a child process for each crash scenario. It works after jet build. Under jet run every child prints a jet usage error, and his harness reports success with empty traces.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Core/sys/sys.jet:53 declares executable() -[Env]> String. The native leaf in crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/OsExtra.rs:18-22 returns std::env::current_exe(). Under jet run the program runs inside the jet process, so that path is the jet binary. Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1499 only says executable() returns process and operating-system facts. Examples/features/io/sys_executable.jet:1-2 already states that meaning: the jet host under jet run, the built binary after jet build.

process.argv() is already made the same in both modes. jet run hands the program its own argument list through one shared carrier (crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Interpreter.rs:663-690, crates/jet-jit/src/Collections.rs:2286-2289). os.executable() has no such carrier.

Examples/features/io/cleanup_matrix.jet:86-95 relaunches itself with process.cmd([os.executable(), path]). Card #4346 records that under jet run every child ran `jet return` and similar, exited 2, and the example still exited 0. process.cmd takes the full argument list, program first (core-library.md:1574). jet run takes program arguments after `--` (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:27), and --allow, --deny, --profile and similar flags shape the run (cli.md:127-130).

Other examples relaunch the same way. They are Examples/features/foundations/distributed/run.jet:65-72, foundations/storage/run.jet:20 and io/watcher.jet:91. Jetpack does too, in Jetpack/Store/Tests/Broker.jet:386 and Jetpack/Services/Source/Supervisor/Lifecycle.jet:60. The test helper tests/dev_parts/support.rs:3463-3470 works around the watcher case by pointing argv at the AOT binary.

Other Jetpack code reads os.executable() to find files beside the running binary. Examples are Jetpack/Foundation/Source/SourceRoot.jet:13 and Jetpack/Store/Source/ArtifactStore/NativeRuntimeCache.jet:244.

Ratified law. D-VERDICT-1254-1 requires that nothing works under jet build and fails under default jet run. D-VERDICT-687-1 makes jet run and jet build two views over one compiler. D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1=B reuses checked work across fresh compiler processes, so a relaunched jet run child does not recheck from nothing.

No Core call today returns the entry file or the jet run flags, so a program cannot build a correct relaunch list by itself under jet run.

options.name: process.self_cmd(args) reruns this program
options.detail:
A new call, process.self_cmd(args: [String]) -> ProcessSpec, builds a child that runs this same program with these arguments. After jet build the list is the program file followed by args. Under jet run it is jet, run, the same absolute entry and every flag that shaped the parent run, then `--` and args. The child therefore runs the same way as its parent.

os.executable() keeps its plain meaning, the file of the running process, which is jet under jet run. The checker warns when os.executable() is the program element of process.cmd, and names self_cmd as the fix. All in-repo self-relaunches move to self_cmd([...]) in the same change, and the support.rs workaround is deleted. The returned value is an ordinary ProcessSpec, so streams, limits and authority work as usual, and .plan() shows the real list.
options.technical:
The run driver records the entry path, project root and the program-shaping flags it applied in the process-start facts. Those flags are rights, profile, preset, fixtures, locked and offline, and they travel through the carrier that already feeds process.argv(). self_cmd reads those facts; an AOT program records its own path instead. Under jet test the child reruns jet test on the same file, and the caller selects a test through its own arguments or environment, as Broker.jet:386-387 does.

The call carries the same -[Exec] effect as process.cmd. One registry row, one Core declaration, one leaf per back end, one registered warning, a spec row beside executable() and goldens for every migrated example on both modes land together.

options.name: jet run hands out a launcher file
options.detail:
Under jet run, os.executable() returns the path of a small launcher file that jet writes before the program starts. Starting that file runs jet run on the same entry with the same flags. Existing code like cleanup_matrix works unchanged.

The cost is that os.executable() no longer names the running file under jet run. Code that hashes its own file, reads files beside it, or reports its path gets the launcher instead; Jetpack's SourceRoot.jet:13 and NativeRuntimeCache.jet:244 do that today. jet must write and mark executable a launcher per entry and flag set, with a .cmd or .exe form on Windows.
options.technical: jet run writes the launcher under the project's .jet directory keyed by entry and flags, reused across runs. The leaf returns that path on the run path and current_exe after jet build. Launcher creation failure must be reported, not silently fall back to the jet path.

options.name: Document the difference only
options.detail:
os.executable() is documented as the running file: jet under jet run, the program after jet build. No new call is added. A program that wants to relaunch must detect the mode and build the jet run command itself.

Today no Core call gives the entry file or the run flags, so this needs at least a mode check and an entry-path fact. The same source still has two meanings, which the parity law forbids.
options.technical: Adds documentation and, to be usable, two facts: whether the program runs under jet run, and its entry path. cleanup_matrix branches on the mode.

comparisons.note: Node keeps process.execPath as the real node binary and offers child_process.fork(file) to rerun a script in a new process.
Python keeps sys.executable as the interpreter, so a script relaunches with the interpreter plus its own path.

recommendation.why: A gives relaunching one call that means the same thing in both modes, which the parity law requires. os.executable() keeps telling the truth about the running file, so code that inspects its own file keeps working.
gains: Self-relaunch works the same under jet run and after jet build.
os.executable() keeps one honest meaning: the file the system started.
The child is an ordinary ProcessSpec, so plans, limits and authority still apply.

losses.loss: Code that relaunches with os.executable() must move to the new call, and code outside the repository that keeps the old pattern still fails under jet run.
losses.mitigation: The in-repo examples and Jetpack callers migrate with the call. The registered warning on os.executable() as process.cmd's program points every other caller at self_cmd.

losses.loss: A relaunched child under jet run starts the jet tool again, which is slower than starting a built program.
losses.mitigation: D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1=B reuses checked work across fresh compiler processes, and jet build removes the cost entirely.

decisions.title: One meaning for date and time format patterns
decisions.gist: Should every time formatter read one percent-code pattern language, or should two named dialects remain?
decisions.lesson: A format pattern like "%Y-%m-%d" turns a date into text. Jet's two formatters read patterns differently, so the same pattern prints different text. One even rewrites ordinary letters such as "ss" inside words. Both options keep every field Jet can print today; they differ in whether one language or two remain.
decisions.explainer:
A directive is a percent sign followed by a letter, such as %Y for the year. Everything else in the pattern is copied as written. One pass means the formatter reads the pattern once, left to right, so text it already produced is never read again as a new directive.

Today time.strftime, written in Jet, reads patterns in one pass but knows only some codes. It has no %S, %p, %z, %e, %F, %T, %R or %D. The .format method, written in Rust, knows those but works by find-and-replace. It replaces %% first, so "%%Y" turns into a year instead of the text "%Y". It also replaces bare tokens such as yyyy, MM, dd, HH, mm and ss anywhere, even inside words.

Some codes also disagree. %f prints 6 digits (microseconds) in strftime but 9 digits (nanoseconds) in .format. Year 5 prints as "5" in strftime and "0005" in .format. A Date has no clock time, yet .format quietly uses midnight. A LocalTime has no date, yet .format uses 1 January 1970.

A literal pattern is one written directly in the code, like "%H:%M". The compiler can read it before the program runs. A runtime pattern comes from a variable, such as a user setting.
decisions.story: Sam prints log timestamps with "%H:%M:%S". In one file he calls time.strftime and gets "03:04:%S". In another he calls dt.format and gets "03:04:05". He expects one pattern to mean one thing.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-and-strptime-format-codes
from datetime import datetime
datetime(2026, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 123456).strftime("%H:%M:%S %%Y %f")
# '03:04:05 %Y 123456'  (one pass: %%Y is the text %Y)
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Core/time/time.jet:117-175 strftime is one-pass. It supports %% %A %a %b %B %c %d %f %H %I %j %m %M %U %W %w %y %Y and %Z, which always prints UTC. It lacks %S, %p, %z, %e, %F, %T, %R and %D and copies an unknown code as text. %f is six microsecond digits and %Y is unpadded.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/Time.rs:1768-1868 builds .format output by chained replacement. %% is replaced first (line 1823), so %%Y then becomes a year. %f is nine nanosecond digits (1845), years pad to four digits (1760-1766), and %z prints +HH:MM (1722-1725). Lines 1849-1866 also replace EEEE, MMMM, MMM, yyyy, DDD, EEE, MM, dd, HH, mm, ss, SSSSSSSSS, SSSSSS, SSS, VV and XXX anywhere in the pattern.

Date.format fills in midnight (Time.rs:274-279) and LocalTime.format fills in 1970-01-01 (466-471). format_checked exists on Date, LocalTime, DateTime and ZonedDateTime (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreCallRows.jet:1606-1714). It returns String TextError! and validates the token grammar with quoted literals (Time.rs:1873-2004). Core/time/time.jet:104 isoformat_date already pads the year to four digits. No proposed output was run.

options.name: One percent-code language, checked early, migrated automatically
options.detail:
Every formatter reads one percent-code language in one pass: time.strftime, and .format and .format_checked on Date, LocalTime, DateTime and ZonedDateTime. The codes are the familiar C and Python ones, plus %N for nanoseconds and %L for milliseconds. The year pads to four digits, like isoformat.

When the pattern is written in the code, the compiler reads it. An unknown code, a stray % at the end, or a field the value lacks, such as %H on a Date, is a compile error with a suggested fix. A bare yyyy or HH:mm gets a warning offering the percent spelling, which helps people coming from Java.

`jet fix` rewrites every existing literal pattern so it prints what it printed before. For example "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS" becomes "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%L". If old output came from a token inside a word, like "class", the fix keeps that output and adds a note so the author can restore the word.

A pattern that comes from a variable or a settings file cannot be rewritten in the source. jet fix wraps it instead: `dt.format(p)` becomes `dt.format(time.from_legacy(p, .DateTime))`, which translates the old pattern while the program runs. So a stored "yyyy %f" still prints what it printed before.

One old output is not kept. The old formatter re-read zone names, so Europe/Brussels printed as Europe/Bru05els. The new %Z prints the real name, and jet fix lists every pattern this can affect.
options.technical:
Date codes. %a and %A are the short and full English weekday. %b and %B are the short and full month. %Y is the year with at least four digits, with a minus when negative (-0005). %y is the year mod 100. %m, %d and %y are two digits. %e is the day padded with a space. %j is the day of year, three digits. %w is the weekday with Sunday 0. %U and %W are Sunday-first and Monday-first week numbers; days before the first such day are week 00.

Clock codes. %H, %I, %M and %S are two digits. %p is AM or PM. %f is microseconds, six digits, truncated. %L is milliseconds, three digits. %N is nanoseconds, nine digits. Zone codes: %z is the offset +HHMM, %:z is +HH:MM, and %Z is the zone name. Composites: %F = %Y-%m-%d, %D = %m/%d/%y, %T = %H:%M:%S, %R = %H:%M, and %c is the asctime form. %% is one percent. Composites render fields directly; produced text is never re-read.

The GNU no-padding flag works on every numeric code: %-d prints 2, not 02, and %-Y prints -5, not -0005.

Receivers: Date takes date codes only and LocalTime clock codes only. DateTime takes both, with %z +0000, %:z +00:00 and %Z UTC. ZonedDateTime takes both plus its real zone and historical offset. No synthetic midnight or 1970 fields exist. In a literal pattern, an unknown code, a code the receiver lacks or a trailing % is a compile error. At run time .format copies it as text and .format_checked returns TextError.

Literal migration by jet fix keeps output byte for byte, except the zone case below. Date tokens: EEEE to %A, EEE to %a, MMMM to %B, MMM to %b, yyyy to %Y, MM to %m, dd to %d, DDD to %j. Clock tokens: HH to %H, mm to %M, ss to %S, SSSSSSSSS to %N, SSSSSS to %f, SSS to %L. Zone tokens: VV to %Z and XXX to %:z. Old .format %f becomes %N and %z becomes %:z. Old time.strftime %Y becomes %-Y, its unpadded form.

A %% followed by a letter becomes the code the old formatter actually applied. Codes whose old output was fixed text, such as Date midnight digits or an empty DateTime zone, become that text. Quoted literals in format_checked patterns become plain text with % doubled. Literal text that already holds a % is escaped first.

Runtime migration: time.from_legacy(pattern: String, kind: time.LegacyKind) -> String Never!, with LegacyKind = Strftime | Date | LocalTime | DateTime | Zoned. It applies the same translation while the program runs, using the receiver facts named by kind. jet fix wraps every old call whose pattern is not a literal, choosing kind from the static receiver type. Converting a stored pattern once with from_legacy lets the author delete the wrapper.

One case is not preserved. Old .format replaced %Z with the zone name and then re-read it, so ss in Europe/Brussels became seconds (Time.rs:1840, 1859). The new %Z prints the real name. jet fix lists every literal %Z pattern on a ZonedDateTime for review, and from_legacy documents the same difference. One engine serves every tier.

options.name: Two named dialects
options.detail:
Every formatter takes a dialect: `.Strftime`, the one-pass percent language of A, or `.Legacy`, today's find-and-replace rules frozen as they are. Existing .format calls are rewritten to pass .Legacy, so their output does not change.

The disagreement stays. "%Y %%Y" still means two different things depending on the dialect, and Legacy still rewrites "ss" inside words. Every reader must check which dialect a call uses. Every new formatting feature must be built twice or refused in one dialect.
options.technical: format(pattern: String, dialect: TimeFormat) -> String Never! on each receiver, with TimeFormat = Strftime | Legacy; time.strftime always uses Strftime. Legacy freezes the Time.rs:1823-1866 order, padded year, nine-digit %f, synthetic midnight and 1970 fields. One private engine with two policies.
options.code:
use core.time as time
dt :: time.datetime(-5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) + 123456789ns
print(time.strftime("%H:%M:%S", dt))            // 03:04:05
print(dt.format("%H:%M:%S", .Legacy))           // 03:04:05
print(dt.format("%Y %%Y %f", .Legacy))          // -0005 -0005 123456789
print(dt.format("%Y %%Y %f", .Strftime))        // -0005 %Y 123456
print(dt.format("%H:%M class", .Legacy))        // 03:04 cla05

comparisons.note: Python strftime reads the pattern once, so %%Y is the text %Y and %f is six digits.
GNU date adds %N for nanoseconds and %:z for an offset with a colon.

recommendation.why: One pattern should print the same text everywhere. A gets there while keeping existing output: jet fix rewrites written patterns and wraps runtime patterns in a converter. Only text the old formatter corrupted changes.
gains: One pattern prints the same text in every formatter.
Pattern typos are caught while compiling, not in production logs.
jet fix keeps existing output, for written patterns and for patterns read from settings.

losses.loss: Old calls whose pattern comes from a variable or setting keep a time.from_legacy wrapper until their stored patterns are converted.
losses.mitigation: jet fix adds the wrapper with the right kind, so output stays the same. Running a stored pattern through time.from_legacy once converts it, and the wrapper can then be deleted.

losses.loss: Old output that re-read a printed zone name, such as Europe/Bru05els for Europe/Brussels, is not reproduced.
losses.mitigation: that text was corrupt. The new %Z prints the real name, and jet fix lists every literal %Z pattern on a zoned value for review.

whyNot.reason: Two dialects keep one pattern meaning two things, so every reader must check which rules apply.

recommendation.tradeoff: One language plus an output-preserving fix removes the disagreement; only text the old formatter corrupted changes.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Test every code on Date, LocalTime, DateTime and ZonedDateTime with years -5, 0, 5 and 10000. Cover %U, %W and %w at year boundaries, Unicode literals, %%Y, trailing % and fractions 0, 999 and 999999999.

Prove compile errors for unknown and missing-field codes in literal patterns. Run jet fix over a corpus of old patterns, literal and runtime, and assert byte-identical output before and after. Cover runtime patterns holding %f, %z and yyyy through time.from_legacy for every kind. Zone regression: old "%Z" on Europe/Brussels printed Europe/Bru05els; new prints Europe/Brussels, and jet fix lists the call. Prove one engine serves every tier.

# '03:04:05 %Y 123456'

decisions.situation: A time format pattern is the small template, such as "%H:%M:%S", that turns a date and time into text. Jet has two formatters that read the same pattern differently: time.strftime prints "03:04:%S" because it has no seconds code, while dt.format prints "03:04:05". The method form also replaces bare letter pairs, so the word "class" in a pattern comes out as "cla05". This bites anyone printing timestamps in logs, file names or screens, and the errors are silent. You are deciding whether every formatter shares one pattern language or whether two named dialects remain. We recommend one percent-code language, checked while compiling, with a jet fix migration that keeps old output, even for patterns read from settings. The only output that changes is text the old formatter corrupted, such as the zone name Europe/Brussels printed as Europe/Bru05els.

decisions.title: Moving a field out of a value that has its own Close
decisions.situation: Some Jet types define Close, cleanup code that runs once when a value is done, such as flushing a file. If code moves one field out of such a value, Close would later run on a value with a missing field. Today's Jet checker refuses that move with error E0222, except inside the type's own Close. That rule was added to fix a crash and was never put to a vote. We recommend keeping the refusal, with clearer error text, because Close always sees a complete value.
decisions.gist: May code move one field out of a value whose type defines its own Close, and if so, what happens to that Close?
decisions.lesson: Close is a type's own cleanup, run exactly once when its value ends. It reads the value's fields. Moving one field out leaves a hole that Close would read. Jet can refuse such moves, skip Close when a value is taken apart, or allow it only inside the type's own methods. Fields that can be copied are unaffected under every option.
decisions.story: Sam wraps a file in an Upload type whose Close flushes and logs. Later he writes a helper that takes just the file out of an Upload. Today the checker stops him with E0222. He wants to know whether that is a permanent rule, and if so, how to get the file out properly.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4809; checker rule in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Checks.jet:2393-2402 (sema_ownership_reject_partial_close_move). Today: moving part of a value whose type has its own Close is E0222. The one exemption is the consuming Close body itself, so Close may take its own fields apart, as in Examples/features/memory/resource_close_containers.jet.

Burn-down 2026-10-17 (DoneEvidence) confirmed the refusal on r29g, and also found two gaps. No UI snapshot exists, and the Why text leaks an internal id ('module:14:source-root:0::main.jet::Holder'). Under A, both are fixed: the message names the user's type, and a UI snapshot is added.

Related: D-FIELD-DROP-ORDER1=A explicitly did not permit new partial moves. Copying a copyable field (for example a String under default copy) is allowed under every option. Destructuring with `..` copies the named fields and leaves the owner whole (Examples/features/memory/destructure_drop_order.jet).

The rule applies on every tier (check, run, build, interpreter), so I9 holds under each option.

options.name: Refuse the move, as today
options.detail: Moving a field out of a value whose type has its own Close is error E0222, except inside that type's Close. Callers move the whole value, copy a copyable field, or call a method the type author provides. The error text names the user's type and suggests those fixes.

options.name: Allow it; Close is skipped and the rest is cleaned field by field
options.detail: Any code may move a field out. The value's own Close then never runs; each remaining field is cleaned up on its own. A file wrapper's flush or a lock wrapper's release could be skipped silently by an ordinary-looking line.

options.name: Allow it only inside the type's own methods
options.detail: Inside the type's own impl, a consuming method may move fields out of self, and Close does not run for that value. Everywhere else the move is E0222. Authors get an into-parts pattern, but a method can skip cleanup with no visible marker, unlike Swift, which requires `discard self`.

comparisons.note: Rust refuses moving a field out of a type that implements Drop (E0509); authors use Option fields or mem::take instead.
comparisons.code: error[E0509]: cannot move out of type `Upload`, which implements the `Drop` trait

comparisons.note: Swift lets a noncopyable type's own consuming method take itself apart only after writing `discard self`, which skips deinit.
comparisons.code: consuming func intoFile() -> File { let f = file; discard self; return f }

recommendation.why: Close always sees a complete value, so cleanup can never silently skip a step. This is today's behavior, matches Rust, and keeps copyable fields and the Close body itself unrestricted.
recommendation.tradeoff: Type authors who want an into-parts method must design for it, for example with an optional field, until a separate vote adds an explicit take-apart step.

whyNot.reason: One ordinary-looking line can silently skip a flush or a lock release.
Cleanup can still be skipped with no visible marker in the method.

losses.loss: No built-in into-parts pattern for Close types.
losses.mitigation: Authors use an optional field and take it; an explicit take-apart step can be voted separately.

surface.gist: May code move one field out of a value whose type has its own Close cleanup?
surface.lesson: Close is a type's own cleanup, run once when its value ends, and it reads the value's fields. Moving one field out leaves a hole Close would read. Jet can refuse the move, skip Close, or allow it only inside the type's own methods.

current.note: Today's checker refuses the move with E0222; this was never voted.

wild.note: Rust refuses the same move with E0509.

options.name: Refuse it
options.gist: Keep E0222; Close always sees a whole value.
gains: Cleanup can never be skipped by accident.
Matches today and Rust.
losses: No easy into-parts pattern.

options.name: Allow; skip Close
options.gist: Any code may move a field; Close never runs.
gains: Most flexible.
losses: A flush or unlock can vanish silently.

proposed.code: ^up.file   // allowed; Upload's Close skipped

options.name: Only inside the type
options.gist: The type's own methods may take it apart.
gains: Authors get an into-parts method.
losses: Skipped cleanup has no visible marker.

recommendation.why: Close always sees a complete value, so cleanup never silently skips a step. It is today's rule and matches Rust.
gains: Predictable cleanup.

losses.loss: No built-in into-parts pattern.
losses.mitigation: Use an optional field; an explicit take-apart step can be voted later.

whyNot.reason: Silently skips cleanup.
Skips cleanup without a visible marker.

recommendation.tradeoff: Less flexibility for cleanup that always runs.

decisions.title: Closure audit: what to do with the 3,670 closures from the Rust era that have no durable evidence
decisions.situation: #6563 c1 says every done card and every met criterion, live or archived, must be DURABLE, re-verified against dev with a commit, or reopened. The audit finds 3,729 rows with no durable evidence. 59 of them are live or were closed after the Rust cutover (6a18f4d8e3, 2026-10-23), and Prep has a disposition for each. The other 3,670 rows are on 1,344 archived cards, all closed between 2026-06 and 2026-10-23 against the Rust compiler. Their evidence is mostly prose with no commit (1,952), a merge into a card later deleted (468), or a Rust file path (390). The rest cite a decision (253), are empty (227), name a path not on dev (223), use Rust words (94) or cite a sha not in the repo (63). Only the owner can restore an archived card.
decisions.gist: Should the audit record the Rust-era closures as unproven since the cutover, or reopen them and prove each one again?
decisions.lesson: A durable closure names a commit, file, test or decision still on dev. Rust-era closures named Rust files and cargo runs that the cutover deleted. The cutover removed that evidence, not the need for the behaviour. The 4,414 tracked tests/cases files and the Examples goldens now guard most of it, but #6096 still lists areas whose Rust tests are unported. One group differs: 468 criteria were merged into 60 cards later deleted. Only 84 of them appear, met, on another card; 384 are on no card.
decisions.story: Prep re-proved all 59 live and post-cutover rows on compiler 76b385b498. 27 still hold and 17 must be reopened. Of the rest, 10 no longer apply, 2 are covered by a decision, 2 are duplicates and 1 needs a fresh perf run. Proving the 3,670 older rows the same way means one probe each, and most of their wording describes Rust-era internals.
decisions.inWild: When a project rewrites its implementation, the usual practice is to close legacy-era tracker items in bulk as 'obsolete after the rewrite'. An item is reopened only when the new test suite or a user shows the behaviour is still missing. [INFERENCE: a general practice; Prep cites no specific project.]
decisions.detail: Today's tooling: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/Main/prep/audit/audit2.mjs writes CLOSURE-AUDIT-v2.tsv (15,259 rows), and era.mjs splits its REOPEN rows by the cutover. The live and post-cutover dispositions are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/briefs/6563-c1-dispositions.tsv. The merged-into-deleted figures come from matching each source criterion's normalized text against every criterion on the live and archived board.

options.name: Record the Rust-era rows as unproven, but check the 384 orphaned merges
options.detail: Each pre-cutover row with no durable evidence is recorded UNPROVEN-PRECUT, citing 6a18f4d8e3. UNPROVEN-PRECUT never counts as done; it means the evidence predates the cutover. The exceptions are the 384 orphaned merges, rows merged into a deleted card and on no card, which Prep checks against dev. A row that holds is recorded VERIFIED with a commit; the rest become criteria on live cards. A row in an area #6096 lists as unported also becomes a #6096 criterion. The 59 newer rows follow the dispositions TSV; c1 is amended to match.
options.technical:
audit2.mjs gains the class UNPROVEN-PRECUT (closed before 2026-10-23T07:18:29Z, not live, not merged-orphan). Archived UNPROVEN-PRECUT rows need no Tower write; the audit TSV is their record.

The new c1 text reads: 'Each live or post-cutover row is DURABLE, re-verified against dev with its commit, or reopened with its reason. decisions.title: A drag that leaves with no action
decisions.gist: When a drag leaves a window without dropping, what action should Jet report?
decisions.lesson: While you drag something over a window, the browser says what a drop would do: copy, move or link. When the drag leaves, it says none. Jet's drag event always holds one of three actions, so every web leave event is an error today. Whichever option wins, leave events must arrive without an error.
decisions.story: Maya builds a web to-do list where people drag notes between columns. When a note leaves a column, she clears the column's highlight. Today her program gets an error on every leave, so highlights stick.

options.name: Optional action
options.detail: UIDragEvent.operation becomes UIDragOperation?. Enter and over carry the browser's action, or none when the target refuses the drop. Leave and cancel carry none. A drop always carries an action.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/DragDrop.jet: drag_operation maps "none" to None. A drop record whose effect is none becomes phase Cancel, so Drop implies Val. The provider record format is unchanged. Native providers send the same five fields.
options.code:
if event.operation == .Val(op) -> show_hint(op)
else -> clear_highlight()

options.name: None case
options.detail: UIDragOperation gains a None case. Every event carries an action value, and None means nothing would happen.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/DragDrop.jet: the enum gains None; drag_operation maps "none" to .None. Exhaustive matches on UIDragOperation everywhere gain an arm.

comparisons.note: The browser models dropEffect as a string that includes none. MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DataTransfer/dropEffect.
winit reports a file hover as a separate event, and a cancelled hover as HoveredFileCancelled with no action. See https://docs.rs/winit/latest/winit/event/enum.WindowEvent.html.

recommendation.why: Jet already spells "may be missing" with optional values. One spelling of nothing keeps the drag type honest, and drops keep a guaranteed action.
gains: Leave events work on the web with no new enum case.

losses.loss: Code that reads the action on hover checks for none first.
losses.mitigation: Core guarantees drops carry an action; a browser drop with none becomes a Cancel event.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second way to say nothing and forces a None arm into every drop handler.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hover and leave code checks for a missing action; drop code never does.

decisions.title: Keyboard shortcuts in web pages
decisions.gist: How should a web page hand key presses to Jet's shortcut table?
decisions.lesson: Jet keeps a table of shortcuts, such as Ctrl+S for save. A program registers a key and an action, and Core decides which key matches. A Jet web page never forwards key presses, so a registered shortcut never fires. Ctrl+S opens the browser's own save page instead. Whichever option wins, Core keeps deciding matches.
decisions.story: Sam writes a small web notes app in Jet and binds Ctrl+S to save. On the desktop it saves. In the browser, Ctrl+S opens the browser's save page, and the app never hears the key.

options.name: Key queue
options.detail: Registering a shortcut also tells the page which key to claim. The page blocks the browser's default for claimed keys only and queues each press. shortcuts.poll takes the next press, matches it in Core's table, and returns Dispatched or Unhandled.
options.technical: Core/Ui/Host/Shortcuts.jet gains poll() over provider queue 2 (capability 4), the same provider record and overflow mark as ime.poll and drag_drop.poll. register() also calls one new raw host primitive that passes the normalized key and modifier bits to the provider. The default web provider (JetWeb Host.jet) listens for keydown, compares against claimed keys, calls preventDefault, and enqueues target, key and modifier bits. Desktop providers enqueue the same record.

options.name: UI key events
options.detail: Key presses arrive through core.ui as key events that now carry modifiers. The core.ui event loop asks the shortcut table before the program's own handler.
options.technical: core.ui InputEvent.Key gains a modifiers field; DomRuntime.js forwards keydown into the node tree; the UI loop calls shortcuts.dispatch. Programs that use core.ui.host without core.ui nodes see no key source.

options.name: Desktop only
options.detail: The web provider reports the Shortcuts capability as unavailable, so register and dispatch fail with CapabilityUnavailable on the web.
options.technical: JetWeb Host.jet capability() returns false for code 4.
options.code:
shortcuts.register(save)?
// web: Err(CapabilityUnavailable{capability: "Shortcuts"})

comparisons.note: Pages own shortcuts by listening for keydown and calling preventDefault. MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/keydown_event.
egui reads queued key events each frame and checks shortcuts against them. See https://docs.rs/egui/latest/egui/struct.InputState.html#method.consume_shortcut.

recommendation.why: Drag and drop and typing composition already arrive through page queues and poll. Keys joining the same path keeps one mechanism, and Core still owns every match.
gains: Web shortcuts work with the same code as desktop.

losses.loss: A program that stops polling misses presses after the queue fills.
losses.mitigation: A full queue reports QueueFull on the next poll, like drag and drop, so nothing is lost silently.

whyNot.reason: B leaves host-only programs without shortcuts and changes a public event type.
C makes the same program behave differently on the web.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs poll shortcuts like other host events; a stalled program learns it missed presses.
