decisions.title: One rule for foreign words and retired Jet spellings
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler can spot another language's word, such as `fun`, or an old Jet spelling, such as `#Suppress`, and name the current form. In June the owner paused these teaching messages, but the port of the compiler to Jet brought most of them back. Today `fun add(...)` gets an error that points the wrong way, while `length()` teaches. Nine tests fail on missing teaching text, and 27 pass while pinning teaching the pause removed. The recommendation keeps the pause everywhere, with generic errors that name the legal Jet forms.
decisions.gist: When code uses another language's word or a retired Jet spelling, should Jet name the replacement, and what happens to the tests that pin it?
decisions.lesson: Jet paused its teaching messages in June, but the port to Jet brought 29 of them back. Nine tests fail because their teaching text is gone, while 27 others pass and pin teaching that the pause removed. One rule has to decide which messages Jet prints.
decisions.story: Maya comes from Kotlin and writes `fun add(left: Int, right: Int) -> Int`. Jet tells her the line computes a value she does not use, so she wraps it in `print` and gets a stranger error. A minute later she writes `sizes.length()`, and Jet says `length` is another language's name for `len`. The two answers follow two different rules, and the first one sent her the wrong way.
decisions.detail:
Five owner rulings disagree. The June pause, confirmed in July, removes teaching for foreign words and retired spellings until after the FFI epoch. The owner added that retired spellings leave the tests too. The August retirement rule makes a retirement that changes meaning a hard error with a fix line, and checks that the old form is gone from the repo. The August foreign-keyword rule teaches each known foreign keyword. The October foreign-teaching ballot kept the pause and asked only for better generic errors.

Measured at commit 125e2e8f89, 29 teaching rows still print, and three of them are already marked Retired in the registry. The 27 tests that pin them pass. Method lookup also still says `length` is another language's name for `len`. Nine tests fail. Three are foreign cases: `fun` and friends, `jet install`, and a list of foreign method names. Six are old Jet spellings: `tasks.channel<Int>()`, `Ability`, `#Suppress`, `.origin()` on a tracked value, a bare `?`, and the old HTTP response literal.

The bare `?` test also expects the `Int E!` suffix to be retired. That suffix is current syntax, and the compiler itself uses it, so that half of the test is stale under every option. The test keeps its bare `?` error and is re-recorded from real output. The `semaphore_teaching` test fails only on a trailing blank line, and it follows the same rule as the other teaching tests.

Two codes mean several things at once, and this is not a teaching question. E1206 is registered as a lint-selector error but is also printed for package file, allocator, path and lock errors. E0128 is registered as a zip length error but is also printed for distinct types, so `Meters{a + b}` says a `Meters` cannot be used where a `Meters` is expected. Under every option each meaning gets its own registered code.

Some codes are never printed today. E0983 and nine lint codes are checks the Jet compiler has not built yet, so each keeps its test and gets a real check on the package and lint cards. E0043 (`jet install`) and E0037 (a print macro) are teaching codes and follow this ruling.

Nothing is deleted outright. A test that leaves the suite is moved to the held archive with a log row, and git history keeps it. A registry row that stops printing stays with status Retired, so `jet explain` still answers for old logs. About 115 tests have retired, foreign, teach, legacy, migration or deprecated in their path, and 92 of them pass. Each is checked once during the change.

options.name: Pause everywhere, with generic errors that name the legal forms
options.detail:
Jet stops recognizing foreign words and retired spellings, including the foreign method-name hints. Every unknown word, method, type or rule gets one generic error built from Jet's own grammar and library. It lists the legal forms at that spot and suggests current names by spelling and by signature. An unknown rule no longer stops the check, so the code inside it is still checked in the same run.

Tests that pin only teaching leave the suite. Tests that pin a current rule keep that rule but use an invented word instead of an old spelling.
options.technical:
Remove the recognizers behind the 29 printing teaching rows and the foreign branch of method lookup. Mark those rows, E0037 and E0043 Retired. The parser and checker still reject every form; before the tests leave, one recorded run shows each program still fails.

Add a check that no active registry row is named Foreign or Retired, apart from the FFI rows that describe calls into C. This replaces the fix-line half of the August retirement rule and the August foreign-keyword rule. The check that a retired form appears nowhere in the repo stays.

options.name: Pause foreign words, teach retired Jet spellings
options.detail: Foreign words get the same generic errors as in A. A retired Jet spelling gets a hard error that names its replacement, from one retirement table. The six retired-spelling tests are fixed by restoring their messages, and the three foreign tests leave the suite.
options.technical: Retire the foreign rows as in A. Keep the retired-spelling rows and port the six missing messages into one table of old form, new form and fix line. Pure renames get a machine fix, as the August retirement rule says. The retired spellings stay in the tests, which the June owner comment ruled out.

options.name: Teach both from one table
options.detail: Jet names the replacement for both foreign words and retired Jet spellings. All 29 printing rows stay, the nine failing tests are fixed by restoring their messages, and one table holds every taught word. This reopens the October ruling that kept the pause.
options.technical: Move the 29 recognizers and the method-name hints into one table. Port the nine missing messages, including `fun`, `def` and `var` and `jet install`. Re-record `semaphore_teaching` without its trailing blank line. Someone must keep the table current for every language it covers.

comparisons.note: Python suggests near names by spelling only, and keeps no table of other languages' words.
comparisons.code:
[].apend(1)
# AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'apend'. Did you mean: 'append'?

recommendation.why: Two owner rulings say pause, and the latest one, in October, kept it. One rule ends today's mix, where `length` teaches and `fun` misleads. Generic errors that list legal forms help every unknown word, including typos, not only the words someone thought to list.
gains: One rule for every unknown word, method, type and rule.
No retired or foreign spellings left in the tests, as the owner asked in June.
Generic errors stop pointing the wrong way, which helps typos as well as habits from other languages.
An unknown rule no longer hides the errors inside it.

losses.loss: A form whose meaning moved, such as `#Suppress`, gets no direct pointer to its replacement. This is irreducible: without a table of old forms, no rule can know what the old form meant.
losses.mitigation: Checking continues past the unknown form, so the next error in the same run names the current form, as `.drop("reason")` does here.

losses.loss: The change touches 29 recognizers and about 115 tests in one pass.
losses.mitigation: It lands as one change with the full test suite run before and after, and every removed test is kept in the held archive.

whyNot.reason: It keeps retired spellings in the tests, which the owner ruled out in June, and it still leaves two rules for unknown words.
It reverses the October ruling, and it needs a table of other languages' words that someone must keep current.

recommendation.tradeoff: Clear, uniform errors for every unknown word, at the cost of no direct pointer for the few forms whose meaning moved.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main, reviewing the Prep-2 draft under the four-agent cap. Findings were that the October claim checks out (D-FOREIGN-TEACH1 chose Keep the pause), and the code splits apply under every option, so they do not tilt the vote.

surface.lesson: Jet paused its teaching messages in June, but 29 came back when the compiler moved to Jet. Today `length()` teaches while `fun` gets a misleading error. Nine tests fail on missing teaching. One rule should decide what Jet says for every unknown word.

current.note: Today one foreign word misleads and another teaches.

# AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'apend'.
# Did you mean: 'append'?

options.name: Pause everywhere, better generic errors
options.gist: No foreign or old-word teaching; errors list the legal forms and near names.
gains: One rule for every unknown word.
Errors never point the wrong way.
Errors inside an unknown rule still show.
losses: Old forms whose meaning moved get no direct pointer.

options.name: Pause foreign words, teach old Jet spellings
options.gist: Foreign words get generic errors; retired Jet spellings name their replacement.
gains: Old Jet code gets a direct fix line.
losses: Old spellings stay in the tests.
Two rules for unknown words.

options.name: Teach both from one table
options.gist: Jet names the replacement for foreign words and old Jet spellings alike.
gains: The most direct help for newcomers.

losses: Reverses the October ruling.

Generic errors stop pointing the wrong way.

losses.mitigation: Checking continues past the unknown form, so the next error names the current form.

whyNot.reason: It keeps old spellings in the tests and leaves two rules.
It reverses the October ruling and needs a table of other languages.

decisions.title: How are the ui and cases corpus suites named, and how does a code suite report its rows?
decisions.situation: D-TEST-PROFILE1=A made test profiles data in package.jet. Its example names one stock suite field, golden_corpus, and says code suites register with Test.suite(name, value) in fn test, without saying what value is. Jet's own ui and cases corpora need field names, and the jetpack, selfhost and perf suites need a signature. Today only golden_corpus is ratified, so the testkit package declares only golden, and ui, cases, jetpack, selfhost and perf are left out. This vote names the two corpus fields and fixes how a code suite reports its rows.
decisions.gist: What are the ui and cases corpus fields called, and does a code suite return rows or report each one?
decisions.lesson: A suite is a named set of rows that `jet test --profile` runs and compares. A stock suite is a folder of test files, written as data. A code suite is a function that checks something no folder describes, such as a binary-size budget, and reports one row per check.
decisions.story: Sam adds a size budget to CI. Today it is a Node script that prints its own format. With a code suite he writes one Jet function that reports a row per program. `jet test --profile perf` then shows those rows beside the golden rows, compares them with the last run, and fails when a row that passed now fails.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo: [[test]] harness = false points at a binary that prints its own results.
Go: a TestMain or t.Run(name, fn) reports each subtest as it runs.
Vitest: projects in config name test folders; each test reports as it finishes.
pytest: a plugin's pytest_collect_file turns any file type into reported items.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS DECIDED ALREADY

D-TEST-PROFILE1=A (2026-10-30) made profiles `test:` records in package.jet, such as `quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s }`. The suite `tests`, every #Test, is built in. Stock suites are `suites:` data. The ratified example names one field: `golden: TestSuite{ golden_corpus: "tests/golden" }`. Code suites register in test.jet's fn test with Test.suite(name, value).

WHAT IS OPEN

1. Field names for the other two corpora Jet runs: the ui corpus (tests/ui, a source file with its expected stdout and stderr) and the cases corpus (tests/cases, step files).

2. What value is in Test.suite(name, value). Today Test has one method, t.run(), which runs the stock suite and returns its exit code (sema THandleOp.TestSuiteRun). There is no Test.suite.

TODAY (dev b032d40638)

- `ui_corpus:` or `cases_corpus:` in package.jet is E1206 "unknown Package field" (Jetpack PackageModel apply_field), as `test:` was before D-TEST-PROFILE1.
- The testkit package's ui and cases runners exist (Tools/testkit, Jet). Moving them under `jet test` is #6035 c3, which needs these names.
- The perf, selfhost and jetpack checks are shell and Node scripts today (Tools/perf/ci-perf-check.sh, Tools/agent/s5, the Jetpack tests), outside `jet test`.

THE OPTIONS

A and B both add ui_corpus and cases_corpus beside golden_corpus, and differ only in the code-suite value. C replaces the three corpus fields with one `corpus:` field plus `kind:`. That rewrites the ratified example, and C uses B's code-suite value.

A: the value is a function that receives a row sink, fn(rows: TestRows). It calls rows.pass(id), rows.fail(id, detail) or rows.skip(id, reason) as each check finishes.

B: the value is a function that returns its rows, fn() -> [TestRow]. TestRow is a plain struct: id, outcome (.Pass, .Fail(detail), .Skip(reason)).

C: `TestSuite{ corpus: "tests/ui", kind: ui }`, with kind one of golden, ui, cases; code suites as in B.

EDGE CASES (the same under every option unless noted)

- A suite name in both `suites:` and a Test.suite call is an error that names both places.

- Test.suite names are string literals, so `jet check` and `--profile` list every suite without running code. A computed name is an error with a fix to write the name.

- A profile that names an unknown suite is the D-TEST-PROFILE1 error listing the known suites, code suites included.

- Two rows with one id in a suite: the second is a failing row "duplicate row id".

- A code suite that panics: under A, rows reported before the panic stay and one failing row "stopped: <message>" is added. Under B and C every row of that suite is lost and the suite is one failing row.

- time_limit bounds each corpus row, and each code-suite call as a whole. Under A the rows reported before the limit stay.

- -u rewrites a ui row's expected streams. A code suite has no snapshots; -u accepts its new rows as the stored last result.

- cases_corpus reads .case files only while they exist. When D-TESTKIT1=A's migration moves them to #Test, they join `tests` and the field retires with the corpus.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginner: nothing changes. `jet test` runs every #Test, with no package.jet fields and no test.jet. Expert: package.jet names the corpora and the profiles, and test.jet registers code suites. `jet test --profile full` runs them all in the c4 pool and prints one row stream.

decisions.title: Every jet test flag is also a setting: shard, list, levels, results, compiler and the rest
decisions.situation: Some test runs need choices that change each time. A release check splits the golden tests across eight processes. A census first lists the tests, then runs one build level and saves the verdicts to a file. An A/B check runs the same tests under an older compiler. Today these scripts call a separate test-kit program with its own flags. You ruled that every command-line flag must also be a setting. We recommend that each jet test flag is also a test-profile field and an fn test call, with the same name.
decisions.gist: Should every jet test flag also be a profile field and an fn test call, with one name?
decisions.lesson: A choice can be written in three places: a test profile in package.jet, code in test.jet's fn test, or a flag on one command. Each place uses the same name. Later places win: the profile, then fn test, then the flag. Build settings already work this way.
decisions.story: Ana's release script checks a new compiler on the golden tests. It starts eight processes, each told to take one eighth of the tests, then merges the eight verdict files. Her census lists the tests first, then runs only the jet run level. She wants plain jet test commands, and the same choices written in her package when they never change.
decisions.inWild:
cargo nextest: --partition count:2/8 runs one of eight slices, and the same choice can live in a profile in .config/nextest.toml. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/configuration/

pytest: every flag can also be written in the addopts setting of pytest.ini. Source: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference/customize.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT You ruled that any flag must also be a setting. The last draft added flags only, and only with --profile. Now every jet test flag, old and new, is also a test-profile field and a call on t in fn test. The flags work on every jet test, not only with --profile. TODAY Test profiles live in package.jet (D-TEST-PROFILE1=A). A profile already has suites, baseline, jobs, memory, filter, shard, opt_in, optimize and time_limit fields. fn test in test.jet declares code suites with t.suite and has no settings calls (Compiler/test.jet:26-31). Build settings already come in three layers (D-SETTING-ORDER1=A): the profile in package.jet, a call in fn build such as b.optimize(.Full), then the flag. jet test instead refuses --optimize when the profile sets optimize:, with E2104 (TestProfile.jet:96-100). Most jet test flags have no setting at all: --serial, --shuffle, --coverage, --capture, --fresh, --seed, --iterations and the browser flags, among others (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CLICommands.jet:901-953). Scripts that need per-run choices call the separate Tools/testkit program. They are release-compiler.mjs (--shard, --results), goldens-census.mjs (--list, --tier, --shard, --results), compiler-registries.mjs (--opt-in, --results), and suite.sh A/B runs (--jet for another compiler). SHAPE UNDER A 1. One rule. Every jet test flag has a profile field and a t call with the same name, dashes becoming underscores. --shuffle=7 is shuffle: 7 in a profile and t.shuffle(7) in fn test. A bare flag such as --serial is serial: true and t.serial(). 2. One order. The profile applies first, then fn test, then the flag, exactly as build settings do. jet test runs fn test once to collect its settings and suites before any test runs, as jet build runs fn build. The E2104 refusal for --optimize becomes an override. 3. Four new choices, each in all three places. shard runs the I-th of N slices, the same tests for the same slice and tree. list prints the selected test names after filter and shard, runs nothing and exits 0. results writes every selected test's verdict as JSON, with the same writer and row format as JET_CI_EVIDENCE_DIR. compiler builds and runs the tests with another jet, while slicing, baseline and verdicts stay with the running jet, so an A/B run differs only in the compiler. 4. optimize takes a list of levels, so a census needs no --tier word. none is jet run, basic is jet build, and full is the release build. 5. Settings that are not choices. --profile selects a profile, so its setting is the existing defaults: { test: ... }. --help, --show-default and --browser-scaffold are actions, not run choices, so they have no setting. HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY 1. Many new names. Every name is a flag that exists today. One registry row per flag produces the flag, the profile field and the t call, so the three can never drift apart. jet help test shows all three spellings on each line. 2. A setting that should be one-off, such as -u or list, written into a profile by mistake. Such a profile says so in its name, and jet test prints the settings it used and where each came from. 3. Shards overwriting the baseline. A sharded run compares with the baseline but never writes it. -u with shard stays refused with E2104. 4. Two verdict formats. results and JET_CI_EVIDENCE_DIR share one writer and one row format. No loss remains. EDGE CASES - list with -u is refused with E2104, since listing runs nothing to record. - shard 0/8, 9/8 or a malformed value is refused with E2104, naming the valid range. - results to an unwritable path fails before any test runs. - Parallel shards share no scratch files; each run gets its own temporary directory. - A settings call after t.run() is refused with E2104, since the run has already started. AFTER A LANDS The four scripts switch to jet test /Compiler --profile

with these flags, and the Tools/testkit command is deleted. Its engine stays as the library jet test calls. WHY NOT B OR C B keeps the test-kit command as a second front door with its own words, so every new choice lands twice. C adds the flags but no settings, which breaks your rule, so a fixed choice can only be typed again on every command.

decisions.title: The log level follows the setting order, plus `JET_LOG` for operators
decisions.situation: A Jet program sets its log level only by calling a function in its own code. The level is one value for the whole process. An operator cannot raise it for one run without editing the program. One noisy module cannot be quieted alone. Level names also have aliases, so `warning` and `warn` mean the same. Build options already follow one order. The package sets a default, code overrides it, and the flag wins. The vote decides where log levels are set, how they are spelled, and in what order.
decisions.gist: Should the log level follow the setting order, with an environment variable for operators?
decisions.lesson: Yes: package, then code, then `JET_LOG`, then `--log`; each level can be set per module.
decisions.story: A shop is slow in production. The operator restarts it with `JET_LOG=warn,shop.db=debug` and sees only database debug lines, with no rebuild.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Who wins        Per module   Like
A setting order flag > env      yes          Spring Boot, .NET
B code wins     code > env      yes          Rust env_logger
C code only     code            yes          Go slog, Python
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- `log` becomes a row of the D-SETTING-ORDER1=A option table: package.jet `log:`, `--log` on `jet run`/`jet dev`, the code method. `debug` in text is `.Debug` in code.
- `JET_LOG` read from the captured environment (D-EFF-ENV-SNAPSHOT1=A); a built binary reads it, and its own argv stays the program's.
- Records carry the declared module path of the calling function, passed by the compiler (emit, Log.jet:38-62, has none today). Files with no module declaration share the package root.

- No pin for `log`. A bad filter fails at startup naming the pair (today ignored, Log.jet:138-143). Credential-tagged values stay blocked at every level (D-TAINT2=A).
- Migration: `set_level`, `log.log`, `enabled` and `setup` take the typed level; `canon_level` aliases (:256-265) and `log.warning()` (:49) are removed.

EVIDENCE (r14 jet, probe r11)
- Logging needs `--allow=Log` (E1803). `set_level("warning")` and `setup("level=err")` work; `JET_LOG=debug` is ignored; `--log` is E2102.

IDS
Under A amends D-SETTING-ORDER1=A for the log row: a process-environment source between code and flag, and no pin. D-CONF-MERGE1=A's environment layer is package `environments:` (PackageParse.jet:206), not a process variable. `log:` is a table field, not a `settings:` entry (D-CONF-KEY1=A). Hosts #6056 (L-18).

options.detail: `log` is one row of the setting table. `JET_LOG` sits between code and the flag, and cannot be pinned. Gains: Operators change logging without a rebuild. One noisy module can be set alone. Same order and spelling as every setting. Losses: `JET_LOG` is an environment source no other setting has.
options.technical: The setting table generates `log:` in package.jet, `--log` and the code method. Order: stock info < package.jet < code < `JET_LOG` < `--log`. Filter text is a default, then `module=level` pairs; the longest module path wins. The compiler passes each record's module. decisions.title: Which glyph stands for the value a pipe step receives: <>, $ or {}?
decisions.situation: You called the named steps terrible and asked for a glyph such as dollar, braces or angle brackets, leaning to angle brackets because they echo the fence. This revision drops the named steps, so every option is the same pipe with a different glyph for the value from the line above. The recommendation is the empty angle pair, which means nothing in Jet today, while the dollar sign already marks facts and environment reads, and empty braces already build an empty value. Each claim about today's compiler was checked with a probe, and each option shows one complete program with its output.
decisions.gist: Should a pipe step write the value it receives as <>, as $, or as {}?
decisions.lesson: A dot chain such as text.trim().len() reads in the order it runs. Many steps are not methods, such as Int.parse, so those flows nest inside out or need a name per line. A pipe passes each value down to the next line. This vote picks the glyph that stands for that value inside a step.
decisions.story: Ana reads a port: bytes become text, text becomes a number, and each step can fail. Today she invents a name for every step or nests the calls. With a pipe she writes one step per line, and one glyph marks where the value goes.
decisions.inWild:
Hack: $x |> foo($$) writes the piped value as $$ in every step.
JavaScript (Stage 2 proposal): every step writes the piped value as %.
R 4.2: x |> f(data = _) marks the piped value with _, in a named argument only.
Elixir and Gleam: x |> f(1) passes x as the first argument, with no glyph.
SQL and Pascal: a <> b means not equal. Elixir joins strings with <>, and Haskell combines values with it.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION

You called the named steps terrible and asked for a glyph such as $, {} or <>, leaning to <> because it echoes the fence, as in <: 1, 2 :>. The named steps are gone. Each option below is the same pipe, with one glyph standing for the value from the line above. A recommends <>.

WHAT A MEANS

A step is |> expression, and <> inside it is the value made by the line above. The step's result goes down to the next line. The whole pipe is one ordinary expression, so it can be returned, bound or passed.

raw |> String.from_bytes(<>) ?? return fallback means the same as text :: String.from_bytes(raw) ?? return fallback. Each step lowers to a hidden :: binding before type checking. The compiled code equals the named form at every optimisation level, so a pipe costs nothing while running.

THE RULES

- Every step uses <> at least once. A step without it is an error, with a fix that uses <> or removes the step.

- <> may appear more than once in a step. The value is computed once and read each time, as a named line is.

- <> outside a pipe step is an error that says <> is the value from the line above in a pipe.

- <> means the value of the nearest enclosing step. A lambda inside a step may capture it, as it captures any local (scaled in the program).

- A pipe inside a lambda or inside parentheses has its own steps, and there <> means its own value (total and badge in the program). Its first line may still read the outer <>.

- A step runs to the next |>. So ?? return fallback returns fallback and leaves the function, as return does in an arm or a loop body (probe q04).

- break and continue in a step act on the enclosing loop, as in an arm.

- A step that only calls a method, |> <>.trim(), is joined onto the line above as .trim() by the formatter, because a dot chain already reads in order.

WHY <> COLLIDES WITH NOTHING

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/pipe2, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- Comparisons: a <> b is E0003, "Expected a value, found >" (g01). show(<>) is E0003 too (g02). x < y && y > z and the tight a<c && c>a print true (g03, g06).

- Fence: <: 1, 2 :> and <:3:> print beside Box<Box<Int>>, and 1 <=> 2 works (g06). Fence tokens start <: and end :>, so neither can form <>.

- Generics: fn one<>() is already "A generic parameter list cannot be empty" (g05b), and id<>(1) is E0003 (g05). Box<>{value: 1} is accepted today with a broken type, Box<><Int> (g04). A makes it the same empty-list error, with a fix that removes <>.

- Shifts: 1 << 2, 8 >> 1 and 1 <= 2 print 4, 4 and true (g12). <> becomes one longest-match token, as the fence tokens are.

- Tight runs: <> touching another < or > is an error with a fix that adds a space. So <>>2 can never quietly mean <> > 2 when >> was meant. jet fmt always spaces these operators.

- Strings: "a<>b" prints a<>b (g11). Inside a string <> stays text; inside an interpolation hole, as in "{<>.len()}", it is code.

- Census on dev 63b075b2af: 0 uses of <> in 18,184 .jet files, outside strings and comments.

WHY NOT B, $

A bare $ is free today: print($) is E0003 (g07). But $ already marks three other things. Facts and template splices use it today, as T.$layout, $package.name and {$count}, until the cutover to # under D-META-HASH1=A (#4276 c22) lands.

Config files keep $HOME for environment reads under D-ONCE-DOLLAR1=B, and that stays after the cutover (g08 shows the teaching error outside config). In a config file, $ and $HOME would then mean the piped value and the environment, one letter apart. Waiting for the cutover cannot remove that.

WHY NOT C, {}

{} already has a meaning. With struct Opts { size: Int{4} }, size({}) builds an empty Opts and prints 4 today (g09b). Under C the same text inside a step would mean the piped value, so moving a line into a pipe changes what it does. In a string, {} is already an error that says to write {{}} (g10).

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner can ignore pipes and keep naming each line, as today. When they meet a pipe they learn one sentence: <> is the value from the line above. An expert writes long flows one step per line, gives each step its own fallback, nests pipes in lambdas, and sets a breakpoint per step. Hover shows the type of <> on each line.

THE ONE COST LEFT

Readers from SQL or Pascal know <> as not equal. Elixir joins strings with it, and Haskell combines values with it. That outside meaning cannot be removed, because it lives in other languages. Under D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A no error names another language: a <> b outside a pipe gets the generic error, which lists the legal operators there, including !=. Inside Jet, <> has exactly one meaning.

An error names the step and the type of <>:

```text
Error [jet.TypeMismatch]: This needs String, but `<>` is [U8]
  --> app.jet:3:23
  3 |         |> Int.parse(<>.trim()) ?? return fallback
    |                      ^^ `<>` here is the [U8] made by line 2
 Fix: add a step such as `|> String.from_bytes(<>) ?? return fallback`
```

DROPPED

Named steps, such as |> b -> String.from_bytes(b), are dropped as you asked. A hidden first argument, as in Elixir, and function-only steps, as in F#, stay dropped. The first fits about a third of real chains. The second cannot give a step its own ?? return (research probe p15).

TODAY AND THE CENSUS

t02_today_full runs the same program in today's spelling and prints the six lines shown in each option. |> itself is still free (q02, E0003). The census on dev 0d1ea12f79 finds 516 nested, 824 mixed and 1,850 named runs. About 950 sites read better as a pipe, and 910 named runs end a step in a ?? fallback.

The programs use D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C lambdas, such as fn(v) { v * 2 }, which are not built yet (probe q03). Today's v -> v * 2 form is in t02. Pipes ship after that cutover.

RATIFIED DECISIONS IT TOUCHES

Every option amends D-SHAPE-PIPE1=C (2026-07-14), which says Jet has no general flow operator; its warning against tap, error, async and mutation variants stays. D-UFCS1=B keeps one call spelling, since the value goes exactly where <> is written. A adds <> beside D-FENCE2=A's longest-match fence tokens.

B would give $ a fourth meaning beside D-COMPILER-NS1=A, D-NAME-SPLICE1=B and D-ONCE-DOLLAR1=B. C would overload the typed anonymous value. Docs/proposals/2026-11-04-pipes.md needs updating from named stages to the <> step.

decisions.title: One-liners: one `jet -e` flag, with input read through plain Core names and the result printed
decisions.situation: A one-liner is a tiny program typed straight into the shell. It often reshapes lines of text. Perl, Ruby and awk own this job, using letter flags such as `-n` and `-a`. Those letters are hard to guess and hard to find, and Jet already has many flags. Jet cannot run code typed on the command line today. A user must create a file, wrap it in `fn run`, and write the loop. The vote decides how one-liners read their input and show their result: through flags, or through plain names in the code.
decisions.gist: Should one-liners use letter flags, or one `-e` flag with plain names for reading input?
decisions.lesson: One `-e` flag. The code reads input through plain names such as `input`, `words()` and `input.csv(T)`, which also work in scripts. The code's final value is printed, one item per line.
decisions.story: Bo pipes a log into `jet -e 'input.map((l) -> l.words()[1])'` and gets each second word, one per line. Later he finds `input.csv(Sale)` in `jet help input`, next to everything else that reads input.
decisions.inWild:
Option             Second word of each line                      Like
A -e + input       jet -e 'input.map((l) -> l.words()[1])'       Ruby ARGF, node -p
B letter flags     jet -a -e 'print(words[1])'                   Perl, Ruby
C implicit it      jet -e 'lines { print(it.words()[1]) }'       Kotlin
For scale: perl -lane 'print $F[1]' and awk '{ print $2 }'.
decisions.detail:
OWNER QUESTION (q0fpghts)
The earlier draft explained only three of its eleven flags, and nobody could guess that `-n` means "loop over lines". This redesign has no letter flags. Everything a one-liner needs is a plain Core name in the code. The names are listed together under `jet help input`, so nothing is scattered through `jet help`.

WHAT WE BUILD
- CLI: `jet -e CODE [FILES]` and `jet run -` (program from stdin). The code is the body of `fn run`, checked like a file, as a REPL adapter builds one (D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1=C). Front.jet:999 (jet_cli_run_entry) parses -e; today the code text is taken as a file name (Front.jet:674, E2105).

- Result printing: if the code ends in a value, `-e` prints it, as `node -p` does. A list or line stream prints one item per line; a unit result prints nothing. So no loop or `print` is needed for the common reshape.
- Core `input`: the lines of the files named after the code, or of stdin when none are named, like Ruby's ARGF and Python's fileinput. It is a lazy stream, so `input.map(f)` prints as lines arrive.

- `input.csv(T)` and `input.json(T)` decode each record into `T`, so `r.nmae` is a compile error before any input is read. `input.edit(f)` rewrites each named file in place and asks once for permission to write.
- `text.words()` (existing) splits on spaces; `text.split(sep)` takes a separator.

- `jet help input` lists every input name with one example each. `jet help run` points to it.
- The generated source is an overlay entry (Request.jet:1299-1367). Compiled one-liners are cached by content hash (ScriptCache.jet).

WHY A HAS NO REAL LOSS
- The old loss was length against Perl. Printing the final value removes the loop and the `print`, so a reshape is one method call on `input`.
- The characters left are names that say what they do, which philosophy rule 2 ranks above keystrokes. The shell completes them.

EVIDENCE
- Probes (commit 8fbf094): `jet -n -e 'print(f[1])'` gives E2101; `jet run -e 'print(1)'` gives E2105.
- A new one-line file compiles in 102 to 152 ms; warm runs take 18 to 24 ms (scripting/work/p/cold). Perl starts in 1.7 ms, Ruby in 41.0 ms.

IDS
Hosts card #6067. The `-e` body is a `fn run` body, like a REPL cell under D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1=C. Named files are read under D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 (a typed path grants reading it).

options.name: One `-e` flag; input through plain names
options.detail: `-e` runs code and prints its final value, one item per line. `input` is the lines of the named files or stdin. `words()`, `input.csv(T)` and `input.edit(f)` cover splitting, records and editing in place. Gains: nothing to memorize, since the code says what it does; the same names work in scripts; a reshape is one method call. Losses: none.
options.technical:
`-e CODE` is the body of `fn run`, checked like a file, and `jet run -` reads the program from stdin. If the body ends in a value, it is printed; a list or stream prints one item per line. `input` is a lazy stream of the lines of the files named after the code, or of stdin. `text.words()` splits on spaces and `split(sep)` on anything else.

`input.csv(T)` and `input.json(T)` decode each record into `T`, so a wrong field fails before any input is read. `input.edit(f)` replaces each line of each named file with `f(line)`, after asking once to write. These are ordinary Core names, so a one-liner pasted into a script works unchanged. `jet help input` lists them together.
options.code:
$ printf 'a b\nc d\n' | jet -e 'input.map((l) -> l.words()[1])'
b
d
$ jet -e 'input.csv(Sale).sum((s) -> s.amount)' sales.csv
1240.50

options.name: Perl's letter flags
options.detail: `-n` loops over lines as `line`, `-a` splits into `words`, and `--csv T` gives a typed `row`. Eleven flags in all. Gains: as short as Perl. Losses: letters nobody can guess; eleven flags spread through `jet help`; code that only works under the right flags.
options.technical: `-n` wraps the body in a loop over input lines, named `line`. `-a` implies `-n` and splits into `words`. `-F SEP` sets the separator, `-p` prints `line` after the body, and `--begin` and `--end` run code around the loop. `-i` edits files in place. `--csv T` and `--json T` decode each record into `row: T`.
options.code:
$ printf 'a b\nc d\n' | jet -a -e 'print(words[1])'
b
d

options.name: A block with an implicit `it`
options.detail: `-e` plus a Core `lines { }` block where `it` is the current line. Gains: short, with one idea to learn. Losses: `it` would be a new implicit name in the whole language.
options.technical: A Core function `lines(body)` runs the block once per line with an implicit `it`. Jet has no implicit parameter today, so this adds one everywhere.
options.code:
$ printf 'a b\nc d\n' | jet -e 'lines { print(it.words()[1]) }'
b

comparisons.note: `-p` evaluates the code and prints its result. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#-p---print-script
comparisons.code:
# Node: print the value of the code

comparisons.note: `-c` runs code; fileinput reads named files or stdin. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/fileinput.html
comparisons.code:
# Python: plain names, written out
python3 -c 'import fileinput
for l in fileinput.input(): print(l.split()[1])'

comparisons.note: `-n`, `-a`, `-F`, `-p`, `-i` and `-l` change what the code means. Source: https://perldoc.perl.org/perlrun
comparisons.code:
# Perl: second word, then a column sum
perl -lane 'print $F[1]'
perl -F, -lane '$s += $F[2]; END { print $s }'

# awk: fields are $1, $2, ...
awk '{ print $2 }'
awk -F, '{ s += $3 } END { print s }'

# nushell: built-in commands in a pipe
open --raw log.txt | lines
  | split column ' ' | get column2

decisions.title: Read-only fields: a public computed field over a priv stored field, with writes refused
decisions.situation: A file lock exposes the path it names, and the library documentation intends callers only to read it. The checker currently accepts a write to that Core field, but running the program fails in the compiler backend before the lock is taken. Ordinary user structs do allow public-field writes. Jet also has computed fields that can read private storage without exposing a writable field. Their literal-write error exists, but assignment checking is incomplete. We recommend finishing that existing rule and using a private stored path behind a public computed path, rather than adding a setter qualifier.
decisions.gist: How should a field be readable everywhere but writable only inside its own module, such as a lock's path?
decisions.lesson: Field visibility and write access are different. A public field can be edited only through a mutable owner or write view; priv also restricts which module may access it. A public computed getter can expose a value without exposing storage to write.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module is a file or a name: module { … } block; its code owns the types it declares. priv before a field hides it outside that module. A computed field, name: Type -> formula, is read like a field but holds no value of its own; its formula reads other fields.

Forging means building or changing a value so it claims something untrue. A lock whose path was rewritten forges a claim about which file is locked.
decisions.story: Sam's backup helper tries to overwrite a lock's path. He wants a normal compiler error explaining that the field is read-only, not a backend failure, while print(lock.path) keeps working.
decisions.inWild: Kotlin separates getter and setter visibility: a public var can have private set (https://kotlinlang.org/docs/properties.html). This preserves stored-field organization. Jet's working private-field/reader-method probe r4 offers a different organization without a new setter qualifier.
decisions.detail:
Exercised admitted jet: r1 gives E0605; r2 gives E0414. r3 prints /tmp/app.lock then /etc/passwd for a user struct. r4 and r5 print /tmp/app.lock through a method and computed getter. r8 prints true then /tmp/next.lock after an internal backing-field edit. r9 gives E0339 for the computed literal field and E0605 for explicitly setting private storage.

r6, r7 and r10 pass jet check but jet run reports an internal backend failure for their field writes. r7 is a real FileLock and was run from BallotReview/field-run, not the repository. Therefore the draft must not say a Core lock currently takes effect and then successfully changes its reported path. This is a checker/backend gap, not proven runtime mutation.

E0339's declaration covers computed fields in literals or direct assignments. Constructors.jet:628 checks the literal case. Finish assignment-place checking under every ballot option, independently of the handle API choice (I2/I3 and #6468 c3). A computed field is not writable even inside its defining module; that module changes the separate stored field.

A uses private storage plus a public computed projection. Reject direct and compound assignment, destructive take and write loans into computed properties before lowering, including nested/indexed projections. Plain reads follow existing ownership, copy and view rules; do not promise zero String copies without IR evidence. Keep constructors private where hidden handles enforce provider ownership.

Current Core paths are stored fields on TempDir, TempFile, FileLock, FileReader, FileWriter, Directory and MappedFile. Cutover must cover their constructors, host projections and in-repo readers, not just source declarations. The corpus currently reports E0302, E0205 and E0605: its write owners are immutable. To require E0339 unchanged, check computed-target validity before ordinary mutability; also add mutable-owner tests so E0205 cannot hide the actual gap.

B narrows setter permission on a stored field. That is distinct from computing a value with no stored place, so its benefit is one declaration, ordinary internal writes and unchanged storage metadata. Its cost is another permission qualifier and enforcement across every write/loan path; it is not automatically forbidden by I8. D is an ordinary private field plus reader and remains a working alternative. C retains public mutable path but must still fix computed-field checking, document the changed promise and remove only the explicitly voted forge-by-write expectations.

#6468 c1 is this choice; c2 applies the chosen API to named handles and corresponding tests; c3's sema refusal is unconditional. The corpus is an acceptance target, not an observed pass under unimplemented A. Beginner reads stay .path under A/B/C; D changes them to .path(). Experts retain explicit provider methods and normal ownership checks. No new accessor evaluator or special Core-only protection is authorized.

options.name: A computed field over a priv field
options.detail: No new syntax: a public computed getter reads private storage. No code assigns the getter itself, even inside its module; provider code edits the backing field.
options.technical: Finish E0339 computed-place validation independently of this vote. Migrate all named handle storage, constructors and host projections. Test direct/compound/nested writes, write loans and destructive takes from storage. Consuming an ordinary materialized getter result remains legal. Add mutable-owner cases and define diagnostic priority for the existing immutable-owner corpus.

options.name: A priv(set) qualifier
options.detail: priv(set) path: String reads anywhere and writes only in the type's module, like Swift's private(set).
options.technical: The grammar accepts set as a second priv qualifier on fields only. Reads follow the type's visibility. Writes and literal entries outside the type's module are E0605 with a write message. The syntax registry gains a set qualifier row.

options.name: Keep path writable; drop the write rows
options.detail: path remains publicly writable through a mutable owner. The docs change, and only the specifically voted write expectations leave the corpus. Existing computed-property bugs still must be fixed.
options.technical: Retain public stored paths and implement valid Core-handle lowering without changing checks or allowing forging of the private handle. Fix computed-field assignment checking under #6468 c3 regardless. This option relaxes a path-reporting API promise; it does not authorize descriptor forgery.

options.name: A priv field and a path() method
options.detail: The field is hidden, and a method returns a copy, as in Rust's tempfile crate.

decisions.title: A task group can ask for a larger stack; programs otherwise get the system's stack size
decisions.situation:
Today every task in every Jet program gets a stack of at least 192 MiB, a size chosen for the compiler's own deep recursion. The main thread gets the normal system size, so the same deep call works in a task and stops on the main thread.

The plan is to give programs the normal size everywhere, while the compiler keeps its large stacks. The open question is how the compiler asks for them: a task-group argument, a process-wide call, a package setting, a private back door, or no change.

Whatever is chosen must not leak into programs the compiler starts, and must not need a privilege other packages lack. We recommend A: a task group can ask for a bigger stack, and one deep function uses the depth mark Jet already ratified.
decisions.gist: How should the compiler get its large worker stacks once ordinary programs stop getting 192 MiB for every task?
decisions.lesson: A stack is the memory a thread uses for calls in progress. Today every task gets a very large one because the compiler needs it. This vote decides how the compiler keeps its large stacks while ordinary programs get the normal size.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A stack is the memory that holds calls in progress; deep recursion needs a big one. The soft stack limit is the size the operating system offers, usually 8 MiB.

A worker is a thread that runs tasks, and a fiber is a task with its own small stack on a worker. A task group is the task.group block that owns the tasks started in it.
decisions.story: Mia's program recurses deeply in a task. Today it works, because every task gets 192 MiB, but the same call on the main thread stops. Under A both stop at the same depth. The stop names the fix: mark the function with the depth it needs, and it works in both places on every build level.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust: the thread that needs a big stack asks for it.
std::thread::Builder::new().stack_size(192 << 20).spawn(compile)?;
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How the compiler gets the stack size its recursive passes need, once ordinary programs get a stack chosen for programs. The runtime's default and the docs follow from the choice.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0. Thread.jet's thread_stack_bytes gives each worker and fiber the larger of the soft stack limit and 192 MiB. It is capped at 8 GiB and at a hundredth of a finite address-space limit. The main thread keeps the soft limit, 16 MiB on the probe machine.

Probe t01 recurses 3,000,000 calls deep on the main thread, and jet run stops it with Stop [E3012]: Stack overflow in depth. Probe t02 makes the same call in a task and prints task 3000000, because the task got 192 MiB. On the seed compiler jet run also ran t01 to the end; t6c now runs the program's main thread with every stack default (Host.jet:3383).

Probe t03 writes task.group deep(stack: …) and gets E0003, task-group parameter stack is not supported. Probe t04 calls core.sys.__thread_stack_floor from user code and gets E0067. Probe t06 writes #MaxDepth(3000001) and gets E0927: the ratified depth mark is not built yet.

The rule under A, for one deep function. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A and D-STACKBOUND1=A already ratified #MaxDepth(n): every build level reserves room for n waiting calls when the entry or task starts. That is the fix A's stop suggests when the overflow repeats one function, as in Mia's program. It gives the same depth on every tier.

The rule under A, for other deep code. task.group gains a stack argument next to limit. Every task started in that group runs on a stack of at least that many bytes. A group opened inside one of those tasks uses the same size, unless it names its own. The bytes give a depth that depends on the machine, as D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A allows for unmarked code.

Without a mark or a stack argument, a task gets the soft stack limit, at least 8 MiB, the same room the main thread gets. That meets the card's goal, and the runtime docs state both numbers.

Nothing outside the group changes. The process's stack limit is never written, so no child process inherits anything: not jet dev's program, not a jet test binary, not a core.process spawn. Other groups in the same program keep the default.

The compiler. Host.jet already compiles inside task.group compile_stack. Its deep code is many functions calling each other, so one mark cannot size it. Under A that line asks for 192 MiB, and the compiler's internal groups inherit it. D-COMPILE-STACK1=A already says jet::compile runs on a worker with an explicit stack size; A gives that size a public spelling.

A needs no double-underscore exception, no C import and no package field. Any package can do what the compiler does, which is the rule card c0w1wcfc asks for.

Limits and refusals, following D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A. A literal size the target can never supply is a build error. A request that the address-space limit cannot cover is cut to a hundredth of it, as today, and the stop report names the request and the cut.

A target whose tasks share one fixed stack, such as web, refuses a stack argument at build time, naming the target. The argument reserves address space without touching memory, as today's 192 MiB does, so resident memory does not grow until the stack is used.

What building A takes. The parser and checker accept stack beside limit. The runtime keeps one fiber pool per stack size instead of one size per process. Alloc.jet's arena bands read each thread's real stack size instead of assuming 192 MiB. E3012's fix text names #MaxDepth or the group's stack argument.

Beginner path. Nothing to write. Tasks and the main thread get the same room, so a recursion that works on one works on the other. If one function needs more, the stop writes the #MaxDepth line for it. Expert path. Ask a group for more with stack:, and see the computed worst case with jet inspect memory under D-STACKBOUND1=A.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A program that relied on 192 MiB in its tasks now stops with E3012. The stop names the fix: #MaxDepth on the function that repeats, or the stack argument on the group. Until #MaxDepth is built, it names only the stack argument, so the default should change after #MaxDepth lands.

The census on dev counts task.group headers outside comments: 195 in 146 files, 24 of them with an argument list such as limit:. Only the compiler's compile_stack group is known to need more than the default. The suite's compiler_stack cases and every example's golden output prove the rest under an 8 MiB limit before the default changes.

What remains. Two fiber pools in one process, one per size, keep some idle stacks of each size. That is address space, not resident memory; the cost is bounded by the pool's existing cap.

Other options. B adds a public core.sys call that raises the floor for every worker in the process. C adds a package.jet field fixed at build time. D lets Compiler packages call Core's double-underscore functions. E keeps 192 MiB for every program and retires c6. F makes the compiler's passes iterative so nothing needs more (#5910).

Their best cases. B is one call and is already drafted. C needs no code in Host.jet. D is the smallest change. E costs nothing and keeps every deep task working. F is the cleanest end state, with no stack request at all.

Their costs. B and C act on the whole process, not on the code that needs it. D gives one set of packages a privilege, against D-SHAPE-DUNDER2=A and D-CORE-HELPERS1=A. E keeps the compiler's size in every program. F has no date; until then it is E.

options.name: A stack size on the task group
options.detail: task.group name(stack: bytes) gives that group's tasks, and groups opened inside them, a stack of at least that size. One deep function uses the ratified #MaxDepth mark instead. Every other task gets the system's stack size, at least 8 MiB. The compiler asks for 192 MiB on its compile group.
options.technical: Parser and checker accept stack beside limit; a literal the target cannot supply is a build error. The runtime keeps a fiber pool per stack size; Thread.jet's default becomes the soft RLIMIT_STACK, minimum 8 MiB. No rlimit write, so children inherit nothing. E3012 suggests #MaxDepth(n) for one repeating function, else stack:. Gives D-COMPILE-STACK1=A's explicit worker stack a public form.

options.name: A public process-wide floor
options.detail: core.sys gains set_thread_stack_floor(bytes), which raises every worker's stack in this process. The compiler calls it once at start.
options.technical: Core/Sys/Sys.jet beside set_stack_limit. The runtime floor is already on dev as jet_rt_thread_stack_floor_set, with a core.sys.__thread_stack_floor row (Thread.jet:456-468); B gives it a public name. Needs the Env effect; children inherit nothing.

options.name: A package.jet field
options.detail: package.jet gains thread_stack:, fixed at build time. The program's entry sets the floor before run starts.
options.technical: A BuildOptions row carried as an IRChecks word; the entry calls the floor as it configures the allocator. Compiler package files set 192 MiB.

options.name: Compiler packages may call Core internals
options.detail: The lexer and checker let Compiler packages call Core's double-underscore functions. The compiler calls the floor directly; user code still gets E0067.
options.technical: Payload.jet's identifier_respelling and Sema/Calls/Core.jet:1451 gain a Compiler-package exception. Amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2=A and D-CORE-HELPERS1=A, and works against card c0w1wcfc's c36.

options.name: Keep 192 MiB for every program
options.detail: Keep today's runtime. The docs state the 192 MiB floor as the program default, and c6 is retired as not a defect.
options.technical: No code change. Thread.jet:442-451 stays. The c6 wording changes.

options.name: The compiler stops needing deep stacks
options.detail: The compiler's recursive passes become bounded or iterative, so it runs on the default stack. Until then, today's 192 MiB stays.
options.technical: Tracked under #5910. Proof: tests/cases/compiler_stack passes under prlimit --stack=8388608. No public surface.

comparisons.note: thread::Builder::stack_size sets one thread's stack; other threads keep the default.
A Thread constructor takes a stack size for that thread only.
Goroutine stacks grow on demand; debug.SetMaxStack sets one process-wide cap.

recommendation.why: A asks for room only where code needs it. One deep function uses the depth mark Jet already ratified, and other deep code asks its task group, in a form any package can use. Programs get the system's stack, children inherit nothing, and no privilege is added.
gains: Programs get the normal stack size, as c6 asks.
The compiler uses the same public form as any package.
No child process inherits a changed limit.
A deep function marked with #MaxDepth gets the same depth on every tier.

losses.loss: Tasks that relied on 192 MiB now stop with E3012.
losses.mitigation: The stop names #MaxDepth or the group's stack argument; goldens under 8 MiB prove the change first.

losses.loss: #MaxDepth is ratified but not built (probe t06, E0927), so the best fix is missing today.
losses.mitigation: The default changes after #MaxDepth lands; until then E3012 names the stack argument.

losses.loss: One fiber pool per requested stack size.
losses.mitigation: Idle stacks are reserved address space, not resident memory, under the pool's existing cap.

whyNot.reason: B raises every worker in the process, not just the code that needs it.
C fixes a process-wide size in the package file, far from the code.
D gives Compiler packages a privilege the ratified naming rules forbid.
E keeps the compiler's stack size in every program.
F has no date, and until then it is E.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small new argument on task.group, in return for program-sized stacks and no privileged route.

decisions.title: `priv` works on any declaration, not only modules and fields
decisions.situation: Everything in Jet is public by default. Only a private module or a private struct field hides anything. To hide one helper from other packages, an author wraps it in a private module. Then every call needs the module prefix. A promise to add package privacy through the manifest has no form yet. The documented path from internal to public still names a public marker that was removed. The vote decides how one item is hidden, and what package privacy looks like.
decisions.gist: Should `priv` work on any declaration, so one helper can be hidden without a wrapper module?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `priv` on any declaration hides it outside its module; at top level, outside the package.
decisions.story: Mei writes `priv fn pad` in her library. Her own code calls `pad` freely. Other packages get an error naming the `priv` line.
decisions.inWild:
Option            Hide one helper            Like
A priv anywhere   priv fn pad                Kotlin, Swift, Rust
B modules only    wrap in priv module        no peer
C export list     exports: [banner]          Haskell, OCaml .mli
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Remove E0413 for declarations. `priv` = enclosing module and children; top level = package-only. `priv(package)` on nested declarations; at top level refused with a fix to write `priv`. E0417 on fields stays.
- E0605 names the hidden item and its `priv` line. A `priv` type in a public signature is refused; `pub use` of a `priv` item is refused.
- Loose files: a loose file is its own module, so `priv` hides from path importers; after `jet init` (D-LOOSE-GROW1) it widens to package-only, and `jet init --check` lists those items.

- Lifecycle (D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A, stale since `pub` was removed): `priv` item, public item, `#Deprecated(since:, use:, removed_in:)`, removed. `_name` keeps only its unused and discovery meanings.
- Tools/agent/vis-cutover.mjs:262-281 stops deleting `priv` before non-module declarations.

EVIDENCE (r14 jet)
- Probes q03 and r17: `priv fn` gives E0413 "priv marks only modules and fields"; `priv module helpers` with `helpers.pad` checks clean.
- Audit p07: `_name` has no access meaning; `lib._helper()` is reachable from another package.

IDS
Under A reverses two S18 statements (owner directive 2026-10-07, card #4723): no visibility marker on declarations, and package privacy via the manifest. Under B S18 loses its manifest sentence; under C S18 stands. Hosts #6050 (L-12).

options.name: `priv` on any declaration
options.detail: The module rule for `priv` applies to one item too. At top level, `priv` means package-only. This reverses two lines of the everything-public ruling. Gains: Hiding one helper is one word. One word works on items, modules and fields. Calls keep their plain names. Losses: Any declaration may now carry `priv`, one more word to read.
options.technical: `priv` on any declaration means usable only in the enclosing module and its children. The package top level is its root module, so a top-level `priv` item is package-only. `priv(package)` works on nested items. A `priv` type in a public signature is refused, naming both lines. `jet doc` lists only public items. `jet explain NAME` prints the visibility and the line that set it.

options.name: Modules and fields only
options.detail: Keep today's rule. A `priv(package) module` is the package level, and the manifest promise is dropped. Gains: No change to the ruling beyond one sentence. Losses: One hidden helper needs a wrapper and prefixed calls.
options.technical: E0413 keeps its fix that moves the item into a `priv` module. The sentence promising manifest privacy is deleted.

options.name: The manifest lists exports
options.detail: package.jet gains `exports:`, a list of the names other packages may use. Gains: The public surface is one list in one file. Losses: Visibility lives far from the code it hides. A second mechanism beside `priv` modules and fields.
options.technical: With no `exports:` everything is public. Importers reaching an unlisted name get E0605 naming the manifest line.

comparisons.note: Public by default; private and internal on any declaration. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/visibility-modifiers.html
Access levels go on any declaration. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/accesscontrol/
Private by default; pub and pub(crate) widen one item. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/visibility-and-privacy.html
A module header lists its exports. Source: https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch5.html

# Haskell: Textkit.hs
module Textkit (banner) where
pad s = "  " ++ s

recommendation.why: `priv` already means "this module and its children" on modules. Letting it sit on one item is the same rule, one step smaller.
gains: One word for every level of hiding.
No wrapper modules or prefixed calls.
Fills the package level the manifest promise left empty.

losses.loss: Any declaration may now carry `priv`, one more word to read.
losses.mitigation: Public stays the default, so most code never writes it.

whyNot.reason: Hiding one helper still costs a wrapper and a prefix on every call.
It adds a second mechanism, far from the code it hides.

recommendation.tradeoff: One optional word on declarations, for hiding any helper without a wrapper.

decisions.title: Public routes for a custom HTTP method: mux.custom(token, path, handler) and #Server.Custom(token, path)
decisions.situation:
HTTP lets a server accept methods beyond the nine standard ones, such as PURGE for caches or PROPFIND for WebDAV. Jet's server already reads such a request and answers 405 with an Allow list. But public code cannot register a route for one.

Each standard method has its own call, like mux.get, plus a struct marker like #Server.Get. The one call that takes a method value is mux.__route, and the compiler refuses that name in user code. So card #6206 cannot meet its rule that a custom-method route checks and serves.

We recommend A: mux.custom("PURGE", path, handler) and #Server.Custom("PURGE", path), named for the Custom case of the Method enum. The compiler checks the token while building.
decisions.gist: Should a custom HTTP method get its own route call, mux.custom(token, path, handler), named for the Method enum's Custom case?
decisions.lesson: A web server answers requests by method, such as GET or POST. HTTP also allows other methods, such as PURGE. Jet's server can already receive them, but your code has no public way to route one. This vote picks how you write that route.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A method is the verb at the start of an HTTP request, such as GET. A custom method is any other valid token, such as PURGE; HTTP calls it an extension method. A mux is Jet's route table; a router is the same table with fully checked contracts. A marker such as #Server.Get tags a struct method as a route. A token is the HTTP word grammar: letters, digits and a few symbols, with no spaces.
decisions.story: Sam runs a cache in front of an API. The CDN sends PURGE /cache/:key to drop one entry. Under A, Sam writes mux.custom("PURGE", "/cache/:key", purge) next to mux.get. A typo with a space fails the build, and the route shows in the Allow header and the OpenAPI document.
decisions.detail:
This vote chooses extension-method registration on muxes, routers and mounted structs. All options are proposals, not implemented APIs.

Reran r01-r07 on a0.0.43. PURGE reaches a 405 with Allow. The attempted public registration forms are refused. CONNECT documentation and Method.custom exit 101. A module-constant router path is refused.

A adds custom(token, path, handler) and #Server.Custom(token, path) over one route table. Preserve the exact case-sensitive RFC 9110 token in dispatch, duplicate keys, Allow, operation IDs and OpenAPI. Refuse only exact standard tokens such as GET, already registered by mux.get. Lowercase get is a distinct method, not a typo to rewrite.

Check literal and constant tokens while building, and dynamic mux tokens at registration before changing the table. Routers and markers need static tokens. Invalid tokens need registered Jet diagnostics and snapshots. OpenAPI 3.2 additionalOperations describes extension methods and CONNECT. Downstream 3.1-only tools may not support it.

B replaces per-verb calls with one route(Method, path, handler) and #Server.Route marker. Migrate all callers and remove per-verb registration. Its typed standard cases are a genuine strength. Fix Method.custom regardless of the vote; its defect is not a design objection.

C replaces per-verb registration with one method-and-path pattern grammar. D dispatches inside a catch-all. D needs explicit method metadata for accurate Allow and OpenAPI, recreating registration.

decisions.title: Every effect is allowed by default; written code denies, and a run warns when its effects change
decisions.gist: What may a Jet program do when nobody has written any authority?
decisions.lesson: Every effect is allowed unless code denies it. Jet knows a program's effects before it starts, so a run lists them up front, and lists them again whenever they change. A written authority row is a ceiling and silences the notice for what it lists.
decisions.story: Ana writes a script that reads a file and calls an API. She runs it and sees one line naming what it does, then it runs. Next week a dependency update adds process launching, and the next run names the new effect. Her team adds an authority row to the package, and anything outside that row fails at check time.
decisions.inWild: Deno denies by default and prompts at first access, so most users pass -A. Node allows everything unless started with --permission. Python, Go and Rust have no authority model at all.
decisions.detail:
Option A is the owner's proposal with four refinements. First, the notice repeats when the effect set changes. Second, a written authority row is a ceiling and silences the notice for what it lists. Third, jetpack reports a dependency whose effects widen, and --locked refuses it. Fourth, code run straight from a URL or the registry asks before its first run.

Option B is the proposal as first stated: a notice on the first run only.

Option C keeps today's model, where undecided effects prompt in a terminal and stop without one.

options.name: Allow by default, warn on change, ceilings
options.detail: Every effect is allowed unless denied. The run lists effects before the program starts and again when they change. Authority rows are ceilings, jetpack reports dependency widening, and remote code asks first.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
note: tool.jet reads files and connects to the network (-A hides this)

options.name: Allow by default, warn on first run
options.detail: Every effect is allowed unless denied, and the first run lists the effects once.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
note: first run: tool.jet reads files and connects to the network

options.name: Keep the prompt
options.detail: Undecided effects prompt in a terminal and stop without one.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
tool.jet reads files and connects to the network. Run it? [Y/n/always]

recommendation.why: No friction for beginners, and nothing changes silently: a new effect, from your code or a dependency, is always named.
recommendation.tradeoff: A run is never blocked by default; protection comes from written ceilings and the change notice.

whyNot.reason: A dependency update that adds an effect would never be noticed after the first run.
Prompts train people to answer yes, and stop every run without a terminal.

losses.loss: Unreviewed local code runs with the user's full authority.
losses.mitigation: The notice names every effect before the program starts, and ceilings stop what a team denies.

decisions.title: Run code straight from a URL or the registry, asking before its first run
decisions.situation: D-AUTH-DEFAULT1 refinement (4) says code run straight from a URL or the registry asks before its first run (card #6614 c8). Q25a=B asked for a ballot on the command itself. Today `jet run` takes local paths only, and `jet X` resolves a command, a job, a retired spelling, a path, then `jet-X` on PATH (D-JET-VERBS1). Jet already fetches remote code in one place: a script's inline `pkg#1.4` dependency. It is resolved through the signed registry index, verified, stored in the Hangar by content hash and pinned in `<script>.jet.lock` (D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1). This ballot picks the command that runs remote code, what it fetches and pins, and how the first-run question behaves with and without a terminal.
decisions.gist: How do you run a Jet program that lives at a URL or in the registry?
decisions.lesson: `jet run` also takes an https URL or a registry package. Jet fetches it, checks it, pins its exact bytes, and asks once before the first run, naming what the program can do. Later runs of the same bytes are silent. Changed bytes or new effects ask again.
decisions.explainer:
The question happens after Jet fetches and checks the code and before its first instruction. Jet knows every effect a program can reach before it starts, so the question names them all at once.

Pinning is by content. A registry package is pinned by its signed index entry and artifact hash. A URL is pinned by the hash of the bytes fetched the first time. Nothing is fetched again silently: `--update` re-resolves, and `--locked` refuses any change.

Fetching never runs code. Nothing is written to the current folder. The fetched code lives in the Hangar store, and a small per-user record under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/remote` keeps the pin and the effects the user said yes to.
decisions.story: Sam sees a log-cleaning tool in a blog post. He types `jet run https://example.org/tool.jet`. Jet shows where it came from, its hash and that it reads files and connects to the network, then asks. He says yes and it runs. Next week the author changes the file, and Jet asks again before running the new bytes. In CI, the same command stops and names the `-A` flag to use.
decisions.inWild: npx asks "Need to install the following packages. Ok to proceed?" in a terminal and fails in CI without --yes. Deno runs a URL directly and pins hashes with a lockfile, then prompts per permission while the program runs. Go runs `go run pkg@version` against a checksum database with no question.
decisions.detail:
Option A adds a remote target to `jet run`: an `https://` URL, `name#1.4.2`, `name#1.4` or a bare `name` that is not a local path. A local path always wins. Plain `http://` is refused. In a terminal Jet asks `Run it? [y/N]`, and only `y` runs. Without a terminal it stops before running and its Fix names `jet run -A <target>`.

Under A, `-A` skips the question, `--allow=R` skips it when R covers the effects, and `--deny=R` still wins. `--sha256=<hex>` pins a URL's first fetch, and `--locked` refuses any re-resolution.

Option B adds a separate verb, `jet x <target>`, with the same fetch, pin and question.

Option C has no remote run form. `jet fetch <target>` stores the code and prints a local path, and the first `jet run` of that path asks.

decisions.title: The command that lists the effect caps in force at a site, nearest first
decisions.situation: The effect-rung and type-rung rulings promise `jet explain effects` (every cap in force, nearest first) and `jet explain effects --caps` (each module cap with its file and line), card #6551. They do not fix the site it explains or its JSON shape, and today the command is E2104 (not built). The ratified CLI has `jet explain marker <file>:<line>` for one site and `jet explain log [<file|dir>]` for a listing with file and line. `jet explain <ref> --json` uses the `jet.report/v1` envelope. `jet inspect rights [TARGET]` lists every callable's declared and inferred rows against the application authority. The owner answered Q27 with option A on 2026-11-08; this ballot records that form with its alternatives and costs.
decisions.gist: How do you ask Jet which effect limits apply to a line of code?
decisions.lesson: `jet explain effects` prints every limit in force at a site, nearest first: the `#FX` block, the function row, the module cap, the package row and the run. Each line names the file and line that wrote it, and the last line names the effects the site reaches.
decisions.explainer:
A site is `<file>:<line>`, the innermost scope at that line. A bare `<file>` is that file's module, plus its `run` if it has one. No site means the entry `jet run` would pick, with the same selection rules and the same errors when it is ambiguous.

The output has one line per rung, nearest first. The rungs are `block` (an `#FX` region), `function` (the `-[…]>` row or `-[!E]>` denials) and `module` (`#FX` on the module). Then come `package` (the `authority` row or `deny`) and `run` (everything allowed unless denied; `--deny` wins). A rung that writes nothing prints `(none written)`, so the ladder is always the same shape. The last line names the effects the site reaches, each with the first call that reaches it, which is the same chain E0749 prints.

`--caps` lists every module cap in the project, or under a given file or directory, as `file:line  #FX(…)  module`, sorted by path then line. `--json` uses the `jet.report/v1` envelope. The command shares one walker with `jet inspect rights`; it is the explain view of the same facts.
decisions.story: Ana's `jet check` stops with E0749 in `push`. She runs `jet explain effects Source/sync.jet:14`. Jet lists the block cap, the function row, the module cap and the package deny, each with its file and line. It shows that the line reaches `Net.HTTP.Get` through `http.get`. She sees the module cap is the one that leaves it out and widens it.
decisions.inWild: Rust's `cargo tree -e features` prints which features are on and why, but only for features. Deno's `deno info` lists a module's permissions requests only at run time. AWS IAM's policy simulator shows, for one action, every policy that allows or denies it, nearest first, with the deciding statement.
decisions.detail:
Option A is `jet explain effects [<file>[:<line>]] [--caps] [--json]`, the form ruled in Q27. A line outside any function starts at the module rung. A line inside a lambda gets its own `function` rung, then the enclosing function. A line inside `comptime` adds a `comptime` rung for the `#Impure` gate. A file with no `package.jet` shows `package (none written)`.

A line past the end of the file, or `:0`, gets the existing `jet explain marker` refusal and its code. Generated code maps to the user site that produced it, as diagnostics do. A line holding more than one function explains the first one that starts on it; no column form is proposed. `--caps` with `:line` is a usage error.

Option B folds the ladder into `jet inspect rights [TARGET]`, with `file:line` targets and a `--caps` filter.

Option C names a function instead of a line: `jet explain effects <module>.<function>`.

options.name: `jet explain effects [<file>[:<line>]]`
options.detail: A site is a line, a file or the entry `jet run` would pick. One line per rung, nearest first, then what the site reaches. `--caps` lists every module cap; `--json` uses `jet.report/v1`.

$ jet explain effects Source/sync.jet:14
effects at Source/sync.jet:14, in `push`, nearest first
  block     #FX(Net.HTTP)            Source/sync.jet:12
  function  -[Net, Log]>             Source/sync.jet:9
  module    #FX(Net, Log, FS.Read)   Source/sync.jet:1
  package   deny: [Exec]             package.jet:4
  run       everything else allowed; --deny wins
reaches: Net.HTTP.Get via http.get (Source/sync.jet:14)

recommendation.why: It keeps the spelling both rulings already name and reuses the ratified `file:line` grammar of `jet explain marker` and the `jet.report/v1` envelope. decisions.title: `#FX` above a type bounds everything done in that type's name
decisions.situation: A library author often wants to promise that a whole type is safe, for example that a parser never touches the network or the disk. Today the promise must be written on every method's row. The vote decides whether `#FX` above a type makes that promise once. It would cover the type's methods, its trait impls in any package, and the closures they create. We recommend it.
decisions.gist: Should `#FX` above a type bound everything its methods, trait impls and closures may do?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A function promises what it does with its row, like `-[!Net]>`. `#FX` above a block is a ceiling for the code inside it. This vote asks whether a type takes the same ceiling for all code that acts in its name.
decisions.story: Mia publishes `mia_parse`. Her users want to know the parser never reaches the network or the disk before they run it on untrusted notes. She writes `#FX(!Net, !FS)` once, above `Parser`. Months later a contributor adds a `Stylesheet` impl that fetches CSS. The build fails at that line, naming Mia's cap.
decisions.inWild:
