decisions.title: Keep #Persist values when jet dev restarts the program
decisions.situation: `#Persist` marks a module value, such as a game score, that should survive your edits while `jet dev` runs. It was made for live code swap, which is retired, so `jet dev` now restarts the program on every save and the marked value starts over each time. This vote decides whether Jet saves marked values when it stops the program and restores them at the next start, or leaves the mark idle until a code swap engine returns. We recommend saving and restoring, with `jet dev --fresh` or `d.fresh(true)` to start over.
decisions.gist: Should `jet dev` keep values marked `#Persist` when it restarts your program after a save?
decisions.lesson: `#Persist` marks a module value, such as a score, that should survive your edits while `jet dev` runs. It was made for live code swap, which is retired. Now `jet dev` restarts the program on every save, and the marked value starts over. Today a marked value must start as a simple value such as a number. `jet run` always starts fresh, and release builds ignore the mark.
decisions.story: Ken is building a small game. A bug shows up three minutes into a boss fight. He marks the level number, the score and the boss's health with `#Persist`, so he can tune the enemy logic without replaying. Since live swap was retired, every save restarts the game and the fight is gone. He needs each restart to bring those values back.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides what happens to `#Persist` values when `jet dev` restarts the program. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides entry shape, the reload boundary and the one process model. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides setting rows and removes `--swap`, `--restart` and the package `dev: { swap }` field; option A adds one `fresh` row to its table. D-TARGET-ONE1, D-ENTRY-NAMES1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decide outputs, names and local services.

Why the owner must decide. D-EXEC2=A retired hot swap: `jet dev` rebuilds and restarts on every save. D-PERSIST1, D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1, D-LIVE-PERSIST1 and D-HOTSTATE1 all describe values that survive a live swap. No ratified text says what the mark does under restarts. The adversarial review of the slate proposal flagged this gap and named the two options here.

Today in code. The default `jet dev` engine is run_dev_restart at Source/CmdDevTools.rs:912-970. Each save kills the child with `running.kill()` at line 957 and starts a fresh `jet run`. A `#Persist` binding lowers to the Prelude `JetPersistCell` (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:11-50), which starts from the literal. Nothing restores it, so the mark has no effect in default `jet dev`.

Today in code, continued. The value store is jet_foundation::Persist (crates/jet-foundation/src/Persist.rs). It is a process-wide static (line 19) with typed outcomes Kept, Migrated, Reset and Rejected (lines 112-120) and a preflight `plan_migrate` (line 256). Only the Canvas in-process loop still uses it (Source/CmdDevTools.rs:1696, 1759-1767 and 1952-1966). The dev session records those outcomes as live-value facts (crates/jet-devserver/src/Session.rs:2319).

Today in code, more. E0622 (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:1587-1603) limits a `#Persist` starting value to a scalar literal, such as an integer, float or bool. So D-PERSIST1's own `World.load(...)` example does not compile today, and the story uses only simple values. The test persist_example_survives_hot_reload (tests/dev_parts/routine.rs:835-892) runs `jet dev --swap` and waits for `count=2`. By reading the code, dev_restart_argv drops `--swap` (Source/CmdDevTools.rs:887-889), so the restart engine prints `count=1` there.

Process model, from D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 option A technical. `fn dev` and the program compile into one O0 binary. The `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. It runs the compiled `fn dev` session, which runs the program as its child. Editing program code restarts only the child. Editing `fn dev` or the env definition ends the session and starts it again; the `jet` process stays, so kept values and running services survive. Ctrl-C ends everything.

Option A, mechanism. The `jet` process gives each program child a private pipe, passed down through the session and named in an environment variable that only `jet dev` sets. A runtime thread in the child waits on it. On a stop request, or when `fn run` returns, the thread copies each `#Persist` cell and sends it to the `jet` process. Then the program ends as it does today. The next child reads the values before `fn run` starts.

Option A, why the copy is safe. Each cell is guarded by a lock, and E0222 and E0223 forbid partial moves and mutable borrows of persistent state. So every write replaces the whole value, and the thread copies each value whole without pausing the program. Two bindings may be copied at slightly different moments. Values that must agree belong in one binding.

Option A, one store. The wire format is the existing PersistEntry: module path, binding name, shape fingerprint and payload. Restore runs `plan_migrate` and reports the same outcomes the dev session already records. The store moves from a process-wide static into the `jet` process's session state; only the transport is new. One store exists per program the session runs, keyed by output name (D-TARGET-ONE1).

Option A, type changes. A value of the same shape is kept. Otherwise the ratified live-value rules apply at restore: D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A migration blocks, as widened by D-HOTSTATE1=A, where added fields take their defaults and removed fields are dropped. When no rule applies, the value starts over from its starting value. The line names the change and the migration block to write, as D-PERSIST1 and D-LIVE-PERSIST1 require.

Option A, edges. A renamed or removed binding starts over, and the line says so (D-LIVE-PERSIST1). An edited starting value does not replace a kept value; the line says so and names `--fresh`. After a crash, or if the program does not answer in two seconds, nothing is saved and the next start is fresh. A crash may come from the state itself, so Jet never replays it. A program paused in a debugger is killed after two seconds and starts fresh.

Option A, the fresh row. `fresh` is one row of the D-SETTING-ORDER1 table: `--fresh` or `--fresh=off`, `dev: { fresh: true }`, and `d.fresh(true)`; stock off. When on, no kept value is restored at any start of the session, so every binding begins at its starting value. Writing `d.fresh(true)` in `fn dev` and saving restarts the session with fresh values while the `jet` process and its local services stay. Removing it turns keeping back on.

The fresh row, continued. It follows the one order: a flag beats entry code, which beats package.jet. `jet test --fresh` already bypasses the persisted test-result cache (Source/CmdCompile.rs:6836). Both rows mean start without saved results for their own command, so the word keeps one meaning.

Option A, lifetime. Values live in the memory of the `jet` process, never on disk. Ctrl-C ends them, and the next `jet dev` starts fresh. They survive a re-entered `fn dev` (D-ENTRY-SHAPE1), because the `jet` process stays. `jet run`, `jet build`, `jet test` and `jet run --watch` always start fresh, and release builds ignore the mark, as D-PERSIST1 says.

Option A, other hosts. A web build already sends a `persist_live_value` row for each binding to the dev server for display (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DomRuntime.js:332, crates/jet-devserver/src/BrowserWebAdapter.rs:381). Option A widens that row to the typed payload and restores it after the live reload. The Canvas loop keeps its in-memory store and reports the same outcomes, so every host follows one rule.

Option A, plain data. Values cross a process boundary, so only plain data can be kept. The store already rejects closures and native handles (crates/jet-foundation/src/Persist.rs:390-392). Today E0622 allows only scalar starting values, so every legal binding qualifies. If struct starting values arrive later, a marked type that holds a handle or closure becomes a registered compile error at the declaration (I7).

Option B, mechanism. The mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. Default `jet dev` restarts, so every start is fresh, and Jet prints one registered note at start when the program has marked values. The Canvas loop keeps them until the evaluator retires. The mark wakes when an engine that swaps code in memory returns. D-EXEC2=A plans native in-memory O0 to replace build-and-execute, but no ratified plan restores code swap.

Byte identity. D-DEVMODE1 requires dev output to be byte-identical to the release build. Under A, a restored value is a program input from the session. With no restored values, such as the first start or a `--fresh` session, dev output stays byte-identical. This ballot is where D-DEVMODE1 is amended; sibling ballots point here.

Amends D-PERSIST1=A: a marked value survives a `jet dev` restart, saved at stop and restored at start, instead of a hot reload. Opt-in, module-level only, identity by module path and binding name, and no release meaning all stay. Amends D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A: the purpose reads across a dev restart instead of a hot reload. The rule that a marked binding is writable stays.

Amends D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A: migration runs at restore instead of in place, and its announced-restart fallback becomes a start-over for that value, with the same line. Amends D-HOTSTATE1=A: its rules apply at restore to `#Persist` values only, because nothing else survives a restart. Its restart fallback also becomes a start-over.

Amends D-LIVE1=A and D-HOTSWAP1: the per-save line `saved game.jet  swapped chase  kept world` becomes `saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40`. A layout change starts that value over instead of restarting the program. Amends D-DEVMODE1: a restored value counts as a program input for the byte-identity rule. D-SETTING-ORDER1 removes the swap flags and field and gains the `fresh` row.

If B wins, it amends D-PERSIST1=A and D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A: the mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A and D-HOTSTATE1=A stay law but apply only in the Canvas loop. Unchanged under both: D-EXEC2=A, D-RUN-WATCH1=A, the D-VERDICT-1231-2 spelling, and E0145.

Research, right ways. Vite's `import.meta.hot.data` keeps one object per module across replacements, and `hot.dispose` fills it before the old module goes (https://vite.dev/guide/api-hmr). That is save at stop, restore at start. React Native Fast Refresh keeps state only when safe, resets it otherwise, and remounts after a runtime error (https://reactnative.dev/docs/fast-refresh). Option A follows both.

Research, wrong ways. With domain reload off, Unity keeps every static field between play sessions, and its manual says you must reset static state yourself (https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/domain-reloading.html). That is the keep-everything default D-PERSIST1 rejected. Flutter keeps globals on hot reload, and a changed initializer needs a hot restart (https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload). Option A keeps that rule, names the kept value, and adds `--fresh`.

Research limits. The sources are official documentation read on 2026-10-19. No adoption or friction data was found for any of these features. No repository census was run for this ballot.

Cutover for A. In run_dev_restart, replace the kill with a stop request, then a kill after two seconds. Add the pipe, the runtime copy thread and the restore before `fn run`. Move the store into the `jet` process's session state. Widen the web row. Add the `fresh` row. Register the kept, start-over, crash and starting-value lines under I7. Update persist.jet, its test without `--swap`, Docs/spec/spec.md:452-453 and the E0146 fix text that says hot-reload state.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: process model (the `jet` process holds the store; editing `fn dev` keeps values), story limited to simple values, `--fresh`/`d.fresh(true)` row, output wording, debugger timeout, situation and surface trim. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: canonical process model.

options.name: Save on stop, restore on start
options.detail:
When a save makes `jet dev` restart the program, Jet first asks the program to stop. The program sends each `#Persist` value to the `jet` process and ends. The new program takes back each value whose name and type still fit, and then `fn run` starts. One line per save names every kept value.

Values are saved when Jet stops the program and when `fn run` returns. After a crash, the next start is fresh, because the saved state may have caused the crash. A changed type uses the existing keep, migrate or start-over rules. A renamed value starts over. An edited starting value does not replace a kept value, and the line says so.

To start over, run `jet dev --fresh` for one session or write `d.fresh(true)` in `fn dev`. Values live only while `jet dev` runs, and Ctrl-C ends them. Gains: the mark keeps its promise with restarts. Loss: an edited starting value applies only when you start fresh.
options.technical: The `jet` process holds the store, as in the process model of D-ENTRY-SHAPE1. It gives each program child a private pipe through the session. A runtime thread in the child copies every `JetPersistCell` whole on a stop request or when `fn run` returns. E0222 and E0223 make each write a whole-value replacement, so no pause is needed. The payload is the existing PersistEntry, and restore runs `plan_migrate` with the existing outcome types. A program that does not answer in two seconds is killed and the next start is fresh.
options.code:
#Persist score := 0
$ jet dev game.jet       // play until score is 40, edit tick, save
saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40
saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40 (new start value 5 applies with --fresh)
saved game.jet  restarted  score is now Float: started over at 0.0
game.jet crashed  restarted fresh: values are not kept after a crash

options.name: Keep values only in memory
options.detail:
The mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. Default `jet dev` restarts the program, so every start is fresh. When a program has marked values, `jet dev` prints one note at start. The Canvas view, which runs the program inside Jet, keeps values until that engine retires. The mark wakes if an engine that swaps code in memory returns.

Gains: every start is clean, and nothing new is built now. Losses: the mark does nothing in default `jet dev`. No plan brings code swap back, and game developers replay to reach a bug after each save.
options.technical: No transport and no `fresh` row are added. The start note is registered under I7. The Canvas loop keeps the process-wide store and HotReplaceTxn, so D-LIVE-PERSIST1 and D-HOTSTATE1 apply only there. The test persist_example_survives_hot_reload moves to Canvas or expects `count=1`. The example persist.jet says the mark is idle in default `jet dev`.
options.code:
#Persist score := 0
$ jet dev game.jet
note: #Persist is idle while jet dev restarts; score starts at 0
— game.jet changed, re-running —      // score is 0 again
$ jet dev game.jet --canvas           // keeps score until that engine retires

comparisons.note: `import.meta.hot.data` is one object per module path that survives each replacement. `hot.dispose` fills it before the old module goes. This is save on stop, restore on start. Source: https://vite.dev/guide/api-hmr.
comparisons.code:
let score = import.meta.hot?.data.score ?? 0
import.meta.hot?.dispose((data) => { data.score = score })

comparisons.note: Fast Refresh keeps local state only when it is safe, resets it otherwise, and remounts after a runtime error. A file can force a fresh start every edit. Source: https://reactnative.dev/docs/fast-refresh.

With domain reload off, every static field keeps its value between play sessions. The manual says you must then reset static state yourself. Keeping everything by default is the trap an opt-in mark avoids. Source: https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/domain-reloading.html.
comparisons.code: static int counter = 0;   // keeps counting across play sessions

comparisons.note: Hot reload treats globals and static fields as state and does not run their initializers again. A changed initializer needs a hot restart. Option A keeps the same rule but names the kept value. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload.
comparisons.code: var score = 0;   // edit to 5: hot reload keeps the old value

recommendation.why: The mark exists so a developer keeps playing after an edit. Saving at stop and restoring at start keeps that promise with restarts, using the type checks Jet already has.
gains: Marked game and app state survives every save.
One store and one set of outcome lines serve every dev host.

losses.loss: An edited starting value applies only when you start fresh.
losses.mitigation: The restart line names each kept value. Run `jet dev --fresh` or write `d.fresh(true)` to start over.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the mark idle in `jet dev`, waiting for a code swap engine that no plan brings back.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rule about edited starting values buys state that survives every save.

decisions.title: One meaning for the word service
decisions.situation: Jet uses the word service for two things: a server program your project builds, and a helper such as a database that Jet starts and watches while you work. Both are even spelled with the same type name, so a newcomer who asks Jet to start their own server as a service gets an error. The vote decides whether the two become one idea, one is renamed, or both stay apart. We recommend one idea: a service is a long-running program Jet supervises, from a package or from your own code.
decisions.gist: Should "service" mean one thing, a long-running program Jet supervises, whether it comes from a package or your own code?
decisions.lesson: Jet uses "service" twice. A Service output is a server program your project builds; it takes no flags and runs until stopped. A dev-environment service is a helper, such as postgres, that Jet starts, checks for readiness, and restarts while you work. Both are long-running programs, and both appear in images. The vote decides whether they become one idea, or whether one is renamed or kept apart with an error.
decisions.story: Mia builds a game and a small API server in one project. She wants `jet dev game` to start postgres and her own API, wait until both are ready, and rebuild the API when she edits it. Today postgres can be a helper, but her API cannot, because "service" means something else for it. Her teammate Omar writes integration tests that need the same API running.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot answers the open card question q01laxht on card c07glrub: "service" means two things. It decides the word and whether your own Service output can run as a service. D-DEV-SERVICES1 (open) decides where services are written and how dev and test switch them. Its rules apply to output-backed services unchanged.

A holds against ratified law, part one. D-ECO-DECL1=A already writes a service as `Service{ run: packages.api }` and an image as `Image{ services: [services.web] }`. So the ecosystem ruling already treats a service as a supervised run of the project's own program. D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A says services run unattended, take no parameters, and live while their call lives. That is a supervised long-running program.

A holds against ratified law, part two. D-JPK-SERVICE1=A says `system.*` services are the same Service type with a different lifecycle owner. D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1=A gives one Service record from a bare `run` to full readiness. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A keeps its nine kinds under A, including Service. D-TARGET-ONE1=A keeps one output list and `b.add_service`.

A holds against code. Output.Service entries take no parameters: E1321 says "A Service or Check takes no parameters" (tests/ui/output_entry_contract.stderr). The `run` intent already accepts Executable or Service (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:1876-1881). The package parser's service field list already allows `from` and `run` (mod.rs:3655-3674). Readiness, restart and logs live in the supervisor (crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:4422-4585).

What A must add. The `run` field of a service record accepts an output reference, such as `outputs.api`, beside an argument list. The `outputs.` prefix follows the D-ECO-DECL1 section-qualified form. Today the env.jet reader rejects unknown fields with E1262 and does not know `from`. The package.jet parser accepts `from` without meaning, so A uses `run` and leaves `from` unused.

The implicit entry. Every Service output appears in the dev and test environments as a service of the same name, off until named. This gives the magic default: `jet dev game --service=api` works with no extra data. An explicit entry adds ports, readiness, `after` or `enable`, and is on unless it says `enable: false`. A clash between an output name and a package service name is a registered error naming both.

Roles. `jet dev api` makes `api` the program of the dev session, as D-TARGET-ONE1=A and D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A say. When the session's program is a Service output, its own service is not started, even if an entry, `d.service` or `--service` turns it on. The first line then says `api: running as the program`.

Roles, continued. `--service=api` keeps another output as the program and runs `api` beside it under the supervisor. The supervisor gates the program on readiness. The first `jet dev` line names each role, for example `services: postgres ready · api ready on :8080 · running game`.

Build and restart. An output-backed service is its own binary on the normal build path, with the dev command's settings, its own `options:`, and flags that reach selected outputs (D-SETTING-ORDER1=A). The dev session builds it with the program. Per the D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A process model, the `jet` process holds the supervisor, so the service survives a re-entry of `fn dev`.

Build and restart, continued. Saving its sources rebuilds and restarts it only, as D-EXEC2=A requires. An output-backed service keeps `#Persist` values across its restarts as the program does (D-DEV-STATE1=A). `jet services up api` builds it with the dev command's settings; outside a dev session nothing rebuilds it on save.

Trust. D-DEV-SERVICES1 keeps service commands as data so `jet env` lists them without running code. An output-backed service runs a program compiled from the project's own sources, which `jet dev` already runs as explicit intent (D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D). It adds no arbitrary command. Outputs written in package.jet are listed by `jet env`; outputs made by `fn build` are known after compiling, like the dev program itself.

Images and the trust fingerprint. Implicit entries do not join image projection or the trust fingerprint (Trust.rs:401-405). crates/jetpack/src/CLI/add_remove_push_image.rs:640-664 raises E1336 when an environment has services that an image does not select. That check counts written entries only, so an existing `from: env.dev` image keeps working when the project gains a Service output.

A third use, unchanged. D-SERVICE1=D's `core.service` tree organizes supervised workers inside one program. Under A it reads as the same idea at a smaller scale: workers inside one Service output. D-SERVICE1 says Jetpack owns supervised external development processes, which A keeps. JetOS system services stay the same record with JetOS as owner.

Why not B. It amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A (Service becomes Server), D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A and D-CONF-NAME1=A examples, D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A wording, D-ECO-DECL1=A examples, D-TARGET-ONE1=A (`b.add_server`) and E1321 text. A worker that consumes a queue serves no requests, so `Server` misnames it. Running a server beside your program would need A's `run: outputs.api` rule too, under a second word.

Why not C. C is today's D-DEV-SERVICES1 text. It keeps two types named `Service` and relies on a registered error to teach the split. Running your own server beside your program needs `run: ["jet", "run", "api"]`. That nested `jet` is not rebuilt or restarted by the dev session.

Today in code. Output.Service appears in 18 files under tests, Examples and the spec, by search for `Service\{ ?name:|\.Service\.?\{` on 2026-10-19. `jet services up api` with no environment entry fails with "no dev service named `api`" (crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:607-621). These counts measure repository sites, not users.

Name-clash migration. The name-clash error affects projects that already have an environment service and a Service output with the same name; none found beyond the Canvas `service` output. Search of 2026-10-19: every file with a Service output (tests, Examples, spec) was checked for a `services:` map. Only tests/canvas_scenarios.rs:1308-1313 has both, with output `service` and environment services `custom_server` and `canvas_service`, so no name clashes.

Research, right ways. Docker Compose runs published images and your own `build:` code in one `services:` list, with one health and start-order model (https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/). .NET Aspire models a packaged database and your own project as the same resource kind (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspire/). systemd's `.service` unit runs any long-running program under one supervisor. All three tie the word to supervision, not origin.

Research, wrong ways. devenv uses two words, `services` for packaged helpers and `processes` for your own programs (https://devenv.sh/processes/). Users must learn which list a program belongs in, and only processes can run their own code. That is the split of options B and C. No adoption or friction data was found that measures either model; the evidence is documentation and Jet's code.

Amends under A. D-JPK-SERVICE1=A: a service's `run` may name a Service output, and every Service output is a service of its own name, off until named. D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1=A: the record's `run` field takes an output reference beside an argument list.

Amends under A, continued. D-DEV-SERVICES1 (open): the output-name error is removed, `--service=api` runs the output as a service, and its "local service" wording becomes "service". D-TARGET-ONE1=A wording: a Service output is "a long-running program", not only "a server program", and it can run as a service beside the dev program.

Amends D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (if A wins): a local service's definition is written as data only, or implied by a Service output. In its "Words." paragraph, "a server program" becomes "a long-running program". Its service on/off row covers output-backed services with no new row.

Unchanged under A. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A, D-ECO-DECL1=A (A follows its example), D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A, D-SERVICE1=D, D-EXEC2=A, D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A and D-DEV-STATE1=A.

Cutover under A. Teach both environment readers that `run` may hold an output reference, and add the implicit entry for each Service output. Build output-backed services with the dev and test session, and restart them on source change. Register the wrong-kind and name-clash errors under I7, and print roles on the first `jet dev` line. Update D-DEV-SERVICES1 and the spec's Services sections.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent Round3Review, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: example `enable: false`, program's own service, image and trust scope, `jet services up`, build settings, B loss, late name check, `#Persist`, settings-order amendment, clash search.

options.name: One idea: a supervised long-running program
options.detail:
A service is a long-running program Jet supervises: it starts it, waits until it is ready, restarts it on failure, and keeps its logs. The program comes from a package, such as postgres, or from one of your own Service outputs. A Service output keeps its name because it is the shipped form of the same idea.

Every Service output is available as a service under its own name, off until named. `--service=api`, `d.service("api")` and `t.service("api")` run it beside the program you work on. A service entry such as `api: .{ run: outputs.api, ports: [8080], enable: false }` adds readiness, ports or order. Like any listed service, an entry without `enable: false` is on for every session.

`jet dev api` still makes `api` the program you work on, and then its own service is not started. `jet dev game --service=api` runs your game and your API together under one supervisor. Jet rebuilds and restarts the API when its code changes, as it does for the program. Gains: one word and one type, and a path for several of your programs at once. Loss: a name can play two roles, which Jet names on the first line.
options.technical:
One record type, the D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1 `Service` record. Its `run` field takes an argument list, as today, or an output reference such as `outputs.api`. This follows the ratified D-ECO-DECL1 form `Service{ run: packages.api }`. The reference must name an output of kind Service; another kind is a registered error naming the kind.

Each Service output adds an implicit service entry `{ run: outputs.<name>, enable: false }` to the dev and test environments. An explicit entry with the same name and that `run` replaces it and, like any listed service, is on unless it says `enable: false` (D-DEV-SERVICES1). An explicit entry with the same name and a different `run` is a registered error naming both. A name that matches only an output made by `fn build` is checked after `fn build` runs.

When the session's program is a Service output, its own service is not started, even if an entry, `d.service` or `--service` turns it on. The first line then says `api: running as the program`.

An output-backed service is built on the normal build path with the session. It is its own binary, with the dev command's settings, its own `options:`, and flags that reach selected outputs (D-SETTING-ORDER1). Per the D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 process model, the supervisor in the `jet` process runs it. Saving its sources rebuilds and restarts it (D-EXEC2=A). An output-backed service keeps `#Persist` values across its restarts as the program does (D-DEV-STATE1=A).

Readiness defaults to process start, as D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1 gives a bare `run`; listed `ports` add a port probe. Its entry takes no parameters (E1321), so the supervisor passes no flags. `jet services up api` builds `api` with the dev command's settings and starts it under the supervisor. Outside a dev session nothing rebuilds it on save.

Trust. An output-backed service runs your own compiled program, which `jet dev` already runs; it adds no arbitrary command. The `jet env` summary lists the Service outputs written in package.jet.

Images. Implicit entries count as listed for `--service` and `jet env`, but not for image projection or the trust fingerprint. An image selects one only by name, and E1336's 'declares services but the image does not select them' check counts written entries only. A selected output-backed service needs a verified package build; until then E1336 refuses it and names the fix.

options.name: Rename the output kind to Server
options.detail:
The output kind `Service` becomes `Server`: `.Server{ name, entry }` in package.jet and `b.add_server` in build code. "Service" means only a helper in the environment that Jet supervises.

Gain: each word has one meaning. Losses: it changes the ratified closed list of output kinds and every example that uses `Service`. A queue worker or a scheduler is not a server, but must be called one. Running your server beside your program needs A's `run: outputs.api` rule too, under a second word.
options.technical: Rename `PackageOutputKind::Service` and `Output.Service`, and the new `b.add_service` from D-TARGET-ONE1 becomes `b.add_server`. The D-ECO-DECL1 example `Service{ run: packages.api }` and image `services: [services.web]` lose their meaning as written and need restating. E1321 text changes from "A Service or Check" to "A Server or Check". The environment `Service` record is unchanged.

options.name: Keep both meanings, with a mix-up error
options.detail:
Both meanings stay, and both types keep the name `Service`. Naming an output where a helper is expected is a registered error that points to `jet dev api`. This is the current text of the local-services ballot.

Gain: no rename and no new rule. Losses: one word keeps two types, and newcomers learn the split from an error. Your own server cannot run beside your program, except through a command such as `run: ["jet", "run", "api"]`, which the dev session does not rebuild.
options.technical: No change to the output kinds or the environment record. The error "`--service=api`: `api` is an output your project builds; start it with `jet dev api`" is registered under I7 for `--service`, `d.service`, `t.service` and `jet services up`.

comparisons.note: One `services:` list. Each entry runs a published image or builds your own code with `build:`. Both get the same start order, health checks and logs. This is option A. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/.
The app host treats a packaged database and your own project as the same kind of resource, with references between them. This is option A. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspire/.

Two words: `services` for packaged helpers and `processes` for your own programs. Users learn both, and only processes run your code. This is the split of options B and C. Sources: https://devenv.sh/services/ and https://devenv.sh/processes/.
A `.service` unit runs any long-running program, packaged or your own, under one supervisor. The word means supervision, not origin. Source: man systemd.service.

recommendation.why: Both meanings already describe one thing: a long-running program Jet supervises. Making them one idea removes the mix-up, and lets the same supervisor run your own server beside your program.
gains: One word, one type, one supervisor for helpers and your own servers.
Several of your own programs run together in one `jet dev`.

losses.loss: `jet dev api` and `--service=api` both run `api`, in different roles.
losses.mitigation: `jet dev api` makes `api` the program you work on. `--service=api` runs it beside that program. The first-run line says which.

whyNot.reason: It renames a ratified kind and misnames workers; running a server beside your program would need A's rule under a second word.
It keeps two types under one name and only teaches the split through an error.

recommendation.tradeoff: One name now runs in two roles. Jet says which role it picked.

decisions.title: Build, Dev and Test are ordinary Core types
decisions.gist: Should the build, dev and test handles be ordinary Core types with labeled settings, instead of names only the compiler knows?
decisions.lesson: A build file starts with `fn build(b: Build)`. The value `b` is a handle: you call its methods to add programs, steps and settings. Today `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` live in private compiler tables, so nothing can show their methods and arguments work only by position. The names, the empty return and `b.default(app)` are already decided and do not change here.
decisions.story: Mara keeps a small game package. She wants a helper library that adds a shader step to any build, and she wants hover to tell her what `b.action` takes. Today neither works. Her library cannot name the `Build` type, and hover finds no declaration. When she writes `toolchain: native` to make a long call readable, the compiler rejects the label. With option A she reads the method in the editor, passes `b` to her helper, and labels each setting.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: the build handle is the ordinary standard-library type `std.Build`, and its methods take named option fields. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/

Bazel: rule code calls `ctx.actions.run(executable = ..., inputs = ..., outputs = ...)`, a documented API with named arguments. Source: https://bazel.build/rules/lib/builtins/actions#run
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and set the direction for this question to option A. The losing option keeps the compiler-private names and the string router.

Already settled, not re-decided here: D-ENTRY-CTX1=A names the handles `Build`, `Dev`, `Test`, `Run` and `Bench` and retires `BuildPlan`. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A settles `b.default(app)`, the empty return with `!BuildError`, sealing at return, and `d.run()` and `t.run()`. This ballot decides only where the handles are declared and how their methods take arguments.

Amends D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A in one point: it calls `Dev` and `Test` prelude-owned handles. Under A they are ordinary Core declarations, not compiler-owned names. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 also names `core.build.graph` as the reader of the sealed plan. A replaces it with `b.graph()`, so build code and tools read one value. Nothing else in that ruling changes.

Method-set question folded in: the proposal listed the exact methods and spellings as a possible fifth ballot. It is not a real choice with at most three options. Most rows are already law: D-TARGET-ONE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1, D-JAI-BUILDOPT1, D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1, D-BUILD-IO1, D-BUILD-INCLUDE1, D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 and D-ENTRY-NAMES1. The rest follows from Jet's ordinary call rule, positional values first and then labels. Option A's technical text lists the full set.

Corrections to the proposal, checked against the code on 2026-10-22: today's dev table holds `watch(String)`, `serve(port:)` and `reload(mode)`, not `reload(target:)`. Test has no method table, but test entries already use `run()`, `iteration` and `result`. The proposal's new test methods, such as a suite or golden helper, are out of scope here.

Code facts: the build call checker rejects any label with E0764 and reports argument counts with E0104. The reserved type list still holds `Build`, `Dev`, `BuildPlan` and the other build names. `FileReader` in Core is the host-backed type pattern A follows. The spec's programmable-builds section still shows a `BuildPlan` return and must be updated in the cutover.

Profile: short. This is one mechanism with two options. Removing `BuildPlan` from the Core surface registry is a removal D-ENTRY-CTX1 already ratified, not new grammar, and labels use the existing call grammar.

options.name: Ordinary Core types
options.detail:
Core declares `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` the way it declares `FileReader`: a type with documented methods whose work is done by the build host. Required values come first. Every optional setting has a default and is written with a label. Hover, completion, go to definition and generated docs read these declarations, so they work with no extra code.

A library may take `b: Build` as a parameter and add outputs or steps to it. `b.graph()` returns the checked build graph registered so far. Build errors are cases of one Core `BuildError` enum, so a caller can match them.
options.technical:
Method set (this folds in the separate method-set question). Build outputs, per the one-output ruling: `add_executable`, `add_library`, `add_test`, `add_asset_bundle`, `add_doc`, `add_package`, `add_service`, `add_install`, `add_publish`. Each takes `name` and `sources`, then labeled `actions:`, `deps:`, `probes:`, `toolchain:`, `signing:` and `options:`, and returns `Output`.

Build steps: `action(name, run:, inputs:, outputs:, allow:, toolchain:, probes:, signing:, kind:, pools:, env:, env_allowlist:, helpers:, labels:, cache:)` returns `BuildAction`. The labels are the fields of today's session action record; `allow:` holds the effect list now passed as strings. `legacy` takes the same labels plus `wrapper:`.

Tools: `toolchain(name, target_triple:, role:, host_triple:, sdk:, linker:, sysroot:)`, `probe(name, kind:, value:)` with `kind` one of program, pkg-config or header, and `signing(name, label:)`. Code and checks: `generate(name) { ... }`, `include`, `error(at:, what:, why:, fix:)`, `plugin` and `contribute`, each written with labels.

Whole build: `default(output)`, `output(name)`, `profile(name)`, `options()`, `pin(..., output:)`, `graph()`. Setting methods such as `optimize`, `default_profile` and `default_allow` are generated from the one option table, as the setting-order ruling requires. The generator writes them into the Core declaration, so they are documented like hand-written methods.

Dev: `run()`, `output()`, `pin(...)` and the generated setting rows `port`, `open`, `watch`, `service`, `before`, `record`, `fresh`, `share` and `args`. Test: `run()` returning the results, `pin(...)` and the generated rows `measure`, `filter`, `before` and `service`. Run and Bench, the other entry handles, follow the same rule, so there is one convention.

Removed: `find`, `embed` and `fetch` leave `Build`; they are ordinary functions under the build-input ruling. `plan()` is gone under the entry-shape ruling. Today's dev methods `watch(glob)`, `serve(port:)` and `reload(mode)` give way to the generated setting rows.

Cutover, in one change. Delete the sema method tables in the build and dev call checkers and the codegen route for build calls. Delete the string router in the build session host and the arity text. Remove `BuildPlan` from the reserved type list and the Core surface registry, which the entry-context ruling already retired. Migrate every in-repo caller to labels in the same change. Update the programmable-builds section of the spec, which still shows a `BuildPlan` return.

options.name: Keep the compiler tables
options.detail: The handles keep their already-decided names and shapes, but the compiler still defines them. Private tables list each method and how many arguments it takes. The build host picks the work by matching the method name as text. Arguments keep their positions, and labels stay an error. Libraries cannot name the handle types.
options.technical: Keeps the build and dev method tables in sema, the codegen route for build calls, the string router in the build session host and the arity text, all in step by hand. The ratified renames still apply. Editor features need separate hand-written entries for each method.

comparisons.note: The build function receives the ordinary standard-library type `std.Build`. Its methods take a struct of named fields. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
Rule code calls documented API methods with named arguments, so each input and output is labeled. Source: https://bazel.build/rules/lib/builtins/actions#run
comparisons.code:
ctx.actions.run(
    executable = ctx.executable._tool,
    inputs = [src],
    outputs = [out],
    arguments = [src.path, out.path],
)

comparisons.note: `Project` and task types are declared API classes, so the IDE completes and documents them. Source: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/kotlin_dsl.html

recommendation.why: Build handles then work like every other Core type. People and editors can read the methods, labels make long calls clear, and libraries can extend a build.
gains: One way to declare, check and document every Core API.
One edit adds a build method, not three.

losses.loss: Build methods become a public API that must stay stable.
losses.mitigation: Methods change only with a Core release, and an old call fails with a checked error naming the new label.

whyNot.reason: B keeps private tables that nobody can read, and every method change must edit three compiler places in step.

recommendation.tradeoff: Build, Dev and Test become versioned public API in exchange for being readable and checked like any other type.

decisions.title: Port the editor server now and keep the unbuilt dev server out of the package tests until `jet dev` is rebuilt
decisions.situation: Two tool packages in the compiler tree, the editor server JetLSP and the dev server JetDevserver, are Rust code rewritten line by line into Jet syntax. Neither has ever compiled. Together they are about 48,000 lines. No command runs them today: `jet self lsp` and `jet dev` both report that they are not built yet. The full test profile still runs every package, so both fail it. The clean-clone gate for the Rust removal goal cannot pass while they fail. This vote decides what to port now and what the full profile runs meanwhile.
decisions.gist: Should Jet port the editor server now and keep the unbuilt dev server out of the package tests until `jet dev` is rebuilt?
decisions.lesson: The full test profile compiles and tests every package in the tree, including tools no command uses yet. A package that cannot compile fails the whole profile. Jet already handles a frozen tree this way: the owner names it, the profile skips it as one visible row, and nothing deletes it.
decisions.story: Ana clones Jet on a machine with no Rust and runs the full test profile. Today it fails on four rows for two packages she never uses. With A, the editor server builds and passes, and the dev server shows as one skipped row naming its card.
decisions.inWild:
// Compiler/test.jet today: only JetOS is frozen
FROZEN_TREES: [String]{"Jetpack/JetOS"}
decisions.detail:
Today. Compiler/JetLSP is 18.7k lines in 113 files and reports 565 problems. About 480 of them come from its dependency on Compiler/JetDevserver. JetDevserver is 29.9k lines in 79 files and reports 480 problems. It uses Rust's standard library names (sync, net, io), unwrap and the old error-propagation operator. Four known-failing rows name card 6650. A fifth, the corpus check for retired failure spellings, names card 6582: its 278 lines are all in JetDevserver.

What A does. Port JetLSP against current Core and drop its JetDevserver dependency. It uses the editor host module (EditorHost.jet, 801 lines) and its five method-name constants, and those move into JetLSP. Add Compiler/JetDevserver to FROZEN_TREES in Compiler/test.jet. Teach package_dirs to skip frozen trees, and have the corpus spelling check skip them too. Remove the JetDevserver and #6582 known-failing rows at once, and the JetLSP rows when its port lands. Cost: about 12-20 agent-hours for JetLSP, plus about 1 for the freeze.

What B does. Port both packages. No suite change. Cost: about 45-60 agent-hours. JetDevserver also needs Core sockets and threads it may not have yet.

What C does. Freeze both trees as in A and port neither now. Cost: about 1 agent-hour.

What the gate then proves. With A, every package under Compiler/ and Jetpack/ builds and passes except JetDevserver, shown as one skipped row. With B, every package builds and passes. With C, the same as A minus JetLSP.

Edge cases. A frozen tree is never deleted and still counts in the coverage row as owner-frozen, so nobody mistakes it for passing.

decisions.title: Small Jai conveniences: flag sets, fall-through, member conversion and fixed enum values
decisions.situation: Jai has small conveniences Jet lacks: enums whose cases combine as bit flags, fall-through between switch cases, and structs that pass as one of their fields. It also has enums whose every value must be written. Other Jai conveniences, such as any-type arguments and stable arrays, already have Jet forms. The vote decides whether Jet adds the four missing ones; we recommend all four, each checked.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add Jai's flag enums, fall-through, member conversion and fixed enum values in checked forms?
decisions.lesson: Jai is a game language with many small shortcuts. A flag set stores several enum cases as bits in one number. Fall-through runs the next match arm's body too. Member conversion lets a struct pass where one of its fields' types is expected.
decisions.story: Joe ports a Jai tool of ten thousand lines. Most of it maps cleanly, but permission flags, fall-through switches, embedded structs and enums with fixed on-disk values each need a different workaround.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

THE ITEMS UNDER A. (1) Flag sets (Jai enum_flags): `Set<E>` over a fieldless enum of up to 64 cases is stored as a bit mask. Case i is bit i in declaration order. For C flags, a `#Specified` enum whose values are single bits maps each case to its own value. Any other value is a compile error. This changes Set's storage for small enums only. Its methods and printing are unchanged (amends D-COLLBREADTH1's storage note).

`.bits()` and fallible `Set<E>.from_bits(n)` cross C boundaries. No new enum kind is added. (2) `#Through` after a match arm (Jai #through) runs the next arm's body as well. That arm's bindings are not available, and the last arm cannot fall through. Or-patterns stay the tool for shared bodies. Fall-through is for 'do this, then also that'.

(3) `#As` on a struct field (Jai #as): the struct converts to that field's type where that type is expected. One #As per type, and the conversion is a view of the field, never a copy. (4) `#Specified enum` (Jai #specified): every case states its value, and changing one on a public type is flagged as a breaking change. ALREADY COVERED, NOT RE-PROPOSED. Jai ..Any maps to trait-bounded variadics `...Debug` (D-ANY-JAI1. No top type).

Jai xx maps to `U8.from_int(n)?` (D-SHAPE-CONVERT1). Bucket arrays map to `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>`, which give stable identities. Stable raw addresses stay behind `#Unsafe`, a deliberate difference from Jai. A custom entry symbol is the freestanding target profile's entry fact (D-TARGET-SURFACE1). C++ methods and non-POD returns are handled by the `cpp.*` binder (D-FFI-CPP1). Jai `#type,isa` maps to distinct types with an explicit conversion.

NOT PROPOSED. Identifier backslashes (public sources do not show their meaning) and textual #load (Jet modules use explicit names). Also #char (Jet has 'a'), #bytes (#FFI(asm) covers raw bytes), and #intrinsic and #runtime_support (compiler-internal in both languages).

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai Appendix C rows. Blow 8tMq3QZyz8s 00:02:52 (enum_flags), from the mining notes. C# [Flags], Rust enum-set crates and Odin `using` fields are the precedents.

options.name: All four, checked
options.detail: A Set of a small enum is stored as bits, with bits() and from_bits(). `#Through` ends an arm and runs the next arm's body. `#As` on one field lets the struct pass as that field. `#Specified` makes every enum case state its value.
options.technical: Set<E> over a fieldless enum of up to 64 cases uses a bit mask, with `.bits() -> U64` and fallible `Set<E>.from_bits(n)`. Markers `#Through` (match arm), `#As` (one field per type) and `#Specified` (enum), registered with decision IDs (I7).

options.name: All except member conversion
options.detail: Flag sets, `#Through` and `#Specified` from A. `#As` is left out.
options.technical: As A without `#As`.

options.name: Adopt none
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: [Flags] enums combine with | and print as names.
EnumSet-style crates store enum sets as bits, the model for Set<E>.
using on a struct field promotes its members, like Jai #as.

recommendation.why: These four forms remove the most common Jai porting rewrites, and each is checked by the compiler.
gains: The four remaining small Jai conveniences get a home.

losses.loss: Member conversion is an implicit conversion.
losses.mitigation: Only one `#As` field per type, written on the struct, so each conversion has one visible source.

whyNot.reason: B avoids implicit member conversion but drops Jai's main composition tool.
C adds nothing and leaves every small porting gap open.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three markers and a set storage rule, for one-to-one Jai porting.

decisions.title: Named results for task.all
decisions.gist: Whether task.all branches can be named, so results come back as named fields instead of positions.
decisions.lesson: task.all runs several branches at the same time and returns every result. Today the results are positional: the third result is whatever the third branch was. When several branches return the same type, a reordered branch list silently swaps results. Names remove that failure class. JavaScript is adding Promise.allKeyed for exactly this reason, and its users welcomed it.
decisions.story: Maya builds a status dashboard. She fetches the build state, the deploy state, and the alert state concurrently. All three are String. A teammate adds a fourth fetch and sorts the branches alphabetically. The build column now shows deploy text. No error fired anywhere.

options.name: Named branches, record result
options.detail: A branch may be written name: expression. When branches are named, task.all returns a value with those fields, and you read results.build. Positional branches keep working exactly as today. Reads like a record literal, so there is nothing new to learn.
options.technical: Grammar: task.all block accepts either all-positional or all-named branches (mixing is an error with a registered diagnostic). Named form types as an anonymous record whose fields are the branch names; failure semantics per branch are unchanged (D-CONC-FAIL1). Parity across parser, sema, TIR, AOT, JIT, interpreter, web (I9).

options.name: Keep positional, lean on destructuring
options.detail: No grammar change. The idiom is to destructure results into named bindings right at the call. Zero new surface, but when two branches share a type, a swapped branch still compiles and runs wrong — the names live one line away from the branches instead of on them.
options.technical: Documentation and example work only. The swap-bug class remains undiagnosable by sema because positions carry no intent.

options.name: Library join over a record of tasks
options.detail: No change inside task.all. You build an ordinary record whose fields are running tasks, then join the record to await all fields. Keeps the grammar frozen, but it creates a second way to await a group, and it makes raw Task values something beginners hold and pass around.
options.technical: Requires Task-typed record fields, a generic join over records (comptime field walk), and rules for a Task value that escapes its scope. Two join spellings then exist: task.all and join(record).

comparisons.note: Await Dictionary is Stage 3 precisely because positional Promise.all mis-wires results as call sites grow.
comparisons.code: const {build, deploy} = await Promise.allKeyed({build: fetchBuild(), deploy: fetchDeploy()});

comparisons.note: No named form. errgroup collects by closure side effects; result wiring is manual and positional.
comparisons.code: g.Go(func() error { build, err = fetchBuild(); return err })

comparisons.note: asyncio.gather is positional; the swap bug is a known review item in async code.

recommendation.why: Named branches put the intent on the branch itself, so a reordered list cannot swap results. The spelling copies the record literal the reader already knows, and positional stays valid for small cases. One mechanism gains one additive form.

whyNot.reason: Destructuring names the bindings, not the branches. Two same-typed branches can still swap silently; the compiler has no intent to check.
It creates a second way to await a group and makes raw Task values a beginner-visible concept, which the current surface deliberately avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: The parser and sema must handle a second branch form inside task.all, and mixing named with positional needs its own clear diagnostic. That is accepted because the swap-bug class disappears at the surface where it is caused.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared named branches, positional with destructuring, and a library join over a record of tasks. It recommended named branches because the spelling mirrors record literals and removes the positional swap-bug class.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also examined a string-keyed map form and a caller-supplied result struct type. Both were folded into the library option because they change how results are keyed, not who owns the join.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review checked combining named and positional forms. The recommendation already is that hybrid: positional branches remain valid, named is additive, and mixing inside one block is rejected with a diagnostic.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the positional option with destructuring placed directly at the call and a naming convention. It still cannot make the compiler see intent, so same-typed swaps stay silent.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the name: spelling for collisions with map literals and labeled arguments, and probed partial-failure semantics. Branch names mirror record fields, not map keys, and named branches add no new failure semantics, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One table for which IP addresses count as public
decisions.gist: Which IP addresses should Core count as public when a program checks a network destination?
decisions.lesson: Some addresses reach only a home network, a provider's internal services, or the machine itself. A program that fetches outside URLs must refuse those, or an attacker can reach internal services. Core's ip.is_global misses several such ranges, including carrier NAT and documentation ranges. Whichever option wins, one written table decides, and every Core check uses it.
decisions.story: Ana ports the Jetpack provider fetcher, which downloads packages from URLs that registries supply. A hostile registry could point a URL at 100.64.0.1 or at a cloud metadata address. The Rust fetcher refuses those with one table. Core's is_global accepts several of them, so the port would silently weaken the check.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html
ipaddress.ip_address("100.64.0.1").is_global  # False
# IANA registries: https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/ and
# https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/
# Rust jet_net (today): crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:681-713
jet_net::is_public_ip(ip)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 3, "public-IP classification must match jet_net::is_public_ip (including CGNAT and other special ranges)." The request side of item 3 is D-CORE-HTTPDEST1.

Rust call sites. jet_net::is_public_ip (lib.rs:681-713) is used by resolve_public_addresses (lib.rs:654-676) and directly by Provider/fetch.rs:550-555 for IP-literal hosts. resolve_public_addresses serves NixIndex.rs:494-496, Store/NixCache.rs:1758-1760, and Provider/fetch.rs:159. A mixed answer with any non-public address is refused (lib.rs:674-676).

Current Jet surface. Core/net/ip.jet:62-83 defines is_global as not private, loopback, link-local, multicast, reserved (only 0/8 and 240/8), or unspecified. It returns true for 100.64/10, 192.0.0/24, 192.0.2/24, 198.18/15, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, and 241-255.x.

ipv6_is_global (ip.jet:453-455) returns true for 2001:db8::/32, IPv4-mapped private addresses, NAT64, and most other prefixes outside 2000::/3. Examples/features/net/network_core_contract.jet:6 prints is_global(240.0.0.1).

Differences between the Rust table and IANA, for the owner: Rust marks 192.0.0.9 and 192.0.0.10 non-public (IANA: reachable). Rust marks 64:ff9b::/96 non-public (IANA: reachable). Rust marks 2002::/16, 2001::/32, and 3fff::/20 public. IANA marks 6to4 and Teredo "not applicable" and 3fff::/20 as documentation, not reachable.

Not balloted: Core has two IP value types, net.IPAddr from DNS and ip.IPv4/IPv6 structs. That is existing drift; the HTTP destination policy applies the table internally, so Jetpack needs no public IPAddr predicate.

options.name: The Rust check's table, made Core's one rule
options.detail:
ip.is_global and ip.ipv6_is_global take exactly the rule in jet_net::is_public_ip (crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:681-713).

IPv4 is public unless it falls in a listed range. The list is 0/8, 10/8, 100.64/10, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16/12, 192.0.0/24, and 192.0.2/24. It continues with 192.168/16, 198.18/15, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, and 224/3. IPv6 is public only inside 2000::/3, and never in 2001:db8::/32. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address uses the IPv4 rule.

The HTTP destination policy in D-CORE-HTTPDEST1 uses this same table. A DNS answer counts as public only when every address in it is public.
options.technical:
No new name. The existing pub fns keep their signatures: is_global(addr: IPv4) -> Bool and ipv6_is_global(addr: IPv6) -> Bool. Their bodies become the table above; the narrower helpers (is_private, is_reserved, is_carrier_grade_nat, and others) keep their meanings. The table lives once in Core/net/ip.jet. The Rust jet_net check is deleted when the port lands; until then a table test pins both to the same answers.

Documentation: core-library.md gains a core.net.ip section with the table. Examples/features/net/network_core_contract.jet keeps its output (240.0.0.1 stays non-public). Pure functions: no effects. Tiers: plain Jet source, identical on every path (I9).

print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("::ffff:10.0.0.1")?))   // false
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("64:ff9b::a00:1")?))    // false

options.detail: is_global and ipv6_is_global follow the "Globally Reachable" column of the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose address registries. jet_net::is_public_ip changes to the same table before the parity run.
options.technical: Registry snapshot pinned in Core/net/ip.jet with its retrieval date. IPv6 becomes allow-by-default outside listed ranges, so new special ranges are public until the table is updated.

options.name: IANA reachability plus a strict fetch check
options.detail: `is_global` follows a dated copy of the IANA special-purpose registries, so it answers "can this address be reached?". A separate `is_public_destination` answers "is it safe to fetch?". It starts from the Rust table and also refuses 6to4, Teredo, and NAT64 addresses that map to private IPv4. HTTP fetches, provider downloads, and redirects use only the strict check.
options.technical: New pub fns is_public_destination(IPv4) and ipv6_is_public_destination(IPv6) in Core/net/ip.jet. The IANA table carries its registry date; updating it is a normal Core change. Rust Jetpack gains the same strict check so the parity run compares identical answers.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net.ip as ip
a :: ip.parse_ipv6("2002:c0a8:0101::1")?          // 6to4
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(a))                        // IANA: reachable
print(ip.ipv6_is_public_destination(a))            // false: refused
n :: ip.parse_ipv6("64:ff9b::a00:1")?             // NAT64 to 10.0.0.1
print(ip.ipv6_is_public_destination(n))            // false
http.get("http://[2002:c0a8:0101::1]/")          // refused: not public

comparisons.note: is_global follows the IANA registries; is_private and is_global are both false for 100.64/10. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html.
Ipv4Addr::is_global is still unstable because the right table was disputed. Tracking issue: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27709.
netip.Addr has IsPrivate, IsLoopback, and similar checks but no single public test; SSRF filters combine them. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/netip#Addr.IsPrivate.

recommendation.why: Reachability and fetch safety are different questions. IANA answers the first; a stricter check refuses 6to4, Teredo, and NAT64 paths into private networks.
gains: One table for every destination check in Core.
The parity harness sees the same answers on both sides.

losses.loss: 6to4 and Teredo IPv6 addresses still count as public.
losses.mitigation: Refusing them changes the Rust answers the parity run compares; tighten both sides together later.

whyNot.reason: A keeps 6to4 and Teredo as public and ignores the published registry.
B makes fetch checks follow IANA, so NAT64 can still reach private IPv4.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two named checks buy standard reachability and strict fetch safety.

surface.gist: Which IP addresses should Core count as public when a program checks a network destination?
surface.lesson: Some addresses reach only a home network, a provider's internal services, or the machine itself. A program that fetches outside URLs must refuse those, or an attacker can reach internal services. Core's ip.is_global misses several such ranges, including carrier NAT and documentation ranges. Whichever option wins, one written table decides, and every Core check uses it.

decisions.title: Keep HTTP requests on checked public or loopback addresses
decisions.gist: How should an HTTP client refuse private addresses and keep using the addresses it already checked?
decisions.lesson: A host name can resolve to a private address, or change its answer between a check and the connection. A careful client resolves once, checks every answer, and connects only to those checked addresses. Jetpack does this for package caches and indexes. Core's HTTP client resolves names itself and has no such check. Whichever option wins, "public" means the one table from D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1.
decisions.story: Mei ports the Jetpack Nix cache and index clients. Each resolves the configured endpoint once and refuses any private answer. Each then sends every request to those checked addresses so a changed DNS answer cannot redirect it. Core's HTTP client resolves names on its own, so the port cannot keep this protection.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer (Control runs after resolution)
&net.Dialer{Control: checkPublic}
# curl: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--resolve
curl --resolve cache.example:443:203.0.113.7 https://cache.example/x
# Rust reqwest: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.resolve_to_addrs
Client::builder().resolve_to_addrs("cache.example", &addrs)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 3, "Request over pre-resolved, pinned public-only socket addresses - jet_net::get_stream_pinned + resolve_public_addresses." The table itself is D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1.

Rust call sites. Store/NixCache.rs:696-700 and 1329-1333 send over the endpoint's pinned addresses; resolve_endpoint_addresses (NixCache.rs:1726-1783) resolves once, public-only for HTTPS and loopback-only for plain HTTP. NixIndex.rs:345-437 and 489-517 do the same and cache one checked answer per authority for the client's life. Provider/fetch.rs:158-165 resolves public addresses for every hop and pins curl with --resolve. jet_net::get_stream_pinned (lib.rs:738-755) builds a ureq agent whose resolver returns the fixed list.

Current Jet surface. HTTPClient has cookies, redirects, protocols, timeouts, raw_encoding, proxy, tls, allow_http_downgrade, and retries (net_text_time.rs:800-818). None sets addresses or a destination rule. core.net has dns_a and dns_aaaa (net.jet:357-367) but no general resolve; D-NETDNS2 ratified net.resolve_ip, which is not built.

Prelude study (HTTP.rs rows "resolve" and "DNSEntry/DNSCache"): resolution is a leaf and cache lifetime is policy. The study does not cover a public destination rule, so this is new surface.

Ratified law checked: D-NETDNS2=A (system resolver by default), D-NETERROR1=A, D4 (enum option), D2 (defaults table), D-NET-HANDLE-ABI1 (no raw sockets exposed).

options.name: A destination rule on the client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains destinations(rule). .Any is the default and keeps today's behavior. .Public resolves each host once per client and refuses the request unless every address in the answer is public by the D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1 table. It then connects only to those addresses and reuses them for later requests to the same host and port. .Loopback does the same with loopback addresses. The rule also applies to IP-literal hosts and to every redirect hop. HTTPS still sends the original host name for SNI and certificate checks.
options.technical:
New closed enum HTTPDestinations { Any, Public, Loopback }. HTTPClient.destinations(rule: HTTPDestinations) -> HTTPClient. Refusal: HTTPError.Policy(reason:) naming the host and the first refused address, raised before any connection. A resolution failure stays HTTPError.Resolve(host:).

Pinning: the client keeps a map from (scheme, host, port) to the checked address list for its lifetime, shared by clones, as NixIndex.rs:345-422 does. The ordinary DNS cache TTL (HTTP.rs:1746-1785) does not apply to a pinned entry. Proxies: with .Public or .Loopback, an environment proxy is ignored; an explicit .URL proxy must itself pass the rule.

Defaults table row: "Client.new().destinations | .Any | .Public, .Loopback". Effects unchanged: Net, Time.Wait. The Prelude port moves resolve (HTTP.rs:1739-1745) behind this check. One path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: The caller resolves and pins addresses
options.detail: Add a public resolver call (D-NETDNS2's net.resolve_ip), a classification call for net.IPAddr, and HTTPClient.connect_to(host, port, addresses). The client then connects to the given addresses for that host.
options.technical: net.resolve_ip(host) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [IPAddr] !NetError uses the ratified D-NETDNS2 name, which is not built yet. net.ip_is_global(IPAddr) -> Bool is new. HTTPClient.connect_to(host: String, port: Int, addresses: [IPAddr]) -> HTTPClient works like curl --resolve.

options.name: A resolver function on the client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains resolver(function). The transport calls it for every connection instead of the system resolver. jet_net uses this mechanism through ureq today (lib.rs:748-754).
options.technical: HTTPClient.resolver(f: (String, Int) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [IPAddr] !NetError) -> HTTPClient. The client caches nothing on its own; pinning is up to the function.

comparisons.note: Dialer.Control is the praised SSRF hook because it sees the address actually dialed. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer.
comparisons.code: Control: func(network, address string, c syscall.RawConn) error

comparisons.note: --resolve pins a host to fixed addresses while keeping the host name for TLS. Docs: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--resolve.
A requests wrapper that refuses non-public destinations by policy at connect time. Project: https://github.com/JordanMilne/Advocate.

recommendation.why: Jetpack's caches and index use the same rule everywhere: HTTPS goes to checked public addresses and plain HTTP stays on loopback. One client setting gives that rule to every request and redirect.
gains: NixCache, NixIndex, and the provider fetcher each become one line.
The check happens where the connection is made, so it cannot be skipped.

losses.loss: A long-lived client keeps a stale address after DNS changes.
losses.mitigation: Pinning is the point: a new answer could be a private address, so a new client must opt in.

whyNot.reason: Pinning by hand misses redirect hops to new hosts, and a forgotten host silently falls back to normal resolution.
A resolver function makes every caller rewrite the same check and pinning, and hides the rule from receipts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs rebuild a client to pick up new DNS answers instead of trusting a fresh lookup.

decisions.title: Limit which hosts an HTTP client may follow a redirect to
decisions.gist: How should a program limit which hosts its HTTP client may follow a redirect to?
decisions.lesson: A redirect tells a client to fetch a different address instead. A download tool that trusts one server must not follow a redirect to another server. Today the client redirect policy only caps the number of hops. Jetpack must turn redirects off and follow each hop by hand. Whichever option wins, Core still refuses HTTPS-to-HTTP hops and strips credentials when the origin changes.
decisions.story: Omar ports the Jetpack toolchain updater. It downloads signed manifests from one configured server and must refuse a redirect that leaves that server. The provider fetcher must also refuse hosts outside each provider's allow list. Today the Jet client follows any redirect, so both ports would need hand-written redirect loops.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client (CheckRedirect)
client.CheckRedirect = func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error { ... }
# Rust reqwest: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/redirect/struct.Policy.html
Policy::custom(|attempt| if attempt.url().host_str() == Some("example.org") { attempt.follow() } else { attempt.stop() })
# curl: --max-redirs 5 --proto-redir =https (https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--proto-redir)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 2, "Bounded fetch with an explicit redirect-policy callback - jet_net::fetch_bounded_with_redirect_policy." The byte bound is D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1; this ballot covers the redirect rule.

Rust call sites. ToolchainUpdate.rs:1010-1016 passes resolve_toolchain_redirect (ToolchainUpdate.rs:962-991), which refuses any hop whose scheme, host, or port differs from the configured origin. Provider/fetch.rs:143-206 follows up to five hops by hand; every hop must pass check_url (fetch.rs:209-218), an allow and deny list of provider hosts on HTTPS port 443. Provider/native.rs:672 and 773 call get_stream_follow_redirects with any host allowed. The jet_net helpers are lib.rs:802-890.

Current Jet surface. HTTPRedirectPolicy has one variant, .Follow{max, same_origin_credentials} (core_types.rs:2972-2995, core-library.md:655). Requests also take redirects(n) (net_text_time.rs:785-791). Core/http/client.jet:26-30 declares a second RedirectPolicy enum {Disabled, Limited, All}; the Prelude port removes that duplicate.

Prelude study (HTTP.rs row "send_following_redirects"): two redirect implementations exist today and must become one Jet implementation. That is implementation. Choosing a host rule is new public surface, so it is balloted here.

Ratified law checked: D4 (options are enums), D2 (defaults table row), D-NETERROR1 (typed errors). The same_origin_credentials Bool is existing D4 drift and is left alone here.

options.name: Allowed hosts written in the policy
options.detail: HTTPRedirectPolicy.Follow gains a to: field that names where a hop may go. .AnyHost is the default and keeps today's behavior. .SameOrigin allows only hops that keep the scheme, host, and port of the first request. .Hosts(list) allows only hops whose host and port appear in the list. Core resolves the Location header, checks it against the rule, and refuses a bad hop with HTTPError.Redirect before it connects. The existing rules still apply: no HTTPS-to-HTTP hop without allow_http_downgrade, and credentials are stripped when the origin changes.
options.technical:
New closed enum RedirectTarget { AnyHost, SameOrigin, Hosts([String]) }. HTTPRedirectPolicy.Follow becomes { max: Int, same_origin_credentials: Bool = true, to: RedirectTarget = .AnyHost }. The true default is what the Rust transport already uses (HTTP.rs:326-333). A Hosts entry is "host" or "host:port"; a bare host means the scheme's default port. Hosts compare case-insensitively after IDNA normalization in core.net.url. An empty Hosts list refuses every hop.

Refusal: HTTPError.Redirect(reason:) naming the refused URL; the response that carried the Location is drained and closed. The hop count check is unchanged. Relative Location values resolve with core.net.url join, one rule for both the Rust transport (HTTP.rs:2645-3020) and client.jet session_follow (client.jet:188-217). The Prelude HTTP port (#3665) merges those two.

Defaults table row: "Client.new().redirects | up to 10 hops, any host | .Follow{max:, to:}". Effects unchanged: Net, Time.Wait. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: A callback approves each hop
options.detail: HTTPRedirectPolicy gains .Check{max, allow}. Core calls allow with the current URL and the resolved next URL; false refuses the hop with HTTPError.Redirect.
options.technical: Variant Check{ max: Int, allow: (URL, URL) -> Bool }. The callback must be pure; effects inside it are refused by the checker. Downgrade and credential rules still apply after the callback allows a hop.

options.name: Follow hops by hand
options.detail: Keep the surface as it is. A caller sends each request with redirects(0), reads Location, joins it with core.net.url, checks the rule, and repeats. This is how Provider/fetch.rs:143-206 works today with curl.
options.technical: Uses existing HTTPRequest.redirects(n), HTTPResponse.header(name), and URL.join. The caller owns method rewriting on 303, body replay on 307/308, credential stripping, and downgrade refusal.

comparisons.note: CheckRedirect is a callback; praised for power, but callers often forget to stop cross-host hops. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client.
Policy::limited(n) is data; Policy::custom is a callback for anything else. Docs: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/redirect/struct.Policy.html.
Redirect rules are flags: hop count and allowed protocols. Jetpack's hardened curl uses --max-redirs 0 and loops itself (fetch.rs:221-239). Docs: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html.

recommendation.why: Every Jetpack redirect rule is either same origin or an allowed host list. A data rule checked inside Core covers both, keeps the existing safety rules on every hop, and shows up in receipts.
gains: Toolchain updates and provider downloads get safe redirects in one line.
The redirect rule is visible data, not hidden code.

losses.loss: Unusual rules, such as path prefixes, still need a hand loop.
losses.mitigation: A closed list of rule kinds cannot express arbitrary code, and no Jetpack caller needs more.

whyNot.reason: A callback hides the rule from receipts and makes every caller rewrite the same-origin check that most need.
Hand loops repeat the joining, downgrade, and credential rules in every caller, and one slip leaks a token.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare rules outside same origin and host lists use a hand loop instead of a callback.
