options.gist: The redirect policy names where hops may go: any host, the same origin, or a host list.
gains: The rule is plain data that logs and receipts can show.
Core checks each hop before connecting to it.
Covers every Jetpack redirect rule without callbacks.
losses: A rule outside the three kinds needs a hand loop.

options.name: A callback approves each hop
options.gist: The policy carries a function that sees each hop and returns allow or refuse.
gains: Any rule a program can compute is expressible.
losses: Receipts cannot show the rule; it is code.
Each caller rewrites the common same-origin check.

options.name: Follow hops by hand
options.gist: No new policy; programs turn redirects off and loop over Location headers themselves.
gains: No new Core surface.
losses: Every caller re-implements joining, downgrade, and credential rules.
Easy to forget stripping credentials on a cross-origin hop.

recommendation.why: Every Jetpack redirect rule is either same origin or an allowed host list. A data rule checked inside Core covers both, keeps the existing safety rules on every hop, and shows up in receipts.
gains: Toolchain updates and provider downloads get safe redirects in one line.
The redirect rule is visible data, not hidden code.

losses.loss: Unusual rules, such as path prefixes, still need a hand loop.
losses.mitigation: A closed list of rule kinds cannot express arbitrary code, and no Jetpack caller needs more.

whyNot.reason: A callback hides the rule from receipts and makes every caller rewrite the same-origin check that most need.
Hand loops repeat the joining, downgrade, and credential rules in every caller, and one slip leaks a token.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare rules outside same origin and host lists use a hand loop instead of a callback.

decisions.title: Stream a large HTTP response body under a caller-chosen byte cap
decisions.gist: How should a program stream an HTTP response body larger than 64 MiB under its own byte cap?
decisions.lesson: A response body arrives in pieces, so a program can save it without holding it in memory. A byte cap stops a bad server from sending forever. Today every response stops at a hidden 64 MiB limit, and explicit limits stop at 1 GiB. Jetpack downloads archives up to 16 GiB. Whichever option wins, the cap is written down and an over-cap body fails.
decisions.story: Mei ports the Jetpack Nix cache client. It downloads a signed package archive of several gigabytes, hashes it, and unpacks it while it streams. Today the Jet HTTP client stops every body at 64 MiB, so the port cannot fetch real packages. She needs to set the cap from the signed file size and hand the body straight to the decoder.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader
body := io.LimitReader(resp.Body, limit+1)
# Python requests: https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#body-content-workflow
for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=65536): ...
# Rust jet_net (today): crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:730-797
response.take(limit + 1).read_to_end(&mut body)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 1, "Streaming GET response body with a caller-set byte cap (default body limit is 1 MiB) - jet_net::get_stream, get_stream_follow_redirects."

Rust call sites. Store/NixCache.rs:696-777 streams a Nix archive through a hashing reader and a zstd decoder, capped by the signed FileSize. MAX_NAR_BYTES is 16 GiB (Store/Nar.rs:22). Provider/native.rs:662-716 and 772-790 stream artifacts up to 512 MiB into a staging file (native.rs:35). ToolchainUpdate.rs:993-1019 fetches toolchain artifacts up to 512 MiB (ToolchainUpdate.rs:31). Store/Cache.rs:2251-2272, Store/NixCache.rs:1329-1355, and NixIndex.rs:355-389 read small bounded bodies; the existing bytes(limit) already covers those.

Current Jet surface. Body has bytes(limit), text(limit), json, chunks(size), and copy_to(^writer, limit) (net_text_time.rs:1034-1053, method_calls.rs:5200-5252). Explicit limits are clamped to 1 GiB (HTTPMessage.rs:884-889). The transport cuts every body at 64 MiB (HTTP.rs:73) and refuses a larger Content-Length as InvalidFraming (HTTP.rs:4271-4273). The card's "1 MiB" is the text() default from D-HTTP-MSG1; the binding limit for streams is the hidden 64 MiB.

Prelude study (prelude-core-gap.json, HTTP.rs row "Client limits constants"): the limit constants are policy that must become one set in Core/http/client.jet. That move alone does not decide how a caller raises the streaming cap, so this ballot decides it.

Ratified law checked. D-HTTP-MSG1 keeps text() and the explicit limit forms. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B define one core.io.Reader that fails with IOError. D-IOERROR-TREE1=A fixes the IOError variants. The bounded buffering law (spec.md:2032) says body limits reject over-limit input. Peer draft D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1 (ArchivePluginBallots) adds zstd.reader and gzip.reader over any io.Reader; NixCache.rs:745-775 needs exactly that composition.

options.name: Cap set on the body, which reads like a file
options.detail:
HTTPResponse.body gains an optional labeled cap: resp.body(limit: n). The cap applies to every way of reading that one-pass body: chunks, copy_to, and the core.io.Reader read(limit) from D-NETIO-CONTRACT1/2. A Content-Length above the cap fails before any byte is delivered. A bare resp.body() keeps a 64 MiB cap, now written in the defaults table instead of hidden in the transport.

In-memory reads keep their own explicit limits: text(), bytes(limit), and json stay as D-HTTP-MSG1 ratified them and never exceed 1 GiB. copy_to(^writer) drops its second argument because the body cap already bounds it.
options.technical:
Signature: HTTPResponse.body(limit: Int = 67108864) -> Body. HTTPRequest.body() on the server gains the same label. Body implements core.io.Reader: read(limit: Int) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [U8] !IOError, [] at end. Through the reader, an over-cap body is IOError.InvalidInput with operation Read, the URL as resource, and cause "HTTP body exceeds N-byte limit". Inherent calls keep HTTPError.BodyTooLarge(limit). A negative limit fails the first read with HTTPError.BodyTooLarge(limit), as jet_http_consume_limit does today (HTTPMessage.rs:884-889).

Streaming reads (chunks, copy_to, read) accept any nonnegative Int cap. The 1 GiB clamp stays only on reads that collect into memory (bytes, text, json). The body checks against HTTP_RESPONSE_BODY_LIMIT (HTTP.rs:3934, 4091, 4272, 4423, 4515) are removed; the Jet-side cap is the one bound. The HTTP/2 frame-queue bound at HTTP.rs:1249 gets its own constant. Framing checks stay: a body shorter or longer than its Content-Length is HTTPError.InvalidFraming.

Cutover (E1): copy_to(^writer, limit) becomes copy_to(^writer) in the checker (method_calls.rs:5230-5240), the Prelude (HTTPMessage.rs:861-882), and every caller. The defaults table in stdlib-api-laws.md gains the row "resp.body() | 64 MiB streaming cap | resp.body(limit:)". One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9). D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1 (ArchivePluginBallots draft) supplies zstd.reader over any io.Reader.

options.name: Cap on each streaming call
options.detail: chunks(size) gains limit:, and copy_to keeps its limit argument without the 1 GiB clamp. Body stays its own one-pass type and does not implement core.io.Reader. A bare chunks(size) keeps the 64 MiB default.
options.technical: Body.chunks(size: Int, limit: Int = 67108864) -> HTTPBodyChunks; Body.copy_to(^writer: FileWriter, limit: Int) -> Int !HTTPError. The transport cap is removed as in A. Composition with stream codecs needs an adapter that turns HTTPBodyChunks into a reader.

options.name: One cap for the whole client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains body_limit(n). Every body read from that client stops at n. One-shot helpers keep the 64 MiB default.
options.technical: HTTPClient.body_limit(limit: Int) -> HTTPClient. The client stores the cap and hands it to each response body. In-memory reads keep their explicit limits as today.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
client :: http_client.Client.new().body_limit(16.gib)
resp :: client.send(http_client.request("GET", nar_url)) ?? return
out :: files.create("stage/pkg.nar.zst") ?? return
resp.body().copy_to(^out) ?? return

comparisons.note: resp.Body is an io.Reader; callers bound it with io.LimitReader or http.MaxBytesReader. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader.
stream=True plus iter_content lets the caller count bytes; there is no built-in cap. Docs: https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#body-content-workflow.
comparisons.code:
with requests.get(url, stream=True) as r:
    for chunk in r.iter_content(65536): ...

comparisons.note: bytes_stream() yields chunks; no body cap exists, so callers count. Docs: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Response.html#method.bytes_stream.
comparisons.code:
let mut s = resp.bytes_stream();
while let Some(chunk) = s.next().await { total += chunk?.len(); }

recommendation.why: One cap on the body bounds every read path. A body that is a Core reader lets the archive decoder chain onto it without glue. Small reads keep their own tighter limits.
gains: One cap per download, chosen where the response is handled.
Package archives stream through decoders with no adapter.

losses.loss: copy_to callers drop their second argument.
losses.mitigation: Keeping both limits would give one body two caps that can disagree.

whyNot.reason: Per-call caps leave the body outside the shared reader contract, so stream decoders need glue, and two calls can set different caps.
Jetpack reads 1 MiB metadata and 16 GiB archives from the same server, so a client-wide cap is either too loose or too tight.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few copy_to callers change shape so that each body has exactly one cap.

defer resp.Body.Close()

n, err := io.Copy(out, body)

decisions.title: Take over a listening socket opened by the service manager
decisions.gist: How should a service take over a listening socket that its service manager opened for it?
decisions.lesson: A service manager such as systemd can open a socket before a service starts and hand it over at start. The service then accepts connections without binding the socket itself. Jetpack's shared-store broker works this way. In Core today, a listener comes only from binding. Whichever option wins, Core checks that the handed-over socket really is a listening socket before use.
decisions.story: Luis ports the Jetpack shared-store broker. An administrator installs it as a systemd socket unit, so systemd owns /run/jet/shared-store.sock and starts the broker per connection. The Rust broker turns descriptor 3 into a listener with unsafe code. Core has no way to receive that socket, so the port cannot run under the ratified install design.
decisions.inWild:
# systemd: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html
int n = sd_listen_fds(1);  /* descriptors 3 .. 3+n-1 */
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation#Listeners
listeners, err := activation.Listeners()
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html#socket.fromfd
sock = socket.fromfd(3, socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 4, "Adopt an inherited listening socket (socket activation, fd 3) for non-JetOS dev services (see #329 for the JetOS twin)."

Rust call sites. Store/Broker.rs:490-507 (serve_shared_store_fd) turns a raw descriptor into a UnixListener with unsafe code and accepts one connection. CLI/shared_store.rs:36-56 reads --fd and defaults to 3. The systemd units are generated at Broker.rs:286-299 (ListenStream socket unit) and Broker.rs:360-365 (ExecStart ... broker --fd 3). The only caller is this broker; Services.rs:1806-1926 reserves socket paths for dev services but hands no descriptor to them, so the card's "dev services" wording names no second user today.

Current Jet surface. core.net offers tcp_listen, tcp_listen_addr, and unix_listen (core-library.md:2803, 2831; net.jet:109-116, 312-319). There is no way to receive a listener.

Ratified law checked: D-JPK-MULTIUSER-IMPL1=A (root-owned socket-activated verifier with peer credentials), D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1=A (listeners are opaque handles; no public descriptor construction), D-NETERROR1=A. The sending side (a parent passing a handle to a child) is D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 in ProcessBallots; this ballot is the receiving side. #329 covers the JetOS service manager, which can speak the same convention.

options.name: Take the sockets the manager declared
options.detail: net.inherited_listeners() returns every listening socket the service manager handed over, as a list of InheritedListener values. Each value is .Unix{name, listener} or .TCP{name, listener}, where name comes from the manager (for example the systemd FileDescriptorName). Core checks that each handed-over descriptor is a stream socket in listening state, marks it close-on-exec, and clears the handover variables so children do not see them. A second call returns an empty list. Without a handover, the list is empty.
options.technical:
New closed enum InheritedListener { Unix{ name: ?String, listener: UnixListener }, TCP{ name: ?String, listener: TCPListener } }. net.inherited_listeners() -[Net, Env]> [InheritedListener] !NetError.

Protocol: the sd_listen_fds convention (https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html). LISTEN_PID must equal the current process id, or the list is empty. LISTEN_FDS descriptors start at 3; LISTEN_FDNAMES supplies names. Each descriptor must report SO_ACCEPTCONN = 1 and SO_TYPE = SOCK_STREAM, with family AF_UNIX or AF_INET/AF_INET6. Any other descriptor fails the call with NetError.InvalidInput naming its position. The call unsets LISTEN_PID, LISTEN_FDS, and LISTEN_FDNAMES, like sd_listen_fds(1).

Platforms: Linux and other Unix hosts whose manager uses this convention. macOS launchd uses a different, name-based call and Windows has no handover; both return an empty list. The listener types stay the ones D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 made opaque; no descriptor number is exposed. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

Jetpack cutover: the generated unit keeps ExecStart=... hangar shared broker, and the --fd 3 flag (CLI/shared_store.rs:39-44, Broker.rs:361) is removed.

options.name: Adopt a socket by descriptor number
options.detail: net.unix_listener_from_descriptor(n) and net.tcp_listener_from_descriptor(n) check that n is a listening socket of the right family and take ownership of it.
options.technical: unix_listener_from_descriptor(descriptor: Int) -[Net]> UnixListener !NetError; tcp_listener_from_descriptor(descriptor: Int) -[Net]> TCPListener !NetError. The same socket checks as A run. Core cannot tell whether another part of the program already owns the number.

comparisons.note: sd_listen_fds checks LISTEN_PID, returns the count, and optionally unsets the variables. Docs: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html.
activation.Listeners wraps each passed descriptor as a net.Listener. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation.
The listenfd crate reads the same convention without unsafe in user code. Docs: https://docs.rs/listenfd.
comparisons.code:
let mut fds = ListenFd::from_env();
let listener = fds.take_unix_listener(0)?;

recommendation.why: The handover convention already says which descriptors belong to the service and what they are called. Reading it in Core keeps descriptor numbers out of program code, as the ratified listener design requires.
gains: The broker takes its socket with no unsafe code and no numbers.
Children never see the handover variables.

losses.loss: Supervisors without the LISTEN_FDS convention cannot hand over sockets.
losses.mitigation: Without a convention, only a raw number identifies the socket, and D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 removed numbers from public code.

whyNot.reason: It brings descriptor numbers back into public code, and Core cannot stop two parts of a program adopting one number.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the widely used LISTEN_FDS handover is supported, in exchange for no descriptor numbers in programs.

Jetpack's shared-store broker works this way. In Core today, a listener comes only from binding. Whichever option wins, Core checks that the handed-over socket really is a listening socket before use.

current.note: Listeners come only from binding a path or address; there is no way to receive one. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: The go-systemd package reads the systemd handover and returns ready listeners. See https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation#Listeners.

options.name: Take the sockets the manager declared
options.gist: One call reads the service manager's handover and returns checked, typed listeners.
gains: No descriptor numbers in program code.
Each socket is checked before it is trusted.

gains: Works with any supervisor that passes a known number.
Matches the Rust --fd flag exactly.
losses: Descriptor numbers return to public code.
Two parts of a program can adopt the same number.

Children never see the handover variables.

losses.mitigation: Without a convention, only a raw number identifies the socket, and D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 removed numbers from public code.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the widely used LISTEN_FDS handover is supported, in exchange for no descriptor numbers in programs.

decisions.title: Learn which user is on the other end of a Unix socket
decisions.gist: How should a Unix-socket server learn which user account is on the other end of a connection?
decisions.lesson: On one machine, a server can ask the kernel which user connected to its Unix socket. The kernel records this at connect time, so the client cannot fake it. Jetpack's shared-store broker uses the user number to decide who may read or write. Core's Unix sockets have no such query. Whichever option wins, platforms without the query report Unsupported.
decisions.story: Luis ports the Jetpack shared-store broker. For each connection, it reads the connecting user's number from the kernel. It then checks that user's enrollment record and grants read or write rights. The Rust code does this through an unsafe getsockopt call. Core's Unix streams offer no way to ask.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 5, "Unix-socket peer credentials (SO_PEERCRED) for the shared-store broker."

Rust call sites. Store/Broker.rs:519 reads peer_uid for every connection, then authorize_peer (defined at Broker.rs:927, called at 526 and 533) checks enrollment and rights. peer_uid is Broker.rs:820-866 (Linux SO_PEERCRED through unsafe getsockopt) and 868-873 (other Unix: unsupported). The test at Broker.rs:2607-2690 proves the number is the kernel's view across a user namespace.

Current Jet surface. UnixStream has read, write, shutdown, and close (net.jet:317-355, core-library.md:2831-2834) and nothing about the peer.

Ratified law checked: D-JPK-MULTIUSER-IMPL1=A ("socket-activated transient verifier with peer credentials"), D-DBG-AUTH1 (same-user attach), D-NETERROR1=A (Unsupported and PermissionDenied variants exist in NetError, core_types.rs:2902-2917). Process identity is ProcessBallots' D-CORE-PROCIDENT1.

options.name: Ask the stream for its peer
options.detail: net.unix_peer(stream) returns UnixPeer{user, group}: the user and group numbers the kernel recorded when the client connected. The server compares them with its own policy. There is no process id in the result, because a process id can be reused by an unrelated process. D-CORE-PROCIDENT1 covers process identity.
options.technical:
New plain-data record UnixPeer { user: Int, group: Int } with equality. net.unix_peer(stream: UnixStream) -[Net]> UnixPeer !NetError.

Linux and Android: getsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_PEERCRED), the ucred recorded at connect() time. macOS, iOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, and DragonFly: getpeereid(). Windows AF_UNIX has no peer credential: NetError.Unsupported. A closed stream: NetError.Closed. Numbers are the kernel's view from the server's user namespace, which is what the broker test at Broker.rs:2607-2690 relies on.

No raw descriptor is exposed. Effects: Net only. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: An admission rule on the listener
options.detail: unix_listen and the inherited-listener path take a peers: rule, .Anyone by default, or .SameUser, or .Users(list). Core checks each accepted connection and closes refused ones.
options.technical: Enum UnixPeers { Anyone, SameUser, Users([Int]) }. The accept loop skips refused connections. The server cannot learn which allowed user connected.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net as net
listener :: net.unix_listen(path, peers: .Users(config.enrolled_users)) ?? return
stream :: net.unix_accept(listener) ?? return   // only enrolled users arrive

options.name: Raw socket option under #Unsafe
options.detail: An expert unix_socket_option(stream, level, name, size) returns raw bytes. The caller knows the platform numbers and struct layout.
options.technical: unix_socket_option(stream: UnixStream, level: Int, name: Int, size: Int) -[Net]> [U8] !NetError, callable only in #Unsafe.

comparisons.note: peer_cred returns UCred{uid, gid, pid: Option}; pid is optional because not every platform has it. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/net/struct.UnixStream.html#method.peer_cred.
x/sys/unix exposes the raw Linux ucred; callers write platform branches themselves. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sys/unix#GetsockoptUcred.
Python needs getsockopt with a hand-written struct layout. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html#socket.socket.getsockopt.

recommendation.why: The broker needs the user number itself to look up enrollment and choose read or write rights. A small record read from the stream gives exactly that on every Unix host, with no unsafe code.
gains: The broker port keeps its access rules without unsafe code.

losses.loss: No process id is reported.
losses.mitigation: A process id can belong to a new process by the time it is used, so it is not identity.

whyNot.reason: The broker must know which enrolled user connected to pick rights, so a yes/no admission rule is not enough.
Raw options push platform numbers and byte layouts into every caller and force #Unsafe for a routine check.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers that want the connecting process use the process-identity surface instead of a raw process id.

current.note: A Unix stream exposes only its path; there is no peer identity query. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Rust's UnixStream::peer_cred returns the kernel-recorded user, group, and process. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/net/struct.UnixStream.html#method.peer_cred.
wild.code:
let cred = stream.peer_cred()?;
if cred.uid != allowed_uid { return Err(denied()); }

options.name: Ask the stream for its peer
options.gist: One call returns the connecting user and group numbers the kernel recorded.
gains: The server decides access with ordinary code on plain numbers.

losses: No process id, so it cannot find the connecting process.

options.name: An admission rule on the listener

gains: Unwanted users never reach program code.

use core.net as net
listener :: net.unix_listen(path, peers: .Users(config.enrolled_users)) ?? return
stream :: net.unix_accept(listener) ?? return   // only enrolled users arrive

options.gist: An expert call reads any socket option as bytes inside an audited unsafe block.
gains: Reaches every platform-specific option.
losses: Every caller decodes platform byte layouts itself.
Jetpack would need #Unsafe for an ordinary check.

gains: The broker port keeps its access rules without unsafe code.

losses.loss: No process id is reported.
losses.mitigation: A process id can belong to a new process by the time it is used, so it is not identity.

decisions.title: Is the wait from `jet run` to its answer part of Jet's speed rule?
decisions.situation: Jet's speed rule says Jet must beat every comparable language on every required benchmark, and no release ships while one loses. It does not say whether a quick run counts, where you type jet run and wait for the answer. People compare that wait with python3 and node, which answer a tiny script in about twenty to fifty milliseconds. The vote decides whether that wait is a required benchmark. We recommend yes, for script-sized programs, timed after an edit and on a repeat run.
decisions.gist: Should the wait from typing `jet run` to seeing the answer be a required speed benchmark?
decisions.lesson: The speed rule gates finished programs and build times against matched languages, and a losing required benchmark holds every release. A quick run includes checking, compiling and running, so its wait is a different number. Whichever option wins, the speed rule still gates release programs, and every measured loss stays on a card.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A benchmark cell is one workload and one measurement, such as run time of a log report, compared with the same program in other languages. Time to answer is the wall time from pressing Enter on `jet run app.jet` to the program finishing.

Two cache states are timed. After an edit: the script changed since its last run, and Jet's own libraries are prebuilt, as they ship. Repeat: nothing changed since the last run. A first run on a freshly installed machine with every cache empty is reported, not gated.

Beginner path: nothing to write. Under A, `jet run` is held to the same beat-the-peer rule as release programs.

Expert path: the cells name the exact commands, inputs and cache states, so an expert can reproduce each number.
decisions.story: Lena writes ten-line scripts to clean CSV files. Python answers before she lifts her finger; `jet run` takes seconds while it builds. Nothing in Jet's speed rule says that wait is a bug to fix.
decisions.inWild:
$ time python3 -c pass   # about 0.02-0.04 s on the reference machine
$ time node -e 0         # about 0.02-0.05 s
$ go run hello.go        # compiles, caches the binary, then runs
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), sections 3.4 and 5.4, and its owner decision 5. The adversarial audit (finding 1) warned the research not to treat quick-run evidence as release evidence. That makes the gate question explicit.

Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. The posted A gated a warm and a cold cache without saying what cold meant. If cold meant every cache empty, Jet would also recompile its own libraries, which no peer does on a script run. A now names the two states users meet: after an edit, and a repeat run. The first run after install is reported only. The surface now states plainly that a losing required cell holds every release (AGENTS.md, performance gate).

Jet today. AGENTS.md's speed rule covers foundations including build time and run time, plus one real workload in each critical area, including CLI and scripts. It forbids substituting an easier tier, but it does not name `jet run`. A performance card, milestone or release gate stays open while any required cell fails.

D-EXEC2=A runs `jet run` through the build path until native in-memory O0 lands, with a target of about 1 to 5 seconds for small programs.

The gauntlet measures `runtime_first_stdout_seconds` and `runtime_wall_seconds` per cell (Tools/gauntlet/status.mjs). It has held an interpreter-tier `jet run --interpret` wall-time row (Tools/gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json).

Peer start-up was measured on the reference machine on 2026-10-07, at load 16 to 23, over three runs. `python3 -c pass` took 0.02 to 0.04 s. `node -e 0` took 0.02 to 0.05 s. A historical Jet receipt shows about 1.7 s of fixed start-up work for hello before any code generation (SpeedPlan1/HANDOFF.md).

Right ways elsewhere. Go's `go run` compiles to a cached binary and runs it; since Go 1.24 the linked program is cached too. Python and Node start an interpreter or JIT immediately. Every peer ships its own standard library ready to use, which is why the after-edit cell keeps Jet's prebuilt libraries. The cells under A compare against these exact commands.

options.name: Gate the time to answer
options.detail: Add required cells for `jet run` time to answer on the script and CLI workloads. Time it after an edit and on a repeat run, against `python3`, `node` and `go run` running the same program. Each cell follows the existing rule: Jet must be faster, every loss stays on a card, and releases wait while a cell loses. The first run after install is shown on the dashboard, not gated.
options.technical: Adds `run_time_to_answer_seconds` with `cache: edited|repeat` to the CLI-and-scripts critical area in the canonical manifest. `edited` touches the script before each sample; Jet's shipped libraries and each peer's standard library stay as installed. `repeat` reruns the unchanged script. A reported-only `cache: fresh_install` row empties every cache. Peers: CPython (`python3 main.py`), Node (`node main.js`), Go (`go run .`). Each cell records the same input, output check and process-start method as existing runtime cells. No change to release-program cells.

options.name: Report it, do not gate it
options.detail: Measure and show the time to answer next to each script cell, but do not count it in the speed rule. Only release programs and build times gate.
options.technical: Adds the same metric and cache states as reported-only columns. Gates and cards ignore them.

comparisons.note: Starts the interpreter and runs at once; about 0.02-0.04 s for an empty script on the reference machine.
`go run` compiles to a cached binary, then runs it.

recommendation.why: The quick-run wait is what script users feel first, and the speed rule only drives work it gates. Timing it after an edit and on a repeat run measures what users actually meet.
gains: Slow quick runs become tracked losses with owners.

losses.loss: Releases wait until quick runs beat Python, Node and Go.
losses.mitigation: Native in-memory quick runs are already the planned path (D-EXEC2); each losing cell is a card with its measured gap.

whyNot.reason: A number that never fails a gate does not get fixed.

recommendation.tradeoff: Releases wait on quick-run speed; the wait users feel first becomes a gated number.

decisions.title: Whether the portable sandbox's walls depend on the compiler being bug-free
decisions.situation: A Jet app file is one portable program that any machine checks, compiles and runs inside sealed walls, the way WebAssembly runs code. Today the plan trusts the machine's own compiler to build those walls correctly, so a compiler bug could let an app escape. Another engine's compiler had exactly such a bug, rated 9.9 out of 10. The vote decides whether a small checker inspects the final machine code before it runs; we recommend yes, so the walls hold even when the compiler is wrong.
decisions.gist: Should the host check an app's final machine code before running it, so compiler bugs cannot break the walls?
decisions.lesson: The walls, or isolation, keep an app inside its own memory and away from anything the host did not grant. The host already verifies the app file and grants each power. Whichever option wins, safety inside the app and the same answers as a native build still rest on Jet's compiler and its tests.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. An app file (`.jetapp`) holds checked portable Jet code. The host is the machine that runs it. The walls, or isolation, mean the app can touch only its own memory and the handles the host gave it. Machine code is what the host's compiler produces from the app file. A side channel is a way to leak secrets through chip timing, such as Spectre.

Beginner path: nothing changes. `jet run notes.jetapp` asks for powers and runs the app.

Expert path: hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening with one host setting; one app per process relies on the operating system's process walls.
decisions.story: Omar runs other people's plugins inside his note app. One plugin triggers a rare bug in the host's compiler. Under today's plan that bug can let the plugin read his notes; with a final-code check, the plugin is refused before it runs.
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), section 4.7, and owner decisions 7 to 9. The adversarial audit's blocking finding 10 showed that 'validation removes the optimizer from the trusted base' is true only for the walls. It does not hold for safety inside the app or for keeping the same answers.

Jet today. D-PORTABLE1=A ratified the Jet sandbox. The app file holds a versioned portable encoding of MIR. The host verifies structure, types, memory safety, control flow and host calls, and grants powers through unforgeable handles held in its own trust store.

D-PORTABLE1's trusted base names the verifier, the runtime and its broker, the native compiler and its cache. It explicitly does not promise protection from bugs in them, or from side channels such as Spectre. It starts a first run in an interpreter while native code compiles.

D-EXEC2=A later retired the interpreter once native in-memory O0 lands. So under both options here, the first run uses quick native code compiled on arrival. D-HOST-CAPS1 (open, proposed A) makes hardware such as tensor cores visible as build facts. A hardware fact never grants a power; only host handles do.

Evidence. Crocus (ASPLOS 2024) reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE in Cranelift's lowering rules, a real compiler bug that broke WebAssembly isolation. Native Client (2009) validated x86 code before running it, at under 5% (ARM) and 7% (x86-64) run-time cost for its fault-isolation scheme (Sehr et al. 2010).

VeriWasm (NDSS 2021) checks the native code Lucet produced, so the compiler leaves the isolation trusted base. Its disassembler and control-flow builder stay trusted. It does not check indirect-call types and allows some reads Wasm would not.

Swivel (USENIX Security 2021) shows that side-channel hardening costs depend strongly on the threat model. Process isolation is the common alternative.

What A requires. The compiler emits code in a checkable shape: memory accesses within the app's region or through checked handles, jumps only to known targets, and host calls only through the broker. A published checker validates each compiled function and refuses the app on any failure.

Checked code is cached by app hash, host, compiler, checker version and policy, as D-PORTABLE1 already keys its cache. Checker cost is unmeasured for Jet. A gauntlet cell for bundle start-up and steady speed measures it before ratification of the checker design.

Edge cases under both options. Hosts that forbid making code at run time, such as iOS apps, get a native copy built and signed ahead of time by the host's operator. Under A, the checker runs on that copy too. In browsers, apps still export to WebAssembly and WebGPU (D-WASISRV1, D-PORTABLE1) and inherit their limits.

options.name: Check the final machine code
options.detail: Before an app runs, the host checks the compiled machine code against the wall rules. Memory accesses stay in the app's region or go through handles, jumps go only to known places, and host calls go only through the broker. A compiler bug can then make the app wrong, but cannot let it out. Hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening.
options.technical:
Amends D-PORTABLE1's trusted base. For isolation, the trusted parts become the verifier, the machine-code checker, the runtime and broker, and the loader; the native compiler is untrusted. For memory safety inside the app and for same-answer behaviour, the compiler stays trusted and is covered by D-EXEC3's rule proofs, checkers and example runs.

Adds a host policy for side channels: `isolate: process` (default; one app per process) or `isolate: shared` with side-channel hardening. The checker spec, its admissible machine-code shape and its cost cells land before the checker is built.
options.code:
$ jet run --allow=FS.Write,IO notes.jetapp
  check   machine code · walls hold · cached
saved
// a compiler bug that breaks a wall: refused before anything runs

options.name: Trust the host's compiler
options.detail: Keep D-PORTABLE1 as ratified. The compiler inserts the wall checks itself, and nothing checks its output. Start-up skips one pass, but a compiler bug can let an app escape.
options.technical: No amendment. The trusted base stays the verifier, runtime, broker, native compiler and cache; side channels stay unpromised.

comparisons.note: Google's Native Client validated every x86 instruction of a module before running it. Source: Yee et al., IEEE S&P 2009.
comparisons.code:

// module rejected: instruction at 0x1040 is not on a 32-byte boundary

comparisons.note: Wasmtime trusts Cranelift's output for isolation; Crocus later found a 9.9/10 lowering bug that broke it. Source: doi:10.1145/3617232.3624862.
comparisons.code: $ wasmtime run app.wasm   # walls built by the compiler

recommendation.why: The walls are the sandbox's whole promise, and a small checker keeps them even when the large compiler has a bug.
gains: A compiler bug cannot become an escape.

losses.loss: The first run of a new app pays one checking pass.
losses.mitigation: Checked code is cached by app hash, so later runs skip the check.

losses.loss: A few speed-ups the checker cannot follow are off inside apps.
losses.mitigation: Bundle speed cells measure the cost, and the checker's rules are published for review.

whyNot.reason: B lets one compiler bug turn into an escape, as happened in another engine.

recommendation.tradeoff: A first-run check and a narrower code shape buy walls that do not depend on the compiler.

decisions.title: How Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check them, and choose which examples rerun
decisions.situation: Jet builds a program at three levels: quick runs while you work, everyday builds, and the fastest release builds. They share one runtime and one checked program, but nothing says which speed-ups each level shares or how a level-only speed-up shows it keeps the meaning. Nothing says which examples a change must rerun either, so some changes merge without running a level at all. The vote sets those rules; we recommend shared speed-ups, proved or checked level-only ones, and rerunning exactly the examples whose build changed.
decisions.gist: How should Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check level-only ones, and choose which examples a change reruns?
decisions.lesson: A level is how hard the compiler works: O0 for quick runs, O1 for everyday builds, O2 for release. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output. Whichever option wins, every example still runs on every level before each milestone, and running out of stack or memory is a separate vote.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A level, or tier, is one way of building. O0 serves `jet run`, `jet dev` and compile-time code, O1 serves `jet build`, and O2 serves `jet build --release`. Compile-time code runs while the program is being built. The web is a level too, where a feature applies.

The runtime is the built-in library every program calls, such as `print` and lists. A speed-up, or optimization, rewrites the checked program so it does less work. A shared speed-up is one piece of compiler code that every level runs; a level-only speed-up runs on some levels.

A rewrite rule replaces one small pattern with an equal one, such as `x * 2` with `x + x`. A proof of a rule is a machine-checked argument that the rule never changes the answer. A checker is a small program that inspects one compiler result and refuses it when it is wrong. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output; passing examples is regression evidence, not proof.

A milestone is the point where finished work joins the released line, after one full test run of everything. In the example, `sum(1..=10)` adds the whole numbers 1 through 10, giving 55. `jet build --release sum.jet` makes a program file and `./sum` runs it.

Beginner path: nothing to write. With enough stack and memory, `jet run`, `jet build` and `jet build --release` print the same output.

Expert path: `-O0`, `-O1` and `-O2` still pick a level. `jet inspect passes` lists every speed-up with its levels and its evidence: proved, checked or tested. It also lists what each proof or checker covers and what it does not.
decisions.story: Priya adds a speed-up that only release builds use. She wants to know before merging whether it can change any program's output. She also wants her change to rerun only the examples it can affect, not every example at every level.
decisions.detail:
Source: the owner's execution requirements (a) to (f), relayed by Main on 2026-10-07. Tiers must not be able to differ, without running every test on every tier. Every tier must be as fast as possible. A hardware-agnostic optimizer is shared by all tiers, and release adds hardware-specific work.

Research: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1/RESEARCH.md revision 2, after two audits (AUDIT-adversary.md, AUDIT-Verifier.md). Fresh reviews of this ballot: review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderAdversary.md, repaired as listed in review/D-EXEC3-repairs.md. Section numbers below refer to RESEARCH.md.

Jet today. D-EXEC1=A ratified one runtime and one Jet code generator with O0, O1 and O2, with LLVM first for O2. D-EXEC2=A retired the Cranelift JIT; until native O0 lands, `jet run` and `jet dev` build and then run. D-TIER-FORM1=A and D-TIER-ONEIR1=A give every back end one checked MIR from one semantic lowering.

I5 requires every feature example to prove the same meaning on every applicable tier. I9 requires one executable meaning, compiled once into one runtime that code generators only call. AGENTS.md runs each card's narrow proof after integration and one composed sweep per milestone. No rule says which examples a change must rerun.

Already settled, so not on this ballot. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B covers run-time re-optimization. D-SIMD3=B, D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D keep floating point bit-identical except under named recorded profiles. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-FAIL-BREACH1=A fix one report text and trace shape per failure on every tier. D-PORTABLE1=A fixes the portable form as MIR. D-BACKEND-OWN1 (open) decides whether Jet O2 replaces LLVM.

Not voted here. Which technology builds O0 (the Jet selector, a template baseline or copy-and-patch) is an implementation choice under D-EXEC1, measured on a real corpus. Copy-and-patch would need build-time clang or LLVM, which then needs its own ballot under the no-Rust directive. Running out of stack or memory is D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1; its I9 text starts with the same parity sentence as this one.

Finding 1, sharing (3.1). Sharing removes the duplication class of tier bugs: copied runtimes and per-engine lowering. CPython reports its JIT-only bugs were in the shared micro-op optimizer, not the copy-and-patch step (PEP 744). A shared bug agrees on every level, so differential runs cannot see it; golden outputs, as an independent oracle, can.

Finding 2, proof tools are bounded (3.1, 4.4). Alive2 (PLDI 2021) caught 29 of 36 known LLVM miscompilations. It checks one function at a time, had no function pointers and supported 21% of intrinsics. Crocus verified Cranelift AArch64 integer lowering rules and reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE, but trusts other passes and the runtime. regalloc2's checker validates register moves, not scheduling or calling conventions.

So proofs and checkers reduce risk without replacing whole-program runs. Every stage is therefore labelled proved, checked or tested, with its covered properties.

Finding 3, rerunning exactly what changed. A level's output for an example depends only on the example's checked program after shared speed-ups, that level's compiler, the runtime, the target and the build settings. If none of these changed and the build is reproducible, the result is the same program, so its earlier pass still stands. Reproducibility is already required for trusted cache outputs (D-JPK-REPROCACHE1=D); a rerun skip uses only such outputs.

A shared change that alters an example's checked program reruns that example on every level, which closes the gap a touched-files rule would leave (adversary 2). Milestone sweeps rebuild and rerun everything from scratch, which catches cache or reproducibility defects.

Finding 4, budgets (5.1). One optimizer output at every level would make the first quick run pay release cost, or cap release at quick-run cost. So levels share pass code and differ in budget. Running a shared pass longer at O2 is not a level-only speed-up.

Finding 5, the runtime boundary (4.1). Opaque runtime calls hide work from the optimizer. A adds an I9 clause letting levels inline runtime functions, but only from the runtime's own source and version. They must keep its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination, and never rewrite its policy.

Finding 6, heavy search (4.5). Cranelift's e-graph pipeline gained about 2% run time for 7 to 8% more compile time, and keeping alternative forms gained about 0.1%. Superoptimizers search for seconds to hours per fragment. Under A they run offline to find rules, or at release within budgets counted in deterministic fuel, after a paired measurement shows a win.

Finding 7, optimality (3.2, 3.3). The claim that no faster organization exists cannot be computed (Rice) and is undefined without a hardware cost model. A promises a monotone reduction in named work counters. Each result is labelled completed or stopped by fuel. Removed drops are dead or redundant only; observable cleanup is preserved. Each gauntlet cell reports its measured fraction of a stated hardware bound, and matched peer cells stay the gate.

Scope of parity. It covers every applicable tier: O0, O1 and O2, and compile-time code, which uses the target's layout, not the host's. It also covers the web adapter where a feature applies, and portable apps compiled on arrival. Programs whose `#Unsafe` blocks break their stated obligations are not compared; sentries and hardened profiles report them under their own law.

Concurrent examples compare the output their contract fixes, not one interleaving. Foreign callbacks, task ordering, ownership and drop paths, and failures during cleanup each get named example families.

Costs of A. A level-only speed-up waits until its proof or checker exists. Proofs, models and checkers need upkeep when rules or targets change. The runtime keeps an inlining interface. The pass registry and the input-hash record must be maintained. Optimizing O0 can hide variables in the debugger, so O0 shared speed-ups must keep source stepping and variable visibility.

Right ways elsewhere. One instruction definition generates both interpreter and JIT (CPython, Deegen). Lowering rules are checked (ISLE with Crocus), and a checker runs after register allocation (regalloc2; CompCert validates allocation). Bazel reruns only actions whose inputs changed. Wrong ways: per-engine runtimes (Jet's old Cranelift engine, about 130,000 duplicated lines per D-EXEC1's text). Unchecked compiler facts: Rust disabled mutable-reference noalias from 2018 to 2021 after LLVM miscompilations.

options.name: Shared speed-ups, checked extras, rerun what changed
options.detail: Every level runs the same shared speed-ups, written once. A speed-up that only some levels run needs a proved rule or a checker on each result; an unproved rule never ships. A change reruns an example on a level exactly when that level's build of it changed, and keeps the earlier pass otherwise. Every milestone rebuilds and reruns every example on every level. Release picks hardware-specific code only among choices proved equal.
options.technical:
Amends I5: "Every feature has an example with golden-tested output. Each change reruns an example on each applicable tier whose build inputs for it changed. Those inputs are the checked program after shared passes, the tier's compiler, the runtime, the target and the settings. Every milestone and cutover rebuilds and reruns every example on every applicable tier."

Amends I9 by adding: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. Tiers share one checked MIR, one runtime and one implementation of each shared pass. A transform only some tiers run is a proved rule or passes a recorded checker. Any other stage is tested and labelled so."

"An unknown or timed-out proof keeps a rule out. A checker that cannot handle its input is a Jet defect, never a pass. Tiers may inline runtime functions only from the runtime's source and version, keeping its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination." This replaces I9's call-only wording.

Jet-generated selectors (O0, O1 and any future Jet O2) come from shared lowering rules. Today's O2 emits LLVM IR from Jet rules; LLVM's own passes stay an external stage, tested by examples and by Alive2 runs in CI that are known to be bounded.

Adds one inspect view, `jet inspect passes`, beside the existing `jet inspect` views. Performance claims follow detail finding 7. Unchanged: D-EXEC2, D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1, D-SIMD3, D-RTFAIL1, D-PORTABLE1, D-BACKEND-OWN1, and the O0 technology choice.
options.code:
fn run() { print(sum(1..=10)) }   // adds 1 through 10
$ jet run sum.jet                       # O0: shared speed-ups
55
$ jet build --release sum.jet && ./sum  # O2: shared + proved extras
55

decisions.title: How deep recursion and running out of memory behave on each build level
decisions.situation: When a function calls itself, each waiting call holds a little memory called stack, and too many at once runs it out. Quick runs keep more in each call than release builds, which can even turn the calls into a loop. So one program can stop with a stack-overflow report in a quick run yet finish in a release build. Jet's rule that every level means the same thing says nothing about this. The vote decides how deep recursion behaves on each level; we recommend that a declared depth is exact everywhere and an undeclared one depends on the machine.
decisions.gist: How should deep recursion and running out of memory behave across quick runs and release builds?
decisions.lesson: The stack is the memory running function calls use; deep recursion fills it. Jet stops an overflow with a registered report. A ratified mark, `#MaxDepth(n)`, states how deep a function may recurse, but nothing yet says whether that limit is enforced. Whichever option wins, programs with enough memory give the same output on every level.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A call frame is the slice of stack one waiting call needs. Recursion means a function calls itself. In the example, `depth(n)` calls `depth(n - 1)` until n reaches 0, so `depth(2)` has three calls waiting at its deepest point: for 2, 1 and 0. A quick run (O0, used by `jet run`) keeps every value in its frame. A release build (O2, `jet build --release`) keeps values in registers, which are the processor's own small storage, and can turn recursion into a loop.

The heap is where lists and text live. Ambient memory is whatever the machine gives the program; a budget is a fixed amount the program sets itself, such as a fixed-size arena. A plain allocation that fails stops the program, as today. A `try_` allocation, such as `list.try_push(x)`, returns an error value the program can handle.

Beginner path: nothing to write. A program with enough stack and memory prints the same output on every level. When a quick run or everyday build runs out of stack, it stops with the stack-overflow report.

Expert path: write `#MaxDepth(n)` on a deep recursive function. It means at most n calls of that function wait at once, counting the first call. Under A, every level then reserves room for n calls and stops the call after n with the same report. `jet inspect memory app.jet` shows, per entry point and level, the stack needed, the stack requested and the stack actually granted.
decisions.story: Sam writes a recursive JSON walker. His tests pass in a release build, but `jet run` on a deeply nested file stops with a stack overflow. He cannot tell whether his program is wrong, or how deep it may safely go on every level.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: a configured recursion limit
import sys
sys.getrecursionlimit()   # 1000 by default
# deeper calls raise RecursionError
# docs: the safe maximum is platform-dependent
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), sections 3.1 and 6.3, and its owner decision 2. Fresh reviews: review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderAdversary.md, with repairs listed in review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-repairs.md. This ballot and D-EXEC3 share one parity rule, quoted in both.

Probe. A C program with fully defined behavior was built with clang 21.1.8 and an 8 MiB stack. It overflowed at depth 74,446 at -O0. At -O2 it finished 50,000,000 levels with the correct value, because the compiler turned the recursion into a loop. A sanitizer build overflowed at 130,283. This shows that levels can differ; it is not a Jet limit or ratio. Receipts: ExecArch1/tierdiff.log.

Jet today, as implemented. E3012 is the registered runtime report `Stack overflow in {fn}` (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet). `jet run` builds and then runs the program, until native in-memory O0 lands (D-EXEC2=A).

Jet today, ratified but not yet built. D-STACKBOUND1=A computes worst-case stack per entry point from each target's frame sizes and the sealed call graph. It enforces `!Mem.Stack(above: N)` and needs `#MaxDepth(n)` on recursion to compute that bound. It does not say how depth is counted or what happens past n; this ballot settles that. `#MaxDepth` is not yet registered in Syntax.rs, and this ballot adds no new spelling.

Other law this ballot keeps. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-REPORT-LAW1=A require one registered report with the same text and trace shape on every tier. S36 sends program stops through one report and cleanup boundary. D-ALLOCFAIL1=A keeps the hosted abort for plain allocation and makes `try_` allocation return an ordinary AllocError. D-FIXED-BACKING1 makes fixed-backing allocation fail atomically at its capacity, with no heap fallback.

The shared parity rule, quoted in D-EXEC3 and in A here. Programs run with enough stack and memory must print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable level. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different levels. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before stopping is a prefix of what the complete run prints.

The rule never excuses a wrong value, a different non-resource error, different output before the stop, or a changed budget failure. Goldens run with granted resources; exhaustion has its own fixtures, compared by report code and the prefix rule.

Runaway recursion. A release build may turn recursion into a loop, as clang did in the probe. Then a recursion that never ends does not overflow; it runs like an endless loop. Under A, only O2 may remove recursive calls, so `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it with E3012. A marked function stops at n+1 on every level. Under B, the counter stops it at the limit on every level.

Stack sizing under A. Each level sizes stacks from its own frames, as it compiles, so a quick run never waits for a release build. A marked function's need is D-STACKBOUND1's worst case on that level's actual call graph, plus call, runtime and cleanup overhead. An unmarked program's quick run gets a larger default stack. That is a risk reduction, not a guarantee.

Where the room comes from. On hosted Linux, macOS and Windows, the runtime switches the entry point onto a larger stack on the same operating-system thread. Thread identity, thread-local data and main-thread-only APIs are unaffected; Windows also updates the thread's recorded stack bounds. Signals use their own alternate stack. Embedded and interrupt entries keep D-STACKBOUND1's static `!Mem.Stack` check and never grow.

Browsers and wasm engines own the stack: a marked depth beyond the engine's published minimum is refused at build time. Tasks get a stack sized from their own entry point. Room is reserved address space committed on use, so many tasks cost address space before memory.

Outcomes when room is short. If the platform cannot ever give the declared room, the build fails with a registered error naming the depth, the need and the limit. If the room cannot be reserved when the entry or task starts, a registered start-up stop fires before any of its code runs. If an admitted guarantee is still broken, that is a Jet defect, exit 101.

Foreign code. A marked recursion whose cycle passes through foreign code is refused at build time, because foreign frames are outside the sealed call graph. A marked function called from a foreign thread's callback keeps its limit check but has no room guarantee, and a lint says so. Raw C callback restrictions are unchanged. `#Unsafe` sentries and hardened profiles add their own frame needs, which are included when that profile is built. A memory-safety fault is never treated as exhaustion.

Heap under A. Ambient memory is the machine's. A plain allocation that fails keeps today's hosted abort. A `try_` allocation against ambient memory may fail on one level and not another, but only under real memory pressure; goldens never run under pressure. A level may remove an ambient allocation it proves unused, which removes its chance to fail.

Budgets are part of meaning on every level: arenas, `mem.Fixed` backings and allocator limits. Allocations against a budget are never removed or merged in a way that changes what the budget counts, so a budget failure happens at the same call everywhere.

Reports and cleanup. The overflow report renders from reserved emergency room without allocating. Its trace collapses repeated recursive frames into one line without a count, so the trace shape matches across levels. It never prints a reached depth, because optimized levels cannot know it.

S36's cleanup boundary then runs on that reserved room. If cleanup itself runs out of room or memory, the program ends with the first report; the first fault wins. Under A, the marked-depth stop is identical on every level, including function name and source location.

Right ways elsewhere. Python fixes a configured recursion limit, raising RecursionError when it is reached. Its docs warn that the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash (docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html). Java and Go never turn recursion into loops, so runaway recursion always overflows. Rust and C release builds may turn it into a loop.

Costs, unmeasured. A adds a counter only inside marked functions, and per-level frame sizing during compiles. B adds an increment, check and decrement on every call inside a recursive cycle, and reserves room for the default depth in every program. Neither cost is measured; a gauntlet pair cell measures B's counter before ratification of an implementation.

options.name: Declared depth exact, undeclared depth depends on the machine
options.detail: A program with enough room prints the same output on every level. Without a mark, the point where it runs out of stack may differ, and only release builds may turn recursion into a loop. So quick runs and everyday builds always stop runaway recursion with the report. With `#MaxDepth(n)`, every level reserves room for n waiting calls and stops the call after n with the same report, or refuses the build and says why. Budgets fail at the same call everywhere.
options.technical:
Adds to I9: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different tiers. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before the stop is a prefix of the complete run's output. Allocator budgets are part of meaning. Only O2 may remove recursive calls."

Defines D-STACKBOUND1's `#MaxDepth(n)`. At most n activations of the marked function are live at once on one thread, counting the outermost. Depth 0 is invalid. Mutual recursion counts activations of the marked function only. The (n+1)th activation stops with a new registered depth-limit report, identical on every tier. Room for n activations is computed per tier from that tier's frames and reserved at entry or task start.

Refusals: a build error when the platform can never supply the room; a registered start-up stop when reservation fails at launch. A marked cycle through foreign code is a build error. Stacks grow by switching stacks on the same OS thread; embedded and web entries do not grow. The details are in the long-form detail.
options.code:
#MaxDepth(1000001)
fn depth(n: Int) -> Int { if n == 0 -> 0 else -> 1 + depth(n - 1) }
fn run() { print(depth(1000000)) }
$ jet run deep.jet
1000000
$ jet build --release deep.jet && ./deep
1000000

options.name: One depth limit for every recursive call
options.detail: Every call inside a recursive cycle counts against one limit of 100,000 waiting calls per thread, on every level, even where a release build turns the calls into a loop. A runaway recursion stops at exactly the same call everywhere. `#MaxDepth(n)` raises or lowers the limit for one function. Every program reserves room for its limit. Heap behaves as in A.
options.technical:
Adds the same I9 text as A, except that the depth stop is part of meaning: "every tier stops at the same activation".

A per-thread logical counter is incremented on entry to, and decremented on return from, functions in recursive cycles and dynamic calls that may recurse. Non-recursive calls are not counted, and removed recursion keeps the counter in a register. Default limit 100,000; `#MaxDepth(n)` overrides it per function.

Each tier reserves physical room for the limit from its own frames at entry or task start, with the same refusals as A. A program whose room cannot be reserved is refused before running, so the logical stop is never pre-empted by a physical one. Raw C callbacks on foreign threads cannot update the counter; Jet code reached from them is refused unless it is non-recursive.

options.name: Keep the current plan
options.detail: No rule is added. `#MaxDepth(n)` stays an input to stack reports only. Where a program runs out of stack or memory, and whether that breaks the one-meaning rule, stays unstated. Golden examples must avoid running out.
options.technical: No amendment to I9, D-STACKBOUND1 or D-ALLOCFAIL1. D-EXEC3's parity rule still says resource-adequate runs must match; exhaustion has no comparison rule.

comparisons.note: A configured recursion limit; docs warn the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash. Source: docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html.
One defined program overflowed at depth 74,446 unoptimized and finished 50,000,000 levels optimized, because the optimizer made it a loop (RESEARCH.md 6.3).
comparisons.code:
$ clang -O0 t.c && ./a.out   # stack overflow at depth 74446
$ clang -O2 t.c && ./a.out   # finishes

recommendation.why: Ordinary calls stay free and quick runs still catch runaway recursion. A program that needs depth declares it once and gets the same result on every level.
gains: A declared depth is exact on every level, or refused before running.

losses.loss: Undeclared deep recursion can stop earlier in a quick run than in a release build.
losses.mitigation: Quick runs get a larger stack, and the overflow report explains `#MaxDepth(n)` for code that needs depth.

losses.loss: In a release build, runaway recursion may run forever instead of stopping.
losses.mitigation: `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it, and a marked function stops on every level.

whyNot.reason: B counts recursive calls in every program and reserves room for a depth most programs never use.
C leaves the one-meaning rule silent exactly where levels differ.

recommendation.tradeoff: Undeclared depth depends on the machine; declared depth is exact everywhere.

decisions.title: Should the `jet run` wait be gated against Lua, LuaJIT, Python and Node?
decisions.situation: Two weeks ago the vote made the wait from typing jet run to seeing the answer a number we show but never gate. The owner now wants Jet to be the fastest scripting language, at least as fast as Lua. Lua answers a tiny script in about 2 ms, which is just the cost of starting any process. We recommend gating the wait on real scripts against Lua, LuaJIT, Python and Node. A tiny hello is gated against that start cost instead, since no program can measurably beat it.
decisions.gist: Should the wait from `jet run` to its answer fail the speed rule when Lua, LuaJIT, Python or Node answer first?
decisions.lesson: The speed rule holds every release while any required benchmark loses. Today the jet run wait is shown but never gated. Lua answers a tiny script at the cost of starting a process, about 2 ms. Gating means Jet must compile and run small scripts with almost no extra time.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Time to answer is the wall time from pressing Enter on `jet run app.jet` to the program exiting. A gated benchmark cell can fail and hold a release; a reported cell is only shown.

Two states are gated under A and B. After an edit: the script changed since its last run, and Jet's own libraries are as shipped. Repeat: nothing changed. The first run after install is shown only, because no peer rebuilds its standard library on a script run.

Beginner path: nothing to write; `jet run app.jet` just has to answer first.

Expert path: each cell names its exact commands, inputs and cache state, so anyone can rerun the numbers. `jet run -O0` and `-O1` keep their meaning; the cell times plain `jet run`.
decisions.story: Ana keeps a folder of tiny Lua scripts for renaming photos. She tries the same script in Jet. Lua answers instantly; Jet makes her wait a quarter second. Nothing in Jet's rules says that wait must go.
decisions.inWild:
$ time lua -e 'print(1)'      # about 2.2 ms here; /bin/true is 2.0-2.4 ms
$ time luajit -e 'print(1)'   # about 2.2 ms
$ time python3 -c 'print(1)'  # about 14.5 ms
$ time node -e 'console.log(1)'  # about 25.7 ms
decisions.detail:
This reopens D-PERF-RUNCELL1, ratified B on 2026-10-07, which kept the wait reported only. The owner's direction of 2026-10-23 (Jet must be the fastest scripting language, at least Lua-level) conflicts with B, so the question returns to the owner. If A or B wins, it supersedes D-PERF-RUNCELL1=B. It does not touch D-EXEC1/2/3; it gives their in-memory O0 work a gated target.

Main measured these on the reference machine on 2026-10-23, under load, as spawnSync medians. Process floor: /bin/true 2.0-2.4 ms. Peers and Jet: `jet --version` 2.2 ms. Lua and LuaJIT (`-e print`) 2.2 ms each. `python3 -c print` 14.5 ms and `node -e console.log` 25.7 ms. `jet run hello.jet` took 241-311 ms. A shebang script on its repeat path took about 319 ms (ExecBallots probe, same day): the script cache still hashes the toolchain before it starts the kept binary.

Where Jet's time goes today: the Prelude and Core front end about 160 ms, linking about 70 ms, writing the binary, spawning it as a child, and runtime start. The in-memory O0 plan (card #4741) removes link, file and spawn first, then ships a prebuilt Core image. Its hello budget is 5 ms. That budget still loses to Lua's 2.2 ms, so under A and B the hello cell stays red until Jet's own work is near zero.

State of the gauntlet. No `jet run` time-to-answer cell exists yet, reported or gated (no `run_time_to_answer` in Tools/gauntlet). Lua and LuaJIT are not gauntlet peers today (Tools/gauntlet/matrix.json rails: rust, python, node; perf rails add c and zig). A and B add both. `go run` was a peer in the 2026-10-07 A; it compiles before it runs, so it never binds and stays reported.

Noise. Lua sits on the process floor, where three runs vary by about 0.4 ms. A strict comparator there needs many interleaved samples and a confidence bound; an inconclusive cell counts as a loss under the speed rule.

HOW A AVOIDS AN UNWINNABLE CELL

The performance gate in AGENTS.md is strict. Jet/peer and Jet/ceiling must be at most 1.00, an inconclusive result counts as a loss, and every required cell needs an asm-parity ceiling reference. At the process floor that rule cannot be met. Jet, Lua and the best hand-written program each cost one process start, so no measurement can show one strictly faster.

A therefore amends the gate for process-floor cells only. Every other cell keeps the strict rule unchanged.

A process-floor cell is one whose ceiling reference does nothing but start, write its output and exit. Under A that is only the hello cell. Its ceiling reference is a minimal static program that writes the same line and exits, kept in Tools/perf/asm-parity.

On that cell, Jet passes when the 95 percent upper bound of Jet minus the ceiling is at most 0.5 ms. The same band applies against each peer on that cell only. 0.5 ms is about the floor's own spread on the reference machine (/bin/true measured 2.0-2.4 ms).

MEASUREMENT

A round runs Jet, the ceiling and each peer once, in a fresh random order. A cell needs at least 30 rounds. The bound is a one-sided 95 percent bootstrap bound on the median difference, drawn from 10,000 resamples of the paired rounds.

Noise under load: if the ceiling's own spread (90th minus 10th percentile) exceeds 0.5 ms, the machine is too busy to judge. The run is then inconclusive, which counts as a loss, and the harness records the load average with it. A busy machine can therefore never turn a cell green.

The real script cells (cli.app, text.script, files.script, formats.csv-cli) run long enough to separate. They keep the strict comparator against all four peers and need their own asm-parity ceilings. Under the existing rule, a cell without one is uncovered and fails.

WHY NOT B

No peer has a parity band today: AGENTS.md judges Rust like every other peer. B would add a new 5 percent band for lua and luajit on every run cell, which makes it a second rule. A's band covers only the hello cell, where the physics leaves nothing to compare.

The hello cell sits at the process floor, where nothing can be strictly faster. There Jet must come within 0.5 ms of a minimal hand-written program. That amends the gate for this one cell. The first run after install is shown, not gated.

The hello cell passes when the 95 percent upper bound of Jet minus its ceiling is at most 0.5 ms. Cells take at least 30 randomly ordered rounds.
