decisions.title: What does `jet run` do when the system forbids new machine code in memory?
decisions.situation: With in-memory O0, jet run writes machine code into memory and runs it there. Some hardened Linux systems forbid turning memory into runnable code, while still running program files. Jet can then put the same code in a file and run that, refuse with an error, or interpret the program. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23 for the file: same code, same output, the real signal on a crash, and only verbose mode mentions it. This records it.
decisions.gist: When the system forbids runnable memory, should `jet run` use a file, refuse, or interpret?
decisions.lesson: Some systems refuse to make memory runnable but still run program files. Jet's in-memory run needs runnable memory. Writing the same code to a file keeps the program's meaning and output identical; only the start is a little slower.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Runnable memory: memory the processor may execute. Hardened systems can forbid making memory runnable after it was written, to stop attacks that inject code. Program files stay allowed.

Where this happens: systemd services with `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes`, SELinux with the `deny_execmem` setting, and PaX kernels. Phones and consoles forbid any new code, but `jet run` does not run there.

Beginner path: nothing changes; the script runs and prints the same thing.

Expert path: `jet run --verbose` prints one line naming the refusal and the fallback. Shipped programs built with `jet build` are never affected.
decisions.story: Omar runs a nightly Jet script from a locked-down systemd service. The first in-memory run is refused by the system. He should not need to know why; the script should just run.
decisions.inWild:
$ node --jitless app.js     # V8 without runnable memory: interpreter only
$ go run .                  # always builds a file, then runs it
# LuaJIT on iOS: the JIT is disabled, interpreter only
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: fall back to writing the same O0 code to a file.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

Answer (c) fixes the fallback’s crash behaviour: every step exits with the real signal, as the built binary does. This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record.

What it amends. D-EXEC1=A allows a tiny evaluator only for a platform that forbids creating machine code at run time, and only if Jet must run there. This decision answers hosts that forbid runnable memory but still run files: they get the file fallback, not an evaluator. The evaluator clause stays only for platforms that forbid all new code, where `jet run` is not hosted.

It also narrows D-EXEC2=A: the build-to-file path survives only as this fallback, producing the same image. D-PORTABLE1/2 already keep checked native code in a file cache, so sandboxed apps meet the same rule. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1 keeps its refusal list for phones, consoles, web and bare metal. I9 holds by construction, because the bytes are the ones the in-memory path maps.

How the fallback works. Main’s plan (o0-plan.md) links the program at a fixed base inside jet, maps it RW, copies, then flips text to RX. If mmap or mprotect with PROT_EXEC fails with EPERM or EACCES, jet writes the same image to a `memfd_create` file. It maps that file read-and-execute at the same base, in the same process.

Both systemd filters allow mapping a file that is never writable and runnable at once. If memfd_create is refused, jet writes the image once to a private 0700 file in the cache directory, named by its hash, checks the hash and maps it the same way. Repeat runs reuse that file. Only if every runnable mapping is refused does jet start the file with execve, so the process is the program. If that is refused too, jet prints a diagnostic naming the policy and suggests `jet build`.

`os.executable()` still returns the script path: jet passes it to the image, which does not trust `/proc/self/exe` (see D-EXEC-RELAUNCH1). With tier-up on by default (D-EXEC-TIERUP1), both in-process steps map each tiered function the same way. The exec step exists only where no runnable mapping is allowed at all. No design can add faster code there, so the program keeps its O0 code with the same output.

Evidence. systemd’s MemoryDenyWriteExecute rejects mmap with PROT_WRITE and PROT_EXEC together, and mprotect adding PROT_EXEC. Its manual says files on non-noexec mounts and `memfd_create` still run code (systemd.exec(5)). V8’s `--jitless` mode (v7.4, 2019) runs without runnable memory; V8 measured 40 percent and 80 percent slower benchmarks. LuaJIT disables its JIT on iOS (luajit.org install notes).

Test. `systemd-run --user --wait --pipe -p MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes jet run hello.jet` prints the same bytes. Adding `-p SystemCallFilter=~memfd_create` forces the private-file step.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Start cost. The program stays in jet's process: the image is copied to an in-memory file and mapped, which costs one memory copy and no exec. Where memfd_create is refused, the cached file is written once and reused by every later run.

2. Tier-up. Both in-process steps map tiered functions the same way, so tier-up works on every system that allows any runnable mapping. A system that refuses all runnable mappings cannot run new code under any option.

No loss remains.

options.name: Run the same code from a file
options.detail: When the system refuses runnable memory, Jet writes the same machine code to a file and runs it. Output, exit status and signals are the same. Only `--verbose` mentions the fallback. The program stays in the same process, so start-up and tier-up are unchanged.
options.technical: Same linked image. On EPERM or EACCES from mmap/mprotect with PROT_EXEC, jet writes a memfd and maps it PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC at the base, in-process. Else it maps a hash-named private 0700 file in the cache directory the same way, reused across runs. Else it starts that file with execve. Else a registered diagnostic. The script path is passed to the image for `os.executable()`. Tier-up maps tiered code the same way in both in-process steps.
options.code:
$ systemd-run -p MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes jet run hello.jet
hello
$ jet run --verbose hello.jet
note: runnable memory refused (EPERM); running the same code from a file
hello

options.name: Refuse with an error
options.detail: Jet stops with an error that names the system rule and suggests `jet build` and running the binary. Nothing runs until the user acts.
options.technical: On EPERM/EACCES from mmap/mprotect PROT_EXEC, emit a registered diagnostic with the errno, the detected policy, and the `jet build` command. No file is written.
options.code:
$ systemd-run -p MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes jet run hello.jet
error: this system forbids runnable memory
  help: jet build hello.jet && ./hello

options.name: Interpret the program
options.detail: Jet keeps a small interpreter and runs the program with it on such systems. No file is written, but the program runs many times slower, and a second way of running code must match the first.
options.technical: Keeps an evaluator for O0 IR as a runtime fallback, the clause D-EXEC1 allowed. It is a second mechanism under I8 and needs its own I9 parity proof for every feature.

comparisons.note: Lua only interprets. LuaJIT turns its JIT off where runnable memory is forbidden, such as iOS, and keeps its interpreter.
CPython interprets; its experimental 3.13 JIT is off by default, so nothing changes.
`--jitless` runs V8 with no runnable memory, interpreter only; V8 measured 40 to 80 percent slower benchmarks.
`go run` always writes a binary file and runs it, so it never needs runnable memory.
Compiles methods into memory with LLVM as they are first called; `--compile=min` mostly interprets instead.
`zig run` writes the binary into its cache and runs it.

recommendation.why: You ruled this in chat on 2026-10-23. It is the same code, so meaning, output and crash signals cannot drift, and users on hardened systems need no flags.
gains: Scripts run unchanged on hardened Linux services.
One code generator and one runtime; no interpreter to keep in step.
Start-up and tier-up stay in-process on hardened systems.

whyNot.reason: It stops working scripts for a reason the user cannot fix inside the script.
A second way of running code is many times slower and must match the first forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: A runs the same code from an in-memory or cached file, so hardened systems lose nothing.

decisions.title: Does `jet run` speed up hot code on its own while the program runs?
decisions.situation: In-memory jet run compiles quickly with simple code, so long loops run slower than in a built program. Jet can rebuild busy functions with faster code on a background thread while the program runs. That could be on by default for jet run, behind a flag, or replaced by compiling everything slower but better first. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23: on by default for jet run, entering faster code at loop heads too, with identical output. This records it.
decisions.gist: Should `jet run` rebuild hot functions with faster code by default, only behind a flag, or never?
decisions.lesson: Quick-start code is simple, so long loops are slower than in a built program. Rebuilding only the busy functions in the background keeps start-up fast and lets long scripts catch up. The program's output never changes; only its speed does.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. O0 is Jet's quick-start code level, used by `jet run`. O1 is the level `jet build` uses. Tier-up means rebuilding a busy function at O1 while the program runs, then switching calls to the new code.

Beginner path: nothing to write. Short scripts finish before anything is rebuilt; long ones speed up on their own.

Expert path: `jet run -O0` keeps every function at O0 with no tier-up. `jet run -O1` compiles everything at O1 before starting. Shipped programs from `jet build` never tier up unless their author opts in.
decisions.story: Mia's script sums thirty million numbers. Built with `jet build`, it takes 264 ms. With `jet run` it takes about twice as long, while Node takes 113 ms. Nobody should need a flag to fix that.
decisions.inWild:
$ luajit loop.lua    # interpreter, then a trace JIT after 56 loop iterations
$ node loop.js       # V8 tiers up hot code and loops on its own
$ python3 loop.py    # no JIT unless built with the experimental one
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: tier-up on by default for jet run.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

Answer (b) makes loop-head entry part of A today, not later. This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record.

What it amends. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B made the in-program optimizer opt-in (`--adaptive`) for long-running shipped programs. This decision turns the same mechanism on by default for `jet run` and `jet dev` only. Shipped binaries keep D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's opt-in. D-EXEC1=A's levels stand: O0 serves `jet run`, and `-O0`, `-O1`, `-O2` pin a level.

Bounds. D-EXEC3=A applies: a speed-up used only at O1 needs a proof or a checker. I9 holds through D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's forced mode, which tiers up every function at once; every golden must print the same under it. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A covers recursion depth: O1 frames differ in size, so undeclared depth may change, while `#MaxDepth(n)` stays exact.

Mechanism, from Main's plan (o0-plan.md, lane L4). O0 code counts calls at function entry and calls other functions through a per-program table. One compiler thread stays alive after the jump. It rebuilds hot functions at O1 from the same IR with the same code generator. It maps the new code read-and-execute, never writable and runnable at once, then swaps the table entry.

The O1 code calls the program's own runtime copy, not the compiler's. Under the file fallback (D-EXEC-NOEXEC1), tiered code is mapped from a new in-memory file; after an exec step tier-up is off.

Loops. Swapping at function entry never helps a long loop inside `fn run`, which is entered once. That is exactly Main's loop benchmark: jet run 509 ms against node 113 and luajit 160. Tier-up therefore also needs entry into O1 code at loop heads (on-stack replacement). D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1 excluded that for shipped binaries; here it is required.

Precedent. .NET's quick-start level initially skipped methods with loops, because without loop-head entry they stayed slow; .NET 7 enabled on-stack replacement to fix that. LuaJIT records traces after 56 loop iterations by default. V8 tiers up through several compilers, also at loop heads.

Costs. The compiler thread uses one core while it compiles, and its memory stays mapped. Timing changes as code swaps, so benchmarks need warm-up; `-O0` and `-O1` give fixed code.

options.name: On by default for `jet run`
options.detail: `jet run` starts at O0. Busy functions and loops are rebuilt at O1 on one background thread and switched in. Output is identical. `-O0` turns it off; `-O1` compiles everything up front. Shipped programs are unchanged.
options.technical: Entry counters and loop-head counters in O0 code; calls through a per-program function table; one compiler thread kept after the jump. O1 code is mapped RX and bound to the program's runtime symbols. Swap at the next call, plus loop-head entry with the slot frame copied. A forced mode tiers every function for I9 goldens.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet
30000000 iterations: 4021
// hot loop rebuilt at O1 while it ran
$ jet run -O0 loop.jet   # no tier-up

options.name: Only behind a flag
options.detail: `jet run` stays at O0 everywhere. Users who want faster loops pass `--adaptive`, the flag shipped programs already use. Speed is predictable, but most users never learn the flag.
options.technical: D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's opt-in `--adaptive` applies to `jet run` too; without it no compiler thread survives the jump and no counters are emitted.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet            # O0 all the way
$ jet run --adaptive loop.jet # rebuilds hot code

options.name: Compile everything at O1 first
options.detail: `jet run` skips O0 and compiles the whole program at O1 before it starts. No background work, but every run waits for the slower compile, including tiny scripts.
options.technical: Changes D-EXEC1's level for `jet run` from O0 to O1. No counters, no table swaps, no compiler thread; start-up pays O1 compile time for every function.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet
// every function compiled at O1 before the first line runs

decisions.title: What does `os.executable()` name under `jet run`, and how does a script relaunch itself?
decisions.situation: Some programs start a copy of themselves, for example to test crash handling or run workers. They ask for their own executable and run it again. Under in-memory jet run the process file is jet itself, so the program could get jet instead of itself. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23 that the call returns the script path, and that starting that path runs it through the same jet at the same level. This records it.
decisions.gist: Under `jet run`, should `os.executable()` return the script, the `jet` program, or a built copy?
decisions.lesson: A program that relaunches itself asks for its own executable. Under `jet run` there is no separate program file, only the script and `jet`. Returning the script keeps the call meaning the file that starts this program.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. `os.executable()` returns the path of the file that started the running program. Relaunch means starting a new process of the same program, usually with different arguments.

Beginner path: `process.cmd([os.executable(), "worker"])` starts the same program again, after `jet build` and under `jet run`.

Expert path: after `jet build`, the call names the binary. Under `jet run` it names the absolute script path. A script with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` and the exec bit runs directly when started.
decisions.story: Sam's test program starts itself six times to check that cleanup runs on every kind of exit. Built, it works. Under the old in-memory runner it started `jet` with the wrong arguments and every case failed.
decisions.inWild:
$ python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'   # the python program
$ node -p process.execPath                         # the node program
$ go run .   # os.Executable() is the built copy in Go's cache
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: os.executable() returns the script path under jet run.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record. Source card #4346, found on 2026-10-02 under the old in-memory runner, where the call returned jet.

Today. `jet run` builds `.jet/build/<stem>` and starts it as a child, so the call returns that file. A shebang script on its repeat path returns the kept copy in `~/.cache/jet/scripts`. The ExecBallots probe confirmed both on 2026-10-23. So #4346 does not show today; it returns with in-memory O0, where `/proc/self/exe` is `jet`.

What it touches. I9 holds with one stated meaning: the file that starts this program. After `jet build` that is the binary; under `jet run` it is the script. D-SCRIPT-ENTRY1=A makes a script with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` start through `jet run`, so its path starts the same program. No ratified decision is reversed. The contract row in Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md (line 1754, "Return process facts") gains this sentence.

`Examples/features/io/sys_executable.jet` still says the call names `jet` under `jet run`; that comment comes from the old runner and must be rewritten.

Implementation, from Main's plan (o0-plan.md). The runtime reads the path from `/proc/self/exe` today (JetRuntime CompilerHost.jet). Under the in-memory runner that is `jet`, so jet passes the absolute script path to the image on its start stack. The runtime uses it when present. Built binaries keep `/proc/self/exe`, which is absolute, unlike AT_EXECFN.

The file fallback (D-EXEC-NOEXEC1) passes the same path. `process.argv()[0]` becomes the script path as given, which is what the kernel passes for a shebang script.

Edge case, settled by answer (a). cleanup_matrix.jet relaunches process.cmd([os.executable(), path]), and so do the distributed, storage and watcher examples. Their sources have no shebang and no exec bit, so the kernel alone would refuse to start them.

Rule under A, written beside executable() in core-library.md: starting the running program’s own script path runs it through the same jet at the same level. Every existing relaunch keeps working, and #4346’s six identical traces hold under jet run and after jet build.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Starting a script without a shebang. Jet code never needs the kernel to do it: under ruling (a), process.cmd with the program's own script path runs it through the same jet at the same level. Outside programs start a .jet file with jet run, as they do today.

2. Files beside the executable. Under jet run they resolve beside the script, where its files live. A built binary keeps its own folder.

No loss remains.

options.name: Return the script path
options.detail: Under `jet run`, `os.executable()` returns the absolute path of the script. After `jet build` it returns the binary. Starting that path runs the same program again. `process.argv()[0]` is the script path as given.
options.technical: jet passes the absolute script path to the loaded image; the runtime uses it instead of /proc/self/exe. Built binaries are unchanged. The file fallback passes the same path. Starting the own script path reuses the same jet and level.

options.name: Return `jet`, add a relaunch call
options.detail: `os.executable()` always names the process file: `jet` under `jet run`. A new call returns the full command that starts this program again, such as `jet run app.jet`. Existing relaunching programs must switch to it.
options.technical: Keeps `/proc/self/exe` on every tier. Adds a public API, say `process.self_command() -> [String]`, returning `[jet, "run", script]` or `[binary]`. Migrates cleanup_matrix and three other examples. A new public API needs its own surface review.

options.name: Return a built copy
options.detail: On the first call, Jet writes a real program file for this script into its cache and returns that path, as `go run` does. Relaunches start the built copy. The first call costs a full build and link.
options.technical: The runtime asks the host to link the same image to a file, keyed by the run's inputs, and returns its path. The cost lands on the first call only. Keeps a script-run cache alive.

comparisons.note: `arg[-1]` is the interpreter and `arg[0]` the script; a relaunch joins both.
`sys.executable` is the python program; `sys.argv[0]` is the script.
`process.execPath` is node; `process.argv[1]` is the script; `fork` relaunches a module.
`go run` builds a binary, cached since Go 1.24; `os.Executable()` names that built copy.
`Base.julia_cmd()` gives the julia command with its options; `PROGRAM_FILE` is the script.
`zig run` builds into its cache; `std.fs.selfExePath` names that built copy.

recommendation.why: You ruled this in chat on 2026-10-23. The call keeps one meaning, the file that starts this program, and relaunch code needs no change.
gains: Existing relaunching programs work under `jet run` and after `jet build`.
No new API and no build on first call.

whyNot.reason: It changes the answer per level and breaks every existing relaunch until migrated.
The first call pays a full build, and it keeps a script cache alive.

recommendation.tradeoff: One meaning, the file that starts this program, and relaunch code works on every level.

decisions.title: Layout control: packed structs, overlapping fields and relative pointers
decisions.situation: Low-level programs sometimes need exact memory control: structs without padding, fields sharing the same bytes, or links stored as small offsets so a saved file loads without fixing addresses. Jai offers all three as language features. Jet offers C layout, alignment, column layout and a byte reader, but none of these three. The vote decides which Jet adds; we recommend all three, each checked so safe code never misreads memory.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add packed structs, overlapping fields and relative pointers, like Jai's #no_padding, #place and *~s32?
decisions.lesson: Padding is unused space the compiler adds so fields line up; packing removes it. Overlapping fields share the same bytes, as in a C union. A relative pointer stores the distance from itself to its target. So a block of data still works after it is moved or saved as one piece.
decisions.story: Yuki writes a save-game format and a network protocol. The protocol header must match the wire byte for byte, and the save file holds a linked list she wants to load with one read and no pointer fixing. Jai handles both; in Jet she writes byte code by hand.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

PACKED UNDER A. `#Layout(c, packed)` removes padding. Fields use unaligned loads and stores. Every borrow position takes a copy: reference, method receiver, view parameter and interpolation. Explicit `&` or `^` on a packed field is a registered error, as is a method that would change a packed field through a reference. Assign the field instead. Packed fields cost unaligned loads and stores on some processors. Atomic and Rel fields are not allowed in a packed struct.

With `align(N)`, the struct's alignment is N while fields stay unpadded (D-PLACE1's maximum rule, natural alignment 1). `Header.$layout.size` is 5.

OVERLAY. `#Layout(overlay)` starts every field at offset 0. Its size is the largest field plus trailing padding. Fields must be plain data: integers, floats, fixed byte lists and plain layouts, as `uninit` requires (E0423). Reading a field is safe when every bit pattern is valid for its type (integers, floats, byte lists). A field with invalid patterns, such as Bool or an enum, is read only inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.

Jai `#place` (partial overlap) maps to an overlay of a struct and a list: `#Layout(overlay) struct V { p: XYZ, xyz: [F32#3] }`. One mechanism covers both. No separate field marker is added.

RELATIVE POINTERS. `Rel<T, I32>` holds a signed offset from the field's own address. Zero means none, so a node cannot point to itself and `Rel<T, I32>?` costs no extra space. Rel is a field type, not a pointer: safe code follows it only through `mem.Image`, a loaded byte buffer. `follow` checks the target lies inside the image, is aligned and has room for T.

`img.link(from, to)` sets an offset, failing when the distance does not fit or a side is outside the image. A struct holding a Rel cannot be copied or moved out of an image (registered error), because its offset would point elsewhere. `follow` returns a view whose lifetime is the image's. `rel.get()` without an image needs `#Unsafe`, matching S58's pointer rules.

Image checks are bounds checks, so the unchecked_bounds power of D-JAI-EXPERT1 removes them like others. Layout types must use sized fields. Jet's Int is arbitrary precision and is refused under `#Layout(c)` (D-REPRC1). These forms follow S58's `use core.mem` discovery rule like `#Layout(c)` today. JAI. Source concepts map. Jai's relative-pointer encoding (zero null, high-bit XOR, Blow GQj8fzxpdrk 00:03:11) differs, so saved Jai bytes do not load unchanged.

Tsoding found built-in support catches type errors his hand-written C missed (_HGkhvpCbsk 01:46:44, mining notes). Column layout (Jai's user-level SOA) is already `#Layout(columnar)` (D-SOA1).

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai Appendix C (#no_padding, #place). Blow Z0tsNFZLxSU and GQj8fzxpdrk (relative pointers, 2017). Rust made references to misaligned packed fields an error after years of undefined behaviour.

options.name: All three, checked
options.detail: `packed` removes padding. `overlay` starts every field at offset 0, for plain-data fields only. `Rel<T, I32>` stores an offset from its own address and is followed through `mem.Image`, which checks bounds, alignment and type.
options.technical: `#Layout(c, packed)`. `#Layout(overlay)` with plain-data fields. `Rel<T, I8|I16|I32|I64>` field type, zero meaning none. `mem.Image` wraps loaded bytes: `root<T>()` and `follow(rel)` return views into the image, `link(from, to)!` failing when out of range or outside the image. Raw `rel.get()` needs `#Unsafe`.
options.code:
#Layout(c, packed) struct Header { tag: U8, length: U32 }      // Header.$layout.size == 5
#Layout(overlay) struct Bits32 { f: F32, u: U32 }               // u reads f's bytes
#Layout(c) struct Node { next: Rel<Node, I32>?, value: I64 }
img :: mem.Image.load(bytes)?
first :: img.root<Node>()?
second :: img.follow(first.next)?          // checked; a view into img

options.name: Packed and overlapping only
options.detail: packed and overlay of A, with A's rules. Links in saved data are stored as indexes into a list.
options.technical: As A without Rel and mem.Image.

nodes: [Node]                                // links are indexes

comparisons.note: References to possibly misaligned packed fields are rejected; reading a union field needs unsafe.

comparisons.note: packed struct and extern union are explicit layout forms.

struct Header { uint8_t tag; uint32_t length; };

decisions.title: Require explicit executable entries in ordinary files
decisions.gist: Should ordinary files require an explicit run entry?
decisions.lesson: An entry is the function that starts a program. Jet currently wraps loose file statements in an implicit run function. This choice removes that file shortcut. Interactive cells still receive a wrapper, and libraries still need no entry.
decisions.story: Mira moves a small script into an application. She wants to see where execution starts without discovering hidden startup work.
decisions.detail:
Owner-selected contract awaiting formal Tower ratification. Related historical work: #1627 and #3122. No compiler work or runtime verification was performed during preparation.

Beginner review prompted explicit file-role, initializer, safe-fix, typed-entry, and export explanations. No runtime result is claimed from those illustrative examples. Entry source forms are grounded in examples/features/cli/typed_entry_args.jet and examples/features/comptime/comptime_block.jet.

Fresh review findings were retained. The author resolved each through the contract and linked card criteria. Review metadata describes that sequence; it does not claim an independent rerun or runtime proof.

options.name: Explicit files, implicit interactive cells
options.detail:
Ordinary application targets declare an existing explicit application entry. Existing build/dev/test override-only sources retain their own entry roles. Library compilation, imports, and test discovery do not require an entry. Loose statements in any ordinary source are errors, not ignored code. A runtime top-level initializer is rejected; the author must move its work into a function.

REPL submissions and notebook cells remain interactive inputs, not ordinary files. Their host supplies the entry internally. An ordinary-source executable export needs a legal explicit entry. Refuse unsafe wrapping or a mixed-entry export rather than guessing. Declaration-only exports need no wrapper.
options.technical:
The interview selects this amendment. Amend D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1, D-ENTRY-ORDER1, and run-specific D-CMDOVERRIDE1 wording. Existing explicit entry forms keep their signature, visibility, multiplicity, and binding rules. Basic forms are fn run() and fn run(args: T), where T is a #CLI type. Do not invent a second entry or change typed argument parsing.

A selected application target needs its resolved source-declared application entry. A declaration-only library can be compiled or imported without one. Test discovery runs tests without a dummy application entry. Trying to execute a library as an application requires an entry; the filename alone does not change its role.

Compile-time work finishes while the compiler builds the program, before launch. Existing explicit compile-time definitions remain valid:

```jet
@answer :: 1 + 1
fn run() { print(@answer) }
```

Runtime initialization cannot remain hidden at file scope. This is rejected rather than silently moved:

```jet
use core.testing as testing
root :: testing.temp_dir("demo")
fn run() { print(root) }
```

The author can move that initialization into run when only run uses it. If another function refers to root, blindly moving the binding would break its scope. The automatic fix must refuse that relocation and explain that the value must be passed explicitly or initialized inside a suitable function.

For the simple loose hello program, jet fix hello.jet offers the existing source-edit workflow and produces the fn run() example shown in option A. Preserve statement order, declarations, comments, captures, return behavior, and source locations. Register exact what/why/fix diagnostics and snapshots. Never convert a backend rejection into a user error.

A cell containing print("hello") still runs directly. The host creates its entry internally; users do not edit that wrapper. Exporting executable ordinary source writes fn run() { print("hello") }. Exporting only declarations writes those declarations without a dummy entry. No notebook visual or teaching-path redesign is included.

Remove ordinary-file script lowering and use the canonical explicit-entry path internally. Migrate all callers, examples, generated fixtures, tests, format/LSP projections, and live explanations. Ahead-of-time binaries, run/dev, the interpreter, and applicable web execution preserve the same meaning. These examples isolate entry behavior; effect permission remains a separate requirement.

Command roles remain distinct. jet run and a stock application-launch path require an explicit application entry: fn run or an existing checked metadata-selected callable. jet build compiles its selected output or invokes its existing explicit build override. Libraries need no run. Override-only @build.jet remains valid.

jet dev invokes its selected explicit dev override; override-only @dev.jet needs no dummy run. Otherwise stock dev launches the explicit application entry. jet test invokes its explicit test override or stock test discovery; neither requires a dummy run. Preserve absent-override defaults. Only fn build with its existing BuildContext signature is build-only.

Wrapping fixes inspect checked command and import roles. Never synthesize an entry in library, imported, or test-only sources if that changes selection or multiplicity. If app.jet imports loose helper.jet, do not add a second fn run to the helper. Refuse that automatic edit and explain how to use an explicitly called function.

Interactive execution preserves existing persistent session scope. A host entry must not turn cross-cell bindings into discarded function locals. Prove a binding created in one submission and mutated in the next, imported/declaration visibility, move/borrow state, failures, and reruns. Reuse existing session storage and checked semantics, not a second runtime model.

Declaration-only export preserves existing explicit entries. Executable export without a conflicting entry emits one legal wrapper when meaning is preserved. A notebook mixing an existing run and separately executed cells refuses automatic ordinary-source export rather than guessing a merge. It changes no output file and explains how to consolidate one entry first. Never silently produce a lossy export.

Tier proof observes actual execution identity. Exercise AOT output, normal run/dev, forced interpreter, and existing run_jit_once/dev_iteration JIT paths. Require Cranelift evidence where applicable; interpreter fallback cannot pass a JIT row. Keep applicable web proof separately identified.

decisions.title: User-defined equality for Map and Set keys
decisions.gist: How should a type tell Map and Set when two of its values count as the same key?
decisions.lesson: A Map finds values by key; a Set keeps one copy of each value. Today both compare raw fields, so values a type calls equal can become separate entries. Every option lets a type define key sameness. They differ in how much the author writes, and whether ==, sorting and lookup can ever disagree.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. A Map stores values under keys, like a dictionary stores definitions under words. A Set stores each value once, like a guest list. Equality decides whether two keys are the same. Ordering decides which key sorts first, and Jet keeps Map keys sorted. Hashing turns a value into a number that picks a storage bucket quickly. It never decides sameness on its own.

Today Jet checks a key by looking at its fields. A struct whose fields are numbers, text or other such structs is accepted, and Map compares those fields exactly. A hand-written equal function on the type is ignored by Map. So == can say two emails match while the Map stores both.

Option A adds one small trait, KeyBy. A type writes one function, key, that returns an ordinary value such as lowercase text. Jet builds ==, ordering, sorting, Map lookup and Set hashing from that one value. Because everything comes from one value, the rules cannot contradict each other. The author proves no comparison laws and writes no hashing code. Choosing the right key is still the author's job, checked by ordinary tests.

Option B keeps today's field rules and adds a wrapper, Key<T>. The author writes equal, compare and hash by hand, then wraps every key with Key.new. Option C honours the same three hand-written functions directly, with no wrapper. B and C both need a new public hashing API. Both trust the author to keep three functions consistent.

Reading the code: x := ... creates a changeable variable. [Email:Int]{} creates an empty Map from Email to Int. m[k] = 1 stores 1 under k. m.get(k) ?? 0 looks k up and gives 0 when it is missing. impl Email.KeyBy { ... } attaches the KeyBy trait to Email.

Edge cases. Under A a lookup cannot miss a stored key, because the key value uses Jet's own lawful comparisons. Under B and C a wrong hand-written rule can make a lookup miss, though it never corrupts memory. Re-inserting an equal key replaces the value and keeps the first stored key, under every option.
decisions.story: Ana is porting the Jet command-line tool from Rust. It keeps tables keyed by file paths, and a//b and a/b must land in one entry, exactly as in Rust. Her sign-up demo has the same problem with emails that differ only in capital letters.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comparability.jet:367-375 and 422-465 accept a Map key by walking its fields; a hand-written equal is not consulted. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Literals.jet:552-553 holds the E0502 refusal text, which also refuses lists as keys.

crates/jet-foundation/src/Collections.rs:75-100 keeps separate Map-key and Set-element checks. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:2681 stores Map in a sorted BTreeMap. No public Hash or KeyHasher declaration exists today.

Scope. Card #4499 needs path keys for the command-line port. The OSPath type and its component rules belong to D-OSPATH-NATIVE1 (#4378), which uses whichever mechanism this vote picks. Under A this ballot amends D-MAP-KEY1=A twice: KeyBy types become keys, and lists of eligible keys become keys. Sorted Map iteration stays. Examples are proposed, not run.

options.name: One comparison key (KeyBy)
options.detail:
A type writes one function that returns its comparison key. Jet derives ==, ordering, sorting, Map lookup and Set hashing from that key, so they always agree. Ordinary structs keep today's automatic field rules unchanged.

Beginner: write fn key(self) returning the value that should decide sameness, often one field. Expert: return a tuple for a multi-part key, or a list for a path-like key. No separate equality, ordering or hash laws need proving, because all three come from one value.

Whether that value matches the program's idea of identity is still the author's choice, and ordinary tests check it. For example, key returning text.lower(self.address) makes Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com one entry. Returning self.address unchanged makes them two entries again.

Types that already hand-write equal or compare and are used as keys are migrated by jet fix, so no existing behavior changes. OSPath from D-OSPATH-NATIVE1 uses this mechanism. Its key is its list of path components, so a//b and a/b are one entry.
options.technical:
Core adds trait KeyBy with one method, fn key(self) -> K, where K is the trait's associated key type (D-LIB2). key must be pure and infallible: no effect row and no error suffix. Otherwise E0502 names the effect or error.

K must be Map-eligible for Map use and Set-eligible for Set use. Eligible now includes [T] for eligible T, ordered item by item with a shorter prefix first. K may be another KeyBy type; a cycle is E0502. Float stays ineligible.

A KeyBy type gets Equatable, Comparable and internal hashing derived from key. A hand-written equal or compare, or a signed marker for those traits, on the same type is a new error naming both declarations. A type with hand-written equal or compare and no KeyBy stops being a key; E0502 suggests KeyBy.

Migration for those types, which are keys today through the field walk (Comparability.jet:446-453). jet fix finds each one used as a Map key or Set element. If its equal compares one derived value, f(self.x) == f(other.x), KeyBy returns f(self.x) and the hand-written equal and compare are deleted. Otherwise KeyBy returns the tuple of all fields, exactly today's Map identity. The old equal becomes the named method equal_by_rule, and existing == calls on that type are rewritten to it, so both behaviors stay.

In the second case, equality reached through generic code, such as list contains or assert_eq, cannot be rewritten at its site. jet fix lists those uses for review.

The implementing type may not hold Shared, Cell, Atomic, weak or native-handle fields at any depth, so its key cannot change while stored. Such fields are not key-eligible today either, so no current key type is excluded. Each insert, get or remove calls key once on its argument. A computed key is stored beside its entry; a key that only reads fields is read in place.

Re-inserting an equal key replaces the value and keeps the first stored key. Set union and intersection keep left-side values; difference keeps left-only values. Iteration follows key order. Every tier uses the same derived code, and no public hasher or seed is exposed.

options.name: Explicit Key wrapper
options.detail:
Keep today's field rules for ordinary keys. Add one Core wrapper, Key<T>, whose Map and Set behaviour calls the type's hand-written equal, compare and hash.

Beginner: learn the wrapper and three trait functions for any custom key. Expert: write all three and keep them consistent; wrap at every insert and lookup. A wrong rule can make lookups miss but cannot corrupt memory.
options.technical:
Key.new(^T) owns its value; T needs Equatable, Comparable for Map and Hash for Set. Missing traits are front-end errors. The new public trait is Hash.hash(self, state: &KeyHasher). KeyHasher.write(value) accepts any Set-eligible value; its seed is runtime-owned and never exposed.

Laws are the author's duty: compare says Equal exactly when equal is true, ordering is consistent, and equal values hash alike. The compiler checks signatures, purity and immutability only. Replacement, removal and Set representative rules match A.

options.name: Honour hand-written traits directly
options.detail:
Map and Set call the type's hand-written equal, compare and hash with no wrapper. Ordinary structs keep today's field rules.

Beginner: ordinary Map syntax, but three trait functions to write. Expert: full control over each rule, with the duty to keep all three consistent. A wrong rule can make lookups miss but cannot corrupt memory.
options.technical: Uses the same new public Hash and KeyHasher API, laws and immutability checks as B. Map uses compare; Set uses hash then equal. The compiler checks signatures, purity and immutability, not mathematical laws.

comparisons.note: Rust Path compares components, while BTreeMap and HashSet use key traits.

recommendation.why: One key value makes equality, sorting, Map and Set agree by construction. Authors write one short function, prove no comparison laws and never write hashing code.
gains: ==, sorting, Map and Set can never disagree.
A custom key needs one short function and no hash code.
No new public hashing API is needed.

losses.loss: A computed key is stored once beside each entry.
losses.mitigation: computing and storing are separate costs. key runs once per insert, get or remove, never during the search. Only computed keys are stored, about the key's own size per entry; keys that only read fields are read in place and add nothing.

losses.loss: Existing key types with a hand-written equal or compare stop being keys until migrated.
losses.mitigation: jet fix migrates each one. A simple equal becomes the key; otherwise the key is all fields, as Map uses today, and == calls move to the old equal, now equal_by_rule.

whyNot.reason: Wrapping every key adds ceremony, and authors must still keep three hand-written functions consistent.
Three hand-written functions can quietly disagree and make lookups miss. It also needs a new public hashing API.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks for one key function instead of three. Its costs are one stored copy of a computed key and a jet fix migration for key types that already hand-write equal or compare.

Check list keys order item by item, re-insert keeps the first key, Set union keeps left values and sorted iteration stays.

Migration: an Email with hand-written equal comparing lower(address) becomes KeyBy with that key. A type with an unrecognized equal gets the all-fields key and equal_by_rule, and its Map results and == results match before and after jet fix.

decisions.situation: Jet's Map is a lookup table from keys to values, and its Set is a collection that keeps each value once. Today both decide whether two keys are the same by comparing their raw stored fields, even when the type has its own idea of equality. So Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com, or the file paths a//b and a/b, become two separate entries. That is why the Jet command-line port cannot keep its path-keyed tables faithful to the Rust original. Beginners meet it as == saying true while the Map disagrees, and experts porting code meet it as quiet duplicate entries. You are deciding how a type tells Map and Set what the same key means. We recommend that a type name one plain comparison key, from which Jet derives equality, sorting, hashing and Map and Set behaviour, so they can never disagree.

decisions.title: Choosing the order of a priority queue or ordered set when you create it
decisions.situation: A priority queue hands back items in order, and an ordered set keeps its items sorted. In Jet both always use the item type's own order today. So a queue that should serve the highest score first, or jobs by deadline, needs a new wrapper type just to flip or change the order. You decide whether these containers accept an order when they are made; we recommend the same by and by_desc spelling lists already use for sorting.
decisions.gist: Should a priority queue or ordered set take its sorting order when you create it, instead of needing a wrapper type?
decisions.lesson: A priority queue always gives back the smallest item first. An ordered set, called Rank in Jet, keeps items sorted. Both use the type's own order today. A lets you pass an order when you create one, with the by and by_desc words lists already use for sort_by. B adds one Core wrapper that reverses any order. C makes the order part of the container's type.
decisions.explainer:
A priority queue is a container whose pop always returns the item that comes first in some order. An ordered set keeps its items sorted and unique. Jet's PriorityQueue and Rank both take the order from the item type. Numbers and text sort ascending, and a struct uses the order its type declares (D-KEY-TRAITS1).

That is fine until one program needs two orders for the same type. Popping the largest score, serving jobs by deadline, or keeping names sorted by length all need a new wrapper type today. Lists already avoid this, because sort_by and sort_by_desc take a key function.

Option A brings the list spelling to these containers. PriorityQueue.by(key) and PriorityQueue.by_desc(key) make a queue ordered by that key. Rank.by and Rank.by_desc make an ordered set the same way. new() and from(xs) keep the type's own order. When two containers with different orders combine, the result keeps the receiver's order.

Option B adds one Core wrapper, Desc<T>, that reverses any order, and keeps everything else. Option C writes the order into the container type, as C++ and Gren do.
decisions.story: Priya builds a leaderboard that should always pop the highest score. Jet's priority queue pops the lowest. She writes a HighScore wrapper type with its own comparison, converts every score into it and back, and her teammate asks why a number needed a new type.
decisions.detail:
Current state: PriorityQueue.new() and PriorityQueue.from(xs) take no order or key, and Rank.new() and Rank.from(xs) likewise (core-library.md:282, 284). Order and equality come from the type through D-KEY-TRAITS1=A (KeyBy per type). Lists already have sort_by((item) -> key or (a, b) -> Ordering) and sort_by_desc((item) -> key) (core-library.md:558-559). The v3 A2-langs re-read confirmed the gap (note 1).

Sources: Gren talk (DuGy1tmKP-w 32:06-33:53), where a reverse-sorted dictionary is made by passing a different compare module, and type classes allow only one instance per type. Roc (DzhIprQan68, about 27:00) makes the same point. Claim languages-a:Q28, attached to #4499.

Proven approaches. Java's PriorityQueue and TreeMap and Kotlin's PriorityQueue take a comparator at construction, and this is the most used form in practice. Rust's BinaryHeap takes order from Ord, so a max-heap of a custom key needs Reverse<T> or a newtype. That wrapper friction is a frequent Rust forum topic.

C++ std::priority_queue and Gren's Dict take the comparator as a type or module parameter. That is precise but makes the order part of every signature. Python's heapq takes no key, so programs push (key, item) tuples by hand.

Option A reuses Jet's existing sort_by vocabulary. The key function must be pure, which sema already checks for callbacks. Combining two containers with different orders uses the receiver's order, as Java's addAll does.

options.name: Pass the order when you create the container
options.detail: PriorityQueue.by(key) and PriorityQueue.by_desc(key) make a queue ordered by a key function. Rank.by and Rank.by_desc do the same for ordered sets. new() and from(xs) keep the type's own order. Combining two containers keeps the receiver's order.
options.technical: The container stores one pure key function and compares keys with the key type's order. by_desc reverses that comparison. The key function must have an empty effect row, the rule callbacks already follow. from(xs) gains by and by_desc variants. Equality between two containers compares items and ignores order functions.
options.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.by_desc((s: Score) -> s.points)
&scores.push(Score{name: "Ana", points: 90})
best :: &scores.pop()   // highest points first

by_len :: Rank.by((w: String) -> w.len())

options.name: One Core wrapper that reverses order
options.detail: Core gains Desc<T>, a wrapper whose order is the reverse of T's. Containers keep using the type's order. Any other order still needs a custom wrapper type.
options.technical: One generic struct with a reversed KeyBy implementation. Items are wrapped on the way in and unwrapped on the way out. Orders other than reversal, such as by deadline, still need a new type.
options.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.new()
&scores.push(Desc{Score{name: "Ana", points: 90}})
best :: (&scores.pop()).value

options.name: The order is part of the container's type
options.detail: An ordered container's type names its order, such as PriorityQueue(Score, ByPointsDesc). Two queues with different orders are different types.
options.technical: The order becomes a build-time parameter of the container type (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1). Every signature that holds such a container must name the order.
options.code:
ByPointsDesc :: order((s: Score) -> s.points, .Desc)
scores := PriorityQueue(Score, ByPointsDesc).new()

comparisons.note: PriorityQueue and TreeSet take a comparator when they are created.
comparisons.code:
var q = new PriorityQueue<Job>(Comparator.comparing(Job::deadline));
var s = new TreeSet<String>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

comparisons.note: Order comes from Ord; a max-heap or custom key needs a wrapper.
The comparator is a template parameter of the queue type.

recommendation.why: A lets one program use several orders for one type without inventing wrapper types, and it reuses the by and by_desc words Jet already teaches for sorting lists. Java and Kotlin show this is the form people use most.
recommendation.tradeoff: An ordered container now carries one small key function.
gains: Max-heaps and custom orders need no wrapper type.
Sorting lists and ordering containers use the same words.
The type's own order stays the default.

losses.loss: Two containers built with different orders can be combined, and the result silently follows one of them.
losses.mitigation: The rule is fixed and documented: the receiver's order wins, as in Java. The editor shows each container's order in its hover, so the choice is visible.

whyNot.reason: B only covers reversal; ordering by a field still needs a hand-written wrapper type.
C makes every signature spell the order, which is heavy for a beginner and rarely needed.

Check that a key function with effects is rejected with the callback diagnostic. Check that union and merge keep the receiver's order. Check that new() and from(xs) behavior is unchanged on every tier.

decisions.title: Code values and macros that paste code at the call site
decisions.situation: A macro is a function whose body is pasted where it is called, so it can wrap your code, time it or loop around it. Jai has macros and lets build code pass pieces of code around as values. Jet has neither in everyday code, and its rules still forbid macros forever, so ported Jai code needs awkward rewrites. The vote decides whether Jet adds checked macros and code values; we recommend adding them for everyone, with text-to-code only for experts.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add Jai-style macros and code values, and who may use them?
decisions.lesson: A code value is a piece of source held before it runs. Pasting puts it somewhere. A macro is a function whose body is pasted at each call. Jai is a game language that uses macros widely. Whichever option wins, pasted code is checked like code you typed, and errors point at your line.
decisions.story: Mei ports a Jai profiler that wraps any block in timing code, and a renderer that loops over visible entities with custom loop logic. Both use macros that paste code into the caller and change the caller's variables. Jet gives her closures, which can do neither.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

DESIGN UNDER A. (1) Code values: `code { ... }` and `code(expr)` hold parsed, not yet checked, source. D-META-CODE1 is recorded as A, with the owner's ratification comment 'Both option A and b. A is the simple case, b is the expert case'. This ballot builds option B on that comment and asks the owner to confirm it. Code values are unbuilt, and `Syntax.rs:119-122` still says no code values exist.

Template bodies in derive and b.generate are code values written in place, so there is one concept. (2) `paste c` pastes a code value at a statement, item or expression position (Jai #insert). The word is `paste` because D-API-STORE1 retired `insert`. Names in a code value resolve where it was written (hygiene). `paste c with [i]` lets the pasted code see listed macro names (Jai #insert,scope()). (3) `#Expand fn` is a macro (Jai #expand).

Parameters of type Code receive caller code unevaluated, written `code { }` at the call. No trailing-block syntax is added, so D-TRAILBLOCK2 stands. Other parameters are evaluated once, in order. Macro-local names never clash with the caller's. (4) Caller variables (Jai backtick): `#Expand(uses: [total])` lists caller variables the macro may read or write. The pasted code is checked at the call as if written there, so moves and borrows of those variables follow the caller's ordinary rules.

`defines: [name]` declares new caller names, and an existing name of that spelling is a registered error. `exits` allows return, break and next to leave the caller (Jai's backtick return). Such a macro is called as `timed!(...)`, so control flow stays visible. Inside a macro, `$caller.code` is the call as a Code value (Jai #caller_code). D-JAI-SITE1 defines `$caller`, and if SITE1 loses, this ballot adds `$caller.code` alone.

(5) `c.nodes()` gives a typed, read-only tree with kinds, children, locations and, after checking, types (Jai compiler_get_nodes). `c.map(f)` builds new code from a transform. Compiler nodes are never mutable. (6) Jai for_expansion maps to `Iterable` (D-ITER-HOOK), which stays the one loop protocol. A macro pastes code and defines no loop protocol. Inside pasted code, `?` and `defer` behave as if written at the call.

(7) Limits and tools: 100 nested expansions by default, raised by `#ExpandLimit(n)`. Errors name the call, the macro line and the pasted line. `jet inspect expand` prints any expansion. The debugger steps through macro lines unless the macro carries `#NoDebug` (Jai #no_debug). (8) The raw_code power (D-JAI-EXPERT1) adds two things. `parse(text)` turns text into a Code value in prep and macros (Jai #insert of a string).

`uses: *` lets a macro touch any caller name (Jai backtick). Every new word is registered in Syntax.rs under this decision (I7).

LAWS AMENDED. S26 'Rejected forever: token/AST/attribute macros'. D-METAMUTATE1 'user macros are rejected'. D-METADEPTH2 'no macros'. D-META-GATE1 'token or tree macros'. The D-META-RECONCILE1 universal limit on user macros. D-METHODMACRO1's decline of call-site expansion. D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2, which place code capture and insertion in advanced sessions (pasting moves to standard mode). And, for raw_code only, the D-META-CODE1 and D-METADERIVE1 rule that generated code never re-lexes text.

KEPT. The closed grammar (macros add no syntax), checking of every expansion (I3), no mutable compiler nodes, and D-META-CONTROL2 change sets for rewriting written code.

REGRETS DESIGNED OUT. Backtick clumsiness (OAIqCpqszVw 00:34:34) becomes a checked list. Macro errors without the call site (6qkL_DmHOuo 00:35:04) get three locations. Missing macro debug info (QX46eLqq1ps 00:59:00) is fixed. Blow's Lisp-list versus typed-tree question (pg_Wk2GBZDw 00:22:00) is answered with typed trees.

EVIDENCE. Jai #expand, #insert, #code, backtick and for_expansion (Blow QX46eLqq1ps 00:13:12-01:24:24, 6qkL_DmHOuo. The Way to Jai Appendix C and book/26C:139-268). Nim templates and Racket hygiene show hygiene-by-default with explicit escapes works. Rust's `!` shows a visible call mark. C text macros show the failure mode.

decisions.title: One Compiler value and one event stream for compile-time control
decisions.situation: Ratified Jet rules let an opted-in build provider rewrite function bodies through checked change sets, but none of that is built. Today no build can change a written function or watch the compiler work, so a team that wants tracing on every marked function copies the same lines into each one. This ballot replaces that unbuilt design and decides who may hold compiler control and how it runs. Under every option macros stay removed, code is quoted with #code and values are spliced in with $. The recommendation is one value that only the application's own source can create and must pass on by hand, which watches compiler events and can add code or rewrite checked function bodies.
decisions.gist: How should a build program control the compiler: one passed value with event handlers, hooks only, or a package-wide grant?
decisions.lesson: A compile-time program is Jet code the compiler runs while it builds. A function is checked once the compiler has confirmed its names, types and effects. Jai lets compile-time code watch every checked function and replace its body. Jet's hooks, functions the compiler calls at fixed stages, can only read, report and add code. A marker such as `#Traced` only tags a declaration. Under every option macros stay removed and code is quoted as `#code { }`.
decisions.story: Ines runs a web service with forty route functions marked `#Traced`. Each starts with the same two tracing lines, written by hand, and new routes keep forgetting them. Her package file names compiler control with `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`. Under option A her build creates one compiler value and hands it to the tracing library, which wraps every marked function. She deletes the hand-written lines. `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints each function's final code. Libraries she never handed the value to cannot touch her code.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: the build program loops on `compiler_wait_for_message()` and may replace a checked procedure with `compiler_modify_procedure`. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai

Rust: procedural macros rewrite token streams before type checking, and any dependency may define one. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html

Zig: compile-time code computes values and types but cannot change another function's body. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime
decisions.detail:
For maintainers. Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and set this question's direction to A. The owner ruled out macros: markers plus compile-time functions cover them, and the goal is full Jai power. The owner named the losing directions: hooks only, and a Jai-style loop with no value to hold.

Shared by every option. Macros stay removed, by owner ruling, and code values are quoted `#code { }` with `$` splices. This answers the owner's comment on D-JAI-CODE1=A, which asked for idiomatic, cohesive syntax. `paste`, `#Expand`, `name!()` calls, the `uses:`, `defines:` and `exits` clauses, `#ExpandLimit` and `#NoDebug` are removed. The `Code` type, `c.nodes()` and `c.map` survive; `code(expr)` becomes `#code { expr }`.

What replaces each macro use. Wrapping a declaration becomes a marker plus `rewrite_body`. Timing a block, D-JAI-CODE1's own example, becomes a closure plus `defer`: `timed("load", () -> assets.load_all())`. Generating declarations becomes `b.generate` or `meta.add`. Changing the caller's own variables has no replacement; that is an accepted loss under the owner's ruling.

Splicing. D-NAME-SPLICE1=B is extended: `$name` splices a compile-time binding inside `#code` as it does in templates, so Jet keeps one splice sigil. The retired `#( )` spelling stays retired. D-META-HASH1, still open, proposes `#` for values Jet supplies while `$` keeps splicing; `#code` fits it, and another outcome is a mechanical respelling.

Replaces D-META-CONTROL2=A's API: the advanced session, change sets, `commit` and the `register`, `register_expansion` and `register_specialization` providers. Call-site expansion leaves with macros. Specialization control is left to D-JAI-GENERIC1, which is open. Signature replacement is not carried over. Compared with change sets, A gives up order-free merges and per-item caching of a stateless provider. A keeps CONTROL2's atomic re-check of affected callers.

Replaces the read-only `stages()` view of D-COMPILER-EVENT1=A and D-JAI-EVENTS1=A with `meta.events(watch:)`. The one `compiler.Event` type stays and gains the loop kinds `Checked`, `Stuck`, `Error` and `Done`. Settled becomes `Stuck` and finished becomes `Done`. Parsed, imported and declared stay hook stages and are not loop events. The session wire uses the same four kind names.

Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A. Its rejection of a full message loop with in-place rewriting is reversed for `Compiler` holders. Its rule that stages run once and never return to declared is kept, and extended: a rewrite produces no new event. Its rule that overlapping edits are an error still binds hooks; `Compiler` holders instead stack in registration order. Hooks still only read, report and add.

Keeps D-HOOK-ONE1 and D-JAI-CONFIG1. Keeps D-EXPANDCLI1: final code lives in `jet inspect expand --facts meta`, a new lens, not in a new `jet expand` command as the proposal wrote. Keeps D-FRONTENDAPI1: the shipped `core.compiler.parse` makes code from text, so there is no second parser; inserting that code is what `Meta.Code.Raw` gates.

Amends D-MARKER-LAW1=A: built-in derives move from compiler code to Core library code over the read-and-add view, as the owner directed. The user derive form of D-METADERIVE1 is unchanged.

Amends D-JAI-EXPERT1=A. The `Meta.Paste` leaf is removed with macros. `Meta.Code` gates creating a value; `Rewrite`, `Raw` and `Types` gate `rewrite_body`, adding code made from text, and adding type declarations. Passing the value is the grant to a library, so `grants:` no longer applies to `Meta.Code` leaves under A. Default holding is D-META-HOLD1.

Interplay. Until D-META-CROSSPKG1 rules, rewrites may touch only the application's own package. D-META-OPTIN2's target records stand until then. The story assumes D-META-HOLD1=A, so Ines's package file names `Meta.Code`; without that line `b.compiler` stops with an error printing it.

Amends D-META-OPTIN2=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A. Under RECONCILE1 the older refusals already yielded for opted-in projects. Opted in now means a build that created a `Compiler` value. That covers D-METAMUTATE1, S26's value-only rule, D-METADEPTH1 and D-META-GATE1. The ban on user macros in D-METAMUTATE1 and S26 returns to full force for everyone.

Effects. D-EFFECT-OMIT1=A infers effects for functions with no written bound, so a rewrite can change a function's effects. A therefore checks affected callers again at round end, and a rewrite past an explicit bound is an error. The step budget is D-PREP-FUEL1's.

Research: Docs/audits/2026-10-07-ast-metaprogramming-report.md recommends a typed code model with quotes and checked insertion, not exposing the compiler's internal trees. A follows it. Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md lists the message loop and procedure rewrite as the main Jai gap.

Profile: full, because A changes quote syntax and removes ratified macro syntax. Two fresh readers reviewed this ballot, and their findings are repaired here.

options.name: One passed Compiler value
options.detail:
Only the application's own source can create a `Compiler` value, with `b.compiler(app)`, one value per program being built. A library gets compiler control only when the application passes it the value. The first hand-off is one visible line, and the `meta` lens lists every later hand-off and every function touched.

A holder registers handlers with `meta.events(watch:)`. The call returns at once, and the handlers run while the program compiles, after `fn build` returns. A handler can add code or rewrite the body of a checked function. Several holders stack in the order they were registered.

The compiler checks every added or rewritten piece of code again, like written code. If a rewrite changes a function's effects, every caller affected is checked again too. The editor marks rewritten functions, and `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints final code and who changed it.
options.technical:
Creation. `Compiler` is a Core type. `b.compiler(output)` must be written in the root package's own source. A call written in any dependency is an error, even when that dependency's function holds the root's `b`. Creating the value performs `Meta.Code`. Whether the application holds `Meta.Code` by default is D-META-HOLD1.

Events. `meta.events(watch:, handler)` registers a handler and returns at once. Compiling starts after `fn build` returns. `watch:` filters by declaration kind and marker, and only watched declarations wait for handlers. Each declaration's event goes once to each handler, in registration order. A rewrite never produces a new event, so a rewritten function is never delivered to any holder again.

Kinds. `compiler.Event` gains four loop kinds. `Checked` means one declaration passed checking. `Stuck` means the compiler cannot continue until someone adds names it is waiting for. `Error` carries a diagnostic, and `Done` ends compilation. A round is one pass of adding code and checking it again. Round 17 is a registered error naming what still waits, as the ratified event rules already say.

Actions. `meta.add(code)` adds declarations; adding a type declaration needs `Meta.Code.Types`. `meta.rewrite_body(f, code)` replaces a checked body and needs `Meta.Code.Rewrite`. Text becomes code through the shipped `core.compiler.parse`; adding code that came from text needs `Meta.Code.Raw`. Until D-META-CROSSPKG1 rules, rewrites may touch only the application's own package.

Re-checking. A rewrite goes through parse and check like written code. Its effect facts are inferred again. Every caller whose facts change is checked again, all at once at the end of the round, and the public API snapshot records the new facts. A rewrite that widens effects past an explicit bound is an error at the `rewrite_body` call that names the bound.

Composition. Holders stack in registration order. In a handler, `f.body` is the current body, including earlier holders' rewrites in this round. Read-only consumers such as `#On` hooks, `b.program()` queries and derives see a watched function only after the round's rewrites.

Quotes. `#code { ... }` is a value of type `Code`. Inside it, `$name` splices a compile-time binding, as `$` already does in templates. Names in a quote resolve where the quote is written, and spliced code keeps its own scope. A local named `trace` in `load_user` cannot capture the quote's `trace`.

Everywhere. Rewrites apply to every compilation of the output's modules: build, run, test, dev, check and the language server, which runs the same handlers. Handlers record what they read, so an unchanged function replays its recorded rewrite. The compile-time step budget stops a runaway handler.

Provenance. Each added or rewritten item records the build line and library function that changed it. `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints final code with that record, and lists each value created and every hand-off. This uses a lens, not a new command, as the transparency-command ruling requires.

options.name: Hooks only
options.detail: Compile-time code matches what is built today. Hooks and markers see each declaration and may report problems or add new code. Nothing may change a function that is already written, so the ratified but unbuilt change-set rewrites are dropped. Tracing can be checked but not added; a hook can only ask the author to write the lines.
options.technical: Keeps the hook stages and the read-only stage view. Drops the change-set session of the compiler-control ruling and its body rewrites. Macros stay removed and code values use the same `#code { }` quote with `$` splices as A, for code that hooks add.

options.name: Package-wide grant, no value
options.detail: The application's package file grants rewriting to a whole dependency. That package's compile-time code opens the event loop itself, as in Jai, with no value to create or pass. The grant is visible in the package file, but the build cannot say which call or which functions it covers.
options.technical: Uses the ratified expert-power grants: the main package names `Meta.Code.Rewrite` for a dependency with `grants:`. Event registration and rewrite are free functions in `core.compiler`. Stacking, re-checking, quotes and provenance follow the same rules as A. Macros stay removed.

comparisons.note: The build program intercepts a workspace, waits on messages and may modify a checked procedure. Any metaprogram that runs can do this. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
An attribute macro rewrites tokens before type checking, so it sees no types. Any dependency can ship one. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html
Compile-time code computes values and types, but it cannot change a body written elsewhere. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime

recommendation.why: A gives Jai's full control and keeps the first grant visible: one value, created only in the application's source and passed by hand. Every change is checked again, including affected callers.
gains: Full control without hidden power in dependencies.
One event stream serves hooks, tools and build programs.

losses.loss: A rewritten body differs from the source on screen.
losses.mitigation: The editor marks rewritten functions, and the expand meta lens prints final code and who changed it.

losses.loss: Watched functions and their callers wait for handlers.
losses.mitigation: Only watched functions wait, unchanged ones replay recorded rewrites, and a step budget stops runaway handlers.

whyNot.reason: B drops the ratified rewrites, so tracing can only be checked, not added, and Jai build programs cannot be ported.
C grants rewriting to a whole package; the build cannot say which call or functions, and any code there may use it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Power over written code, in exchange for one passed value, slower watched builds and a final-code view.

decisions.title: Facts about where code is: caller location, current location, constness and the called function
decisions.situation: A logging or checking function is most useful when it reports the file and line of the code that called it. Jai provides this and related facts, such as the current function's name and which function a call will pick. Jet has none of them, and its rules mention a caller-location value that was never built. The vote decides which of these facts Jet adds; we recommend all of them, read with Jet's existing fact mark.
decisions.gist: Which facts about the code's own location should Jet provide, like Jai's #caller_location?
decisions.lesson: A fact is a value the compiler already knows, read with `$`, such as `T.$fields`. A source location is a file, line, column and enclosing function. The caller location is where the current function was called from. A default is the value a parameter takes when the call omits it, written `name: Type{value}`.
decisions.story: Lena writes a check helper used in two hundred places. When a check fails, the log points inside the helper, not at the failing call, so she has to search by message text. Jai's version reports the caller's file and line.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

FACTS UNDER A. `$here`: SourceLocation for the expression where it is written (Jai #file, #line, #filepath, #location and, through `$here.function`, #procedure_name). SourceLocation is new: SourceSpan holds byte offsets and SourceInfo describes generated source identity (D-META-REFLECT2), so neither carries line and column. Unlike D-META-REFLECT2's fallible queries, these roots never fail. Inside a closure, `function` is the enclosing named function.

`$caller`: SourceLocation of the call, legal only as a parameter default and inside an #Expand macro (D-JAI-CODE1), where `$caller.code` is the call as Code. Anywhere else, `$caller` is a registered error naming those two places. A wrapper forwards its own location by declaring `at: SourceLocation{$caller}` and passing `at`. Nothing is implicit. Function values carry no defaults, so a call through one passes the location explicitly. SourceLocation prints as `path:line:column`.

`x.$known` is true when x is a constant expression or a prep value. GENERIC1's `prep?` uses the same front-end definition, identical on every tier. It differs from `$phase`, which says where code runs. For `LIMIT :: 5` and `LIMIT :: prep { 5 }` it is true. For a run-time variable it is false (Jai is_constant). `call.$callee`: FunctionInfo of the function a call resolves to, without running it (Jai #procedure_of_call).

Jai #this maps to `Self` in a type and to the function's own name in a procedure. No new fact is needed. Jai #compile_time maps to the ratified `$phase`. Jai #location(code) maps to `c.$location` on Code values in D-JAI-CODE1.

AMENDS. D-COMPILER-NS1 gains two subjectless roots. E2414 (defaults must be compile-time constants) treats `$caller` as a per-call constant. D-SHAPE2's `#Caller()` mention is replaced under A and B and built as a marker under C.

STATUS. None of these exist in code today. Each needs a registry row, an example with golden output on every tier (I5), and diagnostics. The example's `print` inside prep follows the compile-time output rules of D-CTIO1. The stale `@` fact text at D-ONCE-AT1 is cleaned up in the same cutover.

REGRETS. In 2015 Blow had no call-site file and line for asserts (0KkW_Zo_pDc 00:05:15). #caller_location was not constant inside #run (pgiVrhsGkKY 00:40:09). `$caller` is a constant wherever it is legal. These citations come from the mining notes.

EVIDENCE. Jai Appendix C rows for #file, #line, #filepath, #location, #caller_location, #procedure_name, #procedure_of_call and #this. Blow yJukJS81o-k 00:19:28-00:21:38. Rust, Swift and C++20 prove the caller-location default works with no run-time lookup.
