decisions.title: Fixed-time rules for the Secret tag, from the checker to the final machine code
decisions.situation:
Code that handles keys must take the same time and touch the same memory whatever the key is. Otherwise an attacker who times it learns the key. Today Jet follows a Secret label through the program but checks nothing about timing, so an early-exit compare of a secret runs as written. This matters most to people who write crypto and login code, and it protects every program that uses theirs.

You are deciding whether the Secret label also makes the compiler refuse secret-dependent branches, lookups, divisions and stops, checked down to the final machine code. We recommend A: it does, and it rewrites simple secret branches into fixed-time code instead of refusing them.

One cost cannot be removed. On a chip whose maker publishes no fixed-time guarantee, or whose switch only the operating system can set, Jet checks its own code but cannot confirm the chip. The build report says so, and the hardened profile refuses such hosts.
decisions.gist: Should the Secret tag forbid secret-dependent branches, indexes, divisions and stops, checked down to the final machine code?
decisions.lesson: A timing leak needs no bug in the math, only a branch, a memory lookup, a division or a stop that depends on a secret. A compiler can refuse those only if it knows which values are secret, follows them everywhere, and checks the code it finally emits.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A tag is a label the compiler follows through the program, written #Secret before a value or a type. A secrecy tag protects what a value says; Secret, Credential and PII are secrecy tags. An integrity tag, such as Input, protects where a value goes.

A branch is an if, a loop test or a match. A stop is a run-time halt, such as an overflow. Fixed time means the work does not depend on a value. To scrub is to release a tag on purpose, in a function marked #Scrub.
decisions.story: Ana writes the check for the tag that proves a message was not changed. Her first version compares byte by byte and returns at the first mismatch. Correct-answer tests can miss this leak. An attacker sends forged tags and times the replies; a slower reply means one more byte was right. Today Jet accepts her code (c07), and nothing stops a later optimizer from turning a careful version back into a branch. Under A her first version compiles and runs in fixed time, because the compiler rewrites the early exit.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether values with a fixed-time tag, Secret first, may steer branches, addresses, divisions, shifts, allocation sizes or stops, and how far down the compiler checks it. Protection of memory is D-MEM-WIPE1's ratified duty, and disclosure sinks are D-SECRETEDGE1's. This ballot changes neither; it adds timing.

No starting assurance is claimed. Core tags nothing #Secret today (census: 0 uses), so no checker sees its keys. Its crypto code is written with masks, and its tests check results, not timing. Nothing here claims that today's TLS or crypto code is constant-time.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), with the same results as seed a0_042. Ana's early-exit compare, a secret table index, a secret divisor, a secret shift amount and a loop counted by a secret all check and run (c07). A Secret condition that picks untagged text reaches process.cmd with no report (c01, BallotReview4's attack).

A Credential condition does the same (c06), though passing the token itself is E0721. A secret U8 plus one prints 1, then stops with E3010 at 255, exit 70 (c02). A compare over a shorter input stops with E3010 (c03). Under #Arithmetic(.Wrapping) the same addition prints 0 (c05).

Flow fixes under every option. The tag checker loses tags in seven known ways, and ratified tags promise all of them. Stores into a list, field or & parameter must tag the container. A loop body must be walked until its tags stop changing. A call must walk its callee with the argument tags, receivers included. A branch's condition must tag its results. Every option below fixes all seven.

Implicit flow, exactly. A branch on a secrecy tag sets a control tag for its arms. Every value an arm produces, assigns outside itself, stores or writes through & gets that tag. A call made in the arm is a use of each sink the tag denies. If an arm can leave by return, break, continue, ? or !, everything after the branch is under the control tag too.

Integrity tags such as Input get no control tag, because a branch on untrusted input that picks a constant query injects nothing. A tag says which kind it is with a new tag-only Marker constant, protects, of the Prelude enum TagProtects { Secrecy, Integrity }. Its default is .Secrecy, the stricter kind. The Prelude sets Input to .Integrity, and Secret, Credential and PII to .Secrecy.

Run-time stops and loops that never end are not tracked for leak-only tags; that residue is named below. Migration: no tag on the seed is declared in D-TAG-MARKER1's form yet (no .TypeUse site), so only the four Prelude tags need constants. A user tag that omits protects gets implicit flow, and one that omits timing gets no timing rule.

Alias, call and capture flow. A loan of a tagged value is tagged, and a write through it tags the owner. A callee is checked once per pattern of argument tags, cached, with recursion solved to a fixed point. Generic code is checked per instance. A closure that captures a tagged value tags its results.

Function and trait values. A function value cannot be walked, so passing a fixed-time value to one is refused unless its type names the tag, as in fn(#Secret U8) -> #Secret U8. A function becomes such a value only when its checked summary for that tag pattern has no refusal and tags its results at least as the type says.

A trait method called through a trait value with a fixed-time argument follows the same rule: its signature must name the tag. Every impl is checked against that signature where it is declared. Under C, the function type must also say #ConstantTime, so only marked functions fit it; naming a Secret parameter is not enough.

Exported callbacks. A Jet function exported to foreign code may take a fixed-time parameter only with #Unsafe and a reason, listed in the build report, because its foreign caller is not checked. Its body is checked as usual.

Separate compilation. Each package's checked interface carries a tag summary for each public function: which argument tags reach which results and sinks, and whether it is fixed-time safe for each tag pattern. Callers in other packages use the summary instead of the body. The summary is part of the package's checked content identity, so a changed body changes the identity.

Loaded code. A package loaded while running is reached only through function and trait values, whose types name the tags. The loader refuses a package whose checked summaries do not satisfy those types. Two boundaries stay outside the promise, and are named: a tampered binary, and foreign code behind an audited extern.

Under A, a tag declares fixed time with a second tag-only constant, timing, of the Prelude enum TagTiming { Free, Fixed }, default .Free. Branch, index and divide are not effects, so they stay out of D-TAG-MARKER1's #FX denial row. The Prelude Secret gets timing: .Fixed. Credential and PII keep .Free, because tokens and personal data are parsed by code that branches on their text.

Several tags. A value may carry more than one tag. It follows the timing rules if any of its tags is .Fixed, and gets implicit flow if any is .Secrecy. A branch's results carry the union of its arms' tags plus its control tag; a container's element tags and its own tag are kept apart.

What is refused for a fixed-time value, with E0737. In control: an if, while or loop-until condition, a match subject, the left side of && or ||, and the subject of ??, ? or !. In addressing: a range bound or loop count, a list index, map key or slice bound. Also either operand of / or %, a shift or rotate amount, an allocation size or capacity, and a call target.

Widths, with E0738. A fixed-time scalar must be a fixed-width integer or a Bool. A fixed-time value may be any container of such scalars: a struct, a fixed or growable array, a String's bytes, or an Any payload. Int and Float, and any type that holds them, are refused. Int's exact routes branch on the value's size, and some hardware slows down on very small floats.

Stops, with E0739. Plain arithmetic on a fixed-time value would stop on overflow, and whether it stops depends on the secret. So the plain Stop policy and checked(...) are refused for fixed-time operands. wrapping(...), saturating(...) and #Overflow(.Wrapping) are accepted, all from ratified D-FIXED-WRAP1; saturating lowers to masks. A narrowing conversion T{x} follows the same rule.

Code that needs to know whether a sum overflowed computes the carry bit with masks, as ConstTime.jet does today, and keeps it as a #Secret Bool. That closes the overflow-stop attack: next_counter must write wrapping(k + U8{1}), which gives 0 for 255 and never stops.

What stays allowed. Comparisons such as == and < on fixed-time values give a fixed-time Bool, lowered to a branch-free compare. Bit operations, wrapping and saturating arithmetic, and selection by mask are allowed. A bounds check with a public index on a list of public length stays, because its stop depends only on public data.

Secret branches that are rewritten, not refused. A branch on a fixed-time value compiles when both arms are total. Total means no stop, no loop with a secret count, no call with an effect, no allocation, and writes only to locals and & places. The compiler runs both arms and picks each result with a mask, as FaCT does. An early return or break in such a branch becomes a secret flag, and the code after it runs with its writes masked.

If the code an early exit would skip is not total, the early exit is refused. A function with a rewritten branch returns a fixed-time value, so check_fast below returns #Secret Bool. The build report lists every rewritten branch by line. Every other secret branch is refused with E0737, which names the first part of the arm that blocks the rewrite: the call, the allocation, the stop or the secret count.

The rewrite is not trusted for timing. The final-code validator below checks its output like any other code, so a rewrite bug is an internal compiler error, not a leak. Tier parity checks its answers: the forced interpreter runs the branch as written, and both tiers must agree.

Public lengths. Allocation sizes are never secret, so every buffer's capacity is public. [#Secret U8] tags each element, and its length and is_empty are public too. #Secret [U8] and #Secret String tag the whole value, so their length is secret and only their capacity is public. TlsLead's probe p4 shows the whole-value length is tagged today.

A public length stays public only while no secret decides it. So push, pop, insert, remove, truncate or extend on a [#Secret U8] is refused under a secret control tag, with E0737, and their count arguments must be public. A call made under a control tag is checked as if each write it makes through & were inside that branch.

The length fact lives in the type, so it travels with every loan, parameter and capture. Turning #Secret [U8] into [#Secret U8] declares its length public, so it is done only in a #Scrub(Secret) function, listed for review. The other direction is a plain widening.

The seed accepts [#Secret U8] as a type but drops the element tag: a byte read from it reaches process.cmd with no report (c04). A builds element tags.

Comparing unequal lengths. Core's crypto.equal(expected: [#Secret U8], got: [U8]) -> Bool returns false at once when the lengths differ, which reveals only public lengths. Otherwise it reads every byte, combines the differences with masks, and reveals one Bool through its scrub. That closes the short-compare attack.

The attack's own hand-written loop is refused when expected is #Secret [U8], because its range bound is secret. With [#Secret U8] the loop compiles, and the stop on a short input depends only on public lengths; crypto.equal is the fix.

Declassifying. #Scrub(Secret) is the only place a fixed-time value becomes public, as D-SECRETEDGE1 already lists. A scrub lifts the timing and disclosure rules from its result only. It never ends D-MEM-WIPE1's protection of the values it read, and Credential and PII keep that duty in every option. Core ships reveal for one Bool and the outputs of seal, sign and public-key derivation.

Secret text. Code over a #Secret String or #Secret [U8] works over the public capacity with masks and never stops at the secret length. Core's fixed-time operations on them are move, drop, copy, crypto.equal and its decoders for base64, hex and PEM. Any other String method reached with one is checked like any helper, and its first refused line reports E0737.

Secret input. A keeps D-MEM-WIPE1's spelling, #Secret (sys.get("SIGNING_KEY") ?? return). The tag applies to the read itself, so the value is protected and fixed-time from its first copy, with type #Secret String; key.bytes() gives #Secret [U8]. Core's decoders take tagged input and return tagged output, so no parser sees untagged secret text.

Boxes and enums. A #Secret Any has secret contents and a public payload type, so type tests and take compare public identity and bind #Secret T. A box, or an enum whose cleanup depends on its variant, may not be made inside a Secret branch, with E0737: dropping it would choose cleanup by a secret. Other variants chosen there become secret, and matching them is refused.

Foreign code. Jet cannot see a foreign body, so passing a fixed-time value to an extern function is refused. An extern may accept one only when its declaration names the tag on that parameter and carries #Unsafe with a reason; each such crossing is listed in the build report. This matches D-MEM-WIPE1's audited owning receivers.

Keeping the tag to the end. Today the IR builder strips tags (BuildTypes.jet:21, ir_untag), so the optimizer sees plain integers. Under A, a fixed bit rides every slot, temporary and register that holds a fixed-time value. Inlining, SSA, copy coalescing and scalar replacement keep the bit. An IR check after every optimizer pass, in every build mode, refuses a branch, address, divide, variable shift or call target that reads a fixed slot.

The leakage model. For code holding fixed-time values, A promises that the executed instruction sequence, every memory address and every branch outcome are independent of those values. Every instruction that reads one is in its target's table. The attacker may time the program and watch caches and branch predictors from the same machine.

Excluded, and named. Power and electromagnetic readings, frequency changes driven by power use, speculative execution, and the timing of the operating system and other processes. A does not promise identical wall time. Jasmin's separate speculative check is a stronger model that A does not offer.

The per-target tables. Each supported target ships a table of exact instruction forms, and each entry cites the vendor document revision that names it; a form without a citation is not listed. The admitted classes are add and subtract with carry, bitwise logic, shifts and rotates by a public amount, multiply, compare and test, conditional select and set, and moves.

Never admitted with fixed-time operands: division and remainder, branches on flags set from them, and loads or stores at addresses they decide. Bit scans, population counts and runtime-helper calls are refused too. Intel's data operand independent timing list governs x86-64, and Arm's DIT list governs AArch64. Compares lower to setcc or cset, and selection to cmov, csel or masks.

Admission on AArch64. Where the CPU reports FEAT_DIT, a function that holds fixed values sets the DIT bit on entry and restores it on exit; an ordinary program may do this itself. DIT is per-thread state, saved with the thread, so thread creation, moves between cores and signal handlers need nothing more. A foreign call made while DIT is set keeps it set.

Admission on x86-64. Intel's DOIT guidance (ID 768873, updated 2025-09-10) covers Core processors before Ice Lake and Atom processors before Gracemont. It says they run the listed instructions as if the mode were on, so those hosts are confirmed. Ice Lake, Gracemont and later need the DOITM bit of a model-specific register. Only the operating system can write it, and Intel advises against setting it for the whole machine. Those hosts are confirmed only where the operating system reports the bit on.

Intel also says some vector forms depend on the MXCSR setting; the x86-64 table leaves those out. This repair read Intel's page but found no AMD list, so AMD processors are unconfirmed until AMD publishes one; the probe machine's Ryzen 9 7950X3D is one of them. A WebAssembly engine is always unconfirmed, because it compiles the module again.

What an unconfirmed host does. By default the program runs, as programs built with BoringSSL, subtle or Go's crypto/subtle run on the same chip. The code half of the promise still holds, because the checker, the IR check and the validator all ran. The build report names each target whose hosts may be unconfirmed. sys.timing_host() returns .Confirmed, or .Unconfirmed with the missing control, so a server can log it or stop.

Under the hardened profile, policy: { harden: true } or --profile=hardened, an unconfirmed host refuses to start a program holding fixed-time values, and the error names the missing control. This adds one check to the ratified hardening fact of D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-HARDENED1; it adds no new switch.

Final-code validation. After register allocation, a validator reads the final instructions of every function that holds fixed values. It follows fixed values through registers, condition flags and spill slots, whose addresses are frame offsets and so public. It checks that only listed instructions read them, and that none feeds a branch, an address, a divide or a variable shift.

Compiler-made code is covered the same way. Inline copies, wide multiplies and stack probes are checked as instructions, and a runtime-helper call with a fixed operand fails validation. Unwinding, cancellation and early exits run only on public conditions, since stops on fixed values are refused, and their wipes loop over public capacities.

A failed validation after sema is an internal compiler error, exit 101 under I2/I3, and no program is emitted. The emitted-code test from #6694 c10 (a) stays as a test of this validator. The checker rules are the same on every tier, and the fixed bit, IR check and validator run at O0, O1 and O2, including jet dev's JIT.

Fail closed, in two separate cases. A target without D-MEM-WIPE1's memory protection already refuses sensitive values under that ratified decision. Every supported target ships a timing table; wasm32-wasip2's covers the WebAssembly instructions Jet emits, which are only arithmetic and bit operations on fixed values. No target is carved out, so I9 holds. A new target gets its timing table before it is supported, as it gets its other tables.

Allocation and memory. A fixed-time value cannot size an allocation, so allocation, growth and allocation failure depend only on public data. Storage for fixed-time values is D-MEM-WIPE1's protected storage, wiped and kept out of swap and crash output. The 270 manual wipe calls in 23 files of Core, Compiler and Examples stay until D-MEM-WIPE1 is built.

Helper coverage. There is no allow list: every function reached with a fixed-time value is checked, Core included. ConstTime.jet has 38 functions, and 18 take Int parameters. BallotReview4 found that memmove_left, memcpy_offset and memcmp_partial handle secret offsets and skip counts as Int. Under A those become #Secret U64, with their totals and ranges public.

Build-time code. The timing rules apply to code in the shipped program; build-time code runs on the build machine and is not timed. A build-time result may not carry a secrecy tag, because the program image is not protected storage. That makes it a non-storable result type under D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1's E0944. It follows from D-MEM-WIPE1 and narrows neither D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 nor D-META-PHASE1.

Beginner path. Use core.crypto's seal, open, sign, verify and equal, and never write a tag. A natural early-exit compare of a tagged key compiles and runs in fixed time. A secret branch that prints or allocates gives E0737, whose fix names the masked form or crypto.equal.

Expert path. Tag key material once as [#Secret U8] or #Secret U64, write the primitive with bit operations, wrapping arithmetic, mask selection or total branches, and publish results only through #Scrub(Secret) functions. The build report lists every scrub, every rewritten branch and every foreign crossing. The hardened profile adds the host check.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A secret branch with an effect, a secret index and a secret loop count are still refused, because no rewrite can hide an address or an effect. E0737 names the part that blocks the rewrite, and Core ships crypto.equal and fixed-time decoders for base64, hex and PEM. Secret arithmetic must name wrapping or saturating, and E0739's fix writes it.

The one cost that cannot be removed. On an unconfirmed host the chip's half of the promise is unknown, because its maker publishes no list or only the operating system can set the switch. Mitigation: AArch64 sets DIT itself, older Intel is covered by Intel's statement, the build report and sys.timing_host() say which hosts are unconfirmed, and the hardened profile refuses them.

Two smaller costs. Leak-only tags do not track run-time stops or endless loops in their branches, and timing and termination can reveal more than a branch outcome; a tag that needs that sets timing: .Fixed. Callees are checked again for each pattern of argument tags, and the summaries are cached.

Other options. B adds core.ct types, such as ct.U8 and ct.Bool, that are always Secret and whose comparisons give a ct.Bool that no if accepts. Operators work on them, and they share A's lowering, validator and host policy. C applies A's timing rules only inside functions marked #ConstantTime, with the same whole-program tag flow. D adds no timing rule; an emitted-code test covers listed Core functions.

E is A without the rewrite: every secret branch is refused, so Ana's early-exit compare must be written with masks. The trusted compiler stays smaller, and no code runs work the source seems to skip.

F is the strictest form, the draft this repair replaced. Every unconfirmed host refuses to start a program holding fixed-time values, and wasm32-wasip2 cannot build one. D-WASISRV1 ratified wasm32-wasip2 as a full server target with no carve-out under I9, so F needs you to approve an I9 exception. A, B, C and E keep the target.

The forced interpreter is a test path, not a deployment target. It gives the same results, makes no timing promise, and says so when it starts.

A validator checks the final instructions on every target. Unconfirmed hosts run and are reported; the hardened profile refuses them.

decisions.title: Where should write and take marks go on method calls?
decisions.gist: Where should a method call show permission to change or take its receiver?
decisions.lesson: A function performs an operation. A method is called through a value, its receiver. & permits temporary exclusive changes; ^ transfers ownership and ends later use of a named value. The permission must mark one exact call. Plain . keeps read calls unmarked. Existing &place windows keep their checked lifetimes.
decisions.explainer:
## Read the example
`struct Buffer` defines a value with one named part, `text`. `impl Buffer` groups methods. `self` names the receiver inside a method.

`buf := Buffer{text: "hello"}` creates a changeable value. `chunk: String` names incoming text. `=` replaces the field, while `{self.text}` and `{chunk}` insert their text inside the quoted result. `append` changes the Buffer. `seal` takes it and prints its text. Every option prints `hello world` once. The caller may use `buf` after `append`, but not after `seal`.

Ordinary functions already use `edit(&values)` and `consume(^text)`. Their declarations use `fn edit(values: &[Int])` and `fn consume(text: ^String)`. Read calls stay unmarked. Static calls through a type have no value receiver and stay unmarked.

## Existing law
D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A defines `&place` as an exclusive write window. A place is a named value followed by fields, indexes, or ranges. A window may be bound and passed under its checked lifetime. This choice does not remove or reinterpret those windows.

Option A writes `buf.&append(...)` and `buf.^seal()`. The mark sits after the ordinary dot and before the method name. It replaces prefix-window calls such as `&values[0..1].sort()` with `values[0..1].&sort()`.

Option B writes `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. It keeps the current prefix-window call and extends that position to taking calls. Prefix scope makes nested calls and mixed chains need grouping. A fresh write receiver is not a place, so B must name it first.

Option C writes `buf&.append(...)` and `buf^.seal()`. The adjacent `&.` or `^.` is one call separator. Plain `.` means a read call. `&.` means write through the receiver for that call. `^.` means take the receiver for that call.

Under C, the composite separators are valid only before a method name followed by call parentheses. They do not access fields, create a window, or move a value by themselves. `?.` keeps its existing optional-access meaning. Ordinary bitwise `&` and power `^` remain separate operators; only adjacent `&.` and `^.` form receiver-call separators.

## Holding a write window
All options keep the window construction:
```jet
values := [2, 1, 3]
window := &values[0..1] // Selects values 2 and 1.
```
A calls `window.&sort()`. B calls `&window.sort()`. C calls `window&.sort()`. Each call sorts the selected values and leaves `[1,2,3]`. A read such as `print(values[0])` is rejected before a later window use. After the sort is the window's final use, that read is accepted and prints `1`.

## The same mixed chain
Assume `duplicate` reads a Buffer and returns another Buffer. Assume `grow` changes its receiver and returns another Buffer. `seal` takes its receiver.

A writes `buf.duplicate().&grow().^seal()`. B writes `next := buf.duplicate()` and then `^(&next.grow()).seal()`. The inner prefix permits `grow`; the outer prefix takes its returned Buffer into `seal`. C writes `buf.duplicate()&.grow()^.seal()`. Under C, each separator marks exactly the following method call.

## Calls inside ordinary arguments
A writes `inspect_buffer(buf.&grow())` and `print(buf.^finish())`. B needs `inspect_buffer((&buf.grow()))` and `print((^buf.finish()))`. C writes `inspect_buffer(buf&.grow())` and `print(buf^.finish())`.

C does not change argument prefixes. `inspect_buffer(&buf.grow())` still marks the outer argument, not the nested receiver. The call-only separator removes that scope question for the marked receiver.

## Exact boundary cases
For a changeable list of Buffer values, C writes `items[i]&.append("!")`. The index is evaluated once. A uses `items[i].&append("!")`; B uses `&items[i].append("!")`.

For a read-only list parameter, every option rejects taking `items[0]`. A mark states requested permission; it never creates ownership the receiver does not have.

`make_buffer()` creates `Buffer{text: "hello"}`. A fresh owned receiver may be taken under C with `make_buffer()^.seal()`. B writes `^(make_buffer()).seal()` because the computed receiver needs grouping.

A fresh C write may use `make_buffer()&.append("!")`; A supports its equivalent inline spelling. These two append examples only prove the permitted call form. `append` returns no value, so the changed temporary is then discarded. B needs a named place for a fresh write call.

Receiver marks do not change access timing. Every user or trait method declared with `&self` reserves write access, evaluates allowed arguments, then activates exclusive access. C's `values&.push(values.len())` uses the same two-phase timing for the builtin `push`, so it reads the length before activation.

Some helper-backed builtins require eager write access. The compiler's builtin registry names them; this ballot adds no source marker or user choice. List examples include `remove`, `sort_by`, `sort_desc`, `sort_by_desc`, `update_first`, and `edit_disjoint`. Therefore `values&.remove(values.len() - 1)` is rejected because the argument reads `values` after eager access begins. A and B preserve the same timing with their spellings.

A newly created ordinary argument may omit ^ under current law. `consume("hello")` is accepted for `fn consume(text: ^String)`. A named argument still needs `consume(^text)`. Receiver calls deliberately require the selected receiver mark, including on a fresh receiver.

No option clones a receiver, changes method lookup, changes evaluation order, creates a raw reference, or weakens use-after-take checks. Missing, extra, or mismatched marks are compile errors with a direct fix.

## Trade-offs
A scopes the mark to one method, but `.&name` and `.^name` make the method name look decorated. It also places receiver marks differently from argument and window marks.

B keeps value prefixes, but the prefix can cover more syntax than the intended call. Nested calls and mixed chains need grouping. Fresh write receivers need temporary names.

C scopes the mark to one method while keeping the receiver before the separator and the method after it. It adds two composite separators. Ruby uses `&.` for optional navigation, so Ruby users may first misread C. Jet already uses `?.` for optional access, which keeps Jet's own punctuation family distinct.

## Delivery
The examples are source-derived design examples, not execution receipts. Ratification selects one canonical receiver-call form. Migrate every caller, example, test, formatter case, editor grammar, completion, diagnostic suggestion, and affected explanation. Keep no compatibility receiver spelling.

Sema checks the written separator against the resolved receiver convention for user methods, traits, and builtins. AOT, default run, forced interpreter, and applicable web execution must preserve one meaning. Generated Rust cannot discover a user error.
decisions.story: Maya appends text to a buffer, then consumes it while printing the result. She wants every call to expose its write or take permission without breaking ordinary chains or changing existing write windows.
decisions.inWild: Rust declares write receivers with &mut self and taking receivers with self, but ordinary dot calls hide those permissions. Ruby uses &. for optional navigation. Jet already uses ?. for optional access. Option C instead uses &. and ^. as explicit write and take method separators. These comparisons explain likely expectations; they do not prove adoption or implementation.

options.name: Mark after the dot
options.detail: Write `buf.&append(...)` and `buf.^seal()`. Each call exposes its receiver permission beside the method. Fresh receivers and mixed chains stay inline. Existing &place windows keep their independent meaning.
options.technical: Add receiver-call marks between the dot and method name. Keep method lookup, receiver evaluation, and borrow classification unchanged. Require a matching mark even when the receiver is an existing write window. Amend D-SHAPE-PLACE1 only where a bare-prefix window call previously supplied sufficient method permission. Migrate that form; do not remove or reinterpret write-window expressions.

options.name: Keep value-prefix receiver marks
options.detail: Write `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. Keep the current write-window receiver spelling and extend prefix marking to take receivers. Write receivers must be places, so name fresh values before calling write methods.
options.technical:
Preserve &place construction and maximal-place binding. Each write/take call must have its own receiver mark; a mark on an earlier chain step does not cover later steps. Add ^ in method-receiver position with explicit grouping for computed receivers. Do not add standalone ^value expressions. Preserve builtin two-phase timing for immediate write receivers and existing exclusive lifetimes for stored windows.

Inside an ordinary argument, preserve argument-prefix precedence. Use `inspect_buffer((&buf.grow()))` or `print((^buf.finish()))` to mark the nested receiver. Without that grouping, the leading mark belongs to the outer argument and the receiver remains unmarked.

options.name: Use capability dots
options.detail: Write `buf&.append(...)` and `buf^.seal()`. The separator states how the receiver enters exactly one method call. Plain `.` remains read. Existing `&place` windows and ordinary argument prefixes keep their current meaning.
options.technical: Lex adjacent `&.` and `^.` as call-only postfix separators. They must be followed by a method name and call parentheses. Record Write or Move on the method receiver, then use the existing resolver and CallBinder path. Do not permit these separators for field access, static calls, or standalone expressions. Keep `?.` optional access, bitwise `&`, power `^`, argument conventions, lookup, evaluation order, and two-phase receiver timing unchanged.

options.name: Mark the value, not the call
options.detail: Write `&buf.append(...)` and `^buf.seal()`. The mark sits on the named value that changes or ends, just like `edit(&buf)`. New temporary values need no mark. Chains stay plain after the first named value.
options.technical: A `&` or `^` mark binds the maximal place after it: one name plus fields, indexes, or ranges. It never binds a call result. Sema checks the mark against the one call that receives that place, as receiver or argument. A fresh receiver takes no mark, matching the existing fresh-argument rule. At line start, `&` or `^` directly followed by a name begins a new statement. A continued bitwise-and or power line keeps a space after its operator. Copy `~` grouping is unchanged. Existing `&place` windows and their checked lifetimes are unchanged.

comparisons.note: Official method-call reference, read 2026-09-16: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html#r-expr.method.autoref-deref . Rust inserts receiver borrows and documents lookup surprises. This demonstrates a design contrast, not popularity or performance evidence.

Ruby uses `&.` as its safe-navigation operator. Jet already uses `?.` for optional access, so C deliberately assigns `&.` a different meaning. Official syntax: https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.4/syntax/calling_methods_rdoc.html#label-Safe+Navigation+Operator
comparisons.code: user&.name  # Ruby: call only when user is not nil.

recommendation.why: D marks the named value that changes or ends, as arguments already do. Temporaries stay unmarked.

whyNot.reason: A adds a second mark position and decorates method names.
B marks temporaries and needs extra names and grouping.
C adds two separators and marks temporaries in chains.

recommendation.tradeoff: Choose one value-side mark position and a line-start rule over new call separators.

surface.gist: Where should a method call show permission to change or take its receiver?
surface.lesson: A method call joins a receiver to an operation. Plain `.` reads. `&` permits temporary exclusive changes; `^` transfers ownership and ends later use of a named value. The mark must cover one exact call. Existing `&place` windows keep their checked lifetimes.

current.note: Source-derived, not executed. The current compiler accepts unmarked method calls even when declarations use `&self` or `^self`. The owner requires visible call permission. Ordinary functions already use `edit(&value)` and `consume(^value)`. An `&place` window gives checked exclusive write access and remains part of every option.

decisions.title: A method that changes its receiver is called as `c.bump()` on a changeable value; `grow(&c)` keeps its `&`
decisions.situation: In Jet, `c.n += 1` changes a field with no mark, but `c.bump()`, a method that changes `c`, must be written `&c.bump()`. The compiler already knows `bump` changes `c` from its declaration, and `c` already says it can change, with `:=` or a `&` parameter. Swift and Rust mark changes at arguments but not before the dot. The vote decides whether the mark before the dot is required. We recommend leaving it to the compiler, as for fields.
decisions.gist: Should calling a method that changes `c` need `&c.bump()`, or just `c.bump()`?
decisions.lesson: A value made with `:=` can change. Calling `c.bump()` on it may change it, just as `c.n += 1` does, and the editor shows a faint `&` there. Passing `c` to another function that changes it still takes `&c`, so changes that leave the line stay visible.
decisions.story: Jo's build file has `&runnable.push(member)` and `&entries.push(selected)` on every other line. Reviewers stop reading the marks, and the one that matters, `grow(&state)`, gets lost.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0meo2tr. This replaces the D-RECEIVER-INFER1 package; its option D, a rule only for locals, is dropped as a weaker A. Changes the method-call clause of D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2847) and extends D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A (:2867-2887). Reuses D-MARK-SCOPE1=A (:2540) for `writes: .Explicit`.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/recv. today.jet: unmarked `c.bump()` is E0224 "This call writes `c`, but `c` has no `&` mark", in `run` and on a `&` parameter. `c.n += 1` passes in both. marked.jet: with `&` on every call it passes, and `&k.bump()` on a `::` value is E0202, which A keeps.

Data: a text count over 17,440 .jet files found about 26,400 marks before a method call and 3,500 before a field. Typical: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:1167-1169.

Reads with D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A: bare places read and `&place` writes in arguments, unchanged by A.

Other ballots' samples, such as `&ps.push(…)` in D-ARRAY-COLUMNS1, use today's spelling. If A wins, `jet fix` drops the receiver `&` and those samples follow the outcome.

The editor shows the filled-in `&` as a hint. A team that wants it in text sets `writes: .Explicit`, beside the existing `copies: .Explicit`, and E0224 fires as today.
options.technical: Stops E0224 for unmarked receiver calls (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/Checks.jet:3732). decisions.title: Pages, marked methods and single routes share one table on `web.app()`
decisions.situation: A Jet web program can add routes three ways. Pages go on the web app. Marked struct methods and single routes go on a router. Pages and router routes live in separate tables. A clash inside one table fails the check. A page and a router route at the same address pass with no error. The example app writes the same addresses twice. The vote decides whether pages and router routes share one table.
decisions.gist: Should pages, marked methods and single routes share one route table on the web app?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `web.app()` holds every route, so any clash fails the check and one listing shows all.
decisions.story: Leo adds an `/orders/:id` API route beside an `/orders/:id` page. `jet check` names both lines, and he mounts the API under `/api`.
decisions.inWild:
Option            Tables   Cross-table clash   Like
A one table       one      check error         Rails, Phoenix, Next.js
B prefix mount    two      unchecked           Express sub-routers
C check at serve  two      startup error       Go ServeMux
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- `web.app()` owns the one route table; `server.mux()` removed. `app.get/post/mount` take the D-HTTP-ROUTE-EXPOSE1=A row rules. `app.mount(prefix, value)` takes a marked struct or a computed handler (web_app.jet:21, E2810 today).
- E2804 for any two rows with one verb and address, naming both lines; E2807 merges into it. A route added while running is listed as computed with its call line and fails when added.

- `jet explain --routes` lists every row (verb, address, page or handler, form, file:line). `jet explain --web-graph` is not ported today (Front.jet:1210).
- Handler rows are server-only; only page rows join client navigation. Static files keep D-HTTP-STATIC-FILES1=A.
- Battery example (run.jet): mount Orders once under /api; delete the duplicate `mux.get` lines (158-169); serve the page graph (lines 31-34, 134).

FIXED UNDER EVERY OPTION
- Path parameters are `:id` (D-DX-ROUTER1=A's Tower code writes `{id}`); the marker is `#server.Get` (D-ROUTE-FILES2 writes `#Server.Get`).
- `#server.Get` is E0927 on r14 and base, even in Examples/features/net/http_routes.jet (probe r15; card #5548).

EVIDENCE (r14 jet)
- r13: `mux.get` beside `web.app().route` on one path passes check. r14: two identical `mux.get` give E2804.

IDS
Under A amends D-HTTP-ROUTE-EXPOSE1=A (rows move from `server.mux()` to `web.app()`). Fixed: D-DX-ROUTER1=A, D-ROUTE-FILES2=A, D-WEBAUTHOR1=D (explicit and convention routes collide loudly). Hosts #6055 (L-17).

options.name: One table on the app
options.detail: The router builder folds into `web.app()`. Every route form adds rows to one table. Gains: Any two routes at one address fail the check. One command lists every route. One builder instead of two. Losses: Every router caller moves to the app.
options.technical: `server.mux()` is removed. `mux.get`, `mux.post` and `mux.mount` become `app.get`, `app.post` and `app.mount` with the same rules. `app.mount(prefix, value)` adds rows under a prefix from a marked struct or a handler. Two rows with one verb and address are E2804 naming both lines; E2807 merges into it. `jet explain --routes` lists verb, address, kind and file:line for every row.

options.name: Two tables, joined by a prefix
options.detail: The app forwards everything under a prefix to a router, which keeps its own table. Gains: Router code stays as it is. Losses: Clashes across tables still pass. Two listings and two builders.
options.technical: `app.mount(prefix, mux)` strips the prefix and forwards requests to the router. Clashes are checked inside each table.

options.name: Two builders, one clash check
options.detail: Keep both builders. Serving them together checks clashes across both at startup. Gains: Clashes across tables are caught. Losses: Caught at startup, not at check. Two builders and two listings stay.
options.technical: The app and the router keep separate builders. Serving them together merges the tables and fails on a clash.

Sub-routers mount under a prefix, each with its own table. Source: https://expressjs.com/en/guide/routing.html
ServeMux panics when two patterns conflict at registration. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#ServeMux

gains: Every clash fails at check, naming both lines.
One command lists every route.
Removes a second builder.

losses.mitigation: The row rules are unchanged; only `mux.` becomes `app.`.

whyNot.reason: Clashes between tables still pass silently.
Clashes surface only at startup, and two builders remain.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename for router users, for one table that catches every clash.

decisions.title: Web and app framework shape: business logic once, for native apps and the browser
decisions.situation: This is the plan for how a Jet program becomes an app: one set of business rules that runs as a web site, a desktop app and a phone app. Today Jet has a web toolkit with string routes and form handlers, and no native app story. A team that also wants a phone app writes a second program and keeps the two in step by hand. That costs beginners twice the work, and it costs safety, because each copy must check sign-in and permissions on its own. You are asked to adopt one shape as the target the build cards follow. We recommend the shape in the proposal: a server function is reachable from the app only when marked, and every table read and write passes the table's access rule.
decisions.gist: Adopt one app shape: business logic in one package, one screen tree for web, desktop and phones, and server methods reachable only when marked.
decisions.lesson: An app framework decides what one program means: where code runs, which functions a stranger on the internet can call, and how screens find their data. Deciding this once, before the build, keeps every later card pointing the same way.
decisions.explainer:
A service is an ordinary struct whose fields are server things such as tables and keys. A screen gets the service as a typed handle and calls its methods. On the server the call is direct. In the browser or on a phone the same call becomes a typed request, checked by the compiler on both ends.

The risk in every such framework is a method that becomes public by accident. In the recommended option a method is public only when it carries a marker that says who may call it: signed-in users or anyone. A method without a marker stays on the server, and calling it from a screen is a compile error that names the marker to add.

The second risk is a query that forgets to check who is asking. Each table has an access rule, called a policy, that the server asks on every read and write. A query cannot skip it, because the table only answers rows the rule allows.
decisions.story: Ana builds Crewboard, a small task board for her team. She writes the rules once: who may move a card, and what a valid task is. The web site, the desktop app and the phone app all show the same board. When she forgets to mark a helper, the app does not quietly expose it; the build stops and tells her which marker to add.
decisions.inWild:
Next.js server functions are public endpoints once exported, and their documentation warns to check the caller inside each one.
Convex makes every server function explicit as a query, mutation or action, and internal functions are not reachable from clients.
Flutter and SwiftUI share one screen tree across devices but leave the server to the developer.
The proposal, section 8, compares the shape with the strongest system in each area, with sources.
decisions.detail:
The proposal is Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md (revision 5). Sections 1 and 3 to 6 are the shape. Section 7 holds the open choices O2 to O10 and S1, each with alternatives and a recommendation. Section 10 is the proposed public surface.

Voting A adopts the shape and the recommended answer to each item in the table of section 7.12. That includes S1, typed styles from tokens, and native builds that carry their server address as a build fact. Any single choice can be reopened later through its build card.

A amends one ratified decision. D-DX-SERVERFN1 moves registration from .action, .form and .data to a mounted service whose marked methods are endpoints. The typed client, plain form posts, same-origin request checks, retries and wire checks stay. D-LIVEQUERY1 is unchanged: its closure form, app.live(fn() { crew.board(view.project) }), is the target form, keyed by the one call it makes.

The 48 example Jet files are checked by the seed compiler (seed-b15) against stubs of the proposed API. Every Crewboard file is clean. The only errors are six style bugs seeded on purpose, one probe that proves an unmarked method cannot be called from a screen, and one example that needs closure-parameter inference (#6819 c4).

A second probe prints a secret and is accepted today; the rule that keeps secrets off the client is proposed separately (#6557, D-SECRETEDGE1). Nothing in the shape is built yet. Section 9 lists the cost and the build cards.

options.name: One app, explicit endpoint markers
options.gist: One logic package and one screen tree; only marked methods are endpoints.
options.detail: The shape in the proposal. A service method is an endpoint only when it is marked #App.SignedIn or #App.Public. An unmarked method is server-only, and a client call to it fails to compile with an error that names the marker. The same screens build for web, desktop and phones.

options.gist: The same shape, but every non-priv method is a signed-in endpoint.
options.detail: The same shape with the opposite default. Every method not marked priv is reachable by any signed-in user. A helper is private only when its author remembers priv, so a forgotten word opens a method to every account.

options.name: Web first, today's toolkit
options.gist: Keep the web toolkit's string routes; native apps come later as separate programs.
options.detail: No new shape. The web toolkit keeps string routes, form handlers and its own data helpers. Each handler checks the signed-in user itself. A desktop or phone app is a second program that calls the same URLs, written and kept in step by hand.

recommendation.why: A gives one program for every target and fails closed: a forgotten marker keeps a method on the server, and the compile error says what to add. B fails open on a forgotten word, and C keeps two programs in step by hand.

A forgotten marker cannot expose a method
Every table read and write passes the table's access rule
Screens call services with checked types on both ends

losses.loss: One marker line per endpoint; Crewboard has nineteen.
losses.mitigation: The compile error names the marker to add, and new-project templates include it.

losses.loss: One ratified decision changes its spelling.
losses.mitigation: Its checked behavior stays; only how code registers endpoints changes.

losses.loss: Little of the shape is built yet.
losses.mitigation: The build is split into hour-sized cards, with Crewboard as the acceptance example.

whyNot.reason: A forgotten priv opens a method to every signed-in account, and nothing warns.
A phone or desktop app means a second program, and each copy must repeat its own sign-in checks.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks for one marker line per endpoint in exchange for a default that cannot leak.

decisions.title: One Color value that every Core library uses
decisions.situation: Jet's terminal, game and user-interface libraries each describe a color in their own way today. A color picked for a game cannot be handed to the terminal library without copying its numbers by hand, and the interface library only takes a color as text. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose one Core color value that all three libraries use. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Should Core define one Color value that the terminal, game and interface libraries all use?
decisions.lesson: A color is usually four numbers: red, green, blue and transparency, each from 0 to 255. Option A makes this one Core value with conversions to hex text, to HSL and to linear light. The terminal, game and interface libraries take that one value, and their own color types go away.
decisions.story: Ana picks a brand orange for her game's menu and wants the same orange in her terminal tool. Today she copies three numbers into a second color type and types a third spelling as text. Under option A she writes the color once and passes it to both.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3288): "One core.color.Color". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3288: tui, game and ui each define their own color struct today. Should Core define one `core.color.Color` (sRGB 8-bit + alpha, with linear/HSL/hex conversions) that all of them use?"

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one.

decisions.title: Turn expensive bug checks on only where needed
decisions.gist: Should one switch enable expensive bug checks in your code and its libraries?
decisions.lesson: A deep check inspects data to find a bug, such as a wrong stored tree size. Today, ordinary debug checks can run automatically during development. These extra checks stay off until requested. Required safety checks stay on. A package is a named library or application; a function is a named operation.
decisions.story: A tree library updates a cached node count incorrectly. The developer wants a thorough walk to locate the bug, without making every normal request walk the tree.
decisions.detail: A approves an optional argument to the existing DebugOnly marker and one compiler switch. The switch may target existing packages or functions. B approves no new spelling and uses ordinary package settings. Both preserve required contracts, memory safety and type safety. Neither lets a successful optional check justify otherwise unsafe code.

options.name: One switch, with optional targeting
options.detail: Mark in-memory checks once, then enable all or selected names. Existing package settings still support checks with file or database access. Jet checks for invalid operations even when these checks are off. Target costly checks instead of enabling everything. Enabled checks take time; changing selection can require recompilation. Interactive sessions keep their starting selection; a different selection needs another session. Unverifiable prebuilt code needs rebuilding or is refused, even with checks off.
options.technical:
## Selection

`#DebugOnly(.deep) { ... }` marks optional, read-only bug checks. No switch means every deep check is disabled, in every profile. `--deep-checks` selects all authored deep checks in the program and its Jet libraries. It does not affect foreign libraries or separate build tools.

`--deep-checks=<scope>` limits selection. The grammar is `<package>` or `<package>::<name>(.<name>)*`. The package is its exact declared package.jet name; subsequent names follow the authored module and declaration path. Use dots after the single package separator: `tree::balance.rebuild`. Owner-qualified methods use `tree::balance.Tree.rebalance`; a default method body written in a trait uses that trait as its owner. Same-owner/name implementations are selected together. Diagnostics print copyable matching scopes and the matched declaration locations; they never expose generated backend names.

For example, `tree` selects that package; `tree::rebalance` selects deep checks inside that function. A module selects its descendants. Same-named package instances, overloads and generic instances are all selected, not silently guessed between. Compiler diagnostics identify the matched declarations. Anonymous nested bodies belong to their nearest named function. There are no new per-check labels, patterns or registry. Several occurrences take the union; a bare occurrence selects all. Every supplied scoped occurrence must match at least one declaration containing a deep check.

An empty, unknown or unmatched occurrence is a registered blocking error: neither compilation nor execution proceeds, even if another occurrence matches or a bare switch is also present. A selected declaration with no deep checks is an unmatched scope, not silent success.

Selection uses the declaration that contains the check, not whoever calls it. Calling a selected function does not enable unrelated checks in its callees. A scope selects every marked block within its named declaration; one block needs no public identifier. The example is a package named tree; tree::run selects its shown function. A separately declared library uses its own package and function names in the same way.

## Checking and effects

All deep bodies type-check when disabled. Captured program state is read-only; only fresh, nonescaping locals may be mutated. No initialization, reference, ownership transfer, refinement, permission or optimizer assumption escapes. No return or error propagation may leave the enclosing function; break/next cannot target an outside loop. Local helper returns and local-loop control remain allowed.

External effects, including file/database access, time, randomness and logging, are rejected transitively. Ordinary authorized code outside this diagnostic scope remains available for those jobs. Private memory work follows ordinary memory rules. Assert may report failure through Panic, but the marker grants no Panic permission. Enabled checks obey surrounding effect restrictions. Disabled bodies add no reachable memory or Panic effect. Required Pre/Post contracts and ordinary safety checks are never removed. These restrictions belong to `.deep`, not ordinary active DebugOnly code.

Independent #3043 fixes facts escaping removed code.

## Compilation and reuse

The switch applies to run, dev, test, build, emit, check, debug, repl, eval and notebook. Compiler wrappers propagate the resolved selection. Both debugger engines inherit it. The existing compiler-options input gains one typed deep_checks request with off, all or scoped forms. CLI and embedded callers use that same input; resolution to declaration/site identity occurs once inside the compiler. Entry points without an options input use off, not ambient environment.

Thread the existing options boundary through selection-capable compile/check facade calls and migrate affected callers in one cutover. Do not introduce separate globals, a second selector parser or parallel compile APIs. Exercise an embedded caller selecting the same checks without a CLI. REPL and notebook sessions select it at creation and keep it for their lifetime. A different selection requires a new session. Creating that session does not reset the existing session, migrate its in-memory values or silently replay prior cells.

Each may retain its own compiled units. A dev process likewise keeps its launch selection; restart it to change selection under its existing lifecycle. D-CLI1 applies: before standalone `--` it is a compiler option; after it, an application argument.

Cache and resident identities use the resolved selected check sites in each affected semantic body, unit and artifact. Equivalent selector lists reuse the same identity. Recompile changed units and their affected dependents, not unrelated packages. Already compiled matching code is reused. Per-function targeting does not promise sub-unit compilation. Already launched binaries retain their compiled choice; there is no runtime flag that recreates removed code.

Rebuilding uses admitted source and ordinary authority. Only run may delegate declared environment preparation to Jetpack; --no-prepare forbids it. Other commands gain no preparation permission. Locked mode preserves pins and dependency identities. Existing E0983, E0603 and E1334 resolution failures keep their causes and repairs. An incompatible prebuilt unit without admitted rebuild source gets a registered blocking diagnostic naming the unit and compiled/requested selections. Missing, unreadable or unsupported selection identity is never assumed to mean off.

It is a cache miss requiring admitted-source rebuilding, or a blocking refusal if that is unavailable. This applies even to default-off requests; no legacy artifact reader or guessed compatibility is introduced. This creates no new resolver, download path or prebuilt format.

## Profiles and delivery

Deep selection is independent of ordinary DebugOnly eligibility. Bare DebugOnly is on for dev, debug, test, ci, small, no-os, default, fast, fuzz, coverage and package-defined profiles. It is off for explicit release and hardened. This fact is shared by all execution engines; optimization alone does not change it. Hardened sentries remain separate.

AOT, default run, interpreter and applicable web use one selected meaning. New marker/flag/scopes require registration, diagnostics and snapshots. Preserve the read-only tree fixture and its valid/corrupt, on/off outputs. No speed advantage over B is claimed; any later performance-motivated replacement still requires its paired strict performance gate.

Sources: D-CANVASSTATE1, D-CLI1, D-CONF-KEY1, D-CONF-MERGE1, D-CONF-MODULE1, D-HARDENED1, D-NOPANIC1, D-PANICROOT1; Source/CmdCompile.rs; Source/main.rs; Driver/mod.rs; crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs; examples/features/packages/typed_settings.

options.name: Configure each package separately
options.detail: Keep existing package settings. Each library chooses whether and how to expose its checks. No new marker or compiler switch. Build with the setting on to check that branch for invalid operations.
options.technical:
Use D-CONF-KEY1 and D-CONF-MERGE1 as exercised by examples/features/packages/typed_settings. The setting belongs to the declaring package and defaults false; current contribution/Force rules still apply. Do not assume an application CLI setting reaches separately configured dependencies.

Libraries expose ordinary read-only predicates where callers need checks; the application authors and enables those calls, or explicitly binds a library-supported setting through its existing configuration contract. The predicate remains ordinary typed Jet. The branch follows the existing comptime checking law: an unselected arm is not promised the always-type-check behavior of DebugOnly, so the author must exercise both setting values.

No marker argument, global deep flag or new invariant API is added. Selected values already fold before execution and participate in instance identity. Ordinary code/effect/safety checking remains in force; a setting is not permission to rely on erased initialization or skip a required guard.

decisions.title: How should an opt-in deep check be written?
decisions.situation: A deep check walks data to find a bug, such as a wrong stored tree size. The approved design keeps it off until --deep-checks selects it. Its original marker was #DebugOnly(.deep). A later ruling replaced #DebugOnly with #Off(.Release), leaving the deep spelling unsettled. The selection and safety rules are not being voted on again. Choose a spelling that preserves them. We recommend adding .DeepDisabled to #Off: the block is off when deep checks do not select it. This keeps one presence marker. #On(.Deep) reads more directly, but adds another marker and changes the earlier one-marker direction.
decisions.gist: How should code mark an expensive check that stays off until requested?
decisions.lesson: A deep check inspects data for a bug. It stays off until --deep-checks selects it, even in development. Jet must still check its types while off. Today's #Off(.Release) removes ordinary code in release builds. The choice is how to name the deep-check block, not whether its safety rules apply.
decisions.explainer:
Expected command results after implementation, identical for all five choices. Run these from the tree package beside run.jet. These are requirements, not observations of proposed syntax.

```text
jet run -A run.jet
stdout: 4\n
stderr: empty
exit: 0

jet run -A --deep-checks run.jet
jet run -A --deep-checks=tree run.jet
jet run -A --deep-checks=tree.run run.jet
stdout: empty, for each selected command
stderr first line: Stop [E3001]: `panic: tree size is wrong`
exit: 70, for each selected command

jet run -A --deep-checks=tree.leaf run.jet
stdout: empty
stderr: E2121, a blocking check-free-scope report
exit: 1
```

The selected command results stay the same with --profile release. -A suppresses authority notices; it does not enable deep checks or override a written Panic denial. Full report source excerpts depend on the chosen header's line positions; they must be snapshotted when implemented.
decisions.story: Ana's three-node tree wrongly records four nodes. She wants a full walk while hunting the bug, without paying for that walk on normal runs.
decisions.inWild:
# Python illustration of the same three-node tree, not a library quotation.
import sys

def deep_consistent(tree):
    children, cached_size = tree
    return all(deep_consistent(child) for child in children) and cached_size == 1 + sum(child[1] for child in children)

tree = ([([], 1), ([], 1)], 4)
if '--deep-checks' in sys.argv:
    assert deep_consistent(tree), 'tree size is wrong'
print(tree[1])
# No flag: stdout 4, exit 0. Flag: AssertionError, exit 1.
# This is an ordinary runtime branch, not Jet's checked removal contract.
decisions.detail:
All five choices are proposals, not working deep-check syntax. Each code pane shows the same complete run.jet. Beside it, package.jet contains name: "tree" and version: "0.1.0", on separate lines. Only the check header changes. The check walks the same corrupt tree and has the same required output under every choice.

The shared contract is D-DEEP-CHECK1=A, ratified September 11. No switch means off in every profile. --deep-checks selects all authored deep checks in the program and its Jet libraries, not foreign libraries or separate build tools. --deep-checks=tree selects this package; --deep-checks=tree.run selects this declaration, not its callers or callees. Paths use dots, not the retired ::. Several scopes take their union. An empty, unknown or check-free scope blocks compilation, even beside a bare switch.

Each selected block may read captured state and mutate only fresh, nonescaping locals. External effects are rejected transitively. Local helper returns and local loop control remain allowed; return, propagation, break or next cannot leave the check. No ownership transfer, initialization, permission, refinement or optimizer assumption escapes it. Assert may stop, but the block grants no Panic permission. Disabled checks contribute no reachable Panic or memory effects. Required contracts and safety checks stay on. Selection is independent of release eligibility.

Every option needs the same compiler plumbing. CLI and embedded callers share one typed request. Selection belongs to the authored declaration, including private methods and anonymous bodies under their nearest named function. Overloads and generic instances with the same authored name are selected together. Diagnostics name matched declarations. Sessions retain their creation-time selection; changing it starts another session. Compiled-out code needs recompilation; compatible units may be reused, while unverifiable prebuilt identities need admitted source or a blocking refusal, even with checks off.

Current source: origin/dev Core/Compiler/Lang.jet:24-28 declares only BuildCondition.Release. Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet declares Off at Statement and Block sites. Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet registers Off and also #here and #caller. The parser emits Stmt.Switched; sema's Off arm checks the body in isolated state and emits TStmt.DebugOnly for .Release. JetIR then omits it for release. That internal name does not make #DebugOnly legal source. Adding any condition still requires generalizing that path, not just declaring an enum case.

The earlier D-OFF-RELEASE1=A ruling explicitly chose one conditional-presence marker. New options must say when they amend that direction. SUB G6Decl-44 stages only spelling-independent selection and diagnostics E2119-E2121; it is not proof that any proposed body runs. Proposed diagnostic reuse and removal costs below are design requirements, not observed behavior. Beginner and expert paths are stated per option; the expert selection and safety rules above never change.

options.name: #Off(.DeepDisabled)
options.detail: Add one BuildCondition case to the existing marker. DeepDisabled means this site's deep check was not selected. Beginner: write this header and use --deep-checks. Expert: use the same header with declaration scopes; no second presence marker is introduced. The negative condition is longer and requires care when reading it.
options.technical:
The proposed BuildCondition.DeepDisabled is evaluated per authored site, not once for the whole build. It removes this block when unselected, regardless of profile. .Release and bare Off retain their current meanings. Reuse Stmt.Switched and the isolated checking/removal path, with the shared deep restrictions.

Cost: one condition case, registry and marker-argument updates, generalized selection/removal, plus all shared deep-check work. No measured compile-time or runtime advantage is claimed. Enabled checks pay for the walk; disabled checks must emit no branch or body at any level.

Edge cases: two Off markers on one statement remain refused. DeepDisabled is valid only for a deep-check body, not a general escape from read-only rules. Nesting under Off(.Release) can suppress an otherwise selected check in release, so document both conditions rather than promising it runs there. Statement and Block sites stay; expression and item uses are refused. This extends the closed condition menu but keeps the ratified one-marker direction.

options.name: #On(.Deep)
options.detail: Add an affirmative marker. Beginner: the header says the check is on only when selected. Expert: target declarations with the same switches as A. It reads directly but asks the owner to amend the earlier one-marker direction. It can share A's semantic path; two spellings do not require two implementations.
options.technical:
Propose On at Statement and Block sites and BuildCondition.Deep, with the same isolated deep checker and removal path as A. Cost: a new marker, condition case, registry/parser wiring and shared implementation work. There is no measured cost comparison with A.

Edge cases: this option refuses On(.Release), Off(.Deep) and two presence markers on one statement. Those refusals are proposed, not today's E0344 behavior for On. Expression and item uses are refused. Nested Off(.Release) can still erase an enabled deep block. The new spelling amends D-OFF-RELEASE1's one-marker direction. Sharing the underlying mechanism is required by I8; a second independent selector or checker is not authorized.

options.name: #DeepCheck
options.detail: Name the purpose rather than the build condition. Beginner: one short word with no condition to learn. Expert: declaration targeting and all shared rules stay unchanged. This is the clearest domain name, but adds a marker beside Off and amends the earlier one-marker direction.
options.technical:
Propose DeepCheck at Statement and Block sites, lowered into the shared switched-body path. It needs no BuildCondition case. Cost: one marker and registry/parser wiring, plus shared checking, selection and removal work. Its shorter source spelling is not proof of faster compilation.

Edge cases: arguments are refused; item and expression uses are refused. DeepCheck plus Off on one statement is refused, while nesting keeps both conditions. No ordinary check, required contract or arbitrary effectful debug block is silently converted. This changes the one-marker surface direction but need not violate I8 if it has exactly one semantic path.

options.name: Restore #DebugOnly(.deep)
options.detail: Use the spelling originally approved for deep checks. Beginner: old deep-check examples remain recognizable. Expert: targeting stays identical. It revives a retired name, and DebugOnly is misleading because selected checks may run in release. Bare DebugOnly would remain refused, not become an alias.
options.technical:
This explicitly amends D-OFF-RELEASE1's retirement. Register only the deep form and lower it through the same switched-body path. Cost: marker and argument registration, parser changes and shared work. Lowercase .deep needs an explicit argument rule; do not claim it follows the current BuildCondition menu.

Edge cases: bare DebugOnly stays refused with Off(.Release) as its repair. Other arguments are refused. Two presence markers on one statement, expression uses and item uses are refused. The argument-sensitive retirement rule is additional teaching and diagnostic work, but does not mean one accepted name has two runtime meanings. Selected checks remain legal in release unless an enclosing condition removes them.

options.name: if checks.deep(at: #here)
options.detail: Use an ordinary-looking call with an explicit site. Beginner: familiar if syntax, but a new checks API must be learned and imported. Expert: the site can identify the authored declaration without a hidden caller-dependent function. It still needs special branch rules to satisfy the already approved deep-check contract.
options.technical:
The checks module and deep function are proposed, not existing Core APIs. #here already supplies a SourceLocation with function and module; #caller is also an existing parameter-default mechanism. Thus an ordinary function can receive site information. A Boolean need not have one value throughout a build. The draft's impossibility argument was false.

Site information alone does not mark a checked diagnostic region. Ordinary if allows outward writes and effects and does not promise branch removal at every level. To keep this a spelling-only choice, recognize only this direct condition as a deep site and lower its then branch through the same isolated checker/removal as A. Cost: a new Core API, exact-call recognition and shared work. Purely ordinary if without those rules is not equivalent and would need reopening D-DEEP-CHECK1.

Edge cases: this option refuses a stored result, negation, a compound condition, an else arm, a forwarded or forged site, and indirect calls as deep-check spellings. That is extra expression policy; these are proposed refusals, not current diagnostics. A wrapper's #caller default could capture a site, but does not remove the need for branch-region recognition. Function identity alone also cannot identify each check site for artifact identities.

recommendation.why: Off(.DeepDisabled) extends the existing presence marker instead of introducing a second one. Its longer negative name buys consistency with the ratified direction. All choices still need the same deep safety and selection work.
gains: One presence marker
No revived retirement or call-sensitive branch rules

losses.loss: The negative condition is longer and less direct.
losses.mitigation: Teach it as off unless selected, show the exact command beside it, and keep its condition meaning consistent with Off.

whyNot.reason: It reads well, but adds a marker and explicitly amends the earlier one-marker direction.
The purpose is clearest, but another marker is not necessary to express this build condition.
It revives a retired name whose debug-only promise is false in release.
Site passing is feasible, but ordinary-looking if needs special restrictions and guaranteed removal to preserve the approved behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: Prefer one marker and a longer condition over the shorter affirmative or purpose-specific names. This is a readability judgment, not a measured speed claim.

Replaced unsupported implementation and diagnostic promises with proposals, restored shared edge cases, and recommend one presence marker rather than the original On recommendation.

wild.note: An ordinary if can select the same check; it does not promise Jet's checked removal rules.

if '--deep-checks' in sys.argv:
    assert deep_consistent(tree), 'tree size is wrong'
print(tree[1])
# No flag: 4. Flag: AssertionError, exit 1.
