decisions.title: The public compiler event type
decisions.situation: While Jet compiles, it passes through named moments: a file is parsed, declarations settle, code is emitted, the build finishes. Packages can already hook these moments in Jet code, and a ratified read-only view lists them in order. Outside tools will also see these moments as messages on the session wire. This vote decides whether one public type defines both the hook view and the wire view. We recommend one compiler.Event enum in core.compiler, with the wire's JSON schema generated from it.
decisions.gist: Should one public compiler.Event type define the moments seen by hooks, by the in-process stages() view and by the session wire?
decisions.lesson: A compile moment, such as settled or emitted, reaches three places: typed hooks written in Jet, the ordered stages() view, and JSON messages for outside tools. Each place could get its own list of moments and fields. If the lists are separate, they can drift: a hook and an external tool would describe the same moment differently. One type keeps one list.
decisions.story: Ken's build.jet audits the items each settled round adds, using stages(). His teammate writes a dashboard that reads the same moments from `jet build --json`. When Ken's hook says a round added three items, the dashboard should show the same round, with the same names and fields.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.3 (event taxonomy) and section 5, ballot 4. Ratified: D-HOOK-STAGES1=A gives typed `#On(point)` hooks and the stage table. D-JAI-EVENTS1=A adds compiler.imported, compiler.settled, build.link, build.before_write, build.after_write and compiler.finished. It also adds compiler.advanced.Session.stages().

Under A, compiler.Event is one enum in core.compiler. Its variants carry the ratified payload types. The JSON schema for `--json` and the session wire is generated from the enum's registry rows. Each variant is versioned with its payload, which is the D-JAI-EVENTS1 stability mitigation.

Hooks never cross the wire, under every option: D-HOOK-STAGES1 has no external engine or carrier. Editor answers such as hover and definition are query responses, not events.

Under B, stage payload types stay in Core and the wire schema is private to the driver. Under C, both are public and documented separately.

options.name: One compiler.Event enum for hooks, stages() and the wire
options.detail: One enum in core.compiler lists every public moment. Hooks, the stages() view, `--json` output and the session wire all use its names and fields. The wire's JSON schema is generated from it, so the views cannot drift. Each new variant is a versioned public change.

options.name: Per-stage payload types only; wire schema private
options.detail: Hooks and stages() use the ratified per-stage payload types. The wire uses a private driver schema that may change freely. Outside tools see a different shape for the same moment, with no public stability promise.
options.code:
#On(compiler.settled) fn gen(r: compiler.Round) -> compiler.Output { ... }
// wire: driver-private JSON, free to change between releases

options.name: Public stage types plus a separate public wire schema
options.detail: Both views are public and documented, as two lists. Outside tools get a stable schema, but every change must be made in two places and kept in step.
options.code:
// Core: compiler.Round, compiler.Artifact, ...
// Docs: session-wire.schema.json, maintained by hand beside them

comparisons.note: One message kind enum drives the whole metaprogram loop.
Zig's compiler server tags are one enum shared by server and client code in the standard library.

recommendation.why: It gives one list of moments in one executable home. Under B and C the hook view and the machine view of the same moment can drift apart.
recommendation.tradeoff: Every new event variant is a versioned public change.

whyNot.reason: Outside tools see a different, unstable shape for the same moment a hook sees.
Two public lists must be kept in step by hand.

losses.loss: Adding a moment is a public API change.
losses.mitigation: Each variant is versioned with its payload, as the ratified events decision already requires.

surface.gist: Should one public event type define the compile moments seen by hooks, by stages() and by outside tools?
surface.lesson: A compile moment, such as settled or emitted, reaches typed hooks, the ordered stages() view, and JSON messages for outside tools. Separate lists for each could drift, so a hook and a tool would describe one moment differently. One type keeps one list.

current.note: Hooks and stages() are ratified; the wire's event shape is not decided.
current.code:
#On(compiler.settled) fn gen(r: compiler.Round) -> compiler.Output { ... }
// wire event for the same moment: undecided

wild.note: One message kind enum drives the whole metaprogram loop.
wild.code:
message := compiler_wait_for_message();
if message.kind == .COMPLETE break;

options.name: One compiler.Event
options.gist: Hooks, stages() and the wire share one enum.
gains: Hook and tool always agree.
Wire schema is generated, not hand-written.
losses: Each new moment is a public change.

options.name: Private wire shape
options.gist: Stage types public; the wire is free to change.
gains: Wire can change without a vote.
losses: Tools see a different shape than hooks.

proposed.code: // wire: driver-private JSON

options.name: Two public lists
options.gist: Stage types and a separate public wire schema.
gains: Tools get a stable schema.
losses: Two lists to keep in step.

proposed.code: // Core types + a hand-kept wire schema

recommendation.why: One list of moments in one home. The other options let hooks and tools drift apart.
gains: One name and shape per moment.

losses.loss: New moments need versioning.
losses.mitigation: Each variant is versioned with its payload, as already ratified.

whyNot.reason: Tools and hooks would disagree.
Two lists drift.

recommendation.tradeoff: Versioning discipline for one shared vocabulary.

decisions.title: The fate of the hidden `jet __jetpack` service
decisions.situation: Jetpack is Jet's package and environment tool. A ratified boundary rule says Jetpack may reach the compiler's evaluator and checker only by running `jet`. Today it does that by starting one hidden `jet __jetpack` process for every config value or entry check, so 40 values cost 40 processes. The new compiler session can answer many requests from one process. We recommend folding the hidden service into the session: one `jet` child per Jetpack command, or none when a shared session already runs.
decisions.gist: Should Jetpack's hidden per-value `jet __jetpack` service fold into the compiler session, stay as one process per operation, or be linked into Jetpack?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack must not contain the compiler; it asks `jet` instead. Today each question starts a new `jet` process, which pays startup every time. The session can answer many evaluate requests from one process, and can even reuse a running `jet dev --serve` cache. The alternative of linking the compiler into Jetpack would break the boundary rule.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jetpack env` on an `env.jet` with 40 computed values. Today he waits for 40 `jet` processes to start, check and exit. With a session, one `jet` child answers all 40, and if his `jet dev --serve` is running, Jetpack reuses its warm cache.
decisions.inWild:
# Bazel keeps one long-lived server and sends it many requests
bazel build //game
bazel query //...
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 5. Boundary law: D-VERDICT-2188-1 (Jetpack reaches the evaluator and checker only through `jet`). Related: D-JETPACK-LAYERS1 and D-JETPACK-LAYERS2.

Under A, `jet __jetpack`, its two operations and their tests are deleted in the same cutover. Jetpack starts one `jet __session` child per Jetpack command (entry per D-SESSION-ENTRY1) and sends evaluate and check lines. When a `jet dev --serve` session runs for the workspace, Jetpack attaches to it instead.

Acceptance proposed for the port card (slate S7): the EnvModel and ProjectEntry service tests pass with one `jet` child per Jetpack command, with the spawn count asserted. With an attached `--serve` session the count is zero.

Under C, jetpack links the evaluator and checker directly, which contradicts D-VERDICT-2188-1.

options.name: Fold into the session
options.detail: One `jet` session child per Jetpack command answers every evaluate and check request, or Jetpack attaches to a running `jet dev --serve`. The boundary law holds. The hidden `__jetpack` command and its tests are deleted in the same cutover.
options.code:
$ jetpack env            # env.jet has 40 computed values
# starts: jet __session   (one child)
# sends 40 evaluate lines, reads 40 answers
# with jet dev --serve running: attaches, zero children

options.name: Keep one process per operation
options.detail: Keep `jet __jetpack <op>` as today. Nothing changes, and Jetpack keeps paying one process start per value.
options.code:
$ jetpack env
# starts 40 x: jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate env.jet#<name>

options.name: Link the evaluator and checker into jetpack
options.detail: Jetpack contains the compiler pieces it needs and calls them in-process. There are no children, but the boundary law breaks: Jetpack would contain the compiler, and the two binaries could disagree.
options.code:
$ jetpack env            # no child process
# jetpack binary now embeds JetEval and JetSema

comparisons.note: One long-lived server answers many client requests instead of starting a process per request.

recommendation.why: It keeps the boundary law and removes one process per value without adding a mechanism. The request is the same evaluate the session already needs.
recommendation.tradeoff: Jetpack depends on the session protocol's stability; the toolchain-identity handshake refuses a mismatched `jet`.

whyNot.reason: It keeps paying one process start per value and keeps a second hidden service beside the session.
It breaks the boundary law: Jetpack would contain the compiler.

losses.loss: Jetpack now depends on the session protocol.
losses.mitigation: The hello handshake refuses a mismatched toolchain with E1227, as the engine handshake does.

surface.gist: Should Jetpack ask one compiler session for all its values instead of starting a process per value?
surface.lesson: Jetpack must not contain the compiler; it asks `jet`. Today each question starts a new `jet` process. A session answers many questions from one process and can reuse a running dev server. Linking the compiler into Jetpack would break the rule.

current.note: One hidden `jet` process per value.
current.code:
$ jetpack env      # 40 computed values
# 40 x jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate ...

wild.note: One long-lived server answers many requests.
wild.code: bazel build //game

options.name: Fold into the session
options.gist: One child per Jetpack command, or none if a session runs.
gains: 40 values, one process.
Deletes the hidden `__jetpack` service.
losses: Jetpack depends on the session protocol.

proposed.code:
$ jetpack env
# one jet __session child; 40 evaluate lines
# jet dev --serve running: attaches, no child

options.name: Keep per-value processes
options.gist: No change.
gains: No migration work.
losses: One process start per value.
A second hidden service remains.

proposed.code: # 40 x jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate ...

options.name: Link the compiler into Jetpack
options.gist: Jetpack calls the evaluator in-process.
gains: No child processes.
losses: Breaks the boundary rule.

proposed.code: # jetpack embeds the evaluator and checker

recommendation.why: It keeps the boundary rule and removes a process per value, using a request the session already has.
gains: Faster Jetpack commands.
One fewer hidden service.

losses.loss: Depends on the session protocol.
losses.mitigation: The handshake refuses a mismatched `jet` with a clear error.

whyNot.reason: Slow, and keeps a second hidden service.
Jetpack would contain the compiler.

recommendation.tradeoff: One protocol dependency for far fewer processes.

decisions.title: What the editor runs on save, and what a check may touch
decisions.situation: While you type, Jet's editor support checks your code and shows errors. Checking already runs some compile-time code, and the project's build file adds more: its fn build plan, its compile-time code and its hooks. Some of that code can start programs, use the network or write files. Running it on every save could do things the user never asked for, silently. Today, mistakes in the plan show up only when someone runs jet build. The vote decides when the plan runs and what any check may touch. We recommend that a check never touches the outside world, that a check command runs the plan, and that running it on save is opt-in.
decisions.gist: When should the editor run the project's build plan, and may any check run code that touches files, the network or programs?
decisions.lesson: Checking finds type and ownership errors, and it already runs the compile-time code that types depend on. The build plan is the `fn build` function in build.jet; running it runs more compile-time code and hooks. Some compile-time code reads files, downloads, starts programs or writes files. A full build also links and writes the program.
decisions.story: Ken saves build.jet with a bad `b.add_executable` call and wants to see the error before he runs a build. His teammate Mia's plan downloads textures and runs a converter program. She does not want a download and a converter run every time she presses save. Both want the editor to show plan mistakes without doing anything behind their backs.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 1.3 (ZLS build-on-save), section 2.5 rule 5 and section 5, ballot 7. Owner question q0d271iq asked for a check command or an opt-in save step, because compile-time code can act silently. Ratified context: D-LSP1=C (one compiler service), D-HOOK-STAGES1=A, D-CTEFFECT1=A (compile-time effect tiers), D-BUILD-IO1=A, D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A (checks run comptime tries) and D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1=A (one tighten rule).

ONE RULE FOR EVERY CHECK. Under A, a check is side-effect free wherever it starts: `jet check`, the editor while typing, the plan check and an attached session request. Compile-time code in a check may compute and may read files inside the workspace. It may also use values already in Jet's cache, such as an earlier pinned download.

A check never starts a program, uses the network, writes a project file, calls a foreign library or runs an `#Impure` block. It never asks for trust. Generated code and lock entries a check computes stay in the session's memory and cache. Only build, run, test and dev write `.jet/generated` and `.jet/lock`.

HOW IT IS ENFORCED. The session runs a check request under a read-only ceiling: the package's held rights narrowed to reading the workspace. This is the existing tighten rule of the one authority model, not a second checker. Compile-time effects in a check meet the same rights tree as everywhere else. Metaprogramming that only changes the program being checked keeps working when the package holds it. Compile-time host access never runs in a check.

THE PLAN CHECK. `jet check --plan` and the editor command Jet: Check build plan both send the session request check{plan: true}. It runs the `fn build` plan, its compile-time code and its hooks under the same ceiling. Nothing is linked or written. Plan results are cached by key, so an unchanged plan costs nothing.

The editor setting `"jet.checkPlanOnSave": true` sends the same request on each save. Its default is false. No setting gives a check more rights; outside work runs only in build, run, test and dev.

EDGE CASES. A pinned `fetch` whose bytes are not cached yet is reported as not downloaded yet. Errors that depend on it are held back, not shown as false errors. An `#Impure` block, a `b.action` step or a process probe is listed by name as not run in a check, with its site. Today an `#Impure` block without the gate flag is error E3411; in a check under A it is a note.

Dependency build entries stay checked but not run, as today. The plan check uses the current snapshot, including unsaved editor text. Cancellation and caching follow section 2.5 of the session design.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. A beginner configures nothing: errors appear while typing, and saving does nothing extra. To see plan errors early they run `jet check --plan` or the editor command. An expert turns on the save setting, or runs `jet build` when outside work must run.

WHY NOT B AND C. B runs the whole plan on every save even when nobody asked. That is safe but costs time on large plans, and it is not what the owner asked for. C is what Zig's and Rust's editors do. Once opted in, every save starts programs and downloads with the project's rights, the silent behavior this revision removes.

options.name: Checks touch nothing outside; plan check on request
options.detail: Every check runs compile-time code under a read-only ceiling: it may compute and read workspace files, and nothing else. `jet check --plan` and an editor command run the build plan under that ceiling. An editor setting runs it on save too; it is off by default. Outside work runs only in build, run, test and dev.
options.technical: Session request check{selection, plan: Bool}. The ceiling is the package's holds narrowed to FS.Read of the workspace plus cached recorded inputs, by the D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1 tighten rule. Tier 2 and `b.action` sites become typed not-run notes. Setting key `jet.checkPlanOnSave`, default false. New CLI flag `--plan` on `jet check`, registered under this decision.
options.code:
$ jet check --plan
error: unknown source `run.jt` in add_executable
  --> build.jet:2:40
note: not run in a check: action `convert_textures` (Exec)
  --> build.jet:5:9  runs at `jet build`
// editor settings, off by default:
"jet.checkPlanOnSave": true

options.name: Plan check on every save, touching nothing outside
options.detail: As A, but saving always runs the plan check. No setting is needed to see plan errors. Every save of a changed plan pays one plan run.
options.technical: As A, with check{plan: true} sent on every didSave. The setting turns it off instead of on.

options.name: Opt-in plan on save with the project's rights
options.detail: Checks while typing stay as in A. An editor setting makes each save run the plan with the same rights as `jet build`, including approved downloads, programs and gated blocks. This matches Zig's and Rust's editors.
options.technical: The save request is build{plan_only: true} under the project's effective authority and the gate flags named in the setting.

comparisons.note: ZLS runs the build's check step on save through Zig's build-system protocol. That step runs build.zig with its full rights.
rust-analyzer runs cargo check on save by default, which runs build scripts and procedural macros with full rights. VS Code's restricted mode exists to stop that in untrusted folders.

recommendation.why: Checks become safe to run anywhere, so the editor can never act behind the user's back. Plan errors still come before a build: one command, or one setting for people who want them on save.
gains: No check ever starts programs, downloads or writes files.
Plan errors appear without a build.

losses.loss: Plan errors wait until you ask.
losses.mitigation: One command, or the save setting, shows them; typing errors still appear immediately.

losses.loss: Errors in outside work appear only at a build.
losses.mitigation: The check names each step it did not run and where, so nothing is hidden.

whyNot.reason: B is just as safe but spends a plan run on every save, even when nobody asked for one.
C lets an opted-in save start programs and downloads silently, the risk this revision removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Plan errors on request instead of on every save, so no check can act on the outside world.

surface.gist: When should the editor run the build plan, and may any check touch files, the network or programs?
surface.lesson: Checking finds errors while you type, and it already runs compile-time code. The build plan, `fn build` in build.jet, runs more compile-time code and hooks. Some of that code downloads, starts programs or writes files. Running it on every save could do things you never asked for.

current.note: Plan errors appear only at a build; compile-time code in checks is limited only by flags.

wild.note: ZLS runs the build's check step on every save, with the build's full rights.
wild.code: "enable_build_on_save": true

options.name: Safe checks, plan on request
options.gist: Checks never touch the outside; a command or opt-in setting runs the plan.
gains: No check starts programs, downloads or writes files.
Plan errors without a build.
losses: Plan errors wait until you ask.

proposed.code:
$ jet check --plan
error: unknown source `run.jt` in add_executable
note: not run in a check: action `convert_textures`
// editor setting, off by default:
"jet.checkPlanOnSave": true

options.gist: As A, but every save runs the plan check.
gains: Plan errors with no setting.
losses: A plan run on every save.

losses.mitigation: One command or the save setting shows them; typing errors stay immediate.

losses.mitigation: The check names each step it did not run, and where.

decisions.title: How a program starts a compiler session it talks to
decisions.situation: A compiler session is one running Jet compiler that tools can send requests to. People already have a public way to share one: `jet dev --serve` opens a socket, and `jet build` can attach to it. A parent program such as Jetpack, an editor build task or a test harness also needs to start its own private session on standard input and output. This vote picks that entry point. We recommend a hidden internal command, `jet __session`, which replaces today's hidden `jet __jetpack` instead of adding public surface.
decisions.gist: How should a parent program such as Jetpack start a private compiler session that it talks to over standard input and output?
decisions.lesson: A parent program can start `jet` as a child and send it requests on standard input. Today Jetpack does this with a hidden command, `jet __jetpack`, once per value. The session needs one such entry point for every first-party client. It can stay hidden, become a flag value on `jet dev`, or become a flag on every runnable command, as Zig does.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jetpack env` on his game. Jetpack needs the compiler to evaluate 40 computed values in `env.jet`. It should start one `jet` child, send 40 evaluate lines and read the answers. Ken never types this command; he only sees that `jetpack env` got faster.
decisions.inWild:
# ZLS starts Zig's build runner as a child and talks over stdio:
zig build --listen=-
# Zig's compiler server works the same way on every build verb:
zig build-exe main.zig --listen=-
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 2. Ratified today: `jet dev --serve` (socket) and `--session=auto|off|required` on `jet build`, `jet run` and `jet test` (D-BUILD-SESSION1=A).

Under A, `jet __session` speaks the session protocol on stdio (wire format per D-SESSION-WIRE1). Like `__jetpack` today it is absent from help and answers a malformed request with E2104. It replaces `__jetpack` and its two operations in the same cutover (see D-JETPACK-SERVICE1).

Under B, `jet dev` gains a non-interactive mode that runs nothing, which is new behavior for a command whose job is running the program. Under C, check, build, test, run and dev each gain `--listen=-`, and each must define what an update request means for that verb.

B is the upgrade path if the owner later wants third-party build tools to drive sessions. A hidden verb is still a command, but it is the same kind of surface `__jetpack` already is.

options.name: Hidden internal command `jet __session`
options.detail: One hidden verb serves every first-party parent. It is not in help and adds no public surface; it replaces `jet __jetpack`. Third-party tools are not supported; they use the CLI or attach to `jet dev --serve`.
options.code:
# Jetpack, once per jetpack command:
$ jet __session
> {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"evaluate","program":"env.jet#port"}
< {"kind":"response","id":1,"status":"ok","value":8080}
> not json
< E2104 report (malformed request), as `__jetpack` answers today
$ jet help    # __session is not listed

options.name: `jet dev --listen=-`
options.detail: One documented flag value on `jet dev` serves the session on stdio. Third-party tools get a supported entry. `jet dev` must gain a mode that starts nothing, so Ken's game must not launch when Jetpack uses it.
options.code:
$ jet dev --listen=-      # serves stdio; does not start the game
> {"kind":"request","id":1,"op":"evaluate",...}

options.name: `--listen=-` on every runnable command
options.detail: Check, build, test, run and dev each accept `--listen=-`, matching Zig. Third-party tools are fully supported, but five commands gain a documented flag and each must define what an update means.
options.code:
$ jet check --listen=-
$ jet build --listen=-
$ jet test --listen=-

comparisons.note: Every Zig build command accepts --listen=- and serves its binary protocol on stdio; ZLS uses `zig build --listen=-`.

recommendation.why: Every current client is first-party, and people already have a public spelling in `jet dev --serve`. A replaces the existing hidden `__jetpack` command instead of adding a second surface.
recommendation.tradeoff: Third-party build tools cannot start their own session; they attach to `jet dev --serve` or use the CLI.

whyNot.reason: It gives `jet dev` a second mode that runs nothing, with no current client that needs it.
It adds a documented flag to five commands for clients that do not exist yet.

losses.loss: Third-party tools have no stdio entry.
losses.mitigation: They attach to the public `jet dev --serve` socket; B stays available if the owner wants more.

surface.gist: How should a parent program like Jetpack start a private compiler session it talks to?
surface.lesson: A parent program can start `jet` as a child and send it requests. Jetpack does this today with a hidden command, once per value. People already have a public shared session, `jet dev --serve`. This vote picks the entry point for private child sessions.

current.note: Jetpack starts one hidden `jet` process per value today.
current.code:
$ jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate env.jet#port
$ jet __jetpack comptime-evaluate env.jet#host
# ... 40 processes for 40 values

wild.note: ZLS starts Zig's build runner and talks over stdio.
wild.code: zig build --listen=-

options.name: Hidden `jet __session`
options.gist: One hidden command replaces `__jetpack`.
gains: No new public surface.
One child per Jetpack command.
losses: Third-party tools have no stdio entry.

options.name: `jet dev --listen=-`
options.gist: A documented flag value on `jet dev`.
gains: Third-party tools get a supported entry.
losses: `jet dev` needs a mode that runs nothing.

proposed.code: $ jet dev --listen=-   # does not start the game

options.name: `--listen=-` everywhere
options.gist: Every runnable command can serve, like Zig.
gains: Matches Zig for outside tools.
losses: Five commands gain a documented flag.

proposed.code:
$ jet check --listen=-
$ jet build --listen=-

recommendation.why: All clients today are first-party, and the public shared session already exists. A replaces a hidden command instead of adding one.

decisions.title: Where the MCP methods on today's editor channel go
decisions.situation: Jet's language server is the background program editors talk to. Today's Rust version also answers a few methods from MCP, the protocol AI agents use to read resources. It mixes them into the editor protocol and advertises MCP fields in its start-up reply. The Jet language server card requires advertising only editor-protocol features. This vote decides where those agent methods go in the Jet port. We recommend moving them to a separate MCP adapter over the compiler session, using the MCP surface Jet already ratified.
decisions.gist: Should the MCP methods that today's language server answers move to a separate MCP adapter, be ported as they are, or be dropped?
decisions.lesson: LSP is the protocol editors speak; MCP is the protocol AI agents speak. Today's Rust language server answers MCP's resources/list, resources/read and ping on the editor channel, and puts MCP's protocol version into its LSP start-up reply. Editors ignore the extra fields, but the server is no longer a clean LSP server. Jet already ratified a typed MCP surface for agents.
decisions.story: An agent helping Ken wants to read his `env.jet` environment resource. Today it must connect to the editor's language server and speak MCP on a channel built for LSP. Ken's editor, meanwhile, receives start-up fields it does not understand.

Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 5 ballot 6, and finding F2. The Rust server mixes MCP into LSP at Server.rs lines 364-369, 512-513, 567 and 624-627. Ratified: D-MCP-SURFACE1=A (first-party MCP surface: a layered typed SDK over one protocol core, with its own versioning and authorization).

Card #3410 criteria c2 and c5 require truthful capabilities and forbid canned responses. Under A, the LSP advertises only LSP capabilities. The environment resources move to an MCP adapter that is a client of the compiler session, built on the D-MCP-SURFACE1 SDK.

The adapter's command spelling (the proposal suggests `jet self mcp`) is a separate future vote, not decided here.

Under B, the Jet port copies the mixing, so its start-up reply carries foreign fields. Under C, agents lose the environment resource until someone builds it elsewhere.

decisions.title: Which processes may own the shared workspace session
decisions.situation: A workspace session is one warm Jet compiler that other commands in the same project can attach to, so they reuse its work. Today only `jet dev --serve` may open that shared endpoint. When an editor is open, its language server already holds a warm compiler for the same project. If it cannot share, the editor and `jet dev` check every edit twice with two caches. We recommend letting the language server own the endpoint too, when started with `jet self lsp --serve`.
decisions.gist: Which long-lived processes may open the one shared session endpoint for a workspace: `jet dev --serve` only, the language server too, or any session automatically?
decisions.lesson: A workspace has at most one shared session, guarded by a lock. Other commands attach to it and reuse its checked results. The ratified rule lets only `jet dev --serve` own it. The editor's language server is also a long-lived compiler session for the same files. This vote decides whether it may own the shared endpoint, so one warm brain serves the whole workspace.
decisions.story: Ken edits his game in VS Code, saves, then runs `jet build` in a terminal. The editor has already checked every file. He expects the build to reuse that work instead of checking everything again. When he also runs `jet dev --serve`, he expects the editor and the dev server to share one cache, not keep two.

decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 2.7 and section 5, ballot 3. Ratified: D-LSP1=C (one incremental compiler service, all tools are its clients), D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (only `jet dev --serve` opens a socket; `--session=auto|off|required`), D-JPK-NODAEMON1=A (no resident background daemon).

Under A, `jet self lsp --serve` is opt-in. The first owner holds the workspace lock; a later LSP attaches to it as a client. When the editor closes, the endpoint disappears and a CLI run falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. The editor-owned session is a foreground process, so D-JPK-NODAEMON1 still holds.

Endpoint security is as ratified: a 0700 per-user directory, symlinks rejected, peer credentials checked, a nonce from .jet/session, and one owner per workspace by lock.

Under C, an editor-started server would listen without any flag. That widens D-BUILD-SESSION1's opt-in rule.

options.name: `jet dev --serve` and `jet self lsp --serve`

$ jet dev --serve        # lock held by the LSP: dev attaches as a client

note: no workspace session; running a fresh compiler

options.name: Only `jet dev --serve`, as ratified

decisions.title: The session protocol's wire format
decisions.situation: A compiler session is one running Jet compiler that several tools can talk to: the editor, a build in a terminal, and Jetpack. When a tool attaches from another process, the two sides need a shared message format on the wire. Jet's error reports and build events already have one ratified JSON shape, one object per line. This vote picks the wire format for everything else the session sends. We recommend newline-delimited JSON, so the wire reuses that shape and an attached build prints exactly what a fresh one prints.
decisions.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes: JSON lines, binary frames, or JSON-RPC with editor-protocol framing?
decisions.lesson: When `jet build` attaches to a running session, the two processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. The wire carries no syntax trees or compiled files, only these control messages, so its speed matters little. The choice is mostly about reuse, debugging and keeping one shape per message.
decisions.story: Ken runs `jet dev --serve` for his game, then `jet build --session=required` in a second terminal. When the build fails, he wants the attached build to print exactly what a fresh build prints. When something goes wrong between the two processes, he wants to read the messages with a pipe and `jq`, not a decoder.
decisions.detail:
Source: compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md in the session-design folder, section 3 (transports) and section 5, ballot 1. Builds on D-BUILD-SESSION1=A (versioned protocol, request envelope), D-REPORT-MACHINE1=A (one JSON report per line) and D-BUILD-UI1=A (--json streams NDJSON events).

Under A, the first line is hello with the toolchain identity. A mismatch refuses the attach and the CLI falls back to a fresh process, saying why under --verbose. Jetpack reports E1227 as the engine handshake does. There is no negotiation and no compatibility branch.

Reports are the D-REPORT-MACHINE1 object unchanged, and build events are the D-BUILD-UI1 events unchanged. Artifacts never cross the wire; events carry store identities and paths. A line is capped at 1 MiB, as jet.devtools.v1 caps envelopes, and JSON escapes newlines inside reports.

Reuse: CompilerService.jet's tagged-value and CtValue codecs become the JSON codec, and its narrow diagnostic codec is replaced by the report writer. The proposal sets a revisit trigger: a paired measurement if protocol cost passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time on the corpus.

options.name: Newline-delimited JSON
options.detail: One JSON message per line, UTF-8. Reports and build events reuse their ratified shapes byte for byte. Any JSON tool can read the stream. Encoding JSON costs a little on a channel that carries only control messages.

options.name: Binary frames
options.detail: Each message is a fixed header with a tag, a length and a request number, then a binary body in Jet's record codec, as Zig's compiler server does. It is the cheapest to encode. Reports would need a second, binary encoding beside their JSON form, and reading the stream needs a decoder.

options.name: JSON-RPC 2.0 with the editor protocol's framing
options.detail: Each message has a Content-Length header and a JSON-RPC body, as LSP and BSP use. It reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes. Events become notifications, and request ids reused after a cancel must be handled as in LSP.
options.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build","params":{"targets":["game"]}}

comparisons.note: Zig's compiler server uses binary frames with a tag and a length, and checks only an exact version string.
comparisons.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

comparisons.note: The Build Server Protocol used by IntelliJ and Metals is JSON-RPC 2.0 with LSP framing.

recommendation.why: Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON home, so A adds no second shape for them. The wire carries no syntax trees or artifact bytes, so binary frames would save little.
recommendation.tradeoff: JSON encoding costs a little; the proposal re-measures if protocol cost ever passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It needs a second encoding of every report, and version skew becomes silent corruption unless separately checked.
It adds framing and request-id rules that a line-based stream does not need, for no gain on this channel.

losses.loss: JSON is slower to encode than binary frames.
losses.mitigation: Only control messages cross the wire; a paired measurement is required if cost passes 5 percent.

surface.gist: Which message format should Jet's compiler session use between processes?
surface.lesson: When a build attaches to a running session, the processes exchange requests, events and error reports. Reports and build events already have one ratified JSON form, one object per line. Only these small control messages cross the wire, so speed matters little. The choice is about reuse and debugging.

current.note: Error reports and build events already stream as JSON lines.

wild.note: Zig's compiler server sends binary frames: a tag, a length, then bytes.
wild.code: Header{tag: u32 LE, bytes_len: u32 LE} + body

options.name: JSON lines
options.gist: One JSON message per line, reusing the report shape.
gains: Attached output equals fresh output byte for byte.
Readable with any JSON tool.
losses: Slightly slower than binary.

options.name: Binary frames
options.gist: Tagged binary messages, like Zig's server.
gains: Cheapest to encode.
losses: A second encoding of every report.
Needs a decoder to debug.

proposed.code:
header {tag: u32, len: u32, request: u64}
body   binary record bytes

options.name: JSON-RPC with editor framing
options.gist: Content-Length headers and JSON-RPC bodies, like LSP.
gains: Reuses JSON-RPC ids and error codes.
losses: Extra framing and id rules for no gain here.

proposed.code:
Content-Length: 88

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"build",...}

recommendation.why: Reports and events already have one JSON form, so JSON lines add no second shape. The wire carries only small messages.
gains: One shape per message everywhere.

losses.loss: A little encoding cost.
losses.mitigation: Re-measure if it passes 5 percent of edit-to-result time.

whyNot.reason: It duplicates the report shape and hides version mistakes.
Its framing adds rules this channel does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small encoding cost for one readable shape.

decisions.title: The language server runs on the one compiler session
decisions.situation: The language server answers your editor: errors as you type, hover text, go to definition. It used to live in the Rust host and checked code on its own path, so the editor could disagree with jet check. On 2026-10-17 you ruled that it is ported one-for-one to Jet and runs on the one compiler session that jet check and jet build use. The port now lives in the compiler tree, and the Rust server is gone. This records your ruling.
decisions.gist: Should the language server be ported to Jet and run on the one compiler session, or stay in the Rust command-line host?
decisions.lesson: A language server is the program an editor talks to for errors, hovers and jumps. If it checks code its own way, the editor and the command line can disagree. Running it on the same compiler session as jet check keeps their answers identical.
decisions.story: Chen edits a file in VS Code. The server is part of Jet and reads the same session as jet check, so the red underline in the editor is exactly the error jet check prints.

decisions.detail:
OWNER RULING

Owner ruling, 2026-10-17, recorded in the card #3410 log. It reads: “the LSP is 1:1 Rust-to-Jet parity work and is ported onto the one compiler session (D-LSP1=C)”. It adds: “the plan line keeping the LSP in the Rust host is superseded.” This ballot records it for one-click confirmation. The alternative is kept for the record.

D-LSP1 is not present in decisions.json; its ruling exists only in the card log. The same log records two amendments. D-INCR-PARK1=C (2026-10-17) keeps one compiler service, and editor answers recheck the whole package per edit, with no item-level reuse. D-SESSION-MCP1=A removes the port’s MCP methods and initialize fields, so the LSP speaks only LSP.

Related ratified decisions, all 2026-10-17: D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON jet.session.v1), D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (--listen=- on check, build, test, run and dev) and D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (jet dev --serve and jet self lsp --serve). D-LSP-BUILDSAVE1 is still open on this card.

TODAY

The port lives in Compiler/JetLSP, with 36 source files and 68 test files. The Rust server under Source/LSP is gone from the tree. positionEncoding negotiation is not yet in Compiler/JetLSP/Source, and the LSP 3.18 applicability inventory is still owed. The card is blocked on #3196.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

Parity work is not a cost of A. The Rust server is gone under every option, so any working editor support needs the Jet port to reach parity. A makes parity checkable: the LSP 3.18 inventory lists each item, and positionEncoding is one of them. No loss remains.

decisions.title: A counted surface budget: new words must pay for themselves
decisions.situation: Lua stays small because its authors make each new feature replace several old ones. Jet already requires one mechanism per meaning, but nothing counts how many words, marks, markers and commands a learner faces. The official keyword list has even drifted: it names nine markers and misses five real words. This vote decides whether a test counts Jet's language surface on every change and stops growth that no owner decision approved. Library functions are counted and shown, never gated.
decisions.gist: Should a test count Jet's keywords, marks, markers and commands, failing growth no owner decision approved?
decisions.lesson: The language surface is what a user types or runs that the language itself defines: keywords, marks like # and $, markers, commands. Jet registers each in one place, so counting is cheap. A ceiling that only an owner decision can raise makes growth visible. Library functions are counted but never gated. Whichever option wins, the stale keyword list gets fixed.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, the syntax registry computes counts: live keywords, marks, live markers, fact rows and top-level commands. A checked-in ceiling file records the current numbers. A guard test fails when one of these counts rises, unless the change names the owner decision that raised that ceiling. Retiring something lowers the ceiling automatically, so the budget only tightens by default.

Public Core functions per module are counted and shown with their trend, but never gated. Adding a library function under an approved library contract is routine work, not an owner choice, and gating it would turn every new function into a ballot. `jet self devtools surface` prints every count, and every ballot that adds language surface shows the before and after numbers.

Today's numbers: 49 live keywords after D-MARKER-DECL1 retired two, 43 lexical-ledger rows, 83 live markers (110 rows, 27 retired), 49 fact rows, 61 top-level commands (counted 2026-10-05). For scale: Lua 22 keywords, Go 25, Python 35 plus 4 soft, Rust 38 strict, Zig 49 plus about 120 builtins.

Beginner path: unaffected; they see a smaller, stable surface. Expert path: a ballot that adds a word must say what it costs and, where possible, what it retires.
decisions.story: Three teams each add a marker in the same month for nearly the same job. Nobody notices until a learner asks why #Track, #Persist and #Reactive all seem to watch values.

decisions.detail:
Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. The posted A also put public Core functions under the owner-raised ceiling. Every new library function would then have needed an owner decision, although the ballot rules say routine work under an approved contract is not a ballot. A now gates the language surface only and reports library counts.

Counts are refreshed: D-MARKER-DECL1=A retired two keywords (51 to 49), and owner directive 21 removed `pub`, so the old count of 2,419 `pub fn` no longer measures anything. The guard's example no longer names a Rust test runner (directive 19). Options, letters and the recommendation are otherwise unchanged.

Code facts, checked 2026-10-05. Keyword list drift: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/package_files.rs:464-551 JET_KEYWORD_LIST (55 entries) is documented as the single source for LSP, formatter and grammar. It includes nine marker names (Unsafe, Impure, Context, Transact, Job, Test, Todo, State, Transition) and the literal None. It omits five live words: prep (Syntax.rs:67), next (math_layout.rs:408), fact (effects_surface.rs:143), yield (core_surface.rs:514) and rust (math_layout.rs:571). Card c0bs5inj already tracks keyword-table consistency.

Registry location. AGENTS.md I7 names crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs as the registry of every keyword and sigil today. Under owner directive 19 that registry moves into Jet with the rest of the toolchain; the guard reads whichever registry is canonical, so the choice here does not depend on the move.

Counts: LEXICAL_LEDGER 43 rows (Syntax.rs:20-64). Prelude/Markers.jet 110 marker rows, 27 carry $retired. Prelude/Facts.jet 49 fact rows. CLI COMMANDS 61 top-level. Corpus marker usage: 1,854 #Name uses, 113 distinct names, 56.4 per 10k lines.

Peers: Lua 5.4 manual 3.1 (22). Go spec Keywords (25). Python 3.12 keyword.kwlist 35 and softkwlist 4. Rust Reference Keywords (38 strict, 14 reserved). Zig language reference (49 keywords, builtins listed separately). Swift Lexical Structure about 95-100 counting context-sensitive and # keywords [approximate].

Research. Ierusalimschy et al., "The Evolution of Lua" (HOPL III, 2007) and "Passing a Language through the Eye of a Needle" (ACM Queue, 2011). Lua adds a feature only when it is a general mechanism and removes features in major versions (module() deprecated in 5.2). Go's Go 1 compatibility promise plus a high bar for keywords kept it at 25 for over a decade; generics (1.18) added zero keywords.

Why library functions are reported, not gated. Lua and Go keep their languages small while their libraries grow freely. A library function adds no grammar and is found through completion and docs. Jet's one-mechanism rule (I8) and the library laws already review library growth.

decisions.title: Everything applied with # is declared with marker
decisions.situation: Jet code attaches rules to code with a # tag, such as #PII on a field or #Policy(audit("users")) on a function. Three different words declare those tags today: marker, tag, and policy with a wrap block. A test run also found that a policy wrapper is skipped when its function is called directly; that bug gets fixed whichever option wins. This vote decides whether tag and policy fold into marker, so one word declares everything you apply with #.
decisions.gist: Should tag and policy declarations fold into marker, so one word declares everything applied with #?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # tag on code; its declaration says where it attaches and what it does. Labels on data (tags, such as #PII for private data) and call wrappers (policies) are applied with # but declared with their own words. Whichever option wins, #Policy keeps its scoped compiler settings such as #Policy(gc).
decisions.explainer:
A tag is a label on data. #PII marks private data, and a declaration such as deny: [Log, Net] stops a labeled value from reaching logs or the network. PII is built in; you declare your own labels, such as CardNumber. A policy wraps a function: inside wrap(call) { ... }, call() runs the original function and returns its result.

Jet already ruled that a user-written marker has the same power as a compiler marker: no body records a fact, a body adds code. So tags, policies and markers are one mechanism with three declaration words.

Under A, `tag CardNumber { deny: [Log, Net] }` becomes `marker CardNumber { deny: [Log, Net] }`. `pub policy audit(topic: String) { wrap(call) { ... } }` becomes `pub marker Audit(topic: String) { wrap(call) { ... } }`, applied as `#Audit("users")`; marker names are PascalCase, so audit becomes Audit. The body tells the compiler where the marker may go: deny/from means values and types, wrap means functions and methods. An explicit sites list still overrides.

The skipped-wrapper bug is fixed under A and B alike: the wrapper becomes part of the function's definition, so direct calls and method values run it. Under A, apply() itself retires. A call site can then no longer swap or drop a function's wrappers. Code that needs the bare body keeps it in an unmarked function and marks a one-line front.

The built-in retry and trace policies become built-in markers, #Retry and #Trace. Stacked markers wrap outermost first: in `#[Retry(3), Audit("users")]`, Retry runs around Audit. Under A, #Policy keeps exactly one meaning: scoped compiler settings (gc, copies, sentries, the escape ladder).

Beginner path: nothing changes until they declare their own label; then there is one word to learn. Expert path: one declaration form, one reflection table, one audit grep (`marker`).
decisions.story: Priya writes a billing audit wrapper as a policy, marks charge() with it, and ships. In production nothing is logged, because direct calls skip the wrapper and only apply() runs it.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the main checkout and dev release dev-05ea86f65.

Declaration words: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:707 KW_TAG (D-QUAL2), Syntax/core_surface.rs:481-483 KW_POLICY and KW_WRAP (D-STRUCT-POLICY1), Syntax/effects_surface.rs:138 KW_MARKER (D-META-NAME1). D-QUAL2 text: "A tag is a marker that erases at runtime and carries no methods." D-META-USER1=A: "A rule with no body records a fact. A rule with a body adds code.

This is the same power the compiler has." D-STRUCT-POLICY1=A says a package declares a policy setting the way it declares a marker, reusing the D-META-USER1 machinery.

Probe (dev-05ea86f65, $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/mech-probes/policy_apply.jet): `#Policy(audit("users.load")) fn load_user()` called directly prints 7 with no audit line. `apply(audit("users.load"), load_user)()` prints the audit line. The shipped examples (Examples/features/callable/user_policies.jet, callable_policies.jet) only exercise apply(), so no golden catches this.

#Policy double meaning. D-CALLPOLICY2=C said #Policy means wrappers only, yet #Policy(gc), #Policy(copies: .Explicit) and #Policy(sentries: .Off) are live scoped settings (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Policies.jet:1-5, D-MARK-SCOPE1, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1, D-ONCE-GATE1). Under A the wrapper half moves to user markers and #Policy keeps settings only.

Corpus impact (Examples + Core + Compiler, 1,660 files, 328,724 lines). 7 `tag` declarations (Examples/features/types/*, reflection/fact_reads.jet, suites/finite_state.jet), 2 `policy` declarations (both callable examples). 4 apply() calls: callable_policies.jet:14-16 and user_policies.jet:11. Prelude: 0 tag or policy declarations. Keyword list: 51 live words drop to 49.

Adversarial findings. D-CALLPOLICY1=E gives apply() two powers: apply(chain, f) replaces a function's wrapper chain at one call site, and apply(f) selects the bare function. Under A both go, which the recommendation now lists as a loss. retry(3) and trace(...) in callable_policies.jet are built-in callable policies, so A must give them marker spellings. PII is a built-in tag (Syntax/effects_surface.rs:87 BUILTIN_TAGS), so the examples declare CardNumber instead.

Research. Python decorators (PEP 318) and C# attributes use one application syntax with one declaration form. Python keeps the bare function reachable through functools.wraps and __wrapped__. Rust has one attribute syntax but four declaration kinds (derive, attribute, function-like proc macros, built-in attributes), a common learner complaint. TypeScript decorators went through two incompatible designs (experimentalDecorators, then TC39 stage 3 in TS 5.0) because wrapping and metadata were specified separately. Lesson: one declaration form for everything applied with one glyph.

decisions.title: Numbers take their type from where they are used; only a conflicting use needs a conversion
decisions.situation: You asked whether numbers should take their type from their uses in the common cases, with a conversion only where uses conflict. This revision recommends that. A named number such as `rate :: 0.5` acts as if `0.5` were written at each use, as Go's constants do. A variable started from a number, such as `total := 0.0`, takes the type of its first use. Only a conflicting use needs a conversion. A computed value still never shrinks on its own.
decisions.gist: Should a number take its type from where it is used, with a conversion only where uses conflict?
decisions.lesson: A number you type, like 200, means the same thing as a byte, a whole number or a decimal. Picking its type where it is used converts nothing and loses nothing. A value the program computed is different: it may not fit a smaller type, so making it smaller stays a conversion you write.
decisions.story: Ana writes `rate :: 0.5` and `total := 0.0`, adds a list of `Float` prices into `total`, and scales it by `rate`. Today both names are errors until she writes `Float{0.5}` and `Float{0.0}`. Under A the program runs as she wrote it. Later she passes `count := 0` to a function that takes a `U8`, then stores a computed length in `count`. That `Int` conflicts with the `U8` that `count` took, so the error names both lines and offers `U8{line.len()}`.
decisions.detail:
What changes under A. Probes p01 to p14 ran on o0, o1 and o2 with the dev compiler; every tier printed the same thing. `d :: 2.5; half(d)` is E0108 today (p01) and runs under A. `total := 0.0; total += x` with a `Float` x is E0109 today (p04) and runs under A.

`big :: 300; take8(big)` stops at run time today (p03) and becomes a compile error under A. An `Int` the program computed passes into a `U8` parameter today and stops at run time when it does not fit (p07). Under A that is E0108 with the fix `U8{n}`.

The rule for a named number. A `::` name bound to a number literal, or to arithmetic on such names, means that literal at each use. Each use takes the type expected there, exactly as if the literal were written there. With nothing expected, as in `print(rate)`, it takes today's default, `Int` or `Decimal`. A use where the number does not fit, such as 300 as a `U8` or 2.5 as an `Int`, is a compile error. Module constants follow the same rule.

The rule for a variable. A `:=` variable started from a number literal takes one type: the type its first use needs, in source order. A use needs a type when it meets a typed parameter, a typed value, a field or a return. A use with nothing expected, such as `print(total)`, gives it the default.

A later use that needs a different type is a conflict. Its error names the line that set the type, and the fix is a conversion or a head on the first line.

What stays. Values the program computes keep their type, and widening stays implicit (D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F, D-NUMWIDEN-CROSS1=E). Shrinking a computed value is always written, as `U8{n}` or `U8.from(n, overflow: .Saturate)` (D-CONVERT-TRAIT1). A head such as `U8{200}` stays legal and fixes the type, so every name written with a head keeps its meaning. Empty lists, maps and None still start with their type (D-INFER-LEVEL1=A): they hold no value a use could fit. Checking stays one pass in source order (D-INFER-LINEAR1=A).

Clutter census, Examples and Core without Vendor (1,676 files; probes/infer/census.mjs). Named literals written with a head: 109 `::` names and 231 `:=` variables; 161 of them are `Float{…}`, such as `total := Float{0.0}`. Under A each head becomes optional; under B only the 109 `::` heads do; under C none do.

Bare named literals: 373 `::` names and 1,289 `:=` variables. Under C each one used as a narrower or other kind of number needs a head added, and under B each such variable does. A adds none. Computed values passed through today's implicit narrowing need `U8{n}` under every option. The census cannot see those without the type checker, so the cutover build lists them.

Other languages. Go, Zig and Odin keep a named constant flexible and give a variable its default; Zig even refuses `var total = 0.0` without a type. Swift and Kotlin fix the type where the name is made. Rust lets the uses of a variable decide its type across the whole function. A takes Go's rule for named numbers and a simpler form of Rust's for variables: the first use decides, read top to bottom.

Edge cases. Generic calls with nothing else to go on take the default: `same(limit)` gives `T = Int`. A variable used first inside a loop or a branch takes the type of that use, read in source order. A lambda that captures the variable counts as a use where the lambda is written. Arithmetic on named numbers is exact at compile time, so `KB :: 1024; MB :: KB * KB` is one flexible number. A module-level `:=` variable keeps its start type, since its uses span functions.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane), revising the SurfaceDesign draft after owner question qcjfku67. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this revision.

options.name: Numbers take their type from their uses
options.detail:
A named number means its literal at each use, so `rate :: 0.5` works as a `Float`, a `Decimal` or an `F32`. A variable started from a number takes the type of its first use, so `total := 0.0` followed by `total += price` is a `Float`. A conflicting use, or a number that does not fit, needs a written conversion.

Behavior changes: `d :: 2.5; half(d)` and the `Float` total now compile. `big :: 300; take8(big)` and a computed `Int` passed to a `U8` move from a run-time stop to a compile error. A counter first used as a `U8` does `U8` arithmetic, so it stops at 255 instead of at the call.
options.technical:
Sema gives a `::` binding of a literal, or of exact arithmetic on such bindings, a literal type. Each use resolves it against the expected type with the existing literal-fit check, and hover shows `number 0.5`. A `:=` binding of a literal gets an open number type. The first use in source order that needs a type closes it, recording that span for later errors.

Uses with no expected type close it to `Int` or `Decimal`. The implicit narrowing at call arguments and returns is removed, so those become E0108 as fields and list items already are. Checking stays one pass.

options.name: Named numbers only, as Go does
options.detail:
A named number means its literal at each use, as in A. A variable takes the default type where it is made, so `total := 0.0` is a `Decimal` and adding a `Float` to it needs `total := Float{0.0}`.

This is Go's, Zig's and Odin's rule.
options.technical: A's literal type for `::` bindings only. A `:=` binding takes `Int` or `Decimal` at once. The implicit narrowing at calls and returns is removed as in A.

options.name: Fixed where it is made
options.detail:
Every name keeps the type it got where it was made: `Int` or `Decimal` for a bare number. Using it as anything else needs a head on that line, which `jet fix` writes.

This was the first draft's recommendation, and Swift and Kotlin work this way.
options.technical: No literal types on bindings. E0108 names the binding's line and carries a safe edit that writes the head. The implicit narrowing at calls and returns is removed as in A.

comparisons.note: An untyped `const` fits any numeric type; a variable made with `:=` takes `int` or `float64`. Source: go.dev/ref/spec#Constants.
comparisons.code:
const rate = 0.5
half32(rate)          // ok
x := 200
takeByte(x)           // error: x is int

comparisons.note: A `::` constant is untyped and fits any width; `x := 0.0` is `f64`. Source: odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#constants.
A `const` number is `comptime_float` or `comptime_int` and fits any type; a `var` needs a written type. Source: ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime.
The name takes the literal's default type at once, as in C. Source: docs.swift.org, The Basics, Type Inference.
comparisons.code:
let rate = 0.5        // Double
half32(rate)          // error: Double is not Float

comparisons.note: A variable's type comes from its uses anywhere in the function; conflicting uses are E0308. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/literal-expr.html.

recommendation.why: A is your direction: numbers take their type from their uses, and only a real conflict needs a conversion. A named number is just its literal; a variable takes its first use's type. Computed values never shrink silently.
gains: The common cases need no head: `rate :: 0.5`, `total := 0.0`.
Up to 340 written heads in Examples and Core become optional.
Only a conflict or a misfit number needs a conversion.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the most common head, `total := Float{0.0}`, and adds one wherever a variable is used as a smaller number.
C adds a head wherever a named number is used as another kind of number, which is the clutter you asked to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: A variable started from a bare number takes its type from its first use; a head on its first line still fixes it.

gains: No head for the common cases: `rate :: 0.5`, `total := 0.0`.
Up to 340 written heads in Examples and Core become optional.
A misfit number is a compile error, not a run-time stop.

proposed.code:
rate :: 0.5
print(half(rate))        // Float here
total := 0.0
loop p in prices -> total += p   // total is Float
print(take8(U8{n}))      // a computed Int needs the conversion

options.name: Named numbers only, as Go does
options.gist: A named number fits each use; a variable keeps its default type.
gains: 109 `::` heads become optional.
A variable's type is always on its first line.
losses: Keeps 231 variable heads; a variable used as a `U8` needs one.

proposed.code:
rate :: 0.5
print(half(rate))        // ok
total := 0.0             // Decimal
loop p in prices -> total += p   // error: write total := Float{0.0}

options.name: Fixed where it is made
options.gist: A name's type is fixed on its line; a different use needs a head.
gains: Every name's type is on its line.
losses: Adds a head wherever a named number is used as another kind of number.
No head becomes optional.

proposed.code:
rate :: 0.5
print(half(rate))        // error: write rate :: Float{0.5}

recommendation.why: A is your direction: numbers take their type from their uses, and only a real conflict needs a conversion. A named number is just its literal; a variable takes its first use's type. Computed values never shrink silently.
gains: The common cases need no head: `rate :: 0.5`, `total := 0.0`.
Up to 340 written heads in Examples and Core become optional.
Only a conflict or a misfit number needs a conversion.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the most common head, `total := Float{0.0}`, and adds one wherever a variable is used as a smaller number.
C adds a head wherever a named number is used as another kind of number, which is the clutter you asked to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: A variable started from a bare number takes its type from its first use; a head on its first line still fixes it.

designAway.loss: A variable's type can come from the line after it is made.
attempts: Let any later use decide, as Rust does: rejected, an error could then blame an earlier line for a later one.
Keep the default for variables, as B does: rejected, it keeps 231 heads and adds more.
designAway.result: Only the first use decides, read top to bottom, and checking stays one pass. Hover shows the type and the line that set it. A conflict error names both lines, and a head on the first line always fixes the type.

designAway.loss: Code that passes a computed `Int` into a `U8` today stops compiling.
attempts: Keep the narrowing at calls: rejected, it breaks the ratified rule that Jet never shrinks a value on its own, and it stops programs at run time.
designAway.result: Each site gets E0108 with the fix `U8{n}`, which `jet fix` writes. It stops on a misfit at that line, as today's hidden narrowing did, so the meaning is unchanged and now visible.

designAway.loss: A counter first used as a `U8` now stops at 255 where it is incremented, not where it is passed.
attempts: Keep counters `Int` until a call shrinks them: rejected, that is the hidden narrowing again.
designAway.result: The counter stops with Jet's overflow report at the line that overflowed, so no value is lost either way. Writing `count := Int{0}`, or `U8{count}` at the call, keeps the stop at the call.

decisions.title: How a public Core type holds a native value that user code can neither name nor build
decisions.situation:
The ratified HTTP law wants one public `Body` type over a private native stream that reads the body lazily. Today `Body` is a plain enum that holds every byte in memory, so `chunks()` on a large download first buffers the whole body. The stream needs a native value that only Core may create, and Jet has no checked way to hide one.

We recommend that the native value's type live in a `priv module` inside core.http, and that `Body` hold it in a `priv` field. Both forms already exist in the visibility law. The checker then refuses any user code that names the type or builds a `Body` by hand.
decisions.gist: How should Core's `Body` hold a native stream that user code must never name or build?
decisions.lesson: Some Core values wrap a native resource, such as an open socket stream. If user code could build one with any contents, it could read from a resource it never opened. Jet already has `priv` modules and `priv` fields, which keep names and contents inside one module.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A facade is the public type users hold, here `Body`. A carrier is the native value inside it, here the stream that pulls the body's bytes from the connection. Forging means building a value by hand, with a struct literal, instead of getting it from the library.

A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A `priv` field can be read and written only by code in its type's own module.
decisions.story: Ines downloads a 2 GB file and reads it with `chunks()`. Today her program first holds all 2 GB in memory, because `Body` is a buffered enum. Under A the chunks arrive from the network one at a time. Her test builds a fake body with `http.body_text("…")`, and a typo that builds `Body{…}` by hand is a clear compile error.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4903, which blocks the HTTP Body cutover and six HTTP goldens. The ratified HTTP law wants one public, source-owned `Body` over a private, lazy native transport.

Today. Core/Http/Http.jet:89 declares `enum Body { Empty, Text(String), Bytes([U8]) }`. `chunks()` (line 216) copies the whole body into a byte list first, so a large download is held in memory. A shared cell gives read-once behavior.

The forging gap, measured on the tree14 compiler (probes ballot/xb/carrier.jet and carrier2.jet). A user program that builds `files.Directory{path: "x", handle: 3}`, `files.FileWriter{path: "x"}` or a struct literal that sets another module's `priv` field passes `jet check`. Reading that `priv` field from another module also passes, and `jet run` prints it. The ui row import_private_field, which expects E0605, fails for the same reason.

So the draft's premise, a public carrier "with no public constructor", is not enforced for any Core carrier today.

The law already has the parts. Syntax-decisions S18 says a `priv` field is readable and writable only by its type's module. It says a `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A only needs these enforced on struct literals and field reads, and the native-carrier registry to accept a carrier declared in a `priv module`.

What the registry holds. FileWriter is a known native carrier whose rows give its clone and drop behavior (core_types). The card notes that these rows are accepted only for public carriers today. A lifts that restriction: the carrier row names its module, and Sema applies ordinary privacy. No new attribute and no new IR kind are needed; the card's joint Core and native review found `Type.Named` sufficient.

Test bodies. User tests still build bodies with the public `http.body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty` (Http.jet:734-741). These return a `Body` whose carrier is an in-memory stream.

Same rule for existing carriers. `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv` fields, which closes the measured forging of a folder handle.

options.name: Carrier type in a `priv module`, held in a `priv` field
options.detail:
Core declares the native stream type inside a `priv module` of core.http, and `Body` becomes a struct that holds it in a `priv` field. User code cannot name the stream type and cannot build a `Body` by hand; both give E0605. Bodies come from responses, requests or the public `body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty`.

The checker enforces the existing `priv` rules on struct literals and field reads, which also closes the forging of `Directory` and `FileWriter` measured today.
options.technical:
Sema: report E0605 when a struct literal or field read names a `priv` field outside its type's module. This is the rule S18 states, and it fixes the import_private_field ui row. Registry: a native carrier row may name a carrier declared in a `priv module`; its clone and drop entries match FileWriter's. A known native carrier's native part counts as a `priv` field, so `FileWriter{path: "x"}` outside Core is E0605 too.

Core/Http: `priv module transport { struct BodyStream }` over the runtime body kernel. `struct Body { priv stream: transport.BodyStream }`. `chunks()` pulls from the stream. Core/Files: `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv`.

options.name: A new `#Carrier(native)` attribute checked for every wrapper
options.detail:
Core marks the facade with a new attribute that tells the checker it wraps a native value. The checker refuses literals of any marked type outside Core and tracks the native value's lifecycle.

The attribute is a second privacy spelling beside `priv`, and every carrier must adopt it.
options.technical: Add `#Carrier(native)` to the syntax tables, with a Sema rule refusing literals of marked types outside their module. Lifecycle rows key on the attribute rather than on the registry row. `Directory`, `FileWriter` and `AdvisoryLock` are re-marked.

options.name: Drop the facade; the native stream is the public `Body`
options.detail:
The native stream type itself becomes the public `Body`, registered as a known native type like FileWriter. There is no wrapper.

The type must stay literal-free by a special case in the registry, and its methods are native signatures rather than Jet source.
options.technical: Register `Body` as a known native carrier with native method signatures. The facade's Jet-source methods (`text`, `json`, `chunks`) move into the runtime. The forging gap on other carriers is untouched.

comparisons.note: A struct with a private field cannot be built outside its module, so `hyper::body::Incoming` comes only from the library. Source: Rust Reference, Visibility and privacy; hyper docs, body::Incoming.
comparisons.code: let b = Incoming { .. };   // error[E0451]: field is private

comparisons.note: `http.Response.Body` is an `io.ReadCloser` interface; the concrete type is unexported, so user code cannot build the library's body. Source: pkg.go.dev/net/http, Response.
comparisons.code: resp.Body.Read(buf)   // concrete body type is unexported

comparisons.note: `private` and `fileprivate` stored properties block memberwise initializers outside the file. Source: The Swift Programming Language, Access Control.
comparisons.code: struct Body { private let stream: Stream }

recommendation.why: A uses two forms the visibility law already has, a `priv module` and a `priv` field. User code cannot name or forge the stream, and the same rule closes the forging of Core's other carriers.
gains: Large bodies stream; memory stays at one chunk.
No new marker and no new public type.
Directory and FileWriter forging is closed too.

whyNot.reason: A second privacy spelling beside `priv`, which every carrier must adopt.
The body's methods move into the runtime, and a special case must refuse literals.

recommendation.tradeoff: The checker starts enforcing `priv` on struct literals and field reads, so Core code that relied on the gap must use the module's functions. In return no user code can forge a native value.

A now enforces the existing priv rules and hides the carrier in a priv module, so no public carrier name or new marker remains.

decisions.title: Values that must finish in a named way, such as commit or rollback
decisions.gist: Should a type list the methods that finish it, like commit or rollback, so forgetting one is a compile error?
decisions.lesson: Some values must not just disappear. A database transaction must end in commit or rollback. Today `#SingleUse` makes a value end exactly once, but any consuming call counts, and errors only say "owes consume". This ballot lets a type name its finishing methods and what runs when an error exits early. It is not a general rule system: effects, call order, and permissions keep their own tools.
decisions.story: Omar writes a payment handler. On one early return he forgets to roll back the transaction, and Jet compiles it, because transactions are plain values (card #4151). He wants the compiler to say "commit or rollback is missing here", and wants errors to roll back without a hand-written branch at every `?`.
decisions.detail:
What the marker does, and only this. `#MustFinish(commit, rollback, on_fail: rollback)` on a type says how a value of that type may end. The compiler tracks each value through four states.

- Created: it must still finish.

- Borrowed (`&txn.charge(...)`) or read: it must still finish.

- Finished: one listed method took it (`^txn.commit()`). Done; any later use is the existing use-after-move error.

- Handed on: passed with `^` to another function, or returned. The receiver now must finish it, by a listed method, by handing it on again, or by returning it. A wrapper function cannot make the duty disappear.

Every path that leaves the scope while the value must still finish is a compile error naming the missing methods. The listed methods are alternatives (commit OR rollback). If a type needs two steps in order, its API expresses that with typestate (`#State`/`#Transition`) or one method that does both.

What it is not. It does not add effects, permissions, value checks, or call-order rules. Those keep their tools: effect rows `-[IO]>` and `#FX`, typestate `#State`/`#Transition`, taint `#Input`/`#Scrub`, and capability authority. `#MustUse` stays separate: it only forbids ignoring a returned value, and reading the value satisfies it.

How `#SingleUse` is replaced. Today `#SingleUse` (D-LIN1) means: end exactly once, by passing with `^`, returning, or `#Unsafe("reason") { consume(x) }`. Any consuming method ends it, and the error says "owes consume" (E0140-E0143).

`#MustFinish(...)` keeps that same exactly-once check and changes three things. Among the type's own consuming methods, only the listed ones finish the value. Errors name those methods. And `on_fail:` can finish it automatically on error exits. Each `#SingleUse` type migrates by listing its consuming methods, for example `#MustFinish(close)`. Abandoning a value keeps the audited gate, `#Unsafe("reason") { consume(x) }` (D-DROP-WORD1=A).

`on_fail: m` runs `m` on a value that is still owned and unfinished when a failure leaves the scope. Failures are `?` propagation, `return Err(...)`, panic unwinding, and task cancellation. It never runs on a value already handed on. For example, if `^txn.commit()` fails, the value was handed to `commit` and counts as finished whether `commit` returns or fails. Mojo's explicit destructors follow the same rule.

`on_fail` does not run on abort, process kill, or power loss. `m` must be one of the listed methods and take only `^self`. If `m` itself fails, its error is attached as a note to the error already leaving; the value counts as finished. Without `on_fail`, every error exit must finish the value by hand, as `#SingleUse` requires today. An early success return is never finished automatically; that is the mistake the marker exists to catch.

Tasks: D-CONC-UNIT1=A already gives task handles the same single-use duty, and D-CONC-JOIN1=A lets reading a task's result count as joining. Under A, Core declares `Task<T>` as `#MustFinish(join, detach)`, and reading the result still counts as `join`. Behavior is unchanged; only the messages name `join` or `detach`.

Unbound spawns keep their scope-end join (D-CONC-SPAWN1). Containers of such values must finish each element, and generic code keeps the D-LIN1 rules.

Spelling: `#MustFinish` is new, chosen by the drafter to pair with `#MustUse` and to say plainly what is required. The earlier draft's `#Owes` is a metaphor; the owner may keep it, and nothing else depends on the name.

Conflicts: E0140 to E0143 merge into one diagnostic family with new snapshots (I4). Receivers follow D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D (`&txn.charge`, `^txn.commit`). In option B's example, `err` names the failure inside a `??` block (D-FAIL-BIND1=A). Card #4151 (transactions) is the first user.

The earlier option "Core marks buffered writers and locks too" is not lost. If A wins, which Core types adopt the marker is a separate ballot, because it changes beginner file code.

options.name: Named finishing methods
options.detail: `#MustFinish(m1, m2, on_fail: m)` on a type lists the methods that finish it and, optionally, the one that runs on error exits. `#SingleUse` is replaced; task handles declare `#MustFinish(join, detach)`.
options.technical: Same exactly-once checker as D-LIN1, in the self-hosted ownership checker (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership), with a per-type list of finishing methods. Existing E0140-E0143 snapshots must stay at least as strict.

comparisons.note: Every resource is linear; operations thread new handles. Strong guarantee, heavy ergonomics.
A type can forbid implicit destruction and name the fix; a `deinit self` method ends the value.

whyNot.reason: B's errors say "consume" instead of naming the job, and every `?` before commit needs its own rollback branch.
C compiles a forgotten commit, so every payment can silently roll back.

recommendation.tradeoff: Types that opt in must be finished on purpose; everything else keeps automatic cleanup.
