decisions.title: Which compiler and tool moments packages may hook, as ordinary Jet metaprogramming
decisions.situation: Packages want to add their own checks, generated code and editor actions at moments such as after a file is parsed or a program is checked. Jet's metaprogramming already lets a marker body read checked facts, reject code and add items while a program builds. A compiler hook is the same compile-time Jet, attached to a compiler moment instead of a written #Name. Today's only compiler hook is a separate plugin outside Jet, chosen by an environment variable, and both options delete it. This vote decides how many moments to publish now. We recommend the full stage table, with every hook following the rules marker bodies already follow.
decisions.gist: Which compiler and tool moments may packages hook with compile-time Jet, and how many should Jet publish now?
decisions.lesson: A hook is package code Jet runs at a named moment, such as after checking a program. Both options use ordinary compile-time Jet and the same runner as marker bodies. A stage determines the read-only input and allowed results: B can return findings and proposed edits only; A also has an additive generation point. Neither silently rewrites source, and the compiler alone decides validity.
decisions.explainer:
Words: the root package is the one being built. Findings are located lint warnings; editor actions are fixes offered for acceptance. Digests/fingerprints are content-derived change identities, not timings.

Markers run where #Name is written; hooks run on each item at a moment. Both use the ordinary compile-time runner, fact views and Meta policy. Powers depend on stages. A's declared point adds items through compiler.generate's checking/provenance path. B's checked point supplies findings and proposed edits only.

Edits apply through jet fix/editor acceptance. Advanced root-opted-in change sets remain D-META-RECONCILE1's contract; vote that first.

A lifecycle: parse -> resolve declarations/signatures/direct named calls -> declared hooks -> check original/added items -> checked -> emitted. Parsed knows syntax, not types; declared knows resolved names, not validated bodies. Checked includes validated added items, which never re-enter declared hooks. Build points view the single fn build graph; fmt/lsp/test/doc are tool views. B begins at checked.

Layout: lint_rules/package.jet identifies the package; lint_rules/no_print.jet is a source module. Included modules supply discovered #On functions without another registration list. Hook modules/imports compile first. Hooks cannot inspect themselves or their support dependency closure; cycles error.

The import use core.compiler supplies payload/result types. Attachment #On selects a typed point. A function returning [compiler.Finding] returns warnings; return [] means none. B's filter selects declarations and map produces one finding per match.

Level 0 is pure computation; level 1 is declared deterministic inputs recorded in .jet/lock. Existing embed_file/embed_bytes/find snapshot inputs. The expression rules :: embed_file("rules.txt") reads a declared package-relative input, not arbitrary fs.read. Hook level 1 excludes network, including pinned fetch. This is explicitly narrower than general metaprogramming.

Steps are deterministic metaprogram evaluator operations under D-PREP-FUEL1. Package maximum and #StepLimit raises retain that contract; no new limit spelling is added. Ambient clock/random/files/network and #Impure are forbidden. Meta.Generate denial blocks additive output.

Jet's own sandbox uses the shared runner. Powers require granted handles; native compile-time machine code is checked before execution. No separate engine/carrier/protocol remains.

Dependencies hold until the root grants their printed jet trust identity. Source/dependency/stage/power/input-authority changes re-prompt with a diff. Compiler-only upgrades rebuild code/cache, not approval. Root hooks run directly within identical ceilings. CI fails with the exact missing grant, not omits checks.

Cache identity includes code, read inputs, full bodies/spans, payload/compiler identity and grants. Trust precedes reuse; revoked/stale grants cannot replay results. Per-item reuse requires unchanged inputs; whole-program hooks rerun when snapshots change. Actual cost appears in jet build --timings; sample figures are illustrative.

Stage-local identities govern merging, not priority. Identical values deduplicate; contradictions/overlapping edits error naming contributors. Presentation follows priority/package/declaration order. Authors still learn stage types, results and trust, but no separate plugin system.
decisions.story: Mia's team bans print in library code. Today she must build a separate compiled plugin outside Jet and set an environment variable on every developer machine and CI job. She wants to write the rule in Jet, next to her other metaprograms.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q47892zx asks for hooks integrated with metaprogramming and Jet's own sandbox. Both alternatives answer unconditionally: ordinary #On Jet functions use the same compile-time runner as markers/prep, with no external plugin engine. The old post-check plugin and JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION retire. Execution architecture independently supplies the baseline runner and native-code isolation check; hooks do not retain a fallback engine while that cutover is voted.

The choice is breadth, not execution technology: A publishes the whole typed table; B publishes only compiler.checked. D-HOOK-ONE1/A already chooses typed #On attachments. This ballot changes the old D-DX5-HOOK1 carrier, not its read-only/checker-authority intent. D-META-USER1, D-MARKER-LAW1, D-META-PUBLISH2 and D-META-GATE1 govern fact reads, additive publication, provenance and denied powers. D-META-CONTROL2/OPTIN2 change-set reconciliation remains D-META-RECONCILE1; directive 23 allows that reconciliation and forbids new AST-report proposals. None are adopted here.

A's CompilerStage mapping is explicit: compiler.parsed -> Parsed; compiler.declared -> Resolved; added-item checking/ordinary preparation passes through Typed/Prepared; compiler.checked is the validated post-Prepared snapshot; compiler.emitted -> Emitted. Hook modules are compiled first without self/closure inspection; cycles error rather than using an incomplete hook. The stage table determines which facts are available, and no stage promises future facts.

Merge rules in the technical table specify all public results. Step exhaustion is E0952, assertion failure E0953, malformed or cap-exceeding output E1402 naming the hook, package, cap and actual count. Per invocation at most 256 findings and 64 proposed edits; the 257th finding or 65th edit rejects the invocation, not truncates it. Failed invocations produce no accepted partial results and are never cached. Findings are L1401 under the package-qualified hook/lint identity; policy deny converts them to E1293.

Grant identity includes source/dependency closure, stage, result powers and declared-input authority; compiler versions invalidate compiled code, not human approval. Cache identity separately includes compiler/payload schema identity and actual granted scope. Revocation disables both execution and cached results. Declared file contents invalidate results without silently adding file-read authority. Package-owned hooks obey effect/sandbox rules even when no dependency prompt applies.

Asset requests enter the one BuildPlan graph and use its dependency/cycle validation. Asset hooks inspect original graph assets once; returned replacements/additions are not recursively fed to the same hook pipeline. Formatter output is for declared non-Jet kinds; it cannot rewrite Jet source through a formatting side door. Editor edits require selection. Added docs and hovers remain presentation outputs, not compiler validity powers.

Attack on A: one runner does not make a broad public stage surface free. B is genuinely easier to stabilize, and evidence from Kotlin KSP supports stable APIs, not publishing every moment. A remains recommended because the owner wants compiler/tool integration and the typed table supplies per-item checks, additive generation and tool moments without a second mechanism. Payloads can evolve independently only when their dependencies permit; there is no promise of version immunity. Publishing all of A commits to every named point now, not a deferred subset.

options.name: Named stages, run as compile-time Jet
options.detail: Publish every typed point in the table, attached with #On and run by the marker/prep runner. Hook modules are discovered in package sources and listed by jet inspect hooks; self/support-closure inspection and cycles are forbidden. Root hooks run directly within the common ceilings; dependency hooks need grants. A commits to more payloads, cache invalidation sites and debugging surfaces. Separate typed payloads localize changes only where dependencies permit, not guarantee isolation from every future API change.
options.technical:
Compiler stage table, payload -> output. compiler.parsed(File): syntax -> findings. compiler.declared(Declaration): resolved signature/body/direct named calls/spans -> findings and added items. compiler.checked(CheckedProgram): validated program -> findings and proposed edits. compiler.emitted(Artifact): read-only artifact -> findings.

Build/tool table. build.planned(BuildPlan): graph -> findings and asset requests. build.asset(Asset): original asset -> replacement or added assets. fmt.file(File): declared non-Jet kind -> formatted text. lsp.code_actions(ActionRequest) -> editor actions; lsp.hover(HoverRequest) -> notes. test.finished(TestReport) -> findings; doc.page(DocPage) -> sections. Types belong to core.compiler. Formatter-kind ownership is declared with attachment; different results conflict.

Merge identity: items by module/name, assets by normalized path, findings by package-qualified lint/span, edits by source revision/span. Overlapping edits conflict. Docs key by page/section ID, hovers by request/location/note ID, actions by request/action ID, formatted text by file/revision/kind.

Distinct IDs coexist in deterministic order. Identical values deduplicate; different values at one identity error naming contributors. Invalid combined generated code reports publication provenance, not selects one hook.

Stages run once. Added items pass ordinary checking/publication, appear in checked, and never return to declared. Edits never apply during builds. Graph outputs use existing cycle/provenance rules. Advanced changes stay outside this contract awaiting D-META-RECONCILE1.

Runner: marker/prep runner, levels 0/file-only 1, existing prep limits and Meta policy. Deterministic-input APIs snapshot declared files and record locks. No external engine/carrier. Atomic caps are in detail. Code caches include compiler version. Result caches include payload/compiler identity, code, bodies/spans/files and grants. Trust precedes replay.

options.name: One checked stage now, more by later votes
options.detail:
Only the shared work: the existing post-check moment becomes the typed point compiler.checked, attached with #On and run as compile-time Jet like any marker body. The environment variable and the plugin protocol retire, as under A. Grants, inputs, limits, merging and caching follow the same rules as A for this one stage. Every further stage needs its own ballot.

B's case: the smallest payload surface to keep stable, the lesson of Kotlin's move from compiler plugins to KSP, with fewer invalidation sites and one place to debug. Its cost: the only moment is the whole checked program, so a per-declaration rule reruns on every program edit, and generators, asset hooks and editor hooks wait.
options.technical: Publishes one point, compiler.checked(CheckedProgram), with findings and proposed edits, carrying D-DX5-HOOK1's read capabilities as its payload. Registration is #On in source. Runner, limits, grants, declared inputs, failure handling, merge identity and the whole-snapshot cache key follow A's technical note. JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION becomes an error whose fix names the #On form. Any other compiler stage name is an error naming the ballot that would add it.
options.code:
// lint_rules/no_print.jet: the same rule over the whole checked program
use core.compiler

#On(compiler.checked)
fn no_print_in_lib(p: compiler.CheckedProgram) -> [compiler.Finding] {
    p.declarations
        .filter(d -> (d.module == "lib" || d.module.starts_with("lib.")) && d.calls.contains("print"))
        .map(d -> compiler.finding(d, "print in library code"))
}

// grant as under A: jet check names the jet trust grant
$ jet check
Warning [L1401] (no_print_in_lib): print in library code
  --> lib/report.jet:12:5
$ jet build --timings
hooks: no_print_in_lib 41 ms (whole program; reruns on any edit)   // illustrative figures

comparisons.note: A stable symbol API replaced internal compiler plugins (kotlinlang.org/docs/ksp-overview.html).
A compile-time program in the same language receives compiler messages for each phase. [INFERENCE: recalled from the Jai beta material, not re-read this session.]

recommendation.why: A publishes the requested compiler and tool moments as one typed metaprogramming surface, allowing per-item checks and additive generation without a second plugin system. Authors still learn stage types and trust; B's smaller stability commitment remains a real alternative.
gains: Lint rules and generators in plain Jet, at the moment they need.
One metaprogramming system: hooks follow the rules marker bodies follow.
No dependency hook runs unasked.

losses.loss: A whole-program hook reruns on any program edit.
losses.mitigation: Per-file and per-declaration points cache per item, and --timings shows each hook's cost.

losses.loss: More hook stages to keep stable across releases.
losses.mitigation: Separate typed payloads localize change where dependencies permit; they do not guarantee that another stage or its consumers can never be affected.

whyNot.reason: B is the smaller, easier-to-stabilize surface, with the same runner and rules for one stage. But per-declaration caching, generators and tool hooks each wait for another vote, and whole-program reruns are the only choice meanwhile.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger hook surface in exchange for rules that run at the right moment and cache per item.

Shared acceptance: #On uses the marker/prep runner and Jet's own sandbox. Pure/declared-file work obeys step limits/Meta policy. Include identical dedup, contradictory doc/hover IDs, overlapping edits, atomic caps, denied powers and revoked-cache replay. Edits never apply at build. B accepts only checked results and rejects generation/absent stages. Implement the entire option, not a subset.

decisions.title: Which ratified ceiling governs metaprogramming: the opt-in advanced mode or the older refusal lists
decisions.situation: Metaprogramming is code that writes or changes code while Jet compiles your program. Jet's ratified rules disagree about how far it may go. Rulings from July to mid-September refuse rewriting written code and splicing code into callers during compilation. Two rulings of September 21 allow those powers behind an approved opt-in, as you asked that day. This vote proposes no new powers and only decides which ratified texts govern; we recommend keeping the September 21 contract, with the older refusals binding projects that do not opt in.
decisions.gist: Which ratified metaprogramming ceiling governs: the September 21 opt-in advanced mode, or the older refusal lists?
decisions.lesson: Standard mode is what every program gets: reading compiler facts, adding new generated code, and type recipes such as prep fn Pair(T: Type). A recipe takes a type and returns a new type. Advanced mode is what an approved root package unlocks with metaprogramming: unrestricted. Today's ratified texts both grant and refuse advanced powers. This vote proposes no new powers, and every change is checked like hand-written code.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A ceiling is the most a metaprogram may do. Standard mode needs no setting. Advanced mode needs metaprogramming: unrestricted in the root package, the package being built, and project trust must approve that root and each provider. A provider is a function the root registers to run in advanced mode for chosen targets. A change set is a checked list of edits that the compiler rechecks as a whole before accepting any of them. A receipt records what changed and the recheck result.

This vote proposes no new metaprogramming powers. Programs still generate new code under the powers already ratified; the vote only decides which ratified texts govern the advanced ones.

The conflict. Older rulings refuse rewriting written code and splicing into callers during compilation. The September 21 rulings allow them behind the approved opt-in. Both are ratified, and the spec prints both. The newer ruling governs today; this vote keeps it (A), withdraws it (B), or withdraws part of it (C).

What every option keeps. No mutable handle into the compiler's internal syntax trees. No forged facts about the program. Every change rechecked by ordinary checking. Generated code keeps a record of where it came from. Host permissions stay separate from metaprogramming.

The grammar stays closed: no token macros and no custom syntax. Advanced parsing reads ordinary Jet with the real parser into checked pieces; it never adds syntax. Type recipes stay in standard mode under every option.

Beginner path: unaffected under every option; standard mode is the same. Expert path: A gives the full checked toolkit behind an approved root and provider; B gives standard mode only; C gives the toolkit without edits to written code. Nothing here proves the advanced API runs; it is unbuilt (card #3520).
decisions.story: Mara's team builds a tracing library that wraps every function in a package with timing code. The spec's advanced API section says a root package can opt in and rewrite those bodies in a checked change set. Three other spec sections say rewriting existing code is rejected forever. She cannot tell whether her design is legal.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision, repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2 passes, 2026-10-07. Quotations below are verbatim, with line breaks and bold flattened; each names whether it is spec text or Tower option text.

Source. Owner directive 23 (2026-10-07) allows reconciliation ballots that resolve a conflict between existing ratified decisions, naming this conflict: S26, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1 against D-META-CONTROL2, D-META-OPTIN2 and D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. It forbids acting on new proposals from the AST research report. So every option is a precedence or a withdrawal among ratified texts, and none adds an API, operation, mode or capability name.

AstResearch1's draft question also asked to name new deniable capabilities (Meta.Rewrite, Meta.Expand, Meta.Types); that is a new proposal and is not offered.

Why the owner decides. Under the project rule, a newer ratified ruling wins, so the September 21 contract governs today; A records that and aligns the older prose. B withdraws that contract and C withdraws part of it, which only the owner can do. None of this shows the advanced API runs: its contract is unbuilt, on card #3520.

THE REFUSING TEXTS

S26 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2913-2920). It says: "comptime never creates, parameterizes, or selects a type, and never affects dispatch — polymorphism is traits-only." Also: "Rejected forever: token/AST/attribute macros, custom syntax, comptime types, const generics in v1."

D-FRONTENDAPI1=A (2026-07-06; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:5216-5219). core.compiler exposes read-only lexer and parser APIs for tools, and "no AST mutation enters compilation." It refuses mutation within compilation, not parsing as such.

D-METAMUTATE1=A (2026-07-06; spec summary, syntax-decisions.md:5222-5225). It says: "Jai-style AST mutation/message loop/user macros are rejected." It also grants a non-mutating power surface: additive generated modules, registered targets and actions, read-only enforcement, DSL blocks and front-end APIs.

D-METADEPTH1/2 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2998-3003): read-only reflection plus derives; "No mutation, no AST injection, no macros"; "libraries can never mutate grammar". Tower records a later August amendment letting user rules record facts and add code, without mutating existing code.

D-META-GATE1=A (2026-09-19; Tower option text): "Refused: splice into existing code, token or tree macros, use-site type factories, in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler. Rewrite and Tokens are never named." Its example adds: "refused, not one flag away."

Docs/spec/reference/metaprogramming.md:304-307, an explanatory page rather than a ratification, rejects "arbitrary message-loop mutation" and says to "generate checked items additively".

THE GRANTING TEXTS

D-META-CONTROL2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3093-3098). It says: "type construction, code parsing/capture/insertion, specialization, workspace/build control, and existing-program rewrites use an authorized compiler.advanced session". Its Tower text adds that changes are atomic, checked against affected callers and receipted, and never expose compiler nodes. It also says: "This does not promise equivalence with the original application."

D-META-OPTIN2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3100-3105): advanced providers require "metaprogramming: unrestricted" in the approved root package and explicit target registration from root preparation. Its Tower text records the owner's request: "full Jai-level capabilities with powers above level 5 gated by metaprogramming opt-in."

OPTIN2's Tower text also requires project trust and enterprise policy to approve the root and provider. "A previously unapproved or changed privileged provider cannot silently run". Noninteractive runs fail closed, and "Revoking authorization invalidates affected preparation artifacts". Registration "uses compiler-issued DeclarationHandles, not unqualified strings", and dependency targets need exact metaprogramming_targets grants.

D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (2026-10-02): types are made by prep fn recipes in standard mode, amending S26 and D-META-GATE1's use-site type-factory refusal. Its Tower text: "Building types from reflection or editing other declarations stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A." D-CONSTGEN1=A already replaced S26's const-generics refusal. Both stay under every option.

UNIVERSAL LIMITS, KEPT IN BOTH MODES UNDER EVERY OPTION

These come from specific clauses and never become standard-only. No token, tree or attribute macros and no custom syntax (S26, D-META-GATE1, D-METADEPTH2). No message loop and no user macros (D-METAMUTATE1). No mutable compiler nodes and no forged facts (D-META-CONTROL2). Host permissions stay separate (D-META-OPTIN2), and no AST mutation enters compilation (D-FRONTENDAPI1).

Advanced parsing runs the real Jet lexer and parser into checked fragments; it is not a token or tree macro, so the closed grammar holds in both modes.

OPTION A: CLAUSE MAP

A keeps D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 in full: approval, changed-provider refusal, revocation, handles, dependency grants and the non-equivalence rule included. The older texts are amended clause by clause, not whole paragraphs. S26: the type clause points to D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, and the dispatch clause binds standard mode, while advanced specialization follows D-META-CONTROL2. Its macro and syntax ban stays universal.

D-METAMUTATE1: the message-loop and user-macro ban stays universal; its refusal of rewriting written code binds standard mode, with advanced rewrites only as D-META-CONTROL2 change sets. D-METADEPTH1/2: "no macros" and the grammar ban stay universal; "No mutation, no AST injection" binds standard mode.

D-META-GATE1: token or tree macros stay refused everywhere. Splice into existing code, in-place rewrite, a type with no file and running the program inside the compiler bind standard mode; advanced mode has them only through D-META-CONTROL2. "Rewrite and Tokens are never named" stays, since there is no capability name. The example's "not one flag away" is amended: the approved root opt-in is that gate.

OPTION B: CLAUSE MAP

The older refusals govern. D-META-CONTROL2's compiler.advanced operations are withdrawn, and the compiler.advanced rows leave the syntax table. D-META-OPTIN2 keeps its manifest member with one value: omitted or metaprogramming: standard. The unrestricted value and metaprogramming_targets are withdrawn, so writing them is an unknown-value error.

Standard mode keeps D-META-REFLECT2 facts, D-META-PUBLISH2 additive generation, type recipes and const generics. In D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, "stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A" becomes stays refused.

OPTION C: CLAUSE MAP

C keeps D-META-OPTIN2 in full and keeps every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that only adds. Kept: the ChangeSet add operation, the types service, parsing into new items, specialization, and workspaces with build control and run_prepared. For those, D-META-GATE1's "a type with no file" and "running the program inside the compiler", and S26's dispatch clause, are amended for advanced mode.

C withdraws every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that edits written code: the ChangeSet operations remove, replace_body, replace_signature, replace_type and insert, and register_expansion's caller expansion. For those, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1's "splice into existing code" and "in-place rewrite" prevail in every mode. C only withdraws named existing clauses; it adds no operation or gate.

THE STORY UNDER EACH OPTION

Mara's tracing library needs to change existing function bodies. Under A, an approved root and approved provider can replace them in a checked change set. Under B and C it cannot; the library can only generate new wrapper functions that callers call explicitly. Those wrappers are not transparent rewrites.

WHAT B AND C OFFER

B keeps the meaning of written code in the file itself. A reader and the editor never apply a transformation to know what code does, the benefit D-METADEPTH2 and D-METAMUTATE1 argued for. B also has the smallest authority surface. C keeps the advanced additions while written bodies never change, the clearest audit story of the three.

Precedent, as illustration only. Swift macros add declarations and expand marked uses but never edit other written code; C also refuses call expansion. Rust procedural macros rewrite only the item they are attached to. Jai's message loop may rewrite code. Zig builds types at compile time with no syntax access, which matches Jet's standard mode.

INTERPLAY

Vote this ballot before D-HOOK-STAGES1. That open ballot's change-set rule defers to D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 as this vote leaves them. Under A, approved providers may return change sets; under C, only additions; under B, findings and Generated items only. This ballot adds no hook API. Card #3520 holds the advanced contract.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2, 2026-10-07). Examples now copy the ratified handle-based registration. A keeps OPTIN2's approval, revocation and dependency rules in full. Every option has a clause-level map, with universal limits kept in both modes, and C is defined only by withdrawing named clauses.

B's manifest change is exact. The non-equivalence of rewrites, provider granularity, the tracing story under each option and the strengths of B and C are stated. Quotation sources are labeled.

decisions.title: How does a level editor change a field it knows only by name?
decisions.situation: You asked us to engineer away the downsides of the recommendation, which were a #Patchable word on every editable type and work not yet built. The engine's own entity marker now includes #Patchable, so an entity type writes nothing extra, and build work no longer counts as a loss. Typos, nested fields, private fields and undo now each get a defined result with a readable error. The reflection write stays as B and the marker template as C, both unchanged.
decisions.gist: Does the editor set Rock's size by name through a typed patch, a reflection write, or marker code?
decisions.lesson: An editor knows a field only by its name, such as size, and must change it on any entity. Reflection reads fields today. #Patchable gives a type a typed patch, apply and undo.
decisions.story: Ana's level editor shows the fields of the selected entity. A designer types 2.0 into Rock's size, then 0.5 into its tint's red part. The editor does not know the Rock type, only the field path and the text.
decisions.inWild:
Bevy: every component an editor may change derives Reflect, and engines bundle that into their own component derive.
Unity: SerializedObject.FindProperty("size") sets a field by name through engine metadata.
Jai: an editor writes a member through its byte offset from the type table.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION

You asked to engineer away A's two downsides. Both are gone.

"Each editable type writes #Patchable." The engine already needs its own entity marker, so it can register, save and list each entity type. D-MARKER-GROUP1=A lets that marker be a fixed group, and the engine's group includes Patchable. Rock writes #engine.Entity, the one line it writes under every option, and gets Patchable with it.

"The Patchable bound and Patch.parse are not built yet." That is build work. Ranking never counts build work, and B and C need unbuilt pieces too.

WHY THE OPT-IN ITSELF STAYS

The opt-in is the guarantee, not a cost. Without it, any function holding a changeable reference could change any field of any type by name, which is B. With the group, consent costs no extra word: the author writes #engine.Entity, hover lists its members, and edit<T: Patchable> shows it in the engine's signature.

WHAT A DOES, EXACTLY

#Patchable already gives Rock a Rock.Patch with every field optional, plus apply, diff and merge (D-PATCH1). A adds one generated method: value.parse_patch(path, text) -> T.Patch PatchError!.

It finds the field named by the path, parses the text with that field's own parse, and returns a patch with that one field set. apply then makes the change. The engine's edit is one line.

For undo, the engine keeps T.diff(before, after), the old values of the changed fields. Applying it restores them.

EDGE CASES

- A typo fails with PatchError, whose text is "no field `sise` on Rock; did you mean `size`?".

- Bad text fails with "`abc` is not a Float, for `size`". The value is unchanged.

- A dotted path such as tint.r walks into a field whose type is Patchable. The patch holds the whole new tint, so diff and undo work unchanged.

- A field whose type has no parse and is not Patchable fails with "`shape` cannot be set from text", and hover on the marker lists such fields.

- A priv field fails with "`hp` is private to Rock". Only the type's own module may write it.

- A computed field is not in Patch (D-PATCH1), so it fails as unknown, with a note that it is computed.

- A type with type parameters cannot be Patchable (E0336), and a field holding a reference or function is refused (E0337). The error points at the field on the #engine.Entity line, so callbacks stay outside entity data.

- A type the engine does not mark cannot be changed by name. The error at edit offers to add #engine.Entity.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes #engine.Entity on a type and never sees Patchable. The editor just works. An expert writes the engine: edit is one line, and an undo stack keeps one patch per edit. Expert code may also read the PatchError to show the designer why an edit failed.

WHAT IS BUILT TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/edit, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- e01: #Patchable apply and diff set and undo size; it prints 2.0, then 1.0.

- e02: a marker group in the ratified form, group :: #[Patchable, Equatable], is not built yet (E0003).

- e03: the old marker Entity = #[…] form is retired (E0381), and its fix writes the ratified form.

Earlier probes from the 2026-11-04 revision: a T: Patchable bound is not built yet (E0904), and a Patch cannot be read from text today (E0905). fn keep<T>(value: &T) cannot write value.size today (E0302). Reflection already reads priv fields.

WHY NOT B

B is easy to read, but it lets any generic function change any field of any type by name, so a signature no longer tells you which values it may change. It reaches priv fields, since reflection already reads them, so it needs a new refusal. It keeps field records while the program runs.

B also needs three amendments. D-METADEPTH1/2 says "read-only reflection + derives" and "No mutation". D-ANY-JAI1 says the core.reflect floor has no "string-named field mutation", and that get and set "remain declined". D-ENUM-CASEMETA1=A says "There is no new get, read, cast, write-by-name, or constructor operation".

WHY NOT C

The engine's marker writes an Edit impl with one typed branch per field. It changes no rule, but each write hides in a template, the hardest code here to read. Templates and #{…} pastes are not built yet.

DROPPED

The JSON round trip stays dropped. Every edit paid a full encode and decode.

COST WHILE RUNNING

parse_patch compares the path with each field name once, then does the typed apply. It is left out of the program when nothing calls it. No field records are kept while running.

RATIFIED DECISIONS IT TOUCHES

A amends no ratified rule. It extends D-PATCH1 with parse_patch and PatchError, the way Codable decode already fills fields by name. It uses D-MARKER-GROUP1=A for the engine's group and D-DECL-TYPES1=A for the T: Patchable bound.

options.name: Build a typed patch from a field path
options.detail: The engine's entity marker is a group that includes #Patchable, so entity types write nothing extra. #Patchable gains value.parse_patch(path, text), which builds a typed patch for one field or dotted path. The engine applies it with the existing apply, and undo is the existing diff. Failures say exactly what went wrong.
options.technical:
Extends D-PATCH1: #Patchable also synthesizes value.parse_patch(path: String, text: String) -> T.Patch PatchError!, one branch per patchable field, using each field type's parse. A dotted path recurses into Patchable field types and stores the whole new field value. PatchError implements Diagnostic, with UnknownField (nearest name), BadText, NoParse, Private and Computed cases.

The engine's Entity marker is a D-MARKER-GROUP1=A group (unbuilt: E0003 today). The T: Patchable bound comes from D-DECL-TYPES1=A's derive-as-trait rule (unbuilt: E0904 today). No Core reflection change and no ratified rule amended.

options.name: Reflection writes a field
options.detail: A reflected value can set a field by name: reflect.of(&value).field(name)?.set_text(text). The engine needs no marker on the type. Any holder of a changeable reference can write any field of any type, and three ratified rules are reversed.
options.technical: Adds a write through a borrowed reflected value, a by-name field lookup and a text setter that calls the field type's parse. Amends D-METADEPTH1/2, D-ANY-JAI1's declined list and D-ENUM-CASEMETA1=A. Adds a priv-field refusal outside the type's module and needs field records kept while running.

options.name: The marker writes setter code
options.detail: The engine's Entity marker writes an Edit impl for every entity type: one typed branch per field. The editor calls it through the trait. Core reflection stays read only, but the write hides in a template.
options.technical: No Core change. Uses expand, #{…} pastes and a loop over target.fields unrolled while compiling. Each branch calls its field type's parse. Templates and pastes are unbuilt today.

recommendation.why: A keeps B's short engine code and gives a typed, visible write. The engine's one entity marker carries the opt-in, so types write nothing extra. Every failure says why, undo is the existing diff, and no ratified rule changes.
gains: Engine code is one line, as readable as B.
Entity types write only the engine marker they already need.
A signature still shows which values a function may change.

losses.loss: A field path is text from the editor, so a typo is found when the edit runs, not when the program compiles.
losses.mitigation: Irreducible: the editor builds the path at run time. parse_patch refuses the typo with a plain error and a "did you mean", and nothing changes.

whyNot.reason: B lets any generic function change any field, reverses three ratified rules and needs a new priv refusal.
C hides each write in a template, the hardest code here to read.

recommendation.tradeoff: The engine marks its entity types once, for typed edits with clear errors and free undo.

decisions.title: The phase read is spelled #phase, a value about the spot where code is evaluated
decisions.situation: Some helpers run while Jet compiles and again in the finished program. A table made early can call the same helper that the program calls later. The helper may need to print only in the finished program. Jet planned a phase read, but its old dollar spelling is retired and neither replacement works today. We recommend #phase, with three answers and an ordinary if, and update five stale criteria across four cards.
decisions.gist: How should code ask whether it is running while compiling, while building, or in the finished program?
decisions.lesson: A phase is the time at which a piece of code runs. Jet has three: while compiling (a comptime block), while building (the build function), and in the finished program. A helper can be called in more than one phase. Reading the phase lets it skip work that only makes sense in one of them, such as printing.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Compiling is when Jet turns source into a program. A comptime block is code Jet must run while compiling. The build function is the fn named build that makes the outputs. Run time is when the finished program runs. A site value is a hash name that Jet fills in for the spot where it is written or evaluated, such as #line. A plain value is an ordinary name whose value is the same in every file, such as build.target.os.
decisions.story: Mia writes a square helper that prints each call. She also fills a lookup table with it while compiling. An unguarded print needs an explicit compile-time effects gate today. She wants the helper to print only in the finished program, without granting that gate.
decisions.detail:
D-META-HASH1=A is ratified and retires every dollar read and paste, but does not name a replacement for $phase. This vote supplies one. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A names Phase.Comptime and distinguishes required early evaluation from an optional early try.

Observed with admitted jet: p1 and p2 give E0107 for $phase. p4 gives E0927 for #line and #phase. p10 prints [1, 4, 9] and 16. p11 gives E3410 for an unguarded compile-time print. BallotReview/phase-type.jet gives E0107 for Phase. p9 instead proves comptime if works, printing linux branch.

Registry entries are not implementations: CoreSurface.jet:139 has FACT_ROOT_PHASE; Spellings.jet:35 lists $phase. AST/Comptime.jet does not declare a source Phase enum.

Proposed A: Prelude Phase: enum { Comptime, Build, Runtime }, read only through #phase. Explicit comptime evaluation, including marker expansion, reads Comptime. Ordinary build-entry execution and its helpers read Build. Finished-program execution reads Runtime. Generated code reads its own execution phase. Explicit comptime inside build reads Comptime. Direct, indirect and recursive calls must agree across O0, O1, O2 and applicable web output (I9).

Before compile-time ambient-effect checks, drop only phase-proven unreachable branches in that copy. Runtime rows retain runtime effects; a pure runtime caller cannot hide IO. Check names and types in every branch. Zero-cost folding, including callbacks, is an acceptance condition, not a measurement.

Reject phase reads reached from comptime if conditions, including through helpers, with a registered error and a plain-if fix. Ordinary if inside comptime is allowed and reads Comptime. Preserve WORD1's distinction: a local optional early try reaching phase falls back to runtime; a required file constant reads Comptime or fails. #phase is not part of #here.

B puts the same read on build, whose Prelude name a user build function can hide (p7 establishes Prelude shadowing). C's Boolean loses the Build distinction. E keeps a function surface without losing any phase. D shares the arithmetic and accepts an explicit trace flag; it needs no duplicated body. BallotReview/phase-explicit.jet already prints [1, 4, 9], square 4 and 16 with D.

Read-only board check: #3520 c23 replaces $phase with the chosen read; #6281 c51 and #6206 c4 replace $build.os with build.target.os. #6039 c6 uses the ratified marker struct/expand shape; c26 uses impl #{target}. These are five criteria across four cards. Keep their behavioral acceptance terms.

Beginners calling libraries need no phase read. Shared-helper authors use one ordinary if. Experts keep normal effect rows and explicit gates: phase grants no permission. Add syntax, errors, UI snapshots, explain text and cross-tier goldens together. A, B, C and E are proposals, not working syntax today.

options.name: #phase, a site value
options.detail: `#phase` is a Phase value that Jet fills in for each compiled copy: `.Comptime`, `.Build` or `.Runtime`. A plain `if` on it folds away. `comptime if #phase` is an error with a fix.
options.technical: Add a site-value row #phase and Prelude Phase: enum { Comptime, Build, Runtime }. Substitute by execution phase, including indirect calls. Fold only phase-proven unreachable effects for the required compile-time copy; preserve runtime effect rows and check names/types in all branches. Reject phase reads reached from comptime if conditions, not ordinary if inside comptime blocks. Preserve D-COMPTIME-WORD1's local-try fallback and required file-constant rule.

options.name: build.phase, a field of the build value
options.detail: The phase is a field of the plain `build` value that HASH1 adds, next to `build.target.os`. Same results as A where `build` is not hidden.
options.technical: Add phase: Phase to the proposed Prelude build value, with A's phase and effect rules. Top-level names can hide Prelude names today (p7); the proposed build qualification and resolution must be specified before implementing B.

options.name: in_comptime(), a Prelude function
options.detail: A Prelude function returns true while compiling and false otherwise, as in Zig and C++. Build code reads true, so it cannot be told apart from a comptime block.
options.technical: Prelude `in_comptime: fn() -> Bool`, substituted per copy like A. The comptime-if trap gets the same registered error. No Phase enum is exposed.

options.detail: No implicit read exists. Share the arithmetic and pass an explicit trace flag. Callers choose whether to print; no helper body is duplicated.
options.technical: Delete FACT_ROOT_PHASE from the public registry and amend the phase-read provisions of D-COMPTIME-WORD1. Ordinary parameters and existing effects remain the only mechanism.

options.name: phase(), a three-case Prelude function
options.detail: A Prelude function returns the same three-case Phase as A. It preserves the Build distinction without a hash name.
options.technical: phase: fn() -> Phase is a compiler-substituted read with A's phase, effects, folding and comptime-if checks. This replaces, rather than accompanies, #phase.

comparisons.note: `@inComptime()` returns whether it ran in a comptime context; the result is a compile-time constant (ziglang.org/documentation/master, @inComptime).
`std::is_constant_evaluated()` always returns true as the condition of `if constexpr`; C++23 adds `if consteval` to avoid the trap (cppreference, is_constant_evaluated, Notes).
comparisons.code: if consteval { /* compile time */ } else { std::printf("square\n"); }

comparisons.note: `__ctfe` is true during compile-time evaluation; it cannot be read in a static if, and every use is evaluated statically at no run-time cost (dlang.org/spec/function.html).

recommendation.why: The phase is a fact about where code is evaluated, so it belongs with #line in the hash family. A names three phases, folds away while running, and turns the known trap into an error with a fix.
gains: One spelling family: hash names are facts about a spot.
Build code can be told apart from comptime code.
The always-true trap is an error with a fix.

losses.loss: One more hash name to learn.
losses.mitigation: Only helper authors need it; hover and jet explain describe each phase.

whyNot.reason: The build value is the same everywhere but the phase is not, and a build file's own build function hides it.
The Boolean cannot distinguish build execution from explicit compile-time evaluation; E shows that a function need not lose that information.
It shares the implementation, but every caller must choose a flag rather than inheriting the execution phase.
It preserves all three phases, but presents an execution-site fact as an ordinary zero-argument call; A makes the special read visible.

recommendation.tradeoff: One explicit site read; zero-cost folding is an implementation acceptance condition, not measured performance.

decisions.title: Read a declaration's source location from its existing reflection record
decisions.situation: Tools need to say where a type, field or function was declared. The location where a query is written is not that declaration's location. Jet already has reflection records and a common SourceLocation record, but the tested reflection result lacks the proposed location field. Choose how to read that declaration location without confusing it with value provenance or caller location. We recommend a location member on the ordinary reflection record. It reuses reflection instead of inventing another compiler-filled sigil.
decisions.gist: Should declaration locations be ordinary members of existing reflection records?
decisions.lesson: #here says where this expression is written; #caller says where the caller called. A declaration location says where Point or helper was defined. A tracked value's origin answers yet another question: where its data came from.
decisions.story: A tool prints Point at line 3 and helper at line 7 of one source file. Every option asks about those same declarations, not about the later query lines.
decisions.inWild: Jet's existing reflection records already carry checked source spans. Its SourceLocation record already supplies file, line and column for site information. The cohesive extension derives a location from that same checked source, rather than creating another source-tracking system.
decisions.detail:
#3520 c24 requires declaration/field/method positions as D-JAI-SITE1 SourceLocation. D-META-HASH1=A selects ordinary reflection; D-META-HASH2=A owns #here/#caller. A adds location: SourceLocation? to type, callable, field and method records. C uses declared_at with that same type. B's #origin returns the same optional record. None means known absence of a source declaration; unavailable analysis still fails the existing reflection query with MetadataError.

The location identifies the declaration-name token in the checked snapshot. Reuse SourceLocation's line, column and path conventions, not another coordinate scheme. Generic instances point to their definition, not a random call. Alias type reflection follows existing resolved-type identity; no new alias-handle syntax is introduced here. Overloads require existing typed selection, never the first same-named declaration.

Derive the member from canonical SourceSpan and SourceId; do not maintain another location store. Generated declarations point into checked generated source and retain existing expansion provenance for navigation. No fallback to #here or fabricated line zero. Snapshot digests remain valid identities even when a mutable disk file changes.

Only the compile-time access required by c24 is authorized here. Do not retain source metadata at runtime just for an early line query. Existing visibility, authority and retention rules apply. Private paths and generated text remain protected. No implicit source reopen to repair stale metadata.

Beginner path: read location and handle known absence, as the complete panes show. Expert path: iterate fields/methods with the same member while using snapshot and expansion metadata. #here/#caller remain use/call sites. Tracked value origin remains data provenance, possibly ambiguous; it is not declaration identity.

B is a new parameterized compiler root, unlike #here's lexical read, but must still use the same checked metadata. It creates no runtime type lookup or extra authority. C is a strong ordinary-field alternative whose name emphasizes the declaration. A uses the common location vocabulary throughout reflected records. Optionality and errors are identical in every option.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43: early Point.reflect() metadata prints struct for kind. INFO.location.line gets E0302. Ordinary runtime Point.reflect() gets E0311, not proof that early reflection is absent. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/Reflection.jet:817-826, 891-906 and 1477-1505 expose field/method/type spans; 89-93 builds offset spans. These are reuse points, not a working location projection.

Adversarial verdict: A holds as a checked-source view. First reuse span and location records. Then preserve identity and expansion provenance instead of silently substituting the query site. Cache snapshot line tables rather than scan text per query. Known absent declarations remain None, never invented positions. No proposed exact-line golden was executed; the named witness file was absent here. The panes supply its complete proposed source with Point at line 3 and helper at line 7.

decisions.title: Opt-in for type construction and existing-code transformations
decisions.gist: Should a checked package opt-in suffice, or must every invocation repeat it?
decisions.lesson: Standard mode permits reflection and additive generation. Advanced mode also permits type construction, caller-code insertion, explicit parsing and replacement of existing contracts. Both options require root approval and explicit provider registration. They share dependency denial, revocation, cache isolation and audit rules. Host permissions remain separate. A stores consent in the approved package; B repeats it per invocation.
decisions.explainer: Standard mode permits reflection and additive generation. Advanced mode also permits type construction, caller-code insertion, explicit parsing and replacement of existing contracts. Both options require root approval and explicit provider registration. They share dependency denial, revocation, cache isolation and audit rules. Host permissions remain separate. A stores consent in the approved package; B repeats it per invocation.
decisions.story: A package author needs the same example to work during preparation and across applicable execution modes. This choice fixes the public contract before implementation.
decisions.inWild:
cargo build --features metaprogramming
Cargo makes feature selection explicit, but features are not a security boundary. Jet authorization must not inherit that assumption. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
decisions.detail:
## Fixed owner direction

The owner explicitly requested full Jai-level capabilities with powers above level 5 gated by metaprogramming opt-in. Neither option removes that requested scope. This decision chooses authorization placement, not whether advanced capabilities will exist.

Standard mode includes ordinary preparation, complete lawful read-only facts and explicit additive Generated publication. It also includes ordinary existing generics and project-defined checks. It forbids first-class type construction, caller-code insertion, arbitrary code parsing and replacement of existing program contracts.

Unrestricted means the complete checked metaprogramming API, not unrestricted operating-system access. Type safety, memory safety, explicit Unsafe regions and enterprise host policy still apply. Advanced metaprograms cannot forge inferred facts or erase external approval records.

## Exact configuration and registration

The manifest member is metaprogramming: unrestricted inside the invocation root package. Omission means standard. An explicit metaprogramming: standard has the same meaning. Unknown values fail rather than falling back. There is one compiler binary and one mode-aware compilation path.

compiler.advanced.register(transform, targets: [(@FUNCTION(price)?).identity, (@FUNCTION(run)?).identity]) registers a provider callback from an explicitly imported module. Registration names the provider's content identity and declared targets. Repeated identical registration is idempotent; conflicting identities under one name are errors. Merely importing a module runs no provider.

A callback receives an authorized session. Its targets must remain within the root's registered workspace and permitted dependency scopes. A dependency may expose a provider, but its own manifest cannot enable it in the root. The root must register it explicitly under the approved policy.

Existing #3418 trust policy decides whether the root and provider are approved. Existing #3419 owns consent presentation. A previously unapproved or changed privileged provider cannot silently run. Noninteractive operation fails closed with an actionable request for approval. A known approved root does not need redundant per-invocation consent under A.

Option B adds --metaprogramming=unrestricted to check, run, dev and build. Editor analysis requires the equivalent explicit session grant. The flag cannot enable a package whose manifest remains standard. Neither option allows a provider to edit its own mode, trust record or external policy.

## Effects, caching and artifacts

The privilege grant is distinct from file, process, network, native-code and sensitive-data authority. Those operations still use inferred effects and approved host policy. A denial stops the operation and records its actual source; no empty success fallback is allowed.

Cache keys include the mode, provider identities, settings, target and relevant grants. Standard mode cannot reuse an advanced result as if it were standard. Revoking authorization invalidates affected preparation artifacts. Existing audit retention policy controls receipts; a metaprogram cannot delete them.

An AOT binary launches without re-running preparation or obtaining compiler privileges. This does not erase ordinary runtime permissions required by its application code. A dev session reload must re-evaluate approval when provider code, mode or grants change.

## Same-program comparison

Both examples register transform and allow the same checked edits after root approval. Without the manifest member, registration fails before the provider executes. Under B, omitting the flag also fails. A dependency's identical manifest member does not enable the parent.

Beginners need no opt-in for read-only reflection or additive generation. Experts choose unrestricted once under A and register only required providers. Tests must exercise denial, dependency self-enablement, revocation, editor behavior and cold/warm execution. No unchecked compiler escape is introduced.

## Reader key and shared policy commitments

The invocation root is the package the user asks Jet to compile. A provider is an imported Jet function explicitly registered to transform named targets. Its content identity is the digest of its code and relevant dependencies. Ambient state means privileges acquired without an explicit passed or registered grant.

This ballot selects the exact opt-in, registration and invalidation rules stated here. The owner already selected advanced power behind opt-in. Existing #3418 and #3419 govern project trust and consent; this vote does not silently expand host rights. The complete transformation in D-META-CONTROL2 defines transform in both examples.

The same transform changes price's signature and updates run in one transaction. The result prints 6 rather than 4. Registration declares price and run as its only targets. Attempting to rewrite a third declaration fails. Attempting a denied file or process operation still fails before that effect occurs.

An approved root and unchanged approved provider may run under A without repeated prompts. An unapproved or changed provider requires interactive approval under the trust policy. Noninteractive compilation refuses it and explains which root/provider requires approval. Approval of a root never approves a dependency provider that was not explicitly registered.

Under B, the editor initialization field metaprogramming is the string unrestricted. Omission or standard permits passive diagnostics but prevents advanced provider execution. The package manifest and trust checks must still agree. Under A, editor execution uses the approved package request without an extra session flag. Revocation immediately prevents subsequent provider execution in either mode.

## Failure coverage

#3526 proves unknown mode values, missing requests, dependency self-enablement, undeclared targets, changed providers and revoked approval fail before privileged code runs. #3419 owns the actual interactive consent surface; #3418 owns a denied host effect. #3532 proves cache isolation and revocation invalidation. #3533 proves editor denial and actionable source locations.

#3521 proves saved AOT artifacts do not prepare at startup. #3527 proves a child workspace cannot widen its parent's grants. #3539 exercises the standard-versus-advanced matrix rather than accepting configuration parsing as proof.


The package file uses the existing top-level record grammar. metaprogramming is a new member next to name and version. No package wrapper keyword or second manifest grammar is proposed.

## Dependency targets and approval ownership

Registration uses compiler-issued DeclarationHandles, not unqualified strings. Handles carry package identity, declaration identity and checked source digest. The root's own declarations are eligible under its approved unrestricted request. Dependency declarations are ineligible unless explicitly granted below.

A root package may add metaprogramming_targets entries. Each record names package identity, source_digest and an exact declarations list. These records use the existing package-record and list grammar. No glob or transitive grant is implied. A conceptual entry is { package: "vendor.math", source_digest: "sha256:...", declarations: ["vendor.math.clamp"] }; the stored digest must be complete and verified.

The invocation-root owner approves this grant under #3418's project trust policy. A dependency cannot supply or approve its own parent grant. Enterprise policy may prohibit dependency transformation. The provider must also register the exact target handles; either missing approval or missing registration denies the edit. Changing the dependency digest invalidates the grant and requires approval again.

Approved edits apply only to the root's compilation workspace snapshot. They never rewrite the dependency cache or another project's source. Receipts retain original package identity, source digest, approved declarations and transformed snapshot identity. Private facts still need the corresponding explicit authorized scope; possession of a display name grants nothing.

#3526 owns exact grant matching, wrong-digest refusal, unauthorized dependency targets and registration checks. #3530 owns unchanged dependency storage and affected-consumer rechecking. #3532 keys the grant and transformed snapshot into cache identity. This grants complete checked dependency transformation without permitting dependency self-enablement.

options.name: Approved package opt-in
options.detail: Authorize the root package and explicitly register providers. Approved projects avoid repeated flags. Ordinary invocations can execute previously approved providers.
options.technical: Only the invocation root manifest can request unrestricted mode. Existing project trust and enterprise policy must approve that root. Registration is explicit in root preparation; import alone remains inert.

options.name: Package plus invocation
options.detail: Require the package request and an execution grant on each invocation. This limits accidental execution but adds CLI and editor setup.
options.technical: The same root authorization and provider registration apply. Every compile, run, dev, check and editor compilation also requires an invocation-level unrestricted grant.

comparisons.note: Cargo makes feature selection explicit, but features are not a security boundary. Jet authorization must not inherit that assumption. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html

recommendation.why: A makes explicitly approved project behavior work consistently in commands and editors. B adds stronger per-invocation refusal, at the cost of repeated execution grants.
gains: Approved projects run without a repeated flag.

losses.loss: Ordinary invocations can execute previously approved providers.
losses.mitigation: Avoiding repeated execution consent lets approved configuration activate providers on later invocations.

whyNot.reason: B can refuse advanced execution per invocation, but adds a grant to every CLI and editor workflow.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts durable activation, not merely a missing reminder. B provides finer control over each execution.

losses.mitigation: Avoiding repeated execution consent lets approved configuration activate providers on later invocations.

whyNot.reason: B can refuse advanced execution per invocation, but adds a grant to every CLI and editor workflow.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts durable activation, not merely a missing reminder. B provides finer control over each execution.

decisions.title: One metaprogramming ladder: Meta effects follow the rule of every effect, compiler control is one passed value, and macros stay out
decisions.situation: While Jet compiles a program, code can act on that program in growing steps. It can read types, add new code through markers, and finally rewrite function bodies through a compiler value. Four earlier votes each set up part of this ladder, and they now disagree. One turns the strong steps on with a package flag, one gives macros to everyone, one adds expert permissions that start off, and one removes macros again. Since then Jet ruled that every effect is allowed unless written code denies it, and that effects are ordinary types. This vote picks one ladder that fits those rules, so the board can build it.
decisions.gist: Which one set of rules should decide who may add or rewrite code while a program compiles?
decisions.lesson: Metaprogramming is code that writes or changes code while Jet compiles. An effect is a kind of outside action a function takes, such as using the network. Jet now allows every effect unless written code denies it, and names new effects when a run starts. The question is whether adding and rewriting code follow that same rule, or a rule of their own.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A marker is a hash name above a declaration, such as #Traced, whose expand code can add new code. The Compiler value is an object that lets code watch the compile and rewrite function bodies. A rewrite replaces a function's body with new checked code. A macro is a function whose body is pasted into the caller's code. An authority row in package.jet lists effects to allow or deny. A grant line limits what one dependency may do.
decisions.story: Ines wants every function marked #Traced to log when it starts and ends. She installs a trace library and passes it her build's compiler value. Today four rulings disagree on what else she must write: a package flag, an expert line, or nothing. She also wonders whether a macro would have been the simpler tool. She wants one rule, the same one her network calls follow.
decisions.detail:
Ratification checked read-only: OPTIN2 authorizes root-approved registration. CODE1 authorizes macros. COMPILER1's ratified detail explicitly removes them and restores the user-macro ban; its A option alone omits that explanation. HOLD1 adds package authorization. AUTH-DEFAULT1 later allows effects unless denied. HASH1 retires dollar pastes. This vote explicitly reconciles those contracts.

Exercised earlier: l1 prints hello and 2; l2 prints start sum, done sum and 5; l3 reports E1221 for Meta.Generate; l4 prints l4 with the package flag accepted. l2 contains no defer. BallotReview/defer.jet separately reports E0003 for general defer. DEFER1=A ratifies reverse-order cleanup on every exit but is not implemented by that probe.

A declares Meta in Core's compiler library, not the machine-only kernel list. Its empty #FX ceiling grants no host power. Generate, Include, Rewrite, Types and Raw are nominal compiler-operation cases. Adding a type from text checks Generate, Types and Raw together. Host work retains machine effects and #Impure gates. No Meta alias hides FS, Exec or FFI.

Only root-package source can call b.compiler(output), using loader/lock identity, not a caller-supplied name. Forwarding Build cannot bypass that check. Compiler recipients can retain and forward control during that build; record every handoff. Stale values fail closed. Root and organization denials and locked dependency rewrite consent apply to every deferred action.

Retain COMPILER1's #code constructor. HASH1 copies ordinary values plainly, so trace.enter(name) captures the early String; only Code body insertion uses the proposed #{f.body} extension. Ordinary meta.add(code) and meta.rewrite_body(f, code) calls avoid a second special trailing-template-block convention. Name/type pastes retain HASH1 hygiene.

The same program in the options has a marked load_level with early return, fallible read and cleanup. trace registers first; timer registers second and wraps outside trace. Under the proposed DEFER1 meaning, every exit prints time start, enter, exit, time stop. This is a design expectation, not current executable output. C also shows explicit macro wrapping, which can leave the caller; closures cannot promise that behavior.

B keeps A's flat effect family but adds HOLD1-style authorization of Compiler possession. It needs neither expert attributes nor a third effect level. D is traceable through root registration and import alone remains inert. Its difference is provider registration/trust state instead of value delegation.

#3526 c1 changes opt-in to possession plus per-action Meta checks. c2 keeps root/external denials. c3 keeps import, possession and registration distinct. c4 freezes authority and consent when build returns and includes them in provenance/cache identity. c5 keeps host, credentials, consent and Unsafe independent. c6 keeps issued declaration identities and replaces target-record spelling with CROSSPKG1's locked-package allow_rewrite consent.

c7/c8 reopen syntax/spec rows for the replacement surface; c9/c10 retain grammar and UI snapshot obligations. c11 keeps no-value, import-only, authorized-value, dependency request, forwarded Build, denial, policy and unknown-root/no-TTY fixtures. No source/header/cache/subprocess self-enablement may succeed. c12 keeps stale-handle refusal and checked backend options.

c13 keeps advanced type factories, deterministic identity and layout under Meta.Types. This does not forbid ordinary type declarations, generic instantiation, or marker-generated declared types without a Compiler value. All applicable effects still check. c14 keeps hygienic Code and scoped meta.add(code, scope:); call-site register_expansion leaves with macros, as COMPILER1 explicitly rules.

c15 keeps atomic rechecking of all a handler's actions and affected callers; a failed handler publishes none. Generated Unsafe is never authorized. c16 keeps revision-aware dependencies, changed-authority invalidation and fresh host effects on cache hits. c17 records the complete producer/handoff chain. c18 maps project checkers to read/report handlers that cannot suppress Core diagnostics.

c19 retains foreign evidence receipts and opaque-evidence refusal through the existing FFI contract. c20 remains with GENERIC1 for explicit specialization, while procedure-of-call identity remains SITE1. No other behavior is deleted merely by retiring an API. #5023 has three bookkeeping criteria, not macro rows to close. B adds its authorization fixture; C restores call expansion; D retains OPTIN2 criteria.

Handlers share PREP-FUEL1's budget and the existing round-17 limit. Budget/round exhaustion is an error with no partial publication. Cache keys cover source, compiler, reflected inputs, lock, authority and consent. The language server follows the same handlers. Beginners apply markers; experts delegate one Compiler value and inspect later handoffs. None of these proposed APIs is claimed as implemented by l1-l4.

options.name: Meta effects like any effect, one passed value, no macros
options.detail: Meta is a flat ordinary effect family, allowed unless denied. Only the root's own source makes Compiler; passing it delegates control. Recipient libraries can forward it, so later handoffs stay visible in provenance. No macros.
options.technical: Proposed Meta: enum { Generate, Include, Rewrite, Types, Raw } implementing Effect, declared in Core's compiler package under D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1, not in Prelude/Effects.jet. Root-only b.compiler(output); every action checks all applicable cases, host gates and dependency consent. Watching grants no mutation. Retain COMPILER1's #code constructor with HASH1 hygiene, and explicitly extend #{e} to paste Code inside it. All #3526 acceptance obligations remain; no behavior is removed merely by deleting its old API spelling.

options.name: As A, but strong steps need one package line
options.detail: As A, but creating the Compiler value also requires an explicit package authorization line, preserving HOLD1's extra review step. The Meta effects themselves keep A's flat family and ordinary defaults.
options.technical: Keep the root-only passed value and flat five-case family. authority.holds.allow: [Meta] authorizes value creation as a separate capability check; it is not an effect ceiling and does not turn off default holding of other effects. This explicitly amends HOLD1's old Meta.Code spelling. No third effect level or expert flag is required.

options.name: As A, plus macros for everyone
options.detail: As A, and a function marked #Expand pastes its body into the caller. It can read and change the caller's variables and leave the caller early. Pasting performs a sixth case, Meta.Paste, allowed by default.
options.technical: Restores D-JAI-CODE1's macros in HASH1 form: `#Expand` on a function, `#{body}` pastes a Code argument, and a call writes `name!(…)`. Hygiene follows HASH1 templates; `uses:` names caller variables the body may touch. Meta gains Paste.

options.name: A package flag and registered providers
options.detail: D-META-OPTIN2 as card #3526 describes it. One package flag turns compiler control on, and comptime code registers provider functions that return checked change sets. There is no Compiler value.
options.technical: package.jet `metaprogramming: unrestricted`. `compiler.advanced.register(provider, targets: [...])` in comptime, with D-META-CONTROL2's change sets. Dependency rewrites need a `metaprogramming_targets` entry. No Meta effect family.

comparisons.note: No macros by design; comptime code and build.zig are ordinary Zig code (ziglang.org/documentation/master, comptime; Zig build system guide).
Procedural macros and build.rs run arbitrary code at build time with no permission step; this is a known supply-chain risk (doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html).
comparisons.code:
#[proc_macro_attribute]
pub fn traced(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream { item }

recommendation.why: A makes the root's creation and handoff the visible opt-in and keeps ordinary effect defaults. Every handler action, later handoff and affected caller stays checked, and every #3526 criterion keeps its behavior.
gains: One default rule for every effect, including Meta.
Every rewrite traces to one build line and the notice.
Templates and pastes use the hash rule only.

losses.loss: A helper cannot leave its caller early.
losses.mitigation: The helper returns a value and the caller writes ? or return, so exits stay visible.

losses.loss: Rewrites run without a separate opt-in line.
losses.mitigation: Only the app's own build can make the value; the notice names it; one deny row refuses it.

whyNot.reason: B adds a package authorization check beyond the root creation call. It is defensible for code-review policy, but is not required to preserve ordinary Meta effects.
C adds explicit caller exits and another expansion surface; it is not interchangeable with marker attachment and needs its own hygiene and exit contract.
D is traceable through root registration but uses provider registration and trust state rather than a value that can be delegated.

recommendation.tradeoff: Root creation replaces a package authorization line; forwarding and execution-time authority must still be visible and checked.
