decisions.title: A wrapping marker gets call: Call<R>, with the arguments already bound, checked once where it is declared
decisions.situation:
A wrapping marker runs its own code around each call of the function it marks, for example to retry it. Jet already agreed that wrappers exist, the order they run in, and that a wrapper never changes a function's signature. Nothing fixes what the wrapper's handle on the call looks like.

Today that handle is the function itself, so a wrapper must pass the function's own arguments and only fits functions it knows. Its body is checked again at every use. We recommend A: the arguments are already attached, so one wrapper fits any function and is checked once.
decisions.gist: Should a wrapping marker's call have its arguments already bound, so one wrapper works on any function and is checked once?
decisions.lesson: A wrapping marker runs code around a function, such as retrying it, timing it or logging it. To do that it needs a way to call the function it wraps. This vote decides what that call looks like, so a wrapper written once works on any function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A marker is a # name with a capital letter, such as #Retry. A wrapping marker runs its own code around each call to the function it marks. call is the handle it uses to run that function.

The arguments are bound when the values the caller passed are already attached to call.
decisions.story: Lena writes a Retry wrapper and marks fetch(id). Today the wrapper must write call(id), so it works only for functions with an id. Under A it writes call(), and the same Retry marks any function.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The type of call in wrap, when the wrapper's body is checked, and whether it may call more than once. Attachment through markers, #Policy and apply() stays as D-CALLPOLICY1 says. Staging is D-META-STAGING1 and spelling is ratified D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH2.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe w02 is Examples/Basics/Functions/CallablePolicies.jet, today's policy declarations with wrap(call). It prints nine lines, and audit:outer:audit:inner:ok shows the outer wrapper runs first. Probe w01 writes wrap in impl Marker and gets E0907: Marker has only expand today.

Probe w03 wraps a function that returns Int with a wrapper that returns a String. The error, E0113, ReturnTypeMismatch, points into the wrapper's body and names a generated function: the body is checked again at each use, like a template.

Probe w04 calls call() twice in a wrapper on bump(n: Int). It gets E0766, MissingArgument, twice: call is bump itself, so the wrapper must write call(n), and a wrapper written once cannot forward the arguments of a function it has never seen.

The rule under A. call has the Core type Call<R>, where R is the wrapped function's result, its error or None included. The arguments are bound before wrap runs, so call() takes none. It runs the next inner wrapper, then the body, in D-CALLPOLICY1's chain order. wrap returns R.

Checked once. The wrapper's body is checked where it is declared, against Call<R> with R generic, as D-MARKER-TARGETS1 checks marker bodies. At each use the compiler checks only that the function's result fits the wrapper's R, such as R? for Retry. A mismatch is an error at the marker, naming the function's result.

Calling more than once. A wrapper may call call() zero, one or more times: zero returns early, as a cache does. A wrapper that may call more than once declares repeats: true, beside sites. It may then mark only functions whose parameters, self included, are borrowed or copyable, so each call sees the same arguments.

Using it on a function that takes an argument by move is an error naming the parameter, with the fix to borrow it. Arguments are cleaned up once, by the caller, after wrap returns.

What a wrapper may read. self holds the marker's arguments, and self.function is D-META-REFLECT2's FunctionInfo for the marked function, so a wrapper can log its name. It cannot read or change the argument values; a marker that needs them adds code through expand instead.

What stays ratified. CALLPOLICY1's law holds: the wrapper's own effects and errors must be covered by the marked function's row, checked at each use. A wrap edits no body, so it needs no Compiler value under D-META-LADDER1; the marker written on the declaration is the visible authority.

Effects inside the once-checked body. Call<R> carries the marked function's effect row with it, and call() performs exactly that row, which the function already declares. So the body needs no effect of its own to call it, and each use checks only what the wrapper adds, as CALLPOLICY1 requires.

Call cannot outlive wrap. Its bound arguments belong to the caller's frame, so storing call, returning it, or moving it into another task is the ordinary borrow error. The arguments are cleaned up once, by the caller, after wrap returns, so no option leaves them dangling.

Census on dev 76955986d0 over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, raw matching lines in Jet files. Policy declarations: 7 in 5 files. wrap(call): 18 lines in 11 files. #Policy(: 88 lines in 71 files. Every user wrap(call) body in Examples and tests writes call() with no arguments, so their text is kept.

Beginner path. Use a wrapper: #Retry(attempts: 3) above a function. Expert path. Write one: a struct with impl Marker and wrap. It is checked once, and it works on any function whose result fits.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A wrapper cannot read argument values. The add rung, expand, can add code that reads them, so nothing is lost. A repeating wrapper cannot mark a function that consumes an argument, which is the price of calling it twice. The error names the parameter and the fix.

Other options. B keeps today's form: call is the function itself, and the body is checked at each use. C is Java's around advice: Call<A, R> exposes the arguments as call.args, and call.with(args) passes changed ones. D removes wrapping, as Rust and Go do: a retry is a plain function taking a closure. E is Python's: wrap returns any function, so a wrapper may change the signature.

Their best cases. B needs no work and lets a wrapper meant for one function use its arguments. C lets a wrapper sanitize arguments. D has no hidden control flow. E is the most flexible. D and E reverse ratified laws: D the wrap rung of DECL-TYPES1, E the signature law of CALLPOLICY1.

options.name: Call<R> with bound arguments
options.detail: call() takes no arguments and returns the function's result. The wrapper is checked once where declared; repeats: true allows more than one call.
options.technical: Core type Call<R>; arguments bound before wrap. call() runs the next inner wrapper per CALLPOLICY1's chain and performs the marked function's own effect row. Body checked at declaration with R generic, per MARKER-TARGETS1; each use checks result fit, effect and error cover. Call is a borrow of the wrap frame and cannot escape it. repeats: true requires borrowed or copyable parameters. self.function is REFLECT2's FunctionInfo.

options.name: call is the function, as today
options.detail: call is the wrapped function with its own parameters. The wrapper's body is checked again at each use.
options.technical: Today's policy wrap(call), probes w02 to w04. A wrapper that calls with arguments names the marked function's parameters. Errors appear inside the wrapper body at each use.

options.name: Java's arguments in call
options.detail: Call<A, R> carries the arguments as call.args, and call.with(args) runs the function with changed ones.
options.technical: As A, plus a typed argument tuple A per use and call.with(a: A). Signature kept; argument values may change.

options.name: No wrapping
options.detail: Markers never wrap. A retry is a plain function that takes a closure, as in Rust and Go.
options.technical: Amends D-DECL-TYPES1=A by removing rule 6, and retires D-CALLPOLICY1=E's wrapper chain.

options.name: Python's decorators
options.detail: wrap takes the function and returns any function, so a wrapper may change arguments and result.
options.technical: Amends D-CALLPOLICY1=E's signature-preservation law. Checks of the result happen at each call of the new function.

comparisons.note: Spring around advice calls proceed() with the bound arguments or proceed(args) with new ones.
comparisons.code:
@Around("execution(* fetch(..))")
Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint p) throws Throwable { return p.proceed(); }

comparisons.note: A decorator returns a new function and may change the signature.
No wrapping attribute in the language; a retry takes a closure.
comparisons.code: fn retry<T>(n: u32, f: impl Fn() -> Option<T>) -> Option<T> { (0..n).find_map(|_| f()) }

recommendation.why: A lets one wrapper mark any function and checks it once, where it is written. It keeps every ratified law about wrapping.
gains: One wrapper works on any function whose result fits.
Errors point at the wrapper's declaration, not inside a generated copy.
CALLPOLICY1's chain and signature law stay as ratified.

losses.loss: A wrapper cannot read or change argument values.
losses.mitigation: A marker that needs them adds code through expand.

losses.loss: A repeating wrapper cannot mark a function that consumes an argument.
losses.mitigation: The error names the parameter and suggests borrowing it.

losses.loss: A wrapper cannot keep call or hand it to another task.
losses.mitigation: Its arguments live in the caller's frame under every option; work that must outlive the call belongs in the function or in expand.

whyNot.reason: B makes a wrapper name its function's arguments and rechecks it at each use.
C lets a wrapper change arguments the caller passed, which no call site shows.
D removes the ratified wrap rung and puts a closure in every retried function.
E breaks CALLPOLICY1's ratified signature law.

recommendation.tradeoff: Wrappers cannot see argument values, in return for wrappers that work everywhere and are checked once.

decisions.title: The values the compiler fills in are spelled with #: #build, #here and #caller
decisions.situation:
Some values are filled in by the compiler: the build being made, the place in the source, and the place a function was called from. An earlier decision spelled the build as a plain name, build, and the places as hash line and hash file. It named nothing for the caller's place.

Your review approved one rule: a hash marks everything the compiler fills in, written #build, #here and #caller. A plain build is hidden inside any file that defines a function named build, as every build file does. We recommend A, that one rule.
decisions.gist: Should the build, this place and the caller's place be read as #build, #here and #caller?
decisions.lesson: A program can ask the compiler what it is building and where a line sits in the source. A logger uses the caller's place to say where a message came from. This vote decides how those values are spelled, so a reader sees at once that the compiler filled them in.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A site value is a value the compiler fills in for the spot where it is written, such as the line number. The caller's site is the place a function was called from. The build value describes what is being built: target system, profile, settings and stamp.

A marker is a # name with a capital letter, such as #Test.
decisions.story: Ines writes a build function named build, as every package's build file does. Inside it she reads build.target.os and gets her own function, not the build being made. Under A she writes #build.target.os, and no name of hers can hide it.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how three compiler-filled values are spelled, where #caller may be written, and the # form of the orphaned $program root. What the values contain stays as D-BUILD-FACT3 and D-JAI-SITE1 ratified. #package and #phase stay as HASH1 and D-META-PHASE1 ratified. Reflection stays reflect(x) per D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1. Staging and wrapping are their own ballots, D-META-STAGING1 and D-MARKER-CALL1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe h03 is the same program in today's spelling: a logger whose at parameter defaults to $caller, a branch on $build.os, and $build.profile. It prints 8: on linux, then dev, then 12: done, so the caller's line reaches the logger.

Probe h01 shows that #if does not parse yet (E0003), which D-META-SPELL1=A changes once built. Probe h02 writes #build.profile and #caller: E0087, MarkerLibraryCasing, and E0927, UnknownAppliedRule. Probe h05 writes HASH1's plain build.profile and gets E0107, UnknownName. Probe h04 prints #line and #file and gets E0915, MissingDisplay: both read as Unit. No option here is built.

Two new probes. h06 calls the logger directly and through a function value, f: log. It prints 7: direct and 9: through a value, so a caller default already fills at each call, even through a value. h07 declares build: fn() -> Int beside $build.profile and prints dev then 1: a marked read and a function named build coexist today.

Why a plain name is fragile here. A package's build file defines a function named build, the entry point D-BUILDENTRY1 ratified. On dev, 181 lines in 180 Jet files of Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests declare build: fn(, Compiler/build.jet among them. Inside those files a plain build value would be hidden by the function.

The rule under A. #build is the build value, with D-BUILD-FACT3's contents: target, profile, settings and stamp. #here is a SourceLocation for the spot where it is written, with file, line, column and enclosing function, per JAI-SITE1. It replaces HASH1's #line and #file, which become #here.line and #here.file: one record, not three names.

#caller is a SourceLocation for the call. It may be written only as a parameter default, as JAI-SITE1 ratified, so each call that leaves the parameter out passes its own place. A wrapper forwards the place by declaring the same default and passing it on. Anywhere else #caller is an error whose fix adds that parameter.

All six are plain values once read, with #package, #phase and #program. #build.profile can be stored, compared, passed and printed like any value; # only says who filled it in. No user name can hide them, because a # name cannot be declared. Under #if, #build.target.os selects an arm while building, as D-META-SPELL1=A says.

The casing rule that keeps # unambiguous. A lowercase # name is a compiler-filled value, and a capitalised one is a marker, as #Test. That is the split E0087's casing check already enforces. So #build can never be read as a marker, and no marker can be named build.

The sixth root. Today's parser also accepts $program, which D-SCRIPT-SCRIPTDIR1 ratified as $program.dir beside $here.dir. HASH1 retired it with no successor under every option. Under A it becomes #program, and #here keeps .dir, so every root has one # form. Under B it would need a plain program name, hideable like build.

#caller stays legal only as a parameter default. Today's second place, inside an #Expand macro, left with macros under D-META-COMPILER1 and D-META-LADDER1.

Census on dev, raw matching lines in Jet files of the same roots. $build is on 183 lines in 76 files, $here 25 in 15, $caller 55 in 20, $package 51 in 26, $phase 22 in 11 and $program 10 in 6. #line and #file appear nowhere. Under A each maps one to one, so the respelling is a token rename with a checked fix.

Beginner path. Print #build.profile to see the profile, and add at: SourceLocation{#caller} to a helper to learn who called it. Everything filled in by the compiler starts with #, so a search for # finds it.

Expert path. Wrappers forward #caller through their own default. Build files read #build freely, even inside a function named build. Code that needs only the line reads #here.line.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A changes HASH1's ratified spelling before HASH1 is built, so no program breaks that does not already use the $ forms, and those need renaming under every option but E. The rename is one to one, so the fix is mechanical and checked.

#build is one character longer than build. Most reads sit in #if lines or in build files, where the mark also tells the reader the arm is chosen while building. Dropping #line and #file costs five characters per read; one record keeps line, file and column together for loggers.

Other options. B keeps HASH1 as ratified: plain build, #line and #file, adding only #caller so JAI-SITE1's caller place has a successor. C is Swift's rule: #line written as a parameter default is the caller's line, so no #caller is needed. D is Rust's: a #TrackCaller marker lets SourceLocation.caller() return the caller's place. E keeps today's $ spelling, which HASH1 retired.

Their best cases. B needs no new rule for build and keeps three ratified names. C adds no name at all and is proven in Swift. D keeps call sites free of extra parameters and is proven in Rust. E needs no work. B and C still leave the build value hidden in every file that defines a build function.

decisions.title: A marker that reflects a type sees every member other markers add to it
decisions.situation:
A marker can read a type while building and can add members to it. When two markers sit on one type, or one marker reads a type another changes, the answer depends on when the read happens. Nothing agreed so far fixes that moment.

Today a marker sees only the members written in the source, in either order. We recommend A: every read sees the finished type, and stacked markers give the same code in any order.
decisions.gist: Should a marker reading a type see the members other markers add to it, whatever order they are written in?
decisions.lesson: Markers can write code for you, such as a method that turns a type into JSON. A marker that reads a type's members needs to know whether another marker's additions count. This vote decides what such a read sees, so stacked markers give the same result in any order.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A marker is a # name with a capital letter that runs code while building, such as #Json. Its expansion is the code it adds. To reflect a type is to read its fields, methods and markers while building.

Stacked markers are several markers on one declaration, written #[A, B].
decisions.story: Omar puts #Timestamps and #Json on Order. Timestamps adds a created_at method; Json lists methods to write. Today Json never sees created_at, in either order, and nothing says why.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What a reflected read made while building sees: in marker expansions, #run values and D-HOOK-STAGES1's declared hook. Checked code after building already sees the finished program. Spelling is settled by D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH1; wrapping is D-MARKER-CALL1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe s01 is the same program in today's $ spelling. AddHello adds a hello method; CountMethods counts the target's methods. It prints first sees 0 and second sees 0: inside an expansion, a marker sees only written members, in either order.

Probe s02 reads the same count from a compile-time value after expansion and prints hello, then reflect sees 1: the added method counts there. Probe s03 removes the marker and prints reflect sees 0. So today has two stages: expansions see the written program, and later values see the expanded one.

The rule under A. Every reflected read sees the finished type, whatever order markers are written in. The compiler records what each expansion reads: which type, and which part, such as fields, methods, markers or layout. A read never sees the reader's own additions.

When an expansion adds to a part another expansion already read, the compiler runs the reader again with the new state and replaces its old output. It repeats until nothing read has changed. Expansions are pure apart from the code they add, and D-HOOK-STAGES1 snapshots their file inputs, so a rerun gives the same answer for the same state.

When the answers cannot settle. If a rerun withdraws a member that another expansion already read, the markers disagree, for example one adds b only when a is missing and the other adds a when b exists. That is an error naming both markers, the type and the part, with the chain of reads.

Reruns count against the existing compile-time step budget from D-COMPTIME-WORD1, so a loop ends in that error, not a hang. jet inspect shows each expansion's reads and additions, so the chain can be followed.

What stays ratified. D-META-LADDER1's rewriting through the Compiler value, and D-META-CONTROL2's checked change sets, run after expansion on the finished program, as today. Layout reads wait for the fields they measure, through the same reruns. D-META-REFLECT2's records are unchanged.

Census on dev 76955986d0 over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, raw matches in Jet files. There are 73 marker expansions, written expand: fn(, in 65 files. Those files hold 102 reads of fields, methods or markers, with or without $, in 21 files.

There are 45 reflect() calls in 28 files. Stacked markers, a #[ list with two or more names, appear on 268 lines in 163 files.

No expansion in the census reads a member another marker adds, because today none can see one. So A changes no existing result: every read that today sees only written members sees the same members under A, until a second marker adds to that part.

Beginner path. Stack markers in any order; the generated code is the same. A marker that lists methods lists all of them. Expert path. Write markers that build on each other's output. A disagreement is a named error with the chain, not a silent difference.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Reruns cost build time. Only readers of a part that changed rerun. No expansion today sees another marker's additions, so existing programs need no rerun, and a program pays only where it builds on another marker.

The cost that remains. Two markers that each add only when the other's member is absent can settle in two ways. The compiler then runs them in a fixed order of their full names, never written order, so reordering a stack or moving a declaration cannot change the output. jet inspect shows the chain. Such a pair is rare and is a design smell in any language.

Other options. B keeps today's two stages: expansions see written members only, and later values see everything. C runs stacked markers in written order, as Python's decorators do, so each sees what earlier ones added. D is Rust's: a marker reads only the tokens written on its own item.

E is Zig's: a read of a type first finishes every marker on that type, on demand, and a loop is an error. A marker may then add members only to its own target. Each option's best case: B and D need no reruns; C is easy to explain; E needs no rerun but forbids adding to another type.

options.name: Reads see the finished type
options.detail: Every reflected read sees every member other markers add, in any order. The compiler reruns a reader when a part it read changes, and a disagreement is a named error.
options.technical: Read sets are recorded per type and part: fields, methods, markers, impls and layout. A read excludes the reader's own output. Readers rerun until stable; withdrawal of a read member is an error with the chain. Where two stable answers exist, readers run in the order of their full names, not written order. Reruns count against the existing step budget. LADDER1 rewrites and CONTROL2 change sets run after, unchanged.

options.name: Two stages, as today
options.detail: Expansions see written members only. #run values and checked code see the expanded program.
options.technical: Today's behavior, probes s01 and s02. No reruns. A marker that needs another's output cannot get it.

options.name: Written order
options.detail: Stacked markers run left to right, and each sees what earlier ones added. Declarations expand in source order.
options.technical: One pass in source order. Moving a marker or a declaration can change generated code. No reruns.

options.name: Rust's tokens only
options.detail: A marker reads only the text written on its own item. Reflecting other types while expanding is an error.
options.technical: Removes reflect from expansions; target is the written item. #run values and checked code keep full reflection.

options.name: Zig's on demand
options.detail: Reading a type first finishes every marker on that type. A marker may add members only to its own target, and a loop is an error.
options.technical: Demand-driven expansion per type; a cycle is an error. Forbids impl blocks for any type but the target from inside an expansion.

comparisons.note: A derive or attribute macro sees only the tokens of its item.
@typeInfo analyzes a type on demand; a dependency loop is a compile error.
Stacked decorators apply bottom to top, each to the previous result.

recommendation.why: A makes stacked markers give the same result in any order. Markers can build on each other's output. A disagreement is a named error, never a silent difference.
gains: Stacked markers give the same code in any order.
A marker can build on another marker's members.
No existing result changes.

losses.loss: Reruns cost build time where a part is both read and added to.
losses.mitigation: Only those readers rerun; existing programs need none, and jet inspect shows the chain.

losses.loss: Two markers that each add only when the other's member is absent settle by a fixed order of their names.
losses.mitigation: Written order never matters, the build stays repeatable, and jet inspect shows both markers and the part.

whyNot.reason: B hides every marker's additions from every other marker.
C makes generated code depend on the order markers are written.
D removes reflection from expansions, so a marker cannot read a field's type.
E forbids a marker from adding to any type but its target.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some reruns while building, in return for markers whose order does not matter.

decisions.title: How a build names a field's type when it declares a struct with meta.add_struct
decisions.situation: A build can declare a new struct while it runs, by calling meta.add_struct with a list of fields. Each field record has a name and a type. Today the type is text, such as "I64", which the build host turns into source for the new struct. That text check only blocks a few characters, so the type "I64, extra: String" quietly adds a second field. The ratified rule also passes a reflected field's type, which reflection gives as a TypeId, not text, so the rule contradicts itself. This vote decides what a field's type is: a TypeId, text, or either. We recommend a TypeId, written in the build file when it can see the type, and looked up by text when it can't.
decisions.gist: When a build declares a struct with meta.add_struct, is each field's type a TypeId, a text spelling, or either?
decisions.lesson: A type passed as a value keeps its identity and is checked where it is written. A type passed as text is checked only when the build runs, and it is read again in the new struct's module, where its name can mean a different type.
decisions.explainer:
A TypeId is the compiler's name for one checked type. Reflection gives one for every field, as field.type. Programs cannot make a TypeId from text; under A they can only ask the compiler for one it already issued.

A text spelling is a String such as "I64" or "[Point]". The build host pastes it into source for the new struct when the build runs.

The build function and the app can live in separate files. A build file sees only the types it declares or imports. A type only the app declares is invisible to it, unless both files import the module that declares it.

A type written as a value means a type name where a value is expected, such as String in CompilerField{name: "label", type: String}. Any other spelling goes in braces, as in TypeId{[String]}. D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A ratifies both spellings for a Type value, Rock and Type{Box<Int>}. Neither is built yet.

A lookup by text, meta.find_type("Point"), asks the compiler for the TypeId of one type the app declares. It returns that identity or None, and the text itself never becomes source.
decisions.story: A build reads the fields of a struct called Source, drops one, and renames another. It adds two hand-written fields, label of type String and tags of type [String]. It also adds a field at of type Point, which only the app declares, so the build file can't name it. It then declares a new struct, Shape, from that list with meta.add_struct. Every option builds the same Shape; they differ in how the hand-written, app-only and reflected types are written.
decisions.inWild: Zig builds a struct type at compile time with @Type, and each field's type is a type value, never a string. That works inside one compilation. Across the build-to-app split, Zig's build.zig passes values to the app by generating Zig source text (std.Build.Step.Options), so Zig also falls back to text there. C++26 reflection (P2996) declares a struct with define_aggregate, and each member's type is a reflection value such as ^^int. Rust procedural macros emit types as token streams, which the compiler checks only after expansion, like a text spelling. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
The ratified row reads: meta.add_struct(name, fields, scope: module) declares the struct name of fields, a list of CompilerField{name:, type:} records. Their names and types may be computed, as in a reflected field's f.type. The build host refuses a type that is not one type's spelling.

D-META-REFLECT2 A (2026-09-21) says FieldInfo's type is a TypeId, an opaque compiler-issued identity that user code cannot make from casts or strings. D-REFLECT-FIELDTYPE1 A named that field type. So the row's own example passes a TypeId into a String slot, which the checker refuses (E0108).

On dev today the two CompilerField rows disagree. The core.compiler index field row says TypeId (commit G6Decl-72), the literal row says String, and a build that writes a literal crashed the IR. The staged fix G6Meta-addstruct1 makes both rows String. It fills the index with the printed type name and has reflected sites write field.type.name. Every other type in that index stays a TypeId.

The host's check is a block-list of characters (jet_driver_meta_type_text_plain in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/BuildAdapter.jet), not a type parser. Probe inject: the type "I64, extra: String" passed it. The generated struct got a second field, extra, and the app printed a value stored there. So the row's promise that the host refuses non-type text fails today.

A TypeId's name is the type as its declaring module wrote it (type_name in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Types/Types.jet). The checker resolves such a name relative to the module that reads it. The new struct lives in a different module, which reads the name again in its own scope. A printed name can then fail to resolve there, or name a different type with the same short name.

Some printed forms are display-only and do not parse at all, such as a quantity's Quantity<dimension, base; identity>. Probe roundtrip: "Point", "Int?", "[String:Int]" and "fn(Int) -> Int" worked as text. The spellings "geo.Point" and "[geo.Point]" for a dependency's type crashed the compiler.

Text can name types a build file cannot see. Probe split: a separate build.jet named the app-only type "Point" and the app printed 9. In that build file, the bare name Point is E0107. Probe forward: a second add_struct named the struct an earlier call made, "Inner", and also "[Inner]" and "Inner?"; the app printed 7.

Type written as a value is not built for any type. Probe typevalue: Type itself is E0119, and Point passed as an argument is E0636. [Point] parses as a list literal, and Int? parses as Int followed by the ? operator. Type arguments, as in name_of<[Point]>(), accept every spelling today.

Migration under A is mechanical. jet fix writes a String literal as a bare name or a braced spelling when the text, read from the build file, names the same type the host finds in the app. Every other literal, and every computed text, becomes meta.find_type(text) with a failure for None.

In this repository the edit is small. Four test files write literal types, all I64 or I32, and jet fix rewrites them. The bad_type case computes its text and moves to find_type, which returns None for it. The typed and raw_denied cases already pass field.type. No example or Core file builds a CompilerField.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S QUESTION (2026-11-12)

The owner called the TypeId direction solid and asked for its downsides to be designed away. The earlier A carried five costs. Four are gone, and one remains with a mitigation.

Computed type text, a type only the app declares, and a list of a struct made earlier in the build all failed under the earlier A. They now go through one lookup, meta.find_type(text). It returns a TypeId the compiler issued, or None. The text never reaches the new struct's source; only the identity it found does.

Function types needed a one-line alias, and compound spellings relied on name lookup to tell a type from a list literal. Braces remove both. TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int} and TypeId{[String]} reuse the ratified Type{Box<Int>} form. A type inside braces parses like a type argument, and probe typepos shows type arguments accept every spelling today. In a bare value position, [Point] reads as a list and Int? as the ? operator (probe typevalue).

The checker work for bare names and braces was listed as a loss. It is shared build work, and difficulty never ranks an option. The split between Type and TypeId predates this ballot. Both values now take the same two spellings, and the expected type picks one, so nothing new is learned.

ATTACKING THE LOOKUP

Forging. D-META-REFLECT2 A says user code can't make a TypeId from casts or strings, so that no program forges an identity. find_type returns only the identity of a type the compiler already declared, or None, so it forges nothing. A amends that sentence to allow this one lookup.

Injection. find_type reads exactly one type spelling. The text "I64, extra: String", which adds a field today (probe inject), returns None.

Scope. Names resolve as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build has already made, so "[Inner]" works after Inner is made. A short name that two modules declare finds nothing, and the build writes the module path, as in shapes.Point. The host still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see.

Timing. The build already reads the app's declared types through b.program.packages() (spec.md, fn build), so a lookup needs nothing the build lacks. find_type, the braced form and add_struct's returned TypeId are proposed and UNCHECKED.

WHAT REMAINS

A type named by text is checked only when the build runs. That cost can't be removed, because the text exists only then, as with a config file. It is minimized: find_type returns None, so the build must handle a miss, and written and reflected types never take this path.

options.name: A TypeId, written in the build file or looked up by text
options.gist: CompilerField.type is a TypeId. Reflected types pass as is, written types are checked where written, and other types are looked up by text.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type becomes a TypeId. A reflected field's type passes as is. So does a field list from the core.compiler index, whose types are already TypeIds on dev.

A type the build file can see is written there, and checked there. A plain name such as String or geo.Point is written bare where a TypeId is expected. Any other spelling uses braces: TypeId{[String]}, TypeId{Int?} or TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int}. These are the two spellings D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A already ratified for a Type value.

A type the build file can't name is looked up by text. meta.find_type("Point") returns the TypeId of that one type, or None. It reads exactly one type spelling and resolves names as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build already made. So it covers a type only the app declares, "[Inner]" after an earlier add_struct, and type names read from a config file.

The text is never pasted into source. meta.add_struct returns the new struct's TypeId, so a later call can use it directly. The host writes each field from its TypeId. It still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see. A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, and a String where a TypeId is expected is E0108.

options.name: A text spelling, as today
options.gist: CompilerField.type stays a String the build host reads. Reflected sites write field.type.name.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type stays a String. A hand-written type is its spelling in quotes, and a reflected field passes field.type.name. Any type the app can see can be named, including a type only the app declares and a struct an earlier call made. A reaches the same types through its lookup, but keeps the identity it finds.

B must replace the host's block-list with a parser that accepts exactly one type, to close the hole probe inject found. That repair is part of this option. Errors still come only when the build runs.

A reflected type loses its identity on the way. Its printed name is read again in the new module, where it can fail to resolve or name a different type. The index's CompilerField.type is then the only String type in an index of TypeIds.

options.name: Either a TypeId or a text spelling
options.gist: CompilerField.type accepts a TypeId or a String. Reflected sites pass field.type; hand-written types stay quoted.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type accepts either, so the field needs a union type, TypeId | String. A reflected field passes field.type, a TypeId. A hand-written type is a quoted spelling, which the host reads when the build runs.

Two ways to name the same type stay in one field, against I8. The text path keeps every cost of B, including the parser repair.

recommendation.why: A keeps every type's identity from reflection to the new struct, and checks a written type where it is written. Text is only ever looked up, never pasted into source, so the hole that added a field cannot occur. Every type in the core.compiler index stays a TypeId.
gains: Reflected and index field lists pass through unchanged
A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, in the editor too
Config text, app-only types and structs made earlier still work, by lookup
No text a build supplies is pasted into source

losses.loss: A type named by text, from a config file or known only to the app, is checked only when the build runs.
losses.mitigation: find_type returns None for a miss, so the build must handle it, and its text can never add a field. Written and reflected types never take this path.

whyNot.reason: B pastes text that is read again in another module, where a reflected type's name can mean a different type. Every mistake shows up only when the build runs.
C keeps two ways to name one type in one field, against I8, and its text path keeps every cost of B.

recommendation.tradeoff: One cost remains. A type named by text is checked when the build runs, and the build must handle a miss. Every other type keeps its identity and is checked where it is written.

decisions.title: Non-prefix uses of `@` and the reserved machine form
decisions.gist: Should references and command filenames keep `@`, and should the future infix machine form stay reserved?
decisions.lesson: Package references use `target@provider#version`; host selectors use `host@root`. Optional command files are `@run.jet`, `@build.jet`, `@dev.jet`, and `@test.jet`. These marks do not request compile-time evaluation. D-ONCE-AT1 also reserves a future infix location form, not an implemented feature. Prefix links are settled; this ballot only decides the other uses.
decisions.story: Noor sees a provider separator in a package reference, a marked command filename, and a link in source code. She needs their contexts explained, not a claim that they do the same job.
decisions.inWild:
npm install @scope/pkg@1.2.0
// npm uses `@` for scopes and versions in package specifiers. Source: docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/package-spec.

options.name: Keep them all
options.detail: Keep package references, host selectors, and optional command home files unchanged. Preserve only D-ONCE-AT1's infix location reservation; this does not approve a machine feature or its final grammar. Prefix `@` in expressions means a link.
options.technical: D-JPK-REF1, D-JPK-OSHOST1, and card #1866 remain unchanged. A future location feature still needs its own ballot. No compile-time prefix form survives.

options.name: Keep references; drop the machine reservation
options.detail: Non-code uses stay; the infix code reservation is released.
options.technical: It releases D-ONCE-AT1's location reservation.

options.name: Keep only links on `@`
options.detail: Use `target from provider#version` for package references and `host from root` for host selectors. Quote them as single CLI arguments. Rename all four command homes to `command.cmd.jet` and release the infix location reservation. Prefix links stay unchanged.
options.technical: Replace the D-JPK-REF1 and D-JPK-OSHOST1 separators and card #1866's filename set in one cutover, including parsers and scaffolding. Whitespace-delimited `from` separates the reference components; paths containing whitespace need the existing quoted-string or CLI argument handling. Remove D-ONCE-AT1's future location reservation.
options.code:
exact = "acme/tool from github#v1.2.0"
"host from root"
run.cmd.jet  build.cmd.jet  dev.cmd.jet  test.cmd.jet
leader :: @p

comparisons.note: `@scope/pkg@version`. https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/package-spec
Flake references use `:` and `#`. https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-flake

recommendation.why: Keeping the established references and filenames avoids unrelated migration. Retaining a reservation approves no new feature; any future infix syntax still needs review.

whyNot.reason: B simplifies the reservation, but gives up the established location spelling before a concrete feature can be judged.
C churns package references and scaffolding for a small consistency gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Avoid unrelated churn while accepting context-dependent meanings and a still-unbuilt reservation.

decisions.title: Where build facts such as the target OS live
decisions.gist: Where should build facts such as the target OS, profile, and settings live?
decisions.lesson: `@build` supplies the target OS, profile, package identity, declared settings, and build stamps. These reads need no error handler; some fields can be absent. This ballot moves only their home. A bare `build` name could be hidden by Jet's existing `fn build` entry. Command filenames belong to D-AT-INFIX1.
decisions.story: Kai reads the target OS in five places and a typed `api_base` setting in two. He wants one short, obvious home for these facts.

options.name: `compiler.build.*`
options.detail: `compiler.build` holds `os`, `profile`, `package`, `settings`, and `stamp`. Settings remain typed values declared by the package. Valid reads need no error handler, but absent stamp data stays optional. Undeclared settings remain compile errors, not missing runtime fields.
options.technical: Move package name/version, OS, profile, declared settings, and stamp git/dirty/toolchain/at paths without changing their values or types. D-CONF-MODULE1 owns settings; the registered COMPILER_BUILD_FACT paths own the complete family. Optional data is not a query failure. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Bare `build.*`
options.detail: Open `core.compiler.build` as the prelude name `build`. User declarations win, as for other prelude aliases. In a file declaring `fn build`, use an explicit module alias for fact reads; the entry function and home filename stay unchanged.
options.technical: Extend the existing prelude alias machinery to this compiler-owned record. Emit the normal shadowing lint when a declaration wins; never reserve or rename the build entry.

options.name: Inside the package view
options.detail: Add a `build` field to the existing package view. It holds A's complete build record, including settings and stamps.
options.technical: Extend the existing CompilerPackage view, not PackageInfo, with the build record. Acquiring that view still returns CompilerPackageError, even when only a total build fact is wanted.

comparisons.note: `cfg!` and `env!` for target and package facts. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
`@import("builtin")` exposes target facts. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Compile-Variables

recommendation.why: Build facts sit beside other compiler facts without inheriting package-query failures. Qualifying the name also avoids the existing `fn build` collision.

whyNot.reason: B saves nine characters but needs another alias where `fn build` hides it.
C makes total facts fallible and mixes target facts into package facts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Eight extra characters over `@build` buy a clear namespace.

decisions.title: One sigil for compiler facts and metadata
decisions.gist: Which sigil should mark every fact the compiler knows, such as build, type, and package facts?
decisions.lesson: Jet reads compiler facts: the target OS, a type's fields, the package version. `prep` already marks code that runs before the program. `@` now means a link. The owner wants facts marked by one sigil, not a plain word. This ballot picks only the glyph; other ballots pick the paths. Family map: `prep` marks code that runs before the program (ratified). A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Mo reads `if os == .Linux` in a game and cannot tell whether `os` is a variable or a build fact. A sigil tells him the compiler supplied it.
decisions.inWild:
#if os(Linux)
print(#file, #line)
#endif

options.detail: `$` marks every compiler fact. Config files keep `$NAME` for environment variables (D-ONCE-DOLLAR1); both mean 'supplied by the build, not the program'. Markers keep `#`, links keep `@`.
options.technical: Amends D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 to allow `$` in code for compiler facts. The retired `$` compile-time mark (E0003) is replaced by this meaning.

options.name: Lowercase `#`
options.detail: Lowercase `#name` is a fact; PascalCase `#Name` stays a marker. Amends D-ONCE-HASH1.
Prefix `%` marks facts; infix `%` stays remainder.

comparisons.note: `#if`, `#file`: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/
`@` builtins: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Builtin-Functions
`#` directives and `ODIN_OS`: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#directives
`$` marks a reassignable local (26:32, Roc talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12yVcgQHAK0). https://www.roc-lang.org/functional.
`#` marks compile-time names in macros (50:46, Skip/Hack talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skiplang/skip/master/docs/blog/2018-07-24-macros.md.

recommendation.why: `$` is free in Jet code, easy to type, and already means 'supplied by the build' in config files, so one idea covers both.

whyNot.reason: B stacks a fourth meaning onto `#` and relies on letter case.
C collides visually with the remainder operator and has no precedent.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pasting Jet into shells needs single quotes in exchange for a clean dedicated sigil.

decisions.title: Spelling a compile-time number parameter
decisions.gist: How should a type declare a compile-time number parameter, such as a buffer size?
decisions.lesson: A number parameter lets one type describe different sizes: `Packet<64>` or `Packet<32>`. D-CONSTGEN1 ratified `<@N: Int>`, but it is not implemented here. #3505 chooses plain `N` uses. The proposed replacement marks the declaration with `prep`. `[U8#N]` means a fixed array of N bytes. This ballot also covers generic functions.
decisions.story: Mia writes a firmware `Packet<64>` type. Reading the declaration, she must tell a number parameter from a type parameter at a glance.

options.name: `<prep N: Int>`
options.detail: Only the declaration carries `prep`; uses write plain `N`. Both types and functions may take Int parameters. Closed expressions remain parenthesized at use sites; bound number arguments remain bare, as D-CONSTGEN1 requires.
options.technical:
Preserve D-CONSTGEN1's value identity, defaults, inference, Int restriction, and rejection of runtime arguments. #3505 owns plain-name uses. In declaration parameter lists only, recognize `prep` followed by a name and colon. Existing `<prep>` and `<prep: Trait>` still mean type parameters; call arguments keep their angle grammar.

This extends the current parser, which accepts only names and trait bounds. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: `<N: Int>`
options.detail: The compiler decides from `Int` being a type, not a trait, that `N` is a number.
options.technical: It relies on sema's type-versus-trait lookup to classify the parameter.

comparisons.note: `comptime n: usize`. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Compile-Time-Parameters
`const N: usize`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics

recommendation.why: `prep` tells a reader this parameter is a number known before running, with the same word used everywhere else.

whyNot.reason: B reads like a trait bound, which the owner already rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four letters buy an unmistakable number parameter.

decisions.title: Spelling a fence that expands one line into several
decisions.gist: How should a fence that expands one line into several be spelled?
decisions.lesson: A fence repeats the entire containing statement once per entry. `@[ t1..t3 ]@ :: task work()` makes three bindings; `print(@[ "a", "b" ]@)` prints twice. Multiple fences advance together and must have equal lengths. Literal range `0..3` expands to four entries; parentheses preserve one range. The proposed delimiters restore D-EACH1's shape, but `:>` currently has a retired-arrow diagnostic meaning.
decisions.story: Tom starts eight transfer tasks and joins each one. He wants one line for the spawns and one for the joins, not sixteen near-identical lines.

decisions.title: How code reads facts about a type, function, or value
decisions.gist: Should compiler facts be read as sigil members on the thing, or through a query that returns a record?
decisions.lesson: Code reads facts such as a type's fields or a function's effects. Examples use `$`, standing for whatever glyph D-COMPILER-NS1 picks. This ballot picks only the path shape. Build and package facts are decided in D-BUILD-FACT3. Family map: `prep` marks code that runs before the program (ratified). A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Ada writes a serializer that loops over a type's fields. She wants to read the fields in the fewest steps, and see at a glance that they come from the compiler.
decisions.inWild: const fields = @typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields;

options.name: Sigil members on the subject
options.detail: Every fact is a `$` member of the thing it describes. Subjectless facts use sigil roots (`$phase`, `$program`). `T.reflect()` and `@TYPE(T)` are removed.
options.code:
prep loop field in T.$fields {
    print(field.$name)
}
range :: Severity.$range
effects :: send_report.$effects
origin :: value.$origin
phase :: $phase

options.name: Sigil query returns a record
options.detail: Sigil queries return records; facts are ordinary fields.

options.name: `.reflect()` method
options.detail: One reserved method returns the record.

comparisons.note: Zig returns one record from a builtin. See https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#typeInfo.

Skip macros read facts and splice names with a sigil: `#thisClassName`, `this.#field` (Skip/Hack talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skiplang/skip/master/docs/blog/2018-07-24-macros.md.

recommendation.why: Members keep the sigil exactly where a compiler fact is read, with the fewest steps and no handler for known subjects.

whyNot.reason: B turns every fact read into a call, a handler, and a field.
C drops the sigil the owner asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few sigil roots join member reads to keep every fact short and marked.

decisions.title: Choosing a branch or repeating declarations before the program runs
decisions.gist: How should code pick a branch or repeat declarations before the program runs?
decisions.lesson: `@if` selects a branch while building. The selected branch gets full checks; discarded branches still get name checks. `@loop` repeats statements or declarations, including methods and tests. D-PREP-SURFACE2 introduced only `prep { }`, not `prep if` or `prep loop`. This ballot extends that word without changing branch checking.
decisions.story: Lena's app calls different platform APIs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Names must resolve in every branch, but only the chosen branch needs full platform and type checks.

options.name: `prep if` and `prep loop`
options.detail: `prep if` evaluates its condition while building and keeps only the chosen arm. The other arms get name checks only, as `@if` does today. `prep loop` repeats statements, impl items, marker-body items, or tests over a closed list known while building.
options.technical: It respells S57's `@if`/`@loop` and D-STRUCT-ONCE1's declaration templates without changing their meaning. It amends D-PREP-SURFACE2's line that prep adds no condition or loop form. That line still holds inside `prep { }` blocks, where ordinary `if` and `loop` run while building. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Plain `if` and `loop` fold when known
options.detail: A known condition keeps only the taken arm, with name-only checks on discarded arms. Otherwise ordinary runtime checking applies to every arm. A top-level `loop` over a known list repeats declarations; nested template loops follow the same rule.
options.technical: The checking rule changes with the condition's phase. D-STRUCT-ONCE1 reversed an earlier same-day ruling that erased `@if` in favor of plain `if`.

comparisons.note: Known conditions prune branches; `inline for` unrolls. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#inline-for
`if constexpr` discards the untaken branch in templates. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/if

recommendation.why: The word makes branch selection visible. Readers can tell which branches receive full checks and which receive only name checks.

whyNot.reason: B hides which arms are checked, which the owner already rejected once.

recommendation.tradeoff: One extra word buys a visible build-time choice.

decisions.title: Marking a function that runs while building
decisions.gist: How should a function that runs while building, such as a literal hook, be marked?
decisions.lesson: A literal hook constructs a value from a written number: for example, `1` becomes a Rational with denominator one. D-FOUND-LITERAL1 uses `@fn from_literal` inside a `Literal.Int` or `Literal.Float` implementation. The hook runs while building and cannot perform effects such as I/O. This ballot changes its mark, not its purity rules.
decisions.story: Ana writes a money type so `12` can mean twelve cents. She wants the hook to say plainly that it runs while building.

options.name: `prep fn`
options.detail: `prep fn` replaces every currently legal `@fn` method declaration. The compiler keeps checking that literal hooks have no effects such as I/O.
options.technical: Respell D-FOUND-LITERAL1 without widening the allowed declaration sites. Cover both Literal.Int and Literal.Float hooks, including decimal text input. Preserve the existing is_comptime flag and purity checks; ordinary runtime functions do not become compile-time functions merely because they are pure. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Plain `fn`
options.detail: The Literal.Int or Literal.Float implementation identifies `from_literal` as a compile-time hook without an extra mark. Purity checks remain mandatory.
options.technical: Infer the existing compile-time requirement from the literal capability and remove its explicit declaration mark. Other methods retain ordinary function behavior; this alternative does not infer arbitrary compile-time functions from purity.

comparisons.note: `consteval` functions. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/consteval

recommendation.why: The mark tells a reader when the body runs, using the word Jet uses everywhere else for build time.

whyNot.reason: B hides when the body runs behind a site rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: One word buys a visible build-time function.
