decisions.title: #run, #if and #loop replace the comptime word, with every ratified meaning kept
decisions.situation: Your 2026-11-09 review asks that # mark what is for the compiler and that the comptime word go. This ballot changes spelling only. A respells D-COMPTIME-WORD1's word and the forms ratified in D-PREP-SURFACE2, D-PREP-LOCAL1, D-PREP-BRANCH1, D-PREP-FN1, D-COMPTIME-USE1 and D-CONSTGEN2. It reverses the choice in D-PREP-BRANCH1 and D-PREP-FN1 of a word over their # option. It respells the regions of D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1=A without changing their scope. D-META-PHASE1, D-META-LADDER1, D-META-HASH1 and D-BUILD-TIER1 stay as ratified.
decisions.gist: Should #run, #if and #loop replace the comptime word in every form, keeping what each form does?
decisions.lesson: Jet can do work while it compiles: build a table, choose code for one system, or repeat declarations for several types. Today the word comptime asks for that, while # already marks markers, site values and pastes. This vote decides whether those requests use # too.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A request asks the compiler to do something while building. A value region computes one value and gives it back. A standing region is a block whose results stay visible after it, as D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 ratified.

A declaration modifier changes one declaration, such as the hook that turns a number literal into a Rational. A number parameter is a whole number fixed for each generic copy, such as the 4 in Ring<4>.
decisions.story: Ada already writes #Test, #line and the ratified #phase. When she wants a table built while compiling, she must learn a separate word, comptime, with braces around a single call. She would like one mark for everything the compiler does for her.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how the existing requests are spelled. Each form keeps the meaning its ratified decision gives it: what runs while building, the budget, the effects allowed, and which names it sees. The staging and Call questions belong to D-META-HASH2 and are not decided here.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe t01 uses a value, a statement region, two branches, a loop of declarations and a literal hook, and prints six lines. Examples/Metaprogramming/Comptime/ComptimeUse shows the build-only import. The tested new spellings are refused: #run reports E0733 as an unknown tag, and #if and #loop report E0003.

Some ratified forms are not built in any spelling yet. A multi-statement value region is E0391 today (t02). A parenthesized region is also E0391 (ms/s03); the attempted function expression gets E0003 and E0391 (ms/s02). These are building gaps, so they count for no option. The ballot specifies every form as ratified, not as the seed limits it.

The three kinds of #run under A. Where #run stands decides its kind, as the ratified comptime forms specify. First, a declaration modifier: #run directly before a declaration's name, as in the literal hook, with D-PREP-FN1's legal sites and purity checks. #run use is D-COMPTIME-USE1's build-only import, in both its forms.

Second, a standing region: #run { } on its own line in a file, module or function body. It follows D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 to the letter. Its direct immutable results become bindings of the enclosing scope, mutable scratch and nested names stay inside, and file and module helpers are build-only, with E0944 for any escape.

Third, a value region: #run in a value position, meaning the right of a binding, an argument, a list element or an operand. #run { } there has its own scope and gives back its last expression, as D-PREP-SURFACE2 ratified, including blocks with several statements.

The unbraced operand rule. Without braces, #run takes exactly one operand: a name, a literal, a parenthesized expression, or a call, member, index or constructor chain on one. So TABLE: #run build_squares(5) is legal. Anything larger needs braces or parentheses: #run a + b is an error whose fix offers #run { a + b } or (#run a) + b.

How the rule treats each case. f(#run g(1), x) computes only g(1). Postfix ! inside the operand makes a failure a build error, under the existing required-evaluation failure contract. A fallback is binary, so #run { load() ?? DEFAULT } and (#run load()) ?? x are the two spellings, and each says what it means.

Functions and closures. D-COMPTIME-WORD1 says functions are storable, and closures are storable when their captures are. A value region keeps that rule. A lambda expression needs a braced value region. A reference to a standing file/module region's build-only helper still cannot escape, under BLOCK1 and E0944.

Why a misread boundary cannot change a result silently. A value region cannot see runtime locals: probe ms/s01 shows comptime { build(3) + y }, with y a runtime local, reported as E0107. The operand rule makes the boundary visible anyway. A function that branches on #phase still does what D-META-PHASE1 says for each copy.

#if and #loop. #if takes every form comptime if takes: a condition with a block, else, else #if, and the matching table #if x == { arms }. It keeps D-PREP-BRANCH1's checks: the arm not taken gets name checks only. Probe ms/s07 shows an unknown name there reported as E0107, and ms/s05 shows a type error there accepted.

#loop takes the pattern, in and closed list that comptime loop takes, in the same places. D-META-PHASE1 is unchanged: a #phase read reached from an #if condition is refused with a fix to a plain if, which folds per copy and checks every arm.

Number parameters. <N: Int> drops the word. Under D-CONSTGEN2's restriction, a parameter whose right side resolves to the core Int, through aliases and by declaration identity, is a number parameter. A trait on the right, as in <T: Comparable>, is a bound. Any other type is an error that says only Int may be a number parameter.

Defaults, inference, identity and the refusal of runtime arguments stay as D-CONSTGEN2 says. A user type named Int is not the core Int, so it cannot make a number parameter by accident. Hover in the editor names the parameter's kind.

The # family. As D-META-HASH1 ratified: # then a lower-case word is a request or a site value, such as #run, #if, #loop, #line or #phase. # then { is a paste. # then a capital letter is a marker, such as #Test. Inside a fixed-size type such as [Int#N], # keeps its size meaning.

What does not change. Automatic early evaluation of immutable values under D-COMPTIME-WORD1 stays; #run requires early evaluation, as comptime does. D-META-LADDER1's #code, Code insertion and Compiler effects stay, and so does D-META-HASH1's hygiene. D-BUILD-TIER1's defaults stay. D-META-PHASE1 keeps #phase, its cases, its crossing checks and the local-try fallback.

Retiring the word. comptime stops being a keyword and becomes an ordinary name, as prep did. Old code that writes comptime gets one registered retirement error with a checked fix. The fix works on parsed nodes, keeps comments and source locations, and renames by declaration identity, never by text.

What the fix does, form by form. A value comptime { e } becomes #run e only when e is a single operand with no comment inside; otherwise it becomes #run { e }. A standing comptime { } becomes #run { }. comptime if, comptime loop and comptime use become #if, #loop and #run use. comptime before a declaration becomes #run. <comptime N: Int> becomes <N: Int>.

Migration changes spelling, not binding identity. BLOCK1 already requires a checked scope migration preserving every old reference. The spelling fix must compose with that migration; neither step may silently rebind a name.

A parsed migration inventory, including examples, tests, diagnostics and prose, is required in the cutover. No regex total proves the number of safe edits. No jet fix for this respelling exists yet; it is part of building A.

Beginner path. The first build-time value is TABLE: #run make_table(). The first system choice is #if build.target.os == { … }. Errors keep their codes and print the new spelling.

Expert path. Standing regions, multi-statement value regions and number parameters keep every ratified rule; only the word changes. Templates through #loop and D-META-LADDER1's Code keep their positions.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A reader must know where an unbraced #run ends; the operand rule limits it to one call or name, and anything larger needs braces. A number parameter has no word of its own; the core Int on its right marks it, and hover names it. Both are real reading costs; no reading-cost comparison was measured.

Respelling touches many sites and much prose. The checked fix handles code, and Docs change in the same pass. #run, #if and #loop are three words where comptime was one; all three share the # mark, and #if and #loop match the plain if and loop the reader already knows.

Other options. B keeps the ratified word and its braces. C keeps the word but lets a plain if select arms when its condition is known while building, which changes checking, not only spelling. D marks the one word as #comptime. E uses A's short requests but always braces values and marks number parameters as <#run N: Int>.

Option C in full. A plain if whose condition is known while building selects its arm, like comptime if today. The arm not taken gets name checks only, and its effects leave the effect row. Today a plain if on a constant checks the types of both arms: probe ms/s06 reports a type error in the arm not taken.

So under C, every existing plain if on a constant loses type checks on its other arm. Whether an arm is type-checked then depends on how its condition is computed. C must also exempt #phase. A condition that reads #phase stays D-META-PHASE1's fold, checking every arm per copy, because a phase-dependent selection of source arms is what that decision forbids.

Boundary cases. Prefix operators, including a negative number or logical not, require braces or a parenthesized operand. Calls and their nested arguments belong to the operand. Binary operators outside that operand require grouping around #run when meant to run later. Value-region scope never becomes standing-region scope just because its contents span several lines.

options.name: #run, #if and #loop; plain number parameters
options.detail: #run, #if and #loop replace the word in every form, and a number parameter is written <N: Int>. An unbraced #run takes one call or name; anything larger keeps its braces. Standing regions keep D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1's scope.
options.technical: Respells D-COMPTIME-WORD1, D-PREP-SURFACE2, D-PREP-LOCAL1, D-PREP-BRANCH1, D-PREP-FN1, D-COMPTIME-USE1, D-CONSTGEN2 and D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1's regions, and reverses BRANCH1's and FN1's word choice. Position decides the kind: declaration modifier, standing region or value region. An unbraced #run takes one postfix operand. A number parameter resolves to the core Int by declaration identity. Retire comptime with one registered error and a node-based fix.

options.name: Keep comptime as ratified
options.detail: Keep the one word comptime for every request, with braces around every value, as ratified. Readers learn one familiar phase word, and there is nothing to respell.
options.technical: No decision changes. Build the ratified forms the seed lacks, such as multi-statement value regions and D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1's standing scope. The word sits beside the # family of D-META-HASH1 for markers, site values and pastes.

options.name: Keep the word; a plain if on a known condition selects an arm
options.detail: Keep comptime, drop its value braces, and let a plain if select its arm when the condition is known while building. Branches on constants need no special word.
options.technical: Amends D-PREP-BRANCH1's checking, not only its spelling. A plain if on a build-known condition name-checks the arm not taken and drops its effects. A condition that reads #phase keeps D-META-PHASE1's fold and checks every arm. comptime loop, comptime use and number parameters keep the word.

options.name: #comptime in every form
options.detail: Keep one phase word, marked with #: #comptime before values, branches, loops, imports, declarations and number parameters. One word to learn, inside the # family.
options.technical: Respells the same decisions as A with one word. The value rule matches A's operand rule, so dropping value braces is a separate edit from adding the #.

options.name: Short requests, with braced values and marked number parameters
options.detail: A's short requests, but a value is always #run { }, and a number parameter is always <#run N: Int>. Every boundary and every parameter kind is marked.
options.technical: Respells the same decisions as A. No operand rule is needed, because every value region has braces. The number parameter keeps an explicit request instead of resolving the core Int.

comparisons.note: Community examples use #run and #if. This is precedent from public examples, not a tested claim about the current compiler.
The comptime word marks an early value or parameter. An if on a comptime-known condition analyzes only the arm taken.
comparisons.code:
const table = comptime makeTable();
fn Ring(comptime n: usize) type { ... }

comparisons.note: A const item or const block computes early; a const generic is written const N: usize.
comparisons.code:
const TABLE: [u32; 5] = make_table();
struct Ring<const N: usize> { slots: [i32; N] }

recommendation.why: A gives the compiler's requests the one # mark you asked for and keeps every ratified meaning. Its operand rule keeps each unbraced boundary to one call or name.
gains: Explicit evaluation, branch, loop and import requests start with #.
TABLE: #run make_table() is the shortest form of the most common request.
No ratified meaning, budget, effect rule or scope changes.

losses.loss: A reader must know where an unbraced #run ends.
losses.mitigation: The operand rule allows one call or name; anything larger needs braces or parentheses.

losses.loss: A number parameter has no word of its own.
losses.mitigation: Only the core Int can make one, an error names any other type, and hover names the kind.

losses.loss: Code and prose across the tree are respelled.
losses.mitigation: A node-based checked fix rewrites code; Docs change in the same pass.

whyNot.reason: B's single word is familiar and needs no respelling, but it keeps a word beside the # family you asked to unify.
C silently drops type checks on the other arm of every plain if on a constant.
D adds the # mark but keeps the long word in every form.
E marks every boundary, but braces a single call and repeats #run on number parameters that Int already marks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three short requests and a parameter marked by its type, in return for one # mark for the compiler.

decisions.title: The place values: #here is where code is written, and a #caller default is the place of each call
decisions.situation:
Jet can tell a function where it was called from, and code where it is written. A logger uses this to print the caller's line, and a check helper to name the failing claim's line.

Today both are spelled with a dollar sign, which a ratified ruling retires. That ruling names hash line and hash file, but nothing for the caller's place. This vote picks the new spelling and closes three traps found while probing.
decisions.gist: Should the two place values be spelled #here and #caller, with assert and panic using the same caller default?
decisions.lesson: A log line is more useful when it says which line wrote it. Jet fills that place in for you, so the logger does not need it passed by hand. This vote decides how that filled-in place is written, now that its old spelling is retired.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A source location is the file, line, column, function and module of a place in code. It displays as file:line:column.

A parameter default is the value a parameter takes when a call leaves it out, written at: SourceLocation{...}. A site value is a value the compiler fills in, marked with #.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a check helper for his tests. It prints the caller's line, but when a claim fails, the stop report names the helper's own assert line instead. He has no way to pass the place on.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How Jet spells the two place values that are $here and $caller today, now that the ratified one-mark ruling retires every $. It also settles their edge rules.

D-META-HASH1=A names #line, #file and #package as site values. It names no successor for the caller's place. #line and #file cover two of the five fields today's record carries.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). $here is a SourceLocation record: file, line, column, function and module, displayed as file:line:column. Probe s01 prints here 13:11 in run, module s01_today.

$caller is legal only as a parameter default, written at: SourceLocation{$caller}. Each call that leaves at out passes its own place. In s01 the direct log prints line 11, and the forwarding warn prints line 12.

The fill rule also holds for methods and pipes, where s04 prints lines 16 and 17. It holds for a generic function called from a lambda (s06, function run) and for a call through a function value (s12).

Anywhere else, $caller is E2427, CallerSiteMisplaced (s03). D-JAI-SITE1=A also allows it inside an #Expand macro, but sema has no such case, and #Expand left with macros under D-META-COMPILER1.

Three traps today. $here written as a default names the declaration, so both calls in s02 print line 2. At module level, $here has an empty function (s09). assert reports its own line, never the caller's (s08).

Census on dev, by git grep for $here and $caller. Jet code has 22 caller defaults: Core/Log 14, Core/Http 3, Examples 3 and tests 2. It has 4 $here reads: Examples 1 and tests 3.

The compiler side holds the parser's root list, sema's site checks in five files, the loader's SourceLocation alias, the syntax tables and E2427's texts. Four editor grammars and 16 Markdown lines in 5 files follow. The $here in Tools/perf is a shell variable.

Core/Log reads at.module to filter records, and the HTTP route check requires its at default to be $caller. Both need one record with a module, not separate line and file values.

The rule under A. #here is the SourceLocation of the place where it is written. #caller, written as a parameter default, is the place of each call that leaves that parameter out. Both are constants and never fail.

#line and #file become #here.line and #here.file. Neither is built: probe mh/h04 gets E0915 for #line, and s05 gets E0927 for #caller. No code uses them, so one record serves every place read. #package stays, since it names a package.

D-SCRIPT-SCRIPTDIR1=A, ratified after the one-mark ruling, still spells $here.file and $here.dir as package-relative Path values. Under A those members ride on #here unchanged, so the record gains dir and file becomes a Path, as ratified.

Edge rules under A. #caller anywhere but a default keeps E2427, respelled, with its fix: declare at: SourceLocation{#caller} and read at. Inside a lambda, the function field is the enclosing named function, as s06 shows today.

#here written as a parameter default becomes an error whose fix writes #caller. Today that default silently names the declaration (s02). No code on dev writes it, so the error refuses only the trap.

A wrapper forwards its caller's place by declaring the same default and passing at: at, as today. A call through a function value fills the call's place, as s12 shows. At module level the function field stays empty.

The one-mechanism check. assert, assert_eq and panic gain the same trailing at: SourceLocation{#caller}. A plain assert(ok) still reports its own line. The check helper above passes at: at, so the stop names its caller.

With that, every place Jet reports comes from one record and one fill rule. There is no second channel for stops, no hidden parameter, and no name whose meaning depends on where it is written.

Lowercase # names are compiler values and capitalised ones are markers, the split E0087 already enforces. So #here and #caller cannot be read as markers, and no user name can hide them.

Migration. jet fix rewrites $here to #here and $caller to #caller one to one: 26 Jet uses, then the compiler's tables, diagnostics, grammars and docs. The retired $ forms get that fix.

Relation to the open hash-spelling ballot, D-META-HASH2. Its option A writes the same #here and #caller. This ballot decides the place values and their edge rules alone, so that ballot can settle build separately.

Beginner path. Call log("starting") and the message names its line; nobody writes #caller to use a logger. Write spot: #here to ask where a line is.

Expert path. Declare at: SourceLocation{#caller} on a helper and pass at: at down to log or assert. Read at.module to filter by module, and build a SourceLocation by hand in tests.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A wrapper that forgets at: at names itself, not its caller. The printed place names the wrapper's own function, so the slip shows on the first run.

assert, assert_eq and panic gain a parameter. Existing calls do not change, since the default fills it; only the stop report reads it.

Other options. B makes here and caller plain Prelude values, like build. Its best case is no mark at all: a reader sees an ordinary name.

B's cost. A default resolves where its function is declared, and a module function named caller is legal; s11 prints 42 from one. So a plain caller can be hidden, silently changing every default in that file.

B also adds a plain value that is filled at each call, which no other value does. And it reverses D-META-HASH1's rule that compiler-filled site values carry #.

C folds both into one name: only #here, and a #here default means the call's place, as a Swift #line default does. Its best case is one name fewer.

C's cost. One token means two places by position, and a reader of at: SourceLocation{#here} must know the rule to know which. It also flips s02's meaning without a word changing.

D is Rust's track_caller. A #TrackCaller marker adds a hidden place parameter, SourceLocation.caller() reads it, and calls between marked functions forward it. Its best case is no at parameter and nothing to forget.

D's cost. The place travels in a parameter no signature shows, so function values and package interfaces must carry it. It adds a second way into a function next to defaults, which the one-mechanism rule refuses.

options.name: A #TrackCaller marker

losses.loss: #line and #file, ratified but unbuilt, become #here.line and #here.file.
losses.mitigation: No code uses them, and one record serves every place read.

whyNot.reason: B's plain caller can be hidden by a file's own name, silently changing its defaults.
C gives one token two meanings by position and flips today's default meaning.
D adds a hidden parameter, a second way into a function next to defaults.

recommendation.tradeoff: Forwarding stays written as at: at, in return for one visible mechanism.

decisions.title: One typed fact query in core.compiler, with inspect as its command-line view
decisions.situation: Jet records rules, facts about a checked program, and evidence from a run. Those records live for different lengths of time, so they should not be squeezed into one mutable table. The owner already approved one typed way to read them, but did not name its public entry point. The tested ledger import and inspect facts command are unavailable. Choose the API and command spelling, without reopening the three-store design. We recommend one query in core.compiler and a command that renders its exact results.
decisions.gist: Should a core.compiler query and inspect command share one typed fact result?
decisions.lesson: The rulebook, a checked program and a run receipt are different shelves. One librarian can answer questions about all three without mixing them up. An empty answer must mean there are no matching rows, not that the librarian never opened the shelf.
decisions.story: A tool counts the marker-rule facts in the schema. Every option answers that same question from the same schema snapshot. Experts can use the same query for a particular checked program or run receipt.
decisions.inWild: A command-line view and a library view can share one typed implementation. Jet's approved compiler-as-library design already requires this direction; a CLI subprocess should not be the only way a build-time Jet tool reads its own checked facts.
decisions.detail:
D-META-REG1=A approves shared schema machinery; D-LEDGER1=D retains schema, checked-program and run-evidence stores behind one typed query. This ballot names its public views. It adds no fourth store, mutable compiler heap or second evidence grader. Read-only queries need no Meta mutation effect.

Canonical API: core.compiler.query(source: FactSource, kind: FactKind, at: QueryTime?{None}, limit: Int?{None}) -> [Fact] MetadataError!. FactSource is Schema(SchemaSnapshot), Program(ProgramInfo) or Run(RunReceipt). Each supplies an explicit immutable authorized snapshot, not a forged name or ambient current program. Omitted time selects that snapshot's complete recorded view; omitted limit requests all authorized matching rows.

Fact is a tagged projection of SchemaFact, ProgramFact or RunFact, preserving canonical typed fields and source identity. FactKind comes from the executable schema. QueryTime selects the approved temporal view, not a schema column. Only claims have evidence grades. Rights retain their existing gate kind and provenance without grades.

Reuse D-META-REFLECT2=A's MetadataError: Unavailable, Unsupported, Stale, Invalid, Denied or Truncated. Empty success means checked emptiness. Missing stages, private facts and absent runs never become empty success. Explicit limits return Truncated instead of a partial list claiming completeness. Identity and order stay canonical across every consumer.

CLI: jet inspect facts --store=schema|program|run --kind=K [SOURCE] [--json]. Schema selects the running toolchain's schema; no SOURCE is allowed. Program requires a target source, checked into a snapshot through the normal pipeline. Run requires an explicit receipt path, validated by the ordinary receipt reader. No default latest run. A failed program check cannot publish recovered rows as valid facts. Both renderers include schema/snapshot identity and completeness.

Beginner path: inspect answers a concrete question. Expert path: ordinary Jet imports core.compiler and reads an authorized immutable source, including permitted #run code. A read snapshot confers no Compiler mutation authority; D-META-COMPILER1's powerful passed control handle keeps its distinct purpose. No new global ledger namespace or discovery mechanism.

B publicly exposes only the Core query; internal consumers still share it. C publicly exposes only the CLI; its internal typed query remains shared, but user Jet libraries must cross a subprocess/JSON boundary. That gives up the library-first ladder, not the three-store rule.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43: core.compiler.ledger import gets E1001. inspect facts with schema/kind/JSON arguments gets E2101. The inspected Core/Compiler/Compiler.jet contains small typed records and extension points, not this query. These targeted reads are not an API census. The ratified_p12 d_meta_reg1_contract path was absent here and not executed.

Adversarial verdict: A holds as multiple views of one query. First require explicit immutable sources instead of ambient mutable state. Then keep CLI rendering outside the typed reader. Lists cost memory; reuse immutable storage where legal and honor explicit limits. Missing/stale facts remain failures. No proposed query or performance advantage was exercised.

decisions.title: What a library marker body receives at each kind of site, and when it is checked
decisions.situation: A marker declared in a library may run a body that reads facts about the declaration it sits on, adds ordinary code, and may refuse the use. Today that body runs only on structs, top-level functions and text blocks. On an enum, variant, method, field, module or package the marker is accepted and the body silently never runs. The open choice is what the body receives at each kind of site, and when mistakes in it are caught. The recommendation gives nine kinds a typed record, checks the body once where the marker is declared, and makes listing any other kind an error.
decisions.gist: When one marker body can sit on several kinds of declaration, what does it receive, and when is it checked?
decisions.lesson: A marker body is compile-time code that runs once for each place the marker is written; that place is its target. Rust attribute macros receive raw text pieces and parse them. Swift macros receive a parsed declaration and test its kind. C# source generators also test kinds. Jet must say what a body receives and when mistakes are caught.
decisions.story: A library author writes a Route marker for a module and for each function inside it. Today the module use compiles and adds nothing, so a whole group of routes silently vanishes. Under the recommendation the body has one arm for modules and one for functions, and a typo in either arm fails where the marker is declared. A beginner who writes a marker for one kind of site never sees the match.

options.name: A typed record per site, checked once
options.detail:
Nine site kinds get records; a several-kind marker matches on the kind, and the body is checked where declared. Beginners write a one-kind marker and use target directly. Experts list several kinds and write one arm each; a missing arm is an error.

Gains: Mistakes show where the marker is declared. Nine site kinds run library bodies; the rest are errors.

Losses: Several-kind markers need one arm per kind. Nine site records, from type to package, must stay complete.

End effect. A wrong read, such as a field list on a function, fails once at the declaration and names the arm and the record. Nine kinds run the body, and a body that lists any other kind is an error at the declaration. Added items land beside the target, and members are added through an explicit impl block for the owner.
options.technical: A new static checker types a marker body once per declared site kind, at the declaration. With one kind, target is that kind's record. With several, target is a closed site value whose cases are generated from $sites; the type has no source name. Expansion still runs per use, through one site-generic collector. A body that lists a kind without a record is an error at the declaration. Added items join the target's module, and a module target receives them inside itself.

options.name: Same records, checked only at each use
options.detail:
Nine kinds run the body with their records, but reads are checked only when a use expands. Beginners see the same body as today. Experts test every kind themselves, because a wrong read fails only at a use that reaches it.

Gains: Smallest change from today's body rules. No match needed for several kinds.

Losses: A wrong read fails at a user's use site. Untested arms ship broken in libraries.

End effect. Nine kinds run the body, and listing any other kind is an error at the declaration, as in A. A read that does not exist for a kind, such as a field list on a module, fails while expanding that use, inside the user's build.
options.technical: The site-generic collector binds target to the record of each kind, plus a $site member naming the kind. The body stays untyped and is evaluated per use, as today (Derives.jet:1554-1572). A missing member is reported at the use, with the marker declaration named in the detail.

options.name: Bodies only on types, functions and blocks
options.detail:
Other kinds keep marker facts only; a body that lists them is an error at its declaration. Beginners get a clear error instead of silence. Experts act on modules, fields and variants from a hook or the build function instead.

Gains: No new records to build. The silent no-op becomes an error.

Losses: Modules and fields need a second mechanism. Library markers stay weaker than Jet's own.

End effect. Struct, enum, function and text block bodies run. A body that lists a module, field, variant, method or package site is an error naming the build function as the place to act.
options.technical: The collector covers struct, enum and function targets and text blocks. The declaration check rejects any other listed site when the marker has a body, with a fix naming fn build. No module record is added for bodies.

comparisons.note: A Swift peer macro receives any declaration node and must test which kind it got.

recommendation.why: Checking the body where it is declared catches mistakes before any user hits them, and nine site kinds finally run.
gains: Library mistakes surface for the library author.
Nine site kinds run bodies; the other nine are errors.

losses.loss: Several-kind markers write one arm per kind.
losses.mitigation: A missing arm is one error that names the kind and the record it would receive.

losses.loss: Nine site records, from type to package, must stay complete.
losses.mitigation: One producer builds them for every rung, so a gap shows everywhere at once.

whyNot.reason: Mistakes surface in someone else's build, at whichever use reaches the bad read.
Modules and fields would need a different mechanism for the same job, a cliff in the ladder.

recommendation.tradeoff: A trades one match per several-kind marker for errors at the declaration.

decisions.title: Read a marker as the typed record its declaration already describes
decisions.situation: A marker often reads another marker on the same item. A `Describe` marker reads the table name from `#store.Table("orders")`, for example. Today it gets a list of marker rows, with names as strings and arguments found by position. The written value, "orders", cannot be read at all while compiling. A typo or a reordered marker returns the wrong row without an error. The marker declaration already lists typed parameters, so Jet knows the record shape. The vote decides how code reads a marker and its arguments. We recommend a typed lookup that returns that record.
decisions.gist: How should code read a marker on an item, and the arguments written in it?
decisions.lesson: A marker declaration like `marker Table(name: String)` lists typed parameters, just like a struct. When other compile-time code looks for `Table` on an item, it can get back a `Table` record and read `.name`. Then a misspelled marker or field is an ordinary error, not a silent miss.
decisions.story: Ada writes a marker that reads `#Table`'s name. A user adds a second marker before `#Table`, and her code reads position 0, which is now the wrong marker. Every generated table name changes without a single error.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. This is the reflection question from the D-COMPTIME-MARKERS1 package ballot, asked alone. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A (`#target`, `#sites`); under another spelling only the marks change.

Today. MarkerInfo rows carry `name`, `args` (each with `name`, `ty` as text, `value`), `sites` and `repeatable` (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/Reflection.jet:311-336). `has_marker` takes a string (Sema/Calls/Reflection.jet:229-250). Examples/features/comptime/reflect.jet reads `info.methods[0].markers[0].name` and `info.has_marker("Debug")`.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. reflect_args.jet: `has_marker("Table")` and `markers[0].args[0].name` check clean and print "name true", the parameter's name, not the written "orders". reflect_c.jet: reading `markers[0].args[0].value` is E0956 "A derive template binding is not a known-time value", so today no compile-time code can read a written argument. The same file with `markers[0].name` prints "Table" for `#[Table("orders"), TableName]` and "TableName" for `#[TableName, Table("users")]`: the position read shifts silently.

Reads with the related ballots. D-MARKER-LADDER1 A lists every use of a marker as the same record, so `Route.#uses` returns `[Route.Use]` holding a `Route` and its site. D-MARKER-DIAG1 A refuses a bad argument by name. Both hold under every option here.

options.name: Typed lookup
options.detail:
Every marker declaration also declares a record with the same name and fields. `#target.marker(Table)` returns `Table?`: the record if `#Table` is written on the item, otherwise `None`. A repeatable marker returns `[Table]`.

On a type or function named in code, the same read is `Order.#marker(Table)`. A misspelled `Tabel` or `.nmae` is the ordinary unknown-name error.
options.technical: The marker rule's parameter list becomes the record type (MarkerInfo rows already carry name and type per argument, Reflection.jet:311-336). `#sites` and other `#` metadata are not record fields. `has_marker("X")` and string `markers[i].args[j]` reads retire; `jet fix` rewrites them to `marker(X) != None` and field reads. Uses D-META-HASH1 A spelling; under B it reads `target.$marker(Table)`.

options.name: Match the marker list
options.detail:
`#target.markers` stays a list. Each entry can be matched against a marker pattern like `Table(name)`, which binds the arguments with their declared types.

Finding one marker means a loop and a mutable value. A pattern for a marker that is never written on any item still compiles silently.
options.technical: Marker rules become pattern constructors over the MarkerInfo list. `has_marker` stays. Uses D-META-HASH1 A spelling.

options.name: Rows, with values readable
options.detail:
Code keeps asking `has_marker("Table")` and reading `markers[0].args[0]`. The one change is that `.value` becomes readable while compiling.

Nothing checks the string or the position, and values arrive as text.
options.technical: Today's MarkerInfo{name, args: [MarkerArgInfo{name, ty, value}], sites, repeatable} (Reflection.jet:311-336) and `has_marker` (Calls/Reflection.jet:229-250), plus making `args[i].value` a known-time value (today E0956).

String n = t.name();

comparisons.note: Derive macros receive raw attribute tokens and parse them by hand, for example with the darling crate. Source: https://docs.rs/darling

recommendation.why: A reuses what the declaration already says: `marker Table(name: String)` is the record. Lookups are one line, typos are errors, and the order of markers no longer matters.
gains: One typed read in place of strings and positions.
Works the same on `#target` and on any named type.

whyNot.reason: B types the arguments but makes every lookup a loop with a mutable value.
C makes values readable but keeps silent misses from typos and shifted positions.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` rewrites `has_marker` calls and position reads.

decisions.title: A marker body sees its target in full, plus every type the target names
decisions.situation: A route marker must check that each path hole, like `{id}`, matches a parameter whose type it can parse. Today a function marker body sees only parameter names, an empty module and only the effects written by hand. The build function sees the same function in full. So the route marker cannot check types at all. The vote decides how far one marker body may read. We recommend its whole target, plus every type the target names, through the same records the build function uses.
decisions.gist: How much of the program may one marker body read: its target, what the target names, or everything?
decisions.lesson: A marker body runs once for each item that carries the marker. It needs to know that item fully, including the types of its fields and parameters. It rarely needs the rest of the program. Limiting what a body reads keeps rebuilds small, because a body reruns only when something it read changes.
decisions.story: Mia writes `#web.Route("/orders/{id}")` on a handler whose `id` is an `OrderID`. The route marker cannot see the type, so it accepts the route, and the request fails at run time with a parse error.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. This is the reach question from the D-COMPTIME-MARKERS1 package ballot, asked alone. The whole-program listing stays with the root build function (D-METADEPTH2=B). Collecting every use of a marker is split out as D-MARKER-USES1. Whether reading needs a grant is already settled by D-META-OPTIN2=A: read-only facts are standard.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. ladder_app.jet: the beginner app, with a local `Route` standing in for `web`, runs and prints "order 1". ladder_type.jet: `target.params[0].ty` in a function marker body is E0956 "A derive template binding is not a known-time value", because params are plain names. program_today.jet: `$program.functions` in a body is the same E0956.

Reads with the related ballots. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A (`#target`) and D-MARKER-DIAG1 A (`reject(BadParam(...))`); the reach rule holds under any spelling. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A typed records are what the body follows. `p.type.implements("Parse")` uses today's TypeInfo `implements` list.

Today the body's FunctionInfo has an empty module, names-only params and declared effects only (Registration/UserTemplates.jet:148-169), while the build function's is full (JetEval CompilerServices.jet). Reads are recorded per body for incremental rechecks. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A and D-MARKER-DIAG1 A.

Because any body might read anything, any edit reruns all of them, and a body that reads items still being added sees an incomplete program.
options.technical: Opens D-META-REFLECT2=A `@PROGRAM()` to marker bodies, which today only the root build function may read (D-METADEPTH2=B). Needs a fixed order for bodies that add items.

decisions.title: `Route.#uses` lists every use of a marker, read in the marker's own package
decisions.situation: A web library wants one table of every `#web.Route` in the app, so it can serve them all. Today nothing can collect them. A marker body sees only its own item, and only the app's build function may list the whole program. So every app lists its routes again by hand, and a forgotten one is silently never served. The vote decides how a library gathers every use of its own marker. We recommend a typed list of uses that only the marker's own package may read.
decisions.gist: How should a library gather every place its marker is used, such as every route in an app?
decisions.lesson: Some markers only make sense together: every `#Route` belongs in one route table, and every `#Command` in one command list. The library that owns the marker should be able to ask for all its uses as a typed list. Each entry pairs the marker's record with the item it sits on.
decisions.story: Ravi adds `#web.Route("/users")` to a new handler and ships it. The app's hand-written route list never got the new line, so every request to `/users` returns 404.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. Split from D-MARKER-LADDER1, which settles how far one body reads. This ballot asks how a library collects every use of its marker. Approved split by Main.

Why only the owner reads. If any package could read any marker's uses, adding a route would change unrelated packages and their rebuilds. Owner-only reading keeps the list a private part of the library's API. The app sees only what the library chooses to expose, here `web.routes()`.

Completeness with separate builds. The uses are known only after the whole program is checked, so a library's route table folds in the app build, never in the library's own build.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. uses_c.jet: option C's hand list runs today and prints "/orders -> orders" and "/users -> users". program_today.jet: a marker body cannot list the program (E0956). Examples/features/comptime/distinct_reflect.jet shows the build function listing types with `b.program.types()`.

Reads with the related ballots. `Route.Use.route` is D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A's typed record. The read is written in D-META-HASH1 A's spelling without presuming it: under HASH1=B this is `Route.$uses`, and the meaning is the same. Serving a handler from its `site` is the library's own generated glue, as in D-MARKER-LADDER1 A.

options.name: Typed list, owner reads
options.detail:
`Route.#uses` is a list with one entry per use: `route`, the typed `Route` record, and `site`, the item it sits on. Only code in the package that declares `Route` may read it. The list is complete once the program is checked, so it is filled in while compiling.

The app just writes `#web.Route(...)` on handlers.
options.technical: A `Use` record per marker rule: `{route: M, site: ItemInfo}`, built from the same records as D-MARKER-LADDER1 A. Reading `M.#uses` outside M's package is refused. Its value is fixed after checking, so the call folds to a constant. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A.

options.name: The app's build function collects
options.detail:
Only the root build function may list the whole program, so the app collects its own routes there and publishes a table.

Every app repeats the same build code, and a library cannot provide the table on its own.
options.technical: Uses D-METADEPTH2=B program listing and D-META-PUBLISH2=A `compiler.generate`. `b.program.types()` exists today (Examples/features/comptime/distinct_reflect.jet); `functions()` would be added.

Every path appears twice, and nothing warns when a handler is missing from the list.

decisions.title: A library error is a struct that implements the Core trait Diagnostic, with its texts as one-literal methods
decisions.situation: When a marker refuses a use, such as a route path without a leading slash, the user sees an error. Today the library must borrow one of Jet's own codes, so `jet explain` shows an unrelated page. D-DECL-TYPES1 A, now ratified, makes every error a struct that implements a Core trait, Diagnostic. This vote decides where that trait keeps an error's texts: in methods, in trait constants, or in fields with defaults.
decisions.gist: Should a Diagnostic's what, why and fix texts be one-literal methods, trait constants, or fields with defaults?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet error has a code, a short what, a why and a fix, and `jet explain` prints them. Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, an error is a struct, and the Core trait Diagnostic says what it must provide. Its data lives in fields. The texts need that data, as in route `orders` must start with /.
decisions.story: Noor misspells a route and gets `web.BadPath`, pointing at her own line. `jet explain web.BadPath` prints the library's texts with `{path}` where her route goes. She fixes the path in seconds. The web library's author wrote one struct and three one-line methods.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card #6039 (c03pi177). The owner rejected v1, which recommended a new `diagnostic` declaration word. He asked for Diagnostic as a trait, aligned with D-DECL-TYPES1, which he has now ratified with option A. He also asked whether the texts should be fields with defaults or functions. v2 compares both on the merits. Every option here is the Core trait; only where the texts live differs.

What is already settled. D-DECL-TYPES1 A makes an error a struct that implements Diagnostic, with no declaration word (its rules 7 and 13). Its name is its package path, such as web.BadPath. Settings with no data, such as code and severity, are trait constants with defaults. The open question is the three texts, because they read the error's own data.

The deciding fact. In Jet, `{name}` inside a string reads a name in scope. A method has `self` in scope, so `{self.path}` is ordinary, type-checked interpolation. A trait constant and a field default have no `self`. The probes show both fail today with E0107, nothing named `path`. So B must give braces a second meaning, and C cannot put data in a default at all.

Static reading. The foundation registry must read every error's texts without running code. Under A, D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 7 requires each text method's body to be one string literal, and the compiler names any other body. So A and B are equally readable from source. Under C, a raise site may replace a default, so the text a user sees may never appear in the declaration.

jet explain. Under A and B, `jet explain web.BadPath` prints each literal with its holes, shown as `{path}`. Under C it prints only the defaults, which cannot mention the data. Under all three the report points at the user's line, such as app/run.jet:3, with the library line as a note. Today it points inside the library.

Defaults and data. Severity defaults to .Error under every option, as a trait constant in A and B. The value's data is its fields under every option. Under C the texts are fields too, so each raise may restate them, and the same error can read two ways.

Brevity. B is shortest: `what :: "..."` is one short line per text. A writes `fn what(self) -> String { "..." }`, about 25 more characters per text. C is short to declare but long at every raise. A's extra characters buy one meaning for braces, interpolation checked by the existing type checker, and no new rule to learn.

Raising. `reject(BadPath{path: path})` raises any Diagnostic, from a marker's expand or from an ordinary library function that expand calls. It runs only while compiling. An .Error stops that marker's expansion. A .Warning is reported, and the expansion goes on. `#Allow(web.TrailingSlash)` on the user's item silences one warning by name. An .Error cannot be allowed.

Jet's own errors. Under A, each of the 996 Prelude rows becomes a struct with the same three methods and `code :: "E0927"` (rule 13). Jet's errors and library errors then render, explain and allow through one path. No rule of D-DECL-TYPES1 changes under A. B would amend rules 7 and 13; C would amend rule 7 and drop rule 13's fixed texts.

Dropped options. v1's `diagnostic` word is gone, because D-DECL-TYPES1 A retired declaration words. v1's C, inline texts named by the marker, is gone too. It gave two refusals one name, so neither could be explained or allowed alone.

Research. Rust's thiserror writes `#[error("route {path} must start with /")]`, an attribute whose holes name fields. That is B's shape, made possible by a macro that reads the struct. rustc's own diagnostics are structs with fixed message slugs. Swift's DiagnosticMessage is a protocol whose message is a computed property, which is A's shape. Java annotation elements must be constants, which is why C cannot hold data.

Trait constants and the Core trait are proposed, per D-DECL-TYPES1 A.

options.name: Texts are one-literal methods
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic. Its what, why and fix are methods whose body is one string literal, so `{self.path}` reads a field with ordinary interpolation. Settings with no data, such as code and severity, are trait constants with defaults.

This is D-DECL-TYPES1 A's rule 7 exactly, so nothing ratified changes. `reject(BadPath{path: path})` raises it from expand or a helper. `#Allow(web.TrailingSlash)` silences one warning.
options.technical: Core trait Diagnostic: required fn what(self) -> String, fn why(self) -> String and fn fix(self) -> String. Trait constants: code (default, the type path), severity (default .Error) and lint_name (required when severity is .Lint). Each text body must be one string literal whose holes read self's fields (rule 7). The registry reads the impls as source. reject takes any Diagnostic and runs only while compiling. The report's primary span is the marker's use site.

options.name: Texts are trait constants
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic, as in A, but its texts are trait constants: `what :: "route {path} must start with /"`. Inside these constants only, `{path}` names a field of the error rather than a name in scope.

Each text is a short line. The braces then mean two things, and this amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 7 and 13.
options.technical: Diagnostic's what, why and fix become required String trait constants. New rule: in those three constants, a hole names a field of the implementing type and binds when the value is raised. Replacement rule 7: "A diagnostic's what, why and fix are trait constants whose value is one string literal. Their {field} holes name the type's own fields." Replacement rule 13, row fields: "Each hole in a row's texts becomes a String field. The texts are trait constants."

options.name: Texts are fields with defaults
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic, and its texts are ordinary String fields with defaults. A default cannot read another field, so a text that names the data is written where the error is raised.

No new rule is needed. But `jet explain` can show only the defaults, and two raises can word the same error differently.
options.technical: Diagnostic requires fields what, why and fix of type String; defaults use the struct form, name: String{"..."}. reject reads the field values. Amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 7 to: "A diagnostic's what, why and fix are String fields; their defaults are fixed texts." Rule 13 keeps the rows' texts only as defaults.

decisions.title: One view shows every item a marker added, with its source, for the terminal, tests and editor
decisions.situation: When a marker adds a method, the user calls code they never wrote. Today no view shows that code. The templates view lists only names, and it skips any file without a compile-time loop. The derive view names the marker but not what it added. A library author cannot write a test that checks the added code either. The vote decides how users and library authors see the code markers add. We recommend one view that prints each added item with the marker and line that added it.
decisions.gist: How should people see and test the code that a marker adds to their program?
decisions.lesson: A marker such as `#web.Describe` can add methods to your type. When something goes wrong in code you did not write, you need to read it. One view should print each added item as source, labeled with the marker that added it. Library authors should be able to check the same text in a test.
decisions.story: Kai's `Point` suddenly has a `describe_x` method that returns the wrong text. He runs the expand view, sees nothing listed for his file, and has to read the web library's source to guess what it generated.

Reads with the related ballots. The labels name markers as D-MARKER-REFLECT1 records do. Added code is shown in D-META-HASH1's output spelling, which is plain Jet with nothing left to paste.

decisions.title: A marker body pastes a whole parameter list with Jet's spread: `fn $name(...$params)` and `$callee(...$params)`
decisions.situation: Marker bodies add declarations with `comptime loop` and `$` pastes, such as `fn $method(self)`. They can paste a name but not a parameter list. So a marker cannot make a wrapper with the same parameters as the function it marks, and a foreign-language reader cannot add a function of any arity. Jet already spreads lists into calls with `...parts`. The vote decides how a marker pastes a parameter list. We recommend the same spread, inside a template.
decisions.gist: How should a marker body paste a parameter list it read from another function?
decisions.lesson: Markers write code for you. A common job is a wrapper: a function with the same parameters as the marked one, which adds a step and calls it. Jet already spreads a list into a call with `...parts`. Inside a marker, the same `...` spreads a function's parameters into a new signature or call.
decisions.story: Rae writes a `#Logged` marker for her team. It works for functions with no parameters. For the rest she writes one copy of the marker per arity, up to five, and stops there.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. The FFI-UNSAFE1 package named this paste as a prerequisite; D-FFI-BINDER1 A needs it. It is asked here, in the markers group, because it is template grammar.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. params.jet: `fn $name(...target.$params)` is E0003 "Expected a name for a parameter name, found `...`". params_read.jet: looping `target.$params` and binding `"show_{p.$name}"` is E0956 "A derive template binding is not a known-time value". Today `$params` reflects as a list of strings (FactReads.jet:406), not typed rows. Examples/features/basics/variadics_mixed_lists.jet shows today's call spread, `join(...left, ...right)`.

Reads with D-META-HASH1. Today's spelling reads facts with `target.$params` and pastes with `$params`. Under HASH1=A the reads become `#target.params`, `#target.name` and `#target.result`, while pastes stay `$name`, `...$params` and `$callee(...$params)`. Under HASH1=B or C the binding lines follow that outcome. The meaning is the same in every spelling: bind the list once, then spread the pasted list.

options.name: Spread with `...`
options.detail:
Inside a template, `...` before a pasted parameter list spreads it. In a signature it writes each `name: Type`, and in a call it passes each name. Ordinary parameters may sit beside it, as in `fn $name(log: Logger, ...$params)`.

This is the spread Jet already uses in calls, such as `join(...parts)`. A variadic parameter keeps its own form, `parts: ...String`, after a name.
options.technical: Template-only: a spread in a parameter list is E0003 today. Needs `target.$params` as typed rows (name, type, mode); FactReads.jet:406 returns `[String]` today. Adds `target.$result` for the result type. Used by D-FFI-BINDER1 A.

options.name: Paste the whole signature
options.detail:
A signature value pastes after the name, and an argument value pastes into a call.

A wrapper that adds a parameter, such as a logger, can't be written this way.
options.technical: Adds `$signature` and `$arguments` facts and two paste positions.

options.name: Build functions as values
options.detail:
Declarations are built as data and emitted by a call.

The body has to be built as data too, so a three-line wrapper becomes a tree of values.
options.technical: Adds an `emit` call and Function, Param and Body values beside `comptime loop` templates.

`@Type` builds types from data; functions are written with `anytype`. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Type

gains: Wrappers and readers of any arity.
Nothing new to learn beyond `...`.

whyNot.reason: B can only copy a signature whole.
C makes function bodies into data trees.

recommendation.tradeoff: `...` before a parameter list and after a name mean two related things.

decisions.title: Markers, effects, facts, derives and errors are ordinary types that implement a Core trait
decisions.situation: Jet has special declaration words for markers (the # rules above code), effects (what a function may do), compiler facts, derives and, as proposed, library errors. Each word has its own settings syntax, and none of them can be documented or inspected like an ordinary type. You asked whether they could be ordinary types that implement a Core trait, so one interface lists everything each one must define. The vote decides whether all of them become such types, whether effects and facts stay declared rows, or whether the special words stay.
decisions.gist: Should markers, effects, facts, derives and errors be ordinary types that implement a Core trait instead of special words?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet programmer already knows structs, enums and traits. Declarations written that way get docs, reflection and editor help for free. The trait is the checklist: it lists what each one must provide, and the compiler names anything missing.
decisions.story: Priya writes a storage package. She needs a Bucket effect, a Table marker, an Equatable-style derive and a MissingKey error. Today she learns effect rows, marker parameters with dollar settings, a derive link and a separate error form, and none of them can be inspected like her other types. With trait-backed types she writes structs and impls, and the compiler tells her exactly what each trait still needs.
decisions.inWild: C# attributes are classes; Java annotations are typed records; Scala 3 ties derivation to the type class; Rust error types carry fixed message templates with field holes.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. The owner asked in chat on 2026-10-30: "Should we just make effects & maybe markers types? Like structs as backing?" He wanted a trait for effects as one clear interface with more granularity. Tower question q066hpbq on D-MARKER-DIAG1 asked the same about library errors. His follow-up the same day asked to include facts and derives and do it all correctly the first time. Card #6039.

History. v1 covered markers, effects and library errors and passed one adversarial pass. v2 adds facts, derives and Jet's own diagnostic rows. It reconciles with D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A, D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A and D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A, all ratified on 2026-10-30.

Today, markers (dev cbc43e0c5e). Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet declares 81 markers as marker Name(params, $sites: [...], ...). The $ parameters are fixed declaration settings: sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion (Markers.jet:8-21). The repository holds 333 marker declarations in all.

Today, effects and facts. Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet declares 46 effect rows, such as effect FS.Write $irreversible. A root with leaves is closed (Effects.jet:8). Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet declares compiler facts as fact Name($holds:, $safe:, $gates:, ...) rows under D-FACTDECL1 A. The repository holds 61 effect declarations.

Today, derives and diagnostics. Compiler/Prelude/Derives.jet writes derive T.Equatable { ... } template bodies. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A ratified the link marker Equatable($sites: [.Type]) derives Equatable. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet holds 996 tab-separated diagnostic rows. Library refusals call reject(code:, what:, why:, fix:) and borrow Jet codes such as E0927. The repository has 100 reject calls.

What A changes. Core gains five traits: Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments. A derive is a trait that implements Derive. An effect is a struct or enum. A compiler fact is a field-less struct. An error is a struct.

What stays. The words marker, effect, fact and derive retire as declaration words. The diagnostic word proposed by D-MARKER-DIAG1 A is never added. Applying a marker, as in #web.Route("/orders") or #[Equatable], is unchanged. Writing an effect row, as in -[FS.Read]>, is unchanged.

The trait constant. This is the one new language capability. A trait may require a named compile-time constant, optionally with a default. An impl supplies it with name :: value. Rust associated consts and Swift static protocol requirements are the proven precedent. A trait constant is a member of its type, so it is snake_case like a field. The ALL_CAPS rule covers module-level constants only.

Settings become constants. Every $ setting becomes a trait constant whose value is a literal, an enum case or a list of them. Marker takes sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion. Fact takes holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by. Diagnostic takes code, severity and the registry columns. A diagnostic's what, why and fix are ordinary methods (rule 7).

Rule 1, cost. Applying a marker or naming an effect builds its value while compiling. That value costs nothing at run time unless code reads it through reflection. The types stay ordinary, so ordinary code may also construct them.

Rule 2, marker fields. Marker fields hold compile-time values. These are constants or the code-shaped kinds marker parameters take today: Value for an expression such as #Pre's condition, Ident for a name, and Type for a type. Policy's variadic ...PolicySetting becomes a trailing list field. The use site still writes its items as separate arguments.

Rule 2, effect fields. Effect fields must be constants. Effect checking therefore never depends on a run-time value or on code.

Rule 3, effect rows. An effect row names a type, an enum case, or a constant value written as an ordinary struct literal: -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]>. A bare type covers every value, and a case covers that case. A value covers only itself. So a function declared -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]> cannot call one that needs -[Bucket]>.

Rule 3, families. Enum cases are today's closed families. With enum FS { Read Write }, -[FS]> means any case and -[FS.Read]> means one case. Irreversibility is the trait method irreversible(self) -> Bool, default false. So FS.Write can be irreversible while FS.Read is not. Manifest grants and --allow/--deny name a type or case. A value narrows only in source rows.

Rule 4, effect powers. A library effect states the most it may do with #FX above its type, as D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A ratified: #FX(Net) struct Bucket. Its impl Bucket.Effect must sit in the same file as the type. A reader then sees the role next to the #FX.

Rule 4, one reading. #FX above any type means the most that work done in that type's name may do. For an effect type, that work is every function whose row names it. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1, still open, decides what #FX promises for an ordinary type's own methods. It must keep this one reading.

Rule 4, kernel effects. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A holds as ratified. The machine powers are Core types the compiler recognizes by identity (rule 10). They are network, files, terminal, clock, randomness, environment, processes, foreign code, graphics card and browser host. Core declares DB, Log and Secret over them with #FX, like any package.

Rule 5, arguments. Marker arguments fill fields in declaration order or by name, as marker parameters do today. Field defaults use the struct form, name: Type{default}.

Rule 6, expand. The marker body becomes the trait method expand(self, target: Target), which runs while compiling. Unlike other methods, its body is a template, as today's marker and derive bodies are. Every declaration written in it is added at the marker's site, including fn and impl $name blocks. $name pastes a value. A helper that should not be pasted is an ordinary function outside the impl.

Rule 6, wrapping. Wrapping markers use the trait method wrap(self, call). Its default passes the call through.

Rule 7, error texts. A diagnostic's name is its package path, such as web.BadPath. Its what, why and fix are methods whose body must be one string literal. Their {self.field} holes may read only the value's own fields. The compiler names any other body. The texts are therefore fixed, so jet explain web.BadPath prints each literal with its holes. #Allow(web.BadPath) names one refusal when severity is .Warning.

Rule 8, reading a marker. Reading a marker returns its value. Inside expand, target.marker(Route) is Route?, and a repeatable marker gives [Route]. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A's typed lookup is unchanged. The twin record it described is the marker struct itself.

Rule 9, derives. A trait becomes derivable by implementing the Core trait Derive. Derive's one requirement is fn expand(target: Target), a template with no self. Example: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { impl $target.Equatable { ... } } }. Writing #[Equatable] or #Equatable on a type applies it. Derive's sites are always types.

Rule 9, the impl head. In an impl head, the name before the dot is the trait itself. It is never the boxed value type that S48 gives a trait name in parameter, field and element positions. Derive is the only trait a trait may implement.

Rule 9, the link. The impl head is the explicit link D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A required. The trait stays only its function contract, and no derive or derives word remains. A derive request carries no data, so it takes no arguments. target.marker(Equatable) answers Bool. Options are separate markers that expand reads. CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) stay struct markers that write impls.

Rule 10, Core's own. Core's own markers, effects and facts become Core and Prelude types that the compiler recognizes by identity. Examples are Unsafe, Policy, Net, FFI, Exactness and Rights. D-CORE-ROLE1 A already ratified this mechanism for library types with language meaning. Policy keeps its built-in tightening rule that way.

Rule 11, nesting. inherits and resolution keep today's meaning. .SiteBound and .Override need nothing more. A library marker that sets resolution to .Merge or .Tighten must also implement combine(self, inner: Self) -> Self. That method states how two nested writings join. The trait's checklist names it when missing.

Rule 12, facts. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact, with its settings as trait constants. The holds and safe constants are the enum cases of today's rows. The name constant is a string, identity is a Bool, and proved_by is an enum case such as .Ownership.

Rule 12, gates. gates is a list of the Prelude enum Gate. Gate has one case per escape word: .Approx, .Rounded, .Raw, .Wrapping, .Saturating, .Checked, .Detach and .Drop. It also has .Marker(Type) for a marker type. Rights sets gates :: [.Marker(Unsafe), .Marker(Impure), .Marker(Grant)]. Every gate is therefore a checked value, not a bare word.

Rule 12, scope. Facts stay compiler vocabulary declared in the Prelude. A package does not add new facts in this step, because a fact needs a compiler rule that publishes and checks it. The rows' $decision fields are dropped in the cutover, as invariant I7 already requires.

Rule 13, Jet's own errors. Each of the 996 Prelude diagnostic rows becomes a struct that implements Diagnostic. The census is 845 active, 135 retired and 16 reserved rows, and 71 are lints. Jet's errors and library errors then share one shape for jet explain, #Allow and the editor.

Rule 13, row fields. Each hole in a row's texts becomes a String field. Meaning and detail are constant texts. Stage, moment, status and structured fix become enum constants with defaults. A typical row then sets only code, what, why and fix. A lint sets lint_name, which the compiler requires when severity is .Lint.

Rule 13, codes and reading. Codes stay E-numbers, set by code :: "E0927". The type gets a descriptive name, and jet explain accepts either name. Every constant and text is a literal (rule 7). So the foundation registry still reads these impls as source text without running them, as it reads the rows today.

Rule 13, cost. The cost is real. About 1000 one-line rows become about 1000 small struct-and-impl declarations, several thousand lines. jet fix must name each type. Retired and reserved rows convert too, so their codes stay explainable.

Rule 14, one role. A struct or enum implements at most one of Marker, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A trait may implement only Derive (rule 9). A type's role is therefore never ambiguous. Marker types are not generic in this step.

Rule 15, groups. A marker group is a struct with no fields whose Marker impl sets the constant group. Example: struct Fast {} with impl Fast.Marker { group :: #[Label("fixed"), Inline(.Always), Scalar] }. D-MARKER-GROUP1's law is unchanged. A group has two or more members and no parameters. Every member's gates and refusals apply at each use.

Folds in, open ballots. D-MARKER-DIAG1: A's Diagnostic trait is its option B plus one rule, that each text method is one string literal. That keeps the texts fixed and removes the reason B lost. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 (open): rule 4 fixes the one reading of #FX above a type that it must keep.

Folds in, ratified and kept. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A keeps its lookup; the record is the marker, and a derive answers Bool. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A keeps #FX above the effect type. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A keeps its split, with kernel effects as recognized Core types. D-MARKER-GROUP1 keeps its law (rule 15). D-EXTEND-ARCH1 A already uses the impl Type.Trait shape, as in impl SQL.CheckedText.

Folds in, needing re-ruling. D-MARKER-DECL1 A chose one declaration word for everything applied with #. A keeps the one-form rule but replaces the word with struct plus impl Marker. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A's explicit link becomes the impl head, so only its spelling changes. D-FACTDECL1 A's fact word retires. D-META-HASH1: the $ settings disappear, which leaves $ only for template pastes.

Research, markers. C# attributes have been ordinary classes deriving System.Attribute since 2002, with [AttributeUsage] naming legal sites. The design is stable and widely used. Java annotations are typed records whose elements must be compile-time constants. That limit matches rule 2 and has not been a practical burden. Java lacked repeatable annotations until Java 8 and needed a wrapper type. A has a repeatable constant from the start.

Research, derives. Kotlin declares annotation class, and Scala annotations extend scala.annotation.Annotation. Rust derive macros are separate items linked to their trait only by name, so a derive and a trait can drift apart. Haskell's DeriveAnyClass and Scala 3's derives clause tie derivation to the type class itself. Rule 9 takes that shape.

Research, errors. Rust's thiserror and miette give errors fixed message templates whose {field} holes name struct fields. rustc's own diagnostics are structs with fixed message slugs. Swift macro diagnostics are structs conforming to the DiagnosticMessage protocol. That is the shape A gives Diagnostic.

Research, effects. Effekt declares effects as interfaces. OCaml 5 effects are constructors of the extensible type Effect.t. Both are ordinary type-system declarations. Koka and Unison use dedicated effect and ability words, which is option C's shape. The known failure to avoid is C# attribute constructors running arbitrary code during reflection at run time. A runs marker code only while compiling.

Migration. One cutover converts everything, and no old spelling remains. jet fix rewrites every marker, effect, fact and derive declaration and every reject(code: ...) call. The Prelude's 81 markers, 46 effects, fact rows, derive bodies and 996 diagnostic rows move to types. The compiler registries read the trait impls instead of the rows.

options.name: Types with Core traits, for all of them
options.detail: A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments and which implements Marker. A derive is a trait that implements Derive and writes its impl. An effect is a struct or enum that implements Effect, and may carry constant data, so a function can name one bucket known while compiling. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact. Every error, Jet's own and a library's, implements Diagnostic with fixed texts. The trait lists what each must provide.
options.technical: Adds the Core traits Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic, plus the trait constant (name :: value in an impl). Retires the marker, effect, fact and derive words and every $ setting. Marker bodies become expand(self, target), a template. Effect rows accept a type, a case or a constant struct literal. Diagnostic texts are one-literal methods, and Jet's 996 rows become Diagnostic types.

decisions.title: Rotate the working seed once B1 lands; the HTTP client (#3665) keeps gating the release
decisions.situation: The compiler that builds Jet, called the seed, is a0_021. It cannot read trait constants, so Core cannot use them. The diagnostic types you approved, such as `jet.UnusedParameter`, need them in Core. You ruled that the next seed, a0_022, waits for the HTTP client port (#3665), which has 9 of 10 criteria open. We recommend rotating the working seed as soon as trait constants land, with the usual checks, and keeping #3665 as the gate for the release.
decisions.gist: Should the working seed rotate before the HTTP client port lands?
decisions.lesson: Jet builds itself. Core and the compiler are compiled by an earlier, trusted compiler called the seed. New syntax can reach Core only after a seed that understands it replaces the old one. A release is a seed published for others to download (D-SEED-DIST1); none is published yet.
decisions.story: DeclTypes finishes B1, which teaches the parser trait constants. B3 is ready: every Jet diagnostic becomes a type with its `jet.` name. The build fails, because a0_021 compiles Core and reads `code: String` in a trait as E0003. Under A, Main rotates the seed that evening and B3 lands. The release still waits for the HTTP client.
decisions.detail:
What is blocked today. Four pieces of work need a seed newer than a0_021. DeclTypes B3 and its later batches put trait constants in Core (#6039 C9 to C14). IrTypes has a Core alias, `Name<T> :: Type`, staged for golden transform_source_identity (#6176). The `__coded_stop` migration of Server.jet and Web.jet waits as g3b. #6279 C4 deletes the email bootstrap file at the first rotation past a0_021.

Why a0_022 waits now. The HttpDest landing note ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/land/HttpDest-g1.msg, line 8) records your ruling. Two Jetpack test rows, foundation_fetch and the Public-client test, fail until the Jet HTTP client port lands. Those rows fail because their source calls a client that is not written yet, so they fail the same way under any seed.

How a rotation is checked today (ROTATION.md in each seed folder). The candidate is built from a clean dev export with no Rust in the chain. It must rebuild itself to the same bytes, s2 equal to s3. Its full golden suite must be no worse than the current seed's, your rule of 2026-10-22. a0_021 took 9 minutes of wall time for these steps.

What A adds. Before the chain, a collect-all preflight checks Core and the compiler with the candidate and lists every error at once, as seed-preflight.sh does with keep-going. Any row stops the rotation. Every earlier seed stays on disk (a0_005 to a0_021), and current.env names the active one, so switching back is one line.

What A changes. The working seed and the release become two separate events. The seed rotates whenever the checks pass and new Core syntax needs it. A release, the seed published for download under D-SEED-DIST1, still waits for #3665. Your ruling keeps its effect: nothing is released before the HTTP client is in Jet.

Option B keeps the hold. All four pieces of work wait for #3665, a P0 card with 9 open criteria spanning Core HTTP, sockets, TLS and server framing. Option C lands B3 without trait constants by keeping each diagnostic's name in a compiler table, then moves them into Core after the rotation. That is a second cutover and a temporary twin of the table, which AGENTS.md forbids.

Probe. trait_const.jet in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/seed declares a trait constant and reads it. Both a0_021 and today's dev compiler stop with two E0003 errors. B1 has not landed on dev yet, so A's rotation starts after it does.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this ballot.
