decisions.title: How is a value tag declared once the tag word retires?
decisions.situation: D-MARKER-DECL1 A retired the tag word, and D-DECL-TYPES1 A made every marker a struct implementing Marker. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A then let any type write `#FX(!Net)` above itself to forbid an effect in everything done in its name. A tag`s deny list says the same thing about the tagged data, so a separate deny setting would be a second way to forbid an effect. The vote decides how a tag is spelled as a type and where its denials live.
decisions.gist: How is a value tag declared as a type, and where do its denials live?
decisions.lesson: A value tag, such as #PII String, marks data that must not reach some effects. The compiler tracks the mark through every value computed from it, and #Scrub(PII) on a function is the one way to remove it. A tag`s from list names sources whose results carry the tag automatically, such as from: [Store.read]. Jet`s built-in tags are Input, PII, Secret and Credential.
decisions.story: Dana`s payment package must keep card numbers out of logs and the network. She declares a CardNumber tag, marks the card parameter, and writes one #Scrub function that returns the last four digits.
decisions.inWild:
Examples/features/types/value_tag_type.jet:4 tag Raw { deny: [DB] }
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Taint.jet:304-311 the built-in tags: Input, PII and Secret deny [DB, Exec, Net]; Credential also denies Log.
D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A, ratified: #FX(!Net, !FS) above struct Parser bounds all work done in Parser`s name.
Java Checker Framework: @Tainted and @Untainted are annotations declared like every other annotation.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
D-MARKER-DECL1 A: tag retires as a word, and a tag declares a value label with its denials and an optional from list.

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct implementing Marker, and its $ settings become trait constants. Rule 9 gives derives their own trait, Derive.

D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A: #FX above a type bounds everything done in that type`s name, with the same row syntax as a function arrow. `!Net` is a denial that also reaches through calls.

Owner direction: a type contains its own impls, so the impl is written inside the struct body. This amends the spelling of D-DECL-TYPES1`s examples.

THE PROBLEM WITH A SEPARATE DENY
Both a type row and a tag deny list name effects that must never happen. If a tag kept its own deny setting, Jet would have two spellings for one meaning, against I8. A reader would also have to learn which one applies where.

HOW A AND B UNIFY THEM
A tag has no fields and no methods, so the only work done in its name is work done on tagged data. Its #FX row therefore bounds every operation a tagged value reaches. For an ordinary type the same row bounds its methods. The row syntax, the denial meaning and the codes (E0749) are shared. Only the place the check looks differs: methods for an ordinary type, data flow for a tag.

WHAT EVERY OPTION KEEPS
The use sites do not change: #PII String in a parameter, field or return type, a tagged expression, and #Scrub(PII). Site gains a .TypeUse case for value positions.

.Type stays the declaration site, so #CardNumber struct Point is still refused as E0731. A tag has no fields, expand, wrap or methods; any of those is refused as E0732 is today. from stays a tag setting, written from :: [Store.read], because no other rule has it.

REFUSALS UNDER A AND B
A tag with no denial is refused, as E0734 is today. A ceiling entry in a tag`s row, such as #FX(Log), is refused for now. Tagged text passes through allocation and other plain work, so an allow-list would refuse ordinary string handling. The fix says to write denials.

The tag is the struct, so a second declaration with that name is an ordinary E0105. A package struct named Input, PII, Secret or Credential is refused as E0106, redefining a built-in. Nine test fixtures that redeclare a built-in tag are renamed.

COST
Every option converts the 36 tag declarations and declares the four built-in tags in the Prelude. It also removes the copies of their names and laws: EffectsSurface.jet:95, Taint.jet:304-317 and :644, and the TaintKind enum (CoreEnumRows.jet:26). The texts of E0733 and E0734 (Diagnostics.jet:449-450) are rewritten.

Under A and B, a tag`s row needs #FX on types, which c09kjhit builds. The compiler`s internal origin rows also deny the sinks SQL.raw, HTML.raw and Sh.raw, which are functions, not effects. No written tag denies a sink. Those rows stay internal until the library-effect step on c09kjhit makes the sinks effects.

EDGE CASES
The tag Secret and the effect Secret (Effects.jet:54) are both Prelude names. A later step of D-DECL-TYPES1 that turns effects into types must rename one. A tag cannot also be a group, an effect or a fact (rule 14).

options.name: A tag`s denials are its #FX row
options.detail: A tag is a field-less struct whose Marker impl attaches at .TypeUse. Its denials are the #FX(!…) row that any type may write. On a tag the row bounds where tagged data goes, because a tag has no methods.
options.technical: A Marker whose sites include .TypeUse is a value tag. The type`s #FX denials become the tag`s deny list in the taint checker. A tag needs at least one denial, and ceiling entries are refused. from is a Marker constant, used only by tags.

options.name: The same row, with a Tag trait
options.detail: As A, the denials are the type`s #FX row. The role comes from implementing a Core Tag trait instead of a Marker site.
options.technical: Core trait Tag with an optional from constant. The tag`s sites are fixed by the trait. Rule 14 adds Tag to the one-role list.

options.name: Denials as a Marker setting
options.detail: Marker gains deny and from settings. A non-empty deny makes the marker a tag. The type`s #FX row stays a separate, unrelated promise.
options.technical: Marker constants deny and from, both default empty. Writing #FX on a tag is either refused or means something else.

recommendation.why: D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A already lets a type forbid an effect in everything done in its name. A tag is a type whose name only data carries, so its denials are that same row. A keeps one way to forbid an effect, and a tag is only a marker that attaches to values.
gains: One spelling and one diagnostic for forbidding an effect, on a type or a tag.

decisions.title: Should compiler fact planes become markers, or keep their own Fact trait?
decisions.situation: Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, a marker becomes a struct that implements Marker. A compiler fact plane becomes a field-less struct that implements Fact. You asked whether facts should merge into markers to remove a duplicate concept. The vote decides whether the Fact trait stays, or whether planes become markers that nobody writes with #.
decisions.gist: Do compiler fact planes become markers?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a rule you write above code with #, such as #Unsafe("reason") or #web.Route("/orders"). A fact plane is something the compiler tracks, such as whether a number is exact or which rights a scope has. Each plane lists the escape words that can weaken it, such as wrapping or #Unsafe. Only the Prelude, Jet`s built-in library, declares planes; there are 49.
decisions.story: Dana reads the Prelude to learn how #Unsafe works. She finds Unsafe declared as a marker, and Rights declared as a fact plane whose gates name Unsafe. She wants to know whether these are one kind of thing or two.
decisions.inWild:

Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet:23 fact Rights($holds: .Scope, $safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant], …)
Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet:27 marker Unsafe(reason: String, obligations: ObligationMode{.None}, $sites: [.Function, .Method, .Block, .Operation])
Java: @Override and @FunctionalInterface are annotations javac checks; the facts javac tracks, such as definite assignment, are not annotations.
Rust: lang items are marked with the built-in #[lang] attribute, but the facts rustc tracks, such as borrow state, are not attributes.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct that implements Marker. Its fields are its arguments. Its $ settings become trait constants: sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion. Rule 15 adds group. A fact plane is a field-less struct that implements Fact. Fact`s settings are holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by. Planes stay Prelude-only (rule 12). A type has one role (rule 14). Owner direction: a type contains its own impls, so the impl is written inside the struct body.

D-TAG-MARKER1, on the board beside this one, decides how a tag is declared. The tag in the code below shows its recommended option.

WHY THIS IS ASKED AGAIN
Folding facts into markers lost twice. D-FACTDECL1 option C lost because calling a knowledge plane a marker breaks the one word a beginner already learned. D-MARKER-DECL1 option C lost because fact is written only in the Prelude, so folding it helps no learner. D-DECL-TYPES1 has since made both kinds ordinary types with traits. A merge now means one trait instead of two, not one keyword instead of two.

THE STRONGEST CASE FOR B
Picking a role with a setting is already ratified: rule 15 makes a group a marker that sets group. D-FACTDECL1 says markers and facts differ only in what they attach to, in one registration table. Tags are facts on the Taint plane that people write with #, so the line between written and tracked is already blurry. A merge removes one Core trait from the docs.

OPTION B IN DETAIL
Marker gains one optional constant, plane: Plane?, defaulting to None. Plane is a Prelude struct holding the six fact settings. Setting plane makes sites default to [], and any other sites is refused. Only the Prelude may set plane, so rule 12 is stated on one constant. Reflection: target.marker(Exactness) is a compile error naming the plane, because a plane is never written at a site. Plane facts keep their $ reads, such as value.$origin.

OPTION C IN DETAIL
As B, but the six plane settings sit directly on Marker with defaults, and a marker that sets holds is a plane. Every marker`s checklist then lists six settings that only planes use.

COST
Every option converts the same 49 Prelude fact rows in the same cutover. Under every option, the Gate enum first needs cases for 20 rows it cannot express yet. Rights and PackagePolicy name the retired Grant, BuildSettings names Force, three Structure rows use strings, and fourteen Target rows name a provider and digest. B and C also add three refusals: a package marker that sets plane (or holds), a plane with non-empty sites, and a reflection read of a plane.

EDGE CASES
A type that is both a plane and a written marker is refused under every option. Under A, rule 14 refuses it. Under B and C it is refused because a plane`s sites must be empty. Build facts such as Build.OS and Target.Memory are planes under every option. Under B, a marker that sets both plane and deny is refused.

options.name: Keep Fact as its own trait
options.detail: D-DECL-TYPES1 as ratified. Markers implement Marker, and the 49 Prelude planes implement Fact. A marker and a plane meet only through the plane`s gates list.
options.technical: No change to D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 12 and 14.

options.name: Planes become markers with one plane setting
options.detail: One trait for markers and planes. A plane is a marker that nobody writes: it sets one plane setting that holds the fact law, and its sites are empty. Only the Prelude may set it.
options.technical: Marker gains plane: Plane? (default None), where Plane{holds, safe, gates, name, identity, proved_by}. Setting plane makes sites default to [], and any other sites is refused. The Fact trait is never added. Refusals: plane outside the Prelude, and target.marker(P) on a plane P.

options.name: Planes become markers, settings flat
options.detail: One trait, as in B, but holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by are ordinary Marker settings with defaults. A marker that sets holds is a plane.
options.technical: Marker gains six constants with defaults. The Fact trait is never added. The same refusals as B, keyed on holds.

recommendation.why: Groups, and tags under D-TAG-MARKER1 A, pick their role with a Marker setting, but they are still written with # at sites. A plane is never written and uses none of Marker`s members: not sites, repeatable, resolution, expand or wrap. Keeping Fact separate means no Marker member needs a refusal to keep planes out.
gains: Each trait lists only members its role uses.
No marker can declare a plane by accident, so nothing extra is refused.

losses.loss: Core keeps two traits where one could do.
losses.mitigation: Only the Prelude implements Fact for now (rule 12). Users see it only in the Core trait docs.

whyNot.reason: Groups, and tags under D-TAG-MARKER1 A, pick their role with a Marker constant but are still written with #. A plane would use none of Marker`s members, so sites and reflection need refusals to keep it out.
C adds six plane-only settings to every marker`s checklist, for 49 Prelude rows.

recommendation.tradeoff: One extra Prelude-only trait, in exchange for Marker holding only things written with #.

decisions.title: Can a type write its markers inside its body?
decisions.situation: Markers such as #FX, #Layout and #Deprecated set facts on a declaration, and today they can only be written above it. A type with many markers gets a long line or a stack of lines before its name. The owner asked for a formal form inside the body that sets the same facts, so the marker above is only a shorthand for it. The vote decides whether that form exists and how it is spelled. Either way it must stay one mechanism with one meaning (I8).

Rust: inner attributes go inside modules, functions and impl blocks, but not struct or enum bodies.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: a marker is a struct implementing Marker, a type contains its own impls, and $ settings retired so that $ means reads and pastes. D-NAME-SPLICE1 B: a template pastes a binding with $name. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A: #FX above a type bounds everything done in its name.

THE RULE UNDER A

The line inside is the formal declaration, and #X(args) above is the shorthand that writes the same entry. Moving a marker inside is one swap: #X(args) becomes #X :: (args) at the top of the body. The # keeps the marker sigil, and :: reads as "this declaration`s X is".

The value after :: has four shapes. true applies a marker with its defaults, as #MustUse :: true. false refuses one, as #Debug :: false for #!Debug, and only where #!X is allowed. One name, string or number needs no parentheses, as #Layout :: c. Any other argument list is written in parentheses, exactly as above.

So #MustUse :: true and #MustUse mean the same, and no empty () exists. A Bool argument is always written in parentheses, as #X :: (true), so true alone never means two things. jet fmt drops parentheses around one simple argument, so each line has one printed form.

The arguments use the marker argument grammar, so every marker accepts exactly what it accepts above. Library markers work the same way, as in #orm.Table :: "users". No marker opts in, and nothing is translated.

ONE MECHANISM

Both spellings fill the same marker list on the declaration. Checks, templates and reflection read that list and cannot tell which form was used. target.markers sees the same entries either way. No new name is declared, so there is no Point.$FX to read.

ONE PLACE PER TYPE

A declaration writes its own markers either all above or all inside. Mixing them is refused, so a reader never searches two places. jet fix offers to move all of them inside, or all of them above. Markers that tools or templates add go wherever the declaration`s markers already are, and above when it has none.

The # lines come first in the body, before fields, constants and impls. A later one is refused, and jet fix moves it up. A repeated marker gets the error it gets above today.

WHERE IT APPLIES

Inside every braced declaration body: struct, enum, trait, impl block, inline module, function and method. A function body is code, but no statement starts with #X ::, so the header lines never look like code. The function`s effect row stays in its arrow, because #FX`s sites do not include functions.

A marker whose sites exclude the declaration gets the site error it gets above, so #Redact :: true in a struct body fails like #Redact struct X. Blocks, lambdas and tests already carry their marker at their own head, as #FX(IO) { … }, so there is nothing to move.

NO CLASHES

A module body binds Name :: path, a trait or marker body has constants such as sites :: [.Function], and a function body has statements. A # line differs from all three by its first character. Template pastes and environment reads use $, so they never meet a # line.

COST

The parser reads the leading # lines right after the opening brace, then applies them where it applies markers above today. Layout, derives, SingleUse and MustUse therefore still take effect before the members are parsed.

The formatter prints the form the author chose. jet fix gains the two whole-type moves. No existing code changes, and no marker is converted. #FX on a type also needs D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 A`s site change, which is not built yet. The other markers work as soon as this lands.

WHY NOT __

B uses __, which matches the idea of an internal field the marker sets. Core already has __show and __debug, which the compiler reads. But D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 A rejects every __ name written in user code as E0067, with no escape. D-NAME-SIGIL1 A says two underscores are machine space with no user meaning.

B would open one user-written slice of that space, so a reader can no longer assume a __ name is generated. Debuggers and suggestion menus hide __ names, so they also hide these lines. A needs no amendment and keeps # as the only marker sigil.

WHY NOT $

$ stays the template paste and the compiler read. The sigil law says programs never declare a $ name. $Layout :: c would also read like a fact member, inviting Point.$Layout, and a bare $MustUse line in a template has the same shape as a pasted enum variant.

options.name: #X :: value lines at the top of a body
options.detail: Any marker on a declaration with a braced body can be written at the top of that body as #X :: value. It means exactly what #X(args) above means. A declaration puts its own markers all above or all inside.
options.technical: Leading body members # Path :: value, read right after the opening brace and added to the declaration`s marker list before its members. Values are true, false, one name, string or number, or a marker argument list in parentheses.

options.name: __X :: (args) lines in the body
options.detail: As A, but each line starts with __ instead of #. It reads as an internal field the compiler sets, which is what the marker above fills in. This amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 and D-NAME-SIGIL1, which reserve every __ name for the compiler.
options.technical: As A with __Path. User code may write a __ name only as one of these leading lines, and only for a marker in scope. Every other __ name stays refused as E0067.

options.name: Markers stay above
options.detail: No new form. A long list becomes a named group written once, then applied with one marker above each type.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A gives every marker on a braced declaration a formal line inside it, with one swap rule and no per-marker work. It keeps # as the only marker sigil, declares no new name and amends no ratified rule. Both spellings fill one marker list, so there is still one mechanism.
gains: Every braced declaration can declare its markers as a header inside it.
One swap rule covers every marker, including library markers.

losses.loss: Readers meet one more line shape.
losses.mitigation: It is the marker itself with :: before its value, and editor hover names the shorthand it equals.

losses.loss: A declaration cannot split its markers between above and inside.
losses.mitigation: That keeps them in one place to read, and jet fix moves the whole set either way.

whyNot.reason: B amends two ratified decisions to let user code write __ names, which tools treat as generated and hide.
C leaves no formal in-body declaration, which is what the owner asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings for one marker list, in exchange for a formal header inside the type.

decisions.title: How does a package declare its own kind of an existing effect, such as an audit kind of Log?
decisions.situation: D-DECL-TYPES1 A already ratified that an effect is a struct or enum that implements the Effect trait, the same shape as a marker. One case is still open. Today a package can add its own kind of an existing effect with `effect Log.Audit`. A function marked -[Log.Audit]> may log, and a caller allowed -[Log]> may call it. Families with fixed kinds, such as FS with FS.Read and FS.Write, are closed today and become enums. Log has no fixed kinds, so packages may extend it. This ballot picks how the struct form says "Audit is a kind of Log". The only use in the repository is Examples/features/effects/effect_declarations.jet, plus about 12 tests.

decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY DECIDED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A: an effect is a struct or enum that implements Effect. Settings are trait constants written name :: value inside the impl, like sites :: [.Function] in impl Marker. Effects with fixed kinds are enums, such as enum FS { Read Write }. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A: package effects carry their package path, as in audit.Audit.

WHAT A ADDS

The Effect trait gains one optional setting, parent. Writing parent :: Log makes Audit a kind of Log. Allowing Log allows Audit, denying Log denies Audit, and Audit may do at most what Log does. No #FX line is needed, because the parent is the limit. A function may still allow only the audit part with -[audit.Audit]>.

RULES UNDER A

The parent must be an effect struct. An enum family such as FS or DB stays closed, as today, and naming one as a parent is an error with a fix. Chains are allowed: a kind of Audit is also a kind of Log. A cycle is an error. Irreversibility defaults to the parent's. A #FX line may narrow the limit further, never widen it.

SAFETY

Joining Log grants nothing new. A kind of Log can do only what Log does, so an app that allows Log gains no power. Two packages cannot clash, because each kind carries its package path: audit.Audit and billing.Audit are different.

MIGRATION

jet fix rewrites each `effect Log.Audit` into the struct with parent :: Log. It also rewrites each -[Log.Audit]> row to -[Audit]> inside the package and to -[audit.Audit]> outside. No caller that allowed Log changes.

options.name: A struct with parent :: Log
options.detail: A package effect is a struct that implements Effect and names its parent: parent :: Log. Allowing Log allows it, denying Log denies it, and it may do at most what Log does. Callers that allowed Log change nothing. A caller may also allow only the narrow kind, as audit.Audit.
options.technical: Effect gains an optional trait constant parent (default none). Sema walks the parent chain for coverage, denial and the limit. A parent must be an effect struct, not an enum family. Cycles are refused. The dotted effect Log.Audit form retires, and jet fix rewrites declarations and rows.

options.name: A separate effect with its own limit
options.detail: A package effect is its own struct with #FX(Log) above it, giving its limit. It is not a kind of Log, so allowing Log does not allow it. Every caller names it, as audit.Audit. Denying Log still denies it, because its limit is Log.
options.technical: No new setting. Uses the #FX limit from D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A. jet fix rewrites declarations and adds audit.Audit to every caller row the check would refuse.

options.name: No package kinds; Log carries a topic
options.detail: Packages do not declare kinds of Log. Core gives Log a constant topic field, and a function narrows with -[Log{topic: "audit"}]>. Allowing Log covers every topic. There is no audit type to document or import.
options.technical: Uses the ratified constant-value rows (D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 3). Core adds topic: String{""} to Log. jet fix rewrites -[Log.Audit]> to -[Log{topic: "audit"}]> and deletes the declarations.

recommendation.why: A keeps today's meaning exactly: allowing or denying Log still covers the package's kind. It uses the ratified struct-and-impl form with one optional setting, written like a marker's settings. Names cannot clash, and joining Log grants no new power.
gains: Callers that allowed Log keep working unchanged.
Denying Log still denies every kind of Log.
Each kind is a real type with docs and a package path.

losses.loss: Effect gains one optional setting, parent.
losses.mitigation: It is a trait constant like sites in impl Marker, so it adds no new syntax.

whyNot.reason: B breaks every caller that allowed Log; each one must add audit.Audit.
C uses strings, so a misspelled topic silently makes a new topic, and there is no type to document.

recommendation.tradeoff: One optional setting on Effect, in exchange for keeping today's meaning with no caller changes.

decisions.title: What does a derive with no trait become when the derive word retires?
decisions.situation: D-DECL-TYPES1 A makes a derive a trait that implements Derive: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { ... } }. But every user derive in the repository today is a provider with no trait at all. For example, derive T.DebugText adds a debug_string method, derive T.FieldNames adds one method per field, and derive T.LayoutFacts adds only constants. There are 40 such declarations in 37 files: 8 examples, 3 perf constructs, and the rest tests. None of them names a trait, so impl X.Derive has nothing to attach to.
decisions.gist: Should a derive that has no trait become a marker that writes the code?
decisions.lesson: A derive writes code onto a type when you mark it, as in #DebugText struct Point. Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, a derive belongs to a trait. A marker can also write code onto the item it marks, through its expand template (rule 6).
decisions.story: Lee's package has derive T.FieldNames, which writes field_x and field_y methods onto any struct marked #FieldNames. The method names depend on the fields, so no fixed trait can describe them. When the derive word retires, Lee needs a form that still writes those methods.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 9: a trait becomes derivable by implementing Derive, whose one requirement is fn expand(target: Target). The derive and derives words retire. Rule 6: a marker's expand(self, target: Target) is a template, and every declaration in it, including impl $name blocks, is added at the marker's site. Rule 9 also keeps CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) as struct markers that write impls.

WHAT IS OPEN

No rule says what jet fix writes for a derive with no trait. The Prelude's two derives, Equatable and Comparable, are compiler-known traits and are not affected.

CENSUS

At dev 2d8aea4762: 40 user derive declarations in 37 files, all trait-less. Some write a fixed method (DebugText), some write methods with pasted names (FieldNames), and some write only constants (LayoutFacts).

options.name: A marker struct that writes the code
options.detail: A derive with no trait becomes a marker: a field-less struct with impl Marker { sites :: [.Type] } and an expand template that writes impl $target { ... }. Writing #DebugText on a type is unchanged. A derive whose name is a trait becomes impl X.Derive, as rule 9 says. jet fix picks the form by checking whether a trait of that name exists.

options.detail: jet fix writes a new trait from the methods the derive adds (trait DebugText { fn debug_string(self) -> String }) and turns the derive into impl DebugText.Derive. A derive whose methods depend on the fields (FieldNames) or that adds only constants (LayoutFacts) has no fixed method list, so it still becomes a marker as in A.
options.technical: Adds a trait per provider with a fixed method list. Two forms remain for user code that writes methods onto a type, and jet fix must decide which one applies to each provider.

options.name: Keep a trait-less derive form
options.detail: A provider keeps a derive form without a trait, such as impl Derive for a field-less struct named after the request. Derive then has two shapes, one with a trait and one without.
options.technical: Needs a new rule for Derive on a struct, against rule 14 (a struct implements at most one of the four roles, and Derive is the trait-only role).

recommendation.why: A uses only forms that are already ratified. A derive stays tied to a trait, and code that just writes methods onto a type is a marker, which rule 6 already lets write impl blocks.
gains: No new trait or new rule.
One mechanical fix, chosen by whether a trait of that name exists.

losses.loss: Derive-only checks (the orphan rule E2711 and the derive collision checks) no longer apply to these 40 providers.
losses.mitigation: The marker rules cover the same sites, and expand output is checked like any other code.

whyNot.reason: B invents traits nobody asked for, and still needs A for providers with pasted names or only constants.
C gives Derive a second shape and breaks rule 14.

recommendation.tradeoff: Derive-only checks stop applying to trait-less providers, in exchange for using only ratified forms.

decisions.title: What the header of Jet's own errors names: the type, the E-code, or both
decisions.situation: Every Jet error is now a type with a name, such as jet.ValueTypeMismatch, and a code, such as E0112 (D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 13). Batch 2 (37eae4f5d6) changed the first line of every Jet report from Error [E0112] to Error [jet.ValueTypeMismatch], about 2,700 snapshot headers. The rest of the report still uses the code: the More: link, the closing jet explain hint and the JSON code field. Library errors have only a name, and print it as Error [web.BadPath] (D-MARKER-DIAG1). No decision says what the header of Jet's own errors shows. The vote decides that, and whether the link and hint follow it.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet error's first line name the error type, its E-code, or both?
decisions.lesson: Each Jet error has two identifiers: a stable code like E0112 and a type name like jet.ValueTypeMismatch. The first line of a report shows one of them in brackets. You write the name in #Allow(jet.FloatMoney), and jet explain accepts either. Library errors have only a name.
decisions.story: Mia gets Error [jet.ValueTypeMismatch] in her build log. The More: line under it says jet-lang.dev/e/E0112 and the last line says run jet explain E0112. She wonders whether these are three different errors. Later a warning tells her to write #Allow with a name, but the warning's link shows an L-code.

tests/ui/gate_law/allow_reason_cannot_suppress_itself.jet:1 #Allow(jet.AllowReason, ...); tests/ui_lint/*.warn headers are Warning [jet.X].

TypeScript: error TS2322. Clippy and ESLint name the rule: clippy::needless_return, no-unused-vars. Elm heads each error with a name: -- TYPE MISMATCH --.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 13: each Jet error type keeps code :: "E0xxx". D-MARKER-DIAG1 A: a library error's code is its type path by default. Its header shows Error [web.BadPath], #Allow(web.TrailingSlash) silences a lint by name, and jet explain web.BadPath works. D-DIAG-URL1 B: every error ends with a More: line, written as More: jet-lang.dev/e/<CODE>. D-DIAG-LIBLINK1 A: a library error prints More: <its link> (or: jet explain <name>), or More: jet explain <name> when it has no link. Jet's own errors keep the ratified line.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY (37eae4f5d6)

The header prints the name, except for the 24 rows the runtime can also raise, which print the code; one run can mix both. More:, the closing hint and JSON code all use the E-code. JSON has no name field, so a tool that reads JSON cannot write the #Allow name without calling jet explain. Names and codes are one to one: 1,006 rows give 1,006 codes and as many names. A name is about 23 characters long with jet. (36 at most); a code is 5.

WHAT EACH OPTION COSTS IN SNAPSHOTS

A: about 2,800 More: lines and 41 hints change, plus the runtime's report strings and the docs site's page names (old E-code addresses redirect). B: only the 24 mixed headers. C: about 2,700 headers return to codes. D and E: about 2,700 headers again, and E also changes the 2,800 More: lines. Every change is mechanical: a bless plus a generator rerun.

SEARCH

Jet's E0001-E0799 overlap rustc's numbers, so a search for E0107 or E0308 finds Rust pages (rustc E0107 is a wrong count of generic arguments; Jet E0107 is an unknown name). A dotted name such as jet.UnknownName belongs to Jet alone.

UNDER EVERY OPTION

The 24 runtime-stage rows follow the same rule as the rest. JSON reports gain a name field beside code, so agents can key on either. jet explain keeps accepting both.

decisions.title: Does the public list of compiler extension points need a vote on how a marker's expand is written?
decisions.situation: You said the code example was confusing and incomplete, so every example is now a whole file with its output beside it. The problem is simple: Mia has many structs and wants each to print a one-line summary, and a marker can write that method for her. Jet will publish one list of every place library code runs inside the compiler, saying what each may read, and this ballot asks how that list writes the marker's entry. The ratified marker rules already answer it, so the recommendation is that no vote is needed.
decisions.gist: Is a vote needed on how the public list writes a marker's expand, or do the ratified rules settle it?
decisions.lesson: A marker is written above a struct, like #Describe. While the program builds, the marker adds code to that struct, such as a describe method. Jet will publish one list that says what each such marker may read.
decisions.story: Mia has a Point struct and an Order struct, and wants each to print a summary such as Point has 2 fields. Writing describe() by hand in every struct is dull, and it goes stale when she adds a field. She writes one Describe marker instead and puts #Describe above each struct.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: comptime code reads a type's fields with plain code, and cannot read files while compiling.
Swift: a macro is a function that receives syntax nodes and returns new syntax nodes.
Rust: a procedural macro is a function from tokens to tokens, and it may read files and the network.
decisions.detail:
THE PROBLEM

Mia has many structs and wants each to print a one-line summary, such as Point has 2 fields, without writing it by hand. By hand she repeats the method in every struct, and the count goes stale when she adds a field. This file runs today:

```jet
// By hand: the same method in every struct. Runs today (probe x03_by_hand).
struct Point {
    x: Int
    y: Int

    fn describe(self) -> String { "Point has 2 fields" }
}

struct Order {
    id: Int
    total: Int
    paid: Bool

    fn describe(self) -> String { "Order has 3 fields" }
}

fn run() {
    print(Point{x: 1, y: 2}.describe())                       // Point has 2 fields
    print(Order{id: 7, total: 30, paid: true}.describe())     // Order has 3 fields
}
```

THE FIX THAT RUNS TODAY

One Describe marker writes describe() for every struct it marks. Its expand reads the struct's name and field count, and the impl block inside it is added to that struct. Option A's code is the whole file. It runs today and prints Point has 2 fields, then Order has 3 fields.

WHAT THIS BALLOT ASKS

A library marker runs inside the compiler while Mia's program builds. Mia should not have to trust a library with her files or the network. So card #6129 publishes one list of every place library code runs inside the compiler, each with a row saying what it may read. Her editor shows that row on hover.

The question is how that list writes the marker's entry. A writes the expand method exactly as the author writes it. B writes a function that returns a syntax value, which changes how every marker is written.

WHY NO VOTE IS NEEDED

The ratified rules already answer it. D-DECL-TYPES1=A rule 6 makes a marker's body the trait method expand(self, target: Target), whose body is a template. Rule 9 makes a derive fn expand(target: Target). D-CTCODEGEN1 makes added code re-enter the compiler as source. D-DERIVE-PROVIDER1=A (2026-11-04) keeps that form for derives without a trait.

The disagreeing text is Docs/proposals/effect-types-2026-10-29.md, section 9.1, lines 367-368, which list fn(Site) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax and fn(TypeInfo) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax. Its header says "Nothing here is ratified." Card #6129 criterion 44 already records amending section 9.1 to the ratified methods. Approving A changes no rule and closes this ballot.

THE LIST UNDER A

Each entry is the code its author writes, plus its row. Marker expansion is Marker.expand(self, target: Target) -[Compiler.Read]>, with a template body. A derive is Derive.expand(target: Target) -[Compiler.Read]>, with a template body. Lint, code generation and build actions keep their section 9.1 entries, which are already the functions their authors write.

WHAT B WOULD MEAN

Option B's code is the same program under B, as a whole file. It does not run, because Site, Syntax and the row are not built. Each marker would build its method from calls such as Syntax.method, instead of writing the method as code. Every existing marker and derive body would change.

WHAT RUNS TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/expand, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- x03_by_hand prints Point has 2 fields and Order has 3 fields, with describe() written in each struct.

- x04_marker_two prints the same two lines from one Describe marker. It is option A's code.

- x05_surface_a is the short A file on the summary card, and prints Point has 2 fields.

- x02_expand_reads_file: a marker whose expand reads a file is refused with E0956, "A derive template binding is not a known-time value". The published row will say the same thing in the list.

EDGE CASES

- $tname and {$names} are today's splice spelling. D-META-HASH1=A moves splices to # (card #4276 c22), jet fix rewrites them, and nothing else in these files changes.

- A marker that needs outside data, such as a file, uses the separate impure preparation entry. That entry has its own row and needs --gate impure=allow.

- A derive takes no self, because a derive request carries no data.

- The name of the row's effect, written Compiler.Read here, is settled by card #6129 itself, as criterion 44 says.

- Target is the same value T.reflect() returns for the marked item.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes #Describe above a struct and calls describe(). They never see expand or the list. An expert writes expand as a template, and tools show its row on hover. Neither path changes under A.

WHY NOT B

B rewrites every marker and derive body to build syntax values, as Swift macros do. It reopens D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 6 and 9 and needs a Syntax builder. D-CTCODEGEN1 would then require each syntax value to be printed back to source before it re-enters the compiler.

DROPPED

An earlier option kept the template but published a Syntax result in the list. Nobody writes or sees that value, so it described the code wrongly. It stays dropped.

options.name: Not needed: list the ratified expand
options.detail: No vote is needed. The ratified rules already make a marker's entry Marker.expand(self, target: Target) and a derive's entry Derive.expand(target: Target), each with a template body. The list writes every entry as the code its author writes, plus its row.
options.technical: No rule change. Covered by D-DECL-TYPES1=A rules 6 and 9, D-CTCODEGEN1 and D-DERIVE-PROVIDER1=A. Card #6129 c44 amends Docs/proposals/effect-types-2026-10-29.md section 9.1 lines 367-368 and settles the row's effect name. The core.compiler table names trait methods for marker and derive and keeps the other section 9.1 entries. Target is the reflect() value of the site. The code is probe x04_marker_two, which runs.

options.name: Functions that return Syntax
options.detail: The list writes fn(Site) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax for markers and fn(TypeInfo) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax for derives. Authors build and return a syntax value instead of writing the method as code, so every marker and derive body changes.
options.technical: Reopens D-DECL-TYPES1=A rules 6 and 9 and needs a Syntax builder library. D-CTCODEGEN1 then requires each Syntax value to be printed back to source before it re-enters the compiler. Site and TypeInfo become two input types where the ratified form has one Target.

comparisons.note: Zig reads a type's fields with plain code while compiling, as Jet's template does. This file prints main.Point has 2 fields (Zig 0.14).

recommendation.why: The ratified marker and derive rules already answer this question, and card #6129 already corrects the draft that disagreed. Approving A closes the ballot with no rule change, no code change and one uniform list.
gains: No marker, derive or app code changes.
Every list entry is the code its author writes, plus its row.
Tools still show what each marker may read.

whyNot.reason: B rewrites every marker and derive body to build syntax values, and reopens three ratified rules.

decisions.title: Sized booleans for C APIs: one ffi.Bool<U32> wrapper in core.ffi
decisions.gist: How should Jet code hold a C API's 4-byte true-or-false field, such as VkBool32 or Win32 BOOL?
decisions.lesson: Some C APIs store true or false in a fixed-width integer, such as Vulkan's 32-bit VkBool32. A shared struct must match the foreign field's size and alignment. Using an ordinary Bool can change later offsets.
decisions.story: Kai binds Vulkan's 32-bit feature flags. Using ordinary Bool fields risks wrong offsets, so he currently stores U32 and compares with zero. He wants the representation to say it is a Boolean.
decisions.inWild: Vulkan defines VkBool32 as uint32_t and requires inputs of 0 or 1 (https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/VkBool32.html). Keeping that integer in bindings is a strong zero-wrapper alternative; a wrapper can instead make Bool conversion explicit. The C declaration alone does not distinguish a boolean typedef from an ordinary integer typedef.
decisions.detail:
Exercised with admitted jet: b1.jet gives E0119 for B32; b2.jet prints true using U32 != 0. BallotReview/integer-condition.jet gives E0110 for if on U32. Thus C does not silently accept a forgotten condition comparison. ForeignLink.jet:406 maps Bool to _Bool for inline C scalars; that is not proof of every foreign layout or of C bool's size on every ABI.

A adds an ordinary exact-representation core.ffi wrapper under PRIMS1. ffi.Bool<T> accepts fixed-width signed or unsigned integers, preserving T's size, alignment and scalar call/return ABI. Win32 BOOL's signed storage must not be silently replaced with unsigned storage. Structs, arrays, pointers, callbacks and by-value arguments/results all need foreign round-trip proofs; matching size alone is insufficient.

get() returns false for zero and true for nonzero without modifying the stored bits. Constructing from Bool stores 0 or 1. Equality and hashing use the normalized Bool together, so 1 and 2 compare/hash consistently. Fixed-width storage has no invalid Bool bit pattern; never reinterpret noncanonical integers as native Bool. Unsupported T is a registered error.

The binder wraps only declarations whose Boolean meaning is established by a supported schema or explicit binding annotation. It cannot infer Boolean intent from an arbitrary int typedef. Vulkan inputs must still be 0 or 1; its outputs are specified as 0 or 1, so a returned 2 is not a valid Vulkan example. General C BOOL-style nonzero truth is a different API contract.

B adds four compiler-known names. C retains exact integer storage and explicit comparisons, already checked as Bool conditions by Jet. A's benefit is readable typed conversion, not repairing an existing truthiness hole. Plain code keeps Bool; experts choose exact storage through the same public FFI representation mechanism. No new built-in type or binder-only privilege is authorized.

options.name: One wrapper in core.ffi
options.detail: ffi.Bool<U32> preserves U32's representation and explicitly converts with get(). Signed foreign boolean storage uses the matching signed T. The binder needs evidence of Boolean meaning.

options.detail: B8, B16, B32 and B64 are built in, as in Odin, and convert to Bool.

options.name: No new type
options.detail: Bindings keep the exact declared integer and compare it with zero. No wrapper is required for ABI correctness.

recommendation.why: C structs get the exact size and still read as true or false. Only foreign code sees it, so the beginner's type list stays Int, Float, Bool and String.
gains: Exact C layout with Bool reads.
No new built-in names for beginners.

losses.loss: Reads need .get() instead of using the field directly.
losses.mitigation: An if or && on the field gives an error whose fix adds .get().

whyNot.reason: Four built-in names that only C bindings need, in every program's type list.
C is ABI-simple and already rejects an integer condition; it repeats the zero comparison instead of naming the Boolean representation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library wrapper with a .get() call instead of new built-in types.

decisions.title: Run-time type values: a comparable reflect.TypeKey in core.reflect
decisions.gist: How should a running Jet program name a type as a value, for example to key a map by type?
decisions.lesson: A type-keyed table needs a value identifying the exact type. Jet's current reflection gives display names and paths, which are strings, not an exact portable identity contract.
decisions.story: Rui keeps component counts by type. A reflected path works for his small program, but he wants exact identity across generic instances and separately loaded packages, without relying on display text.
decisions.inWild: Rust's opaque TypeId is comparable and hashable, with release-dependent hash/order and no stable layout (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/any/struct.TypeId.html). Its documentation warns that identity-based abstractions still need correct variance. A Jet key must similarly be more than a hash of a printable path.
decisions.detail:
Exercised: t1 prints Point, t1.Point, Int and true; t2 reports E0107 for TypeId; t3's string-keyed map prints 2. Core/Reflect/Reflect.jet has text inspection, while typed of is compiler-projected. Calls/Reflection.jet:48-57 builds display paths from module path and name, even replacing hyphens with underscores. That is not a globally unique or persistent type identity proof.

A adds an opaque TypeKey projection of the compiler's existing canonical type identity, not a second identity registry inferred from display strings. reflect.key<T>() and reflect.of(x).key() agree for x's static concrete type T. Existing reflect.of visibility/secret/display restrictions remain; key<T>() itself does not render a value. A key for Any names the box type; Any.key() separately names its stored concrete payload.

Aliases share the underlying identity; distinct nominal types differ even with identical layout or path text. Generic type/value arguments and complete callable types participate in the existing canonical identity. Two separately loaded package identities cannot collide merely because their paths match. Hash collisions must still compare full identity. Keys cannot be forged from integers, pointers or strings, and equality alone grants no value access or cast authority.

Keys are meaningful only within one linked program/session identity domain. Do not serialize them as a cross-build protocol. No Encode/Decode or integer conversion is provided, but Display remains printable, so lack of Encode cannot prevent users saving its text. Paths are diagnostic names, not promised stable schema IDs. Applications needing persistence must own versioned schema identifiers.

Dynamically loaded metadata must outlive retained keys; unload/reload must not reuse an identity for a different type or leave dangling display pointers. Use the same managed descriptor lifetime as reflection and Any. This metadata retention is a real cost; exact key comparison is not a measured speedup over string maps. No per-key heap allocation is required for statically linked types.

B makes Type a runtime value kind and must explicitly reconcile compile-time type contracts; an archived decision is not authority to dismiss it. C can compute both map keys from reflect.of rather than type path literals, avoiding the draft's alleged unavoidable typo. C still lacks an exact identity guarantee. Beginners need neither API; experts get exact comparison without a new top-level language value kind.

options.name: TypeKey in core.reflect
options.detail: An opaque key projects canonical type identity. Same concrete type means equal keys; different nominal types or generic instances remain distinct. Keys are session-local, not a persistent schema format.

options.name: A built-in Type value
options.detail: Type is a built-in value kind, and type_of(x) returns it, as in Jai and Odin.

options.name: Keep path strings
options.detail: No new value. Programs key by reflect.of(x).path(), as t3.jet does today.

recommendation.why: A small key covers maps keyed by type and checked unboxing. It lives in the reflection library next to type_name and path, so the language gains no new value kind.
gains: Exact opaque identity rather than display-name identity.
No new built-in value kind.

losses.loss: Keys are not a persistent or cross-program schema identifier and may retain type metadata.
losses.mitigation: Expose no serialization conversion; print a diagnostic path, and keep descriptor lifetimes managed by the shared reflection mechanism.

whyNot.reason: B is a broader runtime-Type design, not forbidden by an archived record; A meets this exact-identity use without making all types runtime values.
C can avoid path typos by deriving keys from values, but display paths still have no exact identity guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library key fixed per build instead of a built-in Type value.

Before delivery, check aliases, distinct types, generic values/types, same-path package versions, callable identities, hash collisions, metadata lifetime and plugin unload/reload. No current performance advantage is claimed.

decisions.title: Pointer-sized integers for C layouts: ffi.USize and ffi.ISize in core.ffi
decisions.situation:
A C library describes sizes and offsets with size_t, ssize_t, ptrdiff_t, uintptr_t and intptr_t. Their width depends on the target: 64 bits on x86-64 and AArch64, and 32 bits on wasm32. Jet has no type for them today, so both hand bindings and the header binder write U64 or I64, which is wrong on a 32-bit target.

This ballot adds two target-sized types to the ratified FFI building-block package, the way sized booleans were added. It leaves Int as Jet's one everyday integer. Keeping today's fixed widths is option C.
decisions.gist: Should core.ffi add USize and ISize, sized to the target, so a C binding is right on 32-bit and 64-bit targets?
decisions.lesson: C programs describe memory sizes with types whose width depends on the machine. A binding that guesses the width gets the struct layout wrong on other machines. This vote decides how Jet bindings name those types, without changing the Int that everyday code uses.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A binding is Jet code that describes a C library's functions and structs. A layout is the size and position of each field in memory. The target is the machine a program is built for.

A pointer-sized integer is as wide as a memory address on the target: 64 bits on most desktops, 32 bits on wasm32.
decisions.story: Noor binds a C buffer whose length is a size_t. She writes U64, and the binding works on her laptop. Built for wasm32, every field after the length sits four bytes off.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How Jet code names C's target-sized integers in bindings and #Layout(c) structs. It does not change Int, list lengths or indexes.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe u02 writes USize{8} and gets E0119, UnknownType: there is no type called USize. Probe u03 declares a #Layout(c) struct with a U64 length, converts it with Int{b.len}, and prints count 3.

Probe u01 converts U64{18446744073709551615} with I64{big} and stops with E3010, value doesn't fit in destination type, rc 70. Probe u04 calls I64.from_u64 on the same value and gets an error result: value doesn't fit in destination type. Conversions are checked; the -1 results reported in Docs/research/2026-10-30-type-conversions.md no longer happen.

The binder hard-codes the 64-bit answer. Dev's C header binder maps size_t and uintptr_t to U64, and ssize_t and intptr_t to I64, on every target (Jetpack PackageModel Foreign/C/HeaderParser.jet:521-522). It has no row for ptrdiff_t. So a generated binding is wrong on wasm32 today, not only a hand one.

The rule under A. core.ffi gains two types. ffi.USize is the target's unsigned pointer-sized integer, and ffi.ISize the signed one. On x86-64 and AArch64 they are 64 bits; on wasm32 they are 32 bits. Their width, sign, alignment and calling-convention class come from the target's C facts, not from the host compiling the program.

Which C names map to them. The binder resolves size_t, ssize_t, uintptr_t, ptrdiff_t and intptr_t separately from the target's C facts, replacing HeaderParser's fixed rows. It uses ffi.USize or ffi.ISize only when the width, sign, alignment and calling class match exactly. On a target where they differ, such as one where uintptr_t is wider than size_t, the binder emits the exact fixed-width type and says why.

Arithmetic. ffi.USize and ffi.ISize are fixed-width integers, so they share D-FIXED-WRAP1's rules: + stops on overflow, and wrapping(...), saturating(...) and checked(...) are the explicit forms. A binding can add offsets and compare lengths without leaving the type.

Into Int and back. The conversions are the ones probes u01 and u04 exercise. Int{n} stops if the value does not fit, and checked(Int{n}) returns an outcome you can handle, per D-FIXED-WRAP1, which retires today's I64.from_u64. ffi.USize{i} from a negative Int stops, and so does a narrowing on a 32-bit target. No conversion ever wraps or drops high bits.

Migration. Regenerated bindings change size_t from U64 to ffi.USize. On x86-64 and AArch64 the width, alignment and calling class are identical, so no 64-bit layout changes. Int{b.len} keeps working. Code that mixes the field with U64 values gets a type error, and jet fix writes the U64{…} conversion.

Why the overflow case is rare. An ffi.USize that measures real memory, a length or an offset, always fits Int, because no target's address space reaches 2^63 bytes. The value that does not fit is a sentinel such as SIZE_MAX, which C uses for not found. Compare it with ffi.USize.MAX before converting, as the C code does.

Addresses. Holding an address in ffi.USize grants no right to read it; turning it back into a pointer stays an unsafe step under D-FFI-PRIMS1 and #Unsafe(reason). All tiers, the interpreter, the JIT and native builds, use the same target facts, so a layout and a conversion behave the same everywhere.

Delivery proof, part of building A: compare size, sign, alignment and calling class with the C compiler for structs, arrays, by-value arguments and results, and callbacks, on x86-64, AArch64 and wasm32. The wasm32-wasip2 build is not implemented on the seed (E2104, #6418), so A's 32-bit claims are a contract for that target, not a measurement.

Beginner path. Everyday code never sees these types: counts, lengths and indexes stay Int. Generated bindings use ffi.USize where C says size_t, and one checked conversion turns it into an Int.

Expert path. A hand-written binding uses ffi.USize and ffi.ISize directly and gets the right layout on every supported target from one source. Sentinels are compared in ffi.USize before conversion.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A conversion from ffi.USize to Int can fail. For real sizes it cannot, as above; for sentinels, the comparison comes first. The checked conversion stops with file and line, never with a wrong number.

Two more names in core.ffi. They follow ffi.Bool<U32>'s pattern, so a binder or reader already knows where C-only types live.

Other options. B builds USize and ISize into the language and makes them the type of lengths and indexes, as Rust does. C keeps today's form: the binder writes the exact fixed width, U64 or U32, per target, and hand bindings choose it themselves. D adds one name per C typedef, ffi.SizeT, ffi.PtrDiffT, ffi.UIntPtrT and ffi.IntPtrT, as Rust's libc crate does.

B mixes Int and USize in every program that touches a list, which is the conversion noise Rust users know. C needs one hand binding per target width. D is exact for every typedef but gives four names where every supported target needs two.

options.name: ffi.USize and ffi.ISize in core.ffi
options.detail: Two target-sized types in core.ffi for bindings and C layouts. Int stays the everyday integer, and checked conversions cross between them.
options.technical: Extends D-FFI-PRIMS1=A like D-PRIM-BOOLSIZE1=A. Width, sign, alignment and calling class come from target C facts. The binder maps size_t, ssize_t, uintptr_t, ptrdiff_t and intptr_t separately, replacing HeaderParser.jet's fixed U64/I64 rows, and uses the alias only on an exact match. D-FIXED-WRAP1 arithmetic; existing checked conversions.

options.name: Built-in USize as the type of lengths
options.detail: USize and ISize are built in, and list lengths and indexes use USize, as in Rust.
options.technical: Adds two primitive types and changes len() and indexing to USize across Core. Every program that mixes lengths with Int arithmetic converts.

options.name: Keep fixed widths per target
options.detail: No new type. The binder learns to write U64 or U32 from the target's C facts; today it writes U64 everywhere. A hand binding chooses the width for each target it supports.
options.technical: No change to core.ffi. HeaderParser.jet's fixed rows become target lookups. Hand bindings that support several widths need one declaration per width, chosen by #if on the target.

options.name: One name per C typedef
options.detail: core.ffi adds ffi.SizeT, ffi.PtrDiffT, ffi.UIntPtrT and ffi.IntPtrT, each exactly its C typedef on the target.
options.technical: Four target-derived types, distinct even where they share a width, as Rust's libc crate names them. No mapping rule is needed in the binder.

whyNot.reason: B puts USize into every program that touches a list, with conversions everywhere.
C needs a separate hand binding for each target width.
D gives four names where every supported target needs two.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two C-only types in core.ffi, in return for layouts that are right on every target.

decisions.title: Types as values and type switches, amending the ratified TypeKey
decisions.situation:
A ratified rule gives a running program an opaque key object that carries a type's exact identity; it is not built yet. The owner later asked why types as values would be a downside, since they allow switches on types. This ballot offers that: a type's own name becomes a value of type Type where a Type is expected.

Option A amends the ratified key and two reflection rules: that types stay types, and that one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the ratified key. The owner's question is not itself a ratification.
decisions.gist: Should a type name be usable as a value of type Type, so programs can key maps and switch on types?
decisions.lesson: A running program sometimes needs to treat a type as data: count game components by type, or pick a handler for each kind of message. Today Jet has an approved but unbuilt key object for that. This vote decides whether the type's own name can be that value instead, with a switch on it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A type's identity is what makes two types the same or different; Box<Int> and Box<String> differ, and two names for one type agree. A type switch picks an arm by a type's identity. It does not convert a value.

A descriptor is the small record a running program keeps for one type's identity. Type info, under D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1, is the larger record of fields and methods kept for reflection.
decisions.story: Rui writes a game whose systems count components by type and describe each kind. Today the display path of a value's type is his only key, and probe k07 shows Box<Int> and Box<String> print the same path. He wants to write counts[Position] and a switch on the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a running program names a type with a Type value whose source spelling is the type's own name, and switches on it. It amends D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A, which chose an opaque reflect.TypeKey. It also amends two rules of D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1: types stay types, and one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the key as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Generic type switches work: k01's if T == { } prints a different line for each component type, and k02 and k03 fail with E0003 without else. k07 shows reflect.of(x).path() is the same for Box<Int> and Box<String>. t: Rock is E0636, TypeAsValue (p09), and type_of is E0102 (k08, p08).

More facts on t6c. The ratified TypeKey is not built: dev has no TypeKey or reflect.key in any Jet file. A user type named Type is legal (k05), and a local declaration can shadow a Prelude name such as Dyn (k04). p05 shows a closed enum switch with no else. None of these probes runs A, B's key or E.

The rule under A. Type is a Prelude type whose values are type identities. A bare type name is a Type value only where a Type is expected. Those places are a parameter, field or result of type Type, a [Type: V] map key and a [Type] list element. They also include the other side of == with a Type, and a switch pattern on a Type.

Anywhere else a bare type name stays a type, so t: Rock is still E0636. Its fix offers Rock{…} for a value, or Type{Rock} for a Type value, the same typed-literal form as U8{1}. So a missing constructor brace can never bind a Type by accident, but a Type-accepting call still accepts any type identity, whether intended or not.

Identity. Two Type values are equal when they name the same type, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 already requires. Aliases agree. Nominal types differ even with equal fields. Generic instances differ by their arguments. A function type's identity is its full signature, as D-META-REFLECT2's CallableSignature records it: parameter types and passing modes, result, error contract, effect row, calling convention and generic bindings.

Callable identity reuses canonical sema equality, including labels, zones, access modes, view provenance and identity-bearing policies. Defaults remain facts, not evaluated identity inputs. A Type value grants no authority: it cannot construct, cast, call, or reach private members. It is a plain value that compares, hashes, prints and can be sent between tasks.

type_of. type_of(x) gives the static type of x, worked out while compiling. Its argument must be a name or a field path such as p or p.pos. A call or other expression is an error whose fix is to bind the value first. So type_of reads no value, borrows nothing, runs nothing and has no effects.

Erased values. For a value whose static type is an erased carrier, such as Dyn, a trait value or the Any of D-PRIM-ANY1, type_of gives the carrier's type, never the payload's. The payload's identity comes from the carrier itself, as box.type under D-PRIM-ANY1. So one name never means two different things.

Type switches. if t == { Position -> … else -> … } on a Type value compares identity at run time, arm by arm. Type is an open set, so else is required, as for generic switches today. A duplicate arm is an error. The switch binds no payload; taking a payload out of an erased value is the Any ballot's job. if T == { } on a generic parameter stays a compile-time choice.

Printing and names. print(t) shows the type's full package path, such as game.Position or game.Box<Int>. When two linked packages share a path, such as two versions of one package, the display adds the version. Equality never compares display text, so a display collision cannot make two types equal. Version alone may not distinguish separately loaded packages with equal name and version; display also needs a package-identity qualifier then.

Reflection, an explicit amendment. D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 lets one reflect call handle every value. A amends that for one written type: reflect(t), where t is written with static type Type, is a compile error. The error says t names a type, and offers t.info() for the type it names, or reflect(Type) for the info of Type itself.

Inside generic code, reflect(x) on a parameter of type T keeps its value meaning even when T is Type. It then gives the info of Type itself, an opaque Prelude type with no public fields. So a generic helper never reads a Type value as if it were the type it names.

The schema. t.info() returns the same reflection value that reflect(T) returns for the type t names, or an InfoError. InfoError has two cases, each naming the type and its package. NotKept means the image that declares the type kept no info for it. Unloaded means that package's code has been released. The Type value itself is inspected with print(t), ==, hashing, and reflect(Type).

The strongest same-call alternative makes reflect(t) reflect the type t names, with no second operation. It is shorter. But then either reflect's meaning depends on whether the call sits in generic code, or a generic helper reads a Type value as a Position. A refuses only the written case that would mislead. E shares A's rule; B and F leave reflect unchanged.

A Type value is one word. It is the same 56-bit key of canonical identity that dev's trait values already carry in their first word (JetIR BuildTraits.jet), and the key D-PRIM-ANY1's box checks. Equality is one compare, and hashing reads the word. Two identities sharing a key stop the build, and keys of separately built packages are compared at load.

What the program keeps, by setting. Each type that becomes a Type value keeps a descriptor holding its key and display path, under every setting including none. Fields and methods are not in it. Under none, t.info() is a registered compile error naming the type_info setting.

Under requested, the default, reflect calls keep what D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 says. A program that calls t.info() also keeps the type info of every type that becomes a Type value somewhere in it. The build report lists those types and their sizes, so the cost is visible. reachable and full keep their ratified retention rules.

Descriptors across packages. Each type identity has one descriptor per process. The linker merges descriptors by identity: canonical package identity including checked content, module path, declaration revision, then generic type and value arguments, recursively. A package loaded while running adds its descriptors to the process table and reuses any that already exist.

Packages loaded while running. Each image, the program or a loaded package, keeps type info by its own build's rules. A package built for loading keeps info for every type it exports or makes into a Type value, since its loader may call t.info(). Its build report lists that cost. Kept info includes the field type graph, transitively, as D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1's type graphs do.

Privacy. t.info() shows the members visible to the calling code: public members always, and package-private ones only when the caller is in the type's own package. The check compares package identities at run time, so a Type value from a loaded package grants no new access.

Code lifetime. A type info value holds method, default and body references into its package's code, and so does a function value. The loader counts these references for each loaded package. Unloading retires a package at once for new lookups, but its code and info stay resident until that count reaches zero. Type values hold only descriptors, so they never keep code alive.

After release, t.info() on that package's types returns Unloaded, and no stale method reference can run. Descriptors are never freed, so unloading cannot leave a Type value pointing at nothing. Identity is session-local, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 says: it is not a format to store or send between processes.

Hot reload. A type's identity includes its declaration revision and the identities of its field types, recursively; mutually recursive types are hashed as one group. When Position's shape changes, every type that holds a Position, such as Box<Position>, gets a new identity too. A type whose transitive field types are unchanged keeps its identity.

The real cost of never freeing descriptors, and its bound. Only hot reload grows the table: a reload that changes no type's shape adds nothing, and a release program never reloads. As an unmeasured estimate, 1,000 reloads that each change 50 types keep 50,000 descriptors of a key and a path, a few megabytes.

A jet dev restart frees them, and D-DEV-STATE1=A keeps every #Persist value across that restart. A loaded package adds its descriptors once per distinct identity, so loading the same package again adds none.

The name Type. A user declaration named Type shadows the Prelude Type in its own module, as k04 shows for Dyn; core.Type stays reachable. The census finds one user declaration named Type, in Compiler. jet fix offers a rename, by declaration identity.

Migration from the ratified key. reflect.TypeKey becomes Type, reflect.key<T>() becomes T in a Type context or Type{T}, and reflect.of(x).key() becomes type_of(x). The old names are removed in the same change, with no aliases. The census finds no use of TypeKey or reflect.key in code, because the key is not built, so the code migration is empty.

Other counts, by git grep -c on dev. There are 59 calls to reflect.of in 29 files, which keep working, and 6 mentions of type_of in 3 files. The seed's census found 12 generic type switches, which keep working. These are regex counts.

Beginner path. Write counts[Position] = 2 and if t == { Position -> … }. If you write t: Rock by mistake, the error offers Rock{…} or Type{Rock}.

Expert path. Function types, generic instances and types from loaded packages all have exact identity. The build report lists what t.info() keeps, and type_info none forbids it. t.info() returns NotKept or Unloaded instead of guessing, and an unloaded package's code stays resident while any info or function value still refers to it.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A program that calls t.info() keeps type info for every type it makes into a Type value. The build report names that cost, and generic reflect(T) avoids it. Descriptors are never freed, so repeated hot reloads grow memory without bound until the dev process restarts.

Type joins the Prelude, so a user type named Type now shadows it; that affects one declaration in the tree. A bare type name is a value in some places and a type in others. Those places are exactly where a Type is expected, and every other place reports E0636 with both fixes. reflect(t) on a written Type is refused, so reflection gains a second operation, t.info().

Option B in full. Keep D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A: reflect.TypeKey, reflect.key<T>() and reflect.of(x).key(), with the same exact identity, session-local meaning and descriptor lifetime. Branching uses chains of if key == comparisons; there is no type switch on a key. Nothing is migrated, and type names never appear in value position.

Option C repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1. Maps are keyed by display paths from reflect.of(x).path(), derived rather than typed by hand. Two types with the same path collide, as k07 shows for generic instances. D also repeals the runtime key and keeps only generic switches on type parameters, so a runtime registry falls back to paths.

Option E. Runtime Type handles and type switches through a library constructor: reflect.type<T>() makes a reflect.Type, and type_of(x) returns one. Type names stay types except in switch patterns. It shares A's identity, retention and descriptor rules, and replaces TypeKey rather than living beside it.

Alternative F separates two choices that A bundles: exact-key switching and bare type names as values. Its only new surface is a checked comparison table on TypeKey. Its descriptors and lifetime are the ratified key mechanism, not another type representation.

options.technical: Amends D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A and two D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 rules: types stay types, and one reflect call for every value. reflect(t) on a written Type is refused, and t.info() returns info or an InfoError, NotKept or Unloaded. Prelude Type keeps D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's identity, including full callable signatures and transitive field identities. Bare names are Type values only in Type contexts. Descriptors are linker-merged, never freed and kept under every type_info setting; loaded code stays resident while info or function values refer to it.

options.name: Keep the ratified reflect.TypeKey

options.technical: No decision changes. The key has D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's exact identity, session-local meaning and managed descriptor lifetime. There is no runtime type switch; comparisons are explicit.

options.name: Repeal exact keys; key maps by display path

options.name: Compile-time type switches only

options.technical: Repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's runtime key, not D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1's run-time reflection. A generic switch cannot serve a registry built while the program runs.

options.name: Runtime type handles made by a library call

options.technical: Replaces TypeKey with reflect.Type, sharing A's identity, descriptor and retention rules. No Prelude name is added and no type name appears in value position outside a switch pattern.

options.name: Keep TypeKey and add a checked key switch

options.technical: Extend key comparison tables, not the identity mechanism. Evaluate the subject once. Arm keys are build-known reflect.key<T>() expressions; compare canonical identity, reject duplicate keys, and require else. No payload is bound. Keep TYPEKEY1 and REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 retention unchanged.
