decisions.title: Core gets no private powers: every list Jet knows is a Core trait that any package can add to
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler keeps many lists of library things it knows by name, such as the checked text kinds SQL and HTML, or the data formats. Core's members of those lists get powers a package cannot reach. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A, ratified, already fixed this for checked text. This vote decides whether the same rule holds for every list. We recommend yes: each list becomes a Core trait, and Core adds its members exactly as a package would.
decisions.gist: Should every list of library things the compiler knows become a Core trait that Core and packages extend the same way?
decisions.lesson: A list here is a set of library things the compiler knows, such as the kinds of checked text. Today Core's members are written into the compiler, and a package's members are weaker. Under A each list is a Core trait. Core and packages add members with the same `impl`, so they get the same powers.
decisions.story: Mira writes a graph database package. Her users write `graph.Cypher{"...{age}..."}` just as they write `SQL{"...{age}..."}`. Under A her kind checks the query while compiling and sends 18 as a bound value, exactly like SQL. She changed nothing in Jet to get there.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today Mira's package can check `Cypher{"..."}` while compiling, but each hole becomes text. Probe probe/ext/arch_a.jet prints `MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.age > $p RETURN p`, so the 18 is lost. Pasting it instead invites injection. Core's SQL keeps 18 as a bound value only because the compiler knows SQL by name (Facts/Checked.jet:90-101).

With A. The user writes the same literal. Jet runs graph's check while compiling, then calls graph's build. The query goes out as `$p0` with the value 18 beside it. Core's SQL uses the same two members and gains nothing extra. The compiler's TypedHeadKind list is deleted. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A, ratified, supplies the two members.

Why it matters. A package can match Core, so a database, shell or markup package is as safe as Core's own. Core feels every gap in a trait first, so gaps get fixed for everyone. Name lists also misfire. Facts/Checked.jet:96 tests `name == "SQL"`, so today any type named SQL gets Core's SQL handling.

What A says. Every list of library things in the compiler becomes a Core trait. A member is a type with `impl Member.Trait`, and its settings are trait constants, as D-DECL-TYPES1 A ratified. No new declaration word is added. The compiler reads impls, never library names. lane-check fails any new name list and names the trait to use.

Already moved. D-DECL-TYPES1 A moved markers, effects, facts, derives and Jet's 996 diagnostic rows to Core traits. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A moved checked text. What remains are smaller lists, such as data formats (Core/Encoding/Encoding.jet:77). The 2026-10-29 census found 1,145 such lists, about 30,700 members, before those two decisions.

What stays closed, on purpose. Grammar and keywords, IR operations, soundness rules, ABI and layout, output kinds, and data fixed by an outside standard, such as Unicode tables. A package adding to these could break the language for everyone. Each has one ledger row with its reason. Opening one takes an owner ballot. Compiler facts stay Prelude-only too (D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 12).

Downsides, designed away. Matches: code never matches over an open list; behavior is a trait method, and the trait's checklist makes every new member complete. Plain data enums stay closed and exhaustive. Speed: Core's impls stay pre-generated into compiler tables (D-OPENTABLE1 D). A package's impls are read once per build, only when imported. A member known while compiling is called directly. One chosen at run time costs one trait-slot call, with no box (Examples/features/traits/trait_value_slots.jet).

Downsides, designed away, continued. Trust: compile-time members are pure (`-[]>`) and run sandboxed (D-META-HOLD1), and laws travel with the trait (D-CORE-LAWS1). A package's failing check is reported in its own name at the user's line, never as a Jet crash. Clashes: members are named by package path. Tools read impls as declarations, without running package code.

Option B, plugins. Each list gets a WebAssembly plugin interface, as Roslyn analyzers and Kotlin compiler plugins work. A plugin can be in any language and can see raw tokens. But it is a second extension system beside impls. Every use is a sandbox call, and the editor sees members only while the plugin runs.

Option C, two tiers. Packages get the open traits, but Core keeps its remaining lists as closed enums, as Swift's standard library keeps private attributes. Core keeps exhaustive matches over its own lists. A package needing a new format must ask for a Core change. Checked text has already left this tier through D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A.

Research. Prettier writes its built-in languages through the same plugin interface outside plugins use (prettier.io/docs/plugins). Elixir protocols stay open to every package, and the build fixes each protocol's impls once (hexdocs.pm/elixir/Protocol.html). Julia's open methods are resolved without a fixed set per build. Loading one package can force thousands of methods to recompile (julialang.org/blog/2020/08/invalidations).

Probes. The files are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ext. On arch_a.jet, `jet run` prints the query with `$p`, which shows today's lost value. On arch_bad.jet, `jet check` shows E2712 for a literal without RETURN. So package checks already run while compiling. `type Hole` and `build` are D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A's features; trait constants are D-DECL-TYPES1 A's.

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It found the old v1 language unreadable and the Cypher gain already ratified elsewhere. So v2 states what remains: every other list, with each downside matched to a ratified mechanism.

options.name: Every list is a Core trait
options.detail:
Each list of library things the compiler knows becomes a Core trait. Core and packages add members the same way, with `impl Member.Trait` and trait constants. The compiler never tests a library name.

Users see no change. A package's Cypher gets the same bound values as Core's SQL. Grammar, soundness and machine code stay closed, each with a written reason.
options.technical: Every domain list becomes a Core trait; members are types with impl Member.Trait, settings are trait constants (D-DECL-TYPES1 A). Compiler and tools read impls. Core impls stay generated into tables (D-OPENTABLE1 D); package impls join per build from interface records. TypedHeadKind (Facts/Checked.jet:90) is deleted. A closed-list ledger names each kernel list with a reason class. lane-check fails new name lists; the baseline may only shrink.

options.name: Compiler plugins
options.detail:
Each list gets a plugin interface. A package ships a sandboxed WebAssembly component, and the compiler loads it during the build, as Roslyn loads analyzers.

A plugin may be written in any language and can see raw tokens. It is a second extension system beside impls, and every use is a sandbox call.
options.technical: Each list gets a component interface loaded with plugin.load<I>(path, authority, sha256) (D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1). The compiler calls the component at each use. Members are not Jet declarations, so the editor, jet inspect and API snapshots must run the component. I9 requires each component to agree on every tier.

options.name: Core keeps its other lists
options.detail:
Checked text stays open, as D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A ratified. Core's other lists, such as data formats, stay closed enums inside Core, generated from one home so copies cannot drift.

Core keeps exhaustive matches over its lists. A package that needs a new member asks for a Core change.
options.technical: D-OPENTABLE1 D as it stands: each Core list has one declared home, and compiler tables are generated from it. The CI guard blocks hand copies but not closed lists. The compiler may still branch on Core names for lists other than checked text.

comparisons.note: Built-in languages use the same plugin interface as outside plugins. Source: https://prettier.io/docs/plugins
Protocols stay open to every package, and the build fixes the set of impls for speed. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/elixir/Protocol.html
The standard library uses private attributes such as @_semantics that packages cannot use; this is option C's shape. Source: swift/docs/ReferenceGuides/UnderscoredAttributes.md
Open methods without a fixed set per build: loading one package could force thousands of methods to compile again. Source: https://julialang.org/blog/2020/08/invalidations/

recommendation.why: A gives packages exactly Core's powers, in the trait shape you ratified. Every downside is covered by a ratified mechanism. Users see no new syntax.
gains: A package's Cypher is as safe as Core's SQL.
A new format or lint needs no compiler change.
No compiler code tests a library name.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second extension system and a sandbox call at each use, for cases impls already cover.
C keeps packages weaker than Core for every list but checked text.

recommendation.tradeoff: The remaining lists move one card at a time; until a list moves, packages cannot add to it.

decisions.title: A checked text kind can build a typed value from its parts and holes
decisions.situation: A checked text literal such as `SQL{"… {age} …"}` has fixed text with holes for values. Core's SQL turns each hole into a bound database value instead of pasting it into the text, which is what stops injection. A package's kind cannot do this: today every hole becomes more text. The vote picks how any kind, Core's or a package's, may keep its holes as values. We recommend two optional members on the existing CheckedText trait, so simple kinds stay as they are.
decisions.gist: How should a checked text kind keep its {holes} as typed values instead of pasting them in as text?
decisions.lesson: A checked text literal is fixed text with `{holes}` for values. Pasting a value into text is how injection bugs start, so Core's SQL keeps each hole as a separate bound value. Packages cannot do that today. This vote picks how any text kind may do it. Kinds that only need text, which is most of them, write nothing new.
decisions.story: Mira's graph package defines `Cypher{"…"}`. Her users write `Cypher{"MATCH (p) WHERE p.age > {age} RETURN p"}`. The database must receive `$p0` in the text and the number 18 beside it, never the text `18` pasted in. Core's SQL already works this way; her kind should work the same way, with no second concept to learn.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Split out of the D-EXTEND-ARCH1 package ballot so the owner votes on the architecture and on this mechanism separately. Ratified D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1=A made checked text an ordinary String-backed type with one CheckedText impl. This ballot adds how a kind keeps its holes as values. Rebuilt after Main's review: one trait, not a second one.

Today. Core's SQL is `struct SQL { text, values }` built by `__sql_literal(literals: [String], values: [DBValue])` (Core/Db/Db.jet:245-264), which is option A's build kept private. The compiler converts each SQL hole to a DBValue by name (Sema/Expressions/Constructors.jet:1692-1719). A package kind has only `encode_hole`, which must return String (E0112 at Constructors.jet:1151). When a hole is a run-time value, `check` runs while the program runs (Examples/features/text/checked_text_runtime_hole.jet).

The check moves fully to compile time under A. It sees the fixed text with `{}` for each hole, once per literal. A run-time check failure (checked_text_runtime_hole_stop.jet) can no longer happen. A kind whose rule depends on a hole's value, such as a length limit, enforces it in `encode_hole` or `build` instead.

The probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ext. holes_a.jet runs option A's build body as a plain function and prints the `$p0` query. holes_b.jet does the same for option B's steps. trait_defaults2.jet shows default method bodies work today. trait_defaults.jet shows a default associated type is E0003 today. self_static.jet shows `-> Self` from a static trait method is E0108 today (card #6284). zip.jet shows lists have no `enumerate` (E0311), so build keeps one index loop.

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A, Core's SQL, Sh and HTML become ordinary impls of the winning form, and their compiler lowering is deleted. Under D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C, A or B here serves packages only. Option C here composes only with D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C. D-SQL-SCRIPT1 shows SQL text in scripts; its holes behave as picked here.

options.name: Two optional members on CheckedText
options.detail:
CheckedText keeps its name and its two methods. It gains two optional members. `type Hole` says what a hole becomes; it is text unless the kind says otherwise. `build` receives the fixed parts and the holes and returns the kind's value; unless the kind writes it, it joins them into text as today.

A text kind writes exactly what it writes today. A kind that binds values names its hole type and writes `build`. `check` sees the literal with each hole shown as `{}`, so every literal is checked while compiling, never while running.
options.technical:
Prelude/core/prelude.jet:19-23 gains `type Hole = String` and `fn build(parts: [String], holes: ^[Hole]) -[]> Self { … }` with a default body that joins. `encode_hole` returns `Hole`. Two small language features: a default associated type (today `type Hole = String` in a trait is E0003, probe/ext/trait_defaults.jet) and a static method returning Self (E0108, card #6284). Default method bodies already work (trait_defaults2.jet).

`Kind{"…"}` lowers to `Kind.build(PARTS, [Kind.encode_hole(h1), …])` with PARTS a module constant. `check` runs once per literal at compile time on PARTS joined by `{}`. Core's SQL, Sh and HTML become ordinary impls, and the name-based lowering in Sema/Expressions/Constructors.jet:1692-1719 is deleted. Core has no list `enumerate` or zip today (probe/ext/zip.jet: E0311), so build keeps one index loop.

options.name: Append pieces in order
options.detail:
This is Swift's design. The compiler starts from the kind's empty value, then calls `literal` for each fixed part and the hole step for each hole, in source order. A text kind keeps the default steps, which append text.

Nothing is collected first, and each hole sees all the text before it, which suits HTML escaping by context. A binding kind needs an empty starting value, and its steps change it in place.
options.technical: CheckedText gains `fn literal(&self, part: String) -[]>` and an `&self` form of the hole step, each with a default body. `Kind{"…"}` lowers to `k := Kind{}; &k.literal(p0); &k.encode_hole(h1); …`. Every field needs a default, written `values: [DBValue]{[]}` (probe/ext/holes_b_default.jet; `[DBValue]{}` there is E0003, card #6285). Core's SQL, Sh and HTML builders become appenders. Model: Swift SE-0228.

options.name: Holes stay text
options.detail:
Every package kind keeps today's one hole hook: each hole becomes text, which the kind can quote. The finished text is the value. Core's SQL, shell and HTML kinds keep their compiler support for bound values, separate arguments and context escaping.

This is the smallest rule, and quoting is enough for many small languages. A database or shell package must rely on its quoting being right, and cannot pass values separately.
options.technical: No change. `encode_hole<T: Printable>(value: T) -[]> String` stays the only hole hook (Prelude/core/prelude.jet:22). TypedHeadKind (Facts/Checked.jet:90) keeps SQL, HTML and Sh lowering by name. Consistent only with D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C.

comparisons.note: One protocol; a type opts into typed holes by naming its interpolation type. Source: SE-0228.
PEP 750 template strings hand code the fixed parts and the values, as option A's build does. Source: https://peps.python.org/pep-0750/
comparisons.code: q = cypher(t"MATCH (p) WHERE p.age > {age} RETURN p")

comparisons.note: Tagged templates pass the fixed parts and the values separately. Source: MDN "Template literals".
comparisons.code: const q = cypher`MATCH (p) WHERE p.age > ${age} RETURN p`

comparisons.note: html/template escapes each value for its place in the page, using the text before it. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/html/template

recommendation.why: A keeps one trait. A text kind writes what it writes today; a binding kind adds a hole type and `build`. Core's SQL becomes an ordinary impl, and every literal is checked while compiling.
gains: Package kinds bind values as safely as Core's SQL.
No literal can fail its check while the program runs.

losses.loss: Checks on a hole's value move into `encode_hole`.
losses.mitigation: Few kinds check values; escaping or binding there is the safe place anyway.

whyNot.reason: B needs an empty starting value and a builder that changes itself; A gets the same result from one pure call.
C leaves every package kind one quoting bug away from injection.

recommendation.tradeoff: Checking the literal with holes shown as `{}` gives up checks that depend on a hole's value; escaping or binding covers those.

decisions.title: A lambda stored where no type is expected follows the declaration rule: it writes parameter and result types, as `fn square` would
decisions.situation: Most lambdas are passed to a call, which tells them their types. About 219 in Jet's code are stored in a local, where nothing does. Under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A a lambda is a function without its name. The vote decides what such a stored lambda must write. We recommend the rule a named function already follows: parameter types always, and the result type when the body gives a value, so adding a name never changes the meaning.
decisions.gist: When a lambda is stored with no expected type, must it write its result type?
decisions.lesson: When you pass a lambda to a call, the call tells it the types. When you store one in a local, nothing does. So you write them, as for a named function: `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`. Forget the `-> Int` and Jet says the value is thrown away, as for `fn square`.
decisions.story: Rae stores `scale :: fn(x: Float) { x * 2.0 }` and later names it `fn scale(x: Float) { x * 2.0 }`. If the two rules differed, the lambda would return a Float and the named copy would fail to build.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: a stored function literal writes its full type.
square := func(n int) int { return n * n }
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rqt0kq. This is the stored-lambda question from the D-LAMBDA-FN1 package, asked alone. It applies under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A; under B or C the arrow forms keep inferring results as today.

Data, from q/b4/lam/census.mjs: 219 lambdas are stored in a local with `::`, `:=` or `=`, and 150 of them have an expression body.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/lamp, rerun on dev. p4.jet: `fn square(n: Int) { n * n }` is E0433 "This Int value is thrown away". p2.jet: `fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` as a value is E0003 today.

options.name: The declaration rule
options.detail:
With no expected type, a lambda is checked exactly as a declaration. Parameter types are required (E0801), and an omitted result means Unit, so a value body is E0433.

Where a type is expected, as in a call or a typed field, everything it gives may still be left out.
options.technical: Under D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=A the checker uses the declaration rules for a stored lambda. `jet fix` writes the result sema infers today for the 219 stored lambdas.

options.name: Infer the result
options.detail:
A stored lambda's result is the type of its last expression, as in Kotlin.

The same text then means different things with and without a name.
options.technical: Stored lambdas skip E0433 and infer the result.

comparisons.note: Function literals write their types. Source: https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_literals
comparisons.code: func(n int) int { return n * n }

comparisons.note: Results are inferred. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html
Closure results are inferred; parameter types may be too, from first use. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/closure-expr.html

gains: One checking rule.
Stored interfaces are written down.

whyNot.reason: B makes the same text return Int unnamed and fail when named.

recommendation.tradeoff: A stored lambda that returns a value writes `-> T`.

decisions.title: A lambda is the bound value without its name: `(n) { n > 2 }`, leaving out any part the call already fixes
decisions.situation:
A lambda is a small function passed to another function, such as the test in `nums.filter(…)`. Jet writes it today as `n -> n > 2`, a shape no named function uses.

D-DECL-BINDING1 proposes that a function is a binding, `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`. This vote decides whether a lambda is exactly that value without the name, or also keeps a short arrow. We recommend one shape. Decide D-DECL-BINDING1 first; this vote holds under each of its outcomes.
decisions.gist: Should every lambda be written exactly as a function binding's value, `(n) { n > 2 }`, with no separate short arrow?
decisions.lesson: A lambda is a function without a name. Under this rule you write it as the value of a function binding: inputs in parentheses, then the body in braces. Types the call already knows may be left out, as in `nums.filter((n) { n > 2 })`.
decisions.explainer:
The two votes fit together. D-DECL-BINDING1 makes `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` a function. Dropping `square ::` leaves a lambda, and dropping the types the call gives leaves `(n) { n * n }`.

The only question left is the short arrow. Most lambdas today have a one-expression body, and the arrow is a little shorter there.
decisions.story: Dev passes `n -> n > 2` to `filter`, then wants a log line in it. Today he turns it into `n -> { … }`. Under one shape he adds the line inside the braces he already has.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rqt0kq. Version 1 proposed `fn(n) { n * n }` and is kept as D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1.v1.json. The owner asked that the shape align with the binding conversion, which D-DECL-BINDING1 now asks for. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=B both options here gain a leading `fn`. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=C, which keeps `fn name(…)`, the value form is `fn(n) { n > 2 }`, version 1's shape, so the choice here stays the same.

Data, from Main's census (q/b4/lam/census.mjs) rerun on a dev export. There are 4,812 lambdas in 1,197 files. Of these, 3,842 have an expression body and 970 a braced body; 888 have a bare parameter. 2,832 leave at least one parameter type to the call, and 220 are stored in a binding.

Size under A. A bare expression lambda grows by three characters, a parenthesized one by one, and a braced one shrinks by three. Over the corpus that adds 2,813 characters, 0.6 per lambda. Version 1's `fn(…)` form added 12,437. Only the 888 lambdas with a bare parameter and one expression grow by three, and a named function passes with no lambda at all.

Probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m-decl run at o0, o1 and o2. The program in today's spelling is d10_lambda_today.jet, and it prints the commented output on every tier. Main's probe q/b4/lamp/p5.jet shows `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` running today as a typed value. With a `print` line added, p10.jet is E0399.

Known defect under both options: a `return` inside a braced lambda passed to `map` is checked against the enclosing function (q/b4/lamp/p12.jet, E0113). Under A a `return` leaves the lambda, as it leaves any function.

Reads with D-LAMBDA-STORED1=A, whose rule stays: a stored lambda with no expected type writes its parameter and result types. Only its spelling changes, from `fn(n: Int)` to `(n: Int)`.

options.name: Exactly the bound value
options.detail:
A lambda is `(params) arrow result failure { body }`, a function binding's value without the name. Parameter, result and failure types may be left out where the expected type gives them. The arrow appears only with a written result or an effect row, as in a named function.

Behavior changes. The arrow lambdas `n -> e` and `(n) -> { … }` are retired, and `jet fix` rewrites them. A `return` inside a lambda leaves the lambda. `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` is a function, never a typed value.
options.technical: Parser: in value position, `(` followed by a parameter list and then `{`, `->`, `-[` or a failure rail reads a function, the D-DECL-BINDING1 rule. The arrow-lambda path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 goes, and E0399 becomes the teaching error for the retired arrow. `jet fix` rewrites 4,812 lambdas, writing the inferred result for the 220 stored ones. Amends D-LAMBDA-IFACE2=A and replaces S46's form.

options.name: The bound value, plus a short arrow
options.detail:
The value form is used as in A. A lambda whose types the call gives, and whose body is one expression, may also be written `n -> n > 2` or `(a, b) -> a + b`.

After `->`, a type followed by `{` reads as a result type, as in a binding's value. So the 40 short lambdas whose body starts with a typed literal `Type{…}` need parentheses around it. Growing a short lambda to two lines changes its head.
options.technical: Keeps the expression arrow path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 and adds A's value path. `jet fix` rewrites the 970 braced arrow lambdas and parenthesizes 40 typed-literal bodies. Two parse paths decide on the token after `->`.

options.name: The bound value, starting with fn
options.detail:
A lambda is exactly a function binding's value without its name, and like every function value it starts with `fn`: `fn(n) { n > 2 }`. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 option B, `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`.

The call still fixes the parameter types, so a passed lambda writes only the names. There is no separate short arrow.
options.technical: Lambda: `fn` `(` params `)` [`-[E]>` | `->` T] `{` body `}`. The params, effect row and result may be left out wherever the call fixes them. The parser sees `fn` and needs no tuple-or-function rule. `n -> e` retires; `jet fix` rewrites it to `fn(n) { e }`.

comparisons.note: One shape: a procedure literal passed inline is the bound value. Source: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#procedures
comparisons.code: slice.sort_by(xs[:], proc(a, b: int) -> bool { return a < b })

comparisons.note: One shape: a function literal is a declaration without its name. Source: https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_literals
comparisons.code: big := filter(nums, func(n int) bool { return n > 2 })

comparisons.note: The bound value, plus a short `=>` form. Source: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-syntax-briefing-2026-09-16.html:234-238
comparisons.code:
square :: (x: float) -> float { return x * x; }
lam    :: (a, b) => a + b

comparisons.note: A lambda has its own braces-first shape, apart from `fun`. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html

recommendation.why: C makes a lambda exactly a function value without its name, and `fn` marks every function, named or passed. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 B, and dropping `fn` later stays a mechanical `jet fix` if it proves redundant.
gains: One shape for named and passed functions.
`fn` marks every function at a glance.
Growing a body keeps its head.
No tuple-or-function parsing rule.

whyNot.reason: A needs a rule to tell `(…)` lambdas from tuples, and adding `fn` back later is far harder than dropping it.
B keeps two spellings for one thing, and a growing body changes its head.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each lambda gains `fn`: two characters per lambda. `jet fix` rewrites every lambda once.

decisions.situation: Enum declarations write case names bare, while values and case patterns use dots. decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Add a dot to labelled case declarations, including payload cases and nested groups. Methods, marker lines and type cases are not labelled declarations.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview's enum_dot.jet gives E0003 at .Fast; enum_comma.jet gives E0003 at the comma. These are independent parser limitations. Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Patterns.jet:597-607 reports E0367 for a bare payload constructor such as Circle(n), not every uppercase name. A bare unit name can parse as a comparison expression; the earlier claim that Fast -> always gets E0367 was false.

DEPENDENCIES

D-DECL-COLON1=A illustrated bare enum cases; A amends that spelling. D-BRACE-LAYOUT1 decides one-line comma bodies independently. Without it, dotted declarations use separate lines. D-ALT-CASES1 depends on this vote for enum type cases: Int denotes a type case, .Int a labelled case. A alone adds neither type cases nor encoding changes.

Migration adds dots from parsed case declarations, never method names. Preserve comments and nested groups. A missing dot receives a registered diagnostic and edit. B is cohesive and familiar but needs two contextual spellings.

decisions.title: A generic alias writes its type parameters on its name: Grid<T>: [[T]]
decisions.situation: A generic alias gives one name to an existing shape, such as rows of any element type. The compiler accepts parameters on that name, while the declaration ruling puts parameters on a kind word such as struct. An alias has no kind word, leaving that rule incomplete. We recommend stating the exception explicitly: generic alias parameters go on the alias name, without introducing a keyword.
decisions.gist: Should a generic alias write its type parameters on its name, since it has no kind word?
decisions.lesson: A type parameter, such as T, stands for any type the user picks. A struct writes it on its kind word: Box: struct<T> { value: T }. A function writes it on fn. An alias has no kind word, because it only renames a type. Today the compiler accepts Pair<T>: (first: T, second: T).
decisions.story: Ravi writes many functions over [[Float]] and [[String]] grids. He wants one name, Grid<T>, that means a list of rows of T and stays the same type as [[T]].
decisions.inWild: TypeScript places generic parameters after the declared type name; its generic types preserve the selected element type. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Where a generic alias writes its type parameters, given that an alias has no kind word.

TODAY

A scratch file with Pair<T>: (first: T, second: T) and swap: fn(p: Pair<Int>) -> Pair<Int> passed jet check and ran. Another with Grid<T>: [[T]] and total(g: Grid<Float>) accepted a plain list of Float rows and printed 6.0. The parser takes parameters on the alias name (Declarations/Types.jet:51-57).

D-DECL-COLON1=A says kind parameters go on the kind word, never on the name. Its table writes an alias as Meters: Int, with no keyword. That replaces the alias keyword D-ALIAS-BIND2=B had kept, so an alias has no kind word.

D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A had made generic types and aliases into recipe functions and removed <>. It was archived on 2026-10-29, and D-DECL-COLON1's struct<T> and fn<T> use <> again.

A separate lag: a plain alias such as Key: Int | String gave E0324 in a scratch run, an alias needs type parameters. D-DECL-COLON1 ratified plain aliases, so that refusal is a defect to fix under any option.

OPTION A IN DETAIL

The law becomes: type parameters go on the kind word; an alias has no kind word, so its parameters go on its name. Grid<T>: [[T]] is the same type as [[T]] for each T. Writing <T> anywhere else on an alias gets an error with the fix.

decisions.title: May a field list named cases such as Celsius(Float) inline, written exactly as inside an enum?
decisions.situation: A union lists types a value may hold, while an enum lists named cases such as Celsius and Fahrenheit, each holding a Float. The seed accepts a separate Temp enum but rejects those case declarations written directly in a field's union. This vote chooses inline structural cases, a separately named enum, or an inline anonymous enum. We recommend inline structural cases with the existing dot-free declaration spelling, keeping bare names unambiguously types.
decisions.gist: May a union list named cases like Celsius(Float), written exactly as inside an enum?
decisions.lesson: Every option stores Celsius or Fahrenheit in the same field. A writes cases directly there; fields listing the same cases share a type. Bare names still mean types. A named empty state such as Off needs a declared enum; ? means absence only. C instead writes an enum body in the field, making a separate type for each declaration.
decisions.story: Yuki stores a thermostat temperature in a settings record. Only that one field uses Celsius or Fahrenheit, yet today she must declare and name an enum first. She wants to write the two cases in the field itself.
decisions.inWild: OCaml polymorphic variants allow named alternatives without a declared type, with structural type checking: https://ocaml.org/manual/5.2/polyvariant.html. Its manual also warns about weaker typo discipline in open inferred variant sets. Jet's proposed inline sets remain explicitly closed and exhaustive; this vote does not add OCaml's open-row inference.
decisions.detail:
THE CHOICE

A permits Name(T) as a named structural union case. Bare Name stays a type, preserving Int | String. Named cases may mix with type cases but cannot reuse a type-case name in the same union. Sets are closed, flattened and duplicate-free; one name with two payload types is an error. Construct and match .Celsius(value); plain Floats never guess a scale.

RATIFIED BOUNDARIES

D-ENUM-DOT1=B keeps declarations dot-free. A extends D-UNIONTYPE1's existing sum mechanism, not a competing enum runtime. D-ALT-SUBSET1=A widens exact subsets by value, not mutable references or containers. Named cases match by exact name/payload. Declared enums remain nominal, requiring explicit outward conversion; transparent aliases remain structural. Earlier type cases inside enums are dropped because bare enum names declare cases.

EMPTY CASES

A requires a declared enum for a named empty state such as Off. Optional ? means absence, not any business state. This is A's restriction, not proof that unambiguous alternatives are impossible. C supports empty cases without lookup-dependent meaning.

STRONG C

C permits an anonymous enum type in a field, using the existing enum body spelling. Each expression introduces a nominal type fixed by its enclosing field. Context builds .Celsius(21.5) in that type. An alias can name the same type; an independently declared enum is different.

C can include an ordinary empty Off case, but does not mix structural type alternatives or gain structural subset widening. Comma layout belongs to the separate brace vote.

SERIALIZATION

Do not promise every inline/named wire format is identical: enum markers can change tagging and names. This ballot adds no serialization options. Extend existing sum encoding where derivation is requested and reject ambiguous tagged/untagged mixes. SerdeItems.jet:1047-1089 contains the encoding choices; the old 988-1031 citation did not establish them. No serialization probe ran, so no existing wire result is claimed.

ONE COST REMAINS

Named empty cases cannot appear directly in A's union form. Use a declared enum for Off, and ? for absence only. No teaching diagnostics or retired-spelling rewrites are added.

CHECKED TODAY

temp_enum.jet printed 21.5 C. temp_union.jet failed E0003 at the case parenthesis. enum_comma.jet failed E0003 at the comma; enum_empty.jet showed Off() also fails E0003 in today's enum grammar. A and C's new type-position forms are proposed, not working syntax.

decisions.title: A value of a smaller union passes where a larger union holding all its cases is expected
decisions.situation: A plain Int passes to Int or String, but an Int-or-String value is refused by a helper accepting Int, String or Bool. Authors must match and rebuild values that already fit. The vote decides whether whole structural unions widen automatically, without widening mutable references or containers. We recommend exact subset widening; transparent aliases remain structural, while declared enums retain their outward conversion boundary.
decisions.gist: Should a value of a smaller union pass where a larger union with all its cases is expected?
decisions.lesson: A union type such as Int | String says a value is one of those types. Widening means a value fits a broader type with no conversion code. Today a plain Int widens into Int | String. A whole Int | String value does not widen into Int | String | Bool.
decisions.story: Omar's parser returns Int | String for a cell. His table stores Int | String | Bool. Every cell needs a two-arm match that rebuilds the same value, just to satisfy the types.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript accepts any member of a union and restricts operations to those valid for the possible members. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#union-types
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Extend D-UNIONTYPE1=A's member conversion to structural subset values. SolBallotReview's union.jet passed check and run with 7; subset.jet gave E0112 at store(x).

EXACT RULE

At value bindings, arguments, returns and failure propagation, every source case must occur unchanged in the target. Matching uses resolved type identity, not printed names. Preserve the active case and payload; remap its discriminant if necessary. Normal payload ownership costs remain; no hidden container-wide copy or allocation is permitted.

A transparent alias is the same structural union on either side. A declared enum remains nominal and never widens outward into another type. Entry into an enum is allowed only if D-ALT-CASES1=A separately permits it; this vote alone does not amend D-UNIONTYPE1's explicit enum boundary. Exact labelled cases compare by label and payload type, never payload alone.

LIMITS

No widening through editable or retained references, including & and &&. Otherwise a callee could write a Bool into storage declared Int | String. No recursive conversion inside lists, maps, records or function signatures. A collection must explicitly map its elements when a larger element type is needed. Exhaustive matching still covers every target case.

Changing a transparent alias changes nothing; introducing enum creates nominal identity. Neither ballot promises that adding enum is behavior-free.

options.name: Widen automatically
options.detail: A smaller unnamed union widens into a larger alternative at the places plain values already widen. Not through & parameters or inside lists.
options.technical: Exact subset value conversion; no recursive variance or reference widening. Enum entry depends on D-ALT-CASES1; enum exit remains explicit.

options.name: Rebuild by hand
options.detail: A smaller union never widens; the author matches each case.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: Every value of the smaller union already fits the larger one, so the rebuild match adds nothing. Plain values already widen the same way.
gains: No rebuild matches.
Same rule as plain values.
Declared enums stay separate.

losses.loss: A list of a smaller union does not widen into a larger list.
losses.mitigation: The error shows a one-line map that widens each element, so the copy stays visible.

whyNot.reason: Every call needs a match that rebuilds the same value.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more implicit widening, in exchange for no rebuild code.

decisions.title: Commas separate data members; method declarations with bodies take no comma
decisions.situation: The seed accepts commas between struct fields, but its formatter removes them from declarations and enum commas are rejected. Values use comma-separated entries, while method declarations already end at their own body brace. This vote chooses one separator rule for brace data lists without adding commas after methods. We recommend commas between data members, with a trailing comma when the formatter wraps a list.
decisions.gist: Should commas separate data members, while method declarations with bodies take none?
decisions.lesson: A uses commas between fields, enum cases and value entries. A trailing comma is accepted on either line layout; the formatter writes it only across lines. A method declaration with a body takes no comma. A field containing a closure or record is still data and needs a separator. All options show the same enum, fields and method.
decisions.story: Hana wants her Server fields and values to use one list rule, without a comma after its url method.
decisions.inWild: Rust separates struct fields with commas and permits a trailing comma: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/structs.html. Its methods are separate associated items rather than comma-list fields. This is precedent for separating data from code declarations, not proof that every language requires a comma on every multiline field.
decisions.detail:
A'S PRECISE RULE

Require commas between data members in brace member/value lists: struct fields, enum cases, record entries, typed collection elements and map entries. A final comma is optional in source on either line layout. The formatter writes it for multiline lists and removes it for compact one-line lists, following D-TRAILCOMMA1=A. Line wrapping does not change which member is data.

ONLY METHOD DECLARATIONS ARE EXEMPT

A declared method or other declared code-body member ends at its closing brace, with no comma. A data field whose initializer happens to end in a record literal, closure or code block still takes its list separator. A function requirement with no body is a data-like member and takes a comma. Associated types and constants follow that member-list rule in trait and impl bodies. Module/file bodies, ordinary statements and control blocks are unchanged. No comma goes after an ordinary function body just because it is inside braces.

RATIFIED BOUNDARIES

D-ENUM-DOT1=B settles dots, not enum comma parsing; commas remain this vote. D-RECORD-BRACE1=A makes {min, max} a punned record. A keeps commas when the formatter wraps it, so its special formatter clause retaining an explicit member can be dropped. Parenthesis and bracket list semantics do not change. Greenfield cutover updates repository callers together; no compatibility parser, teaching diagnostic or old-spelling rewrite ships. Greenfield does not prove that no user code exists.

SAME PROGRAM

Each option declares Mode and Server, constructs the same server and prints 8080. B retains formatter-style declaration lines and comma-separated values. C makes newlines separators only in multiline brace lists; it must account for ambiguous wrapped punned records. Neither alternative adds commas after methods.

ONE COST REMAINS

Multiline data declarations gain visible commas under A's formatter. It writes them during wrapping; authors do not put commas after methods. This is a visible syntax cost, not a cost removed by mentioning a formatter.

CHECKED TODAY

brace_today.jet ran and printed 8080. Formatting that scratch copy expanded the enum and removed struct-field commas, keeping the method comma-free. brace_mixed.jet ran with comma-separated fields and a comma-free method, printing 3. enum_comma.jet failed E0003. These establish the shown grammar and formatter behavior; A's unified rule is proposed.

decisions.title: Every record uses braces: {x: 1} is an unnamed struct, and paren tuples retire
decisions.situation: Unnamed records use parentheses today, while context-typed struct values use braces. One-member parenthesized records fail, and turning a record into a struct requires changing brackets. The vote decides which brackets hold named members and how records differ from code blocks. We recommend braces, with an explicit rule preserving function bodies, empty blocks and punned fields.
decisions.gist: Should every group of named values use braces, so {x: 1} reads as a struct without its name?
decisions.lesson: A record is a group of named values, like a struct with no declared name. Today one record has two spellings. One is (x: 1, y: 2) in parentheses. The other is {x: 1, y: 2} in braces, where a type is expected. Struct literals use braces: Point{x: 1, y: 2}. Parentheses also hold arguments and grouping.
decisions.story: Kemal returns (min: lo, max: hi) from a helper. Later he wants a method on it, so he declares a struct. He must change every parenthesis to a brace, and he learns that (n: 3) alone is an error.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript describes object types in braces and accepts matching object values in braces; object properties can be named directly or through a type alias. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Move unnamed record types, values and destructuring from parentheses to braces. D-LIT-DOT1=B already chose braces for struct and named-payload values; removing the surviving named-parenthesis payload is owed independently. Amend S73, S74, D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1 and D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1 where their parentheses change.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview's record_clean.jet passed check and run: tuple destructuring printed 1 9, and move_to({x: 3, y: 4}) printed 3. one.jet gives E0003 for (x: 1). record_arm.jet and payload_statement.jet fail at a comma. map.jet returned [ana: 3]. Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Expressions.jet:1036-1074 rejects one-member tuples; :1974-2054 parses record fields and both payload forms. Parser/Statements.jet:844-863 treats dispatch-arm braces as blocks.

A'S BRACE RULE

Braces after a function signature, control head or block marker hold code. Braces after struct, enum, trait, module or impl hold members. Elsewhere a group is a record when all entries are fields or puns and at least one field has a colon or a comma separates puns. Quoted keys select map grammar. Empty {} remains a block; typed empty maps remain [String: Int]{}.

Thus {x} yields x as code, {x, y} is a record, and {x: x} is a one-member record. In multiline punned records the formatter retains one explicit field, rather than removing every comma and turning the result into code. A one-member pun canonicalizes to {x: x}. This also binds D-BRACE-LAYOUT1.

Function bodies always hold code. Returning a record needs inner braces, even for one member. Missing braces get a result-type diagnostic; do not promise an error at a comma when no comma exists. No blanket claim that every changed brace reading is harmless substitutes for migration tests.

A statement-start brace pattern followed by : or := is destructuring through bounded lookahead. Partial patterns keep .. under D-DESTRUCT1. Migrate parenthesized records in one parser-based cutover preserving evaluation order. Prove record/block classification, control-header literals, nested maps, interpolation, singleton puns and multiline puns.

decisions.title: Record member order becomes part of the type and determines comparison
decisions.situation: A record groups named values, such as a guest's last and first names. The seed sorts record members alphabetically, so that guest list compares first names even when last is written first. Written-order comparison requires preserving member order in the record type, not merely changing the sorting function. We recommend that change, with explicit sort keys for other orders and the resulting type and display consequences stated openly.
decisions.gist: Should member order belong to a record's type and determine its default comparison?
decisions.lesson: Python tuples and ordered dataclasses compare in written order; dicts support equality but not <. A preserves member order in record types, comparison, display and encoding. Reordered members therefore form a different type. All options add multi-key sort_by for explicit orders. B instead removes default ordering, including use as ordered map or set keys.
decisions.story: Ines sorts a guest list written {last: "Zed", first: "Amy"} and {last: "Abe", first: "Bob"}. She expects Abe first. Jet puts Zed first, because first sorts before last alphabetically.
decisions.inWild: Python dataclass(order=True) compares fields in definition order, and requires identical classes for the generated comparison: https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html. Tuples and named tuples compare by position; dicts compare for equality but reject ordering. Custom sorts can use several keys with attrgetter: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html. Rust derived Ord follows struct declaration order: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html#derivable. Neither fact establishes that every comparable record in every language follows written order.
decisions.detail:
THE OWNER'S PYTHON QUESTION

Python tuples and named tuples compare by position. dataclass(order=True) opts into field-order comparison; plain dataclasses do not order by default. Dicts preserve insertion order but reject < and related ordering operations, while equality remains available and ignores insertion order. Executed Python probes confirmed ordered guests put Abe first, custom first/last keys put Amy first, tuples/named tuples compare positionally, dict equality succeeds and dict < raises TypeError. These are distinct data models, not a blanket 'Python records compare in written order' rule.

WHY WRITTEN ORDER

Alphabetical ordering is coherent for label-sorted type identity and insensitive to source reordering; that is C's genuine strength. It can nevertheless surprise users: year/month/day compares day first, and min/max compares max first. The old draft's major/minor/patch example was wrong because that written order is already alphabetical. No claim about all mainstream languages is needed.

A CHANGES TYPE IDENTITY

D-TUPLE-ORDER1=A and S73 currently use label-sorted identity. A amends both: an ordered sequence of names and member types defines the record type. Its comparison, printing and encoded field order use that sequence. Moving a member changes those outcomes and type identity. An initializer with an expected record type evaluates expressions in source order, then arranges matching named fields in the expected type's order. The same named fields may convert by value at bindings, arguments and returns; this is not mutable-reference or container covariance.

An untyped list takes its record order from the first entry and converts later matching entries to that element type. Comparing independently typed records with different orders requires a common explicit target type first; do not silently pick the left operand's order, which could break comparison symmetry. Equality, ordering and ordered-key behavior all use the same resulting type, without a private second order for maps or sets. Wrong member types still fail rather than being repaired by reorder conversion.

SHARED KEY API

All options add sort_by and sort_by_desc with one or more key functions, applied in the written key order. The existing two-argument comparator form remains. .member is the ratified shorthand under D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A, not a second key mechanism. The examples propose guests.sort_by(.first, .last); extra arguments are not implemented by the seed. They do not require another sorting algorithm or hidden per-value order metadata.

FAIR B AND C

B retains label-sorted record identity and equality but removes default ordering. It also removes records as ordered map/set keys rather than keeping an invisible alphabetical order for those APIs. Use an explicitly ordered named key type when that is needed. C retains the coherent label-sorted identity and comparison. Every option supports explicit multi-key sorting.

CUTOVER AND ACCEPTANCE

D-RECORD-BRACE1=A moves the proposed record spelling to braces; seed probes use today's parentheses only as evidence. Migrate all affected repository callers, synthesized signatures, nested records, printing/encoding expectations and ordered keys in one cutover. Do not defer Core signature changes to later edits or promise retired-spelling rewrites. Require comparisons with reversed field orders, operand-swap consistency, expected-type conversion, first-list-item inference and effectful initializer order.

ONE COST REMAINS

Member order becomes significant for type identity, sort order and output order. Name explicit sort keys where ordering must not change, and use a fixed declared record type at stable boundaries.

CHECKED TODAY

order.jet printed Zed, the label-sorted first/last record, a 2024 date chosen by day, Abe after sort_by(.last), and Bob after sort_by_desc(.first). order_keys.jet failed E0104 and E0107 for two keys. S73 is at Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1171-1176 in the reviewed checkout. No proposed order-sensitive type or multi-key API ran.

decisions.title: Show library promise changes during ordinary checks, and calculate the minimum release version
decisions.situation: A library makes promises to programs that use it. Those promises include what its functions need permission to do, not just their argument types. Adding a clock read inside a greeting function can change that promise without changing its written signature. The probe runs that function successfully; it does not demonstrate an early API-change gate. Choose whether ordinary checks should show such changes and whether publishing should calculate the version. We recommend a generated promise file checked during development, with a calculated minimum release version.
decisions.gist: Should ordinary checks show library promise changes and calculate the minimum release version?
decisions.lesson: An API is the part of a library other programs use. Think of package.api as its generated promise sheet. A source edit can change that sheet. Reviewing the difference makes the change visible before a release surprises users.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. The public surface is everything another package can call or name. A version bump is how a library signals change: major means breaking, minor means added, patch means fixed. An effect is a power like reading the clock.
decisions.story: Ana publishes greeting as 1.0.0, then adds a clock read. Every option runs the same greeting. They differ in when Ana sees the changed promise and who chooses the next version.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript API Extractor generates a committed API report and distinguishes local updates from read-only validation. It makes public changes reviewable, but does not claim that a signature report proves every behavioral promise.
decisions.detail:
A beginner writes ordinary library functions and runs jet check. For a declared library output, A derives package.api from the compiler's existing public API rows. A harmless internal edit changes no rows. An added public function appears as an addition. A newly required clock effect is shown as a breaking promise change, including the path through helpers. Executable-only packages need no promise file merely because functions default to public.

Concrete proposed sequence: start at released 1.0.0; change greeting from a fixed message to a clock-stamped message; jet check shows that greeting now needs Time. A breaking change fails until jet check --accept-api records the new generated baseline. Commit source and package.api together. Later jet registry publish compares fresh checked source against the immutable released 1.0.0 receipt and calculates a minimum of 2.0.0. Accepting the local baseline never resets release history.

For compatible additions, a successful local check updates the generated view with a visible note. jet check --locked is always read-only and refuses missing or stale views. Failed or partial checks never replace the last complete file. Use atomic replacement and one deterministic row order so concurrent checks cannot corrupt the view. The file is generated, not a second authored contract.

Experts can raise the calculated minimum for behavior the rows cannot detect. C has the same early gate but retains deliberate author version selection, with the calculated minimum enforced at publish. This is a real release-planning benefit, not permission to choose an invalid version. The first release uses the declared starting version. Pre-release and supported release-line selection keep their existing version semantics; the calculation compares against the selected released line.

Include public types, names, solved effects, error sets, layout and checked ownership contracts. Adding a publicly exhaustible enum or error case can break callers. A narrower effect is compatible only where actual type and reflection rules prove it. Record compiler/schema identity and supported target/configuration coverage. Publication refuses missing coverage or incomparable old receipts, rather than guessing patch compatibility. Runtime behavior not represented by the rows still needs human review.

Evidence: t17a a0.0.43, jet run - on the clock-stamped greeting, exits 0 and prints a clock-stamped hello. decisions.title: One-liners move under their own verb, jet eval, with every power of today's jet -e
decisions.situation:
Your 2026-11-09 review suggested that one-liners move off the bare jet command and under their own verb, jet eval. Today there are two half-tools. jet -e reads input and accepts semicolons, but refuses a final if. jet eval prints a final if, but reads no input, refuses semicolons and prints () after print.

A amends D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1=A, which ratified one jet -e flag, and reverses D-CLI-FOLD1=A's fold of eval into jet run --eval. The other five folds and D-CLI-ALIAS1=A's one-spelling rule stay. Keeping the ratified forms is option B.
decisions.gist: Should one-liners run as jet eval 'code', one verb with every power of today's jet -e, retiring jet -e?
decisions.lesson: A one-liner is a short program typed straight into the terminal, such as counting the lines of a file. Today Jet has two ways to run one, and each lacks something the other has. This vote decides whether one verb, jet eval, does all of it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A verb is the word after jet, such as run or check. A flag is an option that starts with a dash, such as -e. Standard input, or stdin, is text piped into a command.

The final value is what the last line of the code works out to, which a one-liner prints for you.
decisions.story: Ada pipes a log into jet eval to count its lines, and gets 0. She switches to jet -e, which counts 2, then adds an if at the end and gets an error. The help for each says nothing about the other.
decisions.inWild:
# Perl, Ruby and Node: one flag on the main command.
perl -ne 'print if /error/' app.log
node -e 'console.log(1 + 2)'

# Deno: its own verb.
deno eval 'console.log(1 + 2)'
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The command that runs code typed on the command line, and what that command can do. The Core names a one-liner uses, such as input, words() and input.csv(T), stay as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 ratified them.

Today, on seed a0_042, jet -e. Piping two lines into jet -e 'input.to_list().len()' prints 2. jet -e 'x := 2; x += 1; x * 10' prints 30. jet -e 'if 1 > 0 -> "yes" else -> "no"' is E0003, because the code becomes a run body where a bare if value is not a statement. jet run -e works the same way.

Today, jet eval. It exists, and its help says Evaluate pure Jet and print the value. jet eval '1 + 2' prints 3, the map example prints [2, 4, 6] on one line, and the final if prints "yes" with quotes. --json prints a jet.status/v1 object with the value, and jet eval hello.jet runs the file.

Its gaps: the same piped input gives 0, because eval reads no stdin. The semicolon form is E0373. jet eval 'print("hi")' prints hi and then (), and --pure does not refuse print. In both commands, core.files and other Core modules are E0107 without a use line, which a one-liner has no room for.

Other spellings today. jet run - reads a program from stdin and works. jet hello.jet runs a file. jet '1 + 2' and jet print are E2101 UnknownCommand with exit code 2, so the bare command never ran code.

The rule under A. jet eval 'code' is the one way to run a one-liner. The code is the body of a run function, checked like a file, with the files and arguments after it. input is the lines of those files or of stdin, as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 says.

What jet eval gains over both commands today. Semicolons separate statements, as jet -e allows. A final expression of any kind, an if or a match included, is the final value, as jet eval allows. A unit final value prints nothing, so print never adds (). Core modules resolve by full name, core.files, with no use line.

Printing the final value. A list or a stream prints one item per line, and a string prints without quotes, as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 ratified and jet -e does today (probe cli3). So the map example prints 2, 4 and 6 on three lines. --json prints today's jet.status/v1 object with the value.

Effects and --pure. jet eval has jet run's default authority and flags, -A, --allow and --deny, so a one-liner may read and write files and says so in its effects note. --pure refuses any effect, print included, with the effect named. jet eval file.jet stays a short form of jet run file.jet.

What is retired. jet -e and jet run -e become teaching errors in D-CLI-ALIAS1's retired-spelling table, each naming jet eval with the same code. jet run - stays, because it reads a whole program, not a one-liner. D-CLI-FOLD1's jet run --eval is never built.

Migration, counted over the seed's git-tracked files. jet -e is mentioned 94 times in 28 files, jet eval 197 times in 54 files, and jet run - 36 times. The retired forms print the new spelling, and docs and tests move in one cutover with no alias period, as D-CLI-ALIAS1 requires.

Beginner path. Type jet eval and the code. It prints the answer, reads whatever is piped in, and says which effects it used. jet help eval lists input, words() and the other one-liner names.

Expert path. jet eval --json returns the value as structured data for scripts. --pure checks that a snippet touches nothing. --allow and --deny bound what a pasted one-liner may do, with the same flags as jet run.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. jet eval is five letters longer to type than jet -e. A shell alias covers that for heavy users, and the verb is listed in jet help, where a flag on the bare command is not.

People and scripts that type jet -e meet a teaching error. It prints the jet eval form of the same command, and the docs that teach jet -e change in the same cutover.

Other options. B keeps the ratified forms: jet -e on the bare command, plus D-CLI-FOLD1's jet run --eval once built. C is jet run -e only, the Perl, Ruby and Node style of a flag on the run command. D keeps two tools: jet eval for expressions and jet run -e for statements and input.

B and C put a one-liner behind a flag that jet help does not show as a command. D keeps the split that made Ada switch tools, with two sets of rules to remember.

decisions.title: A typed collection head takes a loop and builds that collection directly: Set<String>{loop …}, [String:Int]{loop … -> k: v}
decisions.situation:
A loop with an arrow builds a list, such as loop w in words -> w.len(). The ratified rule says a loop always gives a list. A set then goes through a conversion, and a map is filled by a second loop.

The review asked for a loop that builds a set or a map directly. This ballot lets the type written before braces take a loop. A bare loop stays a list; keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: Should a typed collection head take a loop, so Set<String>{loop …} and [String:Int]{loop … -> k: v} build directly?
decisions.lesson: A loop with an arrow builds a list of its results. Sometimes you want a set, which drops repeats, or a map from keys to values. Today that takes a conversion or a second loop. This vote decides whether the loop can build them directly.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A comprehension is a loop that gives a collection. A typed head is the type written before braces, as in [Int]{1, 2}. A set holds each value once; a map pairs keys with values.
decisions.story: Mae counts distinct words in a log. In Python she writes {w for w in words}. In Jet today she writes Set.from around the loop, and for a map she writes an empty map and a second loop. Under A she writes the type and the loop.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a loop can build a set or a map in one expression, and how it is spelled. A bare loop with -> stays a list.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe c02 does it the ratified way. A loop gives the list [5, 3, 5, 3], Set.from around a loop gives 3 items, and a second loop fills a map of 3 keys. Probe c05 already accepts a typed list head, [Int]{loop … -> w.len()}.

Probe c04 writes Set<String>{loop w in words -> w}. It parses, and fails E0108: this needs Set<String>, but the value is [String]. Probe c01 adds [String:Int]{loop w in words -> w: w.len()}, which gets E0107 because key: value is not a loop body.

Probe c06 shows a terminal: (loop …).to_set() runs and gives 3. to_map does not exist, E0311.

The rule under A. A typed collection head may hold one loop in place of its items. The loop's results go into that collection in loop order, through the FromIterator protocol of D-ITER-COLLECT1=A, so any user collection works the same way.

A map's loop body yields key: value, the map literal's own item form. The key is an expression, as it is in a map literal today: probe c07 writes [String: Int]{w: 5} with w bound to apple and prints [apple]. A later key replaces an earlier one, as the map assignment loop in c02 does.

User collections. A struct literal's braces hold name: value fields and never start with loop, so Bag<String>{loop …} cannot be misread as a struct literal. The head is a collection head exactly when the type implements FromIterator.

What stays. A bare loop still gives a list and still ignores the expected type, so D-COMPREHENSION1's rule that context never changes a loop's result holds. The head is written on the same line, so a reader always sees the destination.

Census on dev, comment lines included. 1,057 lines in 301 Jet files bind or pass a loop with ->, all unchanged. Set.from around a loop appears 3 times and .to_set() 7 times, which jet fix may rewrite to a head; Map.from appears nowhere. No file writes a loop inside a typed head today.

Beginner path. A loop gives a list; write Set<String>{…} around it for a set. Expert path. Any collection that implements FromIterator takes a loop in its head, with no extra method.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A typed head now holds either items or one loop. Mixing them, as [Int]{0, loop …}, is a build error with a fix to concatenate, so a head is never half literal and half loop.

A map loop that repeats a key keeps the last value without a word. That matches map assignment and Python. A program that must refuse repeats uses a loop with an explicit check.

Other options. B keeps today's rule. C is Rust's collect, naming the destination after the loop. D is Python's: braces around a loop make a set, and key: value makes a map. E is Kotlin's to_set and to_map terminals.

Their best cases. B adds nothing. C works for any destination. D is shortest. E is a plain method. Their costs: B needs a second loop for maps. C puts the type last. D collides with Jet's block braces. E needs pair values and a to_ method per collection.

decisions.title: Core loads a trait implementation only when a program reaches both its type and its trait, and Core's modules sit in checked layers
decisions.situation:
On seed a0_042, a five-line program that imports core.tasks makes jet check load 62 Core source files: 3.2 MB and 47,088 lines from 12 Core areas. It peaks at 277 MB and takes about a second. With no import, the same check takes 10 ms and 28 MB.

The chain runs through trait implementations: Time's decode implementation names core.encoding, which names core.files, which names system, process, testing and mem. Your review proposed two rules to cut it.
decisions.gist: Should Core load an implementation only when both its type and its trait are used, and keep its modules in checked layers?
decisions.lesson: A program that uses one small part of Jet's core library today pulls in most of the rest. Each part's extras point at other parts. This vote decides two rules: extras load only when used, and lower parts may not lean on higher ones.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A trait is a promise of methods, like Decode. An implementation keeps that promise for one type. A layer is a group of Core modules that may use only lower groups.
decisions.story: Kim's script imports core.tasks to run two jobs at once. Its check takes a second and loads file, crypto and encoding code she never calls. Under A the decode chain to those modules stays unloaded.
decisions.inWild:
// Go keeps its standard library layered with a test, go/build/deps_test.go:
// "unicode/utf8 < strconv < fmt < os" and so on; a forbidden import fails the build.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Two rules for Core. They change what loads and which imports Core may write; no public API changes.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe c01 imports core.tasks and starts one task. Its jet check trace shows 62 Core source files from 12 areas: Tasks, Text, Math, Prelude, Time, Encoding, Files, Process, Sys, Testing, Mem and Crypto.

That is 3.2 MB of source, 277 MB at peak and about a second, on a warm second run too. Probe c02, with no import, loads none and checks in 10 ms at 28 MB.

The chain. Time.jet line 1723 is ZonedDateTime's decode implementation, and it names core.encoding. Math.jet line 15423 does the same for Decimal. Encoding's Cbor.jet imports core.files, and Files names sys, process, testing and mem.

Rule 1, the reach rule. The implementation of a trait for a type is loaded and checked for a program only when the program reaches both the type and the trait. Reaching means naming or calling it, directly or through something else reached.

A generic function that requires the trait reaches it. The implementation stays where it is written, beside its type. Under rule 1, c01 names no decode trait. Unless something it calls does, Time's decode implementation and the encoding chain stay unloaded.

Rule 2, layers. Every Core area sits in one of four layers. Layer 0 is the prelude, with mem, rt, reflect, meta and sync. Layer 1 is data: text, math, collections, time, encoding, regex, units, data, compute, crypto, log and event.

Layer 2 is system: sys, files, net, process, tasks, term, watcher, args, perf, testing, plugin, mod, archive, font and vendor. Layer 3 is services: http, db, ui, web, app, auth, service, jobs, game, reactive, tui, devtools, build and compiler.

A module may name its own layer or a lower one. The table lives in Core's package.jet, and jet check on Core reports each upward name as a registered error, with the file, line and the two layers.

Census on the seed, Core .jet files, comment lines skipped. Under that table, Core has 78 upward references in 16 files across 13 area pairs. Crypto naming files is 31 of them and encoding naming files is 27.

Most upward references are file adapters, such as encoding to or from a file. They move up to the files module, which implements the encoding stream trait for its own reader and writer. Rule 1 then loads them only for programs that use both.

Files names core.testing for the fault hooks of D-TESTFAULT1=A. Those hooks move down into the prelude layer, beside the effect carrier they guard.

Ratified decisions. D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A checks Core whole once per compiler and target, and a warm run reads back only what its program needs. Rule 1 is what makes that read-back small, so the two fit. D-EFF-CORE-INIT1=A already makes a Core import start nothing.

Beginner path. Nothing to learn: imports work as today, and small programs check faster. Expert path. A Core author sees the layer error when a lower module names a higher one, and jet inspect structure with --core shows what a program loaded and why.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The 78 upward references must move before the check turns on. The check lists every one in a single run, and most are file adapters that move as a group.

What remains. A Core author must place a new module in a layer, and some helpers end up one layer lower than their natural home. The table is one reviewed list in package.jet.

Other options. B keeps today's ball and relies on D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A's cache. C adopts the reach rule only. D adopts the layers only. E splits Core into separate packages with declared dependencies, as Rust's core, alloc and std do.

Their best cases. B costs nothing now. C gets most of the load cut with no moves. D gets an enforced shape with no loader change. E makes each dependency a package fact. Their costs: B keeps every program reading the ball; C lets the cycles regrow; D still loads unused implementations; E reverses D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A.

decisions.title: One migration block is the only description of a type's history, used for stored data, messages, live reload, database rows and service handoff
decisions.situation:
Jet's migration block already moves old stored data: on seed a0_042, decoding old JSON with name gives display_name. D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A runs the same steps on live state. Two ratified designs describe their own step: D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step for tables and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's typed migrate function.

Neither of those two is built yet. This ballot decides whether both read the migration block.
decisions.gist: Should the migration block be the only description of a type's history, including database tables and service handoff?
decisions.lesson: When a type changes, old copies of it still exist: in files, in messages, in a running program and in a database. This vote decides whether one written migration moves all of them. The alternative is one migration per place.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A migration says how an old shape of a type becomes the new one. A service handoff moves a running service's state to its next version. Reversible means the step can be undone.
decisions.story: Omar renames a field on a published record. Under A, the one migration line updates old files, old messages, his live dev session, the table and the service handoff.
decisions.inWild:
// Protocol Buffers keep one schema history for disk and wire:
reserved 2; reserved "name";
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function are both the migration block. Disk, wire and live state already share it.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe d01 declares UserRecord with migration rename name -> display_name. It decodes old JSON with a name field and prints user: Ana, age: 30. That is D-MIGRATE4=A's chain in decode.

Census on the seed. 15 files hold a migration block. No Examples file uses #Table, and no Jet source names ForwardOnly or DualWrite. So the database and service halves are not built.

What must exist first. D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's #Table records and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's generation handoff. A decides only what they read when they are built.

What A does for tables. A #Table record that is also #PublishedSchema takes its schema steps from its migration block. A rename becomes a column rename and an added field with a default becomes a column with that default.

A removal drops the column, and a change via a converter rewrites each row. D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's derived migration is printed from the block and still reviewed.

What A does for services. D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function is generated from the block, and each step gets that decision's class. A rename or an added field with a default is Reversible, with its inverse generated.

A removal, or a change with only a forward converter, is ForwardOnly. A change becomes Reversible when the block also writes a back converter, for example change score: Int -> MemberRank via { .. } back { .. }.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-MIGRATE1 to D-MIGRATE4, D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A, D-BOUND-EVOLVE1=A and D-SELFVER1=A. It fills in D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function without changing their outcomes. The back converter is a new clause of the block.

Beginner path. A beginner writes one migration line and every place follows. Expert path. jet inspect schema status, which exists today for saved schema versions, would also list tables and services, and the back converter turns a forward-only step into a reversible one.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A table or service may need a step the block cannot say, such as a backfill from another table. Such steps stay ordinary code that D-DB-SCHEMA1=A already allows, listed after the block's steps.

What remains. The block gains one clause, back, used only when a team wants rollback.

Other options. B lets each place keep its own step, as ratified today. C shares the block for tables but keeps the service's own migrate function. D replaces the block with ordinary conversion functions between versioned types.

Their best cases. B lets each design pick its best form. C covers the common database case with no service coupling. D needs no special syntax. Their costs: B writes one rename up to three times. C still writes it twice for services. D reverses the ratified migration block and makes every old version a type to keep.
