decisions.title: A function's error contract is written String ! ParseError
decisions.situation:
A function that can fail with a named error writes it after the result with a trailing mark: -> String ParseError!. That is the only place in the grammar where two types sit side by side joined by a space. Your review proposed String ! ParseError.

The suffix form was ratified as D-TYPE-SUFFIX1=A; A amends its error half and keeps its optional half. Keeping today's form is option B. D-SIG-ARROW1's unit form follows whichever wins.
decisions.gist: Should a function's error contract be written String ! ParseError instead of String ParseError!?
decisions.lesson: A function that can fail says which error it fails with. Today that is written after the result type with a trailing mark, so two type names sit side by side. This vote picks how the result and its error are joined.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A contract is the part of a signature that says which errors a function can fail with. A union, such as DBError | TimeoutError, means either one.

Writing no contract means the default error, Err; most code never writes one.
decisions.story: Ben reads -> String ParseError! and asks whether ParseError is a second result. Under A he reads -> String ! ParseError: a String, or a ParseError. The mark sits between the two, so the eye splits them without counting spaces.
decisions.inWild:
// Zig: an error union joins the error set and the payload with !.
fn parseDigits(text: []const u8) ParseError![]const u8 { ... }
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a signature joins its result and its named error. The default contract stays unwritten, and which errors exist and how they convert is unchanged.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe e01 writes -> String ParseError! and prints 42 then bad. Probe e03 writes a union, -> String (DBError | TimeoutError)!, and prints row 3 then failed. Probe e04 writes a failing unit function as save: fn(n: Int) SaveError! and prints saved 5 then full.

Probe e02 writes -> String ! ParseError and gets E0003, whose fix text talks about a unit-fallible signature. Probe e05 shows ! already beside a contract in three roles: !strict, !=, and the -[!Panic]> denial, and prints true.

The rule under A. A contract is written after the result as ! and the error: -> String ! ParseError. The mark has a space on each side, and the formatter keeps it. It binds looser than |, so a union needs no parentheses: -> String ! DBError | TimeoutError.

A failing unit function writes nothing before the mark: -> ! SaveError, read as returns nothing, or fails with SaveError. With an effect row it is -[FS.Write]> ! SaveError. The default stays unwritten, and Err pins it: -> Int ! Err. A function that cannot fail writes -> Int ! Never.

Function types use the same form: fn(String) -> Int ! ParseError. A contract is still only legal in a signature, never in a field or a generic argument, as D-TYPE-SUFFIX1 ruled. Optional results keep their suffix: -> Entry? ! DBError.

Why the reading stays clear. In type position ! has no other meaning. Not is a value operator, != is its own token, and a denial sits inside -[ ]> with no space after !. A spaced ! between a type and an error can only be a contract, so the parser needs no lookahead.

The mark is the same one the error wore before, moved between the two names. A reader who knows Err! reads ! ParseError at once.

What A removes. The two-types-by-a-space form goes. So does D-TYPE-SUFFIX1's rule that A | B! must be written (A | B)!, since ! now binds loosest. E0003's misleading text for e02 becomes a retirement error for the old form, with a fix that rewrites it.

Census on the seed. Signature lines with a contract, comments skipped, in Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests: 39,940. Of these, 29,920 write Never!, 9,371 a named error, 564 Err! and 85 a union; 7,031 put the error first. Contract lines in Examples are a small share; the bulk is generated Core and Compiler signatures.

Migration. jet fix rewrites every contract from the parse tree, not from text, in the same cut as D-SIG-ARROW1's reorder. One tool pass covers both. Grammars, highlighting, the spec and snapshots move in that cut too.

Beginner path. Write no contract; calls propagate errors. Expert path. Write -> T ! E for a named error, ! E1 | E2 for several, and ! Never to promise none.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. About 40,000 signature lines change. The rewrite is mechanical and lands with D-SIG-ARROW1's cut, so files move once, not twice.

A unit contract starts with the mark, -> ! SaveError, which could read as not at a glance. The space after ! is required and the formatter enforces it. A !SaveError written without the space is refused with a fix, so the denial look-alike never compiles.

What remains. Lines get two characters longer, about one percent of a typical signature. The Never contract is the largest share; whether Core should keep writing it is a separate question for the generated-signature cards.

Other options. B keeps today's suffix. C is Zig's error union, error first: -> ParseError!String. D is Swift's typed throws: -> String throws ParseError. E is Rust's Result: -> Result<String, ParseError>.

Their best cases. B costs nothing and is ratified. C is proven in Zig and puts the error where the eye lands first. D reads as English. E needs no special grammar at all. Their costs: B keeps two types joined by a space. C puts the result last, against D-SIG-ARROW1's result-first order.

D adds a reserved word against your fewer-keywords steer. E turns the default Err route into a type every beginner must write or infer.

Retirement error for T E! with a parse-tree fix, landing with D-SIG-ARROW1's cut. Unit contract -> ! E needs the space; !E is refused with a fix.

decisions.title: Retire the fence <: … :>: loops and lists cover repeated statements, and #loop covers repeated declarations
decisions.situation:
A fence repeats the statement around it once per entry: show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) is two calls. It was ratified as D-EACH1=C, and its spelling as D-FENCE2=A, so eight task handles could be written in four characters.

Your review called it the least guessable form and asked whether #loop and #{…} make it unneeded. A retires it, reversing those decisions; keeping it is option B.
decisions.gist: Should the fence <: … :> go, with loops, lists and #loop doing the repeating it does today?
decisions.lesson: A fence makes one written line stand for several copies, one per entry between <: and :>. Loops and lists also repeat work, and #loop repeats declarations while building. This vote decides whether Jet still needs the fence.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A fence is <: a, b :> inside a statement; the statement runs once per entry. A binding fence names several values at once, as <: t1..t8 :>. #loop repeats declarations while the program builds, and #{…} pastes a name.
decisions.story: Lena reads show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) in a code review and has to look up what it does. Under A the same code is two calls, or a loop over two pairs, and needs no lookup.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether the fence stays in the language. Loops, lists, #loop and #{…} are unchanged; D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH1=A already ratified them.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe f01 uses a binding fence with numbered names, an expression fence, a lock-step pair of fences and a fence in an assignment. It prints 7, 7, 7, left=1, right=2 and 60.

Probe f02 writes the same program in plain Jet: three bindings, three prints, two calls and a loop over a list. It prints the same six lines. Probe f03 writes the lock-step pair as a loop over two named pairs and prints left=1 and right=2.

Census on the seed, .jet files only, comment lines skipped. Fence lines: 67 in 22 files. 41 are in the compiler's own fence parser, formatter and tests; 12 are in tests and 11 in the FencedNames example. Core and Jetpack have none, so no library or program uses it.

The rule under A. The fence and its tokens go. A repeated statement becomes a loop over a list, or the copies written out. Several values become a list. Repeated declarations use #loop with #{…}, as ratified.

jet fix rewrites every fence to the copies it stands for, since a fence is defined as those copies. So the rewrite never changes meaning. Where the copies are three or more, it writes a loop over a list instead.

What goes. The fence parser, its formatter rows, its diagnostics and their UI snapshots, the numbered-name expansion that jump-to-definition had to look through, and the <: and :> tokens. :> stops needing its double job beside the retired-arrow error.

Beginner path. One way to repeat: a loop. Expert path. #loop for declarations, and a list of handles for tasks, which D-FANOUT3 already waits on together.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The case D-EACH1 was ratified for, eight task handles at the spawn and the wait, now uses a list. A list of handles is one line to spawn and one to wait, and it needs no numbered names.

Text search for t5 found nothing under the fence; with a list it is handles[4], which search and jump-to-definition handle without special rules.

What remains. A short lock-step call such as show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) becomes two lines or a loop over pairs. The fence's visual pairing with <> goes; <> itself stays under D-PIPE1=A.

Other options. B keeps the fence. C keeps expression fences and drops binding fences and numbered names. D drops the fence and lets #loop in a function body write one copy per entry, as Zig's inline for does.

Their best cases. B is built and shortest. C keeps the call-site use and drops the part that hides names from search. D gives build-time repetition one spelling everywhere.

Their costs. B keeps the least guessable form. C keeps a form with no users outside its tests. D makes #loop in a body mean unrolling, while ratified D-META-SPELL1=A gives it today's comptime loop meaning: it runs while building.

decisions.title: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language?
decisions.situation: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language? Calling a native library brings outside code into the program. Our example calls the C absolute-value function and prints 7. A broad permission also admits unrelated C libraries, even when their behavior differs. We recommend narrowing the existing foreign permission by locked library identity, while keeping evidence and isolation separate.
decisions.gist: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language?
decisions.lesson: A permission says which outside library is admitted. Its checked contract says what that library does. Neither a name nor an effect list stops native code from issuing system calls.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A binding is the #Import block that gives C functions Jet signatures. An effect is something a call does to the world, such as reading files. A row is the list of effects a call may use.

A grant allows effects, either for the package's own code or for one dependency. A written allow list is a ceiling: code may use only what it lists.
decisions.story: Lee calls the same absolute-value function in both options. The result is 7; the difference is whether another C library shares the permission.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative native call; library-specific permission does not contain the library after loading.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Effects/Checks.jet:1750-1760 adds the foreign effect root and preserves opaque reach. Both choices reuse that effect solver. origin/dev:Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet:71-98 owns the FFI family.

Foreign function interface (FFI) permission and evidence-backed behavior are separate questions. D-FFI-CONTRACT1=A and D-FFI-FACTS1=A already require one artifact-bound contract and the strongest justified safe shape. They are shared obligations, not options to disable accurate facts. This ballot now asks only about library-specific grants.

A explicitly extends the existing FFI.C value spelling into manifest allow/deny and command grants. It amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 3, which otherwise limits value narrowing to source rows. Resolve the local dependency key to its locked artifact identity; equal keys in different packages confer no shared authority. The `c` binding in both panes denotes the same toolchain C library. B preserves broad FFI.C grants. It still uses every justified contract fact; it does not force unknown effects where evidence exists.

Beginners use generated bindings whose required grant is shown with the dependency. Experts inspect evidence or select existing isolated placement. Unknown native reach stays conservative. An empty declared row alone proves nothing. Callback, retained-callback and cleanup effects join through the same descriptor; stale evidence fails admission. In-process trust is not enforcement. A separate process alone does not deny files or network. Unsupported mediation must refuse, never silently choose in-process execution.

The existing descriptor supplies the function contract under both options; this vote adds no import-arrow syntax and requires no duplicate handwritten effect database. The intended C ABI mapping must be established by that descriptor before executing the panes. No native call, containment or fixed ABI layout is claimed from the ordinary-function syntax probe.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Separated already-settled effect evidence from the remaining grant gate and made the required value-grant amendment explicit.

decisions.title: Keep jet explain and jet inspect as ratified, and add a per-line view of the run-time checks a build keeps, with a promise that none remains
decisions.situation:
Jet has two ratified commands for compiler knowledge. jet explain answers about one thing, and jet inspect shows a whole plane. The review asks to fold both into jet explain, and to show every run-time check the compiler could not remove.

Today jet explain effects answers per line. No command says which index on a line still carries a bounds check. This ballot keeps both commands and adds that view, plus a marker that refuses any kept check.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep its two inspection verbs and add a per-line view of kept run-time checks, plus a promise that none remains?
decisions.lesson: Jet adds a safety check where it cannot prove an index fits. That keeps programs safe but costs a little speed. This vote decides whether you can see each check that stayed, and ask Jet to refuse any in a hot loop.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A bounds check tests an index against a list's length while the program runs. A kept check is one the compiler could not prove away. A promise is a #Policy marker that the build enforces.
decisions.story: Dana's game loop is slow. Under A, jet explain checks shows the one index the compiler could not prove, and #Policy(checks: .Forbid) keeps new checks out of the loop.
decisions.inWild:
// Swift and Rust leave this to reading assembly:
$ cargo asm my_crate::sum_first
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether to keep D-CLI-ONE1=A's two verbs, and whether to add a view and a promise for kept run-time checks. The review's query questions are covered at the end.

The verbs today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). jet help inspect lists 28 subcommand words, including the plane views, decisions, expand, audit, query, impact and semindex. jet explain takes a code, a fact, a marker, a policy key, or effects at a file and line.

Kept checks today. Probe g01 indexes xs[i] with i below a parameter n, so the index is not proven. jet inspect decisions lists vectorized sum reductions and a stepped index guarded before the loop. It names no kept bounds check. jet explain effects g01_sum.jet:5 reports effects only.

A name collision, engineered away. On t6c, jet explain checks g01_sum.jet:5 is read as a package name and fails E1274, no package record. jet explain matches its fixed topics, log, effects and marker, before package names, and A adds checks to that list. A policy key followed by a file already routes to the policy explanation, so the view also prints the checks policy in force, as explain effects prints caps.

One answer on every build profile. The view lists the checks sema could not prove, which never depend on the profile. It then marks which of them the optimizer removed on the profile asked for, with --profile. The promise judges only sema's list, so a function that passes in a debug build passes in a release build.

The facts exist. The IR builder records which list accesses sema proved in bounds and lowers those with no check. IR.jet's loop proof rows count proven and unchecked accesses. No command prints them per line for a user.

What A does. A keeps both ratified verbs. It adds jet explain checks with a file and an optional line, beside jet explain effects. For each line it lists each bounds check and other trap check the build kept, each implicit copy and each allocation, with the reason it stayed.

For g01 line 5 the reason reads: xs[i], i is below n, and n is not known to be at most xs.len(). The fix names the proven form, such as loop over xs or a test against xs.len() first.

The promise. #Policy(checks: .Forbid) on a function or block makes each kept check inside it an error with the same line and reason. It joins the policy ladder as a new key, beside the no_alloc promise of D-NOALLOC-SEM1.

The promise uses only proofs sema makes today. D-OOBPROOF1=A's refinement-based proofs would remove more checks once refinement types land; A does not wait for them.

Census on t6c. The repository has no per-line check report. jet inspect audit copies already counts implicit copies, and prints implicit read-view copies: 0 for g01.

Query questions from 8.10. Which functions touch this name: jet inspect impact g01_sum.jet sum_first lists one caller. What can fail: jet inspect semindex prints each function's failure contract. What changed in meaning: jet review v1.jet v2.jet prints effect and authority changes. These exist, so 8.10 needs no new verb.

Tracing from effects. Callable policies already wrap calls, and CallablePolicies.jet applies #Policy(trace(...)). A span on every effect call is a separate ballot.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-CLI-ONE1=A, uses D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A's ladder and D-LEDGER1=D's one query, and does not depend on D-OOBPROOF1=A. Option C would reverse D-CLI-ONE1=A.

Beginner path. A beginner never needs the view; a slow loop leads to one command. Expert path. The promise keeps a hot loop free of checks, and the error says why each one stayed.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The promise can reject code that is correct but unproven. The error names the proven form, and #Policy(checks: .Forbid) applies only where it is written.

What remains. The view adds one more jet explain topic. It sits beside jet explain effects and reads the same way.

Other options. B keeps the ratified verbs with no view or promise. C folds jet inspect, audit and expand into jet explain topics, as the review asks. D adds the view but not the promise.

Their best cases. B adds nothing. C gives one word to learn. D shows the checks without new errors. Their costs: B leaves kept checks invisible. C moves 28 words that D-CLI-ONE1=A just placed. D cannot keep a hot loop clean.

decisions.title: Every breaking language change lands with a rewrite registered in jet fix; errors still never teach retired spellings
decisions.situation:
Jet changes its spelling often before 1.0, and the repository migrates itself with one-off scripts. Users' code gets no rewrite. A file that still writes the retired word prep gets an error saying there is no type called prep, and jet fix makes no change.

Today an owner rule says retired spellings get no teaching message and no jet fix rewrite, and it holds until this vote. D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A already bars teaching. The recommendation keeps that bar and adds rewrites only, which changes the rule's rewrite half.
decisions.gist: Should every breaking language change land with a jet fix rewrite, so old code moves forward in one command?
decisions.lesson: When Jet changes how something is written, old programs stop compiling. This vote decides whether each such change must ship with an automatic rewrite. Then jet fix updates old code instead of leaving a confusing error.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A breaking change makes code that compiled before stop compiling. A rewrite is a saved, replayable edit that turns the old form into the new one. A codemod plan is Jet's existing file format for such edits.
decisions.story: Chen opens a project he last touched in October. Under A, jet check gives the ordinary error and says the project was locked with an older jet. jet fix rewrites the old word, and one command later the project builds.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust ships each edition's rewrites in the compiler:
$ cargo fix --edition
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a breaking language change may land without a rewrite users can run. Library items already have one: D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A and D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1=A. This is the language half.

The rule in force. On 2026-11-10 Main recorded the owner rule on cards #6622 and #6281. Until this ballot is decided, retired spellings get the generic error, no teaching text and no jet fix rewrite. D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A, ratified on 2026-11-05, already says no teaching of retired Jet spellings anywhere.

So the ballot has two halves. Teaching, a message that names the retired word and its new form, is settled against by D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A. Rewriting, jet fix editing old code on request, is the open question. A adds rewrites and keeps the teaching bar. E adds both and would reverse D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A for Jet's own spellings.

Today, on the a0.0.43 compiler (dev c460ba91e5). Commit 5a467902a3 retired prep, and its message says the rewrite was a script in a scratch directory. Probe m05 writes LIMIT: prep { 2 + 3 } and gets E0119, there is no type called prep. jet fix --dry-run prints no changes made, with or without --edition=2026.

jet fix --edition=2027 fails E2104: this jet migrates to edition 2026 only. The next spelling change is already ratified: D-META-SPELL1=A replaces comptime with #run. Probe m06, comptime { 2 + 3 }, still prints 5. Probe m07, #run { 2 + 3 }, fails E0733, no tag called run, and suggests the unrelated tag PII.

How often spelling breaks. Since 2026-09-10, 131 commits that touch the parser or checker say retire. comptime appears 2,816 times in 1,013 Jet files, the size of the next migration. History holds 30 respell commits and 284 that mention a codemod. All 22 codemod plan files in the tree sit under tests.

What A does. Each breaking language change adds one rewrite file in a new Compiler/Migrations directory. The file uses the codemod plan format of D-CODEMOD-BATCH1=A. Its name carries the decision ID and the toolchain version that made the change.

jet fix applies every rewrite between the toolchain recorded in .jet/lock and the running one, in order. jet new already writes that record: a fresh project's lock has toolchain = a0.0.43 and a [[toolchain]] section. A file with no lock names its start: jet fix --since 0.4 file.jet.

Rewrites chain. When D-META-SPELL1=A lands, its rewrite turns comptime into #run, so jet fix on prep code applies both in order. A rewrite that cannot be automatic is marked manual; jet fix lists each such site in its own report and changes nothing there.

No teaching, by design. Under A the old word keeps the generic error, which names no retired form. A failing check adds one toolchain line only when the project's lock is older than the running jet. The line reads: this project was locked with a0.0.41; jet fix --dry-run shows 3 pending rewrites.

That line names no spelling, old or new, so it is not teaching under D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A. It compares two version strings and counts rewrite files, only on failure, so a clean build pays nothing. A project with no lock gets no line.

The landing rule. A change that breaks code lands together with its rewrite. Its fixture holds the old spelling, and the suite requires the result to check clean. A change of meaning under an unchanged spelling counts too: its fixture must print the same output before and after jet fix. The repository migrates itself with the same file users get.

After the 1.0 boundary, the same files become edition migrations that jet fix --edition reads. That matches the release policy: breaking changes need an edition bump and jet fix. A keeps D-REL5, so source is rewritten only by jet fix, on request, and D-CODEMOD1=A and D-CODEMOD-BATCH1=A as the format.

Beginner path. Old code fails with the ordinary error and the toolchain line; jet fix updates it in one command. Expert path. Each rewrite is a reviewable file with a fixture, and jet fix --dry-run shows every edit first.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each breaking change costs its author one rewrite file and one fixture. The repository already writes that script for its own migration; A checks it in. A user whose project has no lock sees no toolchain line and must know to run jet fix --since.

What remains. A rewrite is only as good as its fixture. A missed form leaves the ordinary error, and jet fix --dry-run lists which rewrites ran, so a user can report the gap. A project made without jet new has no toolchain record until a build writes one.

Other options. B keeps today's practice and the owner rule as it stands. C keeps a teaching error for each retired spelling but no rewrite, like Python 3's print message. D waits for editions: no rewrite rule before 1.0. E is A plus a hint naming the retired form and its rewrite.

Their best cases. B costs nothing and lets spelling move fastest. C tells users exactly what to write. D follows the release policy as written. E tells users why their code broke. Their costs. B strands old code. C and E reverse D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A for Jet's spellings. C also leaves every edit to the user. D strands everything written before 1.0.

decisions.title: A named number adapts like the literal it names; a variable takes the type its function needs only where the default is refused
decisions.situation:
A number literal adapts to where it goes: half(3.0) passes a Float. A module constant does too: GRAVITY: 9.81 passes to a Float parameter. A local name does not: after y: 2.5, half(y) is an error, because y is an exact Decimal by default.

The review asked that naming a number not change what it is. This ballot lets local names adapt the way literals and constants already do. The exact default and the rule that precision is lost only at a written step stay as ratified.
decisions.gist: Should a local name for a number adapt the way the literal and module constants already do, so half(y) just works?
decisions.lesson: Jet's plain decimal numbers are exact by default, and Float is the fast approximate kind games use. A written 2.5 becomes a Float where a Float is needed. A name for it, y: 2.5, does not. This vote decides whether naming a number keeps that.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A literal is a number written in code, such as 2.5. Decimal is Jet's exact default for written decimals; Float is approximate binary. A binding gives a value a name: y: 2.5 cannot change, speed := 2.5 can.
decisions.story: Jo writes a game. half(3.0) works, so she names it: y: 3.0, then half(y), and gets E0112 saying y is a Decimal. The fix text suggests Float{3.4}. Under A her code runs as written.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: a named constant is untyped until used, like the literal.
const y = 2.5
var f float32 = y   // fine: y adapts
var g float64 = y   // fine too
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What type a name for a number has. Number types, the exact default of D-TYPE2-DEFAULT1=A, and the rule that precision is lost only at a spelled step are unchanged.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe l01 passes 3.0 to half and gets 1.5; naming it y: 2.5 and calling half(y) is E0112. Probe l08 passes a module constant GRAVITY: 9.81 to the same kind of parameter and prints 4.905. So module constants already adapt, and local names do not.

Probe l04 writes speed := 2.5 and speed = step(speed, 0.5): E0112. Probe l06 passes n: 200 to a U8 parameter: E0108, while the literal 200 works. Probe l07 multiplies a local Decimal by a Float: E0131.

Today's ways out. Probe l10 writes Float{2.5} into each value and prints 1.25, 3.0, 200. Probe l09 converts with y.to_float(). Probe l03 shows approx refuses a Decimal; it is for whole numbers.

The rule under A, for a name that cannot change. A local binding whose value is a number literal, or arithmetic on such literals and constants, adapts at each use exactly as the literal would there. That is the rule module constants follow today.

The rule under A, for a name that can change. A local := binding of such a value keeps today's default, Int or Decimal. Only where that default is refused does it take the type the use needs, at the binding.

If two uses need different types, the error names both lines. So a program that compiles today never changes meaning; A only accepts programs that are errors today.

Names built from names. b: y * 2, where y is an adapting name, adapts too, because it is arithmetic on literals once y is replaced. A closure that captures y captures the literal. A generic parameter that decides nothing gives the default, Decimal, exactly as the literal 2.5 would there.

Why the precision law holds. A name behaves exactly as its literal written at the use, which the compiler already converts with its exactness check. No value at run time loses precision without a spelled step, as D-TYPE2-EXACT1=A requires.

Census on dev, git grep -cE over Jet files, indented lines only, so comments and module lines are skipped. Local bindings that write Float, F32 or F64 into a literal: 827 in 190 files. Local bindings that write a fixed-width integer type into a literal: 2,910 in 429 files. Under A, jet fix may drop the type where a use decides it.

Module number constants, which already adapt: 4,592 lines in 495 files, all unchanged. Plain whole-number := bindings: 7,085, which keep Int unless today they are errors. Bare decimal-literal locals, the cases A reaches directly: 39 in 33 files.

Beginner path. Name a number and use it; it fits where it goes. Expert path. Write Float{2.5} or F32{2.5} to fix a type on purpose; hover shows which line decided a name's type.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A later line can decide a variable's type, so speed / 3 above it becomes Float division. This happens only where the default would be an error, and hover names the deciding line.

E0112's fix text today always says Float{3.4}. Under A the error remains for real conflicts, and its text names both uses with their own numbers.

What remains. A reader of speed := 2.5 cannot tell its type from that line alone when a later use decides it. That is Rust's rule for every number binding; A applies it only where the default fails.

Other options. B keeps today's rule. C is Go's: names that cannot change adapt, variables keep the default. D makes decimal literals Float by default, as Swift and Python do, and writes exact numbers as Decimal. E is Rust's: every use decides one type for the binding.

Their best cases. B tells a reader every type at the binding. C covers constants with no inference. D makes games simplest. E is the most uniform.

Their costs. B makes naming change meaning. C leaves the speed := 2.5 case an error. D reverses the exact world of D-TYPE2-DEFAULT1. E changes programs that compile today, such as y / 3 becoming Float division.

decisions.title: Every module-level value is computed while building, and one that fails or has effects is a build error
decisions.situation:
A value written at the top of a file belongs to the whole program. The rules already say a fixed value there is worked out while building, and a failure is a build error. Today's compiler has not built that yet, so a failing value still builds and stops the program later.

Three kinds of top-level value are still left out of that rule. A shared holder is built the first time it is used, and a foreign call is run once at startup. A value kept across reloads may only be a plain number. This ballot asks whether all three are worked out while building too, so no code runs before the program starts.
decisions.gist: Should every module-level value, including shared holders, foreign calls and reload-kept values, be computed while building?
decisions.lesson: A value written outside any function belongs to the whole file. Most such values are already worked out while building, so a mistake shows up before the program runs. This vote decides whether the last few exceptions follow the same rule.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module-level value is a name: value written outside every function. Computing while building means the compiler works the value out and stores the result in the program. An effect is something a function does to the world, such as reading a file.

A shared holder is a value that several tasks lock and change. A foreign call runs code from another language. A pinned build input is a file the build reads and records by hash, so the same build always sees the same bytes.

Under A, every top-level value is worked out while building. One that stops, reads the world or cannot be stored is a build error with three fixes: move the work into run, make it a function, or use a pinned build input.

Under B, the ratified rules stay as written. Fixed values and plain changeable values are already worked out while building. A shared holder is still built on first use, a foreign call still runs at startup, and a reload-kept value stays a plain number.

C runs every top-level value at startup, as Go does. D computes each one when it is first read, as Swift does.
decisions.story: Ada's game keeps a shared high-score table and a reload-kept list of best runs at the top of a file. Today the table is built when first touched, and the list must start as a plain number. Under A both are stored in the program, ready before run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. When the three remaining kinds of top-level value are computed: shared and Atomic holders, foreign-call values, and #Persist initializers. It also restates the whole file-scope rule in one place. Values inside functions keep the ratified tries and quiet fallback, and a file of statements is unaffected.

Ratified law today. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A already rules that a file-scope immutable value is computed while building, and that a fallback reason there is an error, with E0952 for an exhausted budget. D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A bakes storable changeable globals the same way, but leaves #Persist unchanged.

Still outside that rule. D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A builds a module Shared holder once, on first access. D-FFI-COMPTIME2=A computes a foreign row once at startup when it cannot fold. #Persist initializers keep E0622, scalar literals only. A closes all three; B keeps them.

Dev has not built the file-scope rule yet, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe m01 has BAD: 10 / zero(): jet check passes, and jet run stops with E3010 at run time. Probe m07 wraps it in comptime, and jet check reports E3010 at build time. Probe m04's print runs before run.

More dev facts. m03 reads a file and m05 reads the environment at module level, and both build. m11 gets E0622 even for count := square(3), so baked changeable globals are unbuilt too. m12 writes a #Persist shared holder from two tasks and prints dark light. m14's #Persist best := [Int]{} is E0622.

Spelling. #run is D-META-SPELL1=A's ratified spelling, and an unbraced #run takes one call. Dev still spells it comptime { }, and m10's #run embed_file(...) is E0733 today. The embed_file read is recorded with its SHA-256 in the comptime input lock, which is the pinned build input.

The rule under A. Every module-level initializer runs in the build-time engine with the target's facts, as if written with #run. The result is stored in the program, and every tier reads that stored value. Dependencies are computed first, and a cycle is one registered error. No user code runs before run.

Build errors under A, all reported at once. A stop, such as divided by zero. An exhausted budget, E0952, fixed with #StepLimit or a function. An effect: a file, the clock, the environment, the network or print. A value that cannot be stored, such as a file handle. A foreign row that cannot fold.

The three fixes the error offers. Move the work into run and pass the value on. Make it lazy explicitly: a function, marked #Memo when pure, so the first result is kept. For outside data, use a pinned build input: #run embed_file("config.txt"), or a hashed net.fetch. Probe m06 runs all three fix forms today, in today's spelling.

Shared and Atomic holders. A module holder with storable contents is computed while building, and its lock starts as a zeroed word in the program's data, as Rust's const Mutex::new does. This is the one place a shared cell is stored. Inside any other value it stays unstorable, as D-COMPTIME-WORD1 rules.

Each controlled test world starts from its own copy of the baked holder, where today it builds its own cell on entry. So tests still never share a holder with the process default. A retained cell keeps its live value across a reload, as D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1 rules.

#Persist values. A storable initializer such as #Persist best := [Int]{} is baked like any changeable global, which lifts E0622 there. jet dev computes a changed initializer at its next build, and a #Persist binding keeps its live value across the reload, as today.

Foreign rows. A foreign row at file scope folds while building when it passes D-FFI-COMPTIME2's fold gate. Otherwise it is the build error, with the same fixes. Foreign rows inside functions keep the startup-once fallback.

What this settles. Nothing runs before run, so loading a library runs none of its code. Every tier reads one stored value, so a value cannot fail on one tier and not another. Startup order disappears, because there is no startup work.

Census on dev, over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, package files excluded. 13,519 module value bindings in 2,678 files; 1,284 contain a call. 21 call a files, env, net, sys, time or process function. Seven are pure time functions, and twelve already sit inside comptime, testing its refusals or its hashed fetch.

The last two read the environment at module level: StartupConstants.jet in Examples and one constant-folding fixture. They are build errors under A and under B, because the ratified rule already refuses them. 29 shared module holders in 25 files and 14 #Persist bindings change only in when they are built. embed_file or embed_bytes appears 444 times.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each effectful module value must move, and its build error names the effect and the three fixes. jet fix moves a value into run when only run reads it. When other functions read it, the fix refuses and explains how to pass it, as D-ENTRY-EXPLICIT2 requires.

A heavy initializer makes builds slower, where it might otherwise run at startup or on first use. Outcomes are cached per package version, target and compiler, as D-COMPTIME-WORD1 rules, so only a changed initializer is recomputed. #StepLimit bounds the cost, and each build prints the total bytes of stored values.

A large stored value grows the program file. A zero-filled holder or buffer goes in zero-filled data, which costs no file bytes. Anything too large to store is a #Memo function instead.

Other options at their best. B needs no amendment, and a holder nobody touches costs nothing. C is Go's simple startup order. D is lazy, like Rust's LazyLock or Swift's globals, and a value never read is never computed.

Their costs. B keeps two hidden run-time steps and literal-only #Persist. C runs effects before run, so loading a library can touch files and the network. D checks a flag on every read and moves failures to the first read, after the program has started.

options.name: Always computed while building; failure is a build error
options.detail: Every module value, including shared holders, foreign rows and #Persist initializers, is computed while building and stored. A stop, an effect or a value that cannot be stored is a build error with three fixes: move it into run, make it a function, or use a pinned build input.
options.technical: Keeps D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A's file-scope rule and D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A's baked globals. Amends D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A's first-access cell, D-FFI-COMPTIME2=A's startup fallback at file scope and the #Persist E0622 rule. A module holder is the one stored shared cell; each test world copies it.

options.name: The ratified rules as written

decisions.title: A plain module variable is owned by the main task, and the compiler refuses any task that touches it
decisions.situation:
Today a changeable value at the top of a file can be declared, but any function that writes it is refused, even run. The error suggests a shared holder instead. Games and scripts want a plain variable that functions read and write.

The owner asked for one without a written effect on every function. This ballot lets functions write it, and has the compiler refuse any task that touches it. Keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: May a function read and write a plain module variable directly, with the compiler refusing any task that touches it?
decisions.lesson: A module variable is a name at the top of a file that the program changes as it runs, such as a game's score. This vote decides whether functions may change it directly, and how Jet keeps two tasks from changing it at once.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module variable is a := name declared at the top of a file. The main task is the one that runs run. A task is work started with task, which may run at the same time as other tasks.

To touch a variable is to read or write it, directly or through a function you call.
decisions.story: Lena writes a small game. Her score lives at the top of the file, and hit adds to it. Today Jet refuses the write and tells her to wrap the score in Shared. Under A it just works. If she later starts hit as a task, the error names score and the path to it.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether functions may read and write a plain module variable, and the rule that keeps that free of data races. Survival across a hot reload is D-PERSIST-ONLY1. How a module value is first computed is D-MODULE-BUILD1.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe m01 declares score := 0 and writes it from hit; it gets E0111, module state, so a function can't change it directly. Probe m02 shows even run cannot assign it. Probe m03 marks it #Persist, and the write works and prints score 7.

Probe m05 writes the #Persist binding from a task and from run at the same time. It compiles and runs, so today's grant already allows the race E0111 exists to stop. Probe m04 uses the holder E0111 suggests, written from a function and a task, and prints score 7. D-PERSIST-BORROW1=A keeps ordinary module bindings read-only from functions, which A reverses.

The rule under A, in six parts. One: a := name at file scope is a module variable. Any function that can see it reads and writes it directly. Its first value is computed while building, as D-MODULE-BUILD1 rules.

Two: the compiler infers which module variables each function touches, through calls, closures and function values. Hover and docs show it. It is never written in a signature.

Three: the main task owns every module variable. Starting a task whose work touches one, or sending a closure that touches one to a task, is a build error. It names the variable and the call path and offers two fixes: pass the value in, or keep it in Shared.

So no data race is possible: only the main task ever runs code that touches a module variable. The fact is deny-only, like Panic and Mem. Nobody writes State on a function; a ceiling may write !State to promise no module state, and that denial is optional.

Four: function values carry the fact in their type, as they carry inferred effects. A helper that starts f as a task requires f to be free of module state, so passing a touching closure fails at the caller's line. A dynamic call counts as touching whatever any of its possible targets touch.

Five: no write behind a reader's back. Holding a borrow of a module variable, such as looping over enemies, while calling a function that writes the same variable is a build error naming that call. It is the rule locals already follow, made static because touches are known.

Six: packages and tests. A library's module variables belong to the main task of the program using it, and a public function's touches appear in its docs. jet test gives each test its own copy of every module variable, as D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A gives each test world its own shared cell. Each test is the main task of its world, so tests stay parallel.

Files of statements. D-FILE-STATEMENTS1, still open, makes a top-level binding in a file of statements a local of that program, which functions do not see. A keeps that: this rule governs := bindings in files with run: fn and in libraries. So one line never switches between a local and a module variable under this ballot.

Hot reload. Under D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A a module variable keeps its live value across a swap unless its starting value changed. #Persist also keeps it across a stop and start, as D-DEV-STATE1=A rules, and under D-PERSIST-ONLY1 that is all #Persist means. The runtime's own raw words keep the #Unsafe escape E0111 offers today, with their stated reasons.

Census on dev, over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, package files excluded. File-scope := bindings: 164 in 93 files, 125 of them in 63 Compiler/JetRuntime files, where writes sit in #Unsafe blocks. #Persist bindings: 14 in 14 files, all scalar literals. shared module holders: 29 in 25 files.

None of these breaks under A. The holders stay correct, and each may become a plain variable when no task touches it.

Beginner path. Write score := 0 and change it from any function. Expert path. Write !State on a ceiling to promise a function never touches module state, and ask jet inspect which functions touch which variable.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A task cannot touch a module variable at all, even to read it. That is the price of no races. Fixed module values written with : stay readable from every task, and under D-MUT-NEVER1=A a := that nothing changes is already an error. So only values that really change are owned.

For those, the error says which variable and the call path, and offers Shared, the cross-task holder, so the fix is one line.

Inference across packages could make a library change break a caller, if a function starts touching a variable. The touch fact is part of the public surface, so docs and hover show it, and jet update reports a dependency whose public function newly touches module state.

What remains. In test builds, a module variable is reached through the test's world, one extra load per access. Release and jet run builds keep the plain address, so only the test tier pays it.

Other options. B keeps today: functions read but never write module state, and every write goes through Shared. C is Swift's way: a marker names the owner on the variable and on every function that touches it. D is Go's: plain variables, with a race detector for tests. E is Rust's thread_local: each task gets its own copy.

Their best cases. B needs no new rule and makes every shared write visible. C makes ownership explicit where it is declared. D has zero friction. E never refuses a program. Their costs: B and C add ceremony to the common single-task case, D allows real races, and E silently loses a task's writes.

whyNot.reason: B makes the common single-task case wrap every counter in Shared.
C writes an owner the compiler can infer on every declaration.

decisions.title: No warnings: jet fmt rewrites style, tidy errors never stop jet run or jet dev, and jet check and jet build list them and fail
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that Jet should have no warnings: a finding is an error or nothing. The owner added a builder-friendly rule. Tidiness never stops jet run or jet dev, while jet check and jet build list everything and fail, so the list is a to-do list.

The ratified rule says warnings and lints never fail a build by default. This ballot reverses it and changes how four ratified checks report their findings, without changing what they find. Keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: Should Jet drop warnings, so jet fmt fixes style and jet check fails on untidy code that jet run still runs?
decisions.lesson: A warning is a message that says something may be wrong but lets the program build anyway. People learn to ignore them, and real problems hide among them. This vote decides whether Jet keeps warnings, or makes each finding a style fix, a listed error, or nothing.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A lint is a check for code that works but is probably not what was meant, such as an import nothing uses. Style is how code is laid out and spelled when the meaning is the same.

A tidy error is a new kind of finding under A. It never stops jet run, jet dev or jet test, and it makes jet check and jet build fail.
decisions.story: Ada's game runs, and jet check prints four warnings and says ok. She ships it. Months later the warnings number two hundred, and the one that mattered, a never-read result, is lost among them.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How findings that are not plain errors reach the user, and which commands fail on them. It does not change what any check finds. Real errors, where a program has no single meaning, stop every command as today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe n01 has an unused import, an unused local, a final return, a positional Bool argument and an unused private function. jet run prints TOTAL 6 and exits 0. jet check prints four warnings, now shown by name: PositionalBoolParameter, RedundantFinalReturn, UnusedLocalBinding and UnusedImport. It ends ok with 4 warnings and exits 0; jet build prints none and exits 0.

No unused-function finding fires for the unused helper in a loose file. Probe n02, a := that never changes, gets no finding at all, so D-MUT-NEVER1's ratified error is still not built. Probe n03 writes loud: true at the call, and PositionalBoolParameter still fires on the declaration.

Under A, every current lint goes to exactly one of three places. First, style: a rewrite with one certain result goes to jet fmt, which applies it. Second, tidy errors: a finding that needs a person's choice is listed with its fix. Third, advice that is not about wrong code leaves the diagnostic stream and becomes a report command.

Style moves to jet fmt. Examples are a redundant final return (L0530), a redundant unit binding (L0531), compound assignment (L0503) and a positional Bool argument (L2401). For L2401, jet fmt writes the parameter's label at each call, as n03 shows by hand, and the declaration lint is deleted. Style never fails any command; jet fmt --check exists for CI.

Tidy errors keep their code, Why and Fix. Examples are unused imports, locals, parameters and private functions (L0101 to L0104), unreachable arms and code, a constant loop condition, a discarded value, a zero divisor, and floats compared with ==. D-MUT-NEVER1's never-changed :=, D-MEMBER-LIVE1's unread fields and D-IDENT-CHARS1's look-alike names become tidy errors too.

D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1's one unsuppressible warning on pub _name becomes an unsuppressible tidy error. Tidy errors are reported with error severity in the editor, and in JSON output they carry kind tidy, so a tool can tell them from real errors.

Advice becomes reports. Performance hints such as growth in a loop (L0505), hidden allocation (L0506) and whole-file reads (L2501) leave the diagnostic stream. So do complexity (L2902), undocumented public items (L2201) and doctor advice (L2101). They move under jet lint, which already takes --complexity and --a11y, and which fails only when --max is given.

Which command does what under A. jet run, jet dev and jet test never stop or print for tidy errors; jet dev's status line shows their count. jet check and jet build list every tidy error with every real error, collect-all, and exit 1 if there is any. The list is the to-do list the owner asked for.

Whose to-do list. Tidy errors are listed only for the packages being checked or built: the entry package and workspace members. A dependency's tidy errors never fail its consumer; its own jet check lists them for its author. Findings inside code made by #run, derives or templates are reported at the written template when it is in the package, and dropped otherwise.

Saying a finding is intended. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") is a marker that exists today, with 52 uses on dev, such as #Allow(jet.RedundantFinalReturn, ...). It removes one tidy error at one site, and its reason is required. The build report lists every #Allow, so a reviewer sees each exception. Real errors and unsuppressible tidy errors ignore it.

Migration. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet registers 69 L and W codes on dev, and DiagnosticRows.jet mirrors the same 69. Each code gets one of the three places in the cutover, by the rule above. On the seed, docs mentioned L and W codes 14,182 times, mostly in generated pages that regenerate.

Existing code that warns today will fail jet check and jet build under A. The first run lists every item, so a package sees its whole to-do list at once. jet fix applies every fix that is certain, such as deleting an unused import, and jet fmt applies style.

Beginner path. jet run always runs a program that has a meaning, however untidy. Before sharing it, jet check lists what to clean, each item with its fix, and the list ends at zero.

Expert path. CI runs jet check, jet build and jet fmt --check; all three must pass. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") records a deliberate exception, and jet lint --complexity or --a11y with --max adds stricter reports where a team wants them.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A package that builds today with warnings fails jet build after the cutover. jet fix and jet fmt clear the certain items in one run, and jet run keeps working while the rest is cleaned.

A half-finished edit with an unused local cannot pass jet check, even when the author means to finish it later. The author either names it _name, as the fix says, or keeps running with jet run and jet dev, which never stop for it.

Other options. B keeps D-LINTPOLICY1: warnings stay, and they never fail a build. C is Go's rule: unused imports and locals are real errors in every command, jet run included, and other checks move to a separate vet command. D is Rust's rule: warnings stay by default, and a project setting or flag turns every warning into a failure for CI.

C is the strictest, and it stops a quick experiment for an unused name, which the owner's rule says tidiness must never do. D keeps warnings for people who do not turn on the setting, so the ignored-warnings problem stays for most users.

decisions.title: #Persist means only that a value survives a hot reload, and writes follow the one module-variable rule
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that #Persist should mean only that a value survives a reload. Today the marker also makes the value writable from functions and lets it be handed to a write parameter. No other module value gets either right.

This ballot removes both write rights from the marker. Who may change a module value is then one rule for every module value. That rule is decided by the open module-variable ballot, so the two are coupled, and the cutover waits for it. Keeping today's grant is option B.
decisions.gist: Should #Persist only keep a value across a hot reload, leaving who may change it to the module-variable rule?
decisions.lesson: jet dev can swap in edited code while a game keeps running. #Persist marks a value, such as a score, that keeps its contents through that swap. Today the marker also decides who may change the value. This vote decides whether it does only the first job.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A hot reload is jet dev replacing changed code in a running program. A module variable is a name := value written outside every function.

A write parameter, written &Int, lets a function change the caller's value. A shared holder, written shared Score{…}, is a value several tasks may change safely.
decisions.story: Ada marks her score #Persist so playtests keep it through edits. She then marks an unrelated counter #Persist too, only because that is the one way a function may change it. Now the counter also survives reloads, which she never wanted.
decisions.inWild:
; Clojure: defonce survives a reload; the atom does the writes.
(defonce score (atom 0))
(swap! score inc)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only what the #Persist marker grants. It does not decide whether functions may write a plain module variable; that is the open module-variable proposal. Survival itself, its identity by module path and name, the announced restart on a layout change and D-LIVE-PERSIST1's migrations stay as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe p01 to p11 matches the seed. Probe p01 writes a plain score := 0 from a function and gets E0111, whose fix offers a shared holder, #Persist, or #Unsafe. Probe p07 shows that run itself cannot write a plain module variable either. Probe p02 marks the binding #Persist, and the same write works and prints score 1.

Probe p03 hands a #Persist binding to a function taking total: &Int, and it prints score 1; today's call site writes add_point(score) with no &. Probe p04 hands a local of run the same way, and it works. Probe p06 hands a plain module variable the same way and gets E0223, PersistentMutableBorrow. Probe p05 reads a #Persist value without writing it and prints best 10.

Probe p09 builds a module-level holder, SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, writes SCORE.value += 1 from a function, and prints score 1. Probe p08 marks the same holder #Persist and gets E0622, ModuleGlobalNotLiteral, so D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder is ratified but not built. The open D-MODULE-BUILD1=A lifts E0622 for storable initializers. E0111's fix shows the holder with a lowercase name, which fails the constant casing rule.

What survival means, exactly. Under D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A, a jet dev swap already keeps every module variable's live value unless its starting value changed. #Persist adds the two cases a plain value loses. It is kept when its starting value is edited, and kept across a jet dev restart as D-DEV-STATE1=A rules, while its name and type still fit.

The rule under A. #Persist grants survival and nothing else. It grants no write access and no write parameter passing. A #Persist binding is written exactly where a plain module variable of the same kind may be written, and refused with the same error where one may not.

With today's module rule, a function cannot write a #Persist scalar. The form for changing pinned state is a holder: #Persist SCORE: shared Score{value: 0}, written SCORE.value += 1, in today's holder spelling. Probe p08 shows it is not built yet. Survival comes from the marker and safe writes come from the holder, as Clojure's defonce and atom split them.

If the open module-variable ballot passes as recommended, score := 0 becomes writable from functions on the main task, and #Persist score := 0 is writable by that same rule. A task still cannot touch it, which closes the race today's grant allows: a task can write a #Persist score while run does. No marker then changes who may write.

The coupling, engineered so no game loses pinned state. A's cutover lands in the same change as the module-variable outcome. If you accept the proposal, the write grant moves from the marker to the plain rule, and no #Persist program changes. If not, the cutover lands with D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder built, and jet fix rewrites each written #Persist scalar into a holder.

D-PERSIST-BORROW1's write parameter rule follows the same law. A #Persist binding may be handed to a &Int parameter exactly when a plain module variable may. Today that is E0223 for both; the module-variable outcome decides it for both at once.

Error texts. E0111's fix drops the or mark it #Persist choice from both of its copies, because the marker no longer grants writes. Its holder example is written SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, with the constant casing; if D-SHARED-TYPE1 respells holders, the text follows it. E0223 stops naming #Persist as the exception.

Migration, a census on dev. There are 14 #Persist module bindings, all scalar; one is Examples/Tooling/DevLoop/Persist.jet and the rest are tests. #Persist appears 62 times in 32 Jet files, mostly Compiler source and fixtures, and 55 times in 18 Markdown files. On the seed, 10 of the bindings were written by a function in the same file.

Beginner path. Mark game state #Persist to keep it while editing. Change it the same way as any module value; the error that refuses a write names the holder, and later the plain variable, as the fix.

Expert path. Survival and write access are separate decisions, so a cache can be persisted read-only, and a holder can be shared between tasks without surviving reloads. Each property is visible in one place.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Until the module-variable outcome lands, a written #Persist scalar needs a holder, which is longer than score += 1. The cutover never lands before the holder or the plain rule is built, and jet fix writes the holder.

A holder for a scalar needs a one-field struct today, because probe p10 shows shared 0 refuses SCORE += 1 and printing. That scalar ergonomics question is part of the open module-state proposal, and A does not depend on its answer.

Other options. B keeps D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1: #Persist both survives reloads and grants writes. C is Elm's model: no module value survives; run keeps its state in a local, and jet dev hands run's state value to the reloaded code. D is a Smalltalk or Lisp image: every module variable survives a reload, with no marker.

C changes how every game is written, since state must flow through run and its callees. D keeps stale values the author meant to reset, such as a constant table they just edited.

decisions.title: Keep <> in every pipe step, and let E0438's fix write it into the missing first slot
decisions.situation:
A pipe step is a line starting with |>, and <> inside it stands for the value from the line above. The ratified rule says every step writes <> at least once; a step without it is an error.

The review asked whether a step without <> should pass the value as the first argument, as Elixir does. The owner kept <>, because it marks where piped data goes. A keeps the rule and makes the error's fix write <> for you; B is the review's proposal.
decisions.gist: Should a pipe step keep writing <>, or should a call step without <> take the value as its first argument?
decisions.lesson: A pipe passes a value down a chain of steps. Jet marks where the value lands with <>, as in |> add(<>, 10). Some languages drop the mark and put the value first. This vote decides whether Jet's steps keep the mark.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A pipe step is a line starting with |>. <> stands for the value from the step above. E0438 is the error for a step that never uses <>. A fix is the rewrite an error offers to apply for you.
decisions.story: Ivo writes |> double() and |> add(10) out of Elixir habit and gets E0438 twice. Under A, jet fix turns the first into double(<>). For add, both slots take an Int, so his editor offers add(<>, 10) first, and a later reader sees exactly where the value went.
decisions.inWild:
# Elixir: the value is the first argument of each call step.
3
|> double()
|> add(10)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a pipe step may leave out <>. Pipes themselves, the <> glyph and the ?? return fallback of D-PIPE1=A are unchanged.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Probe p02 writes 3 |> double(<>) |> add(<>, 10) and prints 16, and 3 |> add(10, <>) prints 13. Probe p01 writes |> double, |> double() and |> add(10), and each is E0438, PipeStepWithoutValue. Its fix today is general: write <> where the value goes, or end the pipe before this step.

Probe p03 writes |> print("done") in the middle of a pipe. That is also E0438, and here the error is doing its job: the step ignored the value, which is almost always a mistake.

The rule under A. Every step writes <>, as ratified, and E0438's fix gets exact. A bare function name of one parameter becomes name(<>). A call exactly one argument short becomes a call with <> in the one slot whose parameter accepts the value's type. A name that is only a method of the value's type becomes <>.name(…).

No silent wrong placement. jet fix applies the fix only when exactly one placement fits. When several slots accept the type, as in add(10) with two Int parameters, the error lists each placement. The editor offers each, first slot first, and jet fix leaves the site for a person. Otherwise the fix stays the general one.

So the typing cost of the mark becomes one jet fix, and the reader still sees where the value lands in every step.

Census on dev, unchanged from the seed. Pipes are rare. 13 lines in 4 Jet files start with a step. Outside the compiler's message strings, 18 steps sit in 7 files. 5 pass <> as the whole first argument and 5 call a method on it there, as Int.parse(<>.trim()). 4 put it in a condition, a lambda or a comparison, and 4 are error tests with no <>.

So 9 of the 14 working steps would need <> even under a first-argument rule, and those steps would mix two styles.

Beginner path. Write <> where the value goes; if you forget, jet fix writes it. Expert path. The same rule everywhere: a step is any expression, and <> may appear more than once or deep inside.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A step written the Elixir way fails once. The improved fix rewrites it exactly, so the cost is one command, not a lookup.

What remains. The common first-argument step carries two characters, <> and a comma, that Elixir leaves out. That is the price of the mark you chose to keep.

Other options. B is the review's proposal, guarded: a call one argument short takes the value first, so a complete call like print("done") still fails. C is Elixir's rule unguarded. D is F#'s bare function name. E fills the last argument, as OCaml and F# do.

Their best cases. B shortens 5 steps with no silent change to a complete call. C is the shortest. D reads cleanly for one-argument functions. E suits curried libraries.

Their costs. B leaves no mark, so a reader must know the callee's arity to see where the value goes. C turns a forgotten value into a silent wrong call. D adds a second step form. E puts the value where Jet's argument order rarely expects it.

decisions.title: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.situation: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head? A lookup may return a value, no match or an error. Kai needs three different answers without repeating the lookup. Both choices make that same pattern table fit on one line and retire the result-only short form. We recommend adding compact layout to the existing table, without another expression head.
decisions.gist: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.lesson: Missing data is different from a failed lookup. List each outcome when they need different answers. Compact and expanded tables must use the same patterns, ownership checks and control-flow rules.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A result is a value or an error. An arm table is if subject == { … } with one arm per case. A single-arm if tests one case, as in if r == .Ok(n) -> …. The ?? fallback gives a value when the result is an error.
decisions.story: Kai calls lookup for -1, 0 and 7. Every choice prints -1, 0 and 7 after exactly one lookup per input.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative comma-separated general match for the same three outcomes.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/ExpressionForms/ResultHandlers.jet:1-3 and :99-105 already lower the short handler to ordinary pattern branches. Both options extend that canonical pattern route; neither adds a second result evaluator.

C adds comma separators and optional trailing commas to ordinary pattern tables. F additionally permits `subject ? { arms }` as a general short head. Both retire the result-only `? name -> ... ! name -> ...` spelling in a coordinated cutover, explicitly amending D-RESULT-DECON2=B. The compact feature is general to enums, not only error carriers. Ordinary automatic propagation and ?? remain unchanged.

The shared program uses the ratified flat Int? Problem! cases: .Val, .None and .Err. There is no nested .Ok(.Val(...)) carrier. Evaluate the subject once, run only the selected arm and retain branch-local bindings. Return, break and next retain their enclosing targets; no callback is inserted. Ordinary move/borrow, cleanup, finishing duties and secrecy tags apply.

Beginners use propagation or ?? for simple fallbacks. Experts expand the same table for multi-step arms. Closed sets list every case explicitly; an else arm cannot hide a newly added closed case. Open sets keep the existing else requirement. Missing and duplicate arms use the same checker. Format by width and comments; do not maintain separate compact and expanded AST meanings.

The strongest smaller change was already option C. The prior recommendation preferred a new head mainly because it was shorter, without evidence that the existing head imposed meaningful friction. C supplies the compact three-outcome expression without that extra spelling. F remains a genuine organization alternative under I8, not a second runtime mechanism. The migration must preserve subject evaluation, control targets, binding hygiene and drop timing.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Changed the recommendation to the strongest smaller extension and removed the false second-runtime-mechanism framing.

decisions.title: The shared keyword is retired, and Shared{value} builds a shared cell
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review ruled that the shared keyword goes and that Shared{value} is the spelling. Today counter: shared Counter{hits: 0} builds a lock-guarded cell of type Shared<Counter>. That spelling was ratified, with the rule that shared expr constructs the cell.

A amends only that construction form. Plain field access, one atomic step per statement, #Transact, the Shared<T> type and the sharing menu stay, respelled. Keeping the keyword is option B.
decisions.gist: Should a shared cell be built as Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}, retiring the shared keyword and the Shared.new leftover?
decisions.lesson: A shared cell lets several tasks read and change one value safely, one statement at a time. Today a keyword builds it, while its type is written Shared<Counter>. This vote decides whether the type's own name builds it, the way other Jet values are built.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside other work. A shared cell is a value that several tasks may use at once; a lock inside it lets one statement in at a time.

Shared<Counter> is the type of a shared cell that holds a Counter. A keyword is a word the language reserves for its own grammar.
decisions.story: Ada sees Shared<Counter> in a parameter and writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} to make one. The compiler says it needs Shared but got Counter. The working spelling is the lowercase word shared, which she would not have guessed from the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how a shared cell is written when it is built. What a shared cell does, how its fields are read and written, how several steps commit under #Transact, and how lock order is checked do not change.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe h01 builds counter: shared Counter{hits: 0}, passes it to two tasks, and prints 1, 2 and hits 2. Probe h02 writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} and probe h03 writes Shared<Counter>{Counter{hits: 0}}; both are E0108, This needs Shared, but the value is Counter.

Probe h04 uses shared as a local name, and it works and prints shared 3, so the word is already contextual. Probe h05 writes Shared.new(Counter{hits: 0}) and it works and prints hits 1. E1115 RetiredSharedNew is registered for that form, with status Retired, so it never fires.

The rule under A. Shared{value} builds a cell that holds exactly one value, and its element type is inferred from that value. Shared<Counter>{value} names the element type, for when the value alone does not settle it. The value moves into the cell, and cloning the cell clones its handle, as today.

Why braces. In Jet a type name followed by braces builds a value of that type: Counter{hits: 0} builds a struct, and [Int]{1, 2} builds a list from its elements. Shared{value} is the list form with one element. The project's rule says a construct is a word, a marker or a library name. A shared cell is a runtime value with a type, so its library name builds it.

What is refused, each with a fix. Shared{} and a cell with two values say a cell holds one value. A field list such as Shared{hits: 0} says to build the value first, and its fix writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} when the expected type names Counter. E0108 for a Counter where a Shared<Counter> is needed gains the fix: wrap it as Shared{value}.

Retiring the old spellings. shared expr becomes one registered retirement error whose fix rewrites it to Shared{expr} by parse node. shared becomes an ordinary name everywhere; it leaves the reserved list, and the KW_SHARED spelling and its four references are deleted. Shared.new(value) gets E1115 back with an active status and the same fix.

Fix texts that spell the keyword are updated. E0111's fix today shows score: shared Count{value: 0}, which itself fails, because a module constant needs an ALL_CAPS name (probe p09). Under A it shows SCORE: Shared{Count{value: 0}}. E1101's menu becomes: give it (^), freeze it (freeze), or share it (Shared{value}).

D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A writes a module-level shared holder with the keyword; under A the same holder is written #Persist STORE: Shared{Storage{...}}. Probe p09 shows today's module-level holder works: SCORE: shared Count{value: 0} is written by a function and prints score 1.

Scalars are unchanged by this ballot. Probe p10 shows shared 0 builds a Shared<Int>, but SCORE += 1 and printing it are refused today. Under A, Shared{0} builds the same Shared<Int> with the same rules, so wrapping a scalar in a struct stays the working form.

Migration. The seed's census script counted 402 constructions: tests 149, Compiler 134, Core 59, Jetpack 26, Examples 16, Tools 7 and Docs code blocks 11, plus 23 prose mentions. On dev, git grep -cE for shared followed by a capital, digit, bracket or paren finds 413 in Jet files, comments included. Shared.new( appears 9 times. jet fix rewrites every construction in one run.

Beginner path. The type a parameter asks for, Shared<Counter>, is also how to build one: Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}. There is one spelling to learn, and the old one prints the new one in its fix.

Expert path. Shared<Counter>{make_counter()} pins the element type when a generic value would infer something else. Expert guards, Condition, #Transact and freeze are unchanged, and a cell inside a struct field or a list is built the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} has one more pair of braces than shared Counter{hits: 0}. The braces show where the held value starts and ends, which the keyword left to the reader's sense of precedence.

402 constructions and the docs that teach the keyword must change. jet fix rewrites them by parse node, and the retirement error teaches the new form to anyone who types the old one.

Other options. B keeps the keyword as D-CONC-SHARE1 ratified. C is Rust's style, Shared.new(value), which works today through h05's leftover path. D is a marker on the binding, #Shared counter: Counter{hits: 0}, at its best case: no new construction syntax, and the binding reads as a Counter that tasks may share.

D hides a change of type behind a marker: the binding's type is Shared<Counter>, yet it is written as a Counter. Under the project's rule, markers carry compile-time properties of a declaration, not the type of a runtime value. C adds a second way to build values next to the brace form every other type uses.

One construction form across open ballots. Jet's conversions and typed literals already use braces: Int{b.len}, U8{1}, and Type{Rock} in the open type-value ballot. The open Any ballot spells its box Any(value). If both pass, the box follows this ballot's form, Any{value} and Any.Owes{value}, so every wrapper is built the same way; its type patterns keep parentheses.
