decisions.title: The arrow always comes first after the parameters, and the error-first unit order is retired
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review agreed that the arrow should always come before the result, and that the error-first order should be invalid. Today a function that returns a value writes its arrow first. A unit function that can fail writes its error first, or has no arrow at all.

A later ruling already writes a failing unit function as -> ! SaveError, which assumes the arrow-first order. A reverses the ratified error-first order and keeps one arrow and the fused effect arrow. Keeping the error-first order is option B.
decisions.gist: Should every signature put its arrow before the result and the error, so a failing unit function writes -> ! IOError?
decisions.lesson: After a function's inputs come up to three things: what it may touch, what it returns, and how it can fail. Today their order depends on whether the function returns a value. This vote decides whether one order holds for every function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The effect arrow, such as -[FS.Write]>, lists what a function may touch; -> is the arrow with no effects listed. The result is the type a function returns on success.

The error contract, such as ! IOError, names how the function can fail, and ! Never says it cannot. A unit function returns no value.
decisions.story: Ada writes load with the arrow first and copies its shape for save, which returns nothing. The compiler refuses the arrow before a unit contract and tells her to write the error first. She now keeps two orders in her head for one idea.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only the order of the parts that follow a function's parameters. Which effects, results and errors a function has, and how they are checked, do not change. Lambdas keep D-LAMBDA-IFACE2's rule: they write no result or error type, and their arrow starts the body.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), probes are written in today's built spelling, String IOError!, and match the seed. Probe s01 writes load arrow first, save error first and check_name with no arrow; it runs and prints hello. Probe s02 writes save as -[FS.Write]> IOError! and check_name as -> IOError!.

Both lines of s02 are E0003: a unit-fallible error contract comes before the effect arrow, and a unit-fallible signature has no ->. Probe s03 tries the Swift order for a value and gets E0080, because a type may follow the arrow only where the result goes. Probe s04 shows -> Never! refused like s02. Probe s05 shows the same rule inside a function type.

The rule under A. After the parameters, a signature has either nothing or exactly one arrow, -> or -[Effects]>. After the arrow come the optional result type and then the optional error contract, in that order. A unit function that can fail writes the arrow and then the contract alone.

Every form under A. With nothing to say, fn(x) { } has no arrow. Pure forms: fn(x) -> Int, fn(x) -> Int ! ParseError, fn(x) -> ! IOError and fn(x) -> ! Never. With effects the arrow is -[FS]> in the same position: -[FS]> { }, -[FS]> String ! IOError and -[FS]> ! IOError. The empty row -[]> works the same way.

Function types read the same way, so fn(String) -[FS.Write]> ! IOError is a parameter type. Trait methods and extern declarations follow the same order. The entry point keeps its default: run: fn() { } is fallible with Err, and an expert pins it as run: fn() -> ! Err.

Reading a contract. After the arrow, a spaced ! starts the error contract; a type before it is the result. So -> ! IOError is a unit function that can fail, -> String ! IOError returns a String or fails, and -> String cannot fail. A lone type with no ! is the result.

Spelling. D-ERR-CONTRACT1=A, ratified, writes the error contract as String ! ParseError, and its own unit example is save: fn(n: Int) -> ! ParseError. So that ruling already assumes this order, and its retirement of String ParseError! lands with this ballot's cut. One jet fix run applies both.

That spelling is not built yet. On t6c, probe s09 writes -> String ! SaveError and gets E0003 at the result, so every probe here uses today's String IOError! spelling. The programs in this ballot show the ratified spelling.

What becomes an error. Today's error-first order fn(x) IOError! -[FS]> and the arrowless contract fn(x) IOError! both become one registered retirement error. Its fix moves the contract after an arrow and respells it: -> ! IOError or -[FS]> ! IOError. A bare -> with nothing after it, and -> Unit, stay illegal, as D-SIG-AFTER1 says.

The four E0003 texts that teach the old order are deleted with their fixes; the census finds exactly four, in Compiler, tests and Docs. The retirement fix works on parsed nodes, keeps comments and source locations, and moves only the contract and arrow tokens. It rewrites function types inside parameters, fields and aliases too.

Migration, from the census script re-run on dev. Error first with an effect row: 1,606 signatures (Core 605, Jetpack 698, Compiler 114, Tools 123, tests 45, Examples 9, Docs 12). Arrowless unit-fallible, not Never: 1,807. Arrowless Never!: 3,859. So A changes about 7,272 signatures.

Value signatures with effects, a result and an error already use A's order: 2,250 of them, and they change only in D-ERR-CONTRACT1's respelling. The counts come from regular expressions over source text, so they are estimates; the fix works on the parse tree and reports each edit. The owner's review figures for Core came from a different count.

Beginner path. One sentence covers every function: after the inputs, write an arrow, then what it returns, then how it fails. A function with nothing to say after its inputs has no arrow. The retirement error prints the rewritten line beside the old one.

Expert path. Function types, trait methods, extern declarations and generic signatures share the one order, so a signature copied into a type annotation needs no edit. Effect rows, error unions such as ! DbError | TimeoutError, and ! Never all sit where they sit for a value function.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. About 5,700 unit functions that can fail gain an arrow, 3,859 of them Never functions. jet fix writes the arrow in one run, and the formatter never removes it. A failing unit function is three characters longer, the arrow and its space; that is the price of one order.

Readers and tools that learned the old order meet the retirement error. It is registered, so jet fix applies it across a package in one run, and the error names the new order on the exact line.

Other options. B keeps the error-first order: unit signatures that can fail put the error first or have no arrow, and value signatures put the arrow first. Under the ratified spelling that reads fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Write]>, and B would also amend D-ERR-CONTRACT1's unit example, -> ! SaveError.

C is Swift's order for every function: the error contract before the arrow, then the result, as in fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Read]> String. D moves only the effect form, so -[FS]> ! IOError is required and a pure fn(x) ! IOError keeps no arrow.

C moves the 2,250 value signatures with effects and errors, and every pure value signature with an error. It reverses D-SIG-AFTER1's rule that the result follows the one arrow. D changes the fewest lines, 1,606, but keeps two shapes for a unit function that can fail, chosen by whether it has effects.

C puts errors before results everywhere, reverses D-SIG-AFTER1's result position and rewrites every value signature with an error.
D changes the fewest lines but leaves pure and effectful unit functions in two different shapes.

decisions.title: Teach three ways to hold changing state: a plain value, Shared across tasks, and a Pool with IDs for graphs
decisions.situation:
Jet has seven ways to hold a value that changes: a plain value, Shared, Pool with ID, Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak, beside #Persist and module state. The docs and examples show them as peers, so a beginner must choose among seven.

The owner's language review proposed teaching three, with the rest kept for experts. This is a teaching rule, not a language change, and it extends the ratified short-path rule for examples.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's beginner path teach three ways to hold changing state, with Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak kept for experts?
decisions.lesson: A program's values change as it runs: a score goes up, tasks count hits, a tree grows. Jet has seven tools for holding such values. Most programs need only three. This vote decides which tools a beginner is taught first.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A holder is how a value that changes is kept. Shared lets tasks change one value safely. A Pool stores many values and hands out IDs, so a tree can point both ways. Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak are finer tools.
decisions.story: Sam counts hits from two tasks. Coming from Java, he reaches for Atomic, and Jet answers E1102: Atomic can't cross into a task. Under A the first page on changing state shows him Shared, which works.
decisions.inWild:
// Go's advice: share memory by communicating.
results := make(chan int)
go func() { results <- work() }()
total += <-results
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which holders the beginner path teaches, and in what order. No holder is added or removed; experts keep every one.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe s01 uses the three proposed holders: a plain score, a shared hit count changed by two tasks, and a Pool tree with a parent ID. It prints score 10, tasks 2, hits 2, leaf leaf.

Probe s02 writes the same program with Cell and Atomic, as a reader from Java or Rust would. Cell works. Atomic<Int> passed to a task is E1102, and its Why says the compiler has no registered ownership facts for Atomic.

So that refusal is a missing registration, not a rule, and this ballot does not lean on it. Probe s03 writes Go's way: tasks return values, and it prints score 10, hits 2.

Census on dev, Jet files in Examples, comment lines skipped, by git grep. shared or Shared is on 43 lines, Pool< or ID< on 10, guard_edit, guard_read, guard_write and guard.value on 12. Cell is on 4, Weak or downgrade on 4, #Persist on 1 and Atomic on 0. So the examples already lean toward the three.

What A changes. The guide's chapter on changing state teaches three holders, in order. First a plain value, the default. Then Shared, for one value changed by several tasks. Then a Pool with IDs, for graphs and trees.

Cell, Atomic, guards, Weak, #Persist and module-state rules move to an expert chapter, each with the problem it solves. Examples/Memory keeps the three at its top level and moves the rest under an Expert folder.

A registry check makes it stick. When a beginner holder solves the problem, an error's first fix names it. An expert holder may come first only when none of the three solves it, and then the fix links its chapter.

The check lists today's rows to reword. E0111 suggests the shared keyword with a lowercase module name, which itself fails; under A it shows the ALL_CAPS module holder, a Shared. E1102 suggests rebuilding an owned copy, and under A it names Shared first.

What stays. Every holder keeps its API: D-SHARED-API1, D-POOLID-API1 and D-SHAREDGUARD1 are unchanged. Expert pages link from each error that needs them.

Beginner path. Change a plain value; share it across tasks with Shared; build a graph with a Pool. Expert path. Cell for change behind a read-only view, Atomic for lock-free counters, guards for holding a lock, Weak for back links, #Persist for state across reloads.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A reader from Rust or Java looks for Atomic first. Every error that mentions Atomic links the expert chapter, and E1102 names Shared as the fix for a value several tasks change.

What remains. Shared costs a lock where Atomic would not. For a beginner's counter that cost is small, and the expert chapter shows when Atomic is worth it, once its ownership facts are registered.

Other options. B keeps today's peers. C teaches two, a plain value and Shared, and builds graphs from shared nodes with Weak back links. D teaches one, a plain value, and has tasks return results, as Go and Erlang advise; Shared and Pool become expert.

Their best cases. B hides nothing. C is one holder fewer. D is the smallest first step. Their costs: B leaves the beginner to pick among seven. C teaches Weak, the hardest part, to beginners. D leaves no beginner answer for a value several tasks must change.

decisions.title: One strictness field in package.jet names four levels, script, app, library and hardened, each a fixed bundle of today's policy keys
decisions.situation:
Jet already has many separate rigor settings: 20 scoped policy keys, 10 package policy fields, the authority block and named test profiles. A team that wants a careful package must know which ones to turn on.

A probe package that turns on harden, sentries, a lint and an authority list runs. A package that writes one strictness level is refused as an unknown field.
decisions.gist: Should package.jet get one strictness field whose four levels turn on fixed bundles of today's policy keys?
decisions.lesson: Jet can check a program more or less strictly, but each check is its own setting. This vote decides whether one word in package.jet picks a level. Each level turns on a fixed set of the existing checks.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A policy key is one package.jet setting, such as harden: true. The authority block lists the powers a package may use. A sentry is a runtime check kept in the built program.
decisions.story: Ben's team ships a parser that other teams depend on. Under A he writes strictness: .Library, and jet check refuses any change to a public function's effects or errors that would break those teams.
decisions.inWild:
// TypeScript: one switch turns on a family of checks.
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true } }
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether one field names a level, and what each level turns on. Every level is built from checks that exist today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Policy.jet lists 20 scoped policy keys, such as unsafe, check_removal, sentries and lint_allow. package.jet's policy block also takes contain, harden, unsafe, expert, deps, claims, licenses, sources, exceptions and lints. The authority block holds allow, deny and grants.

Probe today sets policy to harden, sentries .On and a lint deny, plus an authority allow list, and prints 42. Probe dial writes strictness: .Library and gets E1215: strictness is not part of the Package vocabulary.

What A does. package.jet gets one field, strictness, with four values. A missing field keeps today's behavior exactly, so no existing program changes.

jet new writes no level, so a first program meets no new check. The cli and web templates, which ship programs to other people, write strictness: .App with their allow list already filled in.

.Script is today's default: effects are inferred and summarized, and no manifest is needed. .App adds the authority requirement. The package must have an authority allow list, which turns on D-EFFBUDGET1=D's opt-in enforcement. The error offers the inferred list as its fix.

.Library adds a stable public surface. A change to a public function's types, effects or errors that would break callers is refused until the author accepts it. The inferred signature is what is checked, so nothing new is written in source, as D-HONEST-SIG1=A says.

Where that surface lives. If the open API ballot passes, it is package.api, and .Library turns on its --locked check in every jet check. If it fails, .Library requires written effects and errors on public items instead, with the inferred text as the fix.

.Hardened adds the safety keys. It sets harden: true from D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, sentries .On and unsafe .Obligations from D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A. It also makes jet test run D-HARDENED1=A's hardened profile.

Levels only tighten. A package may add any key on top of its level. To loosen a key the level sets, the package picks a lower level and adds the keys it wants. This keeps D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A's rule that policy only tightens.

jet explain strictness lists each level's keys, and jet inspect guarantees prints the level a package chose. The levels are fixed lists in one Jet table, so a new key joins a level by one row.

Ratified decisions. A uses D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A, D-EFFBUDGET1=D, D-EFFECTS-BLOCK1=B, D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A and D-HARDENED1=A unchanged. D-MATURITY1=B's #Hardened marker is a doc label on an item; the .Hardened level is a package setting.

Census on dev, by git ls-files and git grep. The repository holds 2,490 package.jet files, 2,173 of them in tests. 207 write an allow list, and 51 write a policy block. None of them changes under A, because a missing field keeps today's behavior.

Beginner path. A first program never sees the field, since jet new writes none. Expert path. One word picks a level, and extra keys tighten further; jet explain strictness lists what each level turns on.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A team that wants .Hardened minus one key must drop a level and add keys back. jet explain strictness prints the exact key list to copy.

What remains. The levels are a fixed judgment about which checks belong together. A team with a different judgment writes the keys one by one, as it does today.

Other options. B keeps separate keys. C is one strict: true switch, as TypeScript has. D puts the level on the build profile, so one package builds at different levels.

Their best cases. B adds nothing to learn. C is the simplest name. D lets a nightly build run harder checks than a daily one. Their costs: B leaves the team to find the keys. C has only two levels. D lets a published package's level differ by build.

decisions.title: How should a trait be implemented for Pair<T> only when T has another trait?
decisions.situation:
A generic type such as Pair<T> holds values of any type T. Sometimes a trait makes sense for Pair<T> only when T can do something itself. For example, a pair can describe its total price only when each half has a price.

Jet has no way to say this today. An impl block names the type bare, and its methods cannot add a bound to the type's T. The workaround is a separate wrapper type. This ballot picks where that condition is written, or decides that Jet keeps the wrapper.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet write a condition such as 'only when T is Priced' on a trait impl for a generic type?
decisions.lesson: A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have. An impl block keeps that promise for one type. A generic type like Pair<T> works for any T. A conditional impl keeps the promise only for some T, such as every T that is Priced. Calling the method on another Pair is an error at the call.
decisions.explainer:
Today, impl Pair.Describe { … } promises Describe for every Pair. Inside it, a method may use only what every T can do. So calling self.left.price() fails with E0901, because not every T has price.

Writing the bound in the head, impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe, fails with E0003: an impl names the type bare. Adding <T: Priced> to the method makes a new T that has nothing to do with the pair's T, so the call fails with E0904.

Putting the bound on the type, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, works, but then every Pair needs a Priced T. A Pair<Int> could no longer exist.

Option A writes the condition in the impl head: impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe { … }. The head names the type's own parameter and adds a bound to it. Inside the block, T is Priced, so self.left.price() checks.

Option B keeps the bare head and adds a trailing clause: impl Pair.Describe when T: Priced { … }. The meaning is the same as A, with a different spelling.

Option C adds nothing. A program writes a wrapper type, PricedPair<T: Priced>, and implements Describe on it. Callers wrap a Pair before they describe it.

Under A and B a call on a Pair whose T is not Priced is an error at the call. p.describe() on a Pair<Int> reports E0905, the type doesn't implement the required trait, naming Describe and the unmet bound Int: Priced. The same error stops show(p) when show needs Describe.

Overlap. Two impls of one trait for one type may not both apply to the same T. A bare impl Pair.Describe and a conditional impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe overlap for every Priced T, so having both is E0908, a duplicate trait impl. Two conditional impls with different bounds also overlap, because one T could meet both bounds. So they are E0908 too.

The orphan rule does not change. The module must own the trait or the type, exactly as for a bare impl.
decisions.story: Rosa has a Pair<T> type for two items in a shopping cart. She wants pairs of priced items to describe their total, and her generic show function to accept them. Jet tells her an impl names the type bare. Her only choice today is a second type that wraps every Pair she wants to show.
decisions.detail:
Probes were run on dev 76955986d0 with the t6c compiler, as #6281 c58 asks. The files are p/c58/a.jet, b.jet and c.jet in the G1Lead-4 lane.

Probe a writes impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe and gets E0003: impl Pair takes no type parameters. The why text says an impl of a generic type names the type bare.

Probe b writes impl Pair.Describe with a describe method that calls self.left.price(). It gets E0901: calling price needs Priced.

Probe c adds <T: Priced> to the describe method. The method's T is a fresh parameter, so p.describe() gets E0904: Jet can't figure out what T should be.

A bound on the type, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, holds for every Pair, so it does not express only when.

So the answer to c58 is that current law cannot express a conditional impl. This ballot is the missing form that c58 names.

What is the same in A and B. Sema reads the bound on the impl head's parameter as a condition on the impl row. Bound satisfaction, sema_type_bound_satisfied_nominal, then also checks the impl's own bounds against the actual type arguments. Method lookup on a Pair<Int> receiver finds the row, checks the condition and reports E0905 when it fails.

Coherence. Two impl rows of one trait whose targets resolve to one nominal overlap unless their conditions can never both hold. Jet cannot prove two traits are disjoint, so any pair of rows overlaps and E0908 reports the second. A bare row is a row with no condition.

Reproduced in this lane with the same compiler, probes/ic. a_head_bound gets E0003, b_bare_head gets E0901, and c_wrapper runs and prints pair costs 7. d_two_impls, two bare impls of one trait, gets E0908 today, the rule A extends. e_missing_impl passes a Pair<Int> to show and gets E0905, the error A reports.

Generic callers. Inside a function with U: Priced, a Pair<U> meets the condition, because the check reads U's declared bounds. Inside a function whose U has no bound, Pair<U>.describe() is E0905 naming the missing U: Priced, and the fix adds that bound.

Several parameters. For a type with two parameters, such as Entry: struct<K, V>, the head lists every parameter in order and bounds only some: impl Entry<K, V: Priced>.Describe. A head that lists parameters with no bound at all stays E0003, whose fix writes the bare head.

What A does not add. A head with a concrete argument, such as impl Pair<Int>.Describe, stays E0003; a type parameter is required in each place. The head's parameter list is the same form the struct declares, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, so nothing new is spelled.

options.name: The bound goes in the impl head
options.detail: impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe { … } implements Describe for every Pair whose T is Priced. Inside the block, T is Priced. The bare head impl Pair.Describe still means every Pair. A call on a Pair<Int> is E0905, and a bare and a conditional impl of one trait together are E0908.
options.technical:
The parser accepts type parameters with bounds after the target in an impl head and stores them on ImplDef. The head lists every parameter of the type, in order, by its declared name, and at least one carries a bound. Otherwise E0003 names the expected list or, with no bound, writes the bare head.

Registration records the bounds on the impl row. Bound satisfaction and method lookup check them against the actual type arguments, reading a type parameter's declared bounds in generic code; a failure is E0905 naming the unmet bound. Coherence treats every pair of impl rows of one trait for one nominal as overlapping, so a second one is E0908. The formatter prints the head as written.

options.name: A trailing when clause
options.detail: impl Pair.Describe when T: Priced { … } has the same meaning as A. The head stays bare, and the condition follows it as a clause. Calls, overlap and errors are the same as under A.
options.technical: The parser accepts a when clause after the impl head, as a list of bounds on the target type's parameters. Names must be the type's own parameters, or E0003 names them. Registration, bound satisfaction, method lookup, E0905 and E0908 are the same as under A. The formatter prints the clause on the head line.

options.name: No conditional impls; use a wrapper type
options.detail: Jet keeps today's rule. A program declares a wrapper, PricedPair<T: Priced>, and implements Describe on it. Callers wrap a Pair before they describe it. E0003 keeps its current text, and its fix names the wrapper.
options.technical: No compiler change except the teaching. E0003 for a bounded impl head gains a fix that names the wrapper form. The c58 golden records the wrapper as the answer.

comparisons.note: The bound sits on the impl's own type parameter, as in option A.
Conditional conformance uses a trailing where clause, as in option B.
An instance context names the condition before the instance head.
comparisons.code:
instance Priced t => Describe (Pair t) where
    describe (Pair l r) = show (price l + price r)

recommendation.why: A puts the condition where the type is named, next to the parameter it limits. It reads like a generic function's bound, which Jet already writes as <T: Priced>, so there is nothing new to learn.
gains: Pairs of priced items describe themselves with no wrapper type.
The bound looks the same as a generic function's bound.
A call on the wrong Pair gets one clear error at the call.

losses.loss: The impl head grows a new form.
losses.mitigation: The form is the one generic functions already use, and the bare head keeps its meaning.

losses.loss: Two impls of one trait with different bounds cannot coexist.
losses.mitigation: Rust and Swift refuse the same overlap. E0908 names both impls, and a second trait covers the rare case.

whyNot.reason: A when clause is a second way to write a bound, while Jet writes every other bound inside angle brackets.
A wrapper type is boilerplate at every call, and it is the workaround this ballot exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more form in the impl head, for conditional impls that read like every other bound.

decisions.title: Byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a caller-owned buffer, so a steady read loop allocates nothing
decisions.situation:
Every read from a network connection hands back a fresh piece of memory holding the bytes. The runtime fills its own reusable block, then copies the bytes into a new list for the caller. The web server and the encrypted-connection reader then append that list to a buffer they already own.

So each read asks for memory and copies twice. The recommendation is A: a read form that appends straight into a buffer the caller owns, so a steady read loop stops asking for memory.
decisions.gist: Should byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a buffer the caller owns, so steady reads allocate nothing?
decisions.lesson: Reading from a network connection today hands back a fresh piece of memory each time. Busy servers read thousands of times a second. This vote decides whether Jet adds a way to read into memory the program already holds.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A buffer is a byte list a program keeps and reuses. A short read returns fewer bytes than the limit. Allocation is asking for new memory.
decisions.story: Ana's proxy forwards traffic in a loop. Under A, she keeps one buffer, clears it after each forward, and the loop asks for no new memory once it has warmed up.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: Read fills a slice the caller owns.
n, err := conn.Read(buf)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether byte streams get a read form that writes into a caller's buffer, and its shape. read(limit) stays.

Today, with the a0.0.43 compiler (dev c460ba91e5). Probe r02 reads a local TCP pair in a loop of server.read(4096) and prints read 4. Probe r03 calls server.read_into(buffer, 4096) and gets E0102, TCPStream has no method read_into.

Where the cost is. net_tcp_read_result in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/NetHandleRoutes.jet:67-118 now reuses a per-stream read block (net_read_buffer_take, :175). It still allocates a 48-byte scratch per call (:78). net_read_publish_bytes (:208-211) allocates an exact-size list and copies the bytes into it.

The hot callers on dev. Core/Http/Server.jet:1217 and 1226, Core/Http/Client.jet:735 and 746, Core/Net/Tls.jet:1104 and Core/Net/Net.jet:287. Tls.jet:1106 extends its own rx buffer with each result, the exact append A performs in place.

The per-stream block reuse that an earlier draft called pending has landed on dev. It removed the limit-sized allocation, but the exact-size list and its copy remain, so D's internal-reuse path is already spent.

Measured on a0.0.43, built programs, five runs each. 100,000 rounds of a 4,096-byte write and read on a local TCP pair take 1.09 s median (m1), about 11 µs a round. Appending each chunk to a held buffer, as TLS does, measures the same within noise (m2, 0.98 s).

Copying a 4,096-byte list 100,000 times takes 0.026 s median (m3), about 0.26 µs. So the list and copy A removes are about 2% of a local read round. Peak memory stayed near 14.5 MB in every run.

The case for A is therefore a loop that asks for no memory, which D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A asks of Core and which devices need. It is not raw speed.

The paired cell. A arrives with a two-program cell in the canonical performance manifest, as AGENTS.md requires of a surface added for performance. One program loops on read(4096); its twin does the same work with read_into into one held buffer.

The pair records wall time, allocations per read and peak memory. Ratification waits until read_into strictly beats read on it; any loss stays on a card.

What A does. n: stream.read_into(buffer, limit) appends at most limit bytes to the end of buffer and returns the count, 0 at end of stream. A limit below 1 is an invalid-input error, so 0 always means end of stream. A deadline form, read_into(buffer, limit, deadline:), matches read's.

It takes buffer by & as the parameter declares, so the call passes plain buffer. Bytes go straight from the socket into buffer's spare room, and the read's scratch lives with the stream. The list grows only when that room is short. TCP, Unix and TLS streams and file readers get the same method.

Clear already keeps a byte list's room when the list is not shared (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:3093-3117). So a loop that clears buffer after use stops allocating after the first reads. If the loop hands the bytes somewhere that keeps them, clear gives buffer fresh room; the kept bytes need their own memory anyway.

Precedent. Core's encoders already read this way through a private core.encoding.__read_into, used by Csv.jet, Stream.jet and Xml.jet. A makes the same move public, without that helper's empty-list rule.

Ratified decisions. A fits D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A, which prefers caller-owned buffers in Core. It keeps D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B: the Reader trait keeps exactly read, and read_into is an inherent method.

Beginner path. Keep writing chunk: stream.read(4096); nothing changes. Expert path. Hold one buffer and call read_into in the loop; the HTTP server and TLS reader switch the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Generic Reader code cannot call read_into. The four hot stream types cover the measured callers, and a trait default can follow later without breaking them.

What remains. A buffer that is never cleared keeps growing. That is the caller's list, visible in their code, and the limit caps each read.

Other options. B fills from index 0 up to the buffer's length, as TlsLead first drafted and as Go does. C adds read_into to the Reader trait for every Core byte source. D adds nothing and relies on internal reuse.

Their best cases. B matches Go and Rust slices. C makes middleware generic. D adds no surface. Their costs: B needs a zero-filled buffer, which Core can only build by pushing bytes, and appenders still copy. C amends D-NETIO-CONTRACT2's trait law. D keeps one allocation and copy per read.

decisions.title: TCP writes keep the ratified Writer law, mark the short count must-use, and retire the five free-function spellings
decisions.situation:
A network connection in Jet can be written eight ways. Three of them may send only the first part of the bytes and report how many went. Today a program can call one of those three, ignore the count, and compile and run. A partial send then passes unnoticed.

We recommend A. The counted write keeps its count, and ignoring it becomes a build error that points to the write-everything call. The five old free-function spellings retire. On today's code almost nothing breaks: no stream write outside those five functions ignores its count.
decisions.gist: Should TCP writes keep write's short count, make dropping it an error, and retire the five free-function spellings?
decisions.lesson: A network write may send only part of your bytes and tell you how many went. Jet has eight ways to write to a connection, and three can stop early. This vote picks the spellings to keep and how Jet stops a silent partial write.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A short count is a write that reports sending fewer bytes than asked. Must-use means the compiler refuses a call whose result is ignored. Write-everything means the call loops until all bytes are sent.
decisions.story: Ben sends a 2 MB reply with client.write(bytes) and ignores the count. Under A, the build stops on that line and tells him to call write_all, which sends every byte.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust: write may be short; clippy flags an unused count.
stream.write_all(b"ping")?;
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which TCP write spellings remain, and what happens when a caller drops a short count. Reading, Unix sockets and TLS keep their own names.

The ratified law. D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B, with option A's laws, says write may return any positive prefix count and write_all loops until done. Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet's Writer trait has exactly write -> Int and write_all.

Where they live. The methods are sema builtins in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/NetworkHandles.jet:99-104. The free functions are in Core/Net/Net.jet:282-313, each a one-line call to a method.

Census on dev 76955986d0. net.send has 0 callers. tcp_write has 1, tcp_write_bytes 1, tcp_write_all_bytes 50 in 27 files, tcp_write_text 20 in 8 files. Method calls: write_all 187 in 116 files, write_text 49 in 35 files.

Dropped counts today. A statement-start .write( on a stream-named receiver appears 3 times on dev. Two are inside the retiring send and tcp_write_bytes (Net.jet:283, 304); the third, in TrustGate.jet:172, already writes .drop(reason). So A's new error breaks no caller outside the code it retires.

Probes with the t6c compiler. t02 opens a local TCP pair, calls client.write with the count dropped, then write_all, and prints got pingpong. t01 shows a dropped pure result is E0433, but write has effects, so that rule does not apply.

Probe t03 marks an effectful function #MustUse, and the dropped call is E0419. Probe t04 marks a trait method #MustUse and drops it through an impl and through a generic bound: both compile and run. The marker is accepted on a trait method and ignored, a building bug.

Probe t05 gives #MustUse a reason and gets E0930: the marker's signature is MustUse(), so today its fix line cannot name write_all.

A ninth spelling hides in the checker. TCPStream.write also accepts a String and writes its UTF-8 bytes (NetworkHandles.jet:318-320), returning a byte count that can split a character. Its one caller is net.send, which retires.

What A does. TCPStream.write takes bytes only, keeps its count and is must-use, so a dropped count is E0419 with a fix line naming write_all. write_all and write_text stay the write-everything forms for bytes and text. Writer.write in Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet gains #MustUse, so files and TLS match.

Compiler work A needs. #MustUse gains an optional fix text, MustUse(fix: String), shown on E0419's fix line, as Rust's must_use takes a reason. A trait method's #MustUse applies to every impl and to calls through a bound, which fixes t04. The builtin write rows at NetworkHandles.jet:99-100 carry the same flag.

The five free functions go, each with a jet fix rewrite under D-CODEMOD1=A. tcp_write and tcp_write_text become write_text, tcp_write_all_bytes becomes write_all, tcp_write_bytes becomes write, and send(s, text) becomes s.write(text.bytes()). Each rewrite calls what the function called, so it keeps behavior and applies unattended.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B's write law. It uses D-DISCARD1=A's must-use rule as it stands and D-MARK-DISCARD1=A's .drop(reason) for a deliberate discard.

Beginner path. Write stream.write_all(bytes) or stream.write_text(text). If you reach for write and drop the count, the error points to write_all. Expert path. n: stream.write(bytes) keeps the count for a hand-rolled send loop.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Code that drops write's count stops compiling; on dev that is no caller outside the retiring functions. For other code, jet fix offers write_all as a needs-review edit, since it sends the rest of the bytes too. jet fix --all applies it.

What remains. The plain name write stays the partial form, which surprises Go programmers. The E0419 fix line names write_all at the moment of surprise.

Other options. B amends D-NETIO-CONTRACT2: write writes everything, as Go's io.Writer does, and write_some returns a count. C keeps all eight names and makes each write everything. D keeps today's surface.

Their best cases. B gives the short name the safe meaning. C breaks no caller. D costs nothing. Their costs: B changes the Writer law for files and TLS too. C keeps eight spellings for two jobs. D leaves the silent partial write.

decisions.title: A WebSocket route kind on the HTTP mux: the server validates and upgrades, and the handler gets the request and the connection
decisions.situation:
A WebSocket starts as a web request and then becomes a two-way connection. In Jet today, a server handler makes that switch itself and must still return a web response, which the server throws away. The handler also writes its own error replies for a bad handshake.

There is a bigger catch. The server answers one connection at a time, so while one WebSocket stays open, no other client is served (probe w04). That breaks the ratified server design, D-HTTP-SERVER2=A, and its fix serves every option.

The recommendation is A: a WebSocket route kind. The server checks the handshake, and the handler returns nothing.
decisions.gist: Should the HTTP mux gain a WebSocket route whose handler gets the connection and returns nothing, instead of a fake response?
decisions.lesson: A WebSocket starts as an ordinary web request and then becomes a two-way connection. Today a handler must still hand back a web response that nobody sees. This vote decides how a Jet server says a route is a WebSocket.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Upgrade is the step where a web request becomes a WebSocket. The mux is the server's table of routes. A handler is the function a route calls.
decisions.story: Lee writes a chat route. Under A, mux.websocket("/chat", chat) is the whole setup. Bad handshakes get a 400 before chat runs, chat never invents a response, and once the server serves connections side by side, as ratified, a second user joins while the first talks.
decisions.inWild:
// Axum: the upgrade extractor hands the socket to a callback.
ws.on_upgrade(|socket| handle(socket))
decisions.detail:
This vote chooses WebSocket route registration and the handler result. A is proposed, not built. Independently reran w01-w04 on a0.0.43: echo works, websocket registration is E0102, the proposed handler body checks, and GET waits behind an open socket.

A registers mux.websocket(pattern, handler) and #Server.WebSocket(pattern) over the same route table. The handler receives HTTPRequest and WsConn and returns Unit on the WsError rail. Authentication and Origin policy run before the handshake. Use the existing handshake validator once, not a second route-specific validator.

A owns GET for that pattern; another equivalent GET registration is a conflict. Plain GET without upgrade headers returns 400. HEAD must never upgrade; it returns 405. OPTIONS lists GET. OpenAPI records GET with handshake responses, including 101, not the later frame protocol.

The shared upgrade operation must own a transport, not a plain socket descriptor. Carry plain TCP or TLS through that same operation. Rejecting all secure WebSocket servers at bind is a dropped feature, not a fix. This transport repair is required for every option and is not evidence that A is better.

The server must meet ratified concurrency and shutdown rules under every option. Upgraded tasks remain in the server's connection budget and cancellation scope until closed. A task ending normally closes cleanly; application failure uses 1011 only while writable. Preserve protocol close codes and peer closure, and never send a second HTTP response after 101.

B returns an explicit switched response after manual upgrade. C uses an optional response; None without a completed upgrade must be an error, not a silent hang. D keeps the unused response. E returns a typed response-or-upgrade outcome with an owned callback, allowing one handler type and ordinary HTTP denial responses.

Beginner path: A's one route line and socket handler. Expert path: the same upgrade operation supports custom servers; mixed HTTP and WebSocket behavior is E's strongest case. Both require one ownership state and one handshake implementation.

decisions.title: One accessibility provider contract, using AccessKit on supported desktops
decisions.situation: Drawn controls need an accessibility description so assistive tools can find and operate them. Jet has four view roles, but its native host provider reports accessibility unavailable. This vote chooses whether to reuse desktop adapters or write every adapter in Jet. We recommend AccessKit behind the existing provider contract on supported desktops, with Jet providers for phones and semantic elements on the web.
decisions.gist: Should Jet reuse AccessKit's desktop adapters behind one accessibility provider contract?
decisions.lesson: A provider translates one logical view tree into a system's accessibility interface. Different platform adapters are implementations of that contract, not different state or view models. Both choices still need complete roles, focus, actions and manual assistive-tool acceptance.
decisions.story: Hana needs a Pay button that a keyboard user and a screen-reader user can both find and activate. The same action must run whichever adapter exposes it.
decisions.inWild: AccessKit describes itself as accessibility infrastructure for custom-drawn toolkits. Its published adapters cover macOS, Unix and Windows, and it offers C bindings and prebuilt libraries. Source: https://accesskit.dev/
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

A approves a pinned AccessKit desktop dependency and its C bridge. This is a new dependency choice, not a second accessibility mechanism. D-CORE-PROVIDER1=A supplies one replaceable provider contract; D-UI-HOME1 keeps system services in core.ui.host and views in the ui package. D-UI-VIEW1's ui.app/state model stays unchanged.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Ui/Ui.jet:39-44 lists Button, Container, Label and TextInput. Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/gui/gui.jet:542-548 wraps accessibility metadata. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/UiHostProvider.jet:17-25 reports every native capability absent. SolBallotReview compiled and ran ui_values.jet for view construction and ui_gtk_clean.jet for the unavailable GTK result. These checks do not establish browser screen-reader behavior.

RESEARCH AND CORRECTION

https://accesskit.dev/ lists macOS, Unix and Windows adapters, C/Python bindings, prebuilt C libraries, and users including egui and Slint. That page does not list phone adapters; A does not assume they exist. The earlier claim that binding AccessKit needs every user's machine to build Rust was false: prebuilt C-interface libraries are available. Local source rebuilds still require the upstream toolchain. An upstream project can be pinned or patched; fixes need not wait indefinitely for a release.

BRIDGE AND AUTHORITY

D-FFI-RUST1=A currently authorizes static user helpers only on x86_64 Linux. A explicitly extends that scope for this first-party desktop accessibility provider, not arbitrary Rust helpers. Approve the I6 bridge here: pinned source/version and license, reproducible per-target C-interface artifacts, signed distribution, typed ownership and callback lifetimes, no extra user toolchain, and normal provider availability diagnostics. Do not claim this bridge has been implemented or verified. Linux packaging must meet the existing static deployment contract or return for a separate linking decision; no hidden dynamic-loader exception.

ONE CONTRACT

One logical tree owns identity, role, label, state, reading order, focus and actions. A desktop provider forwards it through AccessKit; phone providers marshal it directly; web uses semantic elements under D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1. A target selects one provider, never two competing trees. Provider callbacks invoke the same checked actions.

SHARED ACCEPTANCE

Compare normalized semantic projections, not byte-identical platform trees or exact speech strings. Require focus traversal, action dispatch, live updates, editable text, virtualized lists and manual checks with platform assistive tools. D-A11YGATE1=B keeps optional accessibility linting separate from runtime correctness. Test gates do not magically remove adapter bugs; that obligation is shared by A and B.

B avoids an outside dependency and gives Jet all adapter code, but copying role tables alone cannot make five exports a negligible maintenance cost. A reuses maintained desktop adapters without pretending they cover phones.

decisions.title: Use the graphics chip on phones only after a measured win; keep desktop software defaults
decisions.situation: An app can paint with its main processor or its graphics chip. The approved Linux plan uses the main processor so a graphical app can remain one static file, without loading graphics drivers. The seed refuses phone runs, so this vote sets a future default rather than claiming a working phone renderer. We recommend graphics drawing on phones only after measurement, with automatic software fallback and explicit overrides.
decisions.gist: Should phones use the graphics chip after a measured win, while desktops keep software drawing?
decisions.lesson: The graphics chip is hardware for drawing. A uses it on phones only after Jet measures a win for the same app. Otherwise software drawing stays the default. Experts can choose either path explicitly. All options keep the same screen and actions; phone work still waits for Linux and web.
decisions.story: Jun wants his reading app to scroll well on a phone without learning graphics drivers or losing its portable Linux build.
decisions.inWild: Flutter documents Impeller as the default on iOS and Android API 29+. Android without Vulkan uses the older OpenGL renderer, not software drawing. This is precedent for hardware drawing, not evidence of a Jet speed or battery win. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/perf/impeller
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

D-RAYLIB-DRIVER-LOAD1=A chooses static Linux display and sound clients, with dynamically linked GPU builds as an expert opt-in. It does not establish a software default for every desktop and phone. A sets the phone policy and leaves existing desktop defaults alone. Browser acceleration remains the browser's choice. D-MOBILE-UNDEFER1=B puts phone work after Linux and web, with no pilot.

A'S CONTRACT

Both drawing paths consume the same scene, layout and shaped text. Required acceptance compares clipping, fractional positions, antialiasing, color and actions; these checks are future obligations, not proof that every device produces identical pixels. If graphics startup fails or the graphics device is lost, rebuild the drawing resources in software without losing app state. If neither path can present a window, report the actual failure; fallback is not a promise that a screen can never fail.

The paired phone workload must keep the app, fonts, resolution, refresh rate and scroll trace fixed. Record frame time, energy, cycles and bytes, and apply AGENTS.md:189-192 and the full performance gate. A switches only on a passing result before phone release; otherwise the default remains software. No phone renderer or benchmark was exercised in this review.

EXPERT CONTROL

The proposed package setting drawing: .Software forces software; drawing: .Gpu explicitly requests graphics drawing on a supported target. Forced graphics reports an unavailable driver instead of silently ignoring the request. Automatic fallback belongs to the default policy, not the forced setting. This setting controls the same renderer, not another view model.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B retains software as the default even if a GPU option measures better for a phone workload. It still offers GPU opt-in, so it does not have only one renderer to test. C extends measured hardware defaults to macOS and Windows too; those platforms need their own evidence. Neither Flutter's adoption nor the absence of Jet measurements proves a desktop loss.

EVIDENCE

The seed's jet run club.jet --target=ios returned E2104. The approved Linux rule and phone sequencing were read directly from their ratified options. No build, phone run or battery measurement ran.

ONE COST REMAINS

Hardware and software rendering can differ slightly on real devices. Shared inputs, comparison checks and an explicit software override reduce that risk; they do not prove universal pixel identity.

decisions.title: View literals become typed messages; an opt-in package supplies translation
decisions.situation: Translation shows an app's words in the reader's language, including different forms for counts. The seed has an English plural helper, but a plain string cannot become a checked message just because a parameter expects one. This vote chooses automatic view messages, explicit markers, or named keys in resource files. We recommend automatic messages with translation in an opt-in package, while keeping author review for text built elsewhere.
decisions.gist: Should text in views be translatable automatically, with translation itself in an opt-in package?
decisions.lesson: A turns view literals into typed messages automatically, extending Jet's literal capability to text. An opt-in package later collects and translates catalogs. English-only apps need no catalogs or language data. Runtime data uses ui.verbatim(value), not a translation key. One cost remains: authors must review helpers, runtime text and phrases needing context.
decisions.story: Ana's booking app starts in English. A year later a Brazilian club wants it in Portuguese. She wants that to be a translator's job, not a rewrite of every screen.
decisions.inWild: SwiftUI interprets a literal passed to Text as a localization key, but displays a String variable without localization. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/text. This is precedent for A, including its helper boundary, not evidence that Jet already supports it.
decisions.detail:
WHAT VOTING A INCLUDES

An opt-in first-party i18n package uses public CheckedText parts-and-holes metaprogramming under D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1=A and D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A. The small ui.Text message carrier belongs in ui; the separately ratified kit package uses it too. There is no second interpolation mechanism.

A ALSO EXTENDS LITERALS

D-FOUND-LITERAL1=A ratified numeric literal capabilities, not text literals. A explicitly extends that contextual construction mechanism to checked text. View text parameters take ui.Text only, giving a literal one expected type and retaining its fixed parts and typed holes. Runtime data uses ui.verbatim(value: String), returning the same ui.Text carrier without translation. This avoids an ambiguous ui.Text-or-String overload and prevents database values becoming catalog keys. Translatable helpers return ui.Text. Other checked kinds do not silently opt in.

PACKAGE OR METAPROGRAMMING?

Both: the optional package uses public metaprogramming for extraction and catalogs, supplying locale selection, plural rules and number/date formatting. The proposed jet i18n command is a jet-i18n PATH helper, not a private compiler subsystem. View literals need no later wrappers, making this useful for apps that may translate. No measured zero-overhead result is claimed; artifact checks must prove unused catalogs and language data are absent.

SAME MESSAGE AND FAIR ALTERNATIVES

All options show 1 booking today or 3 bookings today. A and B give the English one: form; C's source catalog gives one and other. Translation catalogs preserve hole names/types and supply each language's required forms. Missing translations fall back to source text; wording changes need review. B explicitly marks phrases. C uses stable keys that survive wording edits. English-only apps may delay either conversion until they translate, so neither charges every app up front.

ONE COST REMAINS

Authors must review helpers, runtime text and ambiguous phrases. Use ui.Text helpers, ui.verbatim for data, and context: for different meanings. Extraction can report explicit verbatim inputs and repeated phrases, but cannot list every runtime phrase or infer human meaning.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Text/Fmt.jet:31-34 selects singular when abs(n) is 1. fmt.jet printed 1 booking and 2 bookings. msg_explicit.jet printed 3 bookings today from an explicit Msg head; msg_plain.jet failed E0112 for String passed to Msg. No proposed ui.Text, ui.verbatim, extractor or catalog ran.

WHAT A APPROVES

A approves contextual checked-text literal construction plus the public ui.Text/ui.verbatim API. It does not add a compiler rule recognizing ui by name or change other checked text kinds without their opt-in.

decisions.title: Rows, columns and grids have defaults; experts can override them or write layouts
decisions.situation: Screens need to place views side by side, in columns, or in grids that adapt to the available space. The seed's box stacks children, while the approved constraint model describes relationships between their sizes and positions. This vote chooses the everyday layout model without removing custom layouts or the solver. We recommend simple containers with defaults and explicit expert settings, including a choice of narrow-screen behavior.
decisions.gist: Should layout have useful defaults, with advanced settings and custom layouts available by explicit opt-in?
decisions.lesson: A two-column signup grid fits labels to their text and gives inputs the remaining width. Below 600 logical pixels of container width it becomes one column, regardless of device. Experts override gaps, tracks, wrapping and that breakpoint. Containers use one layout contract; custom layout functions and the constraint solver remain opt-in. Browser layout follows the companion web-output vote.
decisions.story: Ana's signup form should look tidy on a laptop and stack neatly on a phone, without her learning layout rules. Rui needs exact column sizes and a custom layout for a dashboard.
decisions.inWild:
SwiftUI stacks and grids apply default spacing and alignment when none is given; modifiers override them. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/grid

Flutter separates the box model from HTML and lets experts write custom layouts. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/layout/constraints
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

A amends D-LAYOUT1=A's default surface, not its expert constraint power. Containers and custom layouts implement one measure-and-place protocol in ui under D-UI-HOME1. The solver implements that protocol as a library, not a second state/view system. D-VIEW-SET1=C keeps composed controls in kit.

DEFAULTS AND OVERRIDES

row, column, grid, stack and scroll need no optional settings. Gaps default to 8 logical pixels and padding to 0, with theme overrides. Start alignment follows reading direction. A grid with columns: N uses content-sized tracks followed by one remaining-space track.

Below 600 logical pixels of container width, the default grid becomes one column in child order. A phone is not itself the trigger. responsive: false keeps the columns; collapse_below: changes the threshold. Explicit track lists follow the same responsive rule unless overridden. Rows wrap when needed; wrap: false opts out.

A single oversized or unbreakable child can still overflow. scroll contains it, and preview checks report observed clipping. No finite preview proves every runtime state.

EXPERT PATH

Expose every supported flex/grid property, not every CSS feature: gap, padding, alignment, wrapping, grow/shrink, tracks and spans. Unsupported properties are errors. Custom functions measure and place children. The approved solver uses that same contract and retains its constraint authoring; this vote does not invent Layout{...} as another syntax.

WEB DEPENDENCY

Under D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1=A, standard containers map to CSS under its named layout/text exception. Custom functions run Jet code inside their container, without browser-side copies of app policy. With web-output B or C, shared Jet layout computes geometry. Neither vote promises identical wrapping on every engine.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B gives beginners the same presets, implemented through constraints, and experts direct relationships. It does not start beginners with equations. C includes a first-party default stylesheet and responsive rules, not an unstyled screen. Its selectors and cascade change how styles interact; it need not contain an entire browser engine.

CHECKED TODAY

ui_values_fixed.jet printed 15.0 x 2.0. Core/Ui/Ui.jet:132-146 computes maximum width and summed child heights, with text measured in display cells. That proves this example, not every layout API's absence. SwiftUI Grid documentation confirms default spacing/alignment and overrides.

NO REMAINING DEFAULT-LOCK-IN COST

Every default is overridable, with custom layouts and the solver still available. Implementation and acceptance remain shared obligations, not completed tests.

decisions.title: Phone apps follow Linux and web, with an early one-phone pilot of native contracts
decisions.situation: Phone platform work remains deferred, and current phone runs are refused. A shared app needs an explicit condition for restarting that work, not an implied delivery date. We recommend full phone bring-up after Linux and web app acceptance, within the approved compiler-target order. A bounded pilot on one phone tests native text input, lifecycle, safe areas and screen readers before the shared view contracts freeze.
decisions.gist: Should phone apps follow Linux and web, with an early one-phone pilot that tests native input and lifecycle?
decisions.lesson: A restart gate is not a release promise. Linux and web prove shared behavior, not native phone lifecycle or input. The approved compiler-target order remains binding. Browser access cannot erase later native validation.
decisions.story: Tomas leads a small team. He wants Jet on phones, but he would rather have a working Linux window and web page first than three half-finished targets at once.

Source: https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/05/compose-multiplatform-1-8-0-released-compose-multiplatform-for-ios-is-stable-and-production-ready/
decisions.detail:
OWNER GATE

Amend D-VERDICT-480-1's mobile-native deferral with a measurable restart condition. D-NATIVEUI3 retains phone support, signing and store upload. D-TARGET-ORDER1=A specifically orders wasm32-wasip2, then aarch64, then embedded bring-up; a browser page alone is not proof that the entire WebAssembly target obligation passed.

CHECKED TODAY

SolBallotReview checked union.jet for ios/android successfully, but its phone runs gave E2104. Checking source is not an executable target proof. No phone build ran during this review.

A'S CONDITION

One booking app must pass state, navigation, input, normalized accessibility and golden-view acceptance as a real Linux window and a browser app. Use the renderer and web presentation actually approved by their ballots; neither a drawn renderer nor DOM may be assumed if its vote loses. Compiler WebAssembly and ARM64 prerequisites retain their ratified order. This condition authorizes beginning native phone integration, not shipping phone targets before their own complete acceptance.

Validate portable app logic and phone-sized responsive fixtures while building the shared base. Do not claim these prove native IME, lifecycle restoration, safe areas, permissions or store delivery. Before accepting architecture choices that affect those contracts, review concrete phone requirements rather than waiting until the end to discover them.

A'S EARLY PILOT

As soon as the ratified ARM64 target exists, one phone runs a bounded native pilot. It covers text input and composition, lifecycle restore, safe areas and the screen reader. It runs before the shared view and input contracts freeze, so native risks surface early. It ships no store build.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES AND LOSS

B is the same milestone without the pilot, so native risks surface only at bring-up. C keeps the deferral until another owner vote. A's residual cost is the pilot's bounded effort before Linux and web are done.

decisions.title: One first-party app package serves the web, the desktop and phones
decisions.situation: Jet currently exposes web app builders and a separate UI tree. Ratified rulings already put their higher-level code in shipped packages, with system services remaining in Core. This vote asks whether the web package becomes the shared app layer for web, desktop and phones. We recommend one app package over the existing UI model, without moving authentication or system services back into Core.
decisions.gist: Should one first-party app package serve web, desktop and phone apps, replacing separate web and window libraries?
decisions.lesson: The app layer adds screens, navigation, forms and server calls above views. Jet currently has a web builder and a separate UI tree, not two proven complete app frameworks. This vote extends the shipped web package across targets while retaining the approved UI and authentication package homes.
decisions.story: Dana runs a tutoring business. She wants a booking site for parents, a desktop tool for her staff and a phone app for tutors. She would rather learn one way to write screens, forms and sign-in than three.
decisions.inWild: Expo Router uses the same file-based routes across Android, iOS and web, while allowing platform-specific APIs. Source: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction/
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS DECIDES

Rename the first-party web package to app and extend its app graph across targets. Amend D-WEB-HOME1's package name and scope, D-WEB-NAME1=C's framework name, D-ROUTE-ONE1's builder name, and D-GAME-PLATFORM1's web/app separation. D-UI-HOME1 and D-DB-AUTH-HOME1 retain their homes: ui is a package, core.ui.host stays Core, and auth remains its own package.

CHECKED TODAY

Core/Web/Web.jet:188 defines web.app; :291-360 holds routing and serving methods. Core/Ui/Ui.jet:195-209 supplies backends. SolBallotReview's ui_missing.jet gives E1004 for ui.application, despite D-UI-WINDOW-LIFE1's approved API. web_value.jet checked and ran web.app().facts_json(). The gui editor uses core.ui at Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/gui/gui.jet:460-475. This does not prove a complete desktop app model exists.

A'S BOUNDARY

app.new is the routed-app wrapper over D-UI-VIEW1's ui.app(view, state:). It creates no second mount, diff, state or window mechanism. ui.app is the smallest one-screen entry; app adds routes, navigation and shared form/data policy. The same route identity drives URLs and device deep links. Server handler rows remain server-only; unsupported effects are refused rather than ignored.

Core keeps HTTP and networking. app depends on auth without copying or re-exporting another authentication implementation. The gui editor may consume ui; independent editor helpers are not deleted merely to rename widgets. Standard controls use ui under D-VIEW-SET1. This adjusts D-GAME-PLATFORM1's gui composition while preserving independent video and audio packages.

C can share form and auth primitives without an I8 breach; its cost is separate top-level navigation models. B explicitly reverses the Core-home ruling; changing that ruling is not itself evidence B is technically unsound.

CUTOVER

Migrate existing core.web and first-party web callers together; do not assume no web package callers exist. Preserve server-only APIs. Prove unused target code is excluded rather than asserting this already happens. One booking example must preserve route state, browser Back and device deep links across web, desktop and phones.

decisions.title: Jet draws every control itself by default; an opt-in native library swaps in the system's real control where an expert wants it
decisions.situation: A screen can use Jet-drawn controls, each system's real controls, or a browser view inside the app. The seed's GTK example reports that its runtime is unavailable, rather than opening a window. This vote sets the default drawing model; it does not prove that any future phone renderer already works. We recommend Jet-drawn controls with explicit system-control replacements, subject to the companion vote allowing those controls inside a Jet screen.
decisions.gist: Should Jet draw every control itself by default, with system controls as an opt-in library for experts?
decisions.lesson: A draws the booking screen with Jet's styling; system typing, screen readers and expected platform behavior remain. Experts replace one picker with native.date_picker(day). Inline replacements require the companion system-view option A too. A theme only changes drawn styling; it does not turn a Jet control into a real system control.
decisions.story: Ana builds a booking app and wants it to look the same on every phone and computer without learning five toolkits. Her colleague Rui wants the iPhone build to show Apple's own date wheel.
decisions.inWild:
Flutter draws its widgets itself, while each platform embedder supplies the system keyboard, accessibility bridge and windows. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/resources/architectural-overview

Flutter embeds a real system view when an app needs one, through platform views. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/ios/platform-views
decisions.detail:
SCOPE

A amends the default-widget clauses of D-NATIVEUI3=A and D-NATIVEUI-ANDROID1=C, retaining approved interop and the single view/state model. D-ONEAPP-WEBOUT1 chooses browser presentation. D-VIEW-SET1=C puts standard composed views in kit, not ui. The owner's no-ship instruction applies independently of this drawing choice.

ONE MODEL, DIFFERENT PRESENTATIONS

Jet draws ordinary ui primitives and kit controls. Layout, state and actions remain shared; typography, accessibility settings and platform conventions can change appearance and interaction details. Do not promise one pixel image or identical scroll physics on all systems. Core host services still provide text input and composition; Jet-written adapters export accessibility under D-A11Y-EXPORT1=B. System sheets and permission prompts stay system-owned. Release acceptance must cover typing, selection, input-method composition, focus, screen readers and system navigation. Those are obligations, not measured successes.

THE SHARED NATIVE PACKAGE

The native package is the same one used in D-THEME2 and D-PLATFORM-OVERRIDE1. native.theme() supplies system-like styling for drawn controls; it is not another control implementation. native.date_picker(day) instead uses the one host-view embedding contract to return a ui.Node backed by a real system control. Where no equivalent exists, it falls back to the kit control without changing state or actions. The date state in the examples is core.time.LocalDate. A target-specific native.view(handle) cannot silently fall back and needs a supported target branch.

DEPENDENCY, NOT A SILENT FALLBACK DESIGN

A's inline native-control promise requires D-PLATFORM-OVERRIDE1=A. If the owner chooses that ballot's B or C, this A must be reconciled before implementation; it must not silently turn an inline date picker into a full-screen interaction. The surface states this dependency. Theme styling remains possible without inline embedding.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B maps the same Jet views to native toolkits. Authors still use one API, not five APIs; differences arise in toolkit behavior and available controls. The seed's static GTK refusal is an implementation fact, not proof that a future native Linux toolkit cannot work. C uses the system's browser view, which can reuse an installed engine rather than bundle one; it adds browser integration and resource costs that require measurement, not a fabricated startup number.

ONE COST REMAINS

Default controls look like Jet rather than exactly like the host. Explicit native replacements reduce that cost where supported, but inherit the composition limits and work described in the companion vote. A does not promise every imaginable system control in one line.

CHECKED TODAY

ui_gtk.jet with --allow=Browser printed UI_UNSUPPORTED[gtk.runtime]. ui_values_fixed.jet printed 15.0 x 2.0. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/UiBackends.jet:13-16 documents the current static GTK path. These do not establish that GTK is the only possible desktop renderer. Flutter's architecture and platform-view documentation provide precedent, not a Jet prototype.

decisions.title: Use real browser elements and server HTML; allow browser layout without promising identical line breaks
decisions.situation: Jet's browser host positions elements using pixel coordinates supplied by Jet. Real browser layout would let text and controls adapt naturally to zoom, translation and the available width, but cannot guarantee native-identical line breaks. This vote chooses browser elements or Jet-computed drawing and positioning, keeping server rendering and resumable handlers in every option. We recommend browser elements, explicitly allowing browser layout and text shaping rather than pretending tests make the engines identical.
decisions.gist: Should browser elements handle web layout, accepting occasional line-break differences from native?
decisions.lesson: Every option shows the same order screen and keeps server HTML and resumable handlers. A uses real text and buttons with browser layout. Shared fonts and comparison checks reduce differences, but cannot guarantee identical wrapping. Voting A also permits a web-only exception: browser layout and text shaping replace Jet's implementation there.
decisions.story: Ana wants her order screen to use browser zoom and translation well, without clipped content when its lines wrap differently from her phone app.
decisions.inWild: Qwik resumes server-rendered HTML and lazily loads handlers without replaying the initial component render: https://qwik.dev/docs/concepts/resumable/. Taffy implements CSS block, flex and grid layout outside browsers; its repository has a Chrome-based fixture generator. It does not implement text layout, so its layout tests do not prove identical line breaks: https://github.com/DioxusLabs/taffy.
decisions.detail:
ONE CHOICE AND ITS NECESSARY EXCEPTION

D-UI-HOME1 and D-UI-VIEW1 retain the ui package and shared state/view model. D-RESUME1 keeps server HTML, serialized state and lazy handlers. D-WEBBACKEND1 and D-WASM1 keep effect-checked placement. A permits one named I9 exception, for browser layout and text shaping of page elements on the web tier only. App rules, validation, state and action meaning remain shared Jet code; the exception does not authorize browser-side copies of those rules.

WHAT A CAN AND CANNOT GUARANTEE

Serve the same bundled fonts where the reader allows them, agree on supported layout and line-breaking rules, and compare native geometry with fixtures from Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Tests must cover zoom, long translations, right-to-left text, missing glyphs, font loading and user font overrides. Mismatches outside the accepted rounding range block release. This is future acceptance, not an existing browser suite.

The same font file does not guarantee identical glyph metrics or wrapping: shaping, fallback fonts, engine rounding and user settings can differ. Unicode line-breaking rules permit choices and tailoring. Tests reduce known differences; they cannot prove every line break on every browser version. Do not exclude every disagreement and then claim all expert features work identically. Supported features and limits must be explicit, with readable overflow behavior.

SERVER OUTPUT

Send semantic elements with serialized state and handler references. Static content can appear before app code runs; network, server and font delays still exist. A simple text node is not automatically a heading. The logical tree determines roles and reading order under D-A11Y-EXPORT1=B; page-element order already follows tree order in the current host.

EXPERT DRAWING

A canvas view for charts or games remains opt-in under D-GAME-PLATFORM1. It uses shared drawing geometry and an accessibility projection, not a second app model. It does not make all displays pixel-identical or give canvas text automatic browser find and translation.

FAIR ALTERNATIVES

B paints the same screen after server HTML, using shared Jet geometry and a synchronized accessible tree. Canvas can zoom as pixels; automatic text find, translation and reflow require additional integration. C uses semantic elements with shared Jet-computed positions and recomputes them on size or text-metric changes. Absolute positioning does not inherently prevent responsive layout; C's cost is having Jet maintain that reflow integration rather than using browser flow. Both retain server output and resume.

CHECKED EVIDENCE

Compiler/JetWeb/Source/Web/Host.jet:479-491 creates real elements, sets absolute position and pixel boxes, then appends them in tree order. SolReworkReview read that code but ran no web build or browser. The native ui_values_fixed.jet probe printed 15.0 x 2.0. No claim of current browser failure beyond the source's positioning strategy is made.

ONE COST REMAINS

Text can wrap differently from native even with shared fonts. Allow flexible heights and reflow; check clipping and focus at varied widths, zoom and translations. The owner is accepting that remaining presentation difference, not being promised it away.
